title: I inadvertently misled parliament over a British nuclear scandal. Now I’m calling for justice | Tobias Ellwood | The Guardian
description: Thousands of service personnel took part in dangerous cold war-era nuclear tests. The government owes them the truth – and compensation, says former defence minister Tobias Ellwood
Author: Tobias Ellwood
Headline: Thousands of service personnel took part in dangerous cold war-era nuclear tests. The government owes them the truth – and compensation, says former defence minister Tobias Ellwood
Content: A British H-bomb is tested at Christmas Island in 1957.Photograph: Christmas Island/PopperfotoView image in fullscreenA British H-bomb is tested at Christmas Island in 1957.Photograph: Christmas Island/PopperfotoOpinionMinistry of DefenceI inadvertently misled parliament over a British nuclear scandal. Now I’m calling for justiceTobias EllwoodThousands of service personnel took part in dangerous cold war-era nuclear tests. The government owes them the truth – and compensationWed 2 Sep 2026 22.30 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.07 BSTShareIn December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament. Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was “unable to locate any information” suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them. This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.More than 20,000 armed forces personnel took part in dozens of nuclear tests and nearly 600 radiation experiments, the majority between 1952 and 1967. This was for the entirety of the cold war. The science was deemed necessary. How effective were our own bombs and, just as importantly, how well could our military function if the Soviet Union used theirs against us? Test after test was conducted in the Australian desert, at Christmas Island in the Pacific, and we also sent service personnel into the atomic clouds of allies and enemies. Yet their medical records for the period are missing.Other nuclear nations, such as the US, France and the Soviet Union, did the same. Yet they acknowledged that it happened and created dedicated compensation schemes for nuclear test veterans who subsequently developed serious illnesses. Britain stands apart here. In Britain, the burden was placed on veterans to prove their case. But how do you claim what happened decades earlier when potentially vital records are missing or inaccessible?In 2007, about 1,000 nuclear test veterans and familiestook the MoD to courtseeking compensation. Pilots had been instructed to fly through mushroom clouds. Service personnel sailed and crawled through fallout. Others witnessed nuclear explosions, in some cases just two miles from ground zero. Surely our service personnel deserved better?This is where the scandal turns ugly. To deal with the veterans’ litigation, the MoD instructed the Atomic Weapons Establishment (AWE) to collate relevant documentation into a searchable database called Merlin. More than 28,000 documents were eventually assembled, covering radiation, precautions, health monitoring and what was known about the possible biological effects of the tests. Yet the veterans’ lawyers had no practical access to this vast archive. Thanks to the extraordinary investigative journalism of Susie Boniface, historical documents began emerging referring to blood and urine testing.When I saw the evidence, I raised it in November 2022 as chair of the defence committee. The MoD finally acknowledged that the AWE held copies of blood-test results and urine-radioactivity measurements for “a small number of individuals”. That took me straight back to my parliamentary answer four years earlier.I challenged the then defence secretary,Ben Wallace. If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture? He agreed that withholding relevant medical information would be “deeply wrong” and undertook to investigate.The dam was beginning to burst. Searches of Merlin for “blood” and “urine” subsequently identified 151 documents. Then another extraordinary twist. A software change meant the AWE could no longer provide a historical audit trail showing who had accessed Merlin.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlutonium levels at nuclear test site in WA up to 4,500 times higher than rest of coast, study findsRead moreIn 2024 (after the general election), the government finally ordered a discovery exercise into what blood and urine testing had taken place.Its findings, published this July, are damning. Evidence indicates that medical examinations or blood testing were required for “the majority, if not all” of Britain’s nuclear-testing period, across all three armed services. Bizarrely, the review says it found no evidence of intentional concealment.But after seven decades of incomplete answers and ministers kept in the dark, this cannot be where the story ends. Had veterans and their doctors known the full picture decades ago, cancers and other illnesses could have been diagnosed earlier. Lives could have been saved.Merlin is now being transferred to the National Archives. But declassifying 28,000 documents into the public domain will take time and is not the same as giving veterans answers. Many are now in their 80s and 90s.Given the numbers of veterans involved and the decades this has been allowed to drag on, this is arguably one of Britain’s biggest scandals – alongside infected blood, Windrush and the Post Office. It demands an apology to the nation from the prime minister, an independent tribunal to establish the truth, and a compensation scheme for veterans and widows similar to that provided in the US.These men served their country. Their country failed them. Seventy years on, veterans should not still be fighting their own government for the truth.Tobias Ellwood is a former defence minister and the author of Ten Steps to Prevent World War ThreeDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Premier League money has lost all meaning amid chaotic spectacle of excess | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: The transfer window has broken all rational rules and limits, leaving us to marvel and, ultimately, pick up the bill
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: The transfer window has broken all rational rules and limits, leaving us to marvel and, ultimately, pick up the bill
Content: Wesley Fofana and Malo Gusto (right) are the only Chelsea players left from the first transfer window of the Clearlake age after exits for Mykhailo Mudryk and Enzo Fernández.Composite: Gaurdian Pictures; Tottenham Hotspur FC/Shutterstock; Manchester City FC; Allstar Picture Library/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenWesley Fofana and Malo Gusto (right) are the only Chelsea players left from the first transfer window of the Clearlake age after exits for Mykhailo Mudryk and Enzo Fernández.Composite: Gaurdian Pictures; Tottenham Hotspur FC/Shutterstock; Manchester City FC; Allstar Picture Library/SportsphotoTransfer windowPremier League money has lost all meaning amid chaotic spectacle of excessThe transfer window has broken all rational rules and limits, leaving us to marvel and, ultimately, pick up the billBarney RonayWed 2 Sep 2026 20.00 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a research study a few years back into a key period in the life of the TV show Location, Location, Location. You know the one. Half an hour of mid-morning drift. Hosted by two people whose common quality is they both look as if the minced essence of Wellington boots, the Volvo XC40 and the phrase “picky bits” has been reconstituted into human shapes, then sent out to judge people for buying houses.The big reveal was always the bit where they came back a year later and saw how much the value had shifted. Because all conversations about houses are, in the end, an excuse to talk about money. Oh wow, it’s gone up by £20,000. You are good. Oh no, you’re now bankrupt and your flat looks like a hostage cell with fairy lights. Unlucky. You are bad.Premier League transfer talking points: three things we learned from the dataRead moreWhat the study found was that prices basically always increased. Ripping out the stairs, living in a tent in the garden, arguing about what to do with the two-and-a-halfth bedroom – all of this was irrelevant. These were the boom times of the early 2000s, UK housing recast as a global money trap, an endlessly whirling laundromat, a bricks and mortar central bank bond.These people could have bought their run-down three-bed, left it empty and done absolutely nothing for two years. The price would have still gone up. That drama about exactly which shade of Anaconda Breath Morgue And Cakebread Mega-Gloss to use in the underfloor wine cave? Just doesn’t matter. Buy the soil. Shut the door. Let money do its thing.And yes, this is a way of talking aboutthe 2026 summer transfer window, and the way in which everyone has basically now been Chelsea-ed. Think back four years to the start of the age of Clearlake, the first post-Roman spree. At that time it seemed impossible there could be a profitable outcome. Chelsea were out there buying the vintage copper-plate statement bidet. Chelsea were digging out a third sub-basement. Who will redeem this expense? Who will provide a similarly deranged response to such overinvestment?Well, it turns out the market will do this for you. If you’d predicted then that Chelsea would miss out on the Champions League and go through five permanent managers, but still make a profitfrom selling Enzo Fernández, would anyone have believed it?View image in fullscreenTodd Boehly has overseen big changes on and off the pitch during his time at Chelsea.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesOr that Mykhailo Mudryk could run around briefly like a deranged hamster, get banned for failing a drugs testand still become a potential growth asset? This is pre-subprime crash energy. Yes, you can install a solar-powered mega-wetroom that fires sourdough breadsticks directly into your eyes. Whatever. Ownership is all. Money will take care of you.There are still levels to this. The one Chelsea thing to shift in the window is that the curtain has now been drawn on those initial eight months, the period where Todd Boehly became the world’s worst director of football, a director of football who basically didn’t know what football was.That period has now been safely capped off. Only two players remain. Rough out the numbers and Chelsea spent something like £200m in fees, wages, leaks and cuts, with only Malo Gusto and Wesley Fofana to show for it. No real damage. Money comes, money goes. We roll on.This is the lesson of the latest summer transfer window. Right now it doesn’t really matter what you do in thePremier League. Just being in it is the thing. With one caveat, which is that nobody actually knows what’s happening here. We can marvel at a record window. We can see the biggest spenders are Manchester City on £457.5m, the lowest Crystal Palace on about £50m, the highest net Liverpool on £216.8m. We can pore over Aston Villa buying the bones of a new squad for £56.7m net gain.View image in fullscreenLiverpool’s £123m signing Bradley Barcola checks out Anfield.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesBut we can’t know what it means, at least not financially. This is part of the design of money on this scale. As the then Federal Reserve chair Alan Greenspan put it in a famous speech on the mysteries of big money: “How do we know when irrational exuberance has unduly escalated asset values, which then become subject to unexpected and prolonged contractions?”Nobody knew what this meant then. Nobody knows what it means now. “Irrational exuberance” is a good phrase, one Greenspan later said came to him in the bath. It was designed to convey the essential point: opacity, vagueness, invisible flows. If not for those actually riding the tide, because someone is always making money. Someone out there actively wants the Premier League’s financial chaos, and is benefiting from it gloriously.Otherwise, reading the runes is just a matter of guesswork. Money moves between networked entities. Everyone inside wins. Everyone outside pays for it. But still, this feels new, if only in its extremity.This was captured by the weirdness of Sky Sports’ transfer deadline programme on Tuesday. At one point a man appeared strumming a guitar, smiling as if he had just filleted a litter of kittens in his basement, and sang a Bradley Barcola Liverpool song to the tune of Don’t Dream It’s Over, like this is all just normal and fine.Later there was a golden period at about 5.30pm where every deal just seemed wrong and impossible, a fever dream after an over-ripe seafood risotto. Aston Villa have paid £47m for an 18-year-old winger. Gabriel Jesus is going to Barcelona. Jack Grealish is having a medical at Everton, an event that seems to prove the non-linear nature of time, a medical that is always happening, never not happening, a constant time-space event.View image in fullscreenGabriel Jesus at his Barcelona unveiling.Photograph: Javier Borrego/AFP7/ShutterstockMeanwhile two private jets are on the tarmac in Lyonas three clubs try to sign Malick Fofana. “We STILL don’t know what Malick Fofana is thinking,” the man with the microphone concluded, mournfully, and this seemed profoundly true and on point. We don’t. Does Malick Fofana even know this? If so, how can he? Nobody else has a clue what’s going on.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is worth trying to list the best deals. Harry Wilson on a free can only be good. Djed Spence to Inter is great.Forza, Djed.Barcola to Liverpool for £123mis lots of money, but he’s really young and knows how to score once he’s settled.Newcastle seem to have had a good window, racking up a list of signings that scream inside knowledge and good data, and chime with Matthias Jaissle’s mercurial vibe. Manchester City’s signings have to be good. There’s so many of them, and they’re all excellent players. That midfield is surely just too big to fail.Arsenal will also be fine, despite not signing a 1950s-style hotshot goal ace with dynamite in his boots and the brain of a hungry magpie. Yes, they’ve lost two, maybe three attackers. But these are Jesus and probably Gabriel Martinelli, meat in the room, plus Leandro Trossard, replaced by basically the same guy. Arsenal won the league with Kai Havertz, Martin Ødegaard, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze short of their ceiling. If you can’t score enough to win with that lot then it’s really not the players.Manchester United’s window looks quite good, but also scattergun. Carlos Baleba may be great, or may wander around like a lost child in Lidl before being loaned to Monaco. Tottenham have mined the club’s DNA, gone back to their spiritual roots, and signed players who will be really good for four games, then disappear and get tattoos.Meanwhile Everton have swapped Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. What does it mean? Can you even visualise this as an event? Beto and Iliman Ndiaye have gone, taking away a third of last season’s league goals. Welcome, Everton fans, to the fully immersive Thierno Barry multiverse.Otherwise the main takeaway is the meaninglessness of big football money. Most notably the size of the most basic fees. Little wonder there is a sense of alienation from familiar notions of team building, blocks in place, footballers as recognisable avatars of graft and cultural chemistry. These are stocks, talent units, a flow of resources.View image in fullscreenCaleb Yirenkyi challenges Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly on his Coventry debut, having joined for £23m this summer.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesRemember the Peter Odemwingie deadline day fiasco, where Odemwingie sat fuming in his car while the world was sucked into this human drama? That whole thing was about the unbridgeable leap from £2m to £3m. Coventry have just signed Caleb Yirenkyi from Nordsjælland for £23m. Does “Caleb Yirenkyi” really exist? Are you sure?Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club faredRead moreWho pays in the end for this circulation of funds? You, for starters. There is no such thing as football money. It’s all TV rights, state propaganda funds and hard private investment from the kind of people who really don’t give without taking back in the end.On one level books are being balanced, accounting rules satisfied, clubs swapping assets at fees driven in part by regulatory requirements. More obscurely Boehly once talked about a rush of cash being diverted football’s way as a sub-avalanche from quantitative easing in the US, because money just has to go somewhere. No, me neither.All that seems certain is money is being pushed around the board. And that it feels wildly abstract. The window was thrilling, its possibilities endless, a shot of blood for the new season. Beyond this, big football and big finance are playing their own game, in a way that goes beyond the human scale and into a world of pure money. The message below the headlines is clear. This thing belongs to them. Your job, human consumer unit, is simply to look at it and have feelings.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowPremier LeagueFootball politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Messy, clever and can barely conceal its rage: is Furious the most outstanding TV show of the year?  | Television | The Guardian
description: The story of a serial killer taking revenge on the rich predatory men who abused her just earned a fantastic finale. With career-defining acting, daring Epstein parallels and super dark comedy, it’s a total must-watch
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: The story of a serial killer taking revenge on the rich predatory men who abused her just earned a fantastic finale. With career-defining acting, daring Epstein parallels and super dark comedy, it’s a total must-watch
Content: ‘Five feet tall with her fuckin’ socks on’ … Lola Petticrew as revenge killer Catherine Grace.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyView image in fullscreen‘Five feet tall with her fuckin’ socks on’ … Lola Petticrew as revenge killer Catherine Grace.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyTelevisionMessy, clever and can barely conceal its rage: is Furious the most outstanding TV show of the year?The story of a serial killer taking revenge on the rich predatory men who abused her just earned a fantastic finale. With career-defining acting, daring Epstein parallels and super dark comedy, it’s a total must-watchRebecca NicholsonWed 2 Sep 2026 15.17 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.21 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou could easily watch the first few minutes of Furious without knowing that it would turn out to be so special. It opens with a scene of pure horror: it’s Halloween night and a real monster is hiding among the pretend ones. A woman we come to know as Catherine Grace (an astonishingly good Lola Petticrew) is inside a man’s house, wearing a creepy kitten mask. The man is in bad shape, crawling on the floor, gasping for air and begging for his life. Catherine is alternately chirpy and tender with him, but eventually, she loses her patience with his pleading. She takes a syringe filled with fentanyl out of a pencil case decorated with sparkly stickers and jewels and finishes the job.So far, so creepy crime drama, but Furious is already hiding in plain sight, because the monster is not who we think it is. What looks as if it will be a cat-and-mouse story, in which a tenacious FBI agent hunts a twisted serial killer, quickly rips up any expectations. We learn that Catherine was trafficked into sex work as a teenager, and is now making her way through a kill list of predatory and powerful men. Her life has been shaped by a conspiracy of abuse, violence, neglect and indifference. She has decided to take matters into her own broken hands.View image in fullscreenThe role of her life … Emmy Rossum as FBI agent Alice Black.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyThe case finds its way to the desk of Alice Black (Emmy Rossum, in the role of her life), a tough former NYPD homicide detective turned recent FBI recruit. Her boss, Nora Washington (an equally excellent Quincy Tyler Bernstine), is the head of the sex crimes and crimes against children unit. She drinks to cope with the horrors she has to witness on a daily basis and is in possession of the darkest sense of humour on TV. She sees the potential, and pain, in Alice, and puts her to work. But as the series progresses, we see what it demands of them both to pursue justice, when they are repeatedly told to step back and stand down.View image in fullscreenExcellent … Quincy Tyler Bernstine as Nora Washington.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyIt is hard to think of a recent drama that has placed quite so much trust in the intelligence of its audience. Every character here is flawed. It has moral ambiguity baked into its core. Alice left the NYPD after being beaten by her cop ex-boyfriend Marshall Connelly (a truly sinister Jake Lacy). She has been ostracised by most of their former colleagues, who either do not believe her or, more likely, do not care. She is suffering from a complex response to trauma, and Furious does not shy away from depicting those complexities. It is a raw and unusually vivid portrait of women and PTSD.When Alice begins to investigate Catherine and her crimes, Furious becomes a big, bold examination of justice, and what that might look like for women who have no access to it. It can barely conceal its rage, and by the final episode, few would expect it to. Catherine, and countless other young girls like her, have had their lives stolen and destroyed by men who believed themselves to be invincible. “I didn’t get to decide a fucking thing about my life,” she shouts, in one of the series’ most devastating scenes.There is an obvious timeliness to this story, which may be one of the reasons why it is capable of landing such a blow. The Epstein parallels are not subtle, nor are they intended to be. The rich buy people off to cover up their terrible deeds. They operate in plain sight, daring people to catch them. There is an important photograph of trafficked teenage girls with older, wealthy men. One can only imagine if this show will pop up on the Mountbatten-Windsor streaming queue.View image in fullscreenPower reclaimed … Lola Petticrew’s Catherine poses as a waitress.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyBut what Furious provides is a fantasy of power, reclaimed and repurposed for the women who have had it taken away from them, if they ever had it at all. One cop describes Catherine as “five feet tall with her fuckin’ socks on”; that she can overpower her victims is something of a fantasy in itself. The finale has a near-impossible task in that it needs to maintain the bleak spirit of the story, while offering some sort of relief, or reward, for the women we have come to care so much about. It pulls it off by allowing for some magical thinking, while never veering too far from the grim reality of the situation. Some men pay for what they have done, whether formally or off the books. Some are given medals for their criminal behaviour. As messy as it is, the resolution is satisfying enough. Justice was never going to be clean.Furious is a clever show. It works as a straightforward thriller, gripping and tense, using a murder mystery and a manhunt to expose an institutional conspiracy. It is also an emotionally astute act of catharsis, and this fantasy of revenge can feel, at times, like a much-needed balm. It has been renewed for a second season already. No wonder. It is one of the year’s most outstanding shows, and, after all, there are plenty more monsters out there.Furious is on Disney+ in the UK and Australia and Hulu in the USExplore more on these topicsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Everything countercultural is doomed, isn’t it?’​ Sofie Royer, the bracingly brilliant pop star pondering life’s big questions | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Referencing Tarkovsky and French theory, the Austrian-Iranian singer is writing some of today’s wittiest music – though she’s ‘too pop for the art world, too indie-darling for the mainstream’
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Referencing Tarkovsky and French theory, the Austrian-Iranian singer is writing some of today’s wittiest music – though she’s ‘too pop for the art world, too indie-darling for the mainstream’
Content: ‘I don’t have a lot of stage fright’ … Sofie RoyerView image in fullscreen‘I don’t have a lot of stage fright’ … Sofie RoyerPop and rockInterview‘Everything countercultural is doomed, isn’t it?’​ Sofie Royer, the bracingly brilliant pop star pondering life’s big questionsBen Beaumont-ThomasReferencing Tarkovsky and French theory, the Austrian-Iranian singer is writing some of today’s wittiest music – though she’s ‘too pop for the art world, too indie-darling for the mainstream’Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.08 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.51 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou wait ages for a brilliant pop song about film-making and then two come along at once. Following on from Charli xcx’sCameracomes Actress by Sofie Royer, with lyrics referencing rotoscoping, call sheets, screenplays, establishing shots, cinéma verité and more. “When the dust settles on your heart / I’d like to audition for the leading part,” she purrs over pumping disco, screwball-funny as she stacks up the metaphors to woo some Letterboxd-brained beau. “My mise-en-scène is flawless, don’t you know I’m quite adored / I’ll win you over in 35mm 4K-restored.”It’s a typically smart and witty number from a singer, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and, as it happens, aspiring actor, whose erudition and taste light up one of the best albums of the year, the forthcoming Before/After. Its lead singleCowboy Mouthis a recreation of a Sam Shepard play in song;another songmakes a catchy funk-pop chorus from the word “sesquicentennial”. Her music is cosmopolitan enough to sit Italo disco next to new wave and garage rock, and across her discography there’s a big cast of cultural figures from Andrei Tarkovsky to Kenneth Anger, Luigi Mangione to Ivy Wolk, knowingness offset by her keen sense of humour.“Maybe I’ve just spent too many years on [academic journal database] Jstor, but I love a good reference, right?” she says, having studied philosophy, psychology and English for a teaching degree. “Paying attention to references is one of the coolest things that you can do: a little keyhole into another piece of knowledge.”Royer seems to ask me as many questions as I ask her during a bracingly intellectual video call from her apartment in Vienna, where she smokes elegant slim cigarettes in front of a tasteful array of paintings and furniture. After an unusually itinerant life, she is relatively settled in the city.Now 35, she was born in the US to an Austrian mother and Iranian father, who were IT workers in California, then spent her high-school years in Vienna and attended a conservatoire thanks to her brilliance on violin. It left her with a musical mindset that is “very classically based”. She says she wouldn’t call herself a singer-songwriter. “I struggle with even calling myself a singer!” But, she says, “if you’re doing violin solos [as a child] you have to want to be on stage. So I don’t have a lot of stage fright – for all that I couldn’t really sing when I released my first record, I was just like, whatever, it’s like karaoke with my own songs.”Aged 19, still long before she started writing songs, Royer went back across the world to work in Los Angeles at record label Stones Throw. Did she feel American again? “That’s a really hard question. If you come from a mixed background, and then you’re socialised in a third country, you aren’t ever really belonging to one place. I’m always just ‘part-’, right?”View image in fullscreenOut of place … Sofie Royer.Photograph: Oskar BurgerShe’s also aware of how a mixed identity such as hers can be parcelled up and sold. She cites a recent sarcastic lyric she admires byCharli xcx– “My heritage could give me quite the USP” – and frowns at the concept of female-only DJ nights. “I think you want to be a musician regardless of gender and heritage. I know it’s not fully possible, but I would love for some of the arts to just remain, at least in some small essence, a rare apolitical kind of structure. I love the surreal; I love things that extend beyond the imaginable.”After LA came another move, to London, as one of the first employees at Boiler Room, which has since become one of the world’s biggest music startups thanks to its brand-partnered livestreams of DJ sets. Boiler Room ultimately took on major investment cash, and isseen as having sold outby many in the underground. “There just wasn’t a necessity to scale up in that way,” she says. “It’s a bummer because it makes you think: everything [countercultural] is kind of doomed, isn’t it?”While working there, Royer’s mother was diagnosed with cancer. An only child, Royer quit and moved back to Vienna to care for her and start her degree (plus another one, in painting, left incomplete). Alongside state-funded therapy, songwriting became a way to process. “I was singing a lot of karaoke around that time in the basement of my art university, and then one thing led to another. It was a real way for me to escape. When I’m monkey-cymbal-clapping brain, when every sense is kind of occupied, it’s when I’m playing something and singing to it.”View image in fullscreen‘Very few professions are as measured in metrics as people working in the arts’ … Sofie Royer in a still from the video for Actress.Photograph: Eliott FettweisHer debut album, Cult Survivor, was released in 2020, but performing it live “was like reopening an old wound”, so she started broadening her writing. She dressed up as a pierrot character for 2022’s Harlequin, “a different persona to help me get over the fear of being perceived as a singer on stage, maybe”, and based 2024’s Young-Girl Forever on a French philosophical tract about culture’s obsession with young women. “The beauty of age is that you care less and less about it. You couldn’t pay me to go back to my 20s.” She reconsiders. “I mean, you could pay me, because I’m self-employed, so I’m down for money.”She is much admired by her peers, with Lana Del Rey, Air and LCD Soundsystem all getting her to support them on tour, but she’s not headlining the same venues. She addresses that relative lack of financial success and fame uproariously on the new album. “Always a nominee, never a winner / The longer I keep this up the less I can afford dinner,” she sings on Sold Out the Jazz Club, just one of many references across the album to how Royer is, as that song’s chorus has it, “too pop for the art world, too indie-darling for the mainstream”.“Very few professions are as measured in metrics as people working in the arts,” she says, “specifically music, and these metrics are publicly available” – Spotify listeners, tickets sold. “And not only that, then you’re being interviewed: ‘Where do you see yourself in five years? What does success mean to you?’ That’s what I wanted to perhaps release when it came to these songs.”She has also released herself from therapy, singing “I spent five years on that couch, and I’m not ever going back again” on another new song, C’est la D. “I was actually in therapy for longer than five years, but it just sounded so cool to sing five instead of seven,” she deadpans.She says she certainly needed therapy to begin with, but when she reached the cap to her free hours from the Austrian state, her therapist said she could continue, but he didn’t think she needed it any more. She agreed with him: “We as humans have a certain semblance of resilience, but there’s a lot of financial value placed in today’s market of psychoanalysis. In a lot of other cultures, that maybe aren’t as socialist as the one I currently enjoy living in, there’s more value in keeping somebody unhappy and dependent on therapy for the rest of their life.”‘The beast inside me wants to move!’ The smart, slapstick world of Audrey Hobert, the Steve Martin of popRead moreFinally a full-time musician (“a lot of it is an email job”), she is also branching into acting after a cameo in the 2024 remake of erotic dramaEmmanuelle, playing a bar singer (though a scene opposite Naomi Watts, who was “an absolute delight”, didn’t make the final cut). She’s been making two films with Austrian director Jasmin Baumgartner, a former student of Michael Haneke: Too Hot to Die, a satirical comedy about a reality dating show, and the bigger-budget dramedy Sentimental Fail Club. “I’m not there for myself; I don’t have any demands or wishes when I’m acting,” she says of its appeal. “You’re just the paintbrush and the film is the canvas. You’re just an element in somebody else’s artistic vision.”For all the many-layered meanings and references in her multi-faceted career, she’s also a dab hand at a straightforward love song, such asOpium, in which she compares her affection for her boyfriend to the drug’s high: “A hundred years is nothing with it, I want more,” she sings. Even here, though, there’s a dash of art-historical analysis. “That one just felt like such a direct, honest song,” she says. “And also, like, structurally dadaist. So it made the cut.”Before/After is released via Stones Throw on 4 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsPop and rockCharli xcxfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I thought I was too broken for sex. Here’s how I found pleasure again | Well actually | The Guardian
description: I was forced to examine the idea of sexual pleasure after a tumor was removed from my spinal cord
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I was forced to examine the idea of sexual pleasure after a tumor was removed from my spinal cord
Content: ‘Lately I have found myself re-examining my sex life after surgery. How has medical trauma and disability changed my relationship to sex and pleasure?’Composite: Vanessa Saba/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Lately I have found myself re-examining my sex life after surgery. How has medical trauma and disability changed my relationship to sex and pleasure?’Composite: Vanessa Saba/The GuardianWell actuallyI thought I was too broken for sex. Here’s how I found pleasure againI was forced to examine the idea of sexual pleasure after a tumor was removed from my spinal cordJodi-Ann BureyWed 2 Sep 2026 17.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.51 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTen years ago, my right elbow started to hurt. The internet suggested I had tennis elbow, so I stopped playing tennis. Once the outer elbow pain moved inward, I changed my self-diagnosis to golfer’s elbow. I stoppedlifting weights, competitive dragon-boating and bouldering.For good measure, I consulted an occupational therapist about my nightly bullet-vibrator routine after reading that golfer’s elbow is common among construction workers who operate heavy-duty vibrating machinery. He listened closely and said he’d note VRI on my patient chart. I asked what VRI meant, eager to end my diagnostic journey. “Vibrator-related injury,” he responded. We busted out laughing.After three years, weak hands and shaky legs had joined the elbow pain. None of the diagnoses I researched or received (a pinched ulnar nerve, tendinitis and thoracic outlet syndrome) fully explained my symptoms. Eventually, an MRI found a tumor growing inside my spinal cord. One surgeon estimated that without treatment, my body would undergo complete, permanent paralysis from the neck down within a year.The surgery itself carried the same risk.Against medical advice to schedule surgery immediately, I postponed it for five weeks. Even that was barely enough time for all my worry, denial, resentment, anger andend-of-life arrangements. Most importantly, this tumor confirmed that the pain I had suffered for years had never been my fault. I wanted to relish the hobbies and pleasures I’d abandoned in case I never experienced them again. Moreover, I’d already booked a snowboarding trip to Chamonix-Mont-Blanc, and my immigrant sensibilities would not let that money waste.Dating also became urgent. Within moments of matching with Nicolas on an app, we were on the phone sharing belly laughs and hard truths. I told him about my diagnosis and flight to New York City that evening to prepare for surgery the following week. Hours later, we had our first date over a pot of tea inside my Seattle apartment. Nicolas neatened my favorite cardigan with an electric fabric shaver while I packed. We talked non-stop until my ride to the airport arrived. Our kiss goodbye lingered like we’d never say hello again.When an unexpected job interview brought me right back to Seattle three days later, Nicolas asked me to be his girlfriend.Surgery successfully removed my tumor. Days turned into three weeks in the hospital’s inpatient rehabilitation unit. By day, I was a patient, relearning how to walk and use my hands. By night, I pretended I was just a person on the phone with her boyfriend. Nicolas and I wove dreams about sailing together, sleeping underneath stars at sea. He promised I’d be able to walk again, and when we aged, I’d be sitting on his lap inhiswheelchair.Everything hurt. Many nights, I wailed with regret that Nicolas and I had not had sex before my body changed. Did I lose the chance to enjoy his touch? Was my body now too broken to please him? Would numbness make it too difficult – not worth the effort – for him to please me? My sisters called him Santa, short for Saint Nick. And who but a saint could desire me as my desirability faded?There’s a lot of talk about sex these days, namelyhow little of it we’re having. I too had deprioritized sex and dating, mostly becauseboyfriends are embarrassingandmen ain’t shit. But lately I have found myself re-examining my sex life after surgery. How has medical trauma and disability changed my relationship to sex and pleasure?In the wake of my diagnosis, I experienced first-hand how loved ones and even doctors can dismiss the difference betweenbeingalive andfeelingalive. Medically, not dying is the goal. It is a task so big that we are often too grateful, exhausted, unprepared or ill-supported to think aboutwhat’s next. If we’re lucky enough to survive, pleasure is simply a trivial extra.I had enjoyed a healthy, active sex life before surgery and thought working back towards that would prove cancer and disability hadn’t changed me. That I was more than just a patient.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’But the reality was that my spinal cord injury and surgery had an impact. Dr Lisa Ruppert, a physiatrist and spinal cord injury specialist who treats cancer patients and survivors at the Memorial Sloan Kettering cancer center, helped me understand the sensory disorders that immediately followed surgery: temperature dysregulation, heightened and dulled sensitivity to touch, bladder and bowel incontinence and sexual dysfunction. I told her my concerns about having sex again, which is common for people living withspinal cord injuries.We started with some basics. Ruppert suggested strategies to trigger arousal: keep the lights on for visual stimulation, stay on top of the sheets to mitigate sensory overload and discover whether and where my erogenous zones had shifted.“For someone with spinal cord involvement, we have to think about what’s still working and what’s not,” said Ruppert when I spoke to her recently. “You and I had a lot of conversations about how it’s going to feel, what still feels good, what doesn’t. That also depends on a patient’s willingness to explore their own body.”Able-bodied people don’t often think about how their bodies work. Not until my spinal cord injury did I ever consider the mechanics of sexual pleasure.Sexual arousal is more complicated than just touch and response, said Ruppert. There are two pathways: reflexogenic and psychogenic. Reflexogenic arousal is triggered by “touch stimulus” to the genitals. That information travels to the spinal cord and causes vaginal lubrication or penile erection. Psychogenic arousal, on the other hand, does not necessarily require physical contact. It’s stimulated by sexual thoughts, fantasies, emotions and other inputs – like what you might see, hear and smell.I remember passing Ruppert’s instructions on to Nicolas, whose knowledge of my body became as significant as my patient chart. I loved our sensory games, but started treating them like rehab. Dates with Nicolas slotted into my calendar alongside weekly physical therapy, occupational therapy, aqua therapy and talk therapy sessions. After we broke up, I resigned myself to a medicalized, dissociative relationship with my body, believing sex just wasn’t for me any more.“Sex after surgery was a project,” I admitted during an interview with Rachel Smith, a licensed marriage and family therapist who specializes in sex therapy. Most of Smith’s clients find her when their sex lives are disrupted by critical life transitions. I have a master’s degree and career in public health, and it wasn’t until I was researching this piece that I learned sex therapy could have been part of my post-operative care.“But what if pleasure became an exploration?” Smith offered. “Something to be discovered versus something to work on.”I noted my use of the word “project”, which held associations of achievement, work and productivity, a stubborn tenet of millennial hustle culture. I also often described my experience within the US healthcare system as a project – its maze-like inefficiencies, high cost and bureaucracy typically require patients to become both the project and the project manager.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I could barely think because it was so bad’: how pain changes usRead moreMy goal of rehabilitating my body so it could function as it did before disability was narrow and unfair. Sex only mattered if it helped my body work. “I see this in a lot of my clients, especially Bipoc children of immigrants,” said Gabriela Fullon, a licensed mental health counselor. “Enjoyment must be deserved. It is only something you are allowed to have if you work your ass off for it.”These capitalistic norms particularly do not permit pleasure for disabled people. “The idea is that our lives should be focused on treatment, cure and management of disability – above all else,” said Sami Schalk, PhD, a disability and gender studies scholar and author ofBlack Disability Politics. “That pleasure only comes into our lives when it is therapeutic. That pleasure must somehow move you towards able-bodiness or able-mindedness in some way. But can’t we just make art for the sake of making art? … Can’t we fuck to fuck?”In theory, absolutely. But in practice, did I?I’m not sure I’ve completely forgiven my body for growing something that hurt me. I punished my body into repair, which is not the same as healing. I spent years believing the more embodied, sensual version of myself had to die as the price for survival.I am not alone.Pleasure is not recognized as important within the US healthcare system, which prioritizes reproductive sexual function. This makes accessing sexual healthcare especially challenging for disabled people, cancer patients and survivors, postpartum parents and others whose bodies start behaving in unexpected and inconvenient ways.“There is no standard sexual health curriculum in medical schools,” said Sonjia Kenya, PhD, sexologist and professor at the University of Miami school of medicine. This means that physicians like Ruppert or providers like Smith, Fullon and Kenya are not default care options. Their open, informed and non-judgmental approach to sex are only available to patients who know enough to seek them out. In a 2013 survey of OB-GYNs,only 29%reported asking patients about sexual satisfaction. If they don’t ask, who does?“The system is supportive of men’s sexual functioning,” Kenya said, reminding me thatmore than 80%of women do not experience orgasm through penetration alone. Conversely, “insurance won’t even cover menstrual supplies”.Even the most competent healthcare providers are constrained by an immoral (my word), fragmented (Kenya’s word) healthcare system. Patient access to services, including sex therapy, largely depends on insurance reimbursement and billing: “Is it general medicine? Is it psychology? Do you need a diagnosis before you can get treatment?” said Kenya.These providers want change. Ruppert helps medical residents to practice talking with patients about sex. Kenya said more physicians should expand their referral networks to include providers who can better address sexual health needs. But in the meantime, patients must self-advocate.If you don’t know how to address concerns about sexual pleasure, Kenya suggests that if or when a provider asks whether you are sexually active: “You can say: ‘I do not enjoy sex.’ That should encourage the provider to go a little deeper and ask the next question, or refer you to someone else.”Support for our sexual health also exists outside a doctor’s office. As Schalk reminded me, those “institutions are not focused on our pleasure. They are focused on activities of daily living and survival in order for you to be a productive citizen.”So we must reckon with our relationship to sex ourselves. As a starting place, Fullon suggested some simple curiosity, saying: “What about pleasure feels scary? Why? How do you feel about that? Do you want it to shift?” Instead of asking myselfhowto have sex again, I began asking myselfwhy.Why was sex important to me? Who and what is sexual pleasure for?I’m a sex educator. Here’s what you should know about sexual incompatibilityRead moreI sought out books and podcasts about disability, and community with other disabled women of color who affirmed that my post-operative struggles with sex and feelings of undesirability were normal. I began to question harmful narratives, like why women are taught to tolerate painful sex and that our pain is necessary for someone else’s pleasure. They are so normal that when women experience these things, we feelweare the ones doing something wrong.My experience with disability actually required me to understand my pain, not ignore it. My spinal cord injury is invisible to others now; I no longer need a wheelchair or a cane. But this intimate, informed relationship with my body has made me more confident in communicating what I need.For example, I shared details about my spinal cord injury with the last guy I dated. During sex, I worried that my needs would offend him, and I felt comfortable enough to share those anxieties. “There is nothing about how your body responds to me that makes me question whether we’re having a good time,” he said. Prioritizing intimacy over intercourse made sex more pleasurable.Audre Lorde presented her groundbreaking essay Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power, in 1978, the year she received her first cancer diagnosis. That Lorde’s cancer coincided with her scholarship on the erotic challenged me to rethink pleasure for pleasure’s sake. “[The erotic] is an internal sense of satisfaction to which, once we have experienced it, we know we can aspire,” she wrote. “For having experienced the fullness of this depth of feeling and recognizing its power, in honor and self-respect we can require no less of ourselves.”The erotic teaches us that we deserve, and must fight for, deep joy and satisfaction in every part of our lives. Pleasure is political, and provides the vitality I need as a disabled woman of color to believe I can do more than survive.I don’t accept a culture that ignores women’s sexual pleasure or believes disabled people shouldn’t have it at all. A pleasure-filled life can be lived with or without sex, with or without a partner, and alongside disability and pain. Schalk suggests keeping a pleasure journal as a way to “comfort and care for our bodies, even in the midst of hard moments”. I took her advice.This summer, I did not find the fling I hoped for, but no matter. I wentoutside, blasting Beyoncé down the freeway – as she sings in Church Girl, “I’m gon’ let go of this body, I’m gonna love on me.” I practiced the choreography from Janet Jackson’s Pleasure Principlemusic video in the park. There I heard Schalk’s words echo in my mind: “Pleasure is what brings us back to ourselves.”Jodi-Ann Burey is a writer, speaker and author ofAuthentic: The Myth of Bringing Your Full Self to WorkExplore more on these topicsWell actuallySexDisabilityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burnham tries to calm bond market fears as sell-off threatens crucial first budget | Business | The Guardian
description: Prime minister promises his government will make decisions ‘grounded in fiscal responsibility’
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Prime minister promises his government will make decisions ‘grounded in fiscal responsibility’
Content: Andy Burnham insists the budget in October will keep to fiscal rules while also reducing pressure on the cost of living.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham insists the budget in October will keep to fiscal rules while also reducing pressure on the cost of living.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesBusinessBurnham tries to calm bond market fears as sell-off threatens crucial first budgetPrime minister promises his government will make decisions ‘grounded in fiscal responsibility’Heather StewartandJessica ElgotWed 2 Sep 2026 19.28 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham moved to calm volatile bond markets on Wednesday as surging borrowing costs threatened to wreck plans for his government’s crucial first budget next month.After a days-long sell-off of government bonds – and with the chancellor, John Healey, facing the prospect of sharply reduced spending power, Burnham used his first appearanceat prime minister’s questionsto promise decisions would be “grounded in fiscal responsibility”.That was widely seen as an attempt to soothe investors after his statement to parliament on Tuesday, in which he made bold promises of more public control of utilities, further interventions on the cost of living and a recommitment to a 3% increase in defence spending.While those offers were broadly welcomed byLabourMPs, Burnham was criticised by others for inflaming the sell-off. His former economic adviser, Jim O’Neill, said it was the “last thing” the markets needed.Investors across world markets have been dumping government bonds amid fears about rising inflation, runaway deficits and competing demand for capital from tech companies on a debt-fuelled AI spending spree. The sell-off has driven up yields, or interest rates, including in the UK. At one point on Wednesday, the cost of 10-year borrowing for the government hit its highest level since 2008, at 5.29%, before easing slightly.That is expected to be costly for Healey when the Office forBudgetResponsibility draws up its budget forecasts. The independent watchdog bases its projection for bond yields on a snapshot of market interest rates taken several weeks before each budget and that is expected to be about now for Healey’s 28 October statement.The chancellor has repeatedly stressed that fiscal discipline is the “bedrock” of government policy. He will give a speech on Monday setting out his plans for economic growth – less than six months after senior City and business figures gathered to hear his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, lay out her approach.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a US strike on Iran’s southern Hormozgan province on Wednesday. The resumption of hostilities has pushed up oil costs and raised inflation expectations.Photograph: Masoud Mohamadi/Tasnim News/AFP/Getty ImagesIn his first PMQs clash with Kemi Badenoch, Burnham blamed the Conservative leader’s party for leaving the UK vulnerable to market turmoil.Criticising Burnham’s three-hour statement in the Commons the day before, Badenoch said: “He did not say no to a single spending request … And personally, I think it’s delightful that he wants to make everyone happy. But a prime minister needs to be a leader, not a people pleaser.”Burnham said his budget would “stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents”.Analysts believe higher interest rates on public debt could wipe out up to half of the £24bn headroomRachel Reeves built up against Labour’s fiscal rules.Government insiders told the Guardian they believed it would be very difficult for Healey to deliver a budget that had less than double-digit headroom, given the signal that would send to bond markets. However, that would leave him with almost no leeway for additional spending. No 10 sources declined to be drawn on what Burnham’s preferred level of headroom would be.Healey will also have to show how the Treasury intends to fill a funding gap in defence spending and pay for Burnham’s cost of living measures, including the VAT cut on electricity bills.Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest is now one in every £12 the government is spending, so even relatively small changes can add up quite quickly.”Alongside the narrowing margin for error against the rules, Miller identified two other budget headaches for Healey – the likely hit to growth forecasts from falling immigration and the demand for more spending on defence.She said: “It’s not that any one of these things on their own are the kind of ‘hit the panic button’ moment, but when you add them all together, they do add real pressure on the government.”Ruth Curtice, the director of the Resolution Foundation, said febrile markets meant the government would face additional scrutiny over the sustainability of the public finances.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe added: “The risk of not facing up to the challenges has gone up, but also maybe the reward from showing that you’re serious about addressing them might have gone up too.”The thinktank boss backed a call by Lord O’Neill for the new government to scrap the triple lock pension as a way of showing it was serious about balancing the books: “Jim O’Neill was on to something, in that part of the test for markets is, are they prepared to do politically unpopular things, in the name of trying to sort some of these fiscal problems out?”O’Neill had been mooted as an economic adviser to Burnham but has instead gone public with criticism of the fledgling government.A Treasury source insisted that unlike other major economies, including the US, the UK had a plan – inherited from Reeves – for reducing the deficit and bringing down debt. “To the extent that investors start looking at fiscal plans, we should start to distinguish ourselves in a positive way,” they said.Global markets have been spooked by higher oil costs aftera resumption of the Middle East conflict, resulting in higher expectations for future inflation.Investors now believe the Bank of England will step in and raise interest rates three times, to 4.5% over the next year, to tackle inflation. That would push up mortgage costs just as Burnham hopes to cut the cost of living.Burnham will host Emmanuel Macron for talks in No 10 on Thursday, as he begins to build his own relationships with European allies before the next stage of the UK’s reset with the EU.The prime minister is expected to use the talks to continue pushing for greater cooperation with Europe to support British businesses and drive growth, with the French president a key figure in the government’s pursuit of a closer trading relationship.Downing Street sources suggested that while the EU reset would not officially be on the agenda – because the responsibility for any deal lies with Brussels – it was likely to come up in the margins of the bilateral discussions.Burnham indicated in the Commons on Tuesday that the next reset summit, which was delayed by the EU after Keir Starmer was ousted as prime minister, could be held in November.Explore more on these topicsBusinessBondsBudgetAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Private equity owns 11 of England’s 20 biggest children’s care providers, research finds | Social care | The Guardian
description: Investigation comes amid growing calls for an end to ‘obscene’ profit-making in care sector
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Investigation comes amid growing calls for an end to ‘obscene’ profit-making in care sector
Content: The ‘big four’ independent fostering agencies have paid more than £200m from taxpayers to shareholders in interest payments since 2020.Photograph: Toru Hanai/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe ‘big four’ independent fostering agencies have paid more than £200m from taxpayers to shareholders in interest payments since 2020.Photograph: Toru Hanai/ReutersSocial carePrivate equity owns 11 of England’s 20 biggest children’s care providers, research findsInvestigation comes amid growing calls for an end to ‘obscene’ profit-making in care sectorJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentThu 3 Sep 2026 00.01 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrivate equity companies now own or partly own 11 of the 20 largest providers of fostering and children’s homes in England, as calls to ban “obscene” profit-making in children’s care grow.An investigation by the thinktank Common Wealth found the “big four” independent fostering agencies – which provide almost a quarter of fostering placements in England – have paid out more than £200m from taxpayers to shareholders in interest payments since 2020.Andrea Egan, the general secretary ofUnison, said the findings must be a “wake-up call” for systemic change in children’s social care.“Profiteering from children’s social care is nothing short of obscene. Decades of outsourcing mean essential services funded by taxpayers are being treated as a goldmine by investors,” she said. “They’re using the welfare of vulnerable children to line their pockets. Children’s social care needs fundamental change, and it needs it soon.”The analysis found that at least one in three fostering agency placements and one in five children’s homes placements are run by firms backed by institutional finance, including private equity, hedge funds, venture capital and sovereign wealth funds.It also found that the four largest fostering companies all used shareholder loans, under which shareholders lend money to a business (without buying new shares) at interest rates that are typically much higher than bank rates.Through this method, the companies have paid or reserved at least £205m to their shareholders and investors since 2020.NationalFosteringGroup, the largest independent fostering provider in the UK with more than 4,000 places, is owned by Stirling Square Capital Partners, having previously passed through the hands of Graphite Capital and Sovereign Capital.It has paid more than £116m in interest on investor loans since 2020, Common Wealth found, as well as £71m in interest on preference shares (where a pre-agreed percentage of an investment is paid back to the investor over a fixed period).BSN Social Care, majority-owned by MML Capital Partners, runs a chain of regional fostering agencies across the country supporting more than 850 children. It has paid more than £7m interest on shareholder loans since 2020.Reported interest rates on these loans range from 8% to 14%. The thinktank said this creates a tax shield by artificially depressing taxable profits, and was a “mechanism for extracting wealth for investors”.Sophie Flinders, a senior data analyst at Common Wealth who led the analysis, said there was a clear case to ban private companies profiting from public and essential services.“It’s time to cut out the middleman and ensure that all spending on children’s social care goes directly to improving the quality of care, not to lining shareholders’ pockets,” she said.Egan added that “insourcing” was vital, and that returning services to the public sector would “ensure funding goes where it’s needed and there’s genuine accountability”.A Guardian investigation found that£1 in every £11of UK government spending on contractors went to private equity-controlled companies last year, including key services such as transport, waste management and healthcare.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Competition and Markets Authority previously found that the biggest private providers in children’s social care were “making materially higher profits, and charging materially higher prices”, while many were also carrying “very high levels of debt”.Over the past decade, the biggest companies have established market dominance by buying smaller providers, pushing up prices across the sector.The UK government hasvowed to curb profiteering in children’s social carethrough better oversight and, as a last resort, capping profits. The Welsh government has gone further by promising to end for-profit provision in children’s social care by 2030.Common Wealth is calling for a temporary pause on for-profit providers in children’s social care, as well as a full audit of illegal children’s homes. It urged the government to use its powers of compulsory purchase order to bring those of unacceptable quality into public hands.“The outsourcing premium fails the most vulnerable children. Providing the best possible care, rather than mediating the social care market, should be the priority,” the report concluded.Tim Barclay, the chief executive of the National Fostering Group, said: “We support about 3,600 children across the UK through a network of fostering agencies, all of which are rated ‘good’ or ‘outstanding’ by regulators.“Every pound the group receives is focused on frontline care: recruiting and training foster carers, therapeutic support for children, safeguarding and the 24/7 professional support that helps placements succeed. The costs of fostering reflect the increasingly complex needs of children coming into care and the specialist, wraparound support they require.”BSN Social Care has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsSocial careFosteringOutsourcingChildrenPrivate equityUnisonShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK bans three journalists from its conference after critical reporting | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Guardian City editor Anna Isaac among those who had credentials to cover event declined
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Guardian City editor Anna Isaac among those who had credentials to cover event declined
Content: Since Isaac broke the story that Farage had accepted an undeclared £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, the party leader has drastically reduced his time in front of the press.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenSince Isaac broke the story that Farage had accepted an undeclared £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, the party leader has drastically reduced his time in front of the press.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersReform UKReform UK bans three journalists from its conference after critical reportingGuardian City editor Anna Isaac among those who had credentials to cover event declinedHelena HortonWed 2 Sep 2026 18.07 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 16.53 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK has banned at least three journalists from its annual conference who have reported critically on the party and Nigel Farage.The Guardian’s City editor, Anna Isaac, the investigative reporter Peter Geoghegan and the broadcaster and biographer Michael Crick were told this week that their credentials to cover the event, which begins on Thursday, had been declined.The party has billed its conference, which will take place at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham, as “the most talked about event of 2026”. Reform figures are hoping to use it as a resetafter a difficult summerconsumed by questions about an undeclared £5m gift Farage received shortly before he was elected in 2024.A Reform spokesperson said Geoghegan and Crick were refused accreditation because the party viewed them as minor figures. They declined to comment on why Isaac was not given accreditation.After the Guardian contacted Reform for comment, all three received emails saying their conference passes had been reinstated. However, when contacted again by the Guardian, a Reform spokesperson said this had been an administrative error and that they were still not accredited for the conference. They then received further emails confirming their exclusion.Isaac broke the storythat Farage had accepted an undeclared £5m gift from Christopher Harborne. Her reporting also revealed that a host of transactions involving Reform UK’s most senior figures and donations to the party caused bankers to report potential money-laundering concerns to the National Crime Agency.The story has caused issues for Farage all summer and he has drastically reduced his time in front of the press. He also resigned as an MP over the furore, prompting a byelection which the other main parties boycotted, leaving Count Binface as his main opponent. Farage won, and was sworn back into parliament on Monday.Geoghegan runs the Democracy for Sale newsletter on Substack and has written for the Guardian and the New York Times. He received the news he had been banned from the conference shortly afterpublishing a piecerevealing negative comments the pro-Reform journalist Isabel Oakeshott allegedly made about Harborne. Oakeshott declined to comment about the allegations when the Guardian contacted her.Geoghegan said: “Reform clearly wants press coverage but it doesn’t want the scrutiny and accountability that comes with it. Farage and co like to present themselves as the anti-establishment insurgents, but banning independent journalists like me from party conference isn’t anti-establishment. It’s the establishment playbook.”Crick said: “I can understand why the Reform high command might not want me talking to ordinary party members.” He published an unflatteringbiography of Faragein 2022, including details of a letter a teacher once sent to the head of Dulwich college when Faragewas proposed as a prefect, complaining about his “publicly professed racist and neo-fascist views”. Crick has also saidhe believesFarage “panders to racists”. Hetold the Telegraphthis summer that Farage’s fatal flaw was that he was thin-skinned and purged people he disagreed with.On the party’s apparent reinstatements and then U-turn, Crick said: “What cock-up merchants!”A party spokesperson said: “Reform UK accepted 950 of about 1,000 media applications from a variety of outlets, including the entire Guardian lobby team.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Mr Crick works for a university and Mr Geoghegan is a Substack blogger. Neither qualify for a media pass.”The Reform spokesperson refused to give a reason for Isaac’s ban but said: “Anna will still be able to watch the conference proceedings on our livestream if she wishes.”Laura Davison, NUJ general secretary, said: “Reports that Reform UK has chosen to ban journalists who have scrutinised the party from attending its conference are frustrating and concerning. A functioning democracy depends on a free press that can ask political parties difficult questions and hold those seeking power to account.”Pointing to what she called “a wider pattern of intimidation and obstruction of journalists,” and noting that the Conservatives and Labour blocked or removed journalists from their conferences last year, Davison said: “We urge the government and all political parties to demonstrate their commitment to media freedom and uphold the public’s right to be informed. Reform UK should rethink its position and allow journalists full access to the conference.”A Guardian spokesperson said: “Holding public figures to account is the role of a free press and an essential part of the democratic process. Our journalists should be able to ask questions in the public interest and not be deterred from doing their job.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Thousands remain missing and aid is restricted by treacherous conditions in communities hit by unfathomable damage
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Thousands remain missing and aid is restricted by treacherous conditions in communities hit by unfathomable damage
Content: A rescue helicopter flies above the devastated Betrawati district. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianThousands remain missing and aid is hampered by treacherous conditions in communities almost wiped out of existenceByHannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin Betrawati and Rasuwa district. Photographs byAhmer KhanWed 2 Sep 2026 17.42 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSearching for the body of his wife in the mud, Dil Bahadur Shrestha lamented that he did not even have a shovel left. For now, he has been using his hands to try to find her as he picks through the ruins of his house.On Wednesday morning last week, Jamuna Shrestha, his wife of 50 years, had been at home in Betrawati on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli River, feeding her beloved chickens and goats.Asdeadly flash floods coursed down the river valley, Jamuna was last seen going back into her house, trying to usher her chickens to safety, while others fled uphill. Now that house stands like a muddy carcass, everything inside it destroyed or washed away by the violent force of the water and debris that killed more than 1,200 people in Nepal and Tibet.Dil Bahadur Shrestha, 70, had been tending to his rice fields and feeding his cows on the opposite bank when he felt the ground tremble and saw a black wave, hundreds of metres high, coming down the valley. He ran to safety in the forest, but not before watching two bridges get swept away behind him. “When it hit, everything was destroyed within two minutes,” he said.View image in fullscreenDil Bahadur Shrestha, who is searching for his wife of 50 years, Jamuna.He knows in his heart that his wife is gone, but like thousands caught up in the disaster, her body has yet to be found and she is counted among the missing. More than 5,000 people are reported missing in Nepal and a further 546 in the Tibet region of China.Rescue workers have still not reached Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s home, so he returned to try to retrieve her body himself. “Maybe she thought the flood wouldn’t reach inside the house,” he said, wiping away tears.The couple had already rebuilt their home once after an earthquake in 2015 that killed about 9,000 people. As he spoke, his frail body collapsed to the barren, muddy ground where his neighbour’s house once stood.“Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone,” he said. “I cannot forget her. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.”View image in fullscreenA Rasuwa district sign in the flood debris in Betrawati.The scale of the tragedy in Betrawati is unfathomable. It was 8.37am when a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and Tibet crashed into the valley below, setting off deadly flash floods down Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers. By 8.50am, with only a few minutes’ warning, the settlement of Betrawati was engulfed.People wading through the mud-filled river valley in BetrawatiThis once-thriving market town was submerged in mud so thick that only the top two floors of a six-storey building are visible. Most houses were washed away entirely or flipped on their sides by the sheer force of the floods. School buses lie overturned. A grocery shop was swept 200 metres from its original location and lies in ruins. The river itself has diverted to a new path that cuts through where the highway once was.View image in fullscreenAn overturned school bus hit by the flood water.Fragments of the lives of the thousands who lived here lie scattered in the debris: kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses. At least 250 people are missing, Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s brother and sister-in-law among them.As Dil Bahadur Shrestha surveyed the ruins of his life, search and rescue teams stood on the opposite bank, looking for the dead. By the end of the day, they had pulled 24 bodies from a single house. A helicopter thundered overhead, white body bags swinging underneath.“I feel there could still be hundreds of bodies here,” said Dil Bahadur Shrestha. “So many people were swept away all at once, carried off by the raging water.” His voice broke: “Now I’m alone. I am completely alone.”View image in fullscreenSantamaya Lawat tries to retrieve some of her belongings.A few metres away, Santamaya Lawat, 57, stood shaking a thick cake of dirt from the few clothes and blankets she had been able to retrieve from her brother’s home, now only partly standing, with a gaping hole in the side. Her own house, built just 10 months ago with her life’s savings, was still so filled with mud she had not yet been able to get inside. Five members of her family are gone.View image in fullscreenSantamaya Lawat has lost five members of her family as well as her home and her brother’s home next door.“My heart broke when I came back,” she said. “This was supposed to be the house I lived in for the rest of my life, but everything is gone. It was like heaven here and now it has been turned into hell.”Further up the river, in the district of Rasuwa, on the border with Tibet, the scale of destruction only gets worse. Many of the villages here were swept away entirely and are only accessibly by army helicopter. Some are still so cut-off and the ground conditions so precarious that the fate of hundreds of people remains unknown. On Tuesday, police search and rescue teams confirmed they had finally been able to begin ground operations in the border village of Timure, recovering 90 bodies so far.Map showing extent of flooding following the glacial collapse.The flood extent was most pronounced in the vicinity of the glacier collapseA week after the disaster, survivors who fled up mountainsides were still being collected by army helicopters and evacuated to the army base in Dhunche, Rasuwa district’s administrative headquarters.A helicopter getting ready for take off in DhuncheThe mountain village of Syabru Besi was among those wiped clean away, with even the road to the village gone. According to local government officials, at least 500 people there are missing, a quarter of the population. The village resembles nothing more than a muddy riverbed, just one building left standing.Chhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing. “There were 15 or 16 of us from the village who made it safely to the forest,” said Dorje. “We stayed there for two days before the army came in a helicopter. We had nothing to eat. We survived by drinking water from the forest.”Syabrubesi before and afterThe flood eliminated dozens of buildings on the river banks in Syabru BesiHe stood tightly holding the hand of his nine-year-old granddaughter, Ritu Tamang, who wore a big pink rucksack as they waited at Dhunche army base for a ride down to Kathmandu. Rescue helicopters thundered in and out every few minutes. She said quietly that there was “nothing left where our house used to be. I used to go to school and was in Grade 1. Now the school is gone. There are no teachers either.”View image in fullscreenChhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing.View image in fullscreenChhiring Doreje’s granddaughter Ritu Tamang – waiting to be taken to Kathmandu.With the highways washed away, the only road from Kathmandu to Rasuwa is a perilous unpaved track of mud and stones, weaving through tiny mountain villages. The journey often takes more than 12 hours. The treacherous conditions have made it difficult for aid to reach the worst-hit areas and hindered the rescue and relief operations. Many aid trucks are now stuck in Dhunche, unable to drive further north.At a small relief camp on the road between Betrawati and Dhunche set up by Nepal’s Dhulikhel hospital, people collected medicine and food supplies. Doctors said dozens of the children here had lost their parents in the floods. More than 200 children from the local Nilakanthaschool, most aged between five and 11, are also missing, believed to have been washed away as they walked to morning classes.View image in fullscreenPrakash Nepal, a teacher.Prakash Nepal, a teacher, said the school had received a warning just 10 minutes before the flood waters hit, when the school bus was already picking up students.‘Pitiful’: experts condemn initial US aid contribution for Nepal flood victimsRead more“Luckily, we immediately contacted the bus driver and the vehicle stopped midway so the students were able to survive,” he said. “The surge of water did reach the vehicle, but thankfully it did not cause much damage.”However, many of the local families had been displaced by the 2015 earthquake and still lived in informal settlements along the riverbank. Most of those children had been walking to school when the flood struck. Prakash Nepal’s eyes welled with tears: “We could not save the students who were still on the road.”A helicopter flying through the clouds above a river valleyAmid the tragedy, there were also small stories of hope. Sitting on the porch of their village home in Lachyang, Ram Krishna Neupane, 69, and his wife, Muiya Neupane, 66, said their only son had been working as a vet in Syabru Besi when the village was hit.For two days afterwards they heard nothing and feared he was dead.
