Then they received a phone call. “He called up from a hospital in Kathmandu; he had been rescued by the army,” said Ram Krishna Neupane. “He could not speak, he was crying so much and we were crying.”It was, added his wife, “a miracle”.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalSouth and central AsiaNatural disastersFloodingExtreme weatherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Israel ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’ | Israel | The Guardian
description: Defence minister says he believes US backing could tip regional balance in favour of forced resettlement
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Defence minister says he believes US backing could tip regional balance in favour of forced resettlement
Content: Palestinian children queue to have their faces painted before an outdoor cartoon screening at a displacement camp in Gaza City.Photograph: Bilal Osama/APAImages/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPalestinian children queue to have their faces painted before an outdoor cartoon screening at a displacement camp in Gaza City.Photograph: Bilal Osama/APAImages/ShutterstockIsraelIsrael ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’Defence minister says he believes US backing could tip regional balance in favour of forced resettlementAndrew RothGlobal affairs correspondentWed 2 Sep 2026 19.20 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s defence minister has said his country is seeking Donald Trump’s support to approve plans to expel Palestinians from the Gaza Strip in what has widely been condemned as a potential war crime.Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza in the end without thismigration” during a conference hosted by the Israeli news site Ynet and the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth. He said the Israeli government was “organised and prepared to get them out by sea, by air, by every way possible”.Trump discussed a US takeover of theGazaStrip in early 2025 that would have involved removing Palestinians from the territory, but has since pulled back from the idea. A 20-point peace plan the White House drew up last year did not call for Palestinians’ deportation, an act that would be widely seen as ethnic cleansing.View image in fullscreenIsrael’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said removal of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip was ‘being discussed all the time’.Photograph: Israeli Defence Ministry/ReutersKatz, however, said on Wednesday that he believed US support could tip regional opinion in favour of the forced resettlement of Palestinians from Gaza. He said Trump’s approval was crucial to convince neighbouring countries to accept Palestinian refugees.“Every country that is willing to take them in wants American backing,” he said. “Trump has not cancelled this at the moment. He has frozen it.”The White House did not immediately respond to a request from the Guardian for comment on whether Trump was continuing to hold discussions on Israel’s proposals to forcibly depopulate the Gaza Strip.Ed Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward IsraelRead moreKatz pointed in particular to Egypt, which he said had lobbied Washington to oppose the forced removal of the Palestinian population. “It has not been cancelled,” he said. “It is being discussed all the time, including now, and I think there is no other solution in the end that is in everyone’s interest.”The remarks come during a competitive election season in Israel in which the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his rightwing allies have appealed to voters by calling for more aggressive measures against Palestinians.Some have been openly inflammatory and cruel. The far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, posted footage on X from a women’s prison where he said he was responsible for the dire conditions in the facility.When one prisoner told him they were not receiving medical care, showering or receiving clean clothing, Ben-Gvir said: “The good conditions in the prisons are over. This is the current situation, and I am directly responsible for everything. I am pleased with these conditions.”Netanyahu visited an Israeli military post close to the yellow line in the Gaza Strip on Wednesday. Israel has said it would not pull back from that line until Hamas disarmed, despite calls for a phased withdrawal to facilitate a recent ceasefire with the group.“We control the territory and are staying on this line,” Netanyahu said. “We are doing everything to achieve our goal – disarming Hamas and demilitarising Gaza. Gaza will no longer pose a threat to Israel.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dutch central bank moves 86 tonnes of gold to UK from US and Canada, citing ‘geopolitical unrest’ | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: Bank says gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily and the move will allow it to respond more rapidly in a ‘crisis situation’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bank says gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily and the move will allow it to respond more rapidly in a ‘crisis situation’
Content: The Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US and Canada.Photograph: Mike Groll/APView image in fullscreenThe Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US and Canada.Photograph: Mike Groll/APNetherlandsDutch central bank moves 86 tonnes of gold to UK from US and Canada, citing ‘geopolitical unrest’Bank says gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily and the move will allow it to respond more rapidly in a ‘crisis situation’Agence France-PresseThu 3 Sep 2026 00.47 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 01.09 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US andCanadato London, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest”.De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) said gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily than those held in New York and Ottawa.“This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation,” the bank said in a statement on Wednesday.“With this step, we have improved the deployability of the gold reserves. We assume that we will never need to deploy the gold, but it is nevertheless necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” said DNB’s president, Olaf Sleijpen.Gold price hits three-month high amid fears over Iran war and Trump economyRead moreThe total Dutchgold stockamounted to 612.4 tonnes and was valued at €72.2bn ($83.7bn) at the end of 2025, said the DNB.Before the deployment, the Dutch bank held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa.After the move, each country accounted for 18.5% of the Dutch gold reserve.The share of gold held in London increased from 18.1% to 32.1%. The bank still holds 30.8% of its gold inthe Netherlands.The transfer was carried out partially by buying and selling and partly by physically transferring gold, the bank said.The bank moved more than 27 tonnes of physical gold from the US and Canada to Zeist.The same quantity of gold was moved from Zeist to London, preventing the melting down of gold bars.“By combining buying and selling and physical transport, the risks associated with physically moving a large quantity of gold have been spread,” the DNB said.The operation took place between March and August of this year, it said.Laurent Schwartz, president of the Paris-based NationalGoldCounter, which facilitates gold trading in France, said central banks had been moving their reserves around for about a decade.“The current political context in the United States might also push certain central banks into favouring other storage locations,” he said.The London market was the deepest and most liquid, Schwartz said, making it easier to deploy in times of crisis.“Central banks can more easily lend their gold there to other banking institutions.”John Plassard, an analyst at Cite Gestion Private Bank, said the Dutch move was intended “for there to be more immediate availability in the event of a crisis”.For the moment, it was a “fairly one-off move”, but he warned that if other central banks followed suit, it could damage confidence in the US.At the beginning of the year, there were concerns raised in Germany about the security of its central bank’s reserves in New York.However, the powerful Bundesbank has decided for the moment not to shift its reserves away from New York.“The New York Fed is and remains an important storage site for our gold,” the bank told public TV station ARD in January.Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsEconomicsGoldCommoditiesBankingTrump administrationCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: Maltese tycoon found not guilty of involvement in Daphne Caruana Galizia murder | Daphne Caruana Galizia | The Guardian
description: Yorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrage
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Yorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrage
Content: Yorgen Fenech leaving court in Valletta after he was found not guilty of involvement in the 2017 murder of Maltese journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersView image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech leaving court in Valletta after he was found not guilty of involvement in the 2017 murder of Maltese journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltese tycoon found not guilty of involvement in Daphne Caruana Galizia murderYorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrageJuliette Garsidein VallettaWed 2 Sep 2026 20.26 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.49 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Malta’s richest men has been found not guilty of involvement in the murder of the anti-corruption journalistDaphne Caruana Galizia.The verdict, which is expected to be appealed against by the prosecution, came as a blow not only to the victim’s family, but to the politicians and campaigners who regard the case as a landmark action in the fight to protect press freedom inEurope.Nearly nine years after Caruana Galizia’s death in acar bombing in October 2017, a jury of six women and three men found Yorgen Fenech, 44, not guilty of both counts with which he had been charged: complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, and association with the intention of committing a crime.Delivered at 7.30pm, the verdict was decisive. To gasps from the gallery and cheers from Fenech’s relatives, the forewoman announced jurors had voted to dismiss both counts by an eight-to-one majority.View image in fullscreenCaruana Galizia’s sister Corinne Vella said: ‘Everybody is much more at risk now, because this signals you can kill journalists with impunity.’Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersAs Caruana Galizia’s family listened in shock, with some relatives in tears, the judge, Edwina Grima, immediately ordered Fenech’s release from custody. If convicted, he would have faced a life sentence. He left court through the front entrance, without responding to requests for comment.“Everybody is much more at risk now, because this signals you can kill journalists with impunity,” Caruana Galizia’s sister, Corinne Vella, said. “We knew an acquittal was a huge possibility. But it’s like when someone dies, it still shocks you.”In a message on Facebook, the journalist’s eldest son decried a “terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from. They had a great responsibility to deliver justice. And washed their hands of it”.The leader of the opposition Nationalist party, Alex Borg, requested the urgent reopening of parliament, which is currently in recess, to discuss the verdict. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” said Borg, speaking to a crowd of demonstrators that had assembled on Wednesday night outside parliament. He described the verdict as a black spot on the Labour government, and said the press should be free to do its work “independently and without undue pressure”.Fenech, an influential businessman and property developer whose family owns two Hilton hotels and has a share in a power station inMalta, had been accused by prosecutors of paying €150,000 (£129,000) via a middleman, Melvin Theuma, to have the journalist killed.The murder of Caruana Galizia, who targeted Fenech and leading political figures in her reporting, triggered the most consequential political scandal in Malta’s postwar history, becoming a rallying point for anti-corruption and press freedom activism.View image in fullscreenA person holds up an image of Caruana Galizia at a protest in Valletta in 2019.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersThe fallout resulted in Joseph Muscat, the then prime minister of the EU’s smallest member state, being forced out of office along with two of his ministers and his chief of staff.While Muscat left office, the party he led remains in power. In a statement, the government noted the verdict and appealed for prudence in public comments at a delicate moment, insisting: “The government remains committed to seeing justice served by its institutions.”The two-month trial laid bare the extent of Fenech’s network of political contacts, and raised questions about attempts to sabotage and interfere with the police investigation. Key witnesses, and the defendant himself, claimed the prime minister’s chief of staff had repeatedly leaked sensitive information to Fenech.Summing up the case against him, prosecutor Anthony Vella said Fenech believed he could “buy justice”, telling the jury: “You are being asked to decide whether a man who had extensive contacts in politics and among the heads of public entities had enough power to pay for Daphne to be killed.”The defence argued that the chain of command went higher, with suggestions from Fenech and his lawyers that the person who had ordered the killing was Muscat’s former chief of staff Keith Schembri. They said police had not done enough to investigate allegations about his involvement.“All roads lead to Keith, and all bridges to Keith were burned,” the defence lawyer Charles Mercieca said in his summing up.In his testimony, Fenech told the jury: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.” He said he had merely acted as a messenger between Schembri and Theuma, and that the taxi-driver had blackmailed him.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSchembri, who gave evidence at the trial, denied all wrongdoing, saying he had no involvement in leaks and no knowledge of the murder.Fenech’s defence lawyer, Giannella de Marco, said Schembri and others should have been investigated. She said the prosecution’s chief witness had not been believed.“The jurors did not believe Melvin Theuma. It was an eight-one verdict, which means unanimous … don’t you think jurors saw who the real masterminds were?” she said.The vote was effectively unanimous because juries in Malta rarely convict 9-0, as this would allow the public to know for certain which way individual members voted.Repubblika, a Maltese campaign group, called for a “national reckoning” in which the corruption investigated by Caruana Galizia, who was 59 when she died and one of Malta’s best-known journalists, is prosecuted.View image in fullscreenDaphne Caruana Galizia’s sons, Matthew, Andrew and Paul, step out of court after Yorgen Fenech was acquitted of conspiracy to murder her in 2017.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters“Those politically responsible for the culture of impunity of the Muscat years must not be rehabilitated into public life. The state must sincerely accept its responsibility and apologise to Daphne’s family,” a spokesperson said.Occupy Justice, meanwhile, described the verdict as “deeply painful and disappointing”, saying Malta remained “without full accountability for the person or people who ordered her murder”.An independent public inquiry, for which the family fought, concluded in 2021 that the state had to shoulder responsibility for the killing because it “created an atmosphere of impunity, generated from the highest levels”. It made a number of recommendations, many of which have yet to be implemented.In a statement, the Daphne Foundation said: “Nine years after Daphne’s brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed. Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne’s life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost.”Tom Gibson, the deputy advocacy director of the Committee to Protect Journalists, was in the courtroom for the verdict. In a statement, he said: “This is a heartbreaking verdict for the family after years of waiting for justice. We will continue to stand by them while they seek accountability for all of those involved in the murder.”Explore more on these topicsDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltaEuropeJournalist safetyPress freedomNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: China’s falling emissions amid Iran war spark hope of decarbonisation watershed | Greenhouse gas emissions | The Guardian
description: Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls
Content: An aquaculture-photovoltaic hybrid project in Fengdu County, China. Clean energy use cushioned the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAn aquaculture-photovoltaic hybrid project in Fengdu County, China. Clean energy use cushioned the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockGreenhouse gas emissionsChina’s falling emissions amid Iran war spark hope of decarbonisation watershedOil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price fallsJonathan WattsThu 3 Sep 2026 00.01 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 00.08 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.The reportreveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by thestrait of Hormuzcrisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed forCarbon Briefby theCentre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months afterthe first US airstrikes in late February.How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.View image in fullscreenWind turbines on the Yellow Sea coast of Yancheng, China.Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPAThe country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.Thiselectrifying trendhad begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic andstrategic imperativeof reducing petro-dependence.In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChina has been preparing for a global energy crisis for years. It is paying off nowRead moreAnalysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” saidLauri Myllyvirta, the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.”Myllyvirta noted this was the first timeChina’s overall emissionshad fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption.In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels.Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst atEmber, which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further.“The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”Explore more on these topicsGreenhouse gas emissionsClimate crisisChinaStrait of HormuzUS-Israel war on IranAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nuclear bomb test veterans were victims of one of ‘greatest scandals in Britain’, says ex-defence minister | Ministry of Defence | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Tobias Ellwood says he gave MPs inaccurate information in 2018 provided by his department, the MoD
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Tobias Ellwood says he gave MPs inaccurate information in 2018 provided by his department, the MoD
Content: A British atomic bomb test explosion in the Montebello Islands in Australia, 3 October 1952.Photograph: Granger/Historical Picture Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreenA British atomic bomb test explosion in the Montebello Islands in Australia, 3 October 1952.Photograph: Granger/Historical Picture Archive/AlamyMinistry of DefenceNuclear bomb test veterans were victims of one of ‘greatest scandals in Britain’, says ex-defence ministerExclusive: Tobias Ellwood says he gave MPs inaccurate information in 2018 provided by his department, the MoDI inadvertently misled parliament over a British nuclear scandal. Now I’m demanding justiceKiran StaceyPolicy editorWed 2 Sep 2026 22.30 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former defence minister has admitted misleading parliament over the existence of crucial medical records relating tonuclear bomb test veterans.Tobias Ellwood has said he unwittingly gave MPs incorrect information in 2018 when he told them he had been unable to locate information on veterans’ blood tests after being given incorrect information by officials at theMinistry of Defence(MoD).Veterans have been fighting for years to see the records as many look to prove that years of serious illnesses such as cancer were linked to their experiences testing nuclear weapons. Ellwood’s admission will increase pressure on the MoD to explain whether its officials have helped prevent those veterans get justice.Ina piece for the Guardian, Ellwood says: “In December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament.“Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was ‘unable to locate any information’ suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.“I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them.”He added: “This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.”View image in fullscreen‘Why had ministers not been given the full picture?’ asked Tobias Ellwood, a former defence minister.Photograph: UK ParliamentAn MoD spokesperson said: “This government commissioned and completed an extensive records discovery exercise, examining tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme.“The findings have now been published in full, following regular engagement between ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process.”Between 1952 and 1967, about 22,000 British military personnel took part in 45 large-scale nuclear weapons tests in Australia and the South Pacific. Some pilots flew through mushroom clouds, some troops crawled through fallout and many witnessed the first test wearing little more than short-sleeved shirts and shorts.Large numbers later suffered blood disorders and cancers, which they believed were caused by exposure to radioactive fallout. Most were denied pensions because of their ill health.View image in fullscreenOperation Hurricane, Britain's first atomic weapons detonation, took place off Trimouille Island, in the Montebello Islands off the coast of north-west Australia, on 3 October 1952.Photograph: Fox Photos/Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesUnlike other nuclear-armed countries such as France, the US and the Soviet Union, the UK has never compensated those involved in testing atomic bombs.The case has been compared with theinfected blood scandal, which saw more than 30,000 people contract HIV and Hepatitis C in the the 1970s and early 1990s after being given contaminated blood and blood products.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, haspreviously saidhe was misled by officials when he claimed as health secretary in 2009 that there was no evidence that people were knowingly given contaminated blood. His claims echo those being made today by Ellwood.Burnham has also been a vocal supporter of the nuclear test veterans in recent years.As Greater Manchester mayor in 2022,Burnham said: “If the state was conducting medical tests upon servicemen and not informing them when they found serious irregularity, that is at least misconduct in public office, and more serious, perhaps gross negligence manslaughter, in respect of people who died as a result.“Crimes have been committed.”The prime minister is now coming under pressure to begin an inquiry and allocate government money for compensation to the victims.View image in fullscreenThe countdown to detonation onboard the aircraft carrier Campania during atomic bomb testing in the Montebello Islands, Australia, December 1952.Photograph: Keystone/Getty ImagesOne of the major problems with securing compensation so far has been the lack of medical evidence linking veterans’ health problems to their experiences helping with nuclear tests.The government long maintained that it did not hold any such medical records – a claim that was proved incorrect in 2022 when the journalist Susie Boniface revealed the existence of a database of 28,000 documents known as Merlin.That database had been put together in response to a 2007 lawsuit by 1,000 British test veterans and their families, but the information was classified.Ellwood says he did not find out about the existence of this database until 2022, when details began to emerge in the press.He writes in his piece: “If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture?”Explore more on these topicsMinistry of DefenceNuclear weaponsMilitaryShareReuse this content

title: Leipzig airport attack fallout exposes Germany’s deepening divide over Russia | Germany | The Guardian
description: The government’s tougher stance towards the Kremlin is drawing attacks from both the far right and far left
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: The government’s tougher stance towards the Kremlin is drawing attacks from both the far right and far left
Content: This week, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport.Photograph: Sebastian Willnow/DPA/APView image in fullscreenThis week, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport.Photograph: Sebastian Willnow/DPA/APGermanyAnalysisLeipzig airport attack fallout exposes Germany’s deepening divide over RussiaKate Connollyin BerlinThe government’s tougher stance towards the Kremlin is drawing attacks from both the far right and far leftWed 2 Sep 2026 18.07 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTShareEven before theGerman government laid the blame this week on Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport, the topic of German ties to Moscow was high on the political agenda.But the timing of the unsurprising yet explosive Leipzig announcement – days before a key regional vote – has exposed the extent to which German politics is polarised on the issue.Leading the polls nationally and in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, which votes this weekend, is the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The party has repeatedly called for a closer bond with the Kremlin, and crucially, for its cheap oil and gas to flow toGermanyonce again, despite Moscow’s unrelenting onslaught on Ukraine.Germany is already on tenterhooks. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, had warned that Berlin faced a growing threat of hybrid warfare, and on Wednesday morning, the day after the Leipzig announcement, police were investigating a second sabotage assault on the electricity grid within just 24 hours.An explosion at Augsburg railway station in the early hours of Wednesday morning also initially looked like it might fall into the same category, illustrating the extent to which the country remains nervous and on high ‌alert for attacks on its vital infrastructure.Investigations into all these incidents and others from the near past, many of which are said to be linked, are ongoing, even as authorities warned against drawing premature conclusions.Moscow has denied involvement, and accused Berlin of trying to divert attention from its own domestic problems, including the rise of the far right, and the state’s failure to protect its own infrastructure.The resulting uncertainty, chaos and angst appear to be nothing less than grist to the mill of the AfD. Its foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, accused the government of sorting acts of sabotage “according to political expediency”.While it had “escalated the situation against Russia within days”, he said, the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukrainian operatives are suspected of being responsible for sabotaging a key route for Russian gas to Germany, had so far remained without consequence. (Two Ukrainian nationals named by Germany as suspects have been arrested over the attack, with one last year extradited from Italy and the other currently in Croatia.)“This is not a consistent security policy, but rather a double standard in foreign policy,” Frohnmaier claimed, adding he was convinced the government would use the Leipzig incident “as justification for even more support for Ukraine and an even deeper involvement of Germany in this war”.The AfD, which has called for talks with Moscow, ending sanctions againstRussia, and slashing support for Ukraine, has urged the government to lay bare its proof of Russia’s involvement, saying so far the evidence is lacking.Wary of escalating a conflict with Moscow, the government of Friedrich Merz waited days before making its painstakingly worded declaration. In a more frank admission than the German government has ever made, foreign minister Johann Wadephul stated: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.”The details released on Wednesday of two Russian suspects identified as having been involved in the Leipzig incident are unlikely to assuage the AfD’s complaints or, it would seem, the far-left party Die Linke.Its leading MP, Dietmar Bartsch, said on Wednesday that the suspicions of Russian involvement did not justify the government’s decision to shut down the Russian consulate in Bonn as well as a sprawling Russian cultural centre in Berlin and would not make Germany safer. On the contrary, they increased the risk of a “major war” drawing closer, he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith the AfD on around 42% in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt and possibly poised to form the first far-right-led administration since the second world war, Merz’s Christlich Demokratische Union (CDU), on around 22%, is under intense pressure.Within Merz’s own party, there have been growing calls for him to toughen his stance against Moscow and pure frustration that it has taken so long. For years, members of his Christian Democrats and his current coalition partner, the Social Democrats, along with generations of diplomats, have remained caught up in, and seduced by, the long-standing romantic notion that Russia could be tamed by trade and energy pipelines, according to the CDU’s Roderich Kiesewetter.The former soldier and the party’s respected foreign policy expert told broadcaster InfoRadio that Germany “must give up its caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil, as well as this romantic notion of Russia as a great cultural nation. Russia cares not a damn about this caution, but rather sees it as an invitation to keep escalating.”He criticised Merz’s recent public reference to Russia as a great cultural nation, “because great cultural nations do not subject their neighbouring states to war, violence and child abductions”. He said it was time for Merz to name the current Russian regime for what it was.Konstantin von Notz, foreign policy expert for the Greens, praised the government’s “significantly clear language” over Moscow’s behaviour, even as he described it as “long overdue”.The extent to which voters in Saxony-Anhalt fear how a further deterioration of relations with Moscow could affect them may yet be felt at the ballot box.Explore more on these topicsGermanyRussiaEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Stolen Babies review – the scale of this cruelty is almost impossible to fathom | Television | The Guardian
description: For decades, thousands of unmarried mothers in the UK were forced to give up their newborns after being denied pain relief in labour so they would ‘not be a bad girl again’. This harrowing documentary hears their stories
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: For decades, thousands of unmarried mothers in the UK were forced to give up their newborns after being denied pain relief in labour so they would ‘not be a bad girl again’. This harrowing documentary hears their stories
Content: Marion McMillan with her nine-month-old son, who was not adopted instantly as he was mixed race and most families wanted white children.Photograph: Marion McMillan c/o Finestripe ProductionsView image in fullscreenMarion McMillan with her nine-month-old son, who was not adopted instantly as he was mixed race and most families wanted white children.Photograph: Marion McMillan c/o Finestripe ProductionsTV reviewTelevisionReviewStolen Babies review – the scale of this cruelty is almost impossible to fathomFor decades, thousands of unmarried mothers in the UK were forced to give up their newborns after being denied pain relief in labour so they would ‘not be a bad girl again’. This harrowing documentary hears their storiesLucy ManganWed 2 Sep 2026 22.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe scale of the suffering at first threatens to make you numb to it. The 90-minute documentary Stolen Babies is as unsparing as it is unsentimental and opens with a bald statement of verified fact: “Between 1949 and 1976 over 250,000 unmarried mothers in the UK were forced into handing their newborn babies over for adoption.” State apparatus facilitated this every step of the way, supported by religious institutions. These institutions ran, or were involved with running, the mother and baby homes to which the girls and young women were banished (“They do not quickly acknowledge themselves as sinners,” notes one report on its inmates), along with self-proclaimed moral welfare societies and the NHS.The statistics are appalling. The details are worse. Some of the women whose stories are told in the film became pregnant by boyfriends. Some were victims of rape. Joan Chambers was 14 when a teacher took her for a walk in the woods. “I trusted him, I really did … All I remember was the pain. I honestly didn’t know what was happening.”Ann Keen was 17 when she went on a date with a salesman from the factory she was working at. “In today’s term,” she says hesitantly, “it was without consent. You couldn’t say that in the 60s.” Doctors and nurses refused to speak to Keen while she was in labour, and they denied her pain relief – including when she was stitched up after the birth – so that she would “remember it and not be a bad girl again”. Her baby was taken away eight days later. “And you’ll never see him again,” a midwife gleefully told her, before putting the teenager in a bath and starting to squeeze her breasts: “I’m getting rid of the milk. You won’t be needing this.”View image in fullscreen‘All I remember was the pain’ … Joan Chambers in Stolen Babies.Photograph: Finestripe ProductionsChambers gave evidence at her teacher’s trial when she was nearly eight months pregnant. “Children are so apt to make up taradiddles and wicked invention,” the judge advised the jury. “You will not allow sympathy for the girl to cloud your judgment.” The teacher was found not guilty. During the birth she was “absolutely torn to shreds”. Her baby was taken from her three weeks later and she was told to go and strip the bedding from his cot, ready for the next one.The dehumanisation, the cruelty is unfathomable and the film leaves the viewer to sit and wrestle with the accruing conundrums. To say that it is the result of different attitudes is only to push the bafflement back a stage: how could they, we, anyone privilege the importance of marriage over the right of a mother to keep her child; how could class – and it was overwhelmingly young working-class women’s babies being given to middle-class couples – be such a blinding factor; how could religious belief have such a chokehold on a society that rage-fuelled punishment could be visited on women with barely a murmur of reproach; how could babies be treated like commodities?View image in fullscreenChambers as a young girl.Photograph: Joan Chambers c/o Finestripe ProductionsBut so it was, and social historian Dr Michael Lambert has the evidence, which would be used alongside the women’s testimonies when the Sunday Post journalist Marion Scott broke the story of the scandal after a long investigation. Painstakingly gathered from thousands of council and state records of the adoptions, of reports from mother and baby homes up and down the land, it is, he says, “evidence of a system designed to supply infants”. It’s also tangible proof of what the women’s stories have told us: that at every level, written through the national psyche like poisonous letters through a stick of rock, was the idea that women are lesser beings and that “fallen” women are the very least of them all.Marion McMillan, whose mixed race son stayed with her for nine months because most families wanted white babies (“No freckles” was one couple’s further stipulation), has spent 20 years supporting mothers like her and campaigning for government apologies. Nicola Sturgeon supplied one from McMillan’s native Scotland in 2023, andKeir Starmer followed suitthis year. The women speak of it as a release from the shame that has pursued them down the decades. Again, the suffering visited upon them all seems incalculable.Adoption law changed after 1976 and put an end – or the beginning of an end – to the grey and hidden market in babies from young, unmarried, poorer women to affluent older couples. Contraception cutting off the supply seems to have been a more immediate factor than changing attitudes, but minds always take longer than bodies to respond to change. Whether you feel the writing through the rock reads truly differently today – looking at rape statistics; state neglect and underfunding of women’s services; authorities’ complicity in ignoring gangs of groomers and predators in recent decades – is up to you.Stolen Babies aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Intoxicating mix of humour, high camp and danger’: Tim Curry remembered | Film | The Guardian
description: Guardian readers share memories of actor best known for roles in The Rocky Horror Show and Stephen King’s It
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: Guardian readers share memories of actor best known for roles in The Rocky Horror Show and Stephen King’s It
Content: Tim Curry gained wide acclaim as the extraterrestrial mad scientist Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarView image in fullscreenTim Curry gained wide acclaim as the extraterrestrial mad scientist Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarFilm‘Intoxicating mix of humour, high camp and danger’: Tim Curry rememberedGuardian readers share memories of actor best known for roles in The Rocky Horror Show and Stephen King’s ItGuardian readers andAlfie PackhamWed 2 Sep 2026 15.27 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.49 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Always had a glorious glint in his eye’I first saw him in the 1978 series Will Shakespeare, where he played Shakespeare alongside Nicholas Clay. Two very classy actors who, whatever the value of the programme, made me want to know more about the man and his work.Tim Curryalways had a glorious glint in his eye which drew you in as if you were the only person who understood.Margaret Carradus, Lancaster‘A delightful exchange’My best friend lives down the street from the Dakota building [in Manhattan]. One night I was waiting for her outside and two nicely dressed, handsome gentlemen were walking together. I was holding my very sweet poodle, Honey, in my arms. One of the men, who I then realised was Mr Curry, placed his hand under Honey’s chin and said: “She looks like a delicious peppermint!” We all chuckled as they continued on their way. Quite a delightful exchange.Mary Donaghy, New YorkClowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in picturesRead more‘That intoxicating mix of humour, high camp, sex and danger’I’ve always loved Tim Curry. More than any other performer. That intoxicating mix of humour, high camp, sex and danger. So I was excited to spot him in a florist decades ago and told him I was a fan. He was very friendly and said he was buying flowers for the cast of a show he was in – first-night presents – and filled the back of his car with them.Jo Glanville, LondonView image in fullscreenTim Curry in The Rocky Horror Picture Show … ‘no words to describe how important [he was] to me and my freaky relationship with myself and my gender identity’.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Allstar‘No other actor could have pulled that role off’As a child, I remember being captivated and equally terrified seeing him as the grand wizard in The Worst Witch and ever since he has continued to do both. But my favourite character of his has to be Wadsworth in Clue. No other actor could have pulled that role off with its endless dialogue and frenzied physical comedy requirements. A legend in every sense.Robert E Moore, Los Angeles‘He played a role in my self-acceptance’One of the first films that stuck with me as a child was FernGully: The Last Rainforest. Tim Curry has been a part of so much of my life. The Rocky Horror Picture Show was so important to me as a queer person and there are no words to describe how important the role of Frank-N-Furter is to me and my freaky relationship with myself and my gender identity. Even at the end of his life, he played a role in my self acceptance. Since I was 10 years old, I have developed a disability that affects my ability to walk, talk, use my hands and arms, and to see and hear. As my mobility and speech declined, he showed me I can still be an icon and contribute to the world even though I’m different and can’t do what everyone else can.Lilly, 22, PenrithView image in fullscreenTim Curry performs in the musical Spamalot at the Broadway premiere in New York.Photograph: Stuart Ramson/AP‘He could embody the wildest characters’I first remember seeing the Rocky Horror Picture Show as a teenager in the Chicagoland area. It blew my mind. I had no idea what to make of it, nor of the costumed people attending. I saw it again several times and couldn’t get enough. After I moved to Japan, I found a copy of the DVD and shared it with friends, all of whom loved it. What always struck me was how he could embody the wildest characters and give them enough depth that you enjoyed them, even if you didn’t like them. The risks he took were admirable. His characters allowed me to explore who I am and appreciate being not the norm. He was a true thespian and a unique person. No one can replace him. Sayonara, Mr Curry, you will be missed and remembered.Joe Guzman, 63, Japan‘A lovely man’In 1982, I was Pamela Stephenson’s dresser on The Pirates of Penzance, which starred Tim Curry as the Pirate King. I got tickets for my sister and my nephew, who were seven or eight years old, to see the show. Neither had ever been to a West End production before. At one point during the performance, Tim Curry took a breath during a rousing speech and in that silence, my nephew, entirely carried away by the experience, very audibly shouted his support. Without missing a beat, Tim Curry replied: “Well said, my man!” A lovely man and I still have my “buckets of blood” badges he distributed to the cast and crew.Gill, East SussexView image in fullscreenTim Curry with Richard O’Brien and Patricia Quinn in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Allstar‘Charm personified’I briefly met him, twice, at the stage door of the Palace theatre when he was in Spamalot in 2006. Although clearly tired after his wonderful performance, he was charm personified – and very happy to sign not only my Spamalot pieces, but also some of my Rocky Horror memorabilia. His was the last of the four signatures I needed on my 8x10 of the famous throne scene during Sweet Transvestite in The Rocky Horror Picture Show – now one of the most precious artefacts in my collection. More importantly, I got to say thank you to him for his performances. I’m really glad I did. Speaking to such a hero can be an intimidating experience: there’s a risk they will disappoint. Curry never did. He was every bit as wonderful as he was when he first strode out on stage that night, looked out into the audience, and every one of us truly believed that he was “looking directly at me!”Edward Marlowe, 52, LondonExplore more on these topicsFilmTim CurryRocky Horror ShowActingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The year of Domhnall Gleeson: ‘No one talks about actors’ dedication. But I had a perm for five months!’ | Domhnall Gleeson | The Guardian
description: He started in the Harry Potter films and has since become ubiquitous, playing every type of character: romcom leads, evil villains, comical idiots. He even starred in a Taylor Swift video. So how does he stay so under the radar?
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: He started in the Harry Potter films and has since become ubiquitous, playing every type of character: romcom leads, evil villains, comical idiots. He even starred in a Taylor Swift video. So how does he stay so under the radar?
Content: ‘I don’t believe in having a bad time at work’ … Domhnall Gleeson.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian. Photographer's assistant: Flora LunaView image in fullscreen‘I don’t believe in having a bad time at work’ … Domhnall Gleeson.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian. Photographer's assistant: Flora LunaDomhnall GleesonInterviewThe year of Domhnall Gleeson: ‘No one talks about actors’ dedication. But I had a perm for five months!’Steve RoseHe started in the Harry Potter films and has since become ubiquitous, playing every type of character: romcom leads, evil villains, comical idiots. He even starred in a Taylor Swift video. So how does he stay so under the radar?Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.33 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDomhnall Gleeson has got so much new stuff coming up, someone recently joked that this was the “summer of Domhnall”. Now the phrase is all over the internet, and Gleeson is mortified: “The worry is that somebody will say this to me now thinking that I believe it.” He doesn’t know where it came from – possibly his co-star Gayle Rankin on his new movie The Incomer. “It’s certainly not something I’m trying to push … but it would be great if it could be the headline.”He’s in a good mood when we meet at a London hotel on a hot afternoon. You could say he’s good at interviews – charming, funny, garrulous, the perfect chatshow guest. He could just beacting, admittedly, but he seems to be a genuinely good-natured, grounded sort of guy.The Incomer, an eccentric Scottish comedy, is one of three new projects Gleeson has coming out in a matter of weeks. The others are the second season of the US Office spin-off The Paper and Werner Herzog’s new film, Bucking Fastard, which is about to play at the Venice film festival. More of all this later, but first we must address Gleeson’s most prominent, and least probable, recent role: as the star of a Taylor Swift music video.View image in fullscreenGleeson as Daniel in The Incomer.Photograph: Universal Pictures. All Rights Reserved/PADirected by Swift herself, thevideo for Opaliteis a bizarrely goofy concoction with an equally bizarre origin story. It came about because the two of them appeared together on the Graham Norton show last October. Fellow guest Cillian Murphy joked that The Paper was worth watching for Gleeson’s dancing alone. “I’m hoping to get in a Taylor Swift music video,” he joked in reply.That was that, he thought. “Then two weeks later, we got an email. Like, wild!” Not just him: Swift asked every other guest on the show to be in the video – Murphy, Greta Lee, Jodie Turner-Smith, Lewis Capaldi,even Norton himself. “No one else in the world can come up with an idea like that and make it happen,” Gleeson says.View image in fullscreenWith Taylor Swift and Graham Norton, during the shoot for Swift’s music video Opalite.Photograph: SpotifyGleeson has the starring role, as a lonely man who gets an upgrade on his painful relationship with a cactus when he is magically matched with fellow loner Swift. Then they dance together joyfully in matching glittery turquoise tracksuits.“They told me the day before there was going to be a dance. I was like, are you fucking joking?” Gleeson recalls. Are you good at that kind of thing, I ask. “No. I’m terrible at it!” He spent all night practising in front of the mirror. But Swift’s direction did the rest: “She said ‘full send’, though I didn’t knowwhat that phrase meant. She was like, ‘The moves don’t matter. You just gotta go for and love it, and just trust in it and experience it.’” The first take after she said that was the one they used. “The believing in it and the joy of it helps you do it.”So did he go to her wedding?“Er …” He ums and ahs. “Can I plead the fifth?”Sociable as he is, Gleeson is also very good at protecting his privacy. He’d rather not answer questions about his immediate family (he has been married to the producer Juliette Bonass since 2023), and he’s not on social media at all, he says. “I think that’s just like a line in the sand that helps immediately in terms of the personal not being public.”In short, Gleeson does a fine job of staying under the radar while also being everywhere. He is not exactly an inconspicuous figure, with his bright red hair and striking features – his Italian co-worker in The Paper says to him: “Look at your eyes: scary, like goat” – but on screen Gleeson is remarkably adaptable. He doesn’t really have a type. He’s played romantic leads (Richard Curtis’s About Time, for example), evil villains (General Hux in the Star Wars movies, or terrorising Julianne Moore in last year’s Echo Valley), real-life characters (Bob Geldof, AA Milne), comical idiots (Frank of Ireland). Family films, period dramas, westerns, sci-fi – he just seems to fit in wherever you put him. Even his age is strangely malleable: he’s now 43 but looks barely any older than he did playing Bill Weasley in theHarry Potterfilms.View image in fullscreenGleeson: ‘I liked the buzz of hearing people laugh.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianWhat’s more, he’s so good at accents, I’d almost forgotten that he’s Irish. When I first met Gleeson a decade ago, it wason the set of Frank, the indie satire based on the outsider musician Frank Sidebottom. We were in a freezing cabin in rural Ireland but Gleeson was playing a middle-class English guy, and stayed flawlessly in accent throughout (but not in character). That’s the best way, he’s learned from experience: “One day when I was doing Harry Potter I kind of went Australian by accident and couldn’t retrieve it.” It has its disadvantages, though: “You don’t want to do any phone calls with anyone from home during your work day.”In The Incomer he’s passing as Scottish, which is more challenging: “Going to Scotland and doing a Scottish accent in front of an all-Scottish crew is a very different experience.” It was kind of fitting, though: Gleeson plays the unwelcome visitor of the title: a mainland bureaucrat who comes to a remote Scottish isle to evict its only residents, a pair of insular siblings (Rankin and Grant O’Rourke). Written and directed by Louis Paxton, and filmed right at the northern tip of Scotland, the film is a charming mix of surreal comedy, local folklore, rugged landscapes and tender companionship, plus a great deal of seagull action – catching them, eating them, being attacked by them, even pretending to be them.View image in fullscreenGleeson as Ned in The Paper, with (from left) Ramona Young as Nicole, Oscar Nuñez as Oscar Martinez and Alex Edelman as Adam.Photograph: Peacock/SkyAt heart it’s a film about isolation and acceptance, he says. His character is as lonely as the siblings: an awkward, underconfident middle-manager type. He cuts a pretty pathetic figure visually, too: geeky dress sense, feebly unassertive, his hair a mess. “I got a perm for that,” he says. “No one talks about the dedication of an actor any more. I lived with a perm for four or five months after I did that film!” But he wanted to have a “comedic silhouette”, he says. “So the perm made just my head bigger, like a big lollipop sort of thing.”He’s a slightly more dashing middle-manager type in The Paper: the almost naively idealistic editor of a once great Ohio newspaper. The show is a gentle mockumentary sitcom in the mould of co-creator Greg Daniels’ other hits, Parks and Recreation and The Office, but it touches on a serious issue: the decline of local news (the paper in question is an afterthought to the company’s primary business – manufacturing toilet paper). It’s not overtly political, but “making something that is pro-journalism speaks for itself in terms of protecting it and caring about it”, says Gleeson, who considers himself “very much on the left”.As always, Gleeson did his homework. Months before starting, he went and hung out with real journalists on some of Ohio’s surviving daily newspapers, shadowing them, attending editorial meetings, asking questions. It was eye-opening but also depressing. “By the time we were doing press for the first season, this person who I had shadowed a little bit, who was a very well-established journalist, was out of the job,” he says. She’d moved on because she could no longer make a living.View image in fullscreenGleeson in Frank, with Michael Fassbender.Photograph: Cinematic/Alamy“It’s harder than it should be to do good journalism. People don’t want to pay for it, and people who it’s against don’t want it to exist. So you can’t pretend that’s not happening, but the young people I met who were going into it, as well as those who were staying the course and fighting the good fight, I found overwhelmingly inspiring. So it gives me hope, even though maybe not optimism.”It’s a rare thing to interview an actor who actually sympathises with your profession, given how intrusive some of us can be: stalking their socials, ambushing their leisure time or even just asking questions about their lives, like I am now. But he knows the drill. “I’m trying to keep my personal life personal, just to talk about the work.”Having a famous dad may have coloured Gleeson’s stance towards celebrity – even if he was essentially a grownup before Brendan became well known outside Ireland in the late 90s. “He is much more intensely famous,” says Gleeson of his father. Back home, Brendan can no longer walk down the street without being stopped. Domhnall gets a little of that, he says, “but not to the same extent”. He goes into Dublin all the time and it’s usually fine. “I’m quite unusual or individual-looking, but I’m also quite different-looking in lots of things, so sometimes people don’t put them all together, which is great.” The perm drew some attention, though, he admits.View image in fullscreenGleeson with Clémence Poésy, Robbie Coltrane and Mark Williams in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 1.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyHis parents never encouraged or discouraged him, or his three younger brothers, from following in his father’s footsteps. “The only thing: they asked me not to be a standup comedian. Probably just because I wasn’t funny.” He’s not being entirely truthful here. His intention was to write and direct, but one day he agreed to accept an award on his father’s behalf. He was still at school at the time (a state secondary school just outside Dublin). “I was 16 and really shy, but weirdly it was like, ‘I could do that if he needs me to.’” This was going out live on Irish national television. “Right before I went up, they said, ‘You’ve got 30 seconds for your acceptance speech,’ and I had this three-page speech that my dad had written. I was like, ‘I’m not gonna be able to say that in 30 seconds,’ so I went up and sort of vamped, and made fun of it.”It turned out hewasfunny. “I quite liked the buzz of hearing people laugh,” he admits. His father’s agent, Teri Hayden, was watching, and called him in for a meeting.Three years later, in his first year at the Dublin Institute of Technology, he was cast in Martin McDonagh’s IRA black comedy The Lieutenant of Inishmore. That’s when he got hooked on acting: “I didn’t have a thing of, ‘I don’t want to be an actor because of my dad.’ It was just by doing it I went, ‘Idowant to be an actor.’ And the play was in London, so there was a bit of distance from my dad. It wasn’t like doing it in Dublin and feeling him looking over my shoulder the whole time.” Four years later the play transferred to Broadway, where Gleeson received a Tony nomination. His career was up and running.View image in fullscreenFamily affair … Gleeson (centre) with (right) his dad, Brendan, and brother Brian in The Walworth Farce, in Dublin.Photograph: Artur Widak/Nurphoto/ShutterstockHe has worked with his father and his brother Brian, who is also an actor, many times since: in McDonagh’s short film Six Shooter, which won an Oscar in 2006; in the Harry Potter movies (Brendan played Alastor “Mad-Eye” Moody); he and Brian fought to the death in Darren Aronofsky’s Mother! and were best buddies in the 2021 sitcom Frank of Ireland. And all three of them performed on stage together in 2006 in Enda Walsh’s The Walworth Farce.It’s not necessarily a jolly love-in when they work together. “It can be difficult at times, and I’m sure we all drive each other mad, but that happens with everybody you work with.” But then it’s not meant to be fun, he believes. “There’s no point being there to be nice to each other. The point is to change the other person’s performance with your own, the point is to bounce off each other and create sparks.” Not in a negative way, though. “I don’t believe in having a bad time at work. That’s all bullshit: to make good art, you have to have a bad time – fuck all that.”He’s now worked with some of the biggest names in the business – the Coen brothers, Tom Cruise, Leonardo DiCaprio, Jennifer Lawrence, Julianne Moore, Margot Robbie,Taylor Swift– but Gleeson still gets awed by people, he says. “When I met the Coen brothers I found it hard. I bumped into Paul Thomas Anderson at something once and I found that very difficult to keep my shit together.” That was almost the case with Werner Herzog, but luckily, their first meeting was over Zoom, “which is so depersonalising and demythologising, just because it’s all, ‘Sorry, can you hear me?’ There’s nothing fancy about it. After that I felt prepared to meet him.”View image in fullscreenGleeson: ‘You don’t know what the next challenge is going to be.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianGleeson only worked a few days on Bucking Fastard, but it was a memorable experience. Kate and Rooney Mara play twins who do everything together – speaking, living, dressing. They even fall for the same man. Gleeson plays their social worker. Unbelievably, it’s based on a true story. Herzog met the real-life twins, Freda and Greta Chaplin (the title is a spoonerism they both made, in unison, in court). “I think maybe he was interested in making a documentary about them,” says Gleeson. He began to suspect that although his character is Irish, he was based on Herzog himself. “He told me a couple of stories about meeting them and what it was like to be around them, then I realised my character in the film has some similar experiences. One of the scenes is basically something that happened to him, with them.”Herzog, of course, has one of the most famous and highly imitable accents in cinema. Was Gleeson tempted to try it? “When I realised that my character has aspects of him in it, for a second in your mind you’re like, ‘Should I do it?’ Then you’re like, ‘No. Absolutely not. No, no, no.’”What’s next for Gleeson? He doesn’t really know, he says, though he hopes The Paper will get another season. He’s always got stuff in the pipeline, he’s always in demand for all sorts of roles, genres, accents. Not having a “type” has proved to be a professional asset, and it keeps life interesting. “It’s where I’m happiest,” he says, “because you don’t know what the next job is going to be, you don’t know what the next challenge is going to be.”Before he goes, he apologises again for not answering some of the more personal questions I’d asked him, which really isn’t necessary at all. Maybe it’s the other side of the coin of his versatility. We don’t have to know everything about people just because we see them on screen – and often it helps that we don’t.Season two of The Paper launches on Sky and NOW in the UK on 10 September.The Incomer is in cinemas in the UK from 4 September.Explore more on these topicsDomhnall GleesonBrendan GleesonTelevisionHarry PotterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Espionage, true crime and war: Baillie Gifford longlist revealed | Baillie Gifford prize for nonfiction | The Guardian
description: Patrick Radden Keefe, Ben Macintyre and the Guardian’s Charlotte Higgins are among the 13 authors selected for the nonfiction award
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Patrick Radden Keefe, Ben Macintyre and the Guardian’s Charlotte Higgins are among the 13 authors selected for the nonfiction award
Content: The venerable read … the Baillie Gifford prize longlistPhotograph: PRView image in fullscreenThe venerable read … the Baillie Gifford prize longlistPhotograph: PRBaillie Gifford prize for nonfictionEspionage, true crime and war: Baillie Gifford longlist revealedPatrick Radden Keefe, Ben Macintyre and the Guardian’s Charlotte Higgins are among the 13 authors selected for the nonfiction awardEmma LoffhagenThu 3 Sep 2026 00.01 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins joins American investigative journalist Patrick Radden Keefe and bestselling historian Ben Macintyre on this year’s Baillie Gifford prize longlist.Higgins’ book,Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, examines the role of culture in Ukraine’s resistance to Russia’s invasion, drawing on multiple reporting trips to Ukraine. Keefe, who won the prize in 2021 with Empire of Pain, is listed again forLondon Falling, which tells the story of Zac Brettler, a teenager who fell from a luxury London apartment after having posed as the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch. Macintyre’s Redwood: The Untold Story of the Cold War’s Most Extraordinary Spy, tells the story of a KGB double agent cultivated by MI6 in revolutionary Tehran.The 13 books on the longlist, selected from submissions published in English in the UK over the past year, range from biography and ancient history to espionage, true crime and international reportage. The prize is widely regarded as the UK’s most prestigious award for nonfiction.“Chairing this prize is like being part of a very well-informed and opinionated book group,” said lead judge Kirsty Lang. “Whittling our choices down to 13 books led to some forthright discussion, but we got there in the end and are very proud of our longlist.”Quick GuideThe Baillie Gifford prize 2026 longlistShowBaldwin: A Love Storyby Nicholas Boggs (Penguin Random House)Murder in Paris ’68: A True Story of Death and Glamourby Edward Chisholm (Bloomsbury)The Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet (Monoray)The Traveller: The Revolutionary Life of George Forster and his Search for Humanityby Andrea Wulf (Penguin Random House)Alexander: God, King, Man by Edmund Richardson (Atlantic)The Nord Stream Conspiracy: The Inside Story of the Explosions That Shook the Worldby Bojan Pancevski (Penguin Random House)Days of Love and Rage: A Story of Revolution by Anand Gopal (Bloomsbury)Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of Warby Charlotte Higgins (Penguin Random House)Redwood: The Untold Story of the Cold War’s Most Extraordinary Spyby Ben Macintyre (Penguin Random House)London Falling: A Mysterious Death in a Gilded City and a Family’s Search for Truthby Patrick Radden Keefe (Penguin Random House)Hotel Exile: Paris in the Shadow of Warby Jane Rogoyska (Picador)Never Say War: Life Inside Russiaby Åsne Seierstad (Hachette)Stay Alive: Berlin, 1939–1945by Ian Buruma (Atlantic)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Biography is a major theme of this year’s list. InBaldwin: A Love Story, the first major study of James Baldwin in 30 years, Nicholas Boggs examines Baldwin’s relationships and their influence on his writing, drawing on previously unseen material and interviews.The life of another literary figure is explored inThe Great Dictatorby Matthew Sweet. Sweet’s account of the romance novelist Barbara Cartland’s career is set against the backdrop of the changing sexual and social politics of her era. Meanwhile, Andrea Wulf’sThe Travellerexamines the largely forgotten 18th-century explorer George Forster, who joined Captain Cook’s second voyage around the world as a teenager.Contemporary conflicts also loom large. In Days of Love and Rage, Anand Gopal reports from Manbij, Syria, during the revolution, telling the stories of people who helped overthrow a dictatorship. The Bookseller of Kabul author Åsne Seierstad offers an account of contemporary Russia in Never Say War; whileIan Buruma’s Stay Alive: Berlin, 1939–1945examines how ordinary people navigated life under the Nazi regime. Ancient history is represented by Edmund Richardson’s Alexander: God, King, Man, a portrait of Alexander the Great.In The Nord Stream Conspiracy the Wall Street Journal political correspondent Bojan Pancevski probes the sabotage of North Sea gas pipelines. While Murder in Paris ’68 by Edward Chisholm revisits one of French cinema’s most notorious scandals: the murder of actor Alain Delon’s bodyguard, Stefan Marković.Completing this year’s longlist, Jane Rogoyska’sHotel Exiletells the wartime story of the Hôtel Lutetia in Paris which was transformed from a gathering place for refugee artists, activists and intellectuals into the headquarters of Nazi intelligence.The longlist was selected by Lang, Waterstones’s head of books Bea Carvalho, writer and cultural historian Tiffany Jenkins, Spectator literary editor Sam Leith, editor and reporter Ravi Mattu and novelist Elif Shafak.The prize, established as the Samuel Johnson prize in 1999, has been sponsored by Edinburgh-based investment management firm Baillie Gifford since 2016. The company has faced criticism in recent years over its investments in fossil fuels and companies with links to Israel. In 2024, campaign group Fossil Free Books organised boycotts of literary festivals sponsored by the firm, resulting in Baillie Giffordending its partnerships with nine festivals.The winner will receive £50,000, with the shortlist of six announced on 1 October and the winner on 4 November. Last year’s prize waswon by Australian writer Helen Garnerfor How to End a Story: Collected Diaries.Browse all the books on the Baillie Gifford 2025 longlist atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBaillie Gifford prize for nonfictionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ink review – Danny Boyle turns the birth of the Sun into a lurid tabloid frenzy | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival Jack O’Connell is terrific as editor Larry Lamb in James Graham’s tale of Rupert Murdoch, Page 3 and the newspaper that transformed Fleet Street
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Venice film festival Jack O’Connell is terrific as editor Larry Lamb in James Graham’s tale of Rupert Murdoch, Page 3 and the newspaper that transformed Fleet Street
Content: Excellent casting … Jack O'Connell in Ink.Photograph: StudioCanalView image in fullscreenExcellent casting … Jack O'Connell in Ink.Photograph: StudioCanalVenice film festivalReviewInk review – Danny Boyle turns the birth of the Sun into a lurid tabloid frenzyVenice film festivalJack O’Connell is terrific as editor Larry Lamb in James Graham’s tale of Rupert Murdoch, Page 3 and the newspaper that transformed Fleet StreetPeter BradshawWed 2 Sep 2026 19.24 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDanny Boyle presents us with a lurid, violent and thumpingly unsubtle movie full of Dutch angles, cartoony shocks and gargoyle closeups. It’s a chapter in the prehistory of modern media, adapted by James Grahamfrom his 2017 stage play, filled with shame and fear and self-hate. It is in fact the story of the Sun newspaper, and how Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) bought the ailing minor title in the late 60s and hired a tough Yorkshire newspaperman, Larry Lamb, to turn it into a raucous and gleefully vulgar circulation powerhouse.Ink summons up the energy and frenzy of tabloid papers of the era, but also – and not entirely intentionally – how strangely depressing they were. Audiences used to the super-rich anomie of the Roy family from TV’s Succession might find all this very unsexy. This is a world of officer-class Fleet Street execs having expense-account meals at Rules and the Savoy Grill in pinstripe suits, smoking and drinking and impassively writing salary offers on paper napkins and silently passing them across to each other. Meanwhile, the other ranks of journalists and print unions are covered in sweat and ink.Murdoch and Lamb had something to prove: both wanted to take a slap at the establishment club that had until that moment kept them out. Jack O’Connell is excellent casting as Lamb; muscular and pugnacious as a working-class reporter made good. Pearce is less of a panto monster than you might expect; in fact, he is increasingly squeamish and fastidious at the rude ideas that Lamb keeps coming up with for the paper – even if the Page 3 girls were not immediately introduced. It’s a coolly composed performance, though the traditional question of what makes Murdoch tick is incuriously passed over; again, this suffers in comparison with Brian Cox’s Logan Roy in Succession.Claire Foyplays the fictional-composite figure of Jules, a kind of young Marjorie Proops women’s-page editor powerless to stop the coming tide of sexism.Yet this is a film with a story-within-a-story to tell, about a truly horrifying true-crime nightmare (in this way, oddly reminiscent of Akira Kurosawa’s 1963 film High and Low), an event which perhaps deserves a film of its own. In 1969, Muriel McKay (played here by Lucy Russell), the wife of Murdoch executive Alick McKay (Jonathan Hyde), was kidnapped by people who thought she was Murdoch’s wife Anna;it was a chaotic and incompetent abductionthat resulted in the death of Muriel McKay, whose body was never found.View image in fullscreenSomething to prove … Guy Pearce as Rupert Murdoch (left) and Jack O’Connell as Larry Lamb in Ink.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/Netflix/APThe film is perhaps unsure exactly how much prominence to give this horrible affair in the midst of the bleary, knowing and lenient black comedy that governs everything else. Was the McKay kidnapping a terrible karmic judgment on the Murdoch group and the Sun itself, that did so much to promote materialism and celebrity obsession? (The kidnappers were reputedly inspired by Murdoch’s appearance on TV.) Maybe. Boyle’s movie imagines Lamb unrepentantly running sensational stories about the kidnapping – as he never would have dared if the victim was actually Anna Murdoch – on the grounds that a reader might have important information to give the police. And then, after the tragic outcome becomes clear, he rejects guilt and doubles down on Sun-sationalism and introduces Page 3 girls.So was the McKay kidnapping the primal scene of media degradation, the seed that led to Fox News, Trumpism and the social media manosphere? Again, maybe; but perhaps the kidnapping should occupy a more central dramatic position if the film is not to appear cynical and detached in the way that the Sun was accused of being. Either way, it’s a resoundingly tough and confident performance from O’Connell.Ink screened at the Venice film festival; it is in cinemas on 11 December in the US, 7 January in Australia and 8 January in the UKExplore more on these topicsVenice film festivalBiopicsDanny BoyleGuy PearceJack O'ConnellJames GrahamThe SunreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Eyes Wide Shut conspiracy theory: did someone cut a crucial 20 minutes from Kubrick’s final movie? | Film | The Guardian
description: For years some have claimed a key part of the thriller was excised after the director’s sudden death – and that it provided clues to the real-life behaviour of rich predators. Now, his daughter has spoken out
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: For years some have claimed a key part of the thriller was excised after the director’s sudden death – and that it provided clues to the real-life behaviour of rich predators. Now, his daughter has spoken out
Content: Did you see that? Tom Cruise (left) and Stanley Kubrick on the set of Eyes Wide Shut.Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreenDid you see that? Tom Cruise (left) and Stanley Kubrick on the set of Eyes Wide Shut.Photograph: Album/AlamyPass notesFilmThe Eyes Wide Shut conspiracy theory: did someone cut a crucial 20 minutes from Kubrick’s final movie?For years some have claimed a key part of the thriller was excised after the director’s sudden death – and that it provided clues to the real-life behaviour of rich predators. Now, his daughter has spoken outWed 2 Sep 2026 15.58 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.07 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:The Eyes Wide Shut conspiracyAge:The erotic psychological thrillerEyes Wide Shutstarring Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman (married at the time, though that isn’t so important now) was released in 1999.Stanley Kubrick, no?yes. It was the great film-maker’s final movie. He died of a heart attack just days after screening his final cut to Warner Bros. His sudden death is what started it all.Startedall of what?The conspiracies.Oooh, go on.OK, so there are rumours that the studio cut 20 minutes of the film after his death, including an alternative ending.Why would they do that?It was too dark apparently, even by Kubrick’s standards. The theory goes that in Kubrick’s original, Cruise and Kidman’s characters sacrificed their own daughter to a child sexual abuse ring.Perhaps it was a premonition of thePizzagatetheory?Make that Jeffrey Epstein.Seriously?That’s what they say.That’s what who say?There was an episode of Joe Rogan’s podcast a couple of years ago in which the screenwriterRoger Avary saidthe film had been cut.WasAvary involved in the making of the film?No, but on Rogan’s podcast he claimed that “as a student of Kubrick” he noticed parts of the film Kubrick wouldn’t have done himself (scenes the director would have trimmed, a “missing” narration, among other things). So it looked to Avary as if EWS had been cut after Kubrick’s death.And those comments helped fuel the rumours that Kubrick may have known about Epstein’s crimes, or possibly some other cult involving the global elite?Precisely. It doesn’t help that Kubrick was no stranger to conspiracy theories. It’s claimed that hestaged the first moon landingthen alluded to it surreptitiously in The Shining.Of course. Back to EWS though.What do people who actually worked on the film say?Nigel Galt, the movie’s editor,said in an interview last yearthat nothing was cut. And now Vivian Kubrick, Stanley’s daughter, has weighed in.
