She worked with him on several films.And Vivian says?It’sa long X post, including: “I never heard of a missing 20 minutes at the time, I have never subsequently seen or been shown any evidence that such a section existed, and I know of no surviving material that establishes that it did.”That doesn’t completely rule out the possibility, though, does it?She goes on to say: “If indeed 20 minutes had been removed, I definitely would have found out about it eventually.” And she tags @joerogan and adds a whole bunch of hashtags including #EpsteinFiles, #GhislaineMaxwell, #SexTrafficking and #ConspiracyTheory, just to be clear who she’s talking to.Do say:“Hmmm, should I believe family and the editor, or a load of people on Reddit?”Don’t say:“What do you think,Joe Rogan?”Explore more on these topicsFilmPass notesStanley KubrickJoe RoganPodcastsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham faces an impossible job. At least he’s got a secret weapon – Kemi Badenoch | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Labour is up against a Tory party with a leader who can’t stop getting lost in her own sense of brilliance. And then there’s Andrew Griffith
Author: John Crace
Headline: Labour is up against a Tory party with a leader who can’t stop getting lost in her own sense of brilliance. And then there’s Andrew Griffith
Content: Andy Burnham at his first prime minister’s questions in the House of Commons, London, on Wednesday.Photograph: House of Commons/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at his first prime minister’s questions in the House of Commons, London, on Wednesday.Photograph: House of Commons/PAThe politics sketchPMQsAndy Burnham faces an impossible job. At least he’s got a secret weapon – Kemi BadenochJohn CraceLabour is up against a Tory party with a leader who can’t stop getting lost in her own sense of brilliance. And then there’s Andrew GriffithWed 2 Sep 2026 17.17 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTShareCall it the gentlest of all reality checks. A quantum realignment in expectations. The faintest reminder to bothAndy Burnhamand Labour backbenchers that international bond markets are impervious to Manchester charm and positivity. Despite a summer of feelgood announcements from the government, there is no escaping the fact that the country is still up shit creek. It’s going to be a tough ride ahead. Nothing will come pain-free.Still, a new prime minister has to learn to take the wins – however small – as they come along. In the wider scheme of things, a good prime minister’s questions means next to nothing: it’s nothing more than politics as performance. Yet it can set the tone and buy a prime minister some goodwill from MPs and the media. Plus, it’s a weekly event so you may as well be good at it.Burnham can be very pleased withhis first outing, even if it didn’t go totally as billed. We had been promised a more consensual politics. An end to point scoring. That lasted all of five minutes. After that, it was business as usual. Partly because that’s the way PMQs has always been set up, but mainly because Andy just couldn’t help himself.It would have taken a will of iron to resist. Not least becauseKemi Badenochmade it so easy for him. Not for the first time, Labour’s secret weapon is the Tory leader. She just can’t help herself from speaking without thinking, getting lost in her own sense of brilliance and failing to spot the traps she is setting for herself. Still, at least no one can call Kemi boring. Though it is quite hard to see why so many Tories seem to drink her Kool-Aid.You could tell that Burnham was very nervous at the start. Understandably so. Twitchy. Not totally in command. PMQs is always an ordeal and never more so for a leader on whom so manyLabourhopes have been pinned. Some of them Burnham has even pinned on himself.“It’s good to be back at the dispatch box,” he began, before listing some of the Labour government’s achievements. Like the number of small boat crossings being at their lowest for years. The Tories barely looked up. It was almost as if they had never been that bothered about illegal immigration, and they certainly weren’t about to give Labour any credit. Opposition parties hate it when something goes well. There’s nothing that suits them better than a country in crisis. They never seem to realise that one day they might be called upon to sort it out.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch decided she had had enough sweet-talk.Photograph: House of Commons/PAKemi’s opening gambit was flirtatious. Going out of her way to congratulate Andy on his stamina. Burnham merely nodded. A lot of people had said that to him. Then Kemi decided she had had enough sweet-talk. That was Burnham’s problem. Always promising the earth. Never daring to say no to anyone. Too desperate to be loved to be a good leader. So could he mention anything he had ever cut?First the smile, then the reply. “Tax,” Burnham said. This was effectively game over forPMQs. Kemi had imagined a Keir Starmer-like evasion. A prime minister caught out. She had never dreamed of this. Andy spelled it out. He had removed VAT on electricity bills. He had cut business rates for pubs and hospitality venues. He didn’t choose to point out these cuts had been paid for by cutting a budget for digital ID that had never existed. Best to keep it simple.Next Kemi turned to the bond markets. She seemed to think they had it in for Labour. Burnham kept it pleasant and polite. It was like this. The international bond markets didn’t have a special grudge against him. This wasn’t personal. They hadn’t been waiting for Tuesday’s statement, itching to put interest rates up.This was a global problem. Other countries were also facing rising borrowing costs. And if Kemi really wanted to know where the blame lay, she could take a look at her own party’s 14 years of stagnant growth. It was the Tories who had trashed the economy. He was merely trying to pick up the pieces. He could also have blamed the Iran war and the spike in oil prices. A war for which Kemi had been initially enthusiastic. Her judgment is seldom the best.Now Kemi sounded almost hurt. As if a promise had been broken. Burnham had said there would be no more point scoring, and here he was openly point scoring. I know, I know, said Andy unapologetically. He just couldn’t help himself. It was just too tempting. It made him feel good about himself to hear the laughs and support of his own backbenchers. PMQs wasn’t all about him. It was a team sport.So while he was about it, Burnham had plenty more points to score. Kemi has yet to realise just how vulnerable she has made herself by appointing Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor. The man who co-authored Liz Truss’s mini-budget and was one of itsmost outspoken defenders.For Labour this is an open goal and they are going to be kicking the ball into the net as often as possible. Kemi may be a woman who doesn’t believe in history. Who thinks each day is a surprising new beginning. But the country is still a long way from forgiving the Tory party for the lasting damage caused by 49 days of Tory chaos. So the self-harm is going to continue for a while.After failing to rule out further tax rises and spending commitments, Burnham went back to his happy place. Good vibes, hope and positivity. All of which are enough to make this a comfortable first PMQs. But he will be more than aware that this is a half-hour bubble and that life will only get tougher outside it.Though Andy appears to be a sucker for work. He spent the rest of the session offering meetings to virtually every MP. Soon his whole life will be one long meeting. Or a meeting to find out why a meeting was not necessary. Meetings to rule out further meetings. Still, I am sure he will enjoy his meeting with Samantha Niblett, whose stated mission has been to have a summer of sex. And to tell as many people as possible about it.Not everything went Burnham’s way. A disgruntled Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the defence select committee, was extremely grumpy about the3% promise. Or possibly not being asked to be a minister. Still, Andy looked happy enough when the speaker called time. The first PMQs was over and he was 1-0 up. Not that anyone was keeping the score. Much.Explore more on these topicsPMQsThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamKemi BadenochLabourConservativesHouse of CommonscommentShareReuse this content

title: Farewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something more | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: ‘U-turn’ doesn’t do justice to the myriad ways he found to break a pledge. Now the former PM is resigning as an MP, why did I have such high hopes? asks Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: ‘U-turn’ doesn’t do justice to the myriad ways he found to break a pledge. Now the former PM is resigning as an MP, why did I have such high hopes? asks Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Keir Starmer delivers a speech in Gateshead, England, July 2022.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKeir Starmer delivers a speech in Gateshead, England, July 2022.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesOpinionKeir StarmerFarewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something moreZoe Williams‘U-turn’ doesn’t do justice to the myriad ways he found to break a pledge. Now the former PM is resigning as an MP, why did I have such high hopes?Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.02 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTShareKeir Starmer exits the British political stage as he entered it: doing the exact opposite of the thing he said he was going to do. It’s only 10 weeks since hepledged to remainas MP for Holborn and St Pancras until the next election, despite stepping down as prime minister. That’s plainly the decent course of action: a dedicated Labour man wouldn’t want to force a byelection. Even if it’s a slam dunk for the party, it inevitably draws focus and resources from more important matters. Someone who takes the business of representing constituents even a 10th as seriously as all MPs say they do would feel that the honour of those votes should be repaid.It’s a pretty boring life for an ex-PM turned backbencher. You have to keep your counsel as a large amount of blame is tacitly shovelled your way, while keeping your opinions to yourself. But that second requirement was the one thing Starmer was really good at. Once it transpired that the opinions he said out loud were open to endless revision and denial, I was never able to figure out what the real ones were.The Tories are crying U-turn atthis resignation, and technically it is – but the category needs more subdivisions to properly describe all the different ways Starmer found to break a pledge. There were the grand statements with which he came armed when he was initiallyseeking the Labour leadership: economic justice, social justice, climate justice, migrants’ rights, putting human rights at the heart of foreign policy. It would be tedious and a little depressing to track the moment at which each aim was jettisoned. Suffice it to say, these did not describe the politician he was. In fact, to be a Starmerite Version 2020 – Corbyn in a tie, basically – was enough to get you kicked out of the Labour party by 2024, and to vote in favour of policies he had once championed (ending the two-child benefit limit, for instance) was enough tohave the whip suspended. “U-turn” doesn’t really cover a deception so kaleidoscopic.There were specific reversals on policy, of course, forced by backbench rebellion (on welfare) or the first disastrous local election results (winter fuel allowance). But those didn’t feel like Starmer’s decisions so much as his having been backed into a corner. Then there were statements he made that he later claimed not to have meant. In October 2023 hetold Nick Ferrarithat Israel had a right to defend itself – even, when pressed, if that meant cutting off power and water to Gaza – thena few days latersaid: “I was saying Israel had the right to self-defence and when I said ‘that right’, it was that right to self-defence. I was not saying that Israel had the right to cut off water, food, fuel or medicines.” Not really a volte-face, more of a squirm.View image in fullscreenLabour candidate Keir Starmer canvasses in Holborn and St Pancras, London, in April 2015.Photograph: Frantzesco Kangaris/Frantzesco Kangaris for The GuardianStarmer, in short, was bad at politics in so many ways, and in ways that oughtn’t to coexist within the same politician. He wasn’t a communicator, but nor was he a meticulous or far-sighted planner. He had no backbone, and yet was incredibly rigid. He was extremely tribal in his determination to extinguish the left of his party, and yet he didn’t seem to have his own loyal tribe. None of that really matters, since he’s unlikely to trouble parliament again, but it matters what we thought we saw in him, and why.Sorry, scratch that: I have lately come to abhor the journalistic formulation “we made the following mistakes”, which I hope isn’t the start of any deeper self-reflection. These are simply mistakes I made on my own.I always claim to wantLabourto be truly pluralistic; to discuss its project and purpose meaningfully between the constituency and parliamentary levels; to vote at party conference as if it matters, rather than have its values handed to it on the last day in a carefully manicured, ultimately meaningless speech. When it came to it, though, the promise of a candidate who obviated the messiness of pluralism by satisfying every wing just enough was too appealing.There was also an internalised patriarchalism. I dismissed way too readily the voices that said it was ridiculous, in the year 2020, for the party of equality tohave never had a female leader. That absurdity wasn’t really about whether any woman in the party was better suited to the job. It was about a failure, over decades, to reflect on where that preference for a middle-class white guy was actually coming from. What qualities of steadiness, credibility and intelligence was I projecting on to him? What cosplayed status quo-ism was I hoping would be sold to the rest of the voting public?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s funny to be returning to the saying thatGeorge W Bush famously mangledin a very different political age: “Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me”. The Keir Starmer who fought the general election had already fooled his original supporters more times than they could count. It was obvious by the time he had his core team in place, with Morgan McSweeney at their helm, that it wasn’t even technocracy he was promising, it was a Blairite/Mandelsonian project much further to the right of what those politicians were flogging in the 90s. Perhaps I was hoping it was all just a feint to get into power, after which he’d rediscover his radicalism, or perhaps “hope” is just a pretty word for “I would prefer to believe than to participate”. So I’ll go along with Andy Burnham’s “hope in every heart” – it would be churlish not to – but it will be as well as, not instead of, comparing his actions with his promises.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsKeir StarmerOpinionLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Fair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s status
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Fair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s status
Content: Andy Burnham (right) and his chancellor, John Healey, could face an even uglier bond market if they defer hard decisions in the October budget.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham (right) and his chancellor, John Healey, could face an even uglier bond market if they defer hard decisions in the October budget.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesNils Pratley on financeGiltsBurnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budgetNils PratleyFair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s statusWed 2 Sep 2026 18.14 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTShareIt’s too soon to say the bond markets have turned on Andy Burnham. Tuesday’s spike in gilt yields, taking the UK’s 30-year borrowing coststo their highest level since 1998, was part ofan international sell-off of government debt.The main contributors are well known. The Iran war, by increasing the cost of energy, has overturned the comforting start-of-the-year thesis of falling global inflation and interest rates. A plunging Japanese yen has kicked away another assumed source of financial stability. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, hasn’t calmed nerves with his solo, and so far futile,attempt to bring down US yields. Meanwhile, the early stage of the AI revolution is an exercise in issuing squillions of debt before long-term returns on capital can possibly be assessed meaningfully.From the point of view of the mythicalbond vigilante, in these circumstances it’s only logical to demand a higher return to lend to profligate governments with high debt ratios, which is most of them.In a narrow sense, then, UK gilts were just moving with the market at a moment of rising financial risks in all directions. It’s just that the UK was already uncomfortably placed at the cold edge of the pack with the highest borrowing rates in the G7, a status largely reflecting a dismal 20-year record in keeping a lid on inflation and, especially now, a dependency on energy imports that stood at 43% in 2025.It is also true, unfortunately, that six weeks into the job Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, have said nothing to make bond investors rethink the UK’s status. Investors have heard the dutiful commitment to Rachel Reeves’s fiscal rules, but Burnham’s Commons speech on Tuesday carried little sense of urgency about the UK’s financial predicament, or appreciation of how 10-year gilt yields at 5.2% will cause damage if sustained for long.More“public control”of utilities – the theme Burnham constantly returns to – may be desirable and play well on the backbenches. But, even whenthe ambiguous meaningis made clearer, how does it translate into, say, substantially lower costs of building infrastructure? Should it really be a top economic priority?“Markets are sceptical that ‘devolution’ and ‘control’ are levers for lower government-led inflation,” said the Panmure Liberum economist Simon French. “Burnham/Healey’s unenviable task is to prove they are the right levers. If they fail then a very painful period of financial repression/demand side-led disinflation will be necessary.”There is an uncomfortable sense that the bond market expects next month’s budget to be a bigger event than Burnham and Healey will produce. The tone of Burnham’s Commons speech was “the last thing investors wanted to hear”, said the former Goldman Sachs economist Jim O’Neill – quite a verdict from a friendly critic who was being lined up for a role in government until recently.But one can see his point. He told the BBC that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to get real about dealing with the triple lock on the state pension and “excessive” welfare spending. There has been little rolling of the pitch, as they say in Westminster, in either of those directions to date.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt may be, of course, that impressions are mistaken and that next month’s promised 10-year economic plan turns out to be a big exercise in addressing energy costs, defence spending, social care, housing shortages and all the other main challenges. But it is also easy to imagine an alternative script in which hard decisions are deferred and the UK-specific action in the bond market turns uglier – especially if, say, disruption to global energy markets looks likely to last the winter.Labour has spent 2026 defenestrating one leader and anointing another. It needs something to show for it. Burnham speaks of giving businesses and consumers breathing space from the cost of living pressures. That task is easier when the government itself is getting some breathing space from the bond markets. Whatever the chosen mix of spending cuts and tax rises, the budget needs details.Explore more on these topicsGiltsNils Pratley on financeBondsGovernment borrowingEconomicsEconomic policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: Being subservient to the interests of the wealthy now means that his hands are tied, and he will be unable to tackle Britain’s most pressing issues, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: Being subservient to the interests of the wealthy now means that his hands are tied, and he will be unable to tackle Britain’s most pressing issues, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Alamy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Alamy/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donationsGeorge MonbiotBeing subservient to the interests of the wealthy now means that his hands are tied, and he will be unable to tackle Britain’s most pressing issuesWed 2 Sep 2026 06.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.06 BSTShareDamn the electorate. They’reso impatient. No sooner do they get a new leader than they want another one. Those ingrates arealreadystarting to grumble about Andy Burnham. Maybe the country isbecoming ungovernable. Perhapsit’s social media. Or a consumerist culture, always picking the next shiny thing. Perhaps we’readdicted to drama. As we’re on our sixth prime minister in 10 years, and as similar levels of discontent surface in many other countries, these claims are recited across the media. What’s wrong with us?Yet our disgruntlement is entirely rational. We give up so quickly on our prime ministers because they give up so quickly on us. Though it may involve different issues, it is always the same betrayal: the public interest is sacrificed for the sake of a tiny number of immensely wealthy people. And it tends to happen almost immediately.The latest example, which has triggered both fury and grim resignation, isBurnham’s backtrackingon his intention to cap political donations. It was hardly a radical policy: he proposed that no person would be able to give more than £500,000 to a political party in one year. That would still have granted the very wealthy disproportionate influence over our politics. I have long believed that the only fair system is one in which there should beno private donations at allbeyond a standard, fixed membership fee. Otherwise voters will always take second place to money. But at the moment there is no cap, which ensures that billionaires can buy political parties and their platforms. So a £500,000 maximum, pathetic as it is, is at least a start. In asubsequent pledge, Burnham suggested that it could gradually be lowered.Now, we are told, even this high cap has been abandoned: therepresentation of the people billwill concentrate instead on introducing Keir Starmer’s risible proposals, which are intended to limit donations sent from abroad but not from within the UK: as if billionaire donors and their wealth managers have no expertise in transferring money from one account to another. The loopholes are designed in.Burnham’s buckling on this issue is not a small matter. It cuts to the quick of what this country is and how it works. It has immense implications for democracy, for policy formation and for every other aspect of civic life. What it means is that the ultra-rich will continue to own our politics and our country. Succumb to the power of money and you will find yourself, like Starmer, tongue-tied and immobilised, unable to rise to any challenge that requires a confrontation with oligarchic might. In other words, get this wrong andevery other wrong thing follows.The official reason for Burnham’s U-turn is that trade unions objected: they have long channelled large sums into the Labour party. I doubt this is the real explanation; most of the donations Burnham received for his leadership campaigncame from large private donors. Almost half was supplied by Lord Sainsbury, who was also a major funder of the Starmer project. Union money scarcely featured.But even if Burnhamhasretreated from his promise for the sake of the unions, I believe trade union funding is also problematic. It ensures that sectoral interests are elevated above the general interest. For example, Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers. And if the unions believe that an uncapped system works for them, they are deluded. They can never match thespending power of billionaires, whose interests in most cases are diametrically opposed to those of their members.The power of the ultra-rich is now manifest in every policy governments do adopt and the policies they don’t. We see it in the new protest laws and their applications, which become more absurd by the week. Labelling protesters “terrorists” is part of a long-running programme to ensure thatno one dares protest about anythingany more. This programme has beenrolled out across the world, through model legislation drawn up by junktanks funded by some of the richest people on Earth. Just as itdid in the 18th century, an ever more extreme defence of property keeps pace with agrowing concentration of wealth.We see it in the way that datacentres have been labelled “critical national infrastructure”, enabling the government tobypass the usual planning processand impose them on communities, regardless of their impacts onlocal people’s quality of life, on water resources, energy supply and climate breakdown. Again,similar measures are being imposedin other countries at the behest of the same billionaire-funded groups. The role of governments appears to have been reduced to nodding them through.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham accused of U-turn after initially backing political donations cap to fall below £500kRead moreWe see it in the Burnham government’s insistence this summer, in the midst of shattering droughts, heatwaves and fires, onlaunching a consultationthat proposesradically curtailingthe transition to electric vehicles. I believe there is only one possible explanation for this policy: lobbying by corporations and their shareholders. Their interests appear to outweigh those of the living planet and its 8 billion people.If our country and many others are becoming ungovernable, it is not because of the people. It is because the ultra-rich have smashed the system. The electorate and the MPs who might seek to represent us pull the political levers, but nothing happens. They might replace the leader, but the new one promptly repeats the “mistakes” that caused the eviction of the old one. It makes you wonder: what threat do the oligarchs present that outweighs even the threat of losing power?Whatever the reason may be, disillusionment is an inevitable result of such betrayals. I think most people want stability. I think most people want to be able to trust their governments. We don’t like in-built obsolescence in our leaders any more than like it in our phones. I don’t want to see Burnham go the way of Starmer. But I know he will succeed only if he defends the public interest against the power of money. So what’s stopping him?George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionParty fundingKeir StarmerLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: What did I learn in the kitchen this week? The longer it takes to cook, the less you want to eat it | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: After grilling, skinning, chopping and stirring, stirring, stirring, my feelings towards my favourite Balkan relish, ajvar, changed. Those Macedonian nans must be made of girders, writes Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: After grilling, skinning, chopping and stirring, stirring, stirring, my feelings towards my favourite Balkan relish, ajvar, changed. Those Macedonian nans must be made of girders, writes Adrian Chiles
Content: ‘I found the first 10 minutes of the process quite enjoyable. The last hour and 50 minutes, less so.’Photograph: Nataliia Sirobaba/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘I found the first 10 minutes of the process quite enjoyable. The last hour and 50 minutes, less so.’Photograph: Nataliia Sirobaba/AlamyOpinionNorth MacedoniaWhat did I learn in the kitchen this week? The longer it takes to cook, the less you want to eat itAdrian ChilesAfter grilling, skinning, chopping and stirring, stirring, stirring, my feelings towards my favourite Balkan relish, ajvar, changed. Those Macedonian nans must be made of girdersWed 2 Sep 2026 16.46 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.03 BSTShareIf you ever meet someone fromNorth Macedoniaand find yourself short of conversation, then one word will get things going nicely. That word isajvar. Pronounce it “Ivor”, as in The Engine – not quite right but it’ll do. Depending on who you ask, ajvar is a condiment, spread, sauce or relish. It’s made – also depending on who you ask – with red peppers and aubergine. You can eat it with meat, cheese, fish, vegetables, on toast or, using a large spoon, straight from the jar.I was accompanying a 13-year-old called Ilijana as she played the British chess grandmaster Nigel Short. This was on the waterfront in Split, Croatia. Long story. All you need to know is that my contribution to the contest was zero. All I could do was try to bond with her somehow, by finding some area of common ground. So I said the magic word: ajvar! This was the conversational equivalent of a chess move – something with a knight perhaps? – which she didn’t see coming. It worked a treat. Suddenly she was all smiles, telling me how her grandma’s ajvar was the best in the world.Ajvar is a Balkan thing, but it is especially common in North Macedonia due, I assume, to an abundance of red peppers there, ripening nicely even as we spoke. Ilijana was one of a couple of dozen young players taking on Mr Short. As he made his way around the other boards I quizzed her about ratios of peppers to aubergines, the right oil to use, the cooking process and so on. She seemed happier discussing this than trying to answer my daft questions about the rudiments of chess tactics. My dad used to say that in chess you need to be thinking five moves ahead, whereas he was always five moves behind. Same. But on matters concerning ajvar, I was now right up to speed.By the time I got back from Croatia, I was champing at the bit to make some of my own. My junior chess friend suggested 5kg of peppers was about right for a batch. Further research made it clear that only pointy peppers would do. The bloke in the world foods shop in Swansea registered no surprise, or indeed interest, at the quantity I was after. With a kilo of aubergines added to the box, I was in business.Rose’s Lime Marmalade? Gone. Dark chocolate Bounty? No more. But what about their heartbroken fans? | Adrian ChilesRead moreFirst came the charcoal grilling of the vegetables. My neighbours have one of those fancy Egg barbecues which they very kindly got going for me. Aware of the fire risk, I was relieved the rain was steady. It took me about two hours to blacken all the skins. I found the first 10 minutes of the process quite enjoyable. The last hour and 50 minutes, less so. My fingers were singed and all the tong-wielding had my right arm begging for mercy. Those Macedonian nans must be made of girders.Then everything had to be skinned, which took longer than I might have hoped. Then drained overnight. Then chopped up, and cooked down, while slowly adding sunflower oil and salt and stirring, stirring, stirring for three hours or more. During this period, as the molten lava spat blobs of fire at me, my feelings for ajvar went from strong love to something approximating dislike. The longer you cook something, the less you end up wanting to eat it. I cooled it and put it in sterilised jars, marvelling at how a box of peppers I could barely carry had ended up filling only four jars. Exhausted, I went to bed, but all I could see on the inside of my eyelids was a cauldron of seething red stuff.Day three, without relish, I tried my relish. It was quite good, but food and drink from your travels never tastes quite the same at home. I hope to rediscover my love for ajvar soon. I’ve a fair amount to get through.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I was once ashamed to admit I’d been strangled nonconsensually during sex. Now I’m speaking up to save women’s lives | Hannah Ferguson | The Guardian
description: Young men are being taught that acts with the potential to kill are erotic. The Albanese government must urgently regulate big tech and criminalise pornography depicting strangulation
Author: Hannah Ferguson
Headline: Young men are being taught that acts with the potential to kill are erotic. The Albanese government must urgently regulate big tech and criminalise pornography depicting strangulation
Content: ‘For a long time, I was embarrassed to admit that while I intellectually knew something wasn’t right, I still failed to call it out in a moment of uncertainty,’ writes Hannah Ferguson of her experience of sexual choking.Photograph: Liz Ham/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘For a long time, I was embarrassed to admit that while I intellectually knew something wasn’t right, I still failed to call it out in a moment of uncertainty,’ writes Hannah Ferguson of her experience of sexual choking.Photograph: Liz Ham/The GuardianOpinionSexual consentI was once ashamed to admit I’d been strangled nonconsensually during sex. Now I’m speaking up to save women’s livesHannah FergusonYoung men are being taught that acts with the potential to kill are erotic. The Albanese government must urgently regulate big tech and criminalise pornography depicting strangulationWed 2 Sep 2026 16.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 16.01 BSTShareLast week, a 16-year-old girl was found unresponsive in a home on Sydney’s northern beaches. She was airlifted to hospital and died two days later. New South Wales policeare investigating her deathas the result of a sexual strangulation act.Sources told the ABCthe deceased may have experienced a seizure following asphyxiation, and that officers were told the sex was consensual.While that investigation has yet to run its course, speaking generally, strangulation during sex is not a new phenomenon or conversation. Just a few years ago it was relatively taboo to criticise this normalisation of violence in sex – it was often framed as “anti-kink” to raise concern about this dangerous act that is increasingly depicted in mainstream pornography.In 2024, Australian research affirmed the prevalence of sexual strangulation. TheArchives of Sexual Behaviour published datarevealing that 57% of Australians aged 18 to 35 had been strangled at least once during sex, and 51% said they had strangled a sexual partner.Choking is sold to teens as a safe sexual practice. The research says it never isRead moreNot only are reports of this act increasing, so are the reports of health impacts. Denele Crozier, the CEO of Women’s Health NSW, stated that since 2023 there had been a123% increasein women presenting with concerns of a possible brain injury linked to strangulation.I was previously ashamed to share my own experiences of being strangled during sex nonconsensually. Despite being an outspoken, progressive woman, I froze up and dissociated. Afterwards, I remember questioning whether my response was one of being in shock and afraid for my safety, or if I felt “prudish” if I spoke up and as if I’d be ruining the mood. For a long time, I was embarrassed to admit that while I intellectually knew something wasn’t right, I still failed to call it out in a moment of uncertainty.That is exactly the concern I have for so many women who may be experiencing sexual strangulation. Affirmative consent is incredibly hard to achieve in these contexts; sexual strangulation is now commonplace and we are not equipped with the sophisticated sex education to match.In 2022, consent advocateChanel Contos wrote about this:“Another US study found that 58% of female college students have been choked during sex, further suggesting that this ‘kink’ is becoming increasingly common in younger age demographics. This study found that while many women enjoyed choking, others did it largely to please their sexual partner. This is the real kicker. The problem here is not only that women are being choked during sex without giving consent, but that a lot of the time they are ‘consenting’ not because they derive their own sexual pleasure from it, but because they think it turns the guy on.”Violence against women and girls has been normalised to such an extent that pornography is convincing us it is normal to be strangled during intimacy, and that we are supposed to like it. I appreciate that messages from leaders like “talk to your kids” are made in good faith, but conversation cannot combat the nature and influence of sex content depicting violence as a standard part of sexual intercourse. We are teaching young men that perpetrating violent acts that have the potential to kill are erotic, and we are teaching women to endure having their lives threatened under the guise of pleasure.There are people who engage with control of breath as part of particular kinks, but even in acknowledging these consensual engagements, it is important to reiterate thatthere is no safe way to engage in strangulation.In response to this expanding dialogue, the social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, has shown her support for Australia to adopt legislation that was introduced to the UK in 2025, making it a criminal offence to possess or publish pornography depicting suffocation or strangulation. I want to add my voice to the many calling for the Albanese government to legislate this imminently.A 16-year-old girl has died from suspected sexual choking. How do we come to terms with this? | Lucy ClarkRead moreThe government is also, rightly, considering a second significant piece of reform proposed by Contos and her organisation Teach Us Consent. Contos has been campaigning for the government’s digital duty of care legislative drafting to adopt their“Fix Our Feeds”pitch, regulating big tech companies to ensure algorithms are an opt-in feature. This would introduce a consent-based model that allows users to have more control over the information these platforms are serving us, reducing the extremist material that so many are exposed to.Our government has established that they are willing to take on the regulation of big tech. Australia was the first country in the world to legislate a social media ban for under-16s. We know we have the capability; now it’s time to introduce something that would actually be effective – and give power back to individual users.These would be two significant steps from the government, after last week’s national cabinet meeting where the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, discussed violence against women and children with state and territory leaders. The subsequent announcements of frameworks and reviews were weak. We need politicians to meet the moment. The safety of women and girls depends on tangible action, now.Hannah Ferguson is the chief executive officer of Cheek Media Co and isrunning as an independent candidate in the federal seat of GrayndlerExplore more on these topicsSexual consentOpinionPornographySexYoung peopleSexualitycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Kemi Badenoch and the economy: a plan stuck in the Tory comfort zone  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election
Content: Kemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons on 1 September.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons on 1 September.Photograph: House of CommonsOpinionConservativesThe Guardian view on Kemi Badenoch and the economy: a plan stuck in the Tory comfort zoneEditorialThe Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last electionWed 2 Sep 2026 18.29 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.08 BSTShareTo outlast a prime minister always counts as some kind of achievement for an opposition leader, although Kemi Badenoch cannot claim credit for Sir Keir Starmer’sdownfall. Sir Keir’s wounds were mostly self-inflicted. To the extent that opposition pressure was involved, it waselectoral threatsfrom Reform UK and the Green party that stoked Labour party frustration to a regicidal pitch. The Tory leader’s role was largely as a spectator.Mrs Badenoch still hopes to use regime change to her advantage. She thinks the economy, and fiscal discipline in particular, will be her most fruitful line of attack. In their first confrontation atprime minister’s questionson Wednesday, the Conservative leader called Mr Burnham a “spendthrift” and “people pleaser” who will dodge the tough decisions required to prove Britain’s creditworthiness on international markets. She expects him to yield to Labour MPs’ demands for budget increases, which will then have to be financed with tax rises.View image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersIn that scenario, Mrs Badenoch imagines a vacancy for a rehabilitated small-state Conservative party offering hard-headed budget management, less profligate than Labour; more sober and respectable than Reform UK. That message would unite what remains of her depleted party. She can’t compete with Nigel Farage on the terrain of anti-immigrant rhetoric (although that doesn’t stop heraping his stances). She shows no interest in finding political accommodation for socially liberal, pro-European one-nation Tories who now have more in common with the Liberal Democrats than the modern Conservative party.This leaves the Tories with a narrow focus on tax cuts, reining in welfare spending and deregulation as a spur to enterprise. Mr Farage supports those things too, but Mrs Badenoch believes that Reform UK’s maverick style and the whiff of impropriety around its financial dealings make it an unreliable vehicle for a classically Thatcherite agenda that belongs, by rights, to Lady Thatcher’s own party.The claim to be the truekeeper of the Thatcherite flamehas become a ritual for Tory leaders. The mantle has passed through so many hands, it is threadbare as a political definition in 2026. It was worn most preposterously by Liz Truss, who posted photos of herself on social media recreating iconic images of the Iron Lady in her pomp. She then detonated her government with a “mini-budget” that was a crass pastiche of the economic ideas she claimed to venerate – a wild foray into fiscal irresponsibility masquerading as free-market radicalism.One of the Treasury ministers who enthusiastically endorsed Ms Truss’s plan, Andrew Griffith, wasthis week appointedMrs Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor. He replaces Mel Stride, a lower-octane performer who was deemed not to have made sufficient impact in the role. It is a revealing choice that undermines the Tory leader’s plan to make economic competence the centrepiece of her pitch to lead the nation. When considering a potential chancellor, she clearly values the ability to grab attention over economic judgment.This is consistent with a pattern of failure to engage with the full spectrum of failures over many years that accounts for the scale of Tory defeat at the last election. What Mrs Badenoch imagines to be a political strategy looks more like retreat to an ideological comfort zone in the hope that a second prime minister will self-destruct while she watches from the sidelines.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Israeli settlements: Britain can no longer look away | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: International law, European action and UK public opinion point the same way. Britain should stop helping to sustain Israeli settlements economically
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: International law, European action and UK public opinion point the same way. Britain should stop helping to sustain Israeli settlements economically
Content: An Israeli settler attacks a leftwing activist in the Israeli-occupied Palestinian village of Jannatah.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn Israeli settler attacks a leftwing activist in the Israeli-occupied Palestinian village of Jannatah.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionIsraelThe Guardian view on Israeli settlements: Britain can no longer look awayEditorialInternational law, European action and UK public opinion point the same way. Britain should stop helping to sustain Israeli settlements economicallyWed 2 Sep 2026 18.29 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.07 BSTShareIn the Commons this week, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, appeared to have accepted the principle of a trade ban between the UK and Israeli settlements, which Britain says are illegal under international law. This is long overdue. The test now is whether his promised “comprehensive reset” deserves the name. Stopping settlement-produced goods at the border is not enough. Britain should prohibit its companies fromsustainingsettlement activity – by financing, constructing, insuring, advertising – in territory whose occupation it regards as unlawful. The ban must have teeth.The UK can no longer ignore theviolence and pressureexerted on Palestinians in the West Bank by Israel’s government, military and settlers. There have been more than 1,400 settler attacks so far this year, according to the UN, against a record 1,800 registered in 2025. An election campaign has only made matters worse. Last month, Israel issued tenders for1,234 homes in the 3,401-unit E1 development east of Jerusalem. The country’s ministers gave the green light for the controversial settlement – long condemned for effectively bisecting the West Bank – expressly to “erase” the idea of a Palestinian state, the creation of which the UK officially supports.Israeli ministers havereactedwith fury, threatening retaliation if Britain imposes sanctions over settlement expansion. This is disappointing, but hardly surprising. Benjamin Netanyahu has accused countries imposing sanctions of “moral bankruptcy”. Yet Britain would be following several comparableEuropeanstates that increasingly regard such bans as a consequence of international law. Spain has banned settlement imports; Norway is legislating against trade and services linked to settlements; nine EU governments have demanded action from Brussels.View image in fullscreenEd MilibandPhotograph: Ian Davidson/SOPA Images/ShutterstockSince 1967, Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jewish people among 3.3 million Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem. There are now calls tosuspendthe EU’s trade agreement with Israel. Britain has such adealand, under Sir Keir Starmer, Labourwantedto “distinguish and protect trade with people and businesses across the state of Israel”. This gave critics reason to warn that targeting settlements could end up as a “de facto” boycott of Israel. But that gets the argument backwards: Israel cannot make the settlements part of its economy and then argue that other nations must treat them as part of the country.Mr Miliband has political room to manoeuvre. Pollingsuggeststhat even Reform UK and Conservative voters are more likely to support than oppose a settlement trade ban. In parliament there wasagreementstretching from the Greens to Labour to Tory MPs that something has to be done.Settlement expansion accelerated after Mr Netanyahu’s far-right coalition took power in 2022 and then again after Hamas’s murderous attack sparked the Gaza war in 2023. The legal case is clear: other nations are acting and the political space is opening up – all while creeping annexation becomes a reality. Israel isextendingcivilian control over occupied territory as settlements expand. Gaza, where more than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed, has understandably commanded the world’s attention. No one disputes that Israel exists in a violent and unstable neighbourhood, though its actions aggravate, rather than alleviate, that instability. But the West Bank and Jerusalem cannot be ignored. Security cannot justify an ideological land grab.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: An autism or ADHD diagnosis without access to treatment is a hollow outcome | Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder | The Guardian
description: Letters: Helen Macdonald responds to a report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsman
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Helen Macdonald responds to a report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsman
Content: ‘Too many people with ADHD and autism receive a diagnosis only to find there is no evidence-based treatment pathway attached to it.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Too many people with ADHD and autism receive a diagnosis only to find there is no evidence-based treatment pathway attached to it.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderLettersAn autism or ADHD diagnosis without access to treatment is a hollow outcomeHelen Macdonaldresponds to a report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsmanWed 2 Sep 2026 18.03 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTShareThe parliamentary and health service ombudsman’s findings are stark and sadly familiar (Autism and ADHD care complaints more than triple in five years in England, 26 August). A more than 200% rise in complaints, years-long waits, patients paying thousands of pounds for private care when the NHS fails them, and a system so complex that people are routinely denied rights they are legally entitled to – these are exactly the issues that the British Association for Behavioural and Cognitive Psychotherapies (BABCP) has been documenting and raising for years.What the ombudsman’s report does not fully address is what happens once people are assessed and diagnosed. Too many people with ADHD and autism receive a diagnosis only to find that there is no evidence-based treatment pathway attached to it. Cognitive behavioural therapy is recommended by the National Institute forHealthand Care Excellence for the anxiety and depression that commonly accompany neurodevelopmental conditions, and in specific contexts for adults with ADHD itself. Yet workforce shortages mean that even where the clinical will exists, the capacity often does not. A diagnosis without access to appropriate treatment is a hollow outcome.A final report by the clinical psychologist Prof Peter Fonagy is expected soon and will inform a new national approach. It must go beyond assessment waiting times and address the full pathway, from recognition to diagnosis, treatment and ongoing support. Closing the regulatory gap that the ombudsman identifies is important. Equally important is ensuring that the services people eventually reach are staffed by clinicians with the specialist training to deliver the care that neurodivergent people need.Helen MacdonaldSenior clinical adviser,BABCPHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Andy Burnham must face down unions over donation cap | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Letters: It is no use promising to reform politics and return power to the people without addressing the power of the big beasts, writes Paul Sawbridge. Plus letters from Marcus Hallside and Martin Knott
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: It is no use promising to reform politics and return power to the people without addressing the power of the big beasts, writes Paul Sawbridge.  Plus letters from Marcus Hallside and Martin Knott
Content: ‘It is no use promising to return power to the people and then refuse to address the power of the big beasts of the politics of yesteryear.’Photograph: Andrzej Rostek/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It is no use promising to return power to the people and then refuse to address the power of the big beasts of the politics of yesteryear.’Photograph: Andrzej Rostek/AlamyParty fundingLettersAndy Burnham must face down unions over donation capIt is no use promising to reform politics and return power to the people without addressing the power of the big beasts, writesPaul Sawbridge.Plus letters fromMarcus HallsideandMartin KnottWed 2 Sep 2026 18.04 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTShareSo much for a new way of doing politics. Even before parliament had convened under his premiership, Andy Burnham had already stumbled at the first hurdle (Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donors, 26 August).Despite widespread support for hard caps to political donations, and despite years of affirming support for such measures, a whisper of opposition from the union lobby has produced a screeching U-turn.It is no use promising to return power to the people via devolution, employee ownership and so on, and then refusing to address the power of the big beasts of the politics of yesteryear. Come on, Andy! If you are to make any impact on reversing the appalling effects of Thatcherite neoliberalism, you are going to need to show more bottle than this. You should immediately supportStella Creasy’s amendment– and throw in a commitment to a national commission on electoral reform.Paul SawbridgeEaling, LondonThe GMB union’s opposition to a cap on political donations raises a question that goes beyond the immediate dispute: when does legitimate defence of an organisation’s interests become defence of a political system that gives that organisation disproportionate influence?Trade unionshave a legitimate role in politics. But political finance should ultimately be governed by the democratic interests of citizens, not those of organisations. The same principle must apply to wealthy individuals and corporations.There is a troubling historical precedent. In the 2010 Labour leadership election, the GMB was one of the unions that backed Ed Miliband against his brother, David. David led decisively among Labour MPs and party members, but Ed won overwhelmingly in the union section and ultimately became leaderby just 50.65% to 49.35%. The unions did not single-handedly determine that result, but their mobilisation was crucial. It is therefore reasonable to ask whether the GMB has reflected on the consequences of using its organisational power to influence Labour’s political direction.Ed Miliband’s leadership was followed by Labour’s defeat in 2015, the return of Conservative government and years of austerity. His defeat also formed part of the political sequence that culminated in the Brexit referendum. To say the unions “caused” these outcomes would be simplistic. But to pretend that their intervention had no consequences would be equally misleading.The GMB argues that a cap on donations could damage Labour’s ability to raise funds from affiliated organisations. That is institutional self-interest. But it should not be confused with the national interest. Britain needs political finance rules that reduce the influence of money and organised interests, whoever they are.Marcus HallsideRadlett, HertfordshireI am in favour of both empowering unions and capping donations. The objectives of union donors are widely different to those of the mega-rich donors. While the latter seek self-enrichment, the unions’ only aim is to enable a society where workers’ rights are upheld and a fair wage is earned, and to increase employment rates. This fits perfectly with the aims of the Labour party: to support everyday working people and provide for those who cannot work. So I say: cap at around £1m to enable unions to donate and to curb the excessive influence of the mega-rich.Martin KnottEdinburghHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Banning nuts from the skies would not keep people with allergies safe | Allergies | The Guardian
description: Letter: Alison Smith says food bans do not improve compliance, they create a false sense of security in patients
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Alison Smith says food bans do not improve compliance, they create a false sense of security in patients
Content: ‘Last summer I spent six hours compulsively cleaning on a demonstrably filthy flight.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Last summer I spent six hours compulsively cleaning on a demonstrably filthy flight.’Photograph: AlamyAllergiesLettersBanning nuts from the skies would not keep people with allergies safeAlison Smithsays food bans do not improve compliance, they create a false sense of security in patientsWed 2 Sep 2026 18.03 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTShareAs the mother of a child with anaphylactic allergies, I am sympathetic to the terror that Lucy Pasha-Robinson describes (Food allergies when flying are no joke. That’s why nuts should be banned on planes, 27 August). Indeed, last summer I spent six hours compulsively cleaning on a demonstrably filthy flight. Flight crew handed out wipes to passengers “to clean your tray tables”, then proceeded to serve packets of cashews (my child’s anaphylactic nut) with drinks. My nerves were shredded by the time we arrived in Chicago.However, I am firmly against the banning of nuts from the skies.Foodbans do not improve compliance, and they create a false sense of security in patients.Because my son’s most severe anaphylactic allergy is not nuts but lentils (which, like peanuts, can be airborne and serious from the tiniest quantities), we have had to learn to live with risk. Time and again, I note his allergies on intake forms, only to be blithely reassured that “we are a nut-free setting”, as if that constituted a proper allergy-protection policy. Instead, I am the helicopter parent boarding flights early with gloves and wipes, deep cleaning our entire row before we sit down.My son knows not to accept food from others and to touch nothing on board until I give the all-clear; we pack meals, pillows and blankets for every flight; brief every flight crew on his allergies and the location of our EpiPens; and, from the age of three, practised administering Epi at least once a month. We will never travel fear-free, but we feel the fear and travel anyway.Alison SmithWorcester Park, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Don’t shy away from the language of loss | Death and dying | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: Words of condolence | Autumn versus winter | More fitting names
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Words of condolence | Autumn versus winter | More fitting names
Content: Daffodils in churchyard at Holt in Norfolk.Photograph: David Burton/AlamyView image in fullscreenDaffodils in churchyard at Holt in Norfolk.Photograph: David Burton/AlamyBrief lettersDeath and dyingLettersDon’t shy away from the language of lossWords of condolence | Autumn versus winter | More fitting namesWed 2 Sep 2026 18.03 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTSharePolly Hudson writes about how people don’t know what to say to the bereaved (26 August). Trust me, the bereaved don’t either. My parents died in a car crash. I watched people sheer away in absolute mind-numbing embarrassment, not because they didn’t care, but because they were afraid they would make it worse. Well, you can’t make it worse, trust me. And we’re not looking for poetry. A simple “I’m sorry for your loss” is perfect.Isobel CassidyArdtrasna, County Sligo, IrelandIt seems appropriate to write about grief following a bereavement to thank the fellow Guardian letter writers who have contacted me via the letters editor. Their kind words have really helped me over the last few weeks, and are read and reread on a regular basis.Ian GrieveGordon Bennett, Llangollen canalMy husband, Bob, who died in 2017 from motor neurone disease 20 months after diagnosis, said he found that people who asked “How are you today?” were aware that some days are less shit than others.Helen KeatsBrighstone, Isle of WightAutumn is a wonderful season, but it’s even better in the bleak midwinter (Letters, 31 August).Andrew CarrollCastletimon, County Wicklow, IrelandI used to resist the temptation to read any letter about nominative determinism. Now I just give in.Peter CaveIlkeston, DerbyshireIs it not time to stop this correspondence?Roger BrakeShaftesbury, DorsetHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Premier League transfer talking points: three things we learned from the data | Premier League | The Guardian
description: After record spending in the transfer market, England’s top clubs have widened the gap to their European counterparts
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: After record spending in the transfer market, England’s top clubs have widened the gap to their European counterparts
Content: Clockwise from top left: Elliot Anderson, Bradley Barcola, Ezri Konsa, Johan Manzambi.Composite: GettyView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: Elliot Anderson, Bradley Barcola, Ezri Konsa, Johan Manzambi.Composite: GettyPremier LeagueAnalysisPremier League transfer talking points: three things we learned from the dataAndrew BeasleyAfter record spending in the transfer market, England’s top clubs have widened the gap to their European counterpartsWed 2 Sep 2026 16.29 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePremier League clubs have invested more than £3.4bn in players this summer, an increase of 11.9% on last year. There are three aspects of this enormous spending worthy of closer scrutiny.Priorities on player age have changedPremier League clubs are spending less on players in the peak 24-27 age band even though those players are increasingly the core of their selections.As recently as 2021-22, 40% of minutes were taken by players at least 28 years old at the start of the season. That proportion has dropped each year, reaching 26.6% in 2025-26. The reliance on veterans has declined. The bulk of their lost minutes went to players aged between 24 and 27, which is now the dominant age band.Chart showing percentage of Premier League minutes played by different age ranges since 2021-22The spend on that key demographic has fallen by 23% since last summer though. Without Manchester Citysigning the 25-year-old Enzo Fernández for a British transfer record-equalling £125mshortly before the window closed, the drop would have been even greater.Younger players account for some of the shortfall but a surprisingly high slice of it has gone towards older footballers. The Premier League has invested £323.3m in players aged at least 28, only around £50m shy of the outlay on this age range in the previous three summers combined (£370.5m). Their proportion of the total has not been as high for four years.Chart showing percentage of Premier League summer transfer spend by different age ranges since 2022How much this increased spending on veterans affects the playing time figures depends in part on the selection decisions of Mikel Arteta. Arsenal signed two 28-year-olds for a combined £126m:Bruno Guimarães (£75m)andEzri Konsa (£51m). Transfermarkt considers them to be the most expensive central midfielder and centre-back respectively aged over 27 in history.The three most expensive Premier League signings of the summer before Fernández – Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson and Bradley Barcola – were 23 when their deals were completed. With only slightly less spent collectively on footballers who are 22, clubs have gone hard for players on the verge of entering their peak years rather than those in them.Chart showing Premier League summer spending by player age in 2025 and 2026The Premier League is becoming a closed shopPerhaps the most notable aspect of transfer spending this summer is how much of it has remained within English football. Fourteen of the 19 signings that cost Premier League clubs at least £50m were made from within the division or from relegated West Ham. Where 30.2% of spending remained in the Premier League in summer 2022, the figure hit 39.3% this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTransfer window verdict: how every Premier League club faredRead moreWith the combined outlay growing by almost £1.5bn in that period, what appears a relatively small percentage shift becomes a significant figure in the accounts. The squad cost ratio rules are unlikely to stem this flow either, because clubs will be happy to sell for inflated fees that can almost only come from within the division.Barcola was the oldest of the five costliest signings from overseas, with Matias Fernandez-Pardo and Jérémy Jacquet (aged 21), Johan Manzambi (aged 20) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (aged 18) completing the set. The Premier League is able to retain its top stars, its clubs exchanging them among themselves, while having the funds to hoover up the most exciting young talent from elsewhere.Squad-building trends may be evolving in the Premier League, but the money is here and a significant portion of it is not going anywhere else. English football is starting to become an enclosed ecosystem.The rest of Europe cannot keep upVery few clubs across Europe come close to competing financially. The Premier League features a match this weekend between the top two teams in Europe for net spend and it isn’t Arsenal v Chelsea. Liverpool’s trip to Ipswich takes the honour.The promoted sides have invested enormous sums to try to be competitive. They have all played League One football within the previous eight seasons, yet Real Madrid are the only club from another country with a higher net spend than Hull or Coventry.Chart showing the top 10 clubs for net spend in summer 2026. Nine of them are from the Premier LeagueThe cream of the Premier League crop can probably only move within England. The transfer fee for Rogers (£117m) or Anderson (£116m) was above the net spend of 75 of the 76 top-flight clubs in France, Germany, Italy and Spain. Milan narrowly spent more than the cost of Sandro Tonali (£92.5m) net, but no other side beyond Madrid from mainland Europe did. Most non-English sides would have to have a clearout of talent to raise funds for a single elite player from the Premier League, which isn’t practical.This financial dominance can be seen in continental competitions. Five English clubs have featured in the past eight Champions League finals, as many teams as the rest of Europe has provided in that time. The Premier League has supplied three of the past four Europa League finalists and three of the past four Conference League winners. This is unlikely to change when relegation favourites in England can outspend all but the very richest clubs overseas.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTransfer windowanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Maro Itoje ready to ‘come back better’ for England after taking mini sabbatical | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: Maro Itoje, who sat out England’s Nations Championship games in July, is healthy and mentally rested after a rare full pre-season with Saracens
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Maro Itoje, who sat out England’s Nations Championship games in July, is healthy and mentally rested after a rare full pre-season with Saracens
Content: Maro Itoje is now feeling the benefits of ‘taking a breath’ after an intense year on and off the field.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMaro Itoje is now feeling the benefits of ‘taking a breath’ after an intense year on and off the field.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianRugby unionMaro Itoje ready to ‘come back better’ for England after taking mini sabbaticalItoje rested for Nations Championship games in JulyCaptain has had a rare full pre-season with SaracensRobert KitsonWed 2 Sep 2026 17.00 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaro Itoje says it felt “very weird” watching England play from afar this summer but he believes more top players should consider taking a break to prolong their careers. The British & Irish Lions captain was rested for his country’s three Nations Championship games in July and is now feeling the benefits of “taking a breath” after an intense year on and off the field.In addition to the burden of leadership for club and country, Itoje also lost his mother last year and, with the 2027 World Cup looming, the national coach, Steve Borthwick, offered his captain the chance of a mini-sabbatical. He has emerged fit, healthy and mentally rested for the season ahead having enjoyed his first full club pre-season atSaracenssince 2014.Lawrence and Daly lose England central contracts as Borthwick looks to World CupRead more“I don’t regret it at all,” Itoje said at the Prem media launch at Twickenham. “In some respects it was a little bit weird being away from the team, especially whilst games were going on. But at the same time I felt like it was the right thing to do. Mentally it was a busy year, both personally and professionally, so it was nice to have a bit of time to take a breath.”Coincidentally, Itoje bumped into the England squad at Heathrow airport on the day they were returning from theSouth African leg of their tourbut otherwise he did his best to keep his distance, even choosing not to watch the games live to avoid getting too emotionally involved. “When you watch a game live, you’re in every nook and cranny, every tackle. But that also probably has a hidden emotional kind of weight. I felt it would have defeated the purpose of what I was trying to achieve.”Itoje, who turns 32 next month, would certainly recommend a break to other leading players as and when the chance arises, with South Africa and New Zealand having long since pursued a policy of allowing their top stars to sign contracts in Japan. “It is very much case by case but I think that, for players who have the blessing to be at the top of the game for a period of time, a proactive approach like this one works.“I was taken aback initially because it just never entered my mind. It was never something that I thought was an option … I kind of had it in my mind that ‘this is the way the cookie crumbles’ and you just have to power through. [But] the more I thought about it, the more I kind of agreed with it. If I was not going to do it then I’m not sure when the next window would have been.”View image in fullscreenMaro Itoje kept his distance during his break, even choosing not to watch England games live to avoid getting too emotionally involved.Photograph: Dan Mullan/The RFU Collection/Getty ImagesThe next challenge is to hit the ground running when the Prem season kicks off this month before a busy November. England are scheduled to play four Tests on successive weekends, starting with a game against Australia on 8 November, and a refreshed Itoje will be keen to make an immediate impact.“I hope the break is giving me what’s necessary for me to come back better. Since I’ve been involved with England, I’ve pretty much been involved in every campaign. Saracens for a large period of that time were the top team in Europe, so we’re going deep into Europe and deep in the Premiership. And that has also helped with Lions tours and selections.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’ve been very fortunate to have had what I’ve had but the cost of that, I guess, is that you don’t tend to have a break. Apart from missing training today, I’ve had a full pre-season [with Saracens] to work on myself and my body and be around the team, and I think that’s been a good thing.”Itoje will soon have added responsibilities on his plate with his wife, Mimi, who is pregnant with the couple’s first child – but on the England front he says he was encouraged by what he saw towards the end of England’s summer Tests under the leadership of his Saracens teammate Jamie George. “I was delighted with the last two results,” he said.“Obviously theFiji game was a big winand in the Argentina game they showed a lot of character away from home. The challenge and opportunity for us now is to build on that to go forward.”Explore more on these topicsRugby unionMaro ItojeEngland rugby union teamPrem RugbySaracensnewsShareReuse this content

Content: Jacques Ekomié wheels away in delight after scoring Wrexham’s third goal at Millwall.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJacques Ekomié wheels away in delight after scoring Wrexham’s third goal at Millwall.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesChampionshipChampionship roundup: Wrexham rout Millwall to seal first league victoryKieffer Moore and Jacques Ekomié score in 3-0 winQPR beat Cardiff; Middlesbrough draw at BurnleyAgence France-PresseWed 2 Sep 2026 23.10 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 00.19 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWrexhampowered to their firstChampionshipwin this season with a ruthless 3-0 rout of injury-plaguedMillwallon Wednesday.The Welsh side had drawn with Cardiff and Watford before losing at home to Birmingham prior to this match. title: Walsh caps Champions League progress for Chelsea despite Real Sociedad grind | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Keira Walsh scored at a corner to earn Chelsea a 1-0 win against Real Sociedad in San Sebastián and settle a hard-fought tie
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Keira Walsh scored at a corner to earn Chelsea a 1-0 win against Real Sociedad in San Sebastián and settle a hard-fought tie
Content: Chelsea celebrate after Keira Walsh scores the only goal of the game.Photograph: Gari Garaialde/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChelsea celebrate after Keira Walsh scores the only goal of the game.Photograph: Gari Garaialde/Getty ImagesWomen's Champions LeagueWalsh caps Champions League progress for Chelsea despite Real Sociedad grindReal Sociedad 0-1 Chelsea (agg 2-6)Keira Walsh scores at corner to settle tieSuzanne WrackWed 2 Sep 2026 20.54 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChelsea ensured there will be three Women’s Super League teams in the league phase of the Champions League as Keira Walsh’s second-half strike against Real Sociedad extended their three-goal margin from the first leg of the third-round qualifier.The5-2 winagainst the Spanish side in Chelsea’s first game at Wimbledon’s Cherry Red Records stadium gave Sonia Bompastor’s side a commanding lead in the tie, after a rusty start had forced them to come from a goal down. It wasn’t a particularly pretty performance, though, and that continued into the second leg againstLa Real, who will now drop into the Europa League.Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 6: ChelseaRead moreBompastor, who returned to the dugout after serving a one-match ban in the reverse game, made four changes for the trip to San Sebastián, probably with one eye on the WSL opener on Saturday against Aston Villa. The scorer of Chelsea’s second last week, Veerle Buurman, was named on the bench, alongside Katie McCabe, Sjoeke Nüsken and Alyssa Thompson. Among those to come in was the 20-year-old midfielder Lexi Potter, who scored in her first league start for Chelsea, a 2-1 win against Brighton, in March.There were only two changes for the home team. The change that mattered most, though, was the one that had taken place in the ­dugout. In between these two critical ­Champions League qualifying games, Arturo Ruiz, the Real Sociedad ­manager, exited andwas unveiled as the new Brighton managerfollowing the shock departure of Dario Vidosic. If Vidosic’s exit had been a surprise, Brighton poaching Ruiz was a bigger one. Gorka Álvarez, who left Real Sociedad in 2025 following three seasons managing the reserves and a year as an assistant to SD Eibar’s women’s team, was hurriedly brought in to lead them in their Liga F opener against Logroño on Saturday, a 2-0 loss, and the second leg against Chelsea.It was a mountain of a task ­facing the 40-year-old and, in many respects, a bit of a free hit, with few expecting Real Sociedad to come close to overturning a three-goal ­deficit against European heavyweights.However, setting the tone for his tenure and building confidence was important.La Realdid well against the visitors, holding Bompastor’s side at bay until Walsh swept in from a corner in the 54th minute to kill any outlandish hopes there may have been of a comeback.Until then, the London side ­struggled to create clear chances withLa Realmirroring their well-organised display in the first half of the first leg.Ellie Carpenter, playing further forward, ahead of Lucy Bronze on the right, was Chelsea’s best outlet but they couldn’t capitalise on her balls into the middle. Walsh’s side-footed effort in the first half was weak and easy for the goalkeeper Julia Arrula. Aggie Beever-Jones had a good chance to break the deadlock moments before Walsh’s goal but the forward’s strike was too central and Arrula made an easy save.The perfectionist that Bompastor is, she will be unhappy with the nature of the two games, but the reality is that reaching the league phase, for a team desperately wanting European glory, was what mattered most.
