In the end the result was comfortable, even if the performance wasn’t, and Chelsea had the chance to give debuts off the bench to their new signings Nelly Las and Giulia Dragoni, and minutes to the talented 17-year-old Chloe Sarwie.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey will have also benefited from valuable competitive minutes before they kickstart their WSL campaign by hosting Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.Bompastor said: “Today we gave some really good opportunities to the young players to come and experience a Champions League game, so when you have the opportunity to do that, I think it’s always something really positive. I’m happy and really excited now to be in the Champions League this season. The goal was for us to qualify, which is what we have done.”On Friday 4 September at 1pm Suzanne Wrack will be answering readers’ questions about the new WSL season for GuardianConversationsExplore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueChelsea WomenWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: England omit Brydon Carse again for third Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: The Durham seamer was also dropped from the squad for the second Test after a late-night incident in a Derby bar last month
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: The Durham seamer was also dropped from the squad for the second Test after a late-night incident in a Derby bar last month
Content: The Durham bowler Brydon Carse has been left out of England’s latest Test squad.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenThe Durham bowler Brydon Carse has been left out of England’s latest Test squad.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAEngland cricket teamEngland omit Brydon Carse again for third Test against Pakistan at EdgbastonCarse also missed second Test after incident in Derby barMatthew Fisher absence is only change from Lord’s squadSimon BurntonWed 2 Sep 2026 18.56 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrydon Carse has been left out of England’s squad for the final Test of the summer, against Pakistan at Edgbaston next week, with police still investigating allegations of an assault connected with thelate-night incident at a Derby bar last monththat led to the Durham seamer being briefly arrested and placed in handcuffs. The Cricket Regulator is also investigating the incident.As a result of the allegations, and with investigations ongoing, Carse was dropped from the squad for last week’s second Test. The 31-year-old had been in the squad for the first game, but not named in the XI. Sonny Baker, who replaced him for the second Test but also did not play, remains in a squad that has changed only by the absence of Matthew Fisher. Alongside Baker, the other squad members who were not in the team at Lord’s are Shoaib Bashir, Sam Cook and Ollie Pope.Joe Root urges England to celebrate Pakistan series win in ‘sensible, grown-up way’Read moreAfter England sealed the series win withvictory at Lord’sMarcus Trescothick, the interim coach, promised that “we’re not going to ease off the gas” and spoke of the benefit the side’s current first-choice seamers – Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson – would get from regularly playing together. “The more experience everyone gets together, then it sort of fits into place how you want it to be.”But if England are likely to be unchanged the same is not true of their opponents, who announced on Monday that they hadsacked Sarfaraz Ahmed, their head coach, and were immediately dropping seven players, of whom five had played in at least one of the first two Tests. Given they had 18 players in their original squad it is theoretically possible for them to not pick any of their seven replacements, of whom five are currently uncapped, though the outgoing players include two of their four bowlers and both recognised all-rounders.Quick GuideEngland squad for third TestShowJoe Root(Yorkshire, captain),Jofra Archer(Sussex),Gus Atkinson(Surrey),Sonny Baker(Hampshire),Shoaib Bashir(Derbyshire),Harry Brook(Yorkshire),Sam Cook(Essex),Jordan Cox(Essex),Ben Duckett(Nottinghamshire),Emilio Gay(Durham),Dan Lawrence(Surrey),Ollie Pope(Surrey),Ollie Robinson(Sussex),Jamie Smith(Surrey),Josh Tongue(Nottinghamshire)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Should the final Test go to five days England will then have less than 48 hours to prepare for a white-ball series against Sri Lanka starting on 15 September in Southampton. Sri Lanka announced their squad for both T20 and ODI series on Wednesday, with Charith Asalanka – who replaced Kusal Mendis as captain in 2024 but was himself replaced when Mendis returned to the role earlier this year, as well as being dropped from the T20 squad – back as vice-captain in both formats.Asalanka’s return is reward for his form in this year’s Lanka Premier League, the country’s domestic T20 competition, in which he scored 385 runs in the tournament and was named player of the match in last month’s final. Lahiru Udara, the top-scorer in the LPL with 434 runs, is recalled three years after his one previous appearance. England are expected to announce their squad for the series later this week.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamCricketEngland v Pakistan 2026Pakistan cricket teamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Deadline-day shambles leaves Everton and David Moyes fighting the odds again | Everton | The Guardian
description: From accepting a bid for Armstrong to Balogun walking away, TFG has shown an amateurish and unambitious approach
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: From accepting a bid for Armstrong to Balogun walking away, TFG has shown an amateurish and unambitious approach
Content: Everton’s owners have challenged David Moyes to go further with fewer resources.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEverton’s owners have challenged David Moyes to go further with fewer resources.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockEvertonDeadline-day shambles leaves Everton and David Moyes fighting the odds againFrom accepting a bid for Armstrong to collapse of Balogun deal, TFG has shown an amateurish and unambitious approachAndy HunterWed 2 Sep 2026 19.02 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 21.16 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo be placed in the same bracket as owners whose lack of ambition, lack of resources and/or incompetence has contributed to the longest trophy drought in Everton’s history, particularly 20 months into a reign that has accompanied the move to a glittering new stadium and the clearing of onerous debt, should be cause for considerable discomfort and embarrassment at The Friedkin Group (TFG) on Wednesday. The slight on Everton’s owner is neither unkind nor unfair. At least Farhad Moshiri had a go before the taps were turned off.TFG may have restored financial stability to Everton after the near-ruinous chaos of Moshiri’s final years and his attempts to sell to 777 Partners but its reputation as “winners” – as the club’s chief executive, Angus Kinnear, labelled his American employers – has been shredded in the space of four days. The description always appeared generous given its approach to the summer transfer window, part two of Everton’s strategic rebuild according to Kinnear. But from accepting Nottingham Forest’s £35m bid for Harrison Armstrong on Saturday morning to Folarin Balogun walking away from a £40m move from Monaco on Tuesday night, and more in between, TFG has positioned itself as just another Everton owner unable or unwilling to realise the club’s potential and to give an expectant fanbase grounds for optimism.Balogun pulled out of Everton move over handling of his medical, claim MonacoRead moreEvertonians hoped for an overdue departure when TFG acquired the club in December 2024 and proceeded to refinance damaging loans and the long-term repayment costs of Hill Dickinson Stadium. The shambles of deadline day, however, was all too familiar and has caused serious damage to its standing among supporters.David Moyes kept his counsel throughout pre-season as Everton spent £16.5m on Hayden Hackney, rising to £25m for last season’s Championship player of the year, £18m on each of Merlin Röhl and Tyrique George, who he had on loan last season, £7m on Christian Nørgaard and swapped Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. The most Everton paid up front for a player all summer would prove to be £18m.When Moyes did eventually speak in public it was to stress, repeatedly, the need for Everton to sign more players, more quality and to keep their best talents. At the end of last season he had 22 outfield players at his disposal. At the start of deadline day he had 20 outfield players. By the end of transfer deadline day he had 18.That total includes one striker, Thierno Barry, no back-up for either full-back and, strictly speaking given that Ainsley Maitland-Niles did not start out in the position, no natural right-back. Evertonsold their most creative asset, Iliman Ndiaye, to Manchester City in a below-market price £65m deal despite the Senegal international having three years on his contract. They sold Beto, their only striking alternative to Barry, before securing a replacement and were left desperately scrambling around for one when Balogun’s medical went awry.View image in fullscreenEverton have sold Iliman Ndiaye (left) and brought in Merlin Röhl (right) for £18m in the summer transfer window.Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty ImagesManchester United said no to a loan offer for Joshua Zirkzee that arrived a few hours before the deadline. Tammy Abraham said no to leaving Aston Villa. Finally Balogun, having arrived later than scheduled for his medical and seen Everton renegotiate the terms of his fee with Monaco, compounded the chaos by also saying no despite signing a deal sheet shortly before 11pm. Barry looked out of his depth for much of his debut season in the Premier League. Now he is the precious commodity that Everton cannot afford to lose.Kinnear, perhaps in response to Moyes raising concerns over Everton’s business for the first time, gave several local interviews two weeks ago that painted a rosy picture of the club’s finances, transfer strategy and ambition. Subsequent events have cost him credibility on every count. The chief executive also got his manager’s back up by claiming TFG regarded not qualifying for Europe last season as “a failure” and that the squad is better placed to sustain a European challenge while striving to end Everton’s 31-year wait for a trophy.Moyes’s team face-planted during last season’s run-in, failing to win any of their last seven games when Europe was in reach. He has been challenged to go further with fewer resources. An added annoyance for Moyes and supporters is that Everton have started this season brightly, only to be surrounded by problems entirely of the hierarchy’s making.It was Kinnear who implemented a new “senior leadership team” at Everton and the move away from a director of football model. The team consists of the technical director, Nick Cox, director of scouting and recruitment, James Smith, director of football strategy and analytics, Chris Howarth and head of player trading, Nick Hammond. Moyes is also part of the leadership team, although he has appeared to be on a different page this summer. There has been sensible, cost-effective recruitment for Hackney, Röhl and Johnson but the end to the window invites criticism of the leadership team’s effectiveness and expertise. It resembles a case of too many chiefs and no clear direction, especially given some of the targets Everton went for in the final days.View image in fullscreenHarrison Armstrong is Everton’s first academy prospect to establish himself in the first team since Anthony Gordon.Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty ImagesThecollapse of the Balogun dealhas caused turmoil at Everton but a player getting cold feet over a move or a medical jeopardising a deal can happen. It is events under Everton’s control, and decisions they have taken, that are of greater concern. TFG’s decision to accept Forest’s offer for Armstrong, the first academy prospect to graduate through the ranks and establish himself since Anthony Gordon six years ago, was the first indication that Everton were struggling to meet the new squad cost ratios. So much for a new financial era at Hill Dickinson.TFG merits some credit for listening to supporters over theproposed sale of Armstrongand pulling the plug. To then consider selling Ndiaye to Tottenham for £60m and spending £35m on Richarlison, however, was another alarming sign.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEverton have been looking for a right-back since Moyes returned to the club in January 2025, and needed one before then. Moyes wanted Guéla Doué from Strasbourg but the 23-year-old was deemed too expensive. Doué joined Bayer Leverkusen on deadline day for £25.7m. At least five alternatives were explored before Everton, their £9m deal for Fulham’s Kenny Tete having fallen through, signed Maitland-Niles as the £4.3m answer to one glaring problem.A bigger weakness lay up front. No Premier League club of serious intent would enter a second season with their striking options limited to Beto and Barry. An upgrade was essential. Instead, Everton downgraded. So much for the leadership team’s vision and the owner’s ambition.Everton are the lowest net spenders in the Premier League over the past five years and, more by accident than design, ended this summer making a net profit of £25m on transfers. TFG committed £78m on signings in a summer where, by the calculations of the football finance expert Kieran Maguire, the average spend per Premier League club was £181m. Everton’s outlay does not include the significant cost of re-signing Jack Grealish on loan.TFG’s frugal spending and efficiency drive – redundancies were made behind the scenes at Everton this summer – has fuelled talk of Dan Friedkin and co looking to sell the club. However, the owners have allocated £40m to cover the compensation payable to Burnley should Everton fail in their appeal against the outcome of a profitability and sustainability breach case, and are investing almost £14m in infrastructure projects at Hill Dickinson, Goodison Park and Finch Farm training ground.What is certain is the anger TFG would face if they attended Sunday’s home game against Manchester United. Dan Friedkin has yet to attend a match at Hill Dickinson, where some season ticket prices were increased by up to 10% this season.The Everton fans’ forum and Everton fan advisory board issued statements on Wednesday criticising the club’s amateurish, unambitious approach to the transfer window. The 1878s, the group of volunteers responsible for the impressive tifos and banners at the stadium, has withdrawn its support for the foreseeable future. “We do not feel that our fanbase’s ambitions and the club’s ambitions align right now – what happened yesterday has proved that even more,” the group said.It looks a long road back to acceptance for TFG, Kinnear and Everton’s senior leadership team.Explore more on these topicsEvertonDavid MoyesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lando Norris launches LN4 Fusion team to develop young drivers in F1 and motorsport | Lando Norris | The Guardian
description: The F1 champion became the first to back a team in the junior single-seater era and also created a legacy programme to support talent
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The F1 champion became the first to back a team in the junior single-seater era and also created a legacy programme to support talent
Content: Lando Norris has co-founded a new junior, single-seater racing team.Photograph: LN4 FusionView image in fullscreenLando Norris has co-founded a new junior, single-seater racing team.Photograph: LN4 FusionLando NorrisLando Norris launches LN4 Fusion team to develop young drivers in F1 and motorsportF1 champion first to back junior team in single-seater eraNorris also creates legacy programme to support talentGiles RichardsWed 2 Sep 2026 19.06 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLando Norris has co-founded a new junior, single-seater racing team. Named LN4 Fusion it will compete in multiple championships including the feeder series for Formula One, F3 and F2, asthe current F1 world championcommits to helping young drivers make it to the top level in motorsport.Norris’s involvement, including a personal financial undertaking alongside an investment group, represents the first time an F1 world champion has directly backed a team in the modern junior single-seater era. As part of the project he has also established the LN4 Legacy programme, a driver development initiative designed to identify and support talent coming through the ranks from karting upwards and then provide assistance financially as well as in coaching, performance and career support.Lando Norris agrees new deal until at least 2030 with ‘second family’ McLarenRead moreThe McLaren driverlaunched the project at an event in Monza, which will host the Italian Grand Prix this weekend. It constitutes a serious and comprehensive effort to address some of the difficulties facing junior drivers coming through the ranks, which Norris has previously identified as a fundamental problem for the sport.“I know that getting toFormula Onetakes so much more than just talent. You need the right people around you, the right support and the right opportunities at the right time,” he said.“That’s what these two projects are all about. LN4 Fusion is about building a race team that can compete with the best in junior motorsport, with great people and a great environment for drivers to develop. The LN4 Legacy programme is about helping talented young drivers get opportunities they might not otherwise have.“They naturally fit together. I want to help create opportunities for the next generation both on and off the track and hopefully make a real difference to young drivers coming through the sport.”View image in fullscreenLando Norris became the world champion with McLaren in 2025.Photograph: Clive Mason/Getty ImagesThe intent for the LN4 Fusion team will be to compete across a range of championships as of next year with already confirmed programmes in F3 for 2027, as well as the Italian F4 Championship and the FIA Formula Regional European Championship. As part of the process the team has acquired key assets from the German team AIX Racing, which has an F3 entry until the end of the 2027 season and has applied for participation in the F2 Championship.Norris will play an active role in the organisation and his role was welcomed by the F1 chief executive, Stefano Domenicali. “SeeingLando Norrisinvolved in this new project is an incredible statement on how much the pyramid of Formula 3 and Formula 2 is crucial to the future of Formula One,” he said. “Through Lando’s investment and experience we can build a future, with new drivers, engineers, mechanics, and a tradition that will be followed by motorsport lovers.”The seriousness of Norris’s ambition was emphasised with the appointment of René Rosin as team principal. Rosin was formerly the principal and managing director of the Prema team, which has enjoyed more than 40 years of competition in the junior series. They have won multiple titles and are one of the go-to teams for developing young talent. Prema brought on many drivers who went on to F1 including, among others on the current grid, the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc as well as Norris’sMcLarenteammate Oscar Piastri. The team also nurtured Jacques Villeneuve who went on to take the F1 title.Part of the LN4 Fusion team will be formed from the experience and personnel at the Fusion Motorsport team, which has enjoyed huge success for 25 years in UK karting, with multiple national and more recently international titles. The head of Fusion Motorsport karting, Dan Hazlewood, will be team principal of the LN4 Fusion UK operation, including overseeing the planned entry into the British F4 championship and in bringing talent through from karting.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLando Norris’s LN4 Fusion F3 car.Photograph: LN4 FusionWith 2027 set for the opening of racing for the team, the organisation is developing a European headquarters in Veneto, northern Italy with a British base in Cambridgeshire already developing the F4 programme.Rosin emphasised the importance of having Norris as a key part of the new venture and its expectations of success.“Having Lando on board adds a further dimension to this project,” he said. “He has come through the junior single-seater ranks and understands its demands. His involvement will make a real difference to the team. We want to develop a pathway through junior single-seaters and create an environment in which drivers, engineers and sporting personnel can perform at the highest level.”The chief executive, Dan Richards, echoed the optimism, believing they had all the requisite elements for success in place. “What we have created is far more than simply the acquisition of a racing team,” he said.“We have assembled a rare combination and secured the right sporting leadership in the industry: an established operation, a Formula One world champion, the most successful team principal in junior single-seater racing over the past two decades, world-class motorsport expertise, significant investment and a shared ambition to build a team capable of competing at the highest levels of the sport.”Explore more on these topicsLando NorrisMcLarenFormula OneFormula One 2026Motor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Vuelta a España: Britain’s Brennan seals hat-trick of stage wins as Mas retains lead | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Matthew Brennan triumphed on stage 11 of the Vuelta a España, becoming the first cyclist to win three stages in his first Grand Tour since Tadej Pogacar
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Matthew Brennan triumphed on stage 11 of the Vuelta a España, becoming the first cyclist to win three stages in his first Grand Tour since Tadej Pogacar
Content: Matthew Brennan of Team Visma-Lease a Bike reacts after winning his third stage on this year’s Vuelta a España.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAView image in fullscreenMatthew Brennan of Team Visma-Lease a Bike reacts after winning his third stage on this year’s Vuelta a España.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAVuelta a EspañaVuelta a España: Britain’s Brennan seals hat-trick of stage wins as Mas retains leadStage 11 won by 21-year-old as dazzling debut continuesLewis Askey claims opening stage in Tour of BritainAgenciesWed 2 Sep 2026 18.34 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatthew Brennan triumphed again in theVuelta a Españaon Wednesday, becoming the first cyclist to win three stages in his first Grand Tour since Tadej Pogacar seven years ago. The British rider secured his third victory on the 11th stage, a mostly flat route of 153.8km from Cartagena to Lorca.“We took the initiative today again,” Brennan said. “The boys pulled as hard as they could even after a tough day in the legs yesterday. We still went full gas. Coming into the final, we really held our own place and knew that we were all strong enough to kind of get to where we want to be.”US cyclist Ezra Caudell hospitalized with ‘multi-system trauma’ after Philadelphia crashRead moreThe 21-year-old of team Visma-Lease a Bike also won the second and fifth stages to become the youngest cyclist with multiple stage wins in the Vuelta since Pogacar’s three victories in 2019.“It’s massive [to have won three stages],” Brennan said. “I’m with a team full of massive champions. We’ve got guys who have podiumed in Grand Tours and won them as well, and guys who’ve won classics and huge races. And the fact they go for me is an amazing opportunity. I’m really thankful that they go full gas for me.”A sprinter had not claimed at least three victories in his maiden Grand Tour since Fernando Gaviria in the Giro d’Italia in 2017. Pogacar also had already won three stages in this year’s Vuelta beforea crash forced him to withdrawon Saturday while holding a big overall lead. He fractured his left collarbone and could not continue on his quest for a career sweep of the three Grand Tours.Enric Mas, from Movistar Team, took the overall lead from Pogacar and has kept it since. He is 1min 18sec ahead of Primoz Roglic, from team Red Bull-Bora Hansgrohe. Roglic is chasing a record fifth Vuelta title.On Thursday, riders will face a 12th stage featuring a tough mountain route in southern Spain. It includes a traditional double climb at Velefique and Calar Alto, marking an important day for the riders fighting for the general classification.The three-week Vuelta finishes in Granada on 13 September.Britain’s Lewis Askey, meanwhile, won the opening stage of theTour of Britain, the NSN rider attacking on the cobbles of the Michaelgate climb in Lincoln and riding clear to victory. The Italian Filippo Ganna of Netcompany Ineos came home second, two seconds down, while the Belgian Tim Wellens of UAE Team Emirates-XRG was third.View image in fullscreenLewis Askey leads the way on the cobbles in Lincoln.Photograph: Zac Williams/SWpix.com/Shutterstock“It feels amazing, especially to have my grandparents there at the finish line. It was super special,” said Askey. “I ride my bike to win races. It’s great when you come second, come third and do good performances, but nothing matches managing to put your hands up in the air.”Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingTour of BritainnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King Charles | Bayeux tapestry | The Guardian
description: Monarch tells Emmanuel Macron at the British Museum in London that the two nations will share a future ‘woven together’ by history and shared values
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Monarch tells Emmanuel Macron at the British Museum in London that the two nations will share a future ‘woven together’ by history and shared values
Content: King Charles and Queen Camilla examine the Bayeux tapestry during a visit to the exhibition at the British Museum.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKing Charles and Queen Camilla examine the Bayeux tapestry during a visit to the exhibition at the British Museum.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesBayeux tapestryBayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King CharlesMonarch tells Emmanuel Macron at the British Museum in London that the two nations will share a future ‘woven together’ by history and shared valuesCaroline DaviesWed 2 Sep 2026 19.58 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.23 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe loan of theBayeux tapestrywas “the best possible symbol” of the “entente amicale” between France and the UK, King Charles said, as he visited the famous embroidered masterpiece at the British Museum in London.Though the tapestry recounts a conflict, “here it is today, nearly 1,000 years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations,” he said.The “70 metres of memory and artistry” were a reminder “that our two nations have been bound together for almost a millennium”, added Charles, speaking at the new exhibition and accompanied by the French president,Emmanuel Macron, and UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.In a speech partly delivered in French, he said: “We have defended our values together in times of peril; we continue to do so today across the world.”He continued: “May this tapestry – and the treasures that will travel in return – stand as symbols not only of our shared past, but our shared future: a future woven, as it should be, by Britain andFrancetogether.”Macron, also speaking in French and English, said that the return of the tapestry “had required a little patience” , since he first spoke of it in 2018.“Since the first British request dates back to 1931, I choose to regard eight years as something of a speed record,” he said.He added that, with the tapestry in Britain, his hopes were that the two countries could “forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery”.The tapestry – the woven record of the Norman conquest – has returned to the UK for the first time in almost 1,000 years, and is on loan until September 2027 as part of a special trilateral agreement between the UK, France and the museum.Charles’s reference to entente amicale followed his use of the phrase to rebrand the famous “entente cordiale” between the two nations in his banquet speech at Windsor Castle when hehosted the Macronsin July last year.During Wednesday’s visit, he expressed his “deepest appreciation” to Macron and the French people “for the trust you have placed in the United Kingdom by agreeing to this unprecedented loan”.He said: “It once depicted warriors crossing the Channel; yet today it forms part of a cultural exchange that will see some of the British Museum’s own precious artefacts travel to France in return, in a spirit of friendship.”Thanking all those who made the loan possible, he added: “Anyone studying the tapestry’s scenes in detail will notice that, even in the 11th century, historic events rarely happened without extensive discussion, careful planning and a great deal of organisation beforehand.”The party, which also included Queen Camilla, France’s first lady, Brigitte Macron, and Burnham’s wife, Marie-France van Heel, stopped at key moments along the 11th-century artwork to hear from curators about historic events such as the coronation of Harold Godwinson and the much-disputed depiction of his death by an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.At hisfirst prime minister’s questionsearlier on Wednesday, Burnham said: “The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation, the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low.”The Labour leader also said the Bayeux Around Britain programme, which will see the digital exhibition displayed in museums, galleries and castles in all four nations, would “give communities across the UK the opportunity to learn about one of the defining stories of our past”.In exchange, Britain will loan the Sutton Hoo treasures – an assemblage of gold and other historic objects dating from the 7th century AD – and a selection of Lewis ‌chess pieces and other masterpieces owned by the trustees of the British Museum to museums in France.Explore more on these topicsBayeux tapestryKing Charles IIIEmmanuel MacronAndy BurnhamMonarchyFranceBritish MuseumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspect and two victims dead at apartment shooting in downtown Minneapolis | Minneapolis | The Guardian
description: The city’s police department and mayor warn the public to stay away from the Loring Park neighborhood nearby
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: The city’s police department and mayor warn the public to stay away from the Loring Park neighborhood nearby
Content: Police respond to a shooting Wednesday on 2 September in downtown Minneapolis.Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/APView image in fullscreenPolice respond to a shooting Wednesday on 2 September in downtown Minneapolis.Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/APMinneapolisSuspect and two victims dead at apartment shooting in downtown MinneapolisThe city’s police department and mayor warn the public to stay away from the Loring Park neighborhood nearbyUwa Ede-OsifoWed 2 Sep 2026 23.40 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.40 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo people were killed and the suspect was dead after a shooting at an apartment building in downtownMinneapolison Wednesday afternoon, officials said.One shooting victim died at the scene. A second diedafter arriving at Hennepin county medical center, a hospital spokesperson said.Gunfire erupted on the upper floor of a high-rise apartment building, according to city officials.Video posted to social media showed police aiming rifles upward at an apartment tower near the Minneapolis convention center.After receiving several 911 calls, officers entered the building at about 4.39pm. They followed the sound of shots and encountered a “haze”, which limited their sight, officials said.Two officers were wounded by the gunfire, with one sustaining a non-life-threatening injury to the leg and a second undergoing surgery.Authorities have not publicly identified the suspect.Julius Bailey was sitting outside his apartment building when he heard gunshots and saw a man he recognized as a resident of the building holding a pistol. Bailey said he heard a woman screaming and immediately started running away. He said he counted eight shots.Bailey said he recognized the man holding the gun because he was someone who was known for showing off his weapon. Bailey said he had tried to avoid the man since moving into the building in June.“I could tell he was trouble,” he said.Chris Miller, who also lives in the apartment building, said he heard a rapid succession of gunshots and quickly ran outside for safety. He said he believed he knew who carried out the shooting and that he encountered someone in the hallway with a handgun earlier this week and reported that person to management.The Minneapolis police department and mayor Jacob Frey warned the public to stay away from the densely populated Loring Park neighborhood nearby.“Grateful to law enforcement actively working to ensure the safety of our neighbors in Downtown Minneapolis this afternoon,”Minnesotagovernor Tim Walz said in a statement. “Minnesota is praying for our first responders.”The FBI has extended its resources to aid law enforcement on the ground, director Kash Patelwrotein an X post.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsMinneapolisMinnesotaUS crimeTim WalznewsShareReuse this content

title: Gun found in French lake is analysed by 2012 Alps killings investigators | France | The Guardian
description: British tourists reportedly discovered Luger pistol that is latest in long line of potential leads in mystery of al-Hilli deaths
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: British tourists reportedly discovered Luger pistol that is latest in long line of potential leads in mystery of al-Hilli deaths
Content: Investigators in 2012 at the campsite where Saad al-Hilli and his family had been staying near Annecy.Photograph: Lionel Cironneau/APView image in fullscreenInvestigators in 2012 at the campsite where Saad al-Hilli and his family had been staying near Annecy.Photograph: Lionel Cironneau/APFranceGun found in French lake is analysed by 2012 Alps killings investigatorsBritish tourists reportedly discovered Luger pistol that is latest in long line of potential leads in mystery of al-Hilli deathsPatrick DalyWed 2 Sep 2026 20.03 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExperts are examining a gun found by tourists to determine whether it might have been used to kill a British family in the French Alps 14 years ago.In what remains an unsolved murder case, Saad al-Hilli, 50, his wife, Ikbal, 47, and her mother, Suhaila al-Allaf, 74, were shot dead on a road near Annecy, a remote Alpine village in easternFrancein September 2012.The couple’s two young daughters, then four and seven, survived but a passing cyclist, 45-year-old Sylvain Mollier, was also killed.The French prosecutor Marie-Céline Lawrysz confirmed that a pistol, thought to be a Luger, was uncovered on 20 August by two tourists swimming in Lake Annecy. The weapon is currently being analysed by ballistics experts in France in connection with the al-Hilli cold case.During the initial investigation, pieces from the butt of the weapon used in the killings, a vintage Luger P06-29 pistol, were found on the ground near the British-registered BMW estate car that the family had been driving at the time of the attack. The gun was identified as a model used by the Swiss army in the 1930s, but its owner has never been traced.In a statement, Lawrysz said a semi-automatic pistol had been found by the tourists, reported to be British, at a depth of about five feet, a few dozen metres away from the shore of Lake Annecy.She said: “They kept the weapon for 24 hours and conducted online research to identify its type.“They subsequently drew a link between the discovered weapon and the one believed to have been used in the Chevaline [near Annecy] killing on September 5, 2012.“On August 21 2026, they handed the weapon over to gendarmes from the local Saint-Jorioz brigade.”Detectives have so far ruled out the possibility of a contract killing, saying a professional killer would not have used such a vintage weapon as the Luger.The discovery of the pistol is the latest in a long line of leads that investigators have followed in an effort to unravel the mystery that has surrounded the four deaths.Suspects previously arrested in connection with the case include an Iraqi prisoner known as Mr S who was claimed to have said he had been offered “a large sum of money” to kill Iraqis living in the UK.Mr al-Hilli’s brother Zaid was also arrested on suspicion of murder in 2013, but was later told he would face no further action after police found there was insufficient evidence to charge him with a crime.In 2022, another suspect was questioned but released without charge. Two years ago,DNA analysis was orderedby detectives in France’s cold case unit on clothes belonging to the victims, as well as on the pieces of the gun and cigarette butts found at the scene. No arrests were made following the tests.Explore more on these topicsFranceCrimeEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Uber drivers launch European class action over ‘soulless’ and ‘scary’ AI algorithm | Uber | The Guardian
description: Landmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earnings
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Landmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earnings
Content: Mohammed Shirwa, an Uber driver from Rotterdam, claims Uber’s pay-setting mechanism preys on weakness.Photograph: Judith Jockel/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMohammed Shirwa, an Uber driver from Rotterdam, claims Uber’s pay-setting mechanism preys on weakness.Photograph: Judith Jockel/The GuardianUberUber drivers launch European class action over ‘soulless’ and ‘scary’ AI algorithmLandmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earningsRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 2 Sep 2026 16.37 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUber drivers have launched a landmark legal action against the ride-hailing company claiming they live in “constant fear” of a “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs.Drivers from the UK, theNetherlandsand other countries have joined the compensation claim that could run into billions of dollars. It alleges an AI-powered pay-setting system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings.The claim has been filed at Amsterdam’s district court, where the $150bn (£111bn) San Francisco tech company has its European HQ. It is the first collective legal move of its kind, according to the European Trade Union Confederation.The case centres on an opaque “black box” algorithm fed on information about drivers, which sets a personalised rate for each ride. Drivers fear it pushes down fares to the minimum they are willing to accept.Drivers have told the Guardian the algorithm has offered the same job to different people at different pay rates and offers them less for a return journey after a long trip because it calculates they will not want to come home empty.“It is like someone watching you all the time and knowing about your weakness – the boss is the algorithm,” said Mohammed Shirwa, a 41-year-old Uber driver in Rotterdam. “All the time the algorithm is learning about you and what you are willing to accept. So the prices go low but you are stuck. It knows you need the job.”View image in fullscreenKola Oba, from Tottenham in north London, claims Uber exploits information it collects about him to push down fares.Kola Oba, who calls the algorithm “soulless”, was taking a break in Tottenham, north London, with another driver when they were offered the same job.The other driver was offered £27 and Oba was offered £23. The pair suspected it was because Oba, 48, had taken several cheap jobs and the AI assumed he would accept a lower price. Uber has previouslysaidsuch discrepancies were down to other features of its system including GPS, surge pricing, promotions and testing.“It’s scary – they have all my information and they are using it against my own wellbeing,” Oba said. “It defines how much I earn, how long I have to work, my time with my family, my resting time.”AI models take an increasing role in assigning work to humans by using their rapidly increasing power to learn about a business’s needs and staff behaviour and then acting as a “synthetic manager”.The Dutch data protection authorityfined⁠Uber €825m (£708m) last month for deactivating driver ⁠accounts through automated systems without ​adequate notice. Uber said it would appeal. The company is also planning to roll out driverless cars in European cities from London to Zagreb, initially with human supervisions.The legal case is being led by the Worker Info Exchange, a campaign group whose founder, James Farrar,secureda UK supreme court ruling that Uber drivers should have worker rights.Relating to about 241,000 drivers across the EU and the UK, the claim alleges that Uber has unlawfully used automated decision-making, including profiling, in dynamically setting pay and allocating work.The lawsuit, which also claims the company unlawfully used driver data to train its AI models, is seeking damages for affected drivers and an injunction to halt the conduct which it claims breachesGDPRdata regulations.The drivers claim Uber has operated dynamic pay-setting in the UK since 2023, pushing down their annual incomes by about £5,000. The system was introduced in the Netherlands this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUber’s chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi,said in 2023: “I think that what we can do better is targeting of different trips to different drivers based on their preferences or based on behavioural patterns that they’re showing us.”View image in fullscreenUber, which has its headquarters in San Francisco, said it categorically rejected the allegations.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUber said it did not adjust the price offered for a trip based on an individual driver’s behaviour and that a history of accepting or rejecting trips was not used to personalise pay offers. Instead, it said, dynamic pricing allowed it to increase pay on less attractive trips, boosting a driver’s earning potential.“While we haven’t seen the claim yet, we categorically reject the allegations,” an Uber spokesperson said. “The Uber app uses real-time information about the trip such as journey, duration and destination to calculate fares.“Drivers see their earnings and where a trip is going before they decide whether to accept it. The vast majority of total fares continue to go where they belong: into drivers’ pockets, and the percentage that Uber keeps from fares has remained relativelyflat.”A 2025studyby academics at the University of Oxford, which Uber said relied on incomplete and selective data,foundthere had been substantial cuts in driver earnings after the “dynamic” algorithm was introduced.Farrar said: “It’s bad enough that Uber’s dynamic pay algorithms have squeezed driver pay for years now but the intrusive and underhanded way in which Uber uses its technology to monitor and influence drivers’ behaviour is an affront to their dignity as workers and as human beings.”Anton Ekker, a Dutch lawyer leading the case, said: “A computer algorithm should not independently make decisions that strip individuals of their livelihood. Like so many other online platforms, it should be held accountable for the large-scale exploitation of vulnerabilities of European citizens.”Explore more on these topicsUberAI (artificial intelligence)TransportGig economyEuropeNetherlandsGDPRnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cassandra Wilson, Grammy-winning jazz singer, dies aged 70 | Jazz | The Guardian
description: Mississippi-born Wilson, who worked across folk, pop, R&B and country, was once dubbed America’s best singer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mississippi-born Wilson, who worked across folk, pop, R&B and country, was once dubbed America’s best singer
Content: Cassandra Wilson performs at Mississippi's Grammy Legacy celebration in 2010 in Biloxi, Mississippi.Photograph: Skip Bolen/WireImageView image in fullscreenCassandra Wilson performs at Mississippi's Grammy Legacy celebration in 2010 in Biloxi, Mississippi.Photograph: Skip Bolen/WireImageJazzCassandra Wilson, Grammy-winning jazz singer, dies aged 70Mississippi-born Wilson, who worked across folk, pop, R&B and country, was once dubbed America’s best singerAssociated PressWed 2 Sep 2026 22.47 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 23.20 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCassandra Wilson, the two-time Grammy-winning jazz singer, songwriter and producer has died. She was 70.Dubbed America’s best singer by Time magazine in 2001, Wilson was best known for her genre-bending voice, which expanded the boundaries of traditional blues-based jazz and worked effortlessly across folk, pop, R&B, country and beyond. At the heart of all her work was her idiosyncratic contralto, a soulful sound distinctly tied to her roots.As Jon Batiste put it in a eulogy on Wednesday, Wilson sounded like the south.She died in her native Jackson,Mississippi, on Tuesday morning, the Hinds county coroner, Jeramiah Howard, confirmed.“It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Cassandra Wilson, the Grammy Award-winning and legendary jazz artist. Cassandra Wilson transitioned peacefully at home, surrounded by family, close friends, and her manager,” said a statement from her manager to the jazz radio station WBGO.Born and raised in Jackson to musician Herman B Fowlkes and teacher Mary Fowlkes, Wilson showed an early love of music, listening to Motown, Miles Davis and Thelonious Monk. At six, she started piano lessons. She played clarinet in marching bands. She performed at coffeehouses and in cover bands while studying at Millsaps College and Jackson State University.In the early 80s, she mentored under jazz greats in New Orleans before moving to New York City and joining Steve Coleman’s M-Base Collective – eventually becoming its main vocalist.Her instantly recognizable voice earned her four Grammy nominations and two wins for best jazz vocal album. Those were in 1997 for New Moon Daughter and 2009 for Loverly.In 2015, it was Wilson who gave a special concert at the famed Apollo Theater to commemorate the 100th birthday of the blues singer Billie Holiday, the legendary American jazz vocalist who died in New York City at age 44. That same year, Wilson released her last album, Coming Forth by Day, a homage to Holiday.In 2022, Wilson was named a National Endowment for the Arts jazz master, one of the highest honors awarded to jazz musicians in the United States.“She had an unmistakable vocal tone, phrasing and her approach of weaving folkloric, R+B and diasporic music together with experimental and popular genres had a major impact on me,” Batiste said in his tribute to Wilson on Instagram.“Her Mississippi heritage was always present in everything no matter how expansive her artistry evolved,” he wrote in the caption of a clip showing them together on Brazilian TV in 2009. “She was one of the first people to take me on tour around the world, the great Cassandra Wilson.”Jackson’s mayor, John Horhn, said the city “has lost an extraordinary native daughter, and the world has lost a singular musical voice”.“Cassandra Wilson carried the sound, spirit and history of Mississippi with her wherever her music reached,” said the mayor’s statement, shared with WJTV. “Her work had rare depth of character and a profound understanding of how music moves people, tells stories and connects generations.”Explore more on these topicsJazzMississippinewsShareReuse this content

title: Patagonia sues Trump over slashing of protected areas in Utah | Utah | The Guardian
description: President’s order strips nearly 3m acres of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante, sacred tribal sites, of safeguards
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: President’s order strips nearly 3m acres of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante, sacred tribal sites, of safeguards
Content: Monument Valley in Utah, seen from Muley Point in the Bears Ears national monument, before Donald Trump’s drastic reduction of its boundaries.Photograph: George Frey/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMonument Valley in Utah, seen from Muley Point in the Bears Ears national monument, before Donald Trump’s drastic reduction of its boundaries.Photograph: George Frey/Getty ImagesUtahPatagonia sues Trump over slashing of protected areas in UtahPresident’s order strips nearly 3m acres of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante, sacred tribal sites, of safeguardsDani AnguianoWed 2 Sep 2026 21.51 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.39 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatagonia, the outdoor clothing and gear company, has joined a lawsuit challenging Donald Trump’s decision to significantly reduce the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah, removing protections from nearly 3m acres.In July, the presidentapprovedthe reduction of the sites by 90%, clearing the way to open the land to oil and gas companies. He argued in his proclamations that doing so would allow lands to be “put to a higher-priority use” and that they contained critical minerals important to “resource independence …[and] national security”.Trump previously targeted the monuments, which are sacred to tribes, in his first term. Joe Biden ultimately overturned it.Patagoniasued Trumpin 2017 when he first sought to downsize the public lands in Utah. His proclamations earlier this year represented an even more dramatic reduction of the monuments than he sought in his first term.Forest Service chief faces scrutiny over logging ties as Trump plans to scrap protectionsRead moreThe retailer announced on Wednesday it was joining a lawsuit to put a stop to what it described as illegal orders that “betray Tribal sovereignty”.“We will not stand idly by while anti-public lands crusaders attempt to exploit these lands for their extractive-industry friends or disrespect tribal nations,” Ryan Gellert, the company’s CEO, said in astatement.The Antiquities Act allows presidents to establish national monuments, but it does not give the executive the authority to undo them, Gellert wrote. Trump’s move was an effort to “force secession of federal land to the state and allow private companies to extract natural resources from that land”, Gellert said, pointing to mining claims that have already been filed in areas that are no longer part of the monuments.“Protecting Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante is worth more than any amount of money. The vast majority of Americans agree,” Gellert said.Barack Obama established Bears Ears in 2016 during his final weeks in office, after years of advocacy by Indigenous American tribes, while Bill Clinton established Grand Staircase-Escalante.The Natural Resources Defense Council, which filed the federal lawsuit on Wednesday along with several other conservation groups, described Trump’s proclamations as “one of the largest rollbacks of public land protections in US history”.“These monuments protect places that took millions of years to form. President Trump is trying to destroy them with a stroke of a pen. That cannot stand,” said Christy Goldfuss, the NRDC executive director.“Once you open these lands to mining and drilling, what gets lost is not coming back – ancient cliff dwellings, dinosaur fossils found nowhere else on Earth and sacred sites tied to the tribal nations.”The other groups that challenged Trump’s rollback in court include the SouthernUtahWilderness Alliance and Earthjustice, which represents Grand Canyon Trust, WildEarth Guardians, the Sierra Club, Western Watersheds Project, the Center for Biological Diversity, Great Old Broads for Wilderness and the National Parks Conservation Association.Explore more on these topicsUtahNational parksDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find | Pesticides | The Guardian
description: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities
Content: A farmer sprays pesticide on sesame fields in Burkina Faso, west Africa.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenA farmer sprays pesticide on sesame fields in Burkina Faso, west Africa.Photograph: AlamyPesticidesAlmost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts findStudy reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalitiesPippa NeillEnvironment reporterWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 22.43 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, astudyhas found.Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned byPesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and eastAfrica.The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was inBurkina Fasoin west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.View image in fullscreenYoung farm workers harvesting cotton in a field near Boromo in Burkina Faso.Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/GettyThe study,publishedin the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action NetworkIndia, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCalifornia bans paraquat, highly toxic herbicide outlawed in more than 70 countriesRead moreGénon Jensen, the executive director of theHealthand Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, withgrowing evidencelinking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it asan occupational disease for farmers.Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the EarthEuropeearlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.Explore more on these topicsPesticidesAgricultureFarmingParkinson's diseasePoisonHealthEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Global heating will hit at least 1.8C, UN warns, and there are ‘no good outcomes’ | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: But scientists say the world could get back to 1.5C through deep, rapid emissions cuts and removing carbon from the atmosphere
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: But scientists say the world could get back to 1.5C through deep, rapid emissions cuts and removing carbon from the atmosphere
Content: A flooded street in Vasai, India, in July. A UN report has warned global heating will reach at least 1.8C, and every fraction of temperature rise intensifies destructive extreme weather.Photograph: Punit Paranjpe/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA flooded street in Vasai, India, in July. A UN report has warned global heating will reach at least 1.8C, and every fraction of temperature rise intensifies destructive extreme weather.Photograph: Punit Paranjpe/AFP/Getty ImagesClimate crisisGlobal heating will hit at least 1.8C, UN warns, and there are ‘no good outcomes’But scientists say the world could get back to 1.5C through deep, rapid emissions cuts and removing carbon from the atmosphereAdam MortonWed 2 Sep 2026 05.00 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGlobal heating will reach at least 1.8C under even the most optimistic future, well beyond the Paris agreement goal of 1.5C, according to a UN report that warns every fraction of temperature rise intensifies destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and island and coastal city submersion.‘The world needs to pay attention’: Nepalis and Tibetans in New York City respond to the Himalayan disasterRead moreThe report by the Nairobi-based UN Environment Programme confirmed overshooting the 1.5C goal inscribed in the landmark Paris agreement of 2015 was now “unavoidable” and, despite some progress in addressing the human-caused climate crisis driven by burning fossil fuels, likely in the next few years.It said: “There are no good outcomes above 1.5C”.Heating of up to 3C above preindustrial levels could lead to glaciers losing more than a quarter of their mass by 2100, raising sea levels by up to 13cm. Global food production could decline by up to 14% by 2050 if there are not effective strategies to adapt.Human health, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies could all be severely damaged. Some losses would be irreversible. Many communities may have to relocate or change their livelihoods.The report said the best hope for humanity to limit damage was to adopt an “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway that required immediate and sustained greenhouse gas emissions cuts combined with steps to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.It described the goal of net zero emissions – increasingly politically contentious in some countries – as “an essential milestone that cannot be skipped” and stressed carbon dioxide removal through steps such as establishing vast new forests must occur alongside, not as an alternative to, deep cuts in fossil pollution.View image in fullscreenA wildfire near the town of Omis, Croatia, in August.Photograph: Miroslav Lelas/AFP/Getty ImagesCrucially, the authors of the report, titled Limiting Overshoot, said the average global temperature could be returned to 1.5C this century only if heating stayed below about 1.8C. They warned nature’s capacity to store carbon was uncertain and would shrink the more the planet heats.The president of Palau, Surangel Whipps Jr – this week hosting regional leaders including Australia’s Anthony Albanese for a Pacific Islands Forum meeting focused on security and climate – said the report was “a fork in the road moment for the planet”.double quotation markThe rules of the game are now changingProf Debra Roberts“It is hard to overstate the depth of emotion for those of us living on the frontline after having fought so hard to put the 1.5C limit at the heart of the Paris agreement,” Whipps said.“We need to see an urgent and unprecedented increase in political will and investment in a climate safe future. Nobody can read this report and conclude otherwise.”Vishal Prasad, from Pacific Island Students Fighting Climate Change, said the report was terrifying for young people from the Pacific.“The International Court of Justice has made it clear – keeping to 1.5C is not a choice, it is a legal obligation,” he said. “We are not asking for your goodwill. We are not begging you. We are telling you what international law requires of you. End fossil fuel expansion. Your corporate profits cannot be allowed to extinguish our future.”The UNEP executive director, Inger Andersen, said the future would “bring many unknowns”, but extreme heatwaves – such as those that smashed records and exacerbated wildfires and droughts this northern summer – were already proving climate impacts would “strike faster, hit harder and last longer”.View image in fullscreenThe president of Palau, Surangel Whipps Jr, says the report is ‘a fork in the road moment for the planet’.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty Images“We have to act with urgency and determination. Every fraction of a degree avoided, every year by which overshoot is shortened, and every adaptation action taken will save lives, will protect ecosystems, and reduce economic losses,” she told reporters.Prof Debra Roberts, a report author and co-chair of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, said a key message was that “the rules of the game are now changing”.“Existing approaches are no longer fit for purpose,” she said. “I think, for me, that’s the clarion call. We now have to reconfigure our climate governance around dealing with an overshoot pathway.”View image in fullscreenThe Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods at Betrawati in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Prof Richard Betts said the flooding catastrophe was a demonstration of why the world needed to limit overshoot and come back to 1.5C.Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty ImagesShe said that meant not just pollution cuts and carbon removal, but “bold adaptation” to protect infrastructure and livelihoods, help sustain political and social support for reducing emissions, and prevent resources being diverted to crisis response.Climate Analytics, a science and policy institute, applauded the report for clearly describing the problem, but said it did a poor job of “showing us that there is a way out”.El Niño climate patterns supercharged by burning of fossil fuels, study findsRead moreIts chief executive, Bill Hare, said UNEP had barely mentioned the need to phase out fossil fuels or evidence showing “real zero” emissions was possible in many economic sectors by mid-century.The report’s authors cited earlier work that found limiting heating to about 1.8C required global emissions to be halved by 2035. They said existing national policies were projected to lead to at least 2.3C heating, but it would still be possible to limit stay below 2C if countries delivered on net zero emissions commitments by mid-century.Prof Richard Betts, from the University of Exeter and UK Met Office and another report author, said the flooding catastrophe caused by the collapse of rock and glacial ice in Nepal and China was a demonstration of why the world needed to limit overshoot and come back to 1.5C.“That specific event obviously is very complicated [but] we are committed to glacier loss,” he said. “We can stop them getting much worse by reducing emissions and limiting the amount of warming.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisHealthPacific islandsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest | Global development | The Guardian
description: Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site
Content: Rampal power plant on the Pasur River. A study found high levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples in the nearby Sundarbans wetlands.Photograph: NurPhoto/GettyView image in fullscreenRampal power plant on the Pasur River. A study found high levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples in the nearby Sundarbans wetlands.Photograph: NurPhoto/GettyGlobal developmentBarclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forestBangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage siteSupported byAbout this contentMatthew PearceWed 2 Sep 2026 11.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.02 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people inBangladeshand India.Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, aUnesco world heritage sitemade up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supportshundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”Last November, astudy found elevated levels of mercury and arsenicin water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.View image in fullscreenThe Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people.Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/AlamyMillions of people live in the Sundarbans, and manydepend on the riverand forests for food and other resources.The claimants allege thatBarclaysfailed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank ofIndiabetween 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, includingconcerns raised by Unescoin a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France,refused to support the projectbecause of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentClimate crisisBangladeshIndiaFossil fuelsEnergySouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Baby stabbed to death in Sheffield was found on top of washing machine, court told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Two men and two women charged with murder after body of newborn girl found with 33 stab wounds
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Two men and two women charged with murder after body of newborn girl found with 33 stab wounds
Content: Police were called to the Wincobank area of Sheffield on Sunday morning after reports of concern for the safety of an infant.Photograph: Iconic Media/SWNSView image in fullscreenPolice were called to the Wincobank area of Sheffield on Sunday morning after reports of concern for the safety of an infant.Photograph: Iconic Media/SWNSUK newsBaby stabbed to death in Sheffield was found on top of washing machine, court toldTwo men and two women charged with murder after body of newborn girl found with 33 stab woundsJosh HallidayNorth of England editorWed 2 Sep 2026 16.44 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 10.32 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA newborn baby girl died from multiple stab wounds before she was found on top of a washing machine in an outhouse in Sheffield, a court has heard.Two men and two women appeared in court on Wednesday charged with the murder of the newborn, named only as Baby S. She was found with 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings when police were called to a property in the Wincobank area of the city on Sunday.Andrea Skopova, 20, and Peter Horvath Jr, 19, have been charged with the baby’s murder, as have Horvath Jnr’s parents, Peter Horvath Sr, 38, and Nina Horvathova, 37.The four, all from Slovakia, are additionally charged with causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.Police were called to a property in Holywell Heights on Sunday morning after reports of concern for the safety of an infant. The prosecutor Luke Hopkinson told the court that Baby S was found wrapped in a towel in a blue bag in an outbuilding at an address in Holywell Heights.A 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons due to her age, has been charged with perverting the course of justice. The girl sobbed in the dock as representations were made about whether she should be released on bail.The district judge Tim Spruce decided she should be remanded in youth custody until Thursday, when she will appear at crown court with the other defendants. The four adults were all remanded in custody following the short hearing on Wednesday.Two women, 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remain on bail.DCI Tom Woodward, of South Yorkshire police, said: “This is a significant step in our investigation into the tragic circumstances that resulted in the death of this baby girl. I would like to thank our communities, who I know will have been deeply impacted by this traumatic incident, for supporting us as we work through this intricate investigation.“We would ask the public to avoid speculating and posting information online about this case while the legal process takes it course. Protecting the integrity of the criminal justice process is crucial to us securing justice for this little girl.”Bouquets of flowers had been left by a police cordon near the property in Holywell Heights on Wednesday.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Green party members back Zack Polanski to stand in London byelection | Green party | The Guardian
description: Party leader in England and Wales seen as favourite to contest Holborn and St Pancras after Starmer’s resignation
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Party leader in England and Wales seen as favourite to contest Holborn and St Pancras after Starmer’s resignation
Content: The Green party’s Zack Polanski is not a member of parliament at present.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenThe Green party’s Zack Polanski is not a member of parliament at present.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAGreen partyGreen party members back Zack Polanski to stand in London byelectionParty leader in England and Wales seen as favourite to contest Holborn and St Pancras after Starmer’s resignationAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentWed 2 Sep 2026 19.11 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski moved a step closer in his quest to become an MP on Wednesday, with local Green party members supporting him to become the party’s candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.The party leader in England and Wales started campaigning alongside his fellow Green, Hannah Spencer, the MP for Gorton and Denton, in the Holborn area on Tuesday, and is seriously considering putting himself forward as the party’s candidate in the seatvacated by Keir Starmer on Monday.Green party sources said local party members would have the final say on the selected candidate, but the Guardian understands local members are supportive of Polanski running, with no clear local activist with significant support expected to oppose him. It is understood nominations will open soon and candidates will be selected by the end of next week.Lorna Jane Russell, the leader of the Greens on the local Camden council, will not stand, having previously expressed a desire to focus on her role as the leader of the opposition at Camden Town Hall and her pregnancy.On the anniversary of his election on 2 September 2025, Polanski said the byelection would be a “referendum on ending rip-off Britain”, adding: “I am very excited for the next chapter for myself, for the Greens and for people across the country.”Sources inside the party in London said that therise in membership since Polanski became leadermade him the favourite for the role.“There would be a lot of excitement about him standing,” said one Green party source. “This is the kind of seat that has always had high-profile figures and I think having someone with Zack’s profile would play very well with local party members.”The move is not without risk for Polanski, with the former prime minister’s seat traditionally considered to be safe for Labour. The Green party leader may prefer to contest a seat in Hackney, wherethe party has recently won the mayoralty, if a sitting MP such as Diane Abbott were to step down. In a difficult political climate in the May local elections, Labour lost seats but held on to Camden council. “This is not Gorton and Denton,” said one Labour source. “The Burnham bounce will help.”Tulip Siddiq, the Labour MP for Hampstead and Highgate, said party members were already out campaigning and were confident they could retain the seat. “I know Camden through and through and I do believe that we can win this,” she said.Siddiq added: “I think theLabourvote is resilient and I think Andy Burnham’s pledges on the doorstep are being gratefully received by people in Camden.
