Certainly I’ll be out campaigning every day and giving it my best shot.”Labour will not run an all-women shortlist and will announce their candidate by next Wednesday, with applications closing on Friday and shortlisting expected by the start of next week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReform UK bans three journalists from its conference after critical reportingRead moreThe frontrunner is thought to be Sagal Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia and has been theleader of Camden council since May. “She’s got a compelling personal story and can reach people from all faiths and backgrounds in Camden,” said one Labour source. “She’s also been really active in the local party for a long time. Lots of people know her and like her.”Adam Hug, the former leader of Westminster council who lost his job leading the council when the Conservatives took control of itin May’s local election, is also a mooted name. Other possible candidates are Nash Ali, the former mayor of Camden, and Rishi Madlani, a former Camden councillor.Abdi-Wali is close to Starmer and local Labour sources said any attempts to bring in a candidate not from the area would be met with fierce criticism. “It will be interesting to see if Burnham has the same appeal in northLondonas Makerfield,” said one. “A lot of the policies he’s been talking about feel more geared towards the rest of the country, not really London.”Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiHannah SpencerKeir StarmerByelectionsLabourTulip SiddiqnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK government does not know what datacentres are being used for, FoI request shows | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Lack of information raises fears over environmental impact of the AI boom
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Lack of information raises fears over environmental impact of the AI boom
Content: An under-construction Equinix datacentre in Slough. The agglomeration of datacentres just west of London is the largest datacentre hub in Europe.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn under-construction Equinix datacentre in Slough. The agglomeration of datacentres just west of London is the largest datacentre hub in Europe.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesDatacentres - UKUK government does not know what datacentres are being used for, FoI request showsLack of information raises fears over environmental impact of the AI boomPippa NeillEnvironment reporterWed 2 Sep 2026 14.44 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.54 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government does not know what the country’s datacentres are being used for despite fears over the growing environmental impact of the AI boom.When asked in a freedom of information (FoI) request who was using the largest sites and what for, the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology said it did “not hold the requested information”. The ministryhas since been dissolved.With hundreds of datacentres awaiting planning permission and 315queueingto connect to the National Grid, there is growing concern over a lack of transparency and justification for these projects given their environmental impact.Ministers announced plans in January to allow qualifying datacentres to opt into the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project scheme. This lets developments bypass local planning committees by securing approval from the government. Campaigners say this “insulates” datacentres from local scrutiny.Zack Polanski, the Green party leader in England and Wales, said: “The government plans to steamroller over local opposition so private companies can build these facilities – yet they can’t even explain what the benefits are and who is benefiting.”View image in fullscreenPlans have been submitted for a third DataVita datacentre in Chapelhall, Airdrie. The Scottish government is said to be considering a moratorium on new datacentres.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianDatacentres use a huge amount of resources. The Guardianrevealed last monththat two planned sites will have higher carbon emissions than ExxonMobil in the UK, with concerns raised over how this will fit within the country’s carbon targets.The government designated datacentres as critical national infrastructure in 2024 and campaigners fear this could mean the water-hungry sites are prioritised over households in times of drought. Water UK, the trade body representing water companies in Britain and Northern Ireland,warned in Julythat the UK did not have enough water for the datacentre expansion.Polanski said: “What is more ‘critical’ than people’s access to water? What is more ‘critical’ than our need to transition to a low-energy, low-pollution world so we can put the brakes on climate extremes?”While there is consensus that datacentres can provide some essential services, there are concerns that developments with a huge environmental impact andlocal oppositionare being prioritised regardless of their use.Oliver Hayes of Global Action Plan, the environmental charity which submitted the FoI request, said: “It’s highly likely that we’re going to end up seeing datacentres given favourable and preferential treatment when it comes to resources that are actually running chatbots or enabling people to do benign and very wasteful, pointless things.“At the more serious end, these datacentres could be powering chatbots that enable people to nudify teens without their consent and much worse, frankly.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith reports that the Scottish government isinching towarda moratorium on new datacentres, there is growing pressure for the UK government to follow suit.Friends of the Earth is calling for a ban on new sites until environmental safeguards are in place. The campaign group wants the government to publish clear environmental rules for new and existing datacentres, including requirements for 100% additional renewable energy generation for new projects.Anisah Khan, the campaigns manager at Global Action Plan, said: “When individuals across the country are facing hosepipe bans and essential housebuilding is being delayed because datacentres are gobbling up grid connections, what we need is not more chatbots at any cost.”The government did not respond to a request for comment over its failure to say what large datacentres were being used for.A spokesperson said: “A pause on building new datacentres would simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on other countries for the processing of sensitive health and defence data. Put simply: it would be a disaster for jobs and national security.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKAI (artificial intelligence)Freedom of informationClimate crisisWaterGreenhouse gas emissionsWater industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Swedish minister defends strict post-Brexit removals of Britons | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Minister says Sweden has ‘fulfilled its commitments’ amid criticism of ‘unjust’ deportation decisions such as case of Joyce Thomas
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Minister says Sweden has ‘fulfilled its commitments’ amid criticism of ‘unjust’ deportation decisions such as case of Joyce Thomas
Content: Johan Forssell, the migration minister, said the European Commission was onboard with Sweden’s approach.Photograph: Joel Lindhe/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJohan Forssell, the migration minister, said the European Commission was onboard with Sweden’s approach.Photograph: Joel Lindhe/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockSwedenSwedish minister defends strict post-Brexit removals of BritonsMinister says Sweden has ‘fulfilled its commitments’ amid criticism of ‘unjust’ decisions such as case of Joyce ThomasLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentWed 2 Sep 2026 13.59 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Swedish government has doubled down on its position on removing and deporting British citizens on the grounds they were late to apply for permission to stay afterBrexit.The migration minister, Johan Forssell, issued a robust defence of the Swedish migration agency’s implementation of the Brexit withdrawal agreement on Wednesday in response to aquestion from an MPabout the case of Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old British widow who has beenordered to leave the country after 21 years.Forssell said theEuropean Commission, which is legally mandated to ensure EU member states implement the withdrawal agreement correctly, was onboard with Sweden’s approach.“The migration board has followed up on the application of the withdrawal agreement and the assessment is thatSwedenhas fulfilled its commitments. This assessment is shared by the commission,” he said.There has been growing controversy over removal orders issued to British citizens who did not know that Sweden was one of 13 countries in the EU that required formal applications to stay in the country post-Brexit.British man deported from Sweden despite living there since childhoodRead moreIn another case, a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, has been deported despite havinglived in Sweden since he was 10.Thomas’s local MP, Häkan Svenneling, of the Left party, told the Guardian: “It seems to me that the Swedish government thinks everything is fine even though British citizens are being deported from Sweden right now. Not acting is also an action in this situation. What Sweden needs is a new government and a new migration minister who stops deporting people with strong connections to Sweden.”In his written answer to Svenneling, Forssell offered British citizens facing deportation a sliver of hope. He said: “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future.”View image in fullscreenJoyce Thomas, 78, has been ordered to leave Sweden after living there for 21 years.Photograph: Felix AndlerThomas has been told she must remove herself from Sweden by Tuesday 8 September or face deportation and a potential ban from the Schengen area.She is one of several British citizens who have been faced with removal orders after the migration agency rejected their late applications to stay.The UK Foreign Office has raised Sweden’s approach to late applications for post-Brexit residency a number of times in the specialised committee on citizens’ rights, a structure set up to ensure the withdrawal agreement is implemented properly.David Milstead, who runs the grassroots organisation Brits in Sweden, said the Swedish response was not a surprise. “The government was hardly going to disown the decisions of [the migration agency] or the Swedish courts. The real question is whether Sweden’s approach is consistent with EU law and the [withdrawal agreement],” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe pointed out that under the agreement, the UK was obliged to set up a statutory body, the Independent Monitoring Authority (IMA), to independently ensure the Home Office implemented the Brexit deal correctly, while the European Commission performed the correspondent role for EU member states.“The IMA has taken a much more robust approach. It is hard to imagine it not challenging the UK had it operated a policy like Sweden’s, which would have put the rights of around a quarter of a million successful late applicants [in the UK] at risk,” Milstead said.“Sweden’s approach now needs either to be tested before the European court of justice or addressed through measures that remedy the problem. The government’s response leaves open the possibility of change, and that must include fixing unjust deportation decisions.”The European Commission has been approached for comment.According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025 a total of 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. Analysis by the Foreign Office found this was 32.9% of the 7,565 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU member states over this period. Although it is not possible to determine exactly how many were in Sweden prior to the end of the UK-EU transition period, it is likely that the majority will have been.Thomas has been in Sweden for 21 years and says her late husband inquired about the impact of Brexit and was told by the authorities there was nothing they needed to do to remain in the country legally.The couple moved to the country to be close to their son and grandchildren, and Thomas said she had been leftfeeling sick with worryafter receiving the removal order.Explore more on these topicsSwedenBrexitEuropean CommissionEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian airspace becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, Zelenskyy says | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukraine president says aviation industry needs to take account of growing number of Ukrainian drones in Russia
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Ukraine president says aviation industry needs to take account of growing number of Ukrainian drones in Russia
Content: Smoke billows across the skyline in Podolsk, south of Moscow, after a Ukrainian drone attack in July.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke billows across the skyline in Podolsk, south of Moscow, after a Ukrainian drone attack in July.Photograph: ReutersUkraineRussian airspace becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, Zelenskyy saysUkraine president says aviation industry needs to take account of growing number of Ukrainian drones in RussiaDan Sabbaghin Kyiv,Pjotr Sauer, andJennifer Rankinin BrusselsWed 2 Sep 2026 16.52 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.18 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has declared that Russia’s airspace is becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, as Vladimir Putin promised to increase strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities in the run-up to winter.TheUkrainian president saidthere was no intention to directly threaten civilian flights, but the growing number of attack drones being flown into Russia by Ukraine would have to be “taken into account” by the aviation industry.“We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelenskyy said in a statement.Ukraine’s foreign secretary, Andrii Sybiha, said Kyiv had notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that “Russian airspace is not safe for civilian aviation” because of increased military activity.A rapid escalation of Ukrainian military capability in the past few months has allowed Ukraine’s forces to strike at targets around Moscow, St Petersburg and otherlocations deep inside Russia.Reliable figures for the number of drone flights are hard to obtain but Ukraine is already capable of launching a few hundred a day, and military sources say the country is chasing a target of 1,000 drones in an effort to hurt Russia’s economy.Justin Bronk, an aviation analyst at the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, said he believed Ukraine could force “periodic closures of Russian airports on a semi-regular basis” by relying on an element of surprise.It could do so by flying small waves of drones at short notice, though trying to close an airport permanently would be difficult, he said, because a sustained attack would become predictable and easier for air-defence systems to halt.Ukraine’s commercial airspace has been closed since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 because Russia has been able to strike targets throughout the country, making airports unsafe for civilians.This year, Ukraine began bombing oil refineries and warehouses near Moscow and St Petersburg, as well as hitting military and industrial sites at ranges in excess of 2,000km (1,250 miles) from its border.Concerns linger about the safety of civilian aviation in the war zone. A Malaysian Airlines planeflying over eastern Ukraine in July 2014 was shot downby Russian separatists operating a surface-to-air missile launcher. All 298 people onboard were killed.Putin described Zelenskyy’s remarks as “state terrorism”, saying: “Negotiations are not conducted with terrorists.”Giving one of his most detailed updates on the war, the Russian leader told a news conference that Moscow was preparing to increase its bombing of Ukrainian energy facilities this winter, aiming to knock out heating and electricity supplies.“The Russian armed forces have been ordered to prepare and carry out mass strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. They are striking us, and they will get a response,” Putin told reporters after a two-day summit in Kyrgyzstan. “I’m not saying we’ll collapse the economy there, but it’s a serious challenge for them.”View image in fullscreenPutin said Russian armed forces had been ordered to prepare and carry out mass strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities.Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/EPAAsked whether Russia would strike British military facilities in the UK that produced weapons for Ukraine, Putin sidestepped the question, saying: “That’s a military secret.”Russia earlieraccused the UK of “escalation”and threatened “consequences” after reports that British-made drones were used by Ukraine in long-range strikes deep inside its territory.Putin sought to stress that Russian forces retained the initiative on the battlefield in Ukraine, despite Moscow’s slowing progress. He appeared to push back against western intelligence reports suggesting he was being given an overly optimistic picture of the war, saying he relied on numerous sources of information that together provided him with an “objective assessment” of the battlefield.Russia’s sluggish advance on the battlefield has fuelled speculation that the Kremlin could resort to another round of mobilisation, the first since Putin called up about 300,000 reservists in September 2022.Zelenskyy and western officials have said Moscow could be preparing such a move, though its diplomats do not consider it a certainty. Putin dismissed the prospect as “nonsense”.What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?Read moreAlso on Wednesday, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said a drone attack on Leipzig airport marked a new escalation by Russia, and that it fitted a broader pattern of “repeated incursions in our airspace, drones that paralyse our airports, interference with our critical infrastructure”.TheGerman government said on Tuesdaythat Russia was responsible for a drone laden with explosives which was discovered at Leipzig airport last month near a Ukrainian plane used to transport weapons.Von der Leyen said: “Europeans are faced with the hard truth that this is the new normal. We have to step up, and that means being ready to respond to Russia’s recklessness faster and better.”The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, told reporters Russia had grown “increasingly reckless” and there had been an increase “in malign activities targeting our territory directly”.The EU is drawing up further sanctions against Russia targeting about 1,600 companies and individuals. Poland’s foreign minister, Radek Sikorski, said the bloc should pass these sanctions in response to the Leipzig attack and others. “Hybrid war is not just nuisance on the internet,” he said, speaking on the sidelines of a meeting with his European counterparts.“Hybrid war meansassassination squads, it meansarsonists, it meansblowing up moving trains, like in Poland, it meansbreaches of airspace with dronesandcruise missiles. We need to convince Putin that such actions are not for free.”The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the Leipzig attacks had the “hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism”, adding that Brussels had summoned Russia’s ambassador to the bloc.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaAirline industryEuropeDrones (military)Volodymyr ZelenskyyVladimir PutinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities
Author: William Christou
Headline: Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities
Content: 1:28Iran retaliates after US missile strike reportedly hits wedding – videoUS-Israel war on IranIran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at weddingBlast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilitiesWilliam Christouin BeirutWed 2 Sep 2026 16.19 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 12.56 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has accused the US of a war crime after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikesprompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities.Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people.Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi.“It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride,told Mehr News.8:08Iran retaliates after US strikes reportedly kill wedding guests - The LatestA video of the aftermath shows colourful wedding streamers and decorations strewn across the ground, and shoes abandoned in the rush to escape the attack.“You wicked people have attacked people’s homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral,” said a man filming the aftermath of the strike, shared by Fars news agency.The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals.Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”.The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”.“If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.View image in fullscreenFootage of the aftermath of the strike shows a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris.Photograph: Iranian Red Crescent/AFP/Getty ImagesThe US attacksfollowed strikes on Sunday, endinga month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran, and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets.Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devastating” retaliation.Videos of the aftermath of the strikeshow a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watchingas injured children were being treated.“When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency.View image in fullscreenThe strike on Kuhestak appeared to signal another cycle of escalation in the US-Iran conflict.Photograph: Masoud Mohamadi/Tasnim News/AFP/Getty ImagesA woman with her hands decorated in henna for the nuptials posted a video on Instagram after the attack, saying “my hands and feet are still shaking”.A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”.‘Her head was broken’: parents at Iranian school bombed by US describe their worst dayRead moreIn February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation.Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to showthe internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst,identified some of the remnantsas belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missiletouted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate”.It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footagecaptured at least six strikesin the area within a minute. A separate strikeappeared to hit a communications towerabout 150 metres away from the home.Authorities said that several “telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged in the latest strikes”.View image in fullscreenA separate strike on Kuhestak hit a communications tower about 150 metres from the home where the wedding was being held.Photograph: Masoud Mohammadi/APThe US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply.Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board.In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticism | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: Energy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeks to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is transformation of relations
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Energy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeks to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is transformation of relations
Content: Chris Wright and Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s interim president, during a meeting over an oil agreement at the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChris Wright and Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s interim president, during a meeting over an oil agreement at the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesVenezuelaTrump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticismEnergy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeks to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is transformation of relationsTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroWed 2 Sep 2026 15.44 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.23 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking to commandeer huge quantities of Venezuelan oil, amid growing criticism of Donald Trump’senergy dealwith the country’s interim leaders.“Absolutely not,” Wright replied when asked by a CNBC journalist if the US was engaged in a “heavy-handed” attempt to “take” Venezuelan oil in violation of the South American country’s constitution.Wright landed in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Tuesday night, four days after Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.“I think we are seeing an absolutely historic transformation of both Venezuela and the relations between Venezuela and the US,”Wright saidof the deal, which Trump has claimed will give the US control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil. “This is President Trump’s grand plan to replace conflict with commerce,” Wright said.The White Housesaysthe deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves. But there has been criticism from across the political spectrum.The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Trump’s deal with Venezuela’s unelected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, “looks less like a normal commercial transaction than it doesthe famous sceneof US businessmen meeting with the Cuban strongman in The Godfather Part II”.“The US government is essentially getting in bed with a foreign dictator and her favored capitalist,” the newspaper complained, in reference to Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan tycoon at the centre of the deal.View image in fullscreenDelcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s unelected interim president, has said the deal had ‘endless’ benefits.Photograph: Venezuelan Presidency/AFP/Getty ImagesThe economist Francisco Rodrígueztold Democracy Now: “It’s clear that this is not a deal that any Venezuelan government would have entered into unless this country had been subject to an invasion, and unless its authorities had been held at gunpoint. So I think we’ve replaced gunboat diplomacy now for gunpoint diplomacy.”Delcy Rodríguez was installed as interim president on 5 January, two days after the president, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces during a predawn raid on Caracas.Trump warned Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president, she would face an even worse fate if she did not toe the US line.Since Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez has made a series of once unthinkable concessions to US officials who their nominally socialist political movement, Chavismo, had spent years denouncing as predatory imperialists bent on stealing Venezuela’s natural resources.On Saturday,Rodríguez claimedthe oil deal had “endless” benefits and would help produce more than $209bn in revenues that could be used to improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said during a televised broadcast to the nation.The deal has dealt a body blow to Venezuela’s political opposition, who fear Trump is unlikely to push for a democratic transition or fresh presidential elections given his lucrative arrangement with Rodríguez.“This is a game between theTrump administrationand Delcy and her people,” one opposition figure lamented after the deal was unveiled.Speaking at a signing ceremony in the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday, Rodríguez thanked the Trump administration for its part in what she called a “win-win deal”. She said: “I have faith in the future of Venezuela. What we are doing today represents the future and the hope of the people of Venezuela.”Explore more on these topicsVenezuelaUS foreign policyTrump administrationDelcy RodríguezOilAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s a fever dream right now’: sailors of USS Abraham Lincoln voice joy after arriving in Thailand | US military | The Guardian
description: Shore leave in Pattaya, known for its red light district, comes after reports of deteriorating living conditions onboard the vessel during record stint
Author: Natasha May
Headline: Shore leave in Pattaya, known for its red light district, comes after reports of deteriorating living conditions onboard the vessel during record stint
Content: Pattaya’s mayor, Poramet Ngampichet, greets Capt Dan Keeler of the USS Abraham Lincoln.Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/ReutersView image in fullscreenPattaya’s mayor, Poramet Ngampichet, greets Capt Dan Keeler of the USS Abraham Lincoln.Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/ReutersUS military‘It’s a fever dream right now’: sailors of USS Abraham Lincoln voice joy after arriving in ThailandShore leave in Pattaya, known for its red light district, comes after reports of deteriorating living conditions onboard the vessel during record stintMiddle East crisis live – latest updatesNatasha Mayin PattayaWed 2 Sep 2026 12.48 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt Pattaya’s Hard Rock Cafe and hotel, the city’s mayor and police officials, along with women in traditional Thai dress, waited to greet the sailors who were arriving in civilian clothes, bags slung over their shoulders, off the buses.The USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew of 5,000 had not been on shore for nearly nine months, a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea.Crew appeared to have been told not to speak to the gathered journalists about the reportedlydeteriorating living conditionsonboard but said they were looking forward to being on dry land, sleeping and going home.One sailor, Breese, who did not want to give his surname, said “it’s a fever dream right now” and he was looking forward to trying Thai food for the first time and meeting new people.View image in fullscreenUS service personnel from the USS Abraham Lincoln arrive in Pattaya for their first shore leave in almost nine months.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesOnce a quiet fishing village, Pattaya was transformed during the Vietnam war into one of the most infamous red light districts in the world with the arrival of American troops using military bases inThailand.At its peak, tens of thousands ofUS militarypersonnel came through each year, said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor specialising in tourism at Bangkok University. “In my opinion, it’s really the founding influence for the town. The US military turned a quiet fishing village into a global destination for an international nightlife and entertainment hub in about 15 years,” he said.Although the American troops left by the mid-70s, the sex industry infrastructure continued to grow, with European tourists taking their place, and more recently waves of Chinese and Russian visitors, Pipatpong said.The Hard Rock hotel is around the corner from the Soi 6 alley, known for its go-go bars, one of the many areas that contribute toPattaya’s sex tourism industry. Soi 6 and the neighbouring area would be off-limits for crew after sunset, said Pattaya’s mayor, Poramet Ngampichet.However, Walking Street, the town’s other entertainment and red light district, was displaying a massive neon sign at its entrance saying: “Pattaya City is pleased to welcome USS Abraham Lincoln carrier and its personnel.”The sailors were being released in staggered groups, so not everyone was out. Shakeira Fairfax, who had travelled all the way from New Jersey, had to wait one more day to be reunited with her sailor daughter, Jada Fairfax.View image in fullscreenShakeira Fairfax has flown over to Thailand to greet her daughter in person.Photograph: Natasha May/The GuardianFairfax said she was mostly excited. “I just want to pick her up and spin her around. She’s my baby always,” but, she said, “I don’t know who I’m welcoming home.”Jada finished her basic training last October and was shipped out a month later, two months before theUS and Israel launched their war on Iran. Jada celebrated her 25th birthday onboard in June.Fairfax said there was an “abrupt” stop to communication when the war broke out, but she had since been able to check in with her intermittently and send care packages.View image in fullscreenA welcoming ceremony was held at the Hard Rock hotel for the US navy crew.Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/ReutersThe ship’s captain, Dan Keeler, acknowledged to the media that the carrier “looks like a dirty car in a parking lot”. As for the reports of the conditions onboard, he said: “I don’t know how to say it other than there’s a disconnect between reporting back home and what’s happening on the ship.”Keeler added: “First-time sailors are going to complain about the food, the living conditions, similar to sending kids off to college for the first time. We did get caught up in an election cycle and got thrown around like a football.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDan Keeler, centre, speaks to the press outside the Hard Rock hotel in Pattaya on Wednesday.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesKeeler said there was plenty of food on the ship but admitted it became hard to get fresh fruit and vegetables, which stopped being served. “I am looking forward to a fresh salad.” They also had to be careful with supplies of soap and toothpaste to ensure every sailor could receive some, he added.Asked about the reports ofattempted suicidesonboard the ship, Keeler did not answer, saying there was an open investigation. As for comments from Donald Trump, which included claims that the 270-day deployment was “not nearly long enough”, Keeler told the Guardian: “The president speaks for himself.”Crew from the USS Higgins also arrived at the Hard Rock hotel. When asked about the conditions onboard the two vessels, Ethan Johnson, a cook on the Higgins, said: “We joined the military, it’s not a cruise ship.”Johnson said there was plenty of meat and vegetables onboard the Higgins.View image in fullscreenThe nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln in the Gulf of Thailand near the city of Pattaya.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesAs well as being prohibited from entering certain areas, sailors are also being prevented from doing any water sports in the area, owing to the potential danger.Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian electionRead moreThey will also not be allowed to visit pharmacies as Thai authorities do not want sailors accessing medicines that do not require a prescription in Thailand but may need a prescription in the US, Poramet said.Kristopher Robinson, a naval attache with the US embassy, said Pattaya was chosen as the destination for rest and relaxation because the “people of Thailand have a history of being wonderful hosts not just to US sailors but people from all around”.Robinson said the crew would take as much opportunity for rest as possible and conduct themselves in accordance with US and local laws. “Sailors here, like all tourists, they’re going to enjoy Pattaya’s great food and wonderful culture,” he said.8:08Iran retaliates after US strikes reportedly kill wedding guests - The LatestExplore more on these topicsUS militaryThailandDonald TrumpfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration sides with OpenAI in lawsuit against New York Times | Technology | The Guardian
description: The Times and many companies are accusing OpenAI of misusing their material to train AI systems without compensation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Times and many companies are accusing OpenAI of misusing their material to train AI systems without compensation
Content: OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman speaks at the G20 innovation ministerial summit in North Carolina on Wednesday.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman speaks at the G20 innovation ministerial summit in North Carolina on Wednesday.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersTechnologyTrump administration sides with OpenAI in lawsuit against New York TimesThe Times and many companies are accusing OpenAI of misusing their material to train AI systems without compensationGuardian staff and agenciesWed 2 Sep 2026 21.39 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 21.52 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administrationis supporting OpenAI in ⁠a lawsuit against the New York Times, arguing in favor of the use of copyrighted writing to train artificial intelligence.The Times accusesOpenAIand its largest financial backer, Microsoft, of using millions of newspaper articles without permission to train OpenAI’s popular chatbot. Other newspapers have joined in the suit, first filed in 2023.In a brief filed in Manhattan federal court on Tuesday, the US government weighed in for the first time on lawsuits over the tense battle over AI and copyright. A brief has advisory rather than legal weight but could bolster tech ⁠companies as they fight the claims.“The United States has a strong interest in continuing to develop a robust and competitive artificial intelligence industry that sets the standard for the practice and procedure of AI use globally … As such, it is critical for the United States to ‘retain global leadership in artificial intelligence’,” the brief said.Copyright owners, including authors, publishers, music labels and news outlets, have filed dozens of lawsuits over AI training against tech companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms. They say the companies ⁠misuse their material to train AI systems and do so without compensation.For AI chatbots to generate responses, machine learning systems are first fed billions of lines of text. The bots produce their output by statistical analysis of what the next word should be by matching a user’s query to parts of the database.Spokespeople for the Times and OpenAI did not immediately respond ‌to requests for comment on the filing on Wednesday.“AI dominance is critical to promote national security, prosperity, and economic mobility for all Americans,” US associate attorney general Stanley Woodward Jr said in a statement posted to X. “This Administration will never let our Nation be at a disadvantage relative to our foreign adversaries based on a plainly incorrect understanding of copyright law.”The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, separately told G20 officials ‌at a meeting in North Carolina on Wednesday that their countries should embrace fair use and allow AI companies to train their models on creators’ work while finding ​a way to “protect artists”.All of the pending cases will probably ​revolve around whether AI systems make ​fair use of copyrighted material by ​using it to create new, transformative content. The first two judges to consider the ​question issued diverging rulings ‌last year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government ​agreed with ​tech companies in Tuesday’s brief that AI training is “extraordinarily” transformative.“Beyond the subject matter of this litigation, LLMs are already helping researchers across fields achieve major breakthroughs,” the brief said. “Constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAINew York TimesTrump administrationNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order | Apple | The Guardian
description: Tech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with Canada
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Tech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with Canada
Content: Apple has followed Google in changing Lake Ontario to Lake America in its Maps app, right, after an executive order signed by Donald Trump.Composite: The Washington Post/ABACA/Shutterstock, Apple MapsView image in fullscreenApple has followed Google in changing Lake Ontario to Lake America in its Maps app, right, after an executive order signed by Donald Trump.Composite: The Washington Post/ABACA/Shutterstock, Apple MapsAppleApple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump orderTech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with CanadaMarina DunbarWed 2 Sep 2026 22.15 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 20.06 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple has renamed Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after anexecutive orderfrom Donald Trump to change the name of the Great Lake amid his trade spat with Canada.TheAppleMaps app now displays the controversial new name for the lake, which sits between New York state and the Canadian province of Ontario, for users in the US. Apple users outside the country will still see the Lake Ontario name.Apple had been reportedly mulling whether to submit to Trump’s new order after receiving a personalrequestfrom the president for the tech company to change the lake’s name.Trump welcomed the news, declaring ina Truth Socialpost that the adoption of “Lake America” by Google Maps and Apple Maps meant the name change was “complete, ratified, and binding”. However, the US cannot compel Canada – or any other country – to also change the name.Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalatesRead moreThe US president officially unveiled the name swap last week. He did not mention his escalating trade feud with the US’s northern neighbors in the order, but the timing suggested a retaliatory move after Canadian officials denounced Trump’s new sweeping tariffs and promised to instate tariffs of their own.Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, rejected the attempt to rename the body of water, saying in apost on social mediathat the lake’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.Late last month, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed, with the US subsequently imposing a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports. Trump additionally threatened another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney retaliated with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.Rather than mention any of this, Trump instead said inthe orderthat the purpose of the renaming is to honor “the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements”.Earlier this week, Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, said in an interview with Fox Business that “the president has reached out to Apple directly” and predicted with confidence that US users would “be seeing that change coming up soon”.Apple’s competitor, Google, alreadymade the changeover the weekend, with Google Maps now showing the Lake America branding. Google cited Trump’s order and its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).In ablogpostissued on Saturday, Google said US users would see the Lake America name while users in Canada will see Lake Ontario, and “those outside of the US and Canada will see both names.”The digital name change is unsurprising considering Google Maps was anearly adopterof the Gulf of America moniker and still currently displays the title, despite the renaminghardlybeing a success outside US government lingo.On Tuesday, it was reported that MapQuest, the pioneering online mapping app,reached the No 1 spoton Apple’s App Store after openly rejecting Trump’s request to rename the lake. The app simplyposteda screenshot of Lake Ontario on social media last Thursday along with the caption: “We’re not changing it.”The act of defiance was enough to catapult the app into becoming the most in-demand navigation tool in the US.Explore more on these topicsAppleDonald TrumpCanadaMark CarneyAmericasTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Temperature check: alarm as prediction markets lean into weather and climate bets | US news | The Guardian
description: Climate experts warn that US Kalshi and Polymarket users are ‘gamifying disasters’ as they bet on events like heatwaves and daily temperatures
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Climate experts warn that US Kalshi and Polymarket users are ‘gamifying disasters’ as they bet on events like heatwaves and daily temperatures
Content: A Kalshi ad in Manhattan, New York City, in June 2026.Photograph: Richard Levine/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Kalshi ad in Manhattan, New York City, in June 2026.Photograph: Richard Levine/AlamyUS newsTemperature check: alarm as prediction markets lean into weather and climate betsClimate experts warn that US Kalshi and Polymarket users are ‘gamifying disasters’ as they bet on events like heatwaves and daily temperaturesOliver MilmanWed 2 Sep 2026 16.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.04 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnline prediction markets, saturated by money staked on sport, crypto and politics, have now set their sights on a promising new area of growth: betting on the future livability of the planet itself.The rise of gamified predictions on the unfolding climate crisis, and shorter-term weather forecasts, has been underscored bya new dealthat allows Kalshi, a leading online financial exchange, to access data from the Weather Company, owner of the Weather Channel, to verify weather-related betting outcomes.The weather is “one of the fastest-growing and most crucial categories” at Kalshi, the company said, with monetized predictions made by people, and bots, on weather and climate events growing 500% in the past year into a $1.1bn market.“The long-term vision is to financialize everything and create a tradable asset out of any difference in opinion,” Tarek Mansour, co-founder of Kalshi,saidof the company’s broader objectives last year.Startlingly, Kalshi even claims that this gauge of public opinion can not only act as a financial hedge for businesses exposed to extreme weather,but also help shape the weather forecasts themselves. Kalshi’s betting markets will appear on the Weather Channel’s app, which is used by more than 330 million people worldwide.“Given the severity of the climate crisis, it’s crucial for policymakers and the general public to have well-calibrated forecasting data about future climate impacts,” said a Kalshi spokesperson, citing acompany studyon how accurate its markets’ predictions are. Asked whether this meant Kalshi saw its weather markets as part of delivering well-calibrated forecasting data, the spokesperson said this was the case.“Weather is the ultimate equalizer – it fundamentally affects everyone and everything,” the spokesperson said.People visiting Kalshi or Polymarket, its main rival, can bet on weather predictions such ashow hotit will be in certain places on a given day, as well as longer-term bets – fromhow manyclimate-fueled disasters the US will have, towhether the worldwill avoid catastrophic global heating, to howseverethe die-off of corals in Hawaii will be.You can evenwagerhow far Lake Mead, the US’s largest reservoir and a crucial water source for the American west, will drop below itsalready record-low levels. Last year, amid ruinous wildfires in Los Angeles, there were $1.2m in bets laid on Polymarket on the extent of the fires, with one user posting that “volume so high in this market it cause another fire”.While Polymarket’s international platform still hosts wildfire bets, US consumers are barred from accessing them. Kalshi meanwhile has never offered wildfire markets, citing “perverse incentives”.Distinctions can be hard to draw, though – the websites will allowbettingon, for example, the severity of heatwaves in Phoenix, Arizona, even thoughup to 500deaths in Maricopa county, which includes Phoenix, are being investigated as possibly heat-related. Excessive heat is the biggest killer among extreme weather events in the US.For scientists and people affected by climate-related disasters, though, it has been troubling to see the painful consequences of an overheating world turned into an online money-making market.When theEaton fireswept through Los Angeles county last year, killing at least 19 people and razing thousands of buildings, the home of Kaitlyn Trudeau’s grandfather was among those destroyed.View image in fullscreenTrees sway in high winds as the Eaton fire burns homes on 8 January 2025 in Altadena, California.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APWhile he was unhurt, Trudeau, a climate scientist at the non-profit Climate Central, said it “left a bad taste in my mouth imagining people making money off it. People were posting ‘that was fun, until next time!’ I’d be lying if I said it didn’t hurt a bit.“The dehumanization of these events really concerns me. I worry about the gamification of this because it distances us from the impacts of climate change, it affects our empathy,” said Trudeau, who added that she questioned Kalshi’s blurring of distinction of weather and climate and how such bets are adjudicated.“I find it depressing because it’s distracting us from what we should be focusing on,” she said. “I’m not against prediction markets in general but we need to be clear about the downsides. They aren’t going to reduce the risks of climate change or solve climate change.”Kalshi’s claims around weather forecasting are “confusing”, Trudeau added. “I’d be curious to know which resolved markets are related to future climate impacts and what sources they used to calibrate them,” she said. “Since calibration is measured by comparing many predictions against many realized outcomes, how can a market be calibrated on impacts that, by definition, haven’t happened yet?”Placing bets on the weather or the broader climate is harmful “because of all of the perverse incentives this can create, especially among bad actors with malicious intentions”, said Michael Mann, a climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania who said he worried about the bets fueling conspiracy theories about weather manipulation.Other critics contend that the public’s understanding of actual weather data could be obscured or even altered by big-money betting. Kalshi, Polymarket and the Weather Company all dismissed concerns of potential improper practices, pointing to company policies and federal regulation deterringinsider tradingand conflict of interest.View image in fullscreenAn advertisement for prediction market platform Kalshi hangs in Washington on 1 April 2026.Photograph: Allison Robbert/AP“We view weather data through the lens of decision intelligence and risk management – not gamification,” said a Weather Company spokesperson about the deal with Kalshi. “This partnership elevates weather data into a highly reliable tool, allowing both individuals and mission-critical enterprises to better quantify and manage real-world weather outcomes.”Polymarket, meanwhile, said it saw itself in grander terms than a mere betting website for people facing the perils of a hurricane, wildfire or heatwave made far fiercer by the burning of fossil fuels.“When tragedy unfolds, people turn to the news for commentary and they come to Polymarket for information,” said a company spokesperson. “While we are not blind to the risks, removing these markets does not prevent a tragedy but makes the most accurate information less accessible to the people who need it most.”While they are booming in popularity, however, the wagering platforms are under increasing scrutiny from federallawmakersandseveral states. Last week, a federal appeals courtruledthat states can regulate prediction markets like gambling, after a case brought by Nevada, which had attempted to shut down Kalshi.This mounting legal and regulatory pressure means that sites that allow wagers on everything from the value of gold to thewords mentioned in a Donald Trump speechmay find the climate crisis a less politically fraught arena to focus on, even though the topic still only attracts a small fraction of the bets laid online, experts point out.“They have to convince the courts they aren’t a gambling platform for sports and crypto,” said Jamie Pietruska, an economic historian at Rutgers University. “The weather and climate are seemingly innocuous in comparison. There isa longstanding beliefthat the weather can’t be controlled so it’s perfect to bet on and different to other categories, such as geopolitics.”Much like how CNN already includes prediction market outcomes in its political coverage, the Weather Channel could soon feature Kalshi odds amid its own forecasts, Pietruska said, further warping public trust in the National Weather Service, the bedrock federal forecasting agency that has faceddeep cutsunder the Trump administration.“Who is the wisdom of the crowds in that situation? There are casual betters, dumb money and weather trading bots,” said Pietruska. “Is that going to produce a forecast better than a meteorologist? Is that just vibes weather?”What will this all do to the public’s appetite to address global heating? One2023 studyfound that participating in a climate prediction market elevated concerns about the climate crisis and even altered the viewpoint of those who denied established climate science.View image in fullscreenBuildings are seen in the flood-damaged Bright Angel Canyon on 31 August, in Grand Canyon national park in Arizona.Photograph: John Locher/AP“The only thing that seems to work in changing minds of climate deniers [is] to let them put their money where their mouth is,” said Moran Cerf, a Columbia University researcher who led the study.Still, Cerf said, the negatives of wagering on the climate outweigh the positives. “It’s bad, in one word,” he said. “The prediction markets have taken a turn to the dark side by gamifying disasters. The fact it’s unregulated, unlike the stock market, means it is getting worse, too.”Pietruska shares these misgivings. “I’ve been uncomfortable with this sort of betting for some time. It has serious moral consequences,” she said. “An academic study isn’t the same as the speed and scale of the new casinos that are being set up.“If I go online and see the perception that the world will pass 2C (3.6F) warming by 2050, it creates a sense of a predetermined future, even though this is an aggregation of public opinion. It’s not a truth machine.”Listing climate-related disasters next to the timing of Taylor Swift’s next album or the winner of the next Super Bowl “casualizes and trivializes catastrophe and human suffering”, Pietruska said. “The wisdom of crowds isn’t going to encourage the community building and solidarity we need to address the climate crisis. That is not good, to say the least.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsPrediction marketsSport bettingGamblingClimate crisisUS weatherExtreme weatherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Google defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech sale | Google | The Guardian
description: Judge declines to make Google sell AdX in win for firm against US antitrust enforcers’ attempts to break up big tech
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Judge declines to make Google sell AdX in win for firm against US antitrust enforcers’ attempts to break up big tech
Content: Google’s office on 19 May 2025 in New York City.Photograph: Gary Hershorn/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGoogle’s office on 19 May 2025 in New York City.Photograph: Gary Hershorn/Corbis/Getty ImagesGoogleGoogle defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech saleJudge declines to make Google sell AdX in win for firm against US antitrust enforcers’ attempts to break up big techReutersWed 2 Sep 2026 19.37 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 21.03 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlphabet’s Google escaped a breakup of its advertising technology business on Wednesday, when a judge in Virginia ⁠rejected US antitrust enforcers’ attempt to force a sale of Google’s online advertising exchange.While the ad exchange is a small part of Google’s business, the ruling is the second powerful ⁠symbolic victory against the US Department ⁠of Justice in ​its efforts to forceGoogleto sell assets to address illegal monopolies.US judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, declined to make Google sell AdX, where publishers pay Google a ⁠20% fee to sell ads in auctions that happen instantly when users load websites. She accepted most of the parties’ proposed behavioral remedies.The justice department and a broad coalition of states sued Google in 2023 over ⁠its dominance in markets for advertising technology used by online publishers and websites.In April 2025, Brinkema ruled that Google holds ​illegal monopolies on servers that host publisher ads and ad ‌exchanges which sit between buyers and ‌sellers. Google unlawfully locked publishers on its ad server into using its AdX, the judge found.The tech company’s anticompetitive conduct “substantially harmed ‌Google’s publisher customers, the competitive process, and, ultimately, consumers of information on the open web”, Brinkema said at the time.At a trial last year on remedies in the case, the justice department argued that Google cannot be trusted to run AdX, given its past behavior.Google argued that a forced sale would be technically difficult and result in a long and painful transition that would hurt customers. The company also sought to show the justice department’s demand was different from Google’s own previous offer ‌to sell AdX to end an EU antitrust investigation, which Reuters reported in 2024.Ad Manager represented 4.1% of Google’s overall revenue and 1.5% of operating profit in 2020, according to Wedbush research and analysis of ​court documents. More recent figures were redacted from court documents.The ruling is the third time in a row that a judge has rejected a bid by US antitrust enforcers to break up big tech in a crackdown that started during Donald Trump’s first term. It is likely to fuel questions about whether courts are up to the task of checking ⁠the industry’s unprecedented power over the US economy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA federal judge in Washington last year rejected the ​Federal Trade Commission’s attempt to make Meta ​Platforms sell off Instagram and WhatsApp, saying the ​agency failed to prove that Meta holds a monopoly in a social media landscape that has shifted ​drastically since the case ‌was brought in 2020.Likewise, ​another judge in Washington, ​who previously ruled that Google holds an illegal monopoly in online search, rejected the justice department’s attempt to make the company sell its Chrome browser, citing rising competition from generative artificial intelligence companies such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT.US antitrust cases against Amazon and Apple, which involve big smartphone and online retail markets, will not go to trial until 2027 at the earliest.Explore more on these topicsGoogleAlphabetLaw (US)AI (artificial intelligence)AdvertisingnewsShareReuse this content

title: From petrol pump attendant to Dylan-feted rocker and Judd Apatow muse: the delightfully unlikely life of Graham Parker | Music | The Guardian
description: Fifty years ago Parker was hailed as rock’s next big thing, but he picked a different path: cult records, a Hollywood diversion, an aversion to stardom. Ahead of a UK tour, he looks back at his strange trajectory
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Fifty years ago Parker was hailed as rock’s next big thing, but he picked a different path: cult records, a Hollywood diversion, an aversion to stardom. Ahead of a UK tour, he looks back at his strange trajectory
Content: ‘I realised I don’t have to go out and grab the audience by the lapels, I can talk to them’ … Graham Parker.Photograph: Dion OgustView image in fullscreen‘I realised I don’t have to go out and grab the audience by the lapels, I can talk to them’ … Graham Parker.Photograph: Dion OgustMusicInterviewFrom petrol pump attendant to Dylan-feted rocker and Judd Apatow muse: the delightfully unlikely life of Graham ParkerAlexis PetridisFifty years ago Parker was hailed as rock’s next big thing, but he picked a different path: cult records, a Hollywood diversion, an aversion to stardom. Ahead of a UK tour, he looks back at his strange trajectoryWed 2 Sep 2026 15.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo say Graham Parker enjoyed a swift rise to fame is an understatement. He played his first live show with his most famous backing band, the Rumour, in October 1975, at the Newlands Tavern, a pub in Nunhead, south-east London. By the start of the following year, he had a record deal and was in the studio recording his debut album, Howlin’ Wind. The buzz around him was such that the sessions were interrupted by the arrival of a succession of stars – Thin Lizzy’s Phil Lynott among them – intrigued to hear what the fuss was about: a petrol pump attendant from Surrey who sang like Van Morrison and had written a set of smart, sharp, literate songs in between filling up cars.The record arrived in April 1976 to vast critical excitement, a lot of it occasioned by the album’s closing track, the reggae-influenced, attitude-laden Don’t Ask Me Questions. After Howlin’ Wind came out, followed in October by Heat Treatment, things ratcheted up another notch. Parker turned up in Australia to discover the media waiting for him and a press conference arranged in the airport: they had taken the amount of music press coverage Parker was receiving to mean he was “as big as Bruce Springsteen, which was insane”. Low down on a festival bill topped by Bob Dylan, he found himself backstage collared by the headline act, eager to tell Parker how much he loved his work. There also exists a photo of Parker in Los Angeles, with, of all people, Michael Jackson, but their meeting was apparently less successful. “I said to him: ‘Michael, great to meet you, I did a version of [Jackson 5 hit] I Want You Back recently.’ And he just sort of said: ‘Ooh.’ So that,” he laughs, “was the full extent of my conversation with Michael Jackson.”View image in fullscreen‘I’d infused myself with this rather melodramatic idea that I was the kiddy’ … Graham Parker in January 1976.Photograph: Ian Dickson/RedfernsIn truth, Parker seemed an unlikely candidate for a saviour of rock. He was short and wiry, a former hippy who had taken himself off to Morocco in his teens and served time in a band called Terry Burbot’s Magic Mud: “My idea,” he sighs, “a burbot being a fish that I knew had become extinct in England because Angling Times offered £100 to anyone who could prove they’d caught one.” On returning, he went back home to Deepcut in Surrey, shorn of his “arse-length” hair, writing songs influenced not by prevalent trends (“I thought progressive rock needed to be destroyed thoroughly”), but the music he’d loved in his youth: Motown, soul, ska, “pop hits on the radio”.On today’s video call from his home in upstate New York, ahead of a UK tour, Parker’s eyes are shielded by tinted sunglasses. Decades ago, dark glasses were his permanent look, which helped give Parker the air of a man who was almost disproportionately angry, or at least a lot angrier than his songs suggested he was. On Howlin’ Wind, he spat out the lyrics of Lady Doctor as if they were a ferocious broadside against the establishment, rather than about fancying a female GP. “Correct,” he nods. “If you went to see a band in the suburbs back then, the audience sat cross-legged, so I thought, we’ve got to do the opposite, get people up and dancing instead of sitting. So I just went out and yelled.”The thing was, Parker didn’t seem to think his sudden rise to fame was at all unlikely. He may have looked a little incredulous in the photo of himself backstage with Dylan, but that was the exception. “Oh no, I was brimming with confidence,” he says, smiling. “I’d infused myself with this rather melodramatic idea that I was the kiddy, you know: I’m going to be the one who shows people something that can be done – attitude, great lyrics that say something, a tight band. I got an instant record deal, I was getting all this attention and none of these people who’d been slogging around the pubs for years were. I remember one of the early gigs we did, the great Ian Dury and his minder, Fred ‘Spider’ Rowe, standing in front of the stage wearing sunglasses, trying to put the mockers on me. I thought: I’m having a great effect here. This is good! I can’t help being this good, you know!” He suddenly looks a bit concerned at revealing his youthful cockiness. “I hope,” he says quietly, “you can write this up with some humour in it. I do know I was being an idiot.”Graham Parker and the Rumour: Hey Lord, Don’t Ask Me Questions – videoOf course, Parker never quite became the huge star everyone seemed to think he would be in 1976. Instead, he carved out a fascinating 50-year career as a critically lauded, cult singer-songwriter whose work has ranged wildly. He recorded an album of obscure Lennon and McCartney songs with Kate Pierson of the B-52s; published novels and short stories; and maintained a pretty startling level of quality control over the course of 47 albums, despite his belief that “you should press the reset button” with every new release. His most recent, 2023’s Last Chance to Learn the Twist, was a delight, a live-sounding collection of songs that range in style from soul to prewar pop.His career has also regularly involved Parker doing the exact opposite of what one might have expected under the circumstances. In the late 70s, dissatisfied with his then record label, Mercury, he terminated their relationship by releasing Mercury Poisoning, a spectacularly withering song that, among other accusations, suggested the label “couldn’t sell kebabs to the Greeks” (“a bit literal,” he concedes today). His commercial stock rising in the 80s US, thanks to 1979’s superb Squeezing Out Sparks album, he signed a deal with Atlantic Records, whose chair Ahmet Ertegun suggested he make his next album sound “like Phil Collins”. Parker proceeded to make the deliberately rough-hewn The Mona Lisa’s Sister: a wonderful collection of songs utterly out of step with mainstream 80s rock trends, that, one can’t help but notice, has aged rather better than most mainstream 80s rock.View image in fullscreenStardom … Graham Parker and the Rumour performing at Reading festival in 1977.Photograph: Odile Noel/AlamyIn 2012, he unexpectedly found himself in Hollywood at the behest of Judd Apatow, a long-term fan: a golden opportunity that might nevertheless have given another artist pause, given that Parker was required to play himself in This Is 40, one of a plethora of underperforming artists who Paul Rudd’s record label honcho character has put his faith in. “He’s signing all these losers from the 70s and 80s. He’s got Haircut 100, and Frank Black without the Pixies, and me,” Parker says, chuckling. “When Judd told me, I said: I can do this, I could destroy his record company instantly, mate. I’m in.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I knew it was over for us’: the bands who got left behind when punk explodedRead moreHollywood was another entirely unexpected state of affairs. “For me, small timer, quite happy with his little career – playing grungy little solo gigs, doing records my way with no one interfering – to suddenly become this actor, pop singer thing, I didn’t see that coming. I ended up sitting in a dressing room with John Lithgow and Paul Rudd and Megan Fox, thinking, I should call a cab, I don’t belong here. But I sank into it pretty good. Being flown to Hollywood to do talks, first class, put up in these amazing hotels … I’m suddenly somebody, for five minutes. But it was a long five minutes, because the film went on and on in America, it was shown for months.”Parker does, indeed, seem perfectly contented with his little career, grungy solo gigs and all: that’s exactly what he’s doing in the UK this month. For all his vaulting ambition in his early 20s, he is not sure that he was really cut out for fame. “The little bit of stardom I had, when everyone’s after you, everyone’s trying to grab you, that crept in and it was quite unpleasant really. Record labels start giving you too much money for music that I knew wasn’t for everybody and probably wasn’t going to burst out in platinum sales. I ended up telling my manager, tell them to pay me half what they’re offering. Which is weird, I know, but I think I did the best thing.”View image in fullscreenFar from the end … Parker performing in New Jersey in 2019.Photograph: Lisa Piernot/Zuma Wire/ShutterstockIndeed, he is a vociferous advocate for keeping things small-scale. “I can pull a crowd, I can do it without the costs of a band, and it taught me to sing – I realised I don’t have to go out and grab the audience by the lapels, I can talk to them.” Although he has caveats. His mordantly funny 2001 song I’ll Never Play Jacksonville Again details the true story of a gig at which Parker ended up playing to “two couples, two barmen who looked like Ted Nugent, and a guy who looked a bit gormless and kept staring at one of the women’s legs until her boyfriend head-butted him. Five people in the audience and there’s a fight! How fucking often does that happen, man? I thought, this is the end.”He says he’s been true to the song’s title and never played Jacksonville again. “But only because nobody’s offered me a gig there. If the money’s good enough and there’s two other gigs nearby, maybe I’ll do it. And I’ll do that song. It’ll be fun.”Graham Parker is atWaterside Arts, Sale, on 8 September,then touringuntil 1 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mayday review – Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh set cold war bromance alight | Film | The Guardian
description: An American fighter pilot teams up with a retired KGB officer for hijinks and hilarity in Soviet Russia
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: An American fighter pilot teams up with a retired KGB officer for hijinks and hilarity in Soviet Russia
Content: Wacky chemistry … Kenneth Branagh and Ryan Reynolds in Mayday.Photograph: Apple TV+View image in fullscreenWacky chemistry … Kenneth Branagh and Ryan Reynolds in Mayday.Photograph: Apple TV+FilmReviewMayday review – Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh set cold war bromance alightAn American fighter pilot teams up with a retired KGB officer for hijinks and hilarity in Soviet RussiaPeter BradshawWed 2 Sep 2026 17.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.01 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRyan Reynolds andKenneth Branaghstar in this goofy but entertaining action-comedy bromance set in the cold war 80s, when it seemed every red-blooded young guy in America adored Top Gun and wanted to be a US Navy fighter pilot. It’s got some outrageous close-quarter fight scenes – and who knew Branagh could bust out martial arts moves? Is he going to follow Bob Odenkirk into an unexpected action movie career? The final sequences of automotive mayhem in and around Moscow might remind you of the heady days of Roger Moore as James Bond.Reynolds is Troy Kelly (callsign “Assassin”), a supercool fighter pilot in 1987, who is always doing brave and brilliant stuff that isn’t in the rulebook, and cracking wise in the accepted Reynolds manner. But when his spy plane is shot down deep inside snowy and forested Soviet territory, Troy awakens from his coma to find himself in the log cabin of retired KGB man Nikolai Ustinov, cheerfully played by Branagh, who is a secret fan of all things American and obsessively rewatches Top Gun on samizdat VHS. He suggests to the stunned Troy that he simply stays in his cabin, watching the film with him, until the cold war is over.At this stage, this movie could have started to resemble Stephen King’s Misery, or Evelyn Waugh’s A Handful of Dust in which Tony Last has to read Dickens eternally to a madman in the jungle. But Troy and Nikolai wind up making a break for it together, with much hijinks in speeding cars and of course, in accordance with a tradition as old as cinema itself, a rattling train from which they are soon going to have to jump. They even end up on an aircraft which is going to be very hazardous once people starting shooting inside it, while all the time naturally quarrelling and sniping at each other. And of course they are being pursued by a hardfaced Russian security operative called Volkov (played by Marcin Dorocinski). It’s all very silly, and considering that there is an unexpected queer theme at the end, I felt that writer-directors John Francis Daley and Jonathan Goldstein missed a trick in not reviving the gay theories around Top Gun. But there are laughs, stunts and wacky chemistry between Reynolds and Branagh.Mayday is on Apple TV from 4 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmThrillersCold warKenneth BranaghRyan ReynoldsComedy filmsAction and adventure filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Quidditch, Muggles, magic: new Harry Potter trailer gives full look at TV show | Harry Potter TV series | The Guardian
description: HBO’s extended trailer reveals more details of JK Rowling’s wizarding world coming to screens this Christmas
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: HBO’s extended trailer reveals more details of JK Rowling’s wizarding world coming to screens this Christmas
Content: Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter in HBO's forthcoming Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone TV series.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/HBOView image in fullscreenDominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter in HBO's forthcoming Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone TV series.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/HBOHarry Potter TV seriesQuidditch, Muggles, magic: new Harry Potter trailer gives full look at TV showHBO’s extended trailer reveals more details of JK Rowling’s wizarding world coming to screens this ChristmasOwen MyersWed 2 Sep 2026 17.23 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.27 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe second official trailer has been released forHBO’s forthcoming TVadaptationofHarry Potterand the Philosopher’s Stone.Starring newcomer Dominic McLaughlin in the lead role, the new trailer gives an extended look at life at Hogwarts and the challenges that Potter and the gang face in their first year at the school.The newly released footage provides glimpses of well-known moments from the book and shows Potter using the invisibility cloak, playing quidditch and being confronted by Professor Snape.The trailer follows an initialteaserunveiledthis March, which gave a first look at the new eight-episode series based on JK Rowling’s first Potter book.As well as McLaughlin as Potter, the series also features the British newcomers Alastair Stout and Arabella Stanton as Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger.
