The young actors werechosenafter a lengthy casting search among British child actors aged nine to 11.The series also features actors Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall, Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid andJohn Lithgowas Albus Dumbledore, the Hogwarts headmaster.Luke Thallon will play Quirinus Quirrell, while Paul Whitehouse will appear as Argus Filch, Lox Pratt as Draco Malfoy, Johnny Flynn as his father, Lucius, Bel Powley as Petunia Dursley, Daniel Rigby as Vernon Dursley and Katherine Parkinson as Molly Weasley.View image in fullscreenJohn Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/HBOThe series began its big-budgetproductionin Hertfordshire, England, last July. The show is led by twoSuccession alums, writer Francesca Gardiner and director Mark Mylod, who will also direct some episodes.Kit Harington to replace Nicholas Hoult in HBO’s Harry Potter TV seriesRead moreLast month, Nicholas Houltstepped backfrom a previously announced role in the show’s second season amid backlash from those opposed to Rowling’sviewsontrans rights. Kit Harington, the Game of Thrones actor, was announced as Hoult’s replacement to play Gilderoy Lockhart, Hogwarts’ defense against the dark arts teacher.Previously, LithgowcalledRowling’s stance on trans rights “ironic and inexplicable”.“It upsets me when people are vehemently opposed to me having anything to do with this,” he said. “But in Potter canon you see no trace of transphobic sensitivity. [Rowling] has written this meditation of kindness and acceptance. And Dumbledore is a beautiful role.”Last month, Powley also commented on the issue. “I strongly disagree with JK Rowling’s views on gender,” she said tothe Telegraph. “I think that the trans community deserve safety and dignity and respect and total acceptance.”Rowling is involved in theHBOseries in an advisory capacity as an executive producer.The show will premiere at Christmas with each subsequent book adapted for further seasons.Explore more on these topicsHarry Potter TV seriesHarry PotterHBOJohn LithgowJK RowlingTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He was always a bit of a groundbreaker’: David Bowie enters a new dimension in ‘extended reality’ documentary | Film | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of unseen images of the star feature at the Venice film festival, alongside virtual worlds exploring wildfires, wolves and the birth of stars
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Hundreds of unseen images of the star feature at the Venice film festival, alongside virtual worlds exploring wildfires, wolves and the birth of stars
Content: ‘He wasn’t just about the music’ … still from David Bowie: Unseen Unheard.Photograph: Venice film festivalView image in fullscreen‘He wasn’t just about the music’ … still from David Bowie: Unseen Unheard.Photograph: Venice film festivalFilm‘He was always a bit of a groundbreaker’: David Bowie enters a new dimension in ‘extended reality’ documentaryHundreds of unseen images of the star feature at the Venice film festival, alongside virtual worlds exploring wildfires, wolves and the birth of starsXan Brooksin VeniceWed 2 Sep 2026 11.36 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.58 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Bowie shares the bill with starmen, firefighters and Walt Disney wolves at the 10th anniversary edition of Venice Immersive, the film festival’s pioneering showcase for new forms of storytelling. David Bowie: Unseen Unheard – a 3D documentary featuring hundreds of previously unseen images – is among 69 XR (extended reality) pieces playing at the event’s regular base on Lazzaretto Vecchio, a repurposed small island off the Venice Lido.Venice Immersive’s 10th birthday marks a milestone for an event which aims to provide a bridge between emergent technology and traditional narrative cinema. But the programme’s organisers are at pains to emphasise the ongoing scope of a project that has in recent years prompted similar sections at the Cannes, Geneva and Toronto film festivals. “This is not a retrospective,” declares the official festival blurb that welcomes guests to the island. It almost sounds like a warning.“This is such a fast-evolving medium,” says Liz Rosenthal, Venice Immersive’s co-curator. “We’re basically witnessing new forms of art being crafted in real time. So we’re already looking forward to the next 10 years. I think we’re very much at a turning point in terms of the platforms and technology that’s available – and this in turn will shape the nature of the storytelling itself.”View image in fullscreenSound and vision … David Bowie on stage at the Serious Moonlight tour in 1983, a scene from David Bowie: Unseen Unheard.Photograph: Denis O’ReganBilled as an immersive spatial-sound documentary, David Bowie: Unseen Unheard is a personal portrait of the singer by Denis O’Regan, who worked as Bowie’s official photographer. The installation plays out across eight screens and 84 hidden speakers, folding 12 Bowie songs alongside O’Regan’s commentary and archive of nearly 800 photographs. Bowie died in 2016, but the project was conceived and developed with the full support and cooperation of the late singer’s estate.“David would have loved this, definitely,” O’Regan says. “And he would have loved it going into the Venice film festival. He was always a bit of a groundbreaker. David loved his technology. He loved making things happen and experimenting with new ideas, like his Bowie bonds orBowie.net. Listen to theAladdin Sane albumfrom 1973 and he’s already writing lyrics like, ‘Pour me out another phone, I’ll ring and see if your friends are home’. The thing about David is that he wasn’t just about the music. He was about mime, visuals, theatre, film.” It is this hybrid quality, O’Regan adds, that makes him a natural fit for Venice Immersive.Fittingly, David Bowie: Unseen Unheard rubs shoulders with a rogues’ gallery of genre-defying new work from around the globe. The climate crisis is a major focus at this year’s edition, with Felix Gaedtke and Gayatri Parameswaran’s Solomon Islands-set Solwata, Barthélemy Antoine-Loeff and Hugo Arcier’s interactive The White Saboteur and the LA wildfire documentary Out of the Ashes all tackling the issue of human-made climate change.Other potential highlights include the immersive nature documentaries Galápagos: The Last Eden and Disneynature’s Wolf, which conducts a virtual tour of Canada’s remote Ellesmere Island. James Elliott Mizroch’s VR installation Smithsonian Starstruck goes further still, inviting users to step inside the cosmos to watch a star being born.“The first years of Venice Immersive were more about experimentation,” says Rosenthal. “The pieces were either playing with the various formats or they were these small side projects of big media properties. Now we’re seeing big works that have a proper distribution strategy. That means that the work has a life that extends far beyond the island. They can be seen and enjoyed by people around the world.”Venice Immersive2026 runs until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalDavid BowieVirtual realityItalyEuropeFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘OK, fine. I’m a national treasure’: Joe Lycett on fatherhood, Celebrity Traitors – and his TV show live from a pub  | Television | The Guardian
description: The comedian’s new Friday night series will come live from a working pub, with his aunties working the bar and celebrities doing shifts as managers. Or it will be if he can only get his licence …
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The comedian’s new Friday night series will come live from a working pub, with his aunties working the bar and celebrities doing shifts as managers. Or it will be if he can only get his licence …
Content: ‘Let’s go and have a lock-in at mine’ … Lycett at the Lucky Saint in London.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Let’s go and have a lock-in at mine’ … Lycett at the Lucky Saint in London.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianTelevisionInterview‘OK, fine. I’m a national treasure’: Joe Lycett on fatherhood, Celebrity Traitors – and his TV show live from a pubStuart HeritageThe comedian’s new Friday night series will be set in a working pub, with his aunties working the bar and celebrities doing shifts as managers. Or it will be if he can only get his licence …Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.24 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe Lycett sits in a pub, an untouched pint in front of him. “Since I had my son, I’m not drinking anywhere near as much,” he laments. “Children do not respect hangovers, or tiredness in general.”His son is almost two, and Lycett has readjusted his life accordingly. “I’ve started going to bed when he does, which is about seven o’clock,” he explains. “I’ve seen a few nights where I’ve just gone: ‘Right, well, that’s me, then.’”However, this is all set to come to an end thanks to the comic’s new television programme, Live from the Lycett Arms, which will not only be broadcast live three hours after his new bedtime, but absolutely surround him with alcohol. The Lycett Arms is a continuation of what began with his previous live Friday night show,Late Night Lycett, only with a more ambitious premise. This time, Lycett will host while simultaneously operating a working pub. It sounds as if it has been specifically constructed to maximise impromptu chaos – more on that in a bit – but for now Lycett has a pair of larger anxieties to deal with.View image in fullscreen‘I took the licence exam but failed’ … Lycett in a publicity image for the show.Photograph: Matt Crockett/Channel 4/PAThe first is that, even though we’re meeting just a couple of weeks before the first episode, the pub isn’t ready. “It’s not fully constructed yet, so I’ve been to where it will be,” he explains. “It’s going to be in fashionable east London, and that’s everything I can say about it, because I don’t actually know the full address.”Nevertheless, he promises that the finished building will be “identifiably a pub. There’ll be an outdoor area and a cellar. There’s a bar. There’s a kind of back room. There’s a saloon bar. There’s a pool table. There’s darts. There’s karaoke. It should be really fun. That’s the goal. If it isn’t fun, there’s no point in doing it.”A bigger issue, though, is that, since the Lycett Arms will be a real pub, Lycett will be its licensed operator. This is a role that comes with a legal requirement: he needs to pass a mandatory exam to be accredited with a Level 2 Award for Personal Licence Holders. It is an accreditation he does not yet hold.“I took the exam but I failed,” he says. “I didn’t do any work, so that is a problem. I needed about 70% to pass, and I got something like 38%. I tried to use common sense, and I don’t have a lot of it apparently.”View image in fullscreenLycett … ‘If it isn’t fun, there’s no point in doing it.’Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianEager to help him out a little, I ask if he knows the four primary licensing objectives, as per section four of the Licensing Act 2003. The blood briefly drains from Lycett’s face. “Safe … safety … safe drinking environment to create … happy places, for people … to dwell?” he yammers.That isn’t what’s written on the test. The answer is: “Prevention of crime and disorder. Public safety. Protection of children from harm. Prevention of public nuisance.”“Yeah, that’s what I said, isn’t it?”No, not really.“Well, I think I paraphrased that. And I think that’s their problem that I didn’t get the licence because I did essentially paraphrase it right.”double quotation markI’m amazed they commissioned it because nobody’s commissioning anything. TV is in freefall. I don’t know if you’ve heardAfter strenuously assuring me that the show will go on, with a stand-in licensee if he continues to perform as disastrously as this, Lycett starts telling me how excited he is for people to see the show.“So, it’s my pub,” he says. “But from week one, there will be a celebrity manager who’s doing a trial shift. My aunties are going to be working the bar. There will be a weekly quiz and rotating regulars. I’m well up for weird and wonderful celebrities to just turn up, drink a pint and leave. I just want it to be constantly surprising and silly.”It’s also exciting that he gets to be the face of live, late-night television, I tell him. It’s a dying breed of show. “I’m kind of amazed they’ve commissioned it, because nobody’s commissioning anything at the moment,” he replies. “TV is in freefall – I don’t know if you’ve heard.”View image in fullscreenTailor made … Lycett getting involved as a host of The Great British Sewing Bee.Photograph: Mark Bourdillon/Love ProductionsSo in essence, running a pub could be a fallback career if the TV work ever dries up? “I mean, hospitality is in freefall as well,” he points out, not unreasonably. “Like most industries, it’s all just sort of fucked, isn’t it? Should I join the Guardian? Is that doing well?”Still, the thought of turning the Lycett Arms into a permanent nightspot is something that appeals to him. After all,if Jeremy Clarkson has proved anything, it’s that tourists love nothing more than a pub with a celebrity landlord.“I think lots of people feel like they could open up a pub or restaurant or whatever, and obviously it’s really hard,” he says. “But I do like the idea of it. I think it’s the cachet of being, like, ‘Let’s go and have a lock-in at mine.’ When the reality must be doing invoices and working out VAT.”This is a big year for Lycett. As well as Live from the Lycett Arms, he is returning to standup after stepping aside for a couple of years. This is something he is palpably excited about. “I’m touring next year, but since last October I’ve been trying to do one gig a week,” he says. “It took me a good few months to feel even close to like I knew what I was doing. I still don’t feel like I know what I’m doing. But I’m really enjoying being on stage, and I’m not panicked about it in the way I was when I had just come back from paternity leave.”Since his last tour, Lycett has become more recognisable and beloved in a way that nudges him towards national treasure status.“I dispute that,” he growls.Please agree for the sake of my question, I beg.“Fine, OK, I’m a national treasure, yes,” he says, rolling his eyes.View image in fullscreenClogs, gentlemen, please … Lycett.Photograph: Matt Crockett/Channel 4/PABecause people pay more attention to him now than when he last toured, does he feel a greater weight of responsibility for the topics he covers? “No,” he says. “If I started to change who I am on stage to fit what I think people want of me, I’d go mad. When you get reviewed, and the reviewer doesn’t like what you do, there’s this temptation to write the sort of show that the reviewer would like. But there are only about 10 comedy reviewers left in the whole country, and it wouldn’t be good to write something just so that 10 white men will like me.“I think the thing that has changed what I do most is being a father,” he continues. “I feel more risk averse, but I also want to stand up for things more than I used to. It’s like this weird tussle between not wanting to annoy the wrong people because I just want a calmer life, and also really wanting to annoy those people a lot more. But then a big part of this new show is also about swimming, so if you’re into swimming-based material, you’ll love it.”‘You don’t have to sell them on the idea’: how Celebrity Traitors has seduced the starsRead moreLycett will take part in The Celebrity Traitors later this year, which will almost certainly be 2026’s biggest show. He is sworn to such secrecy that he practically ties himself in a knot trying to give the blandest non-answers imaginable. “The production team were very nice, as was Claudia Winkleman. I can’t say anything about the other players, so I can’t say whether they’re nice or not,” he offers apologetically.But before that airs, Lycett has six episodes of Live from the Lycett Arms to deliver. As I leave, he is taking notes on the decor of the pub we are in, particularly the quality of the bar itself. “Apparently it’s been treated with Danish oil,” he says approvingly. “That might be a future requirement for any pub I go into. The bar must have been treated with Danish oil.”Live from the Lycett Arms is on Friday at 10pm on Channel 4Explore more on these topicsTelevisionJoe LycettinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The opposite of ‘damsels in distress’: how TV fell in love with female gangsters | Television | The Guardian
description: The ruthless female characters of The Gentlemen, Beef and Peaky Blinders bring new depth to the evil matriarch stereotype
Author: Louis Staples
Headline: The ruthless female characters of The Gentlemen, Beef and Peaky Blinders bring new depth to the evil matriarch stereotype
Content: These women create space for scenes that sometimes feel even more shocking and subversive, precisely because of their proximity to femininity.Illustration: Guardian Design / Netflix / HBOView image in fullscreenThese women create space for scenes that sometimes feel even more shocking and subversive, precisely because of their proximity to femininity.Illustration: Guardian Design / Netflix / HBOTelevisionThe opposite of ‘damsels in distress’: how TV fell in love with female gangstersThe ruthless female characters of The Gentlemen, Beef and Peaky Blinders bring new depth to the evil matriarch stereotypeLouis StaplesWed 2 Sep 2026 10.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.04 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTelevision loves a gangster story – andapparentlyso does the Duchess of Sussex. This week, Netflix’sThe Gentlemen–Guy Ritchie’s latest addition to the gangster canon, which stars Theo James as a distractingly handsome aristocrat who becomes embroiled in the world of organized crime – returns for its second season. And in August, the show hit the headlines afterrumorsthat Meghan was reportedly in early talks to join its third season when she and Prince Harry made their highly unexpectedreturnto the UK.At first, Meghan’s potential role seemed like a random pivot for the former Suits star, who now seems far more at homeholding a jarof her Montecito-made jam than brandishing a gun. But really, thesecasting rumoursare indicative of a wider shift in the traditionally machismo-fueled gangster genre, where it’s now more common to see women stealing the spotlight – and calling the shots.Meghan’s casting in The Gentlemen reportedly withdrawnRead moreWhen The Gentlemen premiered in 2024, it marked a departure from Ritchie’s previous work. Alongside James and Vinnie Jones, the show starsKaya Scodelario, who is best known for portraying Effy in Skins, the groundbreaking British teen drama.Scodelario plays Susie Glass, a sharp, impeccably dressed, ruthless head of an underground cannabis empire, who introduces Eddie (James) to her world following the death of his father. She isn’t the first female character in Ritchie’s crime shows, but she is the first woman who has parity with her male peers. She’s the polar opposite of a “damsel in distress” – in fact, wherever she leads, Eddie follows. “What I liked about her was that this isn’t a story about her learning how to be a criminal … She’s already at the top of the ladder,” said Scodelario when Iinterviewedher in 2024. She told me that people initially assumed Susie would be “the girlfriend or the wife or the sidekick”, when really the opposite was the case.Susie is part of a new wave of female characters in gangster shows who are intrinsic to the genre increasing its depth and scope. As a society, there’s a tacit acceptance that men will be involved in all kinds of criminal activity and violence, but female gangsters force us to take a much closer look at the characters’ motivations. These women create space for scenes that sometimes feel even more shocking and subversive, precisely because of their proximity to femininity.On Netflix’s assassin seriesBlack Doves, the professional killers are handled by the grudge-holding Lenny Lines (Kathryn Hunter), whose tiny stature only makes her more scary. The show’s most powerful organized crime boss is Alex Clark, played byTracey Ullman, who runs a massive criminal enterprise that has connections reaching into the highest level of the British government.Similarly, in the Paramount+ seriesMobLand,which also returns for its second season in September, the most hair-raising character isn’t crime boss Conrad Harrigan (Pierce Brosnan) or even his rough-around-the-edges “fixer”, Harry Da Souza (Tom Hardy). No, it’s Maeve Harrigan (Helen Mirren), the mob family’s Irish matriarch, who is as bloodthirsty as she is protective.View image in fullscreenHelen Mirren (center), with the cast of MobLand.Photograph: Jason Bell/Paramount+Traditionally, women in gangster shows have tended to be either shallowly written objects of male desire, or cunning matriarchs like Maeve, who command respect and use family ties to control people. The latter category often operate quietly behind the scenes, holding the real financial or political power while the men in their families are front and centre. Think Polly Gray (Helen McCrory), the treasurer of the Shelby family in Peaky Blinders, orYoun Yuh-jung’s portrayal of a deliciously evil and corrupt country club owner in season two of Netflix’sBeef.This year, we’re starting to see the archetype gradually evolve. In HBO’sEuphoria, drug queenpin Laurie, played by a chillingly deadpan Martha Kelly, is very much not a matriarch or a sexualized figure. (With the exception of doting on her beloved pet parrot, Paladin). And rather than fade into the background, she doesn’t hesitate to go up against fellow drug lord Alamo Brown in a murderous turf war. In fact, right up until thegrisly finale, there is nobody above Laurie, and her destiny is entirely in her own hands.View image in fullscreenKaya Scodelario and Theo James in The Gentlemen.Photograph: NetflixAnd in The Gentlemen, Scodelario’s character is the classic millennial girlboss – a fitting role for an actor who had her breakthrough on a show thatdefined2000s youth culture. Susie loves red lipstick and an Instagram-ready outfit, making her simultaneously an object of desire and aspiration. She’s a gangster who doesn’tlooklike a gangster, but at the same time, her visual femininity isn’t her defining characteristic – it’s her ability to strategise and get things done.Summer box office 2026: what can we learn from the hits and misses?Read moreIn a show where the men are often held back by their status and the firmly set roles that they occupy – father, heir, fixer – Susie is a hyper-capable shapeshifter who can cut their egos down to size. In the heart-pumping season two premiere alone, we see her tweed-clad at grouse shooting, suited up at an art auction (to spend a cool £16m on a Botticelli painting), covertly hatching plans in a steamy lakeside sauna (of all places), pursuing masked thieves on bikes in a classic high-speed chase, negotiating with a (terrifying) Italian mafia boss and continuing her flirtationship (or is it?) with Eddie.Really, it’s not surprising that The Gentlemen supposedly piqued Meghan’s interest, because its second season is a high-budget, twist-heavy affair. The series now boasts a prestige production value that feels more aligned with Netflix past mega-hits includingThe CrownandHouse of Cards. And crucially, it’s also a show where women take up more space than ever in the Guy Ritchie cinematic universe. In Susie’s world, aristocrats might be the original organized criminals, but they are by no means the best – as long as she’s around.Season two of The Gentlemen is onNetflixon 3 SeptemberThis article was amended on 1 September 2026. The character Effy, from the British teen drama Skins, was misnamed as Effie.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionNetflixHBOHelen MirrenGuy RitchieWomenUS televisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chasing Freedom: a poignant reflection on empire, education and parental expectations | Books | The Guardian
description: Simukai Chigudu’s filmic memoir details the confines and conflicts of growing up in Zimbabwe during political turmoil
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Simukai Chigudu’s filmic memoir details the confines and conflicts of growing up in Zimbabwe during political turmoil
Content: Diversely gifted … Simukai Chigudu.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Getty Images/PenguinView image in fullscreenDiversely gifted … Simukai Chigudu.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Getty Images/PenguinThe Long WaveBooksChasing Freedom: a poignant reflection on empire, education and parental expectationsSimukai Chigudu’s filmic memoir details the confines and conflicts of growing up in Zimbabwe during political turmoil.Don’t already get The Long Wave in your inbox? Sign up hereNesrine MalikWed 2 Sep 2026 14.42 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 16.20 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast week, I finally managed to snatch one read out of the jaws of a hectic summer. On a series of very long-haul flights (highly recommended as a way to break reading droughts), I fell into the world of Simukai Chigudu’s Chasing Freedom: Coming of Age at the End of Empire. I finishedthe bookjust as I was landing in Nairobi, Kenya. In a daze, I stepped on to the tarmac in the chill of equatorial winter.The book was about growing up in post-colonialZimbabweand navigating life between the ex-colonised and the ex-colonial power. But the account of Chigudu’s life also captured, in ways that sometimes left me breathless with the shock of recognition, what felt like a broader shared experience for those of us born to parents whose traumas we never understood. This week, I reflected on how Chigudu’s experience connects to that of a wider post-colonial African generation.View image in fullscreenStruggles for freedom … Chigudu’s memoir, Chasing Freedom.Photograph: PenguinAn invisible generationChasing Freedom is Simukai Chigudu’s own personal story, but like all great memoirs, it is somewhat uncategorisable. His account of his life (soundtracked by this Spotify playlist) is layered with a story of Zimbabwe: its struggles for freedom, its bitter disappointments, and the lives broken in the process of both. It is also the first rendering I have seen of a generation of Africans born to parents of a certain class, who were bequeathed the contradictory burdens of anti-imperialism and the expectation that their children must achieve outside the continent. That small class is an illegible one to outsiders in the west; neither wealthy nor poor, educated enough to take civil service or academic jobs, but never affluent. Its members had the means to provide their children with private English language education and “exposure”, as Chigudu’s mother calls it, but were not comparable in lifestyle and status to, say, British elites with children in private schooling. Their politics is also a mess: many of them ushered their children away from their local cultures towards the west, while always holding on to a wholesale denouncement of that world, which they fought in liberation struggles.They are also – and here is where Chigudu delivers a devastating portrait that is profoundly familiar to me – cut off and unreliable witnesses to their own lives, ones marked by disorienting and painful political events. This makes them unreliable guides to the path their children are treading after them, a faded blueprint that leaves you to fill in the gaps. Chigudu describes the moment that conversations between these adults turned into anything intimate as “moistureless, even frightened, the result of generation upon generation of repression”. I recalled the long salon evenings during which my father sat with his many brothers, and how even to a child it was jarring to see how awkward and formal they were with each other. It was as if they sought a kind of adolescent safety in talk about sport and politics, sprinkled with some boyish banter that was full of avoidance and devoid of genuine humour. In our household, deaths, illnesses, political detentions and torture passed by without proportional remark. “Emotionally weighty things happened in my life that were never talked about,” Chigudu writes. “Whatever was difficult or painful lay dormant in the dark shadows of my soul.”School as a way outView image in fullscreenA secluded oasis … English language schooling in Zimbabwe meant jostling with feelings of shame and pride.Photograph: Alex Davidson/ICC/ICC/Getty ImagesThat painful and dormant material became metabolised through the only coping mechanism Chigudu had access to – academic excellence, or “punishing the books”. Chigudu paints a chilling and definitive portrait of how school became the high stakes ground for so many of us who did not have the privilege of walking into family businesses, or parents who had the money that made academic scholarships unnecessary. English-language schooling was an oasis and an isolated island in the middle of political turmoil. A place where pride in achievement jostled with shame that it was an achievement on the terms of white colonisers, who in the case of Zimbabwe still owned the lion’s share of assets and land, and still looked down on Black Zimbabweans.School was also not just a rite of passage, a milestone for white counterparts whose lives are plotted neatly to end in university abroad – it was the passage. While reading, I felt my chest tighten each time Chigudu approached a landmark exam, that sense of a school year being the pivot of your entire life, the crushing weight of academic pressure, the understanding, too heavy for a child to bear, that failure in grades meant a failure to launch into another good school, another good university in the west, and therefore a good life. Escape being an actualisation of yourself, and a validation of your parent’s trajectory and hopes which were never made explicit, but still overbearing.Turmoil, regret- and eventual stillness?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGrappling with imperialism … Oxford University’s statue of Cecil Rhodes, the British magnate who colonised Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/Getty ImagesChigudu plots his way to “freedom” as Zimbabwe unravels around him. The plots and personalities in his school all exist against a backdrop ofRobert Mugabe’s land repossessions, a failing government, power cuts, corruption, bribery, nepotism, embezzlement. So many personal journeys took place in the choppy waters of coups, protests, shortages, and the ever-present threat these events would encroach upon you and slow down or terminate your trajectory. Mine was indeed terminated (thankfully in hindsight), after high school. I ended up in higher education in Sudan that was poorly resourced and volatile, but infinitely bountiful in other ways. Chigudu goes on to leave Zimbabwe for the UK, landing straight into a bruising experience in public school and university. But in many ways, he never escapes what was always a mental location, rather than a physical one.It’s a turbulent ride, marked by rejection and success, the latter a restless kind. Chigudu goes on to become a doctor, and then changes lanes to become an associate professor of African politics at Oxford University. He heads up theRhodes Must Fallmovement at Oxford, and is met with the realisation that “the heated rhetoric of the culture wars could never do justice to what decolonisation has meant in my life”. All that promises certainty melts away into ambivalence. At the end, which I will not spoil, the reader is left with a vivid sense of how history bears down on us in ways that are effacing and propulsive. And to those of us from similar backgrounds, who made more elliptical journeys but were still drawn to the imperial metropole, a crushing too-late realisation that we had choices. We just didn’t know we could make them.The book is full of arresting and poignant reflections, potent and often funny – Chigudu is a diversely gifted writer. One thing still lingers in my mind, a question that he asks himself: “I wondered what life I might live if the choice were entirely mine, free of pressure and expectation.”Tap inWhat are your favourite nonfiction books on the diaspora experience? title: The Bridge by Colm Tóibín review – betrayal and survival in the High Pyrenees | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Deep sorrow mingles with illicit desire in this potent novella, the follow-up to a 2006 story about an isolated family in the Catalan mountains
Author: Alexandra Harris
Headline: Deep sorrow mingles with illicit desire in this potent novella, the follow-up to a 2006 story about an isolated family in the Catalan mountains
Content: Austere worlds … The Catalan Pyrenees provide the setting for The Bridge.Photograph: Xavier Fores/Joana Roncero/AlamyView image in fullscreenAustere worlds … The Catalan Pyrenees provide the setting for The Bridge.Photograph: Xavier Fores/Joana Roncero/AlamyBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Bridge by Colm Tóibín review – betrayal and survival in the High PyreneesDeep sorrow mingles with illicit desire in this potent novella, the follow-up to a 2006 story about an isolated family in the Catalan mountainsAlexandra HarrisWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 07.31 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty years ago,Colm Tóibínpublished a steadily desolating novella set in the high villages of the Catalan Pyrenees. A woman walks out of her house and her life, starts along the mountain road and disappears in the snow. Her son Miquel, failing to find her body, waits through the dark months for the thaw. A Long Winter, which appeared in a standalone volume and then as the final story in the 2006 collection Mothers and Sons, followed Miquel through dramatically extreme circumstances and patient endurance. It was told with the most restrained prose ever likely to be employed for a son’s view of vultures circling a corpse.Now, in The Bridge, a single year has passed in Miquel’s life and he is eking out an existence with his hurtful, unyielding father. The sheep are grazing their high summer pastures; a side hustle smuggling contraband brings in a little much-needed cash. In the bare conditions of the lonely farm, any warmth of feeling is a kind of contraband smuggled in by night; love between men is doubly illicit. The grave tenderness that grows between Miquel and his father’s maltreated servant Manolo gives The Bridge its emotional centre. These young men salve the emptiness with a few quiet words and touches. We sense their youthful beauty and resilience, their suppleness in a place of fixity.In fact, and with a fullness that’s striking in this novella of watchfulness and withholding, Miquel enters into a varied erotic life. Visits to the local town bring assignations. A later relationship between cellmates is extraordinarily vivid as Miquel seeks to “assuage his hunger by biting Odo, chewing him”. But it’s the lost, interrupted love of Manolo that gives shape to the rest.double quotation markTóibín practises a sustained reticence, even as fate strikes so cruelly as to give this story an absurdist edgeA great alteration has come to the area in the form of a road bridge linking isolated settlements with the country beyond. Places “cut off and enclosed” for centuries are suddenly opened and connected. This central motif suggests a story concerned with social change, and certainly it could be described in those terms. There’s a potent scene in which dogs from both sides of the valley run wildly across the bridge, frenzied at the possibility of new mates. This is not the only moment of the feral, and the farcical. As for Miquel: the crossing should bring him a larger terrain for youthful exploration, but it casts him into peril and dire confinement. The Bridge stays in the mind less as a historically specific story of 20th-century development than as an ageless study of loss, betrayal and survival. Miquel himself comes to believe that “his isolation was nothing new, that he had always been far away even from those to whom he had been closest”.Tóibín’s relationship with Catalonia now spans five decades. His first novel was set in Barcelona; his latest collection,The News from Dublin, includes several fine Spanish stories. He spends part of each year in the mountains near Llavorsí, and in writing about Miquel he is thinking his way into lives that have unfolded in that long known yet hardly knowable place. The germ of Miquel’s story came in a particular glimpse of local history. Tóibín was told that a ruined building was all that remained of the house where a woman once grew desperate enough to walk away from her family. It was said that the snow came; it was said to be a terrible tale. A Long Winter and The Bridge have grown from that beginning.Tóibín responds powerfully to the qualities of exactitude and seriousness he finds in Catalan writing, in the work of Mercè Rodereda for instance, and these are very much qualities of The Bridge. We know that Miquel feels deeply, but nothing in his life has licensed or recommended the articulation of personal emotion. Tóibín practises a sustained reticence, even as fate strikes so cruelly as to give this story an absurdist edge.Readers of Brooklyn and its follow-upLong Islandwill know that Tóibín has careful ways of handling a sequel: those novels are both richly complete in themselves while opening depths in each other. The Bridge, too, works alone or as part of a pair. To read A Long Winter afterwards, meeting the past that crouches in the shadows of the later story, would be as absorbing as to read chronologically. A further instalment seems possible. Any change would be welcome to lift Miquel from stultifying conditions, though it’s unlikely to offer much relief.This is the kind of small volume temptingly piled by the checkouts at Christmas. I wouldn’t recommend it as a stocking-filler; the stocking would fall to the floor with the weight of sorrow. But this is a memorable short work in which Tóibín’s unsentimental prose is flawlessly matched to the austere worlds of people enduring, in their different ways, lives stripped back to the bone.The Bridge by Colm Tóibín is published by Picador (£12.99). title: Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings by Jared Diamond review – how to change the course of history | Jared Diamond | The Guardian
description: The author of Guns, Germs and Steel falters in this flawed study of whether individuals really make a difference
Author: Steven Poole
Headline: The author of Guns, Germs and Steel falters in this flawed study of whether individuals really make a difference
Content: A performance of Hamlet at Shakespeare’s Globe, London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA performance of Hamlet at Shakespeare’s Globe, London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianJared DiamondReviewProfits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings by Jared Diamond review – how to change the course of historyThe author of Guns, Germs and Steel falters in this flawed study of whether individuals really make a differenceSteven PooleWed 2 Sep 2026 09.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 09.58 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly in this book, Jared Diamond proudly introduces “what I term ‘the Hamlet test’”, which helps decide whether prominent individuals really make a difference, or whether others might have done just as well. Among William Shakespeare’s contemporaries on the Elizabethan stage, he explains, were “Ben Jonson,Christopher Marloweand John Webster. But not even their best plays remotely approach in quality Hamlet and Shakespeare’s other masterpieces.” It follows, for Diamond, that Shakespeare was indeed “uniquely talented”: “We can be confident that no Elizabethan other than Shakespeare could have written a masterpiece like Hamlet if Shakespeare hadn’t done so.”One obvious problem with this is that Marlowe was stabbed to death in a pub in Deptford in 1593 at the age of 29, having already written the absolute bangers Doctor Faustus and Tamburlaine, as well as – so it is now thought – co-writing the Henry VI trilogy with the up-and-coming Shakespeare. Shakespeare himself did not begin to compose his major tragedies, including Hamlet, until he was a decade older. So we can’t rule out the possibility that, had Marlowe lived another 10 years, he would have matched or even exceeded his colleague’s genius. Scholars widely agree that Hamlet and Shakespeare’s other masterpieces were possible only thanks to the outsized influence of Marlowe.But Diamond is not interested in what literary scholars think, and is confident that his “Hamlet test” is a fine intellectual novelty. Indeed, he is not much interested in what scholars of history, or ethics, or business studies think either, because this is one of those books that pretends the subject is one nobody has thought rigorously about before.Diamond argues persuasively that at least the first president of independent Botswana, Seretse Khama, passes the Hamlet test: he made the country safe for democracy by “gut[ting] the power of the traditional chiefs”, for example, but only he could do that, “because he was the most powerful chief”. Much later in the book, we happily agree that only a particular couple of very rich Californians could have invented the pomegranate-juice industry – or, to generalise the lesson, you have to have lots of wealth already to go into a business with very high up-front costs and a lengthy startup period. No shit, Sherlock, as the reader will have cause to exclaim at numerous points throughout the book.As Diamond skips from politics to sport to business, the main interest is supplied by his concentration on the method of “natural experiments”: the statistical comparison of similar past events. In the 1990s, economists David Card and Alan Krueger analysed fast-food joints close together on either side of a state line: New Jersey had just passed a law to increase its minimum wage, while its neighbour Pennsylvania had not. In two celebrated papers, they proved that the increase in the minimum wage led tohigheremployment, contrary to the received economic wisdom. Similar analyses suggest that CEOs are responsible for between 6% and 29% of the variation in a company’s earnings, while sports coaches are on the hook for at most about 30% of a team’s performance. (Here I thought I could hear Thomas Tuchel breathing a sigh of relief.)Analysis of natural experiments is a fun tool, but obviously harder to make work the further you travel from objectively quantifiable things such as money or win/loss records. One Diamond cites used the amount of parking fines incurred by national staff at the UN’s New York headquarters as a proxy for their countries’ level of political corruption, which is already a stretch. Another took the preponderance of cousin marriage as a proxy for lower IQ (because of inbreeding effects), and so found that stupider European monarchs over the past four centuries were less successful in expanding their territory. (Not supplied here is any argument that expanding your territory is always good.)One of Diamond’s more striking examples also betrays some unreliability on his part. He writes that in their 2009 paper Hit or Miss? The Effect of Assassinations on Institutions and War, Benjamin F Jones and Benjamin A Olken showed that successful assassinations don’t make much difference to the outbreak of wars, and concludes that the killing of Franz Ferdinand didn’t cause the first world war. But the study itself explicitly cautions against that inference: Ferdinand is not included in their data, since he was not the “leader” of the Austro-Hungarian empire. Diamond also neglects to mention that paper’s more interesting finding, which is that, in autocracies, assassination can help make a transition to democracy more likely.The book ends by suggesting other questions that “natural experiments” of this kind might address, on the implicit grounds that only quantitative methods from the social sciences can provide satisfactory answers. One of them is “Under what circumstances do military leaders most make a difference?” On this topic, Diamond might have read with profit a book by a military historian, for example, Lawrence Freedman’s superbCommand. But from this book’s Olympian perspective, subject-matter experts in military affairs are as invisible as those in literary history.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a phenomenon – but there is much more to the gaming world | Games | The Guardian
description: As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining
Content: Grand Theft Auto VI’s star-crossed lovers, Jason and Lucia, on a motorcyle.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto VI’s star-crossed lovers, Jason and Lucia, on a motorcyle.Photograph: Rockstar GamesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesGrand Theft Auto VI is a phenomenon – but there is much more to the gaming worldAs Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explainingKeith StuartWed 2 Sep 2026 15.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.04 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePredictably, the Grand Theft Auto VI “extended look” which premiered on Netflix last weekwas a success for all involved. The 30-minute preview scorched to No 1 on the viewing chart and even brought the site down for a few minutes as millions of gamers tried to watch what was, effectively, a very long teaser trailer. According to datacollated by Eurogamer, more than 9,000 Twitch streamers covered the show leading to 5,227,798 hours of viewing there alone. And this was just the beginning of what will surely be two months of escalating hype – and unprecedented media attention.Call me cynical, but I suspect the coverage of GTA VI in the media over the next few weeks will follow a familiar pattern. Mostly, it will be five-minute slots wedged in near the end of news bulletins in which games journalists, industry analysts and other pundits will be asked why the game is such a big deal, how much it cost to make and how much revenue it will generate. Perhaps a few will try to reignite the hoary old “violence in video games” debate, there will be presenters laughingly admitting they’ve not touched a game since Pac-Man, rolling their eyes and wallowing in their ignorance, in a way they never would while discussing any other art form. Somebody will venture the subversive view that “games are no longer just for kids”; somebody else will say “games make more money than films and music put together”. And that will be that, job done for another decade … or until there’s a funny story about Pokémon.I hope I’m wrong. I hope, at least, the BBC, which employs plenty of staff who understand video games, will make time in its schedule to take a good look at GTA VI – its themes and influences, its creators, its place in the wider culture of games and entertainment. Sure, arts coverage on BBC televisionhas been in declinefor years, with the broadcaster shifting this content to digital platforms, but I saw plenty of in-depth analysis of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, looking at the quality of its translation, its depiction of female characters, its use of practical effects. I didn’t see a single presenter shrugging, looking comedically bewildered and admitting they’d not read Homer since secondary school.View image in fullscreenLost Records: Bloom and Rage is one of the games that deserves a least a portion of the attention GTA gets.Photograph: Don't Nod Entertainment SAOn top of this, whatever mainstream media attention GTA VI does get it will come at the expense of covering other titles. Because, when the next video game story comes up in the wake of Rockstar’s behemoth, TV and radio editors and producers will be thinking, “Oh, we covered games last month.”The thing is, GTAisa phenomenon – it looks gorgeous, it looks vast, and it will sell many millions of copies. The series’ notoriety transcends the medium. But is it the most interesting video game since GTA V? So much has changed since then. We’ve explored the fascinating, innovative open worlds of Elden Ring, Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and No Man’s Sky (an open galaxy!); we’ve seen brutal adult themes explored in The Last of Us: Part 2 and Silent Hill; we’ve experienced dizzying narrative innovations via Disco Elysium, Split Fiction and Lost Records: Bloom & Rage. All of these deserved at least a portion of that GTA screen and radio time.True, some gameshavedrawn similar levels of media attention. Minecraft and Fortnite receive regular coverage, but almost always because of concerns over children and games addiction, or because of how they intersect with other media: Minecraft through its hit movie, Fortnite through its many collaborations with music artists. And this is the key problem. Mainstream media is still at the stage where every single games story that does make it to TV or radio has to do the job of explaining and justifying the whole industry. It’s time for programme-makers to understand that video games are a mass cultural phenomenon. Enough people play them and understand them so that they don’t have to be re-introduced every time they’re covered. And most importantly, there is life, love, art and brilliance beyondGrand Theft Autoand beyond the coming storm of hype.What to playView image in fullscreenWhat The Dub?! will definitely be revived at future family celebrations.Photograph: Wide Right InteractiveIt was my birthday a couple of weeks ago, so I set out to find a simple, fun video game that the whole family could enjoy – and I wanted to share my discovery.Inspired by Dominik Diamond’srecent columnon this very subject, I downloaded the party gameWhat The Dub?!, in which players watch old film clips with portions of the sound dubbed out and then enter their own amusing dialogue to fill the gap. The clips are then re-shown with each player’s text added to the soundtrack via a stilted robotic voice – then everyone votes on the funniest entry. It was hilarious, especially because the clips are from weird old public domain films and TV shows, so everything feels stilted and ridiculous. It’s also simple to take part, with each player using their phone to enter their dialogue choices. Apparently, it’s possible to add new clips via the Steam Workshop, the digital store’s user-generated content feature, but we didn’t figure that out. Regardless, What the Dub?! will definitely be revived at future family celebrations.Available on:PCEstimated playtime:All evening!What to readView image in fullscreenThe Sims 4 from EA, which declined to comment on reports of staff concerns.Photograph: EA GamesEA staff have beenspeaking anonymouslyto the industry-news site Game Developer about their concerns after the Saudi-led buyout ofElectronic Arts. Some are troubled by the prospect of popular games such as EA Sports FC, Madden and Battlefield being used by Saudi Arabia to distract from its poor human rights record. There are also worries about the company’s culture and job security.TV producers looking for interesting game stories that don’t involve GTA could check out Eurogamer’sexcellent articleon theNo Man’s Sky’s Galactic Hub project. It’s a community of players exploring and scientifically cataloguing specific regions of the long-running space adventure sim, like a sort of ragtag Starfleet mission. Live long and prosper, lads.As if making and marketing independent video games isn’t hard enough, several developers have reported thefts at this year’sGamescomevent in Cologne.Posting on X, Mimic creator Ryan Laley said: “Our equipment was stolen last night from the booth. Police reports have been filed. At a loss for words to describe the feeling. Just defeated. Gonna do my best with what’s left of the week. But a huge blow financially and mentally.”According to VGC, others affected included publisher iam8bit and Tessera Studios.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickGems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past – Geralt of Rivia returns after a decade in the sunHelp! I have disappeared down a rabbithole of horrible mobile gaming advertsTrainwatch – alone with your thoughts on a railway line to nowhereStar Wars Zero Company – joyfully absurd heroics with a tight-knit team of misfits | ★★★★☆Vholume – a headlong rush of parkour perfection in a brutalist wonderland | ★★★★☆Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan myth | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenA game that soars … Microsoft Flight Simulator.Photograph: MicrosoftA question fromRichardvia email:“My son, aged 6, is a big fan of aeroplanes and is really interested in flight. What games are there that could be used to entertain him, as a thing to do with me. I have (ridiculously) a PS5 and Xbox Series X – is Flight Simulator right? How about Ace Combat? Anything else?”I’d definitely recommendMicrosoft Flight Simulator, which is available on PS5 and Xbox. It can be controlled with just a joypad and you can switch off all the technical elements for your son so he’s basically just steering the craft like in an arcade game. There are lots of aircraft to fly, from tiny prop planes to passenger jets, and you can choose anywhere on Earth to explore. I love simply zooming over cities and scenic highlights, taking it all in.If you’re ok with him doing a bit of shooting,Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theveis out in October, promising highly detailed visuals and exciting dogfighting. Fans say it looks to be a highlight for the series. I’d also recommend No Man’s Sky, which is a space exploration game, but the flight feels lovely, whether you’re scorching over the surface of a planet or out in the depths of the cosmos. The controls are extremely intuitive too. If he gets into space flight, the slightly more involvedEliteDangerousis worth a look, and for an accessible combination of space flight and shooting,Everspace: Stellar Editionis a really nice option on PS5.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterGrand Theft AutoGrand Theft Auto VINetflixFilm adaptationsTwitchfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Star Wars Zero Company review – joyfully absurd heroics with a tight-knit team of misfits | Games | The Guardian
description: Split priorities between scripted and emergent story moments hamper an otherwise brilliant Star Wars-themed successor to XCOM
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Split priorities between scripted and emergent story moments hamper an otherwise brilliant Star Wars-themed successor to XCOM
Content: Star Wars Zero Company.Photograph: Bit Reactor/EAView image in fullscreenStar Wars Zero Company.Photograph: Bit Reactor/EAGamesReviewStar Wars Zero Company review – joyfully absurd heroics with a tight-knit team of misfitsPlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Bit ReactorSplit priorities between scripted and emergent story moments hamper an otherwise brilliant Star Wars-themed successor to XCOMNic ReubenWed 2 Sep 2026 10.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.10 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven if you’re unfamiliar with the term “emergent storytelling”, you’ve likely experienced some of the unscripted tales that can bubble up out of a game’s systems. Perhaps you’ve led a scheming dynasty in Crusader Kings, or watched a favourite hero succumb to madness inDarkest Dungeon. Maybe you’ve surrendered yourself to the infinite yarn-spinner that isDwarf Fortress– or read about it from the mid-00s forums where users helped popularise the term “Let’s Play” bychronicling their gamesin descriptive posts. Or perhaps you’ve played Firaxis’XCOM, the alien invasion tactics hit that several key members of Zero Company studio Bit Reactor had a hand in.Zero Company hinges on a concept as simple as it is perfect: take the complementary class abilities, tough dice rolls, and permanent character deaths of XCOM, and house them in a sci-fi setting known for spaghetti western blaster duels, last stands and heroic sacrifices. As creative director Greg Foertschputs it, “Star Wars is about loss.” Which losses you end up mourning in Zero Company depends on you.In theory, anyway. The game echoes Rogue One in its titular company of doomed misfits, but despite selling permadeath as a looming threat in the scripted tutorial, things rarely get dicey enough to put your squad in real danger. Even on its toughest difficulty, Zero Company feels reluctant to let a stray thermal detonator cut your companions’ stories short, blunting much of its potential for unscripted drama.But in lieu of heroic sacrifices, Zcom (as I like to call it) is exceptional at telling a different kind of emergent story. Ones about iron-clad camaraderie and uneasy alliances. About the time your Mandalorian medic jetted in to heal your Jedi right on time, or the begrudging “nice shot” your clone trooper paid a former enemy sniper. The script feels designed to sell your mercenaries as an inseparable, dysfunctional family. Unironically, this one really is about the friends you make along the way.Each fight is a reminder that Zero Company have each other’s backs. After an opening shot at enemy droids, you might have Kabb – a squat, bulbous alien scoundrel who speaks entirely in cutesy anastrophes – rush over and punch a hulking robot straight down a ravine. “What’s for supper? Cutty-upper!”, he declares for the third time in 15 minutes, met by some variations of “nicely done” from a random squadmate. Kabb’s still in bad shape from last turn, so you have your Astromech launch over healing stim. Kabb grabs it mid-air, slams it into his bicep, thanks the droid, and a notification tells you their bond has gotten stronger. That’ll mean a nice stat bump for them both later.As all this happens, the battlefield buzzes with noise and motion. Idle combatants trade harmless potshots, ducking behind cover. Blaster holes sizzle through steel barriers. Battle Droids mock your missed shots, babbling “oh no!” like exploding lemmings when their comrades fall. There is so much personality in the different ways characters move. Gangers scramble down ladders. Astromechs bump into crates, then jump-jet over. Jedi leap and flip, and droids curl and spin like chrome woodlice. Through it all, veteranStar Warscomposer Gordy Haab underscores every peril and triumph, paying pitch-perfect tribute to the textures of John Williams’ original score.View image in fullscreenStar Wars Zero Company.Photograph: Bit Reactor/EABetween missions, you’ll return to the Den: a streamlined but engaging take on the customisation and upgrades of XCOM’s command centre, with the hangout space of Mass Effect’s Normandy. Via a galaxy map, you’ll spend intel, collect rewards, and make tough choices about which upgrades to deny your foes. It’s also here you’ll learn about your crew’s pasts. If you’ve got the time, you can even join them on personal quests.I haven’t mentioned Zero Company’s overarching plot so far, mainly because there’s little worth mentioning. Its central threat, the Infinite Coil, are a tiresomely exoticised, first-draft cult with ill-defined goals, evidently concocted because the combat needed an enemy faction with some flavour of space magic for variety’s sake. The enemy’s reliance on healing and damage negation – a clumsy workaround for AI that can’t keep up with your team’s escalating stats and skills – results in some laborious late-game encounters.These are by far the weakest parts of an otherwise brilliant debut from Bit Reactor, however. And even when the plot falters, touching character moments join digestible, deeply human explorations of this era of Star Wars’ byzantine factional politics. XCOM’s success has influenced countless turn-based tactics games. Few have made squeezing joyfully absurd heroics out of a handful of action points feel this good. Fewer have made me grin so hard at a final lucky shot during a last-second evacuation. That’smysquad down there, after all.Star Wars: Zero Company is out now: £39.99Explore more on these topicsGamesStrategy gamesStar WarsPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XPCreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ready tae Drap review – clashing neighbours trapped in a lift get roars of approval | Stage | The Guardian
description: Comedy chemistry drives a play that asks if three contrasting characters – conspiracy theorist, pregnant mum, hen-do attendee – can find common ground
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Comedy chemistry drives a play that asks if three contrasting characters – conspiracy theorist, pregnant mum, hen-do attendee – can find common ground
Content: Rift in a lift … Tinashe Warikandwa, Éimi Quinn and Isabelle Joss in Ready tae DrapPhotograph: Eoin CareyView image in fullscreenRift in a lift … Tinashe Warikandwa, Éimi Quinn and Isabelle Joss in Ready tae DrapPhotograph: Eoin CareyStageReviewReady tae Drap review – clashing neighbours trapped in a lift get roars of approvalÒran Mór, GlasgowComedy chemistry drives a play that asks if three contrasting characters – conspiracy theorist, pregnant mum, hen-do attendee – can find common groundKatie HawthorneWed 2 Sep 2026 12.46 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrapping three nightmare neighbours in the dodgy lift of their Glasgow high-rise, Ready tae Drap has lots of sparky, slapstick humour – but not so much nuance.Crotchety conspiracy theorist Pat (Isabelle Joss) is in her 70s and armed with barbed, uninvited observations. Saintly, exhausted Muslim mum of two Aaliyah (Tinashe Warikandwa) is on the verge of giving birth to her third child. Dry-humoured Lauren (performed by playwright Éimi Quinn) is the play’s millennial, fourth-wall-breaking narrator, clad in fishnets and bunny ears for a hen-do. It’s a classic setup: can these contrasting characters find common ground in a tight spot?Not really. Quinn’s vivid new play digs into chalk-and-cheese humour and an ever-present threat of body fluids, cracking jokes as blue as Lauren’s favourite flavour of WKD. Within the lift’s cramped confines (with concise design from Heather Grace Currie), Maureen Carr’s direction is dynamic and physical, bringing out the cast’s comedic chemistry: Pat’s gleeful descriptions of her post-menopausal sex life leave Aaliyah and Lauren wide-eyed and the Òran Mór’s full house roaring.But all this (literal, enjoyable) pissing about disguises the crux of the matter. For most of the hour, the older woman’s racism is watered down – although one sharply written line about Glasgow’s city centre fires has the audience nodding in agreement before it slides into blatant xenophobia. When Pat eventually tears off a vicious tirade against migrants, directed at Aaliyah whom she “doesn’t mean to offend”, both characters feel caricatured and underwritten. Even then, Pat’s lonely backstory is richer than Aaliyah’s, who is given a detail-free story about moving to Glasgow as a refugee – and all the while, Lauren, the audience’s direct contact, has fallen asleep in the corner.When she wakes, her own emotional reckoning is just as thin: Aaliyah and Pat team up to demand why “selfish” Lauren doesn’t want kids, and she skims over a vague answer in less time than the trio spent poking fun at hen-do inflatables.Ready tae Drap wisely doesn’t pretend that small talk will fix society’s deepening trenches. But despite its sleeves-rolled-up approach to life’s grubbier stuff, it shrinks away from emotional viscera.AtÒran Mór, Glasgow, until 5 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rupert Murdoch ‘very happy’ that Guy Pearce plays him in Fleet Street biopic Ink | Film | The Guardian
description: Actor says the press baron’s daughter Elisabeth told him her father was pleased, ‘but he hadn’t seen the film at that point’
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Actor says the press baron’s daughter Elisabeth told him her father was pleased, ‘but he hadn’t seen the film at that point’
Content: Guy Pearce, left, plays Rupert Murdoch in Danny Boyle’s Ink which depicts the origins of the SunComposite: AP/Rex featuresView image in fullscreenGuy Pearce, left, plays Rupert Murdoch in Danny Boyle’s Ink which depicts the origins of the SunComposite: AP/Rex featuresFilmRupert Murdoch ‘very happy’ that Guy Pearce plays him in Fleet Street biopic InkActor says the press baron’s daughter Elisabeth told him her father was pleased, ‘but he hadn’t seen the film at that point’Philip Oltermannin VeniceWed 2 Sep 2026 17.07 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.42 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRupert Murdoch is “very happy” that he’s being portrayed by Guy Pearce in a new film about the origins of British tabloid the Sun, the Australian actor has said.Speaking at theVenice film festivalahead of the premiere of 28 Days Later director Danny Boyle’s Ink, Pearce said he had been messaging with the media tycoon’s daughter Elisabeth “and she did say ‘Dad’s very happy that you’re playing him’.”“But he hadn’t seen the film at that point, so we’ll see,” Pearce added, who had his breakout role in 1994’s The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert.Ink is set in 1969, the year Murdoch took over the ailing newspaper and installed Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) with a mission to outsell the Daily Mirror, then Britain’s leading tabloid.Playwright James Graham, on whose script the film is based, said Murdoch senior twice visited performances of the stage version in the West End and on Broadway.“I remember he was very good at sort of not really giving anything away,” Graham said of the News Corp founder’s reaction. But he said Murdoch “really enjoyed” a particular sequence that showed the workings of the printing process – “the dirt and the steam and the filth that used to go into making a paper on a daily basis.”“He was really charmed by that, which I thought was interesting, because the end of the story is that he’s the first to go digital, and Fleet Street is no longer what it was due to his decisions.”The Murdoch clan’s business travails and familial battles in the US are widely thought to have been portrayed in HBO series Succession,in spite of the programme-makers’ denials.Boyle’s film, by contrast, focuses solely on Rupert Murdoch’s early years in Britain, and finds his role in the battle with Fleet Street’s old guard to be not without appeal.In Venice, Boyle said Murdoch “represented at the time a breath of fresh air in what was a very, very rigid British society”.“He was dealing with a lot of prejudice because he was Australian, which I can certainly understand – I can empathise with that,” said the director, whose 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple, was released this year. “He particularly had a loathing for the British establishment, what’s called the British establishment, which I personally share as well.”Graham said he also wanted his script to show the long-term knock-on effect that the Sun’s disruption of the newspaper industry had on contemporary media.“The tradition of news and journalism in the UK was very much based on the BBC, which is meant to educate and inform, and then these guys just smashed through with an aggressive attempt at entertainment and fun,” said Graham.“The origins of this story, and the news philosophy that was about engagement, entertainment and destruction, that’s never been more embedded in our discourse, with social media and now AI. It’s all about power of engagement.”Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalRupert MurdochGuy PearceItalyEuropeFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pauline Clayden obituary | Ballet | The Guardian
description: Sadler’s Wells dancer who was a snake in Tiresias, a goat in Sylvia and an autumn fairy in Frederick Ashton’s Cinderella
Author: Jane Pritchard
Headline: Sadler’s Wells dancer who was a snake in Tiresias, a goat in Sylvia and an autumn fairy in Frederick Ashton’s Cinderella
Content: Pauline Clayden as Ophelia in Hamlet, Sadler's Wells Ballet, London, 1945.Photograph: Erich Auerbach/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPauline Clayden as Ophelia in Hamlet, Sadler's Wells Ballet, London, 1945.Photograph: Erich Auerbach/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesBalletObituaryPauline Clayden obituaryDancer in the Sadler’s Wells Ballet who was a snake in Tiresias, a goat in Sylvia and an autumn fairy in Frederick Ashton’s CinderellaJane PritchardWed 2 Sep 2026 17.32 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.34 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePauline Clayden was one of the dancers who formed the core of the Sadler’s WellsBalletin the decade after the second world war, leading up to its royal charter in 1956. Never a principal, she was one of those talented, adaptable, highly valued soloists without which ballet companies can never survive.Clayden, who has died aged 103, would feature in the corps de ballet and step out of it to dance leading roles. It says much about her talent that she often stepped into those created forMargot Fonteyn; forFrederick Ashton, the choreographer, she was the ideal dancer to do so.Among her early Fonteyn roles in Ashton’s ballets were Una in The Quest, which she performed with “touching sincerity”, wrote the musicologist Lionel Bradley; the poignant Flower Girl in Nocturne; and leader of the Children of Light in Dante Sonata. In the 1950s she danced as Queen of the Air in Homage to the Queen and with notable success as Chloé in Daphnis et Chloé. But Ashton also created roles for Clayden. With Brian Shaw, she was one of the pair of copulating snakes in Tiresias and a sacrificial goat in Sylvia (she joked about the menagerie of animals she danced).Clayden was also the first to perform the fast, stormy solo for the Autumn Fairy in Ashton’s staging of Serge Prokofiev’s Cinderella – although she acknowledged that much of it had been choreographed on Pamela May.Born in Lewisham, south-east London, to Frederick Clayden, who worked for the Railway Clearing House, and his second wife, Ada (nee Taylor), Pauline was pushed into ballet by her mother, who died when she was 15. Her main training was at the Cone school, where she became lifelong friends withJulia Farronand was spotted by Peggy van Praagh, who was on the lookout for dancers forAntony Tudor’s London Ballet. The company had been invited to serve as the opera-ballet for the 1939 International Opera Season at Covent Garden underThomas Beecham.View image in fullscreenClayden with Robert Helpmann in Miracle in The Gorbals.Photograph: Granger/ShutterstockMost of Clayden’s performances were simply moving across the stage – as in the dance sequence for Parsifal – but she was in a larger ballet included in Aida, in which the ballerina was Fonteyn. Their careers would constantly overlap and Covent Garden became her performing home.When London Ballet re-formed in the early months of the war, in 1939, Clayden was invited to join the company. She was quickly recognised as a valuable member, and in addition to dancing the company’s repertory of ballets by Tudor, she was involved in creations byKeith Lester, Frank Staff,Wendy Toyeand most significantly in Andrée Howard’s La Fête Étrange, evoking the party episode in the novel Le Grand Meaulnes.Clayden was welcomed to the larger Rambert-London Ballet when the two companies amalgamated; the intensity of dancing in up to four hour-long day-time performances for a full year gave her an enormous amount of stage experience. Among the roles she danced were the various variations in Soirée Musicale and a witty role in Staff’s Czerny 2. Other roles, including the Bluebird pas de deux and Canary/Song Bird variation from Aurora’s Wedding, remained in her repertory with the Sadler’s Wells Ballet when she danced in the full Sleeping Beauty. Indeed, she danced the Song Bird variation when it reopened the Royal Opera House in 1946, and when Sadler’s Wells Ballet conquered New York in 1949.When the London-Rambert company closed in 1941, Clayden was one of the dancers who performed Staff’s choreography in The Tales of Hoffmann and the following year she joined Sadler’s Wells Ballet. Her first created role was the allegro Promenade solo inNinette de Valois’s ballet of the same name. She also created roles for Howard and Robert Helpmann. For Howard, she made a considerable impact as Mayfly in an iridescent, mainly purple, costume in Le Festin de l’Araignée (The Spider’s Banquet), suggesting in her solo the few hours of happiness before the end of her short life.For Helpmann she brought nervous tension and pathos to the Suicide in Miracle in the Gorbals. Bradley commented that Clayden “achieved perfection in an adage, a wonderful combination of technique, timing and inspiration”. Clayden never forgot this solo, and when Helpmann’s ballet was reconstructed by Gillian Lynne for BirminghamRoyal Balletin 2014, Clayden was able to set this section accurately, while other parts were evocations of the original ballet.She retained an interest in dance, and from the 90s her clear memory contributed to the reconstruction of Dante Sonata, and the Queen of the Air’s solo for the Royal Ballet; she taught her solo from Promenade to students of the Royal Ballet School, where she was a guest tutor for various projects.In 1948, Clayden married Howard J Gamble, an Indian Army officer who later became a professor of neuroanatomy, whom she had known from childhood. Eight years later she retired from the stage and in 1984 moved to Salcombe, Devon, but continued to take an active interest in dance.Gamble died in 1999. Clayden is survived by their children, Amanda and Roger, five grandchildren and four great-grandchildren.Pauline Elsie Clayden, ballet dancer, born 12 October 1922; died 21 July 2026Explore more on these topicsBalletDanceRambertSadler's WellsRoyal BalletFrederick AshtonMargot FonteynobituariesShareReuse this content
