title: ‘If he can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine by him’: Francis Fukuyama on Trump, democracy - and changing his mind | Books | The Guardian
description: The political thinker became famous for declaring the triumph of liberal democracy. Thirty-seven years on, he explains what he really meant and why he made the rare journey from right to left
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The political thinker became famous for declaring the triumph of liberal democracy. Thirty-seven years on, he explains what he really meant and why he made the rare journey from right to left
Content: ‘We’re actually pretty stable, peaceful’ … Prof Francis Fukuyama at Stanford University. His new book, In the Realm of the Last Man, is part intellectual autobiography and part political history.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘We’re actually pretty stable, peaceful’ … Prof Francis Fukuyama at Stanford University. His new book, In the Realm of the Last Man, is part intellectual autobiography and part political history.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianThe ideas interviewBooks‘If he can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine by him’: Francis Fukuyama on Trump, democracy - and changing his mindThe political thinker became famous for declaring the triumph of liberal democracy. Thirty-seven years on, he explains what he really meant and why he made the rare journey from right to leftJonathan FreedlandWed 2 Sep 2026 10.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are not many public intellectuals who can say they’ve been cited by Capt James T Kirk of the Starship Enterprise, but Francis Fukuyama is one of them. In Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country, William Shatner’s character is in a reflective mood, and speaks to the Klingon chancellor. “Some people think the futuremeans the end of history,” Kirk muses. “Well, we haven’t run out of history quite yet.”When the film came out in 1991 and in the years that followed, you’d often hear comments like that. They were nods to a thesis so famous it hardly needed spelling out. It debuted in a 15-page essay written by Fukuyama, then a 36-year-old thinktanker, which was published in the National Interest, a right-leaning journal of US foreign policy,in the summer of 1989. There was a question mark in the title: it was called The End of History?. In book form three years later, it became The End of History and the Last Man. But these were subtleties that, as we shall see, got lost.The essay made its author internationally renowned and helped power a career as a political scientist, philosopher and analyst, specialising in foreign policy and political economy. Fukuyama’s counsel was sought by governments and boardrooms worldwide, from the C-suite of Ford to the tent of the Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi. But, as is clear from his new memoir –which is less a conventional autobiography thanthe story of a life in ideas, one that revisits intellectual shifts and academic schisms and which, by contrast, scarcely mentions the author’s 40-year marriage –it also became something of a millstone.I ask how he feels about that article. Perhaps the way the Beatles might have come to regard their breakthrough hit She Loves You: grateful for the success, but tired of having to replay it, again and again.“Well, a little bit of both,” Fukuyama, now 73, says on a video call from California, via a computer which, incidentally, he built himself. “I certainly think that I would not have gotten the attention that I did if I’d used a different title. So that made a difference.”But there has been a downside. “You know, I get these ridiculous comments, on the internet. If I post a picture of my grandkids, they say, ‘Oh, I thought it was the end of grandkids.’”View image in fullscreenIdeas man … Francis Fukuyama at Stanford University.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianThe problem, as Fukuyama sees it, is a 37-year-old misunderstanding – one that took root as soon as the essay was published. Thanks to that simple, memorable phrase – “the end of history” – people assumed that Fukuyama was arguing that, with the cold war winding down and the Berlin Wall about to fall, human conflict, even human events, were drawing to a close. That all the big arguments had been settled, there would be no more war, and the entire world was about to live under US-style liberal democracy. As he puts it in his new book, In the Realm of the Last Man, it was taken to be an expression of “naive liberal triumphalism, and I have been asked several times a week over the past three decades whether I wished to recant my argument. I have written thousands of words and given dozens of interviews seeking to answer this question.”Indeed, he tells me, that was “one of the reasons for writing the memoir: to finally get down in a very clear way what I was intending and the ways I was wrong, and the ways I believe I’m still right.” The book makes clear his argument was a subtle one, drawn from Hegelian thought and inspired by an earlier interpreter of Hegel, Alexandre Kojève, from whom Fukuyama borrowed that all-important title.According to Kojève, the end of history was the moment when a principle or set of ideas emerged that could not be bettered, in terms of their ability to satisfy the human beings who lived in a system shaped by them. Kojève himself had playfully proposed the year 1806 as the end of history, since that was the moment when, thanks to his defeat of the Prussian monarchy in the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt, Napoleon brought the code that bore his name to the heart of old Europe, the legal framework that emerged from the French Revolution. As Fukuyama writes, the revolution of 1789 “established the underlying principles of a modern liberal order, namely, the two principles of liberty and equality, or the equality of liberty”.View image in fullscreenFrancis Fukuyama in Munich, 1992.Photograph: Interfoto/AlamyOf course, those principles were not immediately or fully implemented: even as Napoleon was advancing in central Europe, the French colonial authorities were putting down a slave revolt in Haiti. “But Kojève’s point was that once the idea of universal freedom got out, it was only a matter of time before those principles became accepted and practised around the world.” Even if the time it took was measured in centuries, with plenty of events – including two world wars – along the way.This was the nature of the argument Fukuyama was making for 1989. Not that liberal democracy was perfect or that it had been achieved everywhere and that all conflict was over. But rather that the evidence had become compelling that there was no better guiding principle or system. And Fukuyama still maintains that view.“For the last 30-odd years, I’ve been saying that I’m looking for an alternative system that purports to be more humanly satisfying than liberal democracy. And a number of candidates have come along. Some of them, I think, are very implausible.” He cites Iranian-style theocracy as one such candidate. The Chinese model is a more serious contender. As an authoritarian system, he says, it can make decisions more efficiently than liberal democracy. “So the question for me is: is this also a sustainable system? Are we going to see this [replicated] in other places in 30 years? And that is still an open question.” If, over the next generation or so, China turns out to be much more successful than the US, with an exportable model that satisfies human needs, then Fukuyama promises he will be “perfectly happy to concede that I was wrong on the fundamental premise”.He also accepts that the current consensus on liberal democracy is far from universal, and that the “liberal” part of that idea – the belief in constraints and checks on elected power – is especially vulnerable. He writes that is in part because support for those constraints has often been contingent on a collective memory of how dangerous the world can become without them. A younger generation who have known only peace and prosperity, and for whom the tyrannies of the mid-20th century are ancient history, will only be dimly aware of the perils of unrestrained, illiberal rule.View image in fullscreenEnd of an era … the Berlin Wall falls near Potsdamer Square in November, 1989.Photograph: Gerard Malie/AFP/Getty ImagesBut surely Donald Trump, born just one year after the defeat of nazism, is living proof that proximity to that dark history hardly entails respect for the guardrails imposed by liberal democracy? How do we explain the US president’s disregard for that danger?“You know, that is one of the great psychological questions that future historians are going to have to answer. He has had this weird attraction not just to the current Russia and Vladimir Putin but, all the way back in the 1980s, he visited Moscow. He took out these full-page ads attacking Nato way back then, when we were still in the middle of the cold war. I mean, it somehow has to do with his lack of any kind of moral compass beyond his own self-interest. He basically worries about whether he can make money, and if you can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine with him.”It’s worth getting to the bottom of what Fukuyama meant all those years ago because, once you’re there, you find an idea more interesting than the soundbite versions of his thesis ever allowed. The final paragraph of his original essay declared: “The end of history will be a very sad time.” With the fundamental question of politics essentially resolved, even if far from realised, “the worldwide ideological struggle that called forth daring, courage, imagination and idealism, will be replaced by economic calculation, the endless solving of technical problems, environmental concerns, and the satisfaction of sophisticated consumer demands.” As Fukuyama writes now: “The being who emerges at the end of history is typically someone stripped of struggle, risk and ambition, someone whom the philosopher Nietzsche labeled the ‘Last Man’. We have been living in the realm of the Last Man for some time now.” Once this notion is unpacked, even those who dispute Fukuyama’s reading of 1989 will concede that he had an uncanny inkling of what was to come.For what he was anticipating was that liberal democratic societies might prove adept at delivering stability and relative material comfort, but that would still leave something profound missing. He cites Socrates’ notion ofthymos, or spiritedness: that part of the soul which desires the respect or esteem of other human beings. The last man might have his basic economic needs met, but he would become angry if he believed he was not receiving the recognition that was his due. It amounts to thesimple craving for one’s equal dignity to be respected.View image in fullscreen‘If you can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine with him’ … Donald Trump at a Maga rally in North Carolina.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesReading those passages, it’s hard not to think of the worldwide surge of nationalist populism and the Maga movement in particular. “The mass of the people that come to Donald Trump’s rallies feel that the liberal elites have not been respecting them,” says Fukuyama. “One of the things that propelled Trump to the top of the American political system is his recognition that they were being disrespected, and he found a way of talking to them in a manner that didn’t show that kind of contempt. He doesn’t use big words. He tells stupid stories that they think are very funny, and you know, educated people are appalled by.”This, he says, is a key challenge for Democrats. “If you really want to solve this problem of equally distributed respect … it’s about both listening and talking. I think a lot of elite politicians actually don’t listen to people that are not like themselves. They don’t necessarily listen to ordinary people, and they also don’t know how to speak to ordinary people.” He notes the desperation of Democrats “looking for working-class candidates that they can push” in the November midterm elections, but says the “equal distribution of respect requires both policies that distribute actual material benefits more equally and a different kind of political discourse”. In that context, he likes the look of former Chicago mayor and potential 2028 presidential candidate Rahm Emanuel, a man with a streetfighter’s manner who is also, says Fukuyama, “very funny”.The other defining trait of the last man is the hunger for a cause, for a life-or-death struggle that might give his life meaning. In 1989, Fukuyama anticipated “a powerful nostalgia” for the age when such battles raged, and that too reads like a premonition of our own era. “Fundamentally we’re living in a really weird time,” he says now. He looks back to Germany of the 1930s. “They’d just lost a horrendous war, millions of casualties. Then hyperinflation. Everybody’s savings get wiped out. You have instability on the streets of the Weimar Republic, and so – it’s not an excuse – but you can kind of understand why people would be drawn to extremist ideologies at that point. But that’s not the world we’re living in in 2026. You know, we’re actually pretty stable, peaceful. And yet you find people on both the left and the right that are saying, ‘This is the worst possible world.’ In America we have the Maga right that says that America is dying. It’s being killed by the other side. And it’s very hard to understand how they can argue that with any kind of historical awareness.”View image in fullscreen‘Elite politicians don’t listen to people that are not like themselves’ … Francis Fukuyama at Stanford University.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianFor the left, at least, hasn’t the climate crisis played a part in contributing to that mood of existential doom? Fukuyama doubts it. “I am sitting in California. It’s a comfortable 70 degrees [21C]. You know, I’m not burning up like you in Europe, so maybe it’s just my personal situation. But I think that climate still remains a rather abstract thing for many people.” He points the finger in a different direction. “Social media and the internet in general have permitted this vast disconnect between actual material lived reality and what people experience online.” He cites the legions of young men in the manosphere, gaming the days away, simultaneously fed a falsely bleak picture of the world and longing for a cause worth dying for, as an illustration of the phenomenon he warned of in the very last sentence of the 1989 essay: “Perhaps this very prospect of centuries of boredom at the end of history will serve to get history started once again.”There’s a chapter in the new book whose title hints at the other story the memoir tells: On Changing Your Mind. Fukuyama has made the relatively rare political journey from right to left. A former official in the Reagan and Bush administrations, he tells of his time as a disciple of the noted conservative scholar Allan Bloom and as part of the neoconservative gang of thinkers who prepared the intellectual ground for the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Fukuyama renounced his support for that war in February 2004. In the book, he candidly admits that what prevented him from making the break earlier was, in part, less ideological than social and human: he didn’t want to end friendships he had cherished.Still, his departure from the right was not solely in the sphere of foreign policy. While his former colleagues could only see government as an obstacle to be cleared out of the way, his own studies of societies around the world led him to regard a capable state as essential. As if to confirm how far he has travelled, one chapter of the book is titled Learning to Love Bureaucrats.View image in fullscreenLiberty Leading the People, Eugène Delacroix , c1830-31, oil on canvas, Louvre, Paris.Photograph: AlamyI ask whether his perspective on the world might have differed from other Republicans and conservatives because of his Japanese-American roots, which are detailed affectingly in the book. It tells of his grandmother, a “picture bride” who left Japan at 21 when she was put on a “steamer to Los Angeles all alone, where she was to marry a stranger 10 years older than herself”, and of an uncle left “penniless” after the store he built was effectively confiscated when he, like all Japanese-Americans on the west coast, was interned during the second world war. Did he see things differently because he was a member of an ethnic minority that had suffered a bitter history of exclusion?“No, I don’t think so,” he says immediately. “I’ve tried to avoid thinking of myself as an Asian-American my whole life, because I just don’t like that sort of identity politics. It’s true that, after 11 September, you had certain rightwing people in the United States saying, ‘Well, we ought to put Arab-Americans in camps.’ And, yeah, of course, I felt that that was really wrong based on my family history, but I don’t think that made me especially sensitive to those sorts of issues.”What changed his mind was a changing world. Even if he still thinks the big question has been resolved, events matter. The Iraq war and the crash of 2008 upended his worldview. As he puts it, “If you’re an intellectual and you believe certain things about the use of military force in foreign policy and about unregulated markets in economics, and both of them lead to big disasters, you ought to rethink some of those assumptions.” ForFrancis Fukuyama, an end to history never meant an end to thinking.In the Realm of the Last Man by Francis Fukuyama is published by Profile Books (£20) and is out on 8 September. title: A moment that changed me: I had a panic attack on public transport – and it led me to a horrifying secret | Mental health | The Guardian
description: For a decade I lived with a fear so bad that I once tried to climb out of a tube carriage while it was in motion. Then a hypnotherapist told me to ask my parents one very important question
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: For a decade I lived with a fear so bad that I once tried to climb out of a tube carriage while it was in motion. Then a hypnotherapist told me to ask my parents one very important question
Content: Mike McNally circa 1965.Photograph: Courtesy of Mike McNallyView image in fullscreenMike McNally circa 1965.Photograph: Courtesy of Mike McNallyA moment that changed meMental healthA moment that changed me: I had a panic attack on public transport – and it led me to a horrifying secretFor a decade I lived with a fear so bad that I once tried to climb out of a tube carriage while it was in motion. Then a hypnotherapist told me to ask my parents one very important questionMike McNally, as told to Farryn StockWed 2 Sep 2026 06.45 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2000, I had been living in London for just over a decade and working at EMI Records for five years. I had moved to Brixton from Surrey – where space and peace were generally abundant – in the late 80s, and I’d noticed I was becoming increasingly anxious and claustrophobic, particularly on public transport.As things got progressively worse, I had a string of distressing panic attacks. Every time, it felt like the world around me was closing in. Then, in July 2003, during my daily commute between Brixton and the South Bank, I had a panic attack so intense I tried to climb out of the tube carriage doors. Thankfully, other passengers held me back until we arrived at the next platform – but I knew the problem was no longer something I could ignore.The following year, my GP referred me to a hypnotherapist. During regression hypnotherapy sessions, I would sit on a chair, close my eyes and feel as if I was falling back through time to different points in my life. After three months of retracing old memories, my therapist asked me plainly if I had ever been in a train crash. “No, I think I’d know if I’d been in a train crash,” I said, slightly taken aback. Despite my insistence, she asked if I would double-check with my parents next time I saw them, in case I had been too young to remember.double quotation markDuring my daily commute, passengers had to stop me trying to climb out of the tube carriage doorsWhen I returned to my family home the next weekend, I did as my therapist had requested. To my disbelief, my parents looked at each other for a second before admitting that I had, in fact, been involved in a train accident as a child.It was 4 September 1965 and, at four years old, I was returning home from a trip with my grandmother to Ireland, where we’d spent the summer with other relatives. We had taken the ferry from Dublin to Holyhead in Wales, then boarded a train to London. As we sat waiting to depart, another passenger train entered the platform and crashed into us. Our train was thrown a few feet backwards, lifting the carriage off its framework and trapping us inside. My grandmother and I were both unharmed but we were squashed together in the September heat amid rising panic, with other passengers seriously injured around us.My parents said they had tried to talk to me afterwards about what had happened, but I would only scream and run away. Not wanting to upset me further, they stopped talking about it entirely.View image in fullscreenMcNally: ‘With my therapist, I developed the tools I needed to stop living in fear.’Photograph: Courtesy of Mike McNallyThe conversation with my mum and dad changed everything. I suddenly had clarity about the source of more than a decade’s worth of fear and panic. It explained why I had struggled with boarding trains, planes and sometimes even a car. Every time I found myself in a situation where I felt trapped or stuck, my brain had subconsciously taken me back to the crash, despite having no conscious memory of it. Discovering the truth meant I could work with my therapist to develop the tools I needed to stop living in fear.A short while after finishing my hypnotherapy, in 2006, I went on a work trip to Vancouver. We had a team meeting at the top of Whistler Mountain – and the only way up was a 30-minute cable car ride. My colleagues told the cable car workers that I suffered from claustrophobia, and they reassured me there was a halfway point where I could get out if I felt I couldn’t make it to the top. But as the journey began, I found myself feeling surprisingly calm, despite knowing I would be trapped for at least 15 minutes. As the cable car reached the mid-point, I saw that the venue staff had come out to applaud me. I knew then that I could make it the whole way up. Instead of choosing to disembark, I called my hypnotherapist and said: “You’ll never guess where I am – halfway up Whistler Mountain!”Not feeling so terrified all the time meant I could finally live the life I had always wanted. This became even more important when my daughter was born six years later. I wanted to be the best version of myself for her – and that wouldn’t have been possible when I was living in a constant state of fear. Now that she’s 14, our shared love of music means we are always travelling across London by train or tube, going to packed concerts together. If it weren’t for my unexpected discovery, I might never have been able to share those moments with her.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The best kettles in the UK to save energy and speed up your cuppa, tested | Tea | The Guardian
description: We boiled litres of water to find the best electric kettles, from hard-water heroes to vintage-style, repairable and wifi-connected models
Author: Rachel Ogden
Headline: We boiled litres of water to find the best electric kettles, from hard-water heroes to vintage-style, repairable and wifi-connected models
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterTeaReviewThe best kettles in the UK to save energy and speed up your cuppa, testedWe boiled litres of water to find the best electric kettles, from hard-water heroes to vintage-style, repairable and wifi-connected modelsThe best air fryers, tried and tested for crisp and crunchRachel OgdenWed 2 Sep 2026 15.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDespite the march of progress, the humble kettle remains a kitchen staple. It’s what we turn to in times of strife, when spirits are flagging, or to start our day. When a visitor calls, one of the first things we often do is put the kettle on.Many small appliances have evolved beyond their original form, but the kettle’s basic principles remain largely unchanged. Water goes in and heats until a thermostat switches it off; the water then pours out, and we enjoy a cuppa. However, the technology that goes into a kettle has been slowly improving: better insulation to keep water hotter for longer and reduce reboils; different temperature settings to suit every drink from green tea to herbal brews; and more features such as filters and concealed elements to keep scale out of our cups.When your existing kettle makes its last brew and must be taken to the big recycling centre in the sky, it pays to check out what’s on offer to replace it. The next one you buy may make more of a difference to your day than you might think.At a glanceBest kettle overallBoschSky kettle£100 at John LewisBest budget kettleKenwoodRipple kettle£39 at John LewisThe forever kettleDualitClassic kettle£164.99 at CurrysThe fastest-boiling kettleNinjaPerfect Temperature kettle£79.99 at NinjaBest budget variable temperature kettleLakelandDigital double-walled kettle£49.99 at LakelandWhy you should trust meWhen a friend heard I was writing this, she asked me, “Aren’t all kettles the same? They all boil water, don’t they?” And while she’s right about the second part, it took me at least 15 minutes to explain why she was wrong about the first. I’ve been testing kettles for years, and they vary greatly – in design, weight, ease of maintenance, ease of use and build quality. Some will last for decades while others will barely make it past the basic guarantee period. In short, yes, all kettles boil water – but they are far from being all the same.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach kettle was hooked up to a power meter to assess electricity consumption.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianAs you can imagine, I boiled a lot of water. Litres upon litres of the stuff. Enough to turn my kitchen into the steamiest hammam and clear my pores of blackheads I’ve had since I was a teenager.Testing wasn’t just about making gallons of tea and having a deep skin cleanse on the cheap, though. I also brought a lot of gadgets to the party: a power meter to assess electricity use for each kettle when boiling exactly one litre of water from cold; a timer to measure how long that took; and a probe thermometer to gauge how long it took for the kettle to click off once it had reached boiling point.Fancy a cuppa? My epic kettle showdown – and what I learnedRead moreExternal temperature was measured using an infrared thermometer and the highest reading noted, while maximum noise levels were recorded with the Decibel X app. After boiling, water temperature was checked at the 30-minute, one- and two-hour points to see how much it had cooled.I tested 13 kettles in total. The ones that made the cut were selected on the basis of good energy efficiency or low minimum fill, plus ease of use or maintenance. Value for money has also been considered, as have longer guarantees and durable build quality that should translate into a lengthy lifespan for the appliance. Energy costs below have been calculated based on the 1 October to 31 December 2026 price cap in Great Britain. All samples have been returned to their supplier or donated toCaterham Round Tableto raise funds for local causes and charity projects.The best kettles in 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianBest kettle overall:Bosch Sky kettleBoschSky kettlefrom£100£100 at John Lewis£100 at AmazonWhat we loveLower temperatures ideal for green tea drinkersWhat we don’t loveNot the priciest here but it’s still an investmentView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£100 at John Lewis£100 at AmazonOffering variable temperatures and a double-walled stainless-steel housing, the 3kW Sky is a brilliant blend of robust form and function. It boasts a low minimum boil (300ml, which is just over a cup), a keep-warm setting and touch controls.Why we love itI found it difficult to select a best kettle from so many that performed well, but the Bosch Sky clinched it because it’s such a good all-rounder that will suit most people. It pours well, has a button that’s within easy reach of the handle so it’s simple to open the lid without touching it, and it’s insulated so the exterior doesn’t become too hot to touch. From a design perspective, it has a more industrial feel than many others – no frippery here – but not too modern that it wouldn’t fit into most kitchens. Its display is thoughtfully designed, easy to keep clean and lights up as it heats.The exterior doesn’t get too hot (up to 40C), and while it wasn’t the fastest to boil in testing, it was only seconds behind the Dualit below. It clicked off at boiling point, and the water was still a toasty 78C 30 minutes later. At the hour point, it was 66C, and after two hours 52C, meaning you’ll spend less time and energy reboiling.It’s a shame that …its premium look ends at the handle, which seems cheap and plasticky next to the sleek aesthetic of the rest of it.Time to boil one litre:2mins 22secsMinimum fill:300mlMaximum fill:1.7lDimensions:15.8 x 23.8 x 25.8cm (WDH, inc base unit)Total weight:1.5kgPower use:0.112kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWhMatching toaster?YesMaximumnoise recorded:59dBTemperature settings:70C, 75C, 80C, 85C, 90C, 95C, 100C, keep warmWarranty:two yearsBoschSky kettlefrom£100£100 at John Lewis£100 at AmazonWhat we loveLower temperatures ideal for green tea drinkersWhat we don’t loveNot the priciest here but it’s still an investmentBest budget kettle:Kenwood Ripple kettleKenwoodRipple kettlefrom£26.10£39 at John Lewis£26.10 at AmazonWhat we loveSingle cup marking is great for a solo householdWhat we don’t loveIts base is light but also feels flimsyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£39 at John LewisFrom £26.10 at AmazonAvailable in four “ocean-inspired” shades – eggshell blue, storm blue, pure white and midnight black – Kenwood’s Ripple kettle has a subtle design that belies its affordable price. It’s practical, too: there’s a 3kW element, a wide pouring spout to prevent drips, and two water windows showing cups on one side and litres on the other (making it left-hander friendly).Why we love itMore affordable kettles tend to demand a higher minimum fill – usually 500ml – but the Ripple enables those on a budget to boil a single cup (200ml), providing excellent energy economy. There’s even a plastic marker inside for one and two cups and max, so you don’t need to watch the water window as you’re filling. It’s lightweight at 1.08kg without feeling flimsy, has a pull-off lid for easier filling, and it boiled quickly in testing, retaining its heat well for the first 30 minutes (72C) and hour (60C).It’s a shame that …the lightweight plastic body meant that the external temperature was hot after boiling (80C). Its two-hour temperature (44C) was also much cooler than the one-hour point, meaning more energy is needed to reboil.Time to boil one litre:2mins 30secsMinimum fill:200mlMaximum fill:1.5lDimensions:22.4 x 18 x 24.8cm (WDH)Total weight:1.08kgPower use:0.118kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWhMatching toaster?YesMaximum noise recorded:57dBTemperature settings:100CWarranty:one yearKenwoodRipple kettlefrom£26.10£39 at John Lewis£26.10 at AmazonWhat we loveSingle cup marking is great for a solo householdWhat we don’t loveIts base is light but also feels flimsyThe forever kettle:Dualit Classic kettleDualitClassic kettlefrom£164.99£164.99 at Currys£164.99 at John LewisWhat we loveRepairable appliances are win for your pocket and the planetWhat we don’t loveMatching toaster is UK-made but the kettle isn’tView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£164.99 at Currys£164.99 at John LewisAlthough it comes with a higher initial outlay, Dualit’s Classic kettle is more of a “buy right, buy once” appliance. It’s as robust as they come, with a durable stainless-steel body, hinged lid, anti-wobble feet and non-drip spout. But it’s the repairable nature of this kettle that makes it an eco-friendly buy. The 3kW element is replaceable, so a pro can swap it for a new one or repair it if it wears out, meaning you may never need to buy a new kettle again.Why we love itRepairability aside, the Dualit Classic kettle also makes it easy to boil only as much water as you need, with a low minimum fill (250ml) and dual water windows indicating cups and litres via multiple markings. There’s no button to raise the lid, meaning one less thing to go wrong; instead, it has a heatproof plastic handle. It was also the second fastest boiling of all the kettles tested and clicked off bang on boiling point.It’s a shame that …the exterior gets hot after boiling – our sample reached 71C. It also lacked a choice of temperatures and a keep-warm function, despite the higher price.Time to boil one litre:2mins 15secsMinimum fill:250mlMaximum fill:1.7lDimensions:15.4 x 23.5 x 28.1cm (WDH)Total weight:1.61kgPower use:0.114kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWhMatching toaster?YesMaximum noise recorded:57dBTemperature settings:100CWarranty:one yearDualitClassic kettlefrom£164.99£164.99 at Currys£164.99 at John LewisWhat we loveRepairable appliances are win for your pocket and the planetWhat we don’t loveMatching toaster is UK-made but the kettle isn’tThe fastest-boiling kettle:Ninja Perfect Temperature kettleNinjaPerfect Temperature kettlefrom£79.99£79.99 at Ninja£89.99 at ArgosWhat we loveSpeedy boiling means no waiting aroundWhat we don’t loveOnly three colours: black, silver or dark blueView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£79.99 at Ninja£89.99 at ArgosAs you’d expect from Ninja, this kettle has features galore, right down to the same familiar beep all Ninja appliances use when you turn them on. However, most notable is its “hold temp”, which keeps your water at a selected temperature for up to half an hour – great for the easily distracted and busy households alike.Why we love itOut of all the kettles tested, this was the fastest, boiling its litre in just over two minutes with its 3kW element. Also in its favour is a 250ml minimum fill, although this is only shown on the inside of the kettle, not the outside. Both cups and litres are denoted in multiple increments on its water window, so there’s little chance of boiling more than you need. It also uses the least energy of any kettle on test.The six different temperatures each has its own button, meaning no need to scroll until you reach your desired heat. The only place it came unstuck was a lack of insulation. Heat was retained for the first 30 minutes (72C) and hour (58C), but its two-hour temperature was 43C.It’s a shame that …the exterior becomes hot: the meter registered a temperature of 97C just before boiling. Plus, it took a couple of seconds to click off once 100C had been reached.Time to boil one litre:2mins 7secsMinimum fill:250mlMaximum fill:1.7lDimensions:22.61 x 23.6 x 26.7cm (WDH, inc base unit)Total weight:1.88kgPower use:0.102kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWhMatching toaster?YesMaximumnoise recorded:55dBTemperature settings:60C, 70C, 80C, 90C, 95C, 100C, hold tempWarranty:two yearsNinjaPerfect Temperature kettlefrom£79.99£79.99 at Ninja£89.99 at ArgosWhat we loveSpeedy boiling means no waiting aroundWhat we don’t loveOnly three colours: black, silver or dark blueBest budget variable temperature kettle:Lakeland digital double-walled kettleLakelandDigital double-walled kettlefrom£44.99£49.99 at Lakeland£44.99 at AmazonWhat we love5C increments give greater temperature choiceWhat we don’t loveMarkings on inside make accurate filling trickyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£49.99 at Lakeland£44.99 at AmazonLakeland’s digital double-walled kettle proves you don’t have to splash the cash for a well-insulated, variable temperature kettle – or one with a decent warranty length. With a powerful 3kW element, a wide choice of temperatures and a keep-warm setting, plus easy controls, it’s hard to ask for more at this price.Why we love itWhat impressed me most about this kettle, aside from its choice of 13 temperatures, was its large, clear display. It’s easy to read from afar, and the temperature is easy to set with plus and minus buttons. The kettle looks and feels premium for the price, with its measurements all marked on the interior.The double-walled construction served it well: the exterior reached only 27C, while the water was still 78C after 30 minutes, dropping to 67C after an hour and 53C after two hours. However, it did take a couple of seconds to click off after boiling.It’s a shame that …this kettle’s lid catch isn’t as well engineered as the rest of it: its flimsy feel makes me worry that it may not go the distance.Time to boil one litre:2mins 30secsMinimum fill:500mlMaximum fill:1.5lDimensions:23 x 16 x 27cm (WDH)Total weight:1kgPower use:0.112kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWhMatching toaster?YesMaximum noise recorded:57dBTemperature settings:40C, 45C, 50C, 55C, 60C, 65C, 70C, 75C, 80C, 85C, 90C, 95C, 100C, keep warmWarranty:three yearsLakelandDigital double-walled kettlefrom£44.99£49.99 at Lakeland£44.99 at AmazonWhat we love5C increments give greater temperature choiceWhat we don’t loveMarkings on inside make accurate filling trickyThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Used the least energy of those tested’: the Swan Alexa smart kettle.Swan Alexa smart kettleSwanAlexa smart kettlefrom£80£80 at AO£113.33 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks seriously hi-tech on the worktopWhat we don’t loveThe kettle is robust but the handle feels cheapView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£113.33 at AmazonBest for:energy efficiencyThis wifi-connected kettle won’t be for everyone, but it may appeal to those who, hands full with kids or shopping, would like Alexa to put on the kettle for them. Beyond its smart features, it’s a decent kettle, using second lowest energy of those tested and letting you easily set different temperatures. It’s well insulated too, with the exterior only reaching 32C after boiling and the water still registering a balmy 57C after two hours.It didn’t make the final cut because …its 1.8kW element meant it was slow to boil, and it took about six seconds to click off after reaching boiling point. The display is difficult to read in bright light, and there’s a 500ml minimum fill, with no markings between that and the max fill.Time to boil one litre:3mins 59secs;minimum fill:500ml; maximum fill: 1.5l;dimensions:20 x 16 x 27.3cm (WDH);total weight:1.26kg;power use:0.107kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWh;matching toaster?No;maximum noise recorded:55dB;temperature settings:40C, 60C, 85C, 90C, 100C, keep warm;warranty:two yearsSwanAlexa smart kettlefrom£80£80 at AO£113.33 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks seriously hi-tech on the worktopWhat we don’t loveThe kettle is robust but the handle feels cheapSage the Smart kettleSageThe Smart kettlefrom£90£90 at John Lewis£94.99 at LakelandWhat we loveTemperature buttons also show suitable type of teaWhat we don’t loveThe steel exterior can stay particularly hotView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£90 at John Lewis£94.99 at LakelandBest for:hard waterIf you live in a hard-water area, you’ll know that descaling a kettle can be a chore. Sage’s the Smart kettle makes it slightly easier thanks to its wide mouth and removable washable filter. It also features variable temperatures, which can be set with dedicated buttons for particular drinks and dual water windows clearly marked with cups and litres.It didn’t make the final cut because …the minimum boil is 500ml, and its 2.4kW element meant it took longer to boil than others. In addition, the external temperature rose to a fairly hot 61C.Time to boil one litre:2mins 40secs;minimum fill:500ml;maximum fill:1.7l;dimensions:18.3 x 23 x 25cm (WDH);total weight:2.1kgpower use:0.12kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWh;matching toaster?Yes;maximum noise recorded:56dB;temperature settings:80C, 85C, 90C, 95C, 100C, keep warm;warranty:three yearsSageThe Smart kettlefrom£90£90 at John Lewis£94.99 at LakelandWhat we loveTemperature buttons also show suitable type of teaWhat we don’t loveThe steel exterior can stay particularly hotDe’Longhi Eclettica kettleDe’LonghiEclettica kettlefrom£49£49.99 at De’Longhi£49 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy on the eye and a speedy boilerWhat we don’t loveThe max fill marker is inside the kettleView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£49.99 at De’Longhi£49 at AmazonBest for:personalisationPutting the fun into functional, De’Longhi’s Eclettica kettle is one for those who like to be different. Available in colours including “whimsical white” and “playful pink”, its USP is personalisation, with a fluted saucer accessory that you can add and remove as you please. Fortunately, it’s a good, robust kettle too, boiling quickly thanks to its 3kW element and low minimum fill of 300ml.It didn’t make the final cut because …heat retention was disappointing: although the water temperature was 70Cafter 30 minutes, it dropped to 42C after two hours. The exterior also reached 98C after boiling.Time to boil one litre:2mins 28secs;minimum fill:300ml;maximum fill:1.7l;dimensions:15 x 25.5 x 27cm (WDH);total weight:1.163kgpower use:0.114kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWh;matching toaster?Yes;maximum noise recorded:59dB;temperature settings:100C;warranty:one yearDe’LonghiEclettica kettlefrom£49£49.99 at De’Longhi£49 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy on the eye and a speedy boilerWhat we don’t loveThe max fill marker is inside the kettleSmeg 50s-style kettleSmeg50s-style kettlefrom£149£149 at John Lewis£159.95 at SmegWhat we loveFeels robust while oozing styleWhat we don’t loveHigh minimum fill so you’re always boiling for twoView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianFrom £149 at John LewisFrom £159.95 at SmegBest for:vintage styleInstantly recognisable, Smeg’s 50s-style kettle has a vintage aesthetic that has won it a legion of fans. However, there’s no getting away from the fact that it’s one of the priciest while not offering much more than the others. The good stuff: it’s stylish, has excellent build quality and a 3kW element that boiled fast. It also clicked off as soon as it reached 100C, and has a base that allows the cable to emerge from anywhere it pleases. There’s an extensive choice of colours, too, plus a soft-rise lid for minimal splashes.It didn’t make the final cut because …minimum fill appears to be 500ml, although it’s not marked as such, and the external temperature reached a sizzling 99C after boiling. Heat retention was decent at first – 70C after 30 minutes – but after two hours, it had reduced to a tepid 41C, meaning more energy is required for a reboil.Time to boil one litre:2mins 17secs;minimum fill:500ml;maximum fill:1.7l;dimensions:22.6 x 17.1 x 24.8cm (WDH);total weight:1.6kgpower use:0.114kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWh;matching toaster?Yes;maximum noise recorded:60dB;temperature settings:100C;warranty:two yearsSmeg50s-style kettlefrom£149£149 at John Lewis£159.95 at SmegWhat we loveFeels robust while oozing styleWhat we don’t loveHigh minimum fill so you’re always boiling for twoTower Scandi kettleTowerScandi kettlefrom£25.99£25.99 at Wayfair£29.99 at TowerWhat we loveA bargain; frees up money for luxe tea and coffeeWhat we don’t loveLooks lovely but feels a bit plastickyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£25.99 at Wayfair£29.99 at TowerBest for:an affordable luxury kettleIf the price of the two stylish kettles above has you wincing, fear not: you can bag an attractive kettle for less than £30. Enter Tower’s Scandi kettle, available in several shades, all of which have faux wood and chrome-effect detailing. There’s good stuff besides the design, too: it’s lightweight (940g), has a speedy boiling 3kW element, and water windows on both sides that are marked with cups and litres.It didn’t make the final cut because …the minimum fill is 500ml, and it took six seconds to click off after reaching 100C. It’s also not very well insulated: the exterior reached 84C after boiling, and while the water temperature was 72C 30 minutes after boiling, it registered at only 44C two hours later.Time to boil one litre:2mins 21secs;minimum fill:500mll;maximum fill:1.7l;dimensions:16.5 x 25.5 x 24cm (WDH);total weight:0.9kg;power use:0.117kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWh;matching toaster?Yes;maximum noise recorded:59dB;temperature settings:100C;warranty:one yearTowerScandi kettlefrom£25.99£25.99 at Wayfair£29.99 at TowerWhat we loveA bargain; frees up money for luxe tea and coffeeWhat we don’t loveLooks lovely but feels a bit plastickyWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenWhat key features should I look out for?How you use your kettle will probably dictate which functions you’ll find the most useful, but generally, any feature that helps to save energy is valuable. For example, kettles that are dual-walled help to trap heat inside, so the water stays warmer for longer while the outside stays cool to the touch.Those with low minimum fills enable you to boil just enough water for a single cup, so you don’t waste energy heating more than you need. Some kettles also have a keep-warm function that stops the water cooling below a certain temperature, which is ideal for those who become distracted after boiling or drink consecutive cuppas. It’s a good idea to check for safety features too, such as an auto shut-off to prevent it from boiling dry if there’s not enough water.Other features are more “nice to haves”: variable temperature models enable you to choose water heated to lower temperatures than boiling, such as 70C or 80C, for other types of tea or for filling a hot-water bottle. Concealed elements, which are easier to keep scale-free, and removable, washable limescale filters will be useful for those who live in hard-water areas. Then there’s connectivity. While wifi-enabled and voice-controlled kettles can feel a little gimmicky, they can be a gift for busy parents who usually have their hands full.Are rapid-boiling kettles faster than normal ones?Rapid-boil kettles don’t have a strict industry definition, so while a rapid-boil kettle should boil water quickly, it may not differ much from one that’s not labelled as such.A more reliable indicator of how fast a kettle will boil is its power rating: this is listed either in watts (eg 3,000W) or kilowatts (eg 2.2kW). The higher the number, the more power its element can use to heat water quickly. However, this isn’t the whole story: boiling times can also be quicker in double-walled kettles (as they lose less heat to their surroundings) and those with concealed or flat elements (which provide more surface area to heat the water than a coil).How to descale your kettleLimescale reduces your kettle’s efficiency, costing you more to boil each time, and shortening the appliance’s lifespan. Descale it monthly, especially if you live in a hard-water area. Standing water encourages the buildup of limescale, so try not to leave water in the kettle after use.While you can buy descaler in the supermarket, a lower-cost and more eco-friendly option is to combine a weak food-safe acid, such as white vinegar or lemon juice, with water. Fill the kettle three-quarters with either water and the juice of one lemon or equal parts water and vinegar. Let it soak for an hour, then boil the kettle (once for vinegar, three times for lemon). Once it’s cooled, rinse thoroughly. If your kettle has a removable filter, take it out and rinse it under running water at the same time.What material is best for a kettle?The material a kettle’s body and lid are made from can make a difference to the appliance’s durability, daily use and even the taste of your drink. The most common materials for electric kettles are plastic, stainless steel and glass.Plasticis probably the one you’ll encounter the most. It allows kettles to be affordable, lightweight – crucial if you have difficulty lifting or pouring when it’s full – and can be almost any colour or texture.Over time, though, plastic can be prone to damage, such as cracks or scratches, and can absorb odours. This means a plastic kettle will usually need to be replaced more frequently than others. Most modern models are made using food-grade plastic, are BPA-free (check websites and labels to be sure), and meet current safety standards: research remains inconclusive about health risks from using a plastic kettle.Stainless steelis another popular material for kettles. It’s hard-wearing, hygienic and resistant to corrosion, scratches and damage. Stainless steel is also a recyclable material (although the recyclability of your kettle will also depend on its construction and how easily its different materials can be separated). In terms of everyday use, good-quality stainless steel is considered to be taste neutral (although a new kettle may impart a slight metallic flavour at first).Kettles made from stainless steel tend to be heavier overall, and will become hot on the outside when boiling and for some time afterwards. They may also be louder when boiling and can stain over time.Glass kettleshave been steadily gaining in popularity – for many, watching the bubbles rise during a boil is part of the ritual. Taste-neutral – a must for tea lovers who want their blends to shine – glass kettles are usually made from borosilicate glass, just like the glassware in laboratories, which is resistant to thermal shock and rapid temperature changes. The material is also non-toxic, non-reactive and won’t corrode – plus, you can always see how much water is left.A glass kettle tends to be heavier than plastic but lighter than stainless steel. However, while glass kettles are tough enough to withstand daily use, they can still break on impact. You may also find they don’t retain heat as well as other materials, and if you live in a hard-water area, the visible limescale may lead to a more frequent need for descaling.How to know when to replace your kettleAccording to various estimates, the average kettle lasts aroundsixtoeightyears. The higher quality the kettle, the better you maintain it and how often you use it will all determine its lifespan.However, while this is a general guide, you should stop using your kettle if you notice damage, discoloration, leaks or any electrical safety issues – such as burning smells, rattling or buzzing sounds, scorch marks, sparks or exposed wires. A kettle that trips your electrics should be replaced immediately. Contact the manufacturer if you are still within warranty or to explore repairability options.Performance issues are also a sign that your kettle is failing. These can include a kettle that’s taking longer to boil, or that switches off before boiling point is reached (indicative of a faulty thermostat). Even if everything looks fine inside, if water begins to taste different, looks cloudy or has a smell, it’s time for a new kettle. Limescale that is hard to shift is another sign your kettle has to go: this points to deteriorating surfaces.What to do with your old kettleIf the kettle still works, some charities accept unwanted electrical items as donations, or you could give it to a friend. Some kettles can be repaired by the manufacturer, such as theDualit modelreviewed above, or repaired locally, so check if there’s a repair cafe or other repair resource near you.If your kettle is broken or past its best, recycling is the best option. Take it to a recycling centre, drop-off point or a store that offers a retailer take-back scheme if you’re buying a new one. Your council may also be able to pick it up at the kerbside. Use the postcode checker atRecycle Your Electricalsto find your nearest options.For more:The best toasters for toast, bagels and crumpetsThe best frying pans for every kind of cookKitchen gadgets top chefs can’t live withoutRachel Ogden has worked as a consumer journalist for decades, becoming an expert unboxer before it was a thing, although she’s much lessadept at repacking. Her home has hosted hundreds of small appliances, from kettles and toasters to robot vacuums.When outside, you’ll find her messing about with pizza ovens, barbecues and heaters.
