title: The best portable neck and handheld fans in the UK to keep you cool, tested | Gadgets | The Guardian
description: The seasons might be changing, but the muggy weather remains, and heatwaves are on the rise. Stay comfortable on the move with our tried and tested portable neck and handheld fans
Author: Alan Martin
Headline: The seasons might be changing, but the muggy weather remains, and heatwaves are on the rise. Stay comfortable on the move with our tried and tested portable neck and handheld fans
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterGadgetsReviewThe best portable neck and handheld fans in the UK to keep you cool, testedThe seasons might be changing, but the muggy weather remains, and heatwaves are on the rise. Stay comfortable on the move with our tried and tested portable neck and handheld fansThe best fans for your home, testedShark ChillPill 3-in-1 fan reviewAlan MartinWed 2 Sep 2026 11.09 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSo far this year, we’ve seenfive heatwavesin the UK. The climate crisis meansthings are heating up year on year, and while we can hide in air-conditioned shops and offices, our homes can get uncomfortably – sometimesdangerously– hot.We also have to go outside – or worse, pack ourselves like sweaty sardines on sweltering public transport. On those occasions, a portable fan can make all the difference between manageable discomfort and indulging in an inadvisable quantity of ice-cream. Their recent popularity has led to manufacturers churning out cheap-but-not-especially cheerful products that ultimately end up as clutter in your house – or worse, landfill, where anestimated 4.3m will end up this year alone.So which should you buy to cool you for many summers to come? I’ve been testing handheld and neck fans from the likes of John Lewis, Dunelm, Dyson and Shark, assessing them for power, noise, battery life and portability. Here’s what I’ve found.At a glanceBest handheld fan overallJohn Lewishandheld and foldable fan£12 at John LewisBest budget handheld fanFine Elementsfolding rechargeable mini travel fan£6 at WickesBest handheld fan for battery lifeBlueairhandheld fan F7£39 at AmazonBest handheld fan for mistingAecoolyCold Air$34.99 (about £25.89) at AecoolyBest handheld fan for powerDivebluesJetforce£16.99 at AmazonBest neck fanJialexinthree-speed neck fan£28.99 at AmazonBest handheld fan for flexibilitySharkChillPill£129.99 at AmazonThe John Lewis handheld andfoldable fan and Jialexin three-speed neck fan were out of stock at the time of publicationWhy you should trust meI’ve been testing consumer technology for more than a decade now, includingelectric toothbrushesandwater flossersfor the Filter. Yet, without wanting to shatter the illusion that this makes me uniquely qualified for the task, portable fans are among the easiest things to test. There’s little subjectivity involved, as you can measure power, noise, weight and battery life. All you really need is a working hypothalamus and fingers that can manoeuvre buttons – which I have.You also need hot weather, of course, and the Great British summer has been, if anything, a little too accommodating in that regard. It also helps that my PC can turn my tiny office into an overheated sauna in 20 minutes.How I testedView image in fullscreenBlown away: wind speed was tested by active use and with a digital anemometer.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianEach of the 20 fans I tested was assessed for measures that can be objectively tested. Power was not only measured by active use, but via a dedicated digital anemometer to measure wind speed at the highest and lowest supported speeds.More power equals more noise, so I used a sound measurement app held 15cm from the source to assess the decibel level at high, medium and low speeds. I timed how long it took each fan to empty its battery at the lowest and highest speeds (a test my three cats hated even more than I did, due to the constant noise for hours at a time), and popped each one on the scale to get an idea of portability.I also assessed them for more subjective things. Is the fan nice to hold? Can it be folded for increased portability or hands-free use? Does it look visually appealing?Finally, there’s the biggie: price. With portable fans costing between £3 and £100+, there’s a huge range of options. It’s simplistic to suggest that a higher cost automatically equals a better experience, though there is naturally a correlation. Nonetheless, I’m more forgiving of odd quirks in cheap fans than I would be in more expensive ones.There’s also the sticky issue of repairability and thegrowing waste problem of fast tech. Tough-to-replace lithium-ion batteries were present in all but two of the fans tested, which is far from ideal. With that in mind, I kept an eye on build quality too, hoping to endorse fans that will have a long and productive life before they need to be disposed of (electrical recycling, please – you canfind a local spot here).After testing, the fans were either returned to the manufacturer or donated to charity.Here are the 12 best portable fans from my tests.The best neck and handheld fans in 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianBest handheld fan overall:John Lewis handheld and foldable fanJohn Lewishandheld and foldable fan£12£12 at John LewisWhat we loveGood price, decent power and comfortable to holdWhat we don’t loveA slightly awkward shape for baggingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£12 at John LewisCurrently out of stockIt may not look that special, but John Lewis’s offering is a well-made product at a reasonable price that doesn’t put a blade wrong. The handle is a good size for a comfortable grip, and the sage colour my review unit came in is rather stylish. You can also get it in white, light blue or an eye-searing orange if you prefer.Why we love itLooks and build quality aside, the fan provides what you need without fuss. It has three power settings, putting out between 2.5 and 3.7 metres a second (m/s) of wind speed, and the 10cm head covers your whole face at a sensible distance without needing constant adjustment. I measured a peak volume of 62.4dB, which isn’t the lowest, but is still quieter than some of the chunkier fans at their lowest levels.The battery lasted more than four hours on its highest setting, which should be sufficient for most journeys, and it can be charged up via a USB-C cable when it’s empty. Pleasingly, the handle can also be folded down to make it a handy desktop fan with or without a cable attached. It works well, as long asyou have space to keep it close enough to be refreshing.It’s a shame that …at 25cm, it’s a little on the tall side.Power levels:3Measuredair speed:2.5-3.7m/sMeasured volume:51.1-62.4dBTested battery life:maximum, 4hrs 11mins; minimum, 9hrs 37minsMeasured weight:181gJohn Lewishandheld and foldable fan£12£12 at John LewisWhat we loveGood price, decent power and comfortable to holdWhat we don’t loveA slightly awkward shape for baggingBest budget handheld fan:Fine Elements folding rechargeable mini travel fanFine Elementsfolding rechargeable mini travel fan£6£6 at WickesWhat we loveIncredible value and nicely portableWhat we don’t loveQuestionable build qualityView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£6 at WickesCheap and cheerful, this folding fan may feel a little rough around the edges, but it gets the job done. It’s not the cheapest fan I tested, but it proved superior toDunelm’s £2.10 offering(which dropped to a barely noticeable 0.5m/s power as the AA batteries drained) and beatSuperdrug’s £5 fanon battery life (a disappointing 45 minutes at maximum and two hours on minimum).Why we love itIt’s flimsy, but the fan delivers the basics pretty well. It has three speeds, giving between 2.6 and 3.7m/s of wind speed, while the battery lasted six hours at the lowest setting, and just short of three at its highest.It’s a touch noisier than the John Lewis model, maxing out at 64.8dB, but it’s more travel-friendly, folding in half for portability and weighing 48g lighter. That folding hinge means you can also use it as a desk fan, if you like, and there’s even a small flashlight on the bottom for looking around in the dark (though it’s easy to leave this on by mistake).It’s a shame that …the build quality isn’t all that, with some rough plastic moulding.Power levels:3Measuredair speed:2.6-3.7m/sMeasured volume:54.3-64.8dBTested battery life:maximum, 2hrs 50mins; minimum, 6hrsMeasured weight:133gFine Elementsfolding rechargeable mini travel fan£6£6 at WickesWhat we loveIncredible value and nicely portableWhat we don’t loveQuestionable build qualityBest handheld fan for battery life:Blueair handheld fan F7Blueairhandheld fan F7from£39£39 at Blueair£39 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat performance and jaw-dropping staminaWhat we don’t loveThe scroll wheel controls are somewhat inexactView image in fullscreen£39 at Blueair£39 at AmazonThe Blueair handheld fan F7 is not only a great portable fan, it also (appropriately) blows all other fans I’ve tested out of the water in terms of battery life. It beat its nearest competitors by more than two hours on its highest setting and, staggeringly, more than eight on its lowest.Why we love itThe battery life of the F7 is astonishing. On its highest setting, it lasted an impressive 7hrs 2mins – longer than some fans on their lowest speed. At the lowest speed, this fan went for more than 35 hours, eclipsing its longest-lasting rival – the JisuLife Ultra2 – by 497 minutes. Pity the poor reviewer who had to find this out the hard way: I missed it dying twice before figuring out the optimal time to start the test so as not to be out or asleep when it ended.As well as the staggering battery life, the Blueair is simply a great all-rounder. It’s comfortable in the hand, and keeps things relatively quiet, ranging from 43dB on its lowest setting to 70.8dB at level 100. That is loud, to be clear, but not given the 5.9 m/s of wind speed it generates at that noise level.The base is curved, so it can’t be stood vertically, but you can use it as a desk fan by tilting the fan part forward and resting it lengthways. This fan’s 100 levels are more of a marketing gimmick than a particularly useful (good luck picking out a specific number using the scroll wheel controls), but you can quickly zone in on exactly the level of cooling you want.It’s a shame that …scroll controls are a little inexact.Power levels:100Measured air speed:2.6-5.9m/sMeasured volume:43-70.8dBTested battery life:maximum, 7hrs 2mins 51secs; minimum, 35hrs 6mins 3secsMeasured weight:260gBlueairhandheld fan F7from£39£39 at Blueair£39 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat performance and jaw-dropping staminaWhat we don’t loveThe scroll wheel controls are somewhat inexactBest handheld fan for misting:Aecooly Cold AirAecoolyCold Air$34.99$34.99 (about £25.89) at AecoolyWhat we loveMisting is strong and coolingWhat we don’t loveBulky handle is tricky for smaller handsView image in fullscreen$34.99 (about £25.89) at AecoolyWhile traditional fans simply push air from A to B, misting fans add water to the mix, and can make you feel far cooler as a result. A fine spray of water quickly evaporates in hot air, absorbing the heat and cooling the air around you as a result.A water tank is more often a feature in larger static fans, as space is at a premium on handheld models that need to save room for a battery. But the Aecooly Cold Air finds space for both, making it a great choice when regular air movement won’t cut it.Why we love itWhile the power of evaporative cooling drops off in more humid conditions, in dry heat it can be a blessing. And with the water tank in the Aecooly Cold Air, you’re prepared for it: simply use the fan as usual, and hold down the misting button on the side to release a blast of water with the air, offering far more effective cooling in the right conditions.The tank isn’t massive, capable of holding up to 23.5ml of water by my measurements, but holding the button down continuously (not recommended: it really heats up!) produced 19mins 28secs of water flow. While that’s similar to the time I got from the Shark ChillPill’s 14ml reservoir, it’s definitely a stronger spray.It also offers higher wind speeds, reaching 6.2m/s at the highest of its five settings, while staying quieter, maxing at 70.8dB. It lasts more than 22 hours at its lowest setting, too, making it the third-longest battery I’ve tested to date. And while this fan and the Aecooly Air Mate below are sold in dollars, shipping costs aren’t extortionate.It’s a shame that …it’s a chunky beast to hold for extended periods, even with giant paws like mine.Power levels:5Measured air speed:3.2-6.2m/sMeasured volume:54.4-70.8dBTested battery life:maximum, 3hrs 4mins; minimum, 22hrs 23mins 4secsMeasured weight:281gAecoolyCold Air$34.99$34.99 (about £25.89) at AecoolyWhat we loveMisting is strong and coolingWhat we don’t loveBulky handle is tricky for smaller handsBest handheld fan for power:Diveblues JetforceDivebluesJetforce£16.99£16.99 at AmazonWhat we loveImpressive power at a competitive priceWhat we don’t loveIt starts loud and gets louderView image in fullscreenFrom £16.99 at AmazonIf you want power for a reasonable price, then the Jetforce is the answer. Even at its lowest of five speeds, it narrowly betters the speeds of the two fans above by hitting a breezy 3.8m/s.Why we love itA refreshing breeze even at the lowest settings, but when you’re really struggling with heat, crank it up all the way to level five, and it hits a massive 6.6m/s.In truth, you likely won’t need to max it out, and that’s just as well because the noise levels really pick up on the higher settings. Starting at an already noisy 66dB, put it all the way up to level five, and it reaches 74.3dB, about the level of a vacuum cleaner – a vacuum cleaner uncomfortably close to your ears. It’ll also hit the battery hard: at level 1, you can eke out nearly 11-and-a-half hours, but that drops to 2hrs 37mins on max.Still, if you can cope with the noise or routinely wear headphones, it’s a nice option to have in really hot weather. Plus, the flexible head means you can use it as a desk fan, and it has an attachable lanyard so it can be worn around the neck, blasting air upwards.It’s a shame that …it gets noisy fast.Power levels:5Measuredair speed:3.8-6.6m/sMeasured volume:66-74.3dBTested battery life:maximum, 2hrs 37mins; minimum, 11hrs 25minsMeasured weight:184gDivebluesJetforce£16.99£16.99 at AmazonWhat we loveImpressive power at a competitive priceWhat we don’t loveIt starts loud and gets louderBest neck fan:Jialexin three-speed neck fanJialexinthree-speed neck fan£28.99£28.99 at AmazonWhat we loveImpressive cooling of the neckWhat we don’t loveA fan pointed at the ears gets gratingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£28.99 at AmazonCurrently out of stockWant something hands-free to keep you cool? A fan worn around the neck does that, whiletargeting the body’s thermoregulation centre, which can, in theory, make you feel cooler.The Jialexin three-speed neck fan certainly delivered that, if you can cope with fans running so close to your ears.Why we love itIt really does make you feel cooler, even if the fans don’t appear to be more powerful when compared with regular handheld fans. My anemometer test revealed seemingly low speeds of 1.7 to 2.2m/s, but there are more air sources and, as a result, the cooling effect felt more consistent and less disruptive than a jet of constant air to the face.The downside of this, however, is the noise. While the measured volume of 52 to 64.1dB doesn’t sound too bad – around the sound of a busy office – having it this close to your ears for an extended period is tiring, and you do feel a sense of calm when it’s switched off again. That said, if you’re wearing headphones, it becomes a non-issue.This neck fan is extremely comfortable to wear, and it’s more flexible than solid plastic ones, so you can shape it around your neck for more comfortable cooling. That, for me, makes it stand out from its competitors.It’s a shame that …by design, neck fans have to be quite close to your ears.Power levels:3Measuredair speed:1.7-2.2m/sMeasured volume:52-64.1dBTested battery life:maximum, 3hrs 19mins; minimum, 8hrsMeasured weight:291gJialexinthree-speed neck fan£28.99£28.99 at AmazonWhat we loveImpressive cooling of the neckWhat we don’t loveA fan pointed at the ears gets gratingBest handheld fan for flexibility:Shark ChillPillSharkChillPillfrom£129.99£149.99 at SharkNinja£129.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThree heads for flexible coolingWhat we don’t loveMore heads means more to carry aroundView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£149.99 at SharkNinja£129.99 at AmazonShark’s first-ever portable fan brings plenty of innovation to the table. The ChillPill has three interchangeable heads, letting you swap out the familiar blast of air for one with water misting or a cold plate for direct skin cooling. It’s the priciest fan on this list, but its flexibility is impossible to beat.Why we love itWhile it’s not the most powerful fan you’ll find here, it’s still one of the most effective at quick cooling thanks to the two alternative heads. The misting head is extremely refreshing, with a spritz of water accompanying the airflow for more impact – even if the tiny reservoir means you’ll be refilling it frequently. The cold plate, meanwhile, gives the feeling of pressing an ice-cold bottle against your forehead or neck on a hot day – only it stays cool for as long as the battery lasts.On that note, I found Shark’s battery life estimates wildly inaccurate, but not in the way you’d expect. While the manual says you’ll get “up to 10 hours” with the fan on its lowest setting, I was half asleep when it conked out at 2am, nearly 20 hours after kicking off the test. The cold plate’s promised two hours actually ended up at more than nine, making this a great accompaniment for all-day trips.It’s a shame that …the price is a big ask, and if you bought every extra accessory, you’d be down another £96.94.Power levels:10 (2 for cooling plate)Measured air speed:1.6-4.6m/sMeasured volume:46.2-74.1dBTested battery life:maximum, 2hrs 46mins; minimum, 19hrs 19mins(fan mode)Measured weight:237g (with fan head; 253g for misting; 282g for cold plate)Read the fullShark ChillPill reviewSharkChillPillfrom£129.99£149.99 at SharkNinja£129.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThree heads for flexible coolingWhat we don’t loveMore heads means more to carry aroundThe best of the restView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianJisuLife Handheld Fan Ultra2JisuLifeHandheld Fan Ultra2from£92.99$94.49 (about £69.60) at JisuLife£92.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible power and versatilityWhat we don’t loveIt’s bulky, noisy and expensiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian$94.49 (about £69.60) at JisuLife£92.99 at AmazonBest for:a multi-function fanIf you’ve got money to burn, then the JisuLife handheld fan Ultra2 is both ridiculously powerful and extremely versatile.Starting with the power, it has 100 different speeds, ranging from 2.8m/s all the way up to 9.8m/s at full blast, with 98 increments in between. The battery is impressive too, lasting well over a day at the lowest speed – though this did drop to 1hr 34mins when running at full blast.I was secretly quite pleased about that, as the 88.8dB volume (similar to a hairdryer) wasn’t a particularly fun time for my ears, even from a decent distance away. In truth, that kind of power is uncomfortably like staring down a wind tunnel anyway, and the lower settings are considerably easier on the ears: 59.5dB at level 1, rising to 79.1dB at 50.The high price of entry is made a little easier to swallow, though, since the Ultra 2 brings a few extra features for the money. There are a couple of adapters in the box to turn the fan into an air cushion inflater pump or to help kickstart campfires by pushing in more air. A powerful torch on the back can flick between different lighting modes, including a flashing one to attract attention in an emergency.For those of us allergic to camping, there are more sedate indoor uses. One of the adapters is a dust cleaner, which has removed an unspeakable amount of gunk from my keyboard, and the USB-C charging port is two-way, meaning you can steal some of the 9,000mAh battery for your other devices too.It didn’t make the final cut because …you could buy 15 Fine Elements fans for the Jisulife’s RRP of £95.Power levels:100;measuredair speed:2.8-9.8m/s;measured volume:59.5-88.8dB;tested battery life:maximum, 1hr 34mins; minimum, 26hrs 49mins;measured weight:294gJisuLifeHandheld Fan Ultra2from£92.99$94.49 (about £69.60) at JisuLife£92.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible power and versatilityWhat we don’t loveIt’s bulky, noisy and expensiveVonHaus handheld fan and phone holderVonHausHandheld fan & phone holderfrom£10.99£10.99 at VonHaus£10.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEven at its fastest, it’s not aggressively loudWhat we don’t loveIts smaller head weakens coverage somewhatView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£10.99 at VonHaus£10.99 at AmazonCurrently out of stockBest for:peace and quietTake it from someone who’s listened to the incessant hum of fans for weeks now: the noise can become grating. If keeping sound to a minimum is your priority, then this VonHaus 3-in-1 fan might be the one for you. At its lowest setting, it registered just 41dB – less than the sound of a fridge humming.At that volume, you’re looking at a limited power of 2.7m/s, of course, but you can increase that to 4.3m/s over five incrementally louder settings if you need something more. It’s worth noting that by the time you hit maximum, the volume reaches 61.9dB – more comparable with the other fans on test.Overall, it’s a well-designed fan: comfortable in the hand, with a stand to put it upright on your desk, including a phone holder at the base if you want to watch something over the fan’s whisper. You can even use it as a makeshift neck fan with the detachable lanyard and the head pointed upwards. This isn’t a direct substitute for a neck fan, as it’s still aimed at the face, but it’s a nice added use case all the same.It didn’t make the final cut because …the smaller head doesn’t cover quite as much of the face as other models.Power levels:5;measuredair speed:2.7-4.3m/s;measured volume:41-61.9dB;tested battery life:maximum, 3hrs 45mins; minimum, 13hrs 20mins;measured weight:129gVonHausHandheld fan & phone holderfrom£10.99£10.99 at VonHaus£10.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEven at its fastest, it’s not aggressively loudWhat we don’t loveIts smaller head weakens coverage somewhatDyson HushJet MiniDysonHushJet Minifrom£99£99.99 at Dyson£99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible power from such a tiny productWhat we don’t loveIncredible noise from such a tiny productView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£99.99 at Dyson£99 at AmazonBest for:rapid coolingDyson’s first handheld fan has plenty going for it. The company says it’s taken “17 years of airflow expertise” to pack so much power into a device so small. And the volume of air it can push out is genuinely impressive, with my anemometer measuring 6.1m/s at the highest of its five levels.The HushJet’s biggest problem is the name. Put the word “hush” in a product name, and it’s not unreasonable to expect whisper-quiet performance. And while it makes less racket than experienced hardware engineers would dream possible, it’s still incredibly loud for most, with volumes ranging between 61.5dB on level 1 and 76.2dB on level 5. That’sbetween the volume of a dishwasher and a vacuum cleaner– neither of which you’d want close to your ears for extended periods. For context, theUSNational Institute for Occupational Safety and Health recommends hearing protection for extended exposure to volumes over 85dB.If you can get past the noise, there’s no doubting its cooling capabilities, especially if you engage boost mode. This setting requires you to hold down the “speed up” button and puts out an even more impressive 7.5m/s of wind speed (at an even noisier 80.3dB). It will eat through the product’s middling battery (which is already less than an hour for constant level-5 use), but it will rapidly bring down the temperature.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s more jet than hush.Power levels:five plus boost mode;measured air speed:2.0-6.1m/s (7.5m/s in boost mode);measured volume:61.5-76.2dB (80.3dB in boost mode);tested battery life:maximum, 51mins; minimum, 6hrs 9mins;measured weight:220gReadour fullDyson HushJet Mini reviewDysonHushJet Minifrom£99£99.99 at Dyson£99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible power from such a tiny productWhat we don’t loveIncredible noise from such a tiny productAecooly neck fan Click 01AecoolyNeck fan Click 01£14.24£14.24 at AmazonWhat we loveSurprising power from a compact fanWhat we don’t loveIt looks like a panic alarmView image in fullscreen£14.24 at AmazonBest for:neck coolingMost neck fans look like the inflatable pillows seen on long-haul flights. However, the Aecooly neck fan Click 01 is far less intrusive and a whole lot lighter. You can either hang the 94g, 3.2 x 6.1 x 7.5cm block around your neck, or keep the magnetic lanyard under your shirt and clip the fan to the front, keeping part of the neckband visible. The latter method minimises the “panic alarm” look, but it’s still not exactly unobtrusive, despite the heroic efforts of the lifestyle photographers on its product page.It can blast a decent amount of air upwards, with my anemometer measuring speeds of up to 3.4m/s, although noise levels can be a little intrusive for something that’s permanently close to your ears. Battery life is decent, and it should go for at least two hours – or more than 10 if you use it on its lowest setting.While advertised as a neck fan, it can be handheld too. Just unclip it from the magnetic lanyard attachment and you’ve got yourself a pretty competent handheld unit for more targeted cooling – albeit one that’s not much use hands-free thanks to its unusual shape.It didn’t make the final cut because …despite being labelled as a neck fan, it doesn’t offer all-round neck cooling like rival models.Power levels:three;measured air speed:2.1-3.4m/s;measured volume:59-71.4dB;tested battery life:maximum, 2hrs 15mins; minimum, 10hrs 37mins;measured weight:127g with lanyard (94g without)AecoolyNeck fan Click 01£14.24£14.24 at AmazonWhat we loveSurprising power from a compact fanWhat we don’t loveIt looks like a panic alarmAecooly Air MateAecoolyAir Mate$29.99$29.99 (about £22.20) at AecoolyWhat we loveDetachable head offers great portabilityWhat we don’t loveDo you really want to drain your phone battery?View image in fullscreen$29.99 (about £22.20) at AecoolyBest for:portabilityIf you want the most lightweight solution, then the Aecooly Air Mate is the answer. That’s because it’s actually two parts: a detachable fan head (also available separately) and the 5,000mAh power bank it plugs in to.That gives it great flexibility, as the 38g fan head can draw power from a compatible powered USB-C port. This obviously makes the most sense on your phone or a power bank, but you could plug it in to a laptop or PS5 if you wanted. The head is quite small for a targeted blast, but it still reaches measured wind speeds of up to 4.8m/s.The power bank part is quite compact, vaguely resembling aPez dispenserwhen connected, and the whole package weighs 189g when combined. This has one USB-C and one USB-A port plus a built-in USB-C cable for charging, so you can use it to charge other compatible devices. If you’re using it to charge the fan, it’ll last somewhere between five and 17 hours, depending on which of its four settings you use.How long it will last when plugged into your phone depends on the handset, with smartphones typically packing batteries of between 3,000mAh and 5,500mAh. But given your phone also has to power dozens of other functions, you won’t get the same lifespan as plugging directly into a power bank of a similar capacity.It didn’t make the final cut because …do you really want to waste your phone battery on a fan?Power levels:4Measured air speed:2.7-4.8m/sMeasured volume:57.2-67.3dBTested battery life:4hrs 57mins 5secs to 16hrs 56mins 7secs (with bundled power bank)Measured weight:38g (189g when attached to bundled power bank)AecoolyAir Mate$29.99$29.99 (about £22.20) at AecoolyWhat we loveDetachable head offers great portabilityWhat we don’t loveDo you really want to drain your phone battery?What you need to knowView image in fullscreenHigher fan speeds might make you feel cooler, but they can be louder and drain the battery more quickly.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianWhat features should I look for in a fan?Look out for fans with different uses. While the traditional way to use a handheld fan is, of course, in the hand, some models can double as desktop fans, either by folding in half or with a bundled stand. Some even come with a lanyard attachment so they can be worn hands-free around the neck.While power might seem like the key feature, remember this is always a trade-off. Higher fan speeds will make you feel nominally cooler, but will come at the expense of battery life and noise levels.What are the advantages of a neck fan?Neck fans have two advantages over regular handheld fans. The first is that they’re entirely hands-free, meaning you can wear them without temporarily losing the use of a hand in the process.The second advantage is that as they target the neck, there’sevidence to suggestthey may make you feel cooler overall. This is because the thermoregulation centre is at the base of the brain, so a neck fan may make you feel cooler than a regular handheld one, even if your actual body temperature isn’t dropping all that much.The downside to this is that the positioning directly below your ears can be a little tiring, given the constant volume (although this is a problem that’s easily sidestepped with a pair of headphones).How do I dispose of an old handheld fan?If your fan still works, you should try to pass it on to a friend or family member. After all, who would turn down free cooling in the heat? If none want it, someone on Freecycle might, or you may even be able to get some money for it on Gumtree or Facebook Marketplace.If it’s broken, that’s a different story. Unfortunately, most handheld fans don’t have user-replaceable batteries, but it’s worth checking to make sure that’s the case with yours.Shark, for example, sells a replacement battery for the ChillPill(although it’s out of stock at the time of writing).If the fan can’t be fixed, then don’t dispose of it in your regular household waste, as thebuilt-in batteries are both dangerous and an environmental hazard.Some shops such asCurryswill recycle electrical items free of charge. Alternatively, can find local options on theRecycle Your Electricals website. Just enter your postcode and select “electric fan” from the list to see your local options.For more:The best evaporative air coolers – testedDyson HushJet Mini Cool fan review: I’ve never tested a handheld fan this powerful – or this loudDo I really need air conditioning in the UK? title: No eggs, no potatoes but ‘a lot of imagination’: how Spain cooked in war’s hunger years | Spain | The Guardian
description: Book recreates recipes from period following end of Spanish civil war when people faced food shortages
Author: Stephen Burgen
Headline: Book recreates recipes from period following end of Spanish civil war when people faced food shortages
Content: ‘An eggless tortilla’. The recipes in the book span the period from the founding of the second republic in 1931 to the phasing out of ration cards in 1952.Photograph: Berta Álvarez AcalView image in fullscreen‘An eggless tortilla’. The recipes in the book span the period from the founding of the second republic in 1931 to the phasing out of ration cards in 1952.Photograph: Berta Álvarez AcalSpainNo eggs, no potatoes but ‘a lot of imagination’: how Spain cooked in war’s hunger yearsBook recreates recipes from period following end of Spanish civil war when people faced food shortagesStephen Burgenin BarcelonaWed 2 Sep 2026 10.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew dishes are simpler to prepare than Spain’s signature dish oftortilla de patatas, which – aside from disputes about onions – requires nothing more than two basic ingredients and a pinch of salt. But where to begin if you have neither eggs nor potatoes?That is the question the chef and food writer Berta Álvarez Acal sets out to answer inRecetas de Guerra(Wartime Recipes), a compilation of recipes covering the years of hunger after the end of the Spanish civil war in 1939.In the case of thetortilla de patatas, the absent eggs and potatoes were substituted by moistened bread and onion to try to simulate the texture of an omelette.“There was a formula using water, bicarbonate of soda and a bit of oil which simulated an egg perfectly and the potatoes are substituted by bread to make a tortilla that really is delicious,” Álvarez said.View image in fullscreen‘Fried calamari without the calamari’. Álvarez says the recipes were recreated and shared with friends and family.Photograph: Berta Álvarez AcalIn the recipe for “fried squid without squid”, deep-fried onion rings masquerade as squid while the “wartime hake” is instead salt cod.As for the “wartime and postwar breakfast”, this consists of “coffee” made from a blend of barley, malt and chicory.“I got the idea for the book when I came across one of my great-aunt’s handwritten recipe books and I noticed that some of the recipes were marked ‘wartime’,” Álvarez said. “That led me to research recipes from other sources such as Ignacio Doménech, who wrote a book during the war about how to substitute ingredients and how to make the most of leftovers.”She added: “Doménech showed us hundreds of examples of how, with a lot of imagination, we could survive those terrible days of starvation.”Some of Doménech’s recipes, although born of privation, could well find themselves on the menu of an upmarket restaurant today, such as his rose petals with milk and honey.Álvarez did not just compile the recipes. “We recreated them and shared them with friends and family,” she said. “Some dishes, although they were prepared from scraps, surprised us as they were real gems, others were not so great.”The recipes in the book span the period from the founding of the second republic in 1931 to the phasing out of ration cards in 1952. In between, starvation stalked the land, especially in areas that supported the losing republican side in the civil war.According to Miguel Ángel del Arco Blanco, a historian at the University of Granada, between 1939 and 1942 about 200,000 people died of starvation in Spain.While people in the countryside could to some extent subsist on olives and whatever they could grow, Álvarez said “the hunger in Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia was horrific”.“It may seem implausible,” she said. “But for far too long, food in the postwar period was far worse than during the war.”View image in fullscreenChildren queuing for milk rations in Barcelona in 1937.Photograph: Daily Herald Archive/SSPL/Getty ImagesProduce previously fed to livestock such as beetroot and turnips found its way to the table while the shortage of protein meant pets, cats in particular, were at risk.“They were dangerous years for cats,” Álvarez said. “People used to put notices up in the hallway saying ‘please respect your neighbour’s cat’. But the cats lived on rats and were not good to eat.”Álvarez said that what she learned while researching the book was to make the most of every kind of produce, adding that the book was also a homage to the generation that lived through those grim years. “I think it’s important that everyone knows what our grandparents lived through because it marked them as a generation. They were incredibly strong.”Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropeSpanish food and drinkFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: How to turn past-their-best bananas into a glorious ‘ice-cream’ – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Bananas often go off quickly, so use up over-ripe, brown specimens in a sugar-free dessert that will satisfy any sweet-tooth cravings
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Bananas often go off quickly, so use up over-ripe, brown specimens in a sugar-free dessert that will satisfy any sweet-tooth cravings
Content: ‘Really hits the spot’: Tom Hunt’s brown banana ‘ice-cream’.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian. Food styling: Tom Hunt.View image in fullscreen‘Really hits the spot’: Tom Hunt’s brown banana ‘ice-cream’.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian. Food styling: Tom Hunt.Waste notFoodHow to turn past-their-best bananas into a glorious ‘ice-cream’ – recipeBananas often go off quickly, so use up over-ripe, brown specimens in a sugar-free dessert that will satisfy any sweet-tooth cravingsTom HuntWed 2 Sep 2026 13.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.15 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith two young kids, we get through alotof bananas in our household. Perhaps surprisingly, though, most of them are frozen: our daughters eat them straight from the freezer most evenings, with frozen berries and yoghurt, for pudding. We normally order a stack of bananas every Saturday, and before the end of the week they inevitably start to turn brown. At this point, we peel, slice and freeze them for the children’s evening yoghurt, though sometimes, when we have a real excess, I turn them into today’s incredibly satisfying “ice-cream”. Its silky-smooth texture really hits the spot, and satisfies any ice-cream cravings without recourse to added sugar or excessive fat. The trick is to freeze the bananas in a single layer on a flat tray, so they don’t freeze into a homogeneous mass, then transfer to a container to enjoy as and when.Brown banana ‘ice-cream’This has to be in my top five everyday desserts, not least because brown bananas are very gooey and sweet, have a rich and creamy texture and a satiating flavour. Portion for portion, it feels luxurious and indulgent, even without the extra sugar, saturated fat, gums and stabilisers found in much commercial ice-cream and other ready-made desserts. Of course, blended fruit is itself a readily absorbable sugar, but the trade-off is worth it for the extra fibre, potassium, manganese and other vitamins. It’s also a fraction of the price of shop-bought ice-cream.This is best eaten fresh from the blender, but if you need to store a bumper batch, remember to take it out of the freezer at least 10 minutes before you want to scoop it.1 or more brown bananasHalf the bananas’ weight in liquid– water, yoghurt, milk or a plant-based alternativeToppings, all optional and to tasteChopped nutsCoconut flakesGrated chocolatePeel and chop the bananas into 2cm-thick slices (this makes them easier to blend later), then spread out on a tray and freeze for at least five hours. Once frozen, store in a sealed container in the freezer.To make the ice-cream, weigh the amount of banana you’ve taken out, then add half its weight in liquid – that is, water, yoghurt, milk or a plant-based alternative. Transfer to a jug blender and blitz smooth, but not for too long or the fruit will melt too much; stir, if need be, to get an even blend. Serve immediately as it is, or leave to soften like aMr Whippy-alike soft serve, or freeze for an hour or more for a firmer, scoopable texture, adding any optional toppings of your choice.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteFruitIce-cream and sorbetDessertfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Poppy O’Toole’s midweek timesavers: spicy chicken and baked rice, and Thai-style lemongrass fishcakes – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: You’ll thank yourself for making these batch-cooking beauties to store in the freezer until the next busy worknight
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: You’ll thank yourself for making these batch-cooking beauties to store in the freezer until the next busy worknight
Content: Poppy O’Toole’s midweek spicy chicken and baked rice.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenPoppy O’Toole’s midweek spicy chicken and baked rice.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.FoodPoppy O’Toole’s midweek timesavers: spicy chicken and baked rice, and Thai-style lemongrass fishcakes – recipeYou’ll thank yourself for making these batch-cooking beauties to store in the freezer until the next busy worknightPoppy O'TooleWed 2 Sep 2026 06.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve called this spicy chicken and baked rice “midweek”, but you can enjoy this baby all week long. Juicy, spiced chicken, fluffy baked rice and enough flavour to make you bin that takeaway menu and raid your cupboards instead. Then some fragrant, delicate fishcakes with a lovely, bouncy texture, which are such a winner for the freezer. Taking only 10-ish minutes to cook from frozen, they save you from hungeranddistraction on a busy WFH day.Midweek spicy chicken and baked ricePrep10 minMarinate1 hrCook45 minServes8200gGreek yoghurtZest and juice of 1 lemon50g harissa paste1 tbsp garlic granules1 tbsp dried oregano2 tsp ground turmeric1 tbsp ras el hanout2 tsp ground coriander2 tsp ground cuminSalt and pepper16 skinless, boneless chicken thighsOlive oil3 red onions, peeled and roughly chopped into large pieces2 red peppers, deseeded and roughly chopped into large pieces4 garlic cloves, peeled and minced or grated2 tbsp tomato puree400g basmati rice1400g tincrushed tomatoes800ml chicken stockServing suggestions (optional)Sliced or pickled red onionCrumbled fetaFlat-leaf parsley leavesIn a bowl, combine the yoghurt, lemon zest and juice, harissa, garlic granules, dried oregano, ground turmeric, ras el hanout, coriander and cumin with a large pinch each of salt and pepper. Add the chicken thighs, give them a good mix to coat, then pop them in the fridge to marinate for at least an hour.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Meanwhile, put a glug of olive oil in an oven-safe saute pan on a high heat. Chuck in the onions and peppers, fry for two to three minutes, until colooured and slightly blackened, then add the garlic and fry for a minute more, until fragrant.Turn down the heat to medium, squeeze in the tomato puree and cook for one minute, until the mix darkens. Season generously, then tip in the rice and toast for a minute. Pour in the crushed tomatoes and chicken stock, and bring to a bubble.Put the chicken thighs on top of the rice – you want about half of each chicken thigh sitting above the level of the stock – then put the pot in the oven for 30 minutes, until the chicken is slightly charred and cooked through and the rice is tender. Serve immediately, piping hot, with the pickled red onion, feta and parsley, if you like.To eat later, freeze in an airtight container for up to three months. To reheat from frozen, heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 and reheat for 45–50 minutes, until piping hot throughout. Or defrost fully in the fridge overnight, then heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and reheat for 25–30 minutes, again until piping hot throughout.Lemongrass and ginger Thai-style fishcakesView image in fullscreenPoppy O’Toole’s lemongrass and ginger Thai-style fishcakes.Prep5 minChill1 hrCook15 minServes8500g skinless, boneless cod, or haddock200g shelled raw king prawns3 tbsp green Thai curry paste2 lemongrassstalks, bashed and roughly chopped50g fresh ginger, peeled and roughly chopped4 garlic cloves, peeled1–2 tbsp fish sauce, to taste2 tsp palm sugar1 tbsp light soy sauce2 eggsAbout 200g cornflourOlive oilTo serve (optional)Sweet chilli saucePickled vegCooked rice noodlesThai basil and mint leavesLime wedgesTip the fish, prawns, curry paste, lemongrass, ginger, garlic, fish sauce, palm sugar and soy sauce into a food processor. Crack in the eggs, then blitz to a paste. Tip the mixture into a bowl and stir through enough cornflour to make a wet dough (you may not need all of it, so add the cornflour in batches).Wet your hands so the fishcake mixture won’t stick to them, then weigh out 16 equal balls of about 70g each. Shape these into 2cm-thick patties, then arrange on a well-oiled baking tray – they will feel really wet, but that’s normal! - and refrigerate for at least an hour, to firm up.Put a little olive oil in a frying pan on a medium heat, then, working in batches, fry the fishcakes for three to four minutes on each side, until cooked through, piping hot and golden. Serve with sweet chilli sauce, rice noodles, herbs and lime, if you like.To eat later, freeze the raw fishcakes on a tray until solid, then transfer to an airtight container and freeze for up to three months.To cook from frozen,put a little olive oil in a frying pan on a medium-low heat, then fry the fish cakes in batches for about five to six minutes on each side, turning carefully, until cooked through, piping hot and golden.These reccipes are edited extracts from Poppy Cooks: The Actually Delicious Batch Cookbook, by Poppy O’Toole, published by Bloomsbury Publishing at £22. To order a copy for £19.80, visitguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFoodChickenMeatMain courseRiceFishSeafoodrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original work
Author: Aaron Mok
Headline: As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original work
Content: Guardian DesignGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.ReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original workSupported byAbout this contentAaron MokWed 2 Sep 2026 13.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.24 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release ofChatGPTin 2022. She went from receiving slow one-off jobs creating logos and packaging to an onslaught of requests asking her to fix versions that were generated by artificial intelligence – from sharpening fuzzy images for printing to turning flawed designs into usable files.By 2025, Lisa, who asked not to be fully named to avoid solicitations, said 90% of her incoming logo and packaging design requests required cleaning up AI-generated content, work that accounted for 60% to 70% of her annual income. But the grind was exhausting. Clients lowballed her;' some AI-generated designs were so flawed that she had to recreate them from scratch and she worried about being complicit in AI-driven copyright infringement. By the end of the year, she began turning those jobs down.“It was just so soulless,” said Lisa, who now focuses on “human-made designs”.Lisa is part of a growing group of creative freelancers being hired to clean up AI slop, a term used to characterize low-quality, AI-generated output. As businesses use tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude to produce marketing copy, illustrations, books and videos, they are hiring creative professionals to humanize AI-generated copy, repair botched images and salvage flawed footage.The work serves as a stopgap in an increasingly challenging job market, supplementing income for those who freelance full-time or on the side. But clients often underestimate the time and skill involved, expecting cleanup to be quick and cheap when it can require as much work as creating something original, freelancers said. And while the high volume of cleanup gigs can be lucrative, freelancers are divided over the trade-off. Some find it tedious and creatively unfulfilling, while others enjoy the challenge. As AI improves, freelancers question how long the demand will last and where they’ll turn once the jobs dry up.For now, demand for AI cleanup work is growing.On Freelancer.com, a contract work platform with more than 88 million users, job listings tagged with phrases such as “correct AI”, “AI hallucination” and “AI error” rose 87% to 10,760 globally between August 2025 and June 2026, according to internal data shared with the Guardian. The jobs were concentrated in graphic design, followed by video editing, proofreading and content writing. Upwork saw AI remediationgigs jump 70%year over year, and Fiverr saw keyword searches for “AI cleanup” services grow more than 20 times between 2023 and 2026, according to data shared with the Guardian.The specter of AI could spell trouble for the creative freelance labor market. Listings for freelance jobs exposed to automation fell 21% in the eight months after ChatGPT launched and image-creation gigs dropped 17% after AI image generators arrived, according to a2025 studypublished in the academic journal Management Science. And those losses have continued, according to a2026 study.Meanwhile, more workers are turning to freelance work as companies cut staff and hire less, intensifying competition. The average project on Freelancer.com drew 54 bids in 2025, up 8% from the year before, according to the site’sannual report.But as companies cut costs, they’re changing the nature of freelance assignments, from requests for creative work to sprucing up AI output. Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, said the cleanup work is often commissioned by small companies and entrepreneurs using AI to produce a first pass, only to run into problems they don’t have the expertise to solve.“[AI output] needs a human to turn it into something polished that can actually be used,” he said. The time and money saved on the first draft can be eaten up by the “incredibly time-consuming” work of preparing it for commercial use.The rise of the AI cleanup crewsFor some freelancers, cleanup is taking up a growing share of their workload and traditional creative projects are becoming harder to find.Todd Van Linda, a full-time freelance illustrator in Florida, began taking AI cleanup gigs in 2023 as his usual work drawing illustrations, video game art and architectural plans became less steady. The work typically involves filtering out visual noise, improving resolution, and hunting for glitches like an extra toe.“Money”, Van Linda said of his motivation. “The jobs were there to be done.”Though some clients expect AI cleanup to cost less than original work, Van Linda won’t lower his rates. When one prospective client offered about $500 to repair 13 to 15 AI-generated illustrations for a children’s book, with the expectation that each should take about 15 minutes, he turned it down. He said projects can take between a few hours of work to days depending on the scope. His rate is $65 an hour and “doesn’t go down from there”, he said.For Kym Dunbar, a freelance writer and editor based in Australia, AI cleanup now accounts for about 60% of her workload, as writing work like blogs and website copy have dwindled. As a result, Dunbar said her monthly earnings from writing original content have fallen to roughly a third of what she made during the pandemic.Dunbar stumbled into cleanup work in 2024, when a client asked her to revise an AI-generated article. She quickly learned to spot recurring problems, from repetitive language and awkward paragraph structures to a lack of emotional nuance. Since then, she has worked on about 40 AI-generated nonfiction books, longform articles and technical papers.“There’s a lot less good projects available for writers and editors these days,” Dunbar said.But “cleanup” can understate how much work is involved.Nathan McConnell, a multimedia editor who freelances on top of his full-time job, started editing AI-generated videos in 2023. His work has ranged from removing reflections from AI real estate videos to fixing robotic voiceovers and malformed 3D models. The requests have increased from two or three projects in 2023 to eight to 10 so far this year, he said.One client brought him roughly 100 AI-generated images of humanoid animals for a tarot deck riddled with extra fingers, two left feet and other mistakes. McConnell spent two to three hours repairing each image in Photoshop, expecting the project to take nearly two weeks to finish. But after making the first 10 cards, he called the project off because of health issues and constant changes requested from his “persnickety” client.Not everything that lands in McConnell’s inbox can be saved, he said. That could look like videos where the physics feel off, like shadows falling the wrong way, or animations that repurpose another creator’s work without permission.“I’ve told a client before that it’s ‘too’ slop,” McConnell said. “There’s no way I can fix this.”While McConnell and Van Linda would rather make original work, not everyone finds fixing AI outputs dispiriting. Dunbar considers it “interesting” and “challenging”, and takes satisfaction in turning a weak draft into polished prose.What troubles her is that people increasingly see AI not as a tool, but as the “be-all and end-all” of the creative process.“I just feel it’s a shame we need to do it,” Dunbar said.Slop cleanup jobs may not lastIt’s unclear whether cleaning up AI-generated slop will remain a viable source of work.Dunbar isn’t convinced it will. She believes much of the work humanizing AI could dry up within five to 10 years as models improve and allow businesses to generate usable content themselves.McConnell sees it differently, arguing that AI still needs to be “babysat” to catch mistakes an untrained eye might miss, from logos that violate brand guidelines to objects that appear and disappear in videos. “We need people [to fix] problems that AI is creating,” he said.But Van Linda is already creating a different path. After he stopped taking AI cleanup gigs late last year, he has seen more clients, some of whom have been dissatisfied with AI, seeking original, hand-drawn work.“Quite frankly, this kind of thing has gotten extremely distasteful to me,” he said about AI cleanup work.Though Lisa, the freelance graphic designer, updated her profile to say she no longer works with AI-generated images, she still gets requests to edit them. She occasionally takes cleanup gigs for clients who come to her after getting poor results with AI. But some clients “straight up lie” and pass off the images as original creations.“They say ‘I don’t use AI,’ but there’s a “[Google] Gemini logo on the bottom,” she said.But just in case AI makes her job obsolete, she has a plan. Lisa has begun returning to the canvases, watercolors and other physical art she practiced before she pursued a career in graphic design. She predicts that within “another year or two”, AI will be able to do logo and packaging design as well as she can, leaving only “the best of the best” able to make a living.“I don’t know if I’m good enough to survive the digital stuff,” she said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedChatGPTOpenAIfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My autistic son lives in fear of bailiffs from Ovo breaking into his flat | Money | The Guardian
description: He doesn’t have an account with them but he is being bombarded with demands for money and threats of debt collectors
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: He doesn’t have an account with them but he is being bombarded with demands for money and threats of debt collectors
Content: Ovo Energy sent an agent to the flat to ‘prove’ there was no Ovo meter installed.Photograph: Paul Melling/AlamyView image in fullscreenOvo Energy sent an agent to the flat to ‘prove’ there was no Ovo meter installed.Photograph: Paul Melling/AlamyConsumer championsMoneyMy autistic son lives in fear of bailiffs from Ovo breaking into his flatHe doesn’t have an account with them, but is being bombarded with demands for money and threats of debt collectorsAnna TimsWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 16.18 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy autistic son has been bombarded for years by letters to his home from OVO Energy addressed to “The Occupier”, with demands for money and threats of debt collectors. He is supplied by Scottish Gas.He was required to let an OVO agent into his flat to “prove” he didn’t have an OVO meter. Neither this, nor countless phone calls, has stopped the demands.Call centre agents confirm that he doesn’t have an account but seem powerless to update the system. He lives in fear that bailiffs will break his door down.LO,EdinburghBritish Gas mixed up our energy meter – but now I’m being penalisedRead moreOVO swiftly decided that the bombardment was triggered by address error on the national database. In short, it says, the gas and electricity meters supplying another property had been registered to your son’s address. It corrected the address for the gas, but tells me another supplier owned the electricity meter and had “rejected multiple requests” by OVO to update the database.In response to my queries, OVO agreed to suspend demands and issued a letter of deadlock to enable your son to complain to the Energy Ombudsman.The letter, which enables access to the database, discovered that the electricity meter was correctly registered to a neighbouring address and supplied by OVO, but OVO had somehow got your son’s address on its billing system. It was ordered to pay £150 compensation and the bills have now ceased.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. title: Sali Hughes on beauty: think facial sunscreens are greasy? The best are featherlight, fresh and invisible | Skincare | The Guardian
description: There’s no excuse for being UV-reckless with these new options
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: There’s no excuse for being UV-reckless with these new options
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Sali Hughes on beautySkincareSali Hughes on beauty: think facial sunscreens are greasy? The best are featherlight, fresh and invisibleThere’s no excuse for being UV-reckless with these new optionsSali HughesWed 2 Sep 2026 10.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost half of UK adultsdo not apply sunscreen daily. If you think even this woeful figure sounds surprisingly high, I agree with you – some surveys have daily SPF use as low as8% in the male adult population.My own feeling, based on hundreds of conversations with the UV-reckless, is that most would probably offer “greasy texture and feel” as their defence. And yet almost a third of the population wear moisturiser.So what if I told you that sunscreen formulation has improved dramatically in the past five years, offered up some excellent, modern SPFs that feelexactlythe same as a lightweight, non-greasy face lotion, and promised that you’ll barely even know you’re reducing your risk of premature skin ageing and cancers as you wear them?double quotation markIt’s been tried by friends with rosacea, eczema and acne, and in all cases I had to ask for it backLet’s start with the comfiest sunscreen yet from the always dependable La Roche Posay.Anthelios UVAIR Serum Sunscreen SPF50(£26) comes in clear and tinted versions. I won’t dwell on the latter because there’s only one shade of tan and this sullies what is an otherwise flawless formulation. The clear version, however, suits every skin tone and is a near-perfect daily sunscreen for all types – non-oily while still comforting drier skin, invisible, lightweight and obedient under makeup. One can never say anything is suitable forallsensitive skins (someone will always react to any product and this is not without fragrance), but so far it’s been tried by friends with rosacea, eczema and acne, and in all cases I had to ask for it back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: a shortcut to glass skin? Try these one-step moisturisersRead moreSimilarly faultless isAqua Glowing Sunscreen SPF50(£15.30) from Dr Althea, a high-street Korean brand that has yet to disappoint me. This is for drier skins, which may cause you to expect heavy duty grease, but there is none. What a glorious everyday sunscreen at a good price. Fluid, quickly absorbed, soothing (thanks to panthenol and ceramides) and leaving a fresh, not at all makeup-like glow, it stays healthily moist-looking for hours, even on my very dry face.Finally,Naked Sundays’CabanaClear Water Gel Serum SPF50(£30) is just about the wateriest, lightest, freshest-feeling and least visible sunscreen on the market. It leaves even the oiliest sunscreen refuseniks without a leg to stand on.None of these sting my eyes, which is my recurring issue with many other synthetic UV filters, and all can be used instead of moisturiser if you only have the will to apply one layer of a morning.Explore more on these topicsSkincareSali Hughes on beautyBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: swot up with these lessons in back-to-school dressing | Fashion | The Guardian
description: September is the most fun time of year to shop, but it can also be dangerously seductive. Keep your wits about you with these tips
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: September is the most fun time of year to shop, but it can also be dangerously seductive. Keep your wits about you with these tips
Content: Video: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Melanie WilkinsonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley on fashionFashionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: swot up with these lessons in back-to-school dressingSeptember is the most fun time of year to shop, but it can also be dangerously seductive. Keep your wits about you with these tipsJess Cartner-MorleyWed 2 Sep 2026 14.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIused to love back-to-school shopping when my children were little. The miniature highlighter pens, the name labels, those pop-out pencil cases from Smiggle, even the intergenerational wrangling over when the price of a water bottle becomes unreasonable. I love the ceremony of new beginnings. The curtain-raising drama of it all.Luckily for me, you don’t have to grow out of back-to-school shopping even though your children do, because in fashion September is considered the start of the new year. This is eminently sensible, because this time of year is a much better moment for a restart than January. The actual new year is dark and bleak and makes resolutions and projects feel intimidating rather than exciting. But right now, the evenings are still light, and while I’ve still got a bit of a tan pretty much anything feels possible.Back-to-school is a whole vibe, not just a shopping spree. The juice is in the back-to-school thinking, rather than the back-to-school shopping. It is about snapping back into focus, getting your head in the game. Life gets a little loose over summer, which is delicious, but sometime about now you get a restless itch for a new tempo: more coffee and less wine, more can-do and less can’t-be-bothered.double quotation markIt’s good to be extremely picky. The best shoppers are utterly ruthlessThis is the most fun time of year to shop. I love seeing the swimwear and sandals swept away by crisp shirts and I-mean-business kitten heels and loafers. But this also makes it a seductive time to shop, so we need to have our wits about us.I came across a useful protocol on stylistAllison Bornstein’s Substack, where she wrote about her fashion red flags; deal breakers that tell you that a piece isn’t going to work for you, and which you ignore at your peril. They are personal to everyone.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The GuardianBornstein’s first red flag – and I am very much with her on this – is the bra-specific top. Off-the-shoulder necklines, shoulder cut outs, open backs. These are acceptable for special occasion tops, but no one has the time to rummage for a strapless bra before work, and wardrobe-solution type bras are almost never comfortable to wear all day. Not to mention: if the person who designed the top doesn’t think about where bra straps go, it makes me wonder how much they think or care about women’s bodies – so it’s a philosophical red flag as well as a practical one.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: the secret to summer layering? Sheer braveryRead moreGreen flags, meanwhile, are those items which you should snap up when you see them, because they are as rare as hen’s teeth. (Annoyingly, you will almost always spot a green flag item when taking a short-cut through M&S because you are late for a meeting, but you must try to grab them when you can.) Green flags include the perfect jeans, and an all-day bag of the right size that has a secure but unfiddly fastening and doesn’t require you to hunch one shoulder toward your ear to stay in place. I would add shoes with a 5cm-ish mini-heel that is either block-shaped or flared, so that the tip doesn’t come off when wedged in the escalator or between paving stones – you will have your personal green flags, also.Back to the red flags. It is good to be extremely picky. Fashion has a monumental overproduction problem, so there are a lot of clothes out there. The best shoppers are utterly ruthless. One of my red flags is anything with buttons that look a bit cheap or even just boring: a bad button makes a dull coat. Another is anything that misbehaves when you move: skirts that ride up, off-the-shoulder necklines that won’t stay down. “That woman over there yanking at her top every 10 seconds looks so chic,” said literally nobody ever.The key is to combine high standards with gritty, laser-focused realism. Do not buy a sundress you wish you’d had on your holiday last month or a grand linen ensemble perfect for a long lunch which you won’t have time for between now and 2027. Clothes should express your aspirations, but they also need to survive your Tuesdays. More than anything, back-to-school season is about clothes for real life. If a top only works with a weird bra or a bag only looks good until you put anything in it, that’s not wardrobe, that’s a fail. It goes back on the rail and you, my friend, go straight to the top of the class.Styling: Melanie Wilkinson. Styling assistant: Charlotte Gornall. Model: Moli at Milk.
