title: Whisky galore – and now plenty more besides: exploring the Scottish island of Islay | Scotland holidays | The Guardian
description: Distilleries are the backbone of Islay’s economy and tourist trade. Thanks to their success, other businesses – from breweries and farms to restaurants and chocolatiers – are now thriving and adding to the island’s appeal
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: Distilleries are the backbone of Islay’s economy and tourist trade. Thanks to their success, other businesses – from breweries and farms to restaurants and chocolatiers – are now thriving and adding to the island’s appeal
Content: The village of Port Charlotte on Islay, located on the shore of Loch Indaal.Photograph: Mark Unsworth/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe village of Port Charlotte on Islay, located on the shore of Loch Indaal.Photograph: Mark Unsworth/AlamyScotland holidaysWhisky galore – and now plenty more besides: exploring the Scottish island of IslayDistilleries are the backbone of Islay’s economy and tourist trade. Thanks to their success, other businesses – from breweries and farms to restaurants and chocolatiers – are now thriving and adding to the island’s appealAilsa SheldonWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 07.10 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Paps of Jura disappear into the mist as I pedal along the shores of Loch Indaal, and the rain cloud I’ve been racing finally catches up. I stash myhire bikeatPort Charlotte youth hostel, quickly change and make it toLochindaal Seafood Kitchenjust before the downpour.I’m soon warmed, by the welcome then by a bowl of creamy fish chowder. “We’ve plenty of fresh seafood just in,” is all the temptation I need to order the seafood plate. It’s a bowl for one, but a hungry one, and soon I’m picking and cracking my way through piles of fat langoustines and crab claws, with hot whisky-butter scallops and plenty of bread and butter.The island of Islay, off the west coast of Scotland, is far better known for its drinks than its food. With 10, soon to be 11, working whisky distilleries, Islay is synonymous with rich, heavily peated single malts. But, over several days cycling around the island, I find that whisky does much more than fill warehouses and attract tourists. It is helping to support an island where agriculture, fishing and hospitality have long struggled to provide year-round employment.View image in fullscreenLunch at Lochindaal Seafood Kitchen.Photograph: Ailsa SheldonAtBruichladdich, one of Islay’s smallest distilleries but the largest private employer, that begins with the barley. When the distillery was bought by a pair of wine merchants after being mothballed several times in the 1990s, they questioned why the barley arriving at the distillery was being sourced from so many different places. Surely, they thought, like vineyards, where the grain was grown would influence the whisky’sterroir.They began encouraging farmers to grow barley on Islay, which hadn’t been done since before the second world war. Farmers were understandably wary of taking on an unfamiliar crop, particularly as the tens of thousands of migratory geese from Greenland are partial to a field of young barley. When Islay’s last creamery closed in 2000, the dairy industry collapsed, so growing barley offered farmers another way to use their land, and Bruichladdich guaranteed to buy the crop regardless of the yield. Today, 21 Islay farms grow barley for the distillery, producing half of its requirements, and early experiments with rye have been promising.double quotation markGrowing up on Islay, whisky was a way of life. Every family has at least one person working in whiskyEva MacIntyre grew up on Islay, tried living on the mainland and came back. She now works for Bruichladdich as a brand ambassador and takes me up the hill to see the distillery’s water source.“Growing up on Islay, whisky was a way of life,” she tells me. “It’s not just a drink; it’s all about who you share it with.” Before her whisky presentations, she practises with her grandfather. Her story is not unusual. “Every family has at least one person working in whisky,” she tells me.View image in fullscreenRoom with a lighthouse view … at Port Charlotte youth hostel.Photograph: Ridgeline_PrintsI meet Kate Hannett, a full-time forager responsible for gathering the 22 botanicals used in the Botanist gin across peaty bogs and hillsides. Her brother, Adam, is Bruichladdich’s master blender, having started his career as a tour guide. Lisa Matthews, the assistant blender, is also anIleach(a person from Islay) and the distillery’s first female blender. Her brother is a brand ambassador in the US. There are jobs in whisky, and reasons to stay on the island, that most rural communities could only dream of offering their young people.The distilleries are woven into Islay life. I hear frequent stories of distilleries helping each other out and lending equipment when machinery breaks down. “It’s really not competitive,” Eva says. As well as the employment opportunities, whisky benefits the infrastructure. There’s a full-time fire service, unusual across rural Scotland. Even the swimming pool is heated by waste energy from Bowmore distillery.AtIslay Ales, another island-made drink begins with barley and soft west coast water. The brewery, founded in 2004, opened a new brewhouse last year. Its spent grain, or draff, goes to local farms for feed and wastewater is treated through a reed bed. On an island where the growing season is short and the weather can change before you’ve finished your pint, making food and drink locally is not necessarily easy. “After theAgricultural Show, which is the third Thursday in August, it’s winter,” I’m told.View image in fullscreenIslay Cocoa uses several local ingredients in its chocolates.Photograph: Islay CocoaEmma Goudie ofIslay Cocoabegan making chocolates as an easily transportable product that wouldn’t compete directly with other island food businesses. She uses local ingredients where they make sense, rather than simply because they are local.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s quality first, but I’m lucky that the produce we have here is excellent.” Her current range includes Orsay sea salt, Argyll coffee, and sourdough from neighbouring Jura. She also works with the whisky industry, creating chocolates designed to pair with Ardbeg and forCaol Ilatours. “It grew quite organically and in the best way,” she says.Iain and Alexander MacLellan are the fourth and fifth generations of a family whose hospitality business stretches back to the late 19th century. At Lochindaal Seafood Kitchen, Iain tells me he grew up with the fishers who supply the restaurant and remembers cooking mackerel and scallops on their boats. “I’ve been 52 years behind the bar,” he tells me. The restaurant grew out of the family pub atLochindall hotel, partly because, as Iain puts it, “we ran out of space to serve our seafood platters”.View image in fullscreenAilsa Sheldon enjoying a drink at Ardbeg House hotel.Photograph: Ailsa SheldonChef Ajish Johny came toPort Charlotte hotelafter working in India and Dubai, on cruise ships and in Wales, and has now been here for four years. His menus feature a curry of the day alongside Loch Gruinart oysters, locally caught fish and burgers made with beef from nearby Octomore Farm. “We never compromise on quality,” he says. “People on Islay are well travelled. They know what good food is.”And then there isArdbeg Housein Port Ellen, a once tired traditional hotel that has been transformed into a maximalist extension of the Ardbeg brand. There are 12 quirkily themed bedrooms, a fishing boat suspended over the bar and a theatrical restaurant with a beaten-metal ceiling, bold lighting and tables made from marble bathroom offcuts. It’s an exuberant place, but the food is excellent and well priced. I eat bread made with eight-year-old Ardbeg and thyme; langoustine bisque with pickled fennel and tarragon, then the catch of the day, sea bass, with cabbage, kale, roast potatoes and split beurre blanc. My taxi driver insisted that I try the sticky toffee pudding. My server does the same, so I take the hint and am rewarded with a treacly wedge of cake with whisky ice-cream. Outside, it’s raining again.Before the Clearances, about 15,000 people lived on Islay. Today, there are just over 3,000. Islay may have been built, in part, on whisky. But increasingly, the whisky is helping build something back: farms, breweries, restaurants, food businesses and reasons to stay.Ailsa Sheldon was a guest ofHostelling ScotlandandBruichladdich Distillery.Port Charlotteyouthhostelhas dorm beds from £28and private rooms from £78(open late March to early October). Travel to Islay from the Scottish mainland byCaledonian MacBrayne(CalMac) ferry fromKennacraigor by flying withLoganairfrom Glasgow. Hire bikes fromIslay E-Wheelsin Port Ellen from £25a day for non-electric, £35for electric, delivery available across the islandExplore more on these topicsScotland holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysWhiskyFoodEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: The rain has come, and suddenly the land looks (and smells) different | Drought | The Guardian
description: Inkpen, Berkshire: From lurid yellow to a moorland brown; from the scent of fire smoke to sheep urine. It’s amazing what some rainfall can do
Author: Nicola Chester
Headline: Inkpen, Berkshire: From lurid yellow to a moorland brown; from the scent of fire smoke to sheep urine. It’s amazing what some rainfall can do
Content: ‘The land looks strange and unlike itself.’ Gallows Down, on the Berkshire-Hampshire border.Photograph: Nicola ChesterView image in fullscreen‘The land looks strange and unlike itself.’ Gallows Down, on the Berkshire-Hampshire border.Photograph: Nicola ChesterCountry diaryDroughtCountry diary: The rain has come, and suddenly the land looks (and smells) differentInkpen, Berkshire:From lurid yellow to a moorland brown; from the scent of fire smoke to sheep urine. It’s amazing what some rainfall can doNicola ChesterWed 2 Sep 2026 05.30 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.35 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter an entire heat-baked summer without rain, the land looks strange and unlike itself. Fields, banks and grassy margins are the lurid yellow ochre of climate fiction – the mise en scène captured with eerie relevance in the recent BBC TV dramaThe Rapture.There are cracks so deep in Weaver’s Field that the farmer can push his arm in up to his elbow. Spots of bird’s-foot trefoil and sky-blue chicory (the latter on uncannily short stems) polka-dot the otherwise dead pasture. Sentinel field oaks seem unaffected, but shallow-rooted beech trees, familiar in giant caterpillar shapes on the downs, shed shrivelled brown leaves and a poor, early beechnut mast. Gnarly field maples are almost leafless, while sycamores bracket the green with their browning leaf-curl. Even in the keepered woods, laurel has wilted.View image in fullscreenChicory growing on short stems in a parched hayfield.Photograph: Nicola ChesterFor a week, skeins of black smoke drift from the field fires at Enham Alamein, from the eastern end of Greenham Common, and from the New Forest further south. But over the nearby border into Wiltshire, it is white smoke that veils Salisbury Plain all the way to Avebury and itsvillage in the stones. The Westbury White Horse, ofEric Ravilious’s 1939 painting, is on fire – or the down and iron age Bratton Camp next to it is. Probably carved from the chalk in the late 1600s, it is surrounded by an apocalyptic vision.The smell of smoke lingers long after a fire is out. Dad was a fireman who fought the New Forest conflagration in 1976, and Windsor Castle’s blaze in 1992. For me, the smell of burning evokes heightened awareness, comfort and safety, an olfactory memory of him coming home from work in damp, sooty uniform, and the alarm bell that rang in my childhood home whenever he was needed.The rain teases us for a few more days, as towering piles of cumulus sail north like galleons. When it comes, it darkens the down to an unfamiliar moorland brown. The heat rises again afterwards, and with it the strong scent of ammonia from sheep’s urine. The only thing to wet the ground all summer, it had remained undiluted and on the surface. Reanimated, mingled with damp dust and baked grass, it’s a heady, confusing new scent.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comView image in fullscreenThe Westbury White Horse, by Eric Ravilious.Photograph: AlamyExplore more on these topicsDroughtCountry diaryRural affairsSummerWildfiresfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: New constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents say | Guinea-Bissau | The Guardian
description: Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections
Content: Guinea-Bissau’s transitional president, Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, gestures after voting at a polling station in Bairro de Luanda on Sunday.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenGuinea-Bissau’s transitional president, Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, gestures after voting at a polling station in Bairro de Luanda on Sunday.Photograph: ReutersGuinea-BissauNew constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents sayReferendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December electionsEromo Egbejulein AbidjanWed 2 Sep 2026 10.20 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.52 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.View image in fullscreenElection officials wait for voters to cast their ballots in the referendum in Bissau. The turnout was reportedly over 55% of the population.Photograph: Darcicio Barbosa/APThe referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.Explore more on these topicsGuinea-BissauAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find | Pesticides | The Guardian
description: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities
Content: A farmer sprays pesticide on sesame fields in Burkina Faso, west Africa.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenA farmer sprays pesticide on sesame fields in Burkina Faso, west Africa.Photograph: AlamyPesticidesAlmost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts findStudy reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalitiesPippa NeillEnvironment reporterWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 22.43 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, astudyhas found.Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned byPesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and eastAfrica.The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was inBurkina Fasoin west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.View image in fullscreenYoung farm workers harvesting cotton in a field near Boromo in Burkina Faso.Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/GettyThe study,publishedin the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action NetworkIndia, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCalifornia bans paraquat, highly toxic herbicide outlawed in more than 70 countriesRead moreGénon Jensen, the executive director of theHealthand Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, withgrowing evidencelinking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it asan occupational disease for farmers.Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the EarthEuropeearlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.Explore more on these topicsPesticidesAgricultureFarmingParkinson's diseasePoisonHealthEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order | Apple | The Guardian
description: Tech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with Canada
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Tech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with Canada
Content: Apple has followed Google in changing Lake Ontario to Lake America in its Maps app, right, after an executive order signed by Donald Trump.Composite: The Washington Post/ABACA/Shutterstock, Apple MapsView image in fullscreenApple has followed Google in changing Lake Ontario to Lake America in its Maps app, right, after an executive order signed by Donald Trump.Composite: The Washington Post/ABACA/Shutterstock, Apple MapsAppleApple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump orderTech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with CanadaMarina DunbarWed 2 Sep 2026 22.15 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 20.06 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple has renamed Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after anexecutive orderfrom Donald Trump to change the name of the Great Lake amid his trade spat with Canada.TheAppleMaps app now displays the controversial new name for the lake, which sits between New York state and the Canadian province of Ontario, for users in the US. Apple users outside the country will still see the Lake Ontario name.Apple had been reportedly mulling whether to submit to Trump’s new order after receiving a personalrequestfrom the president for the tech company to change the lake’s name.Trump welcomed the news, declaring ina Truth Socialpost that the adoption of “Lake America” by Google Maps and Apple Maps meant the name change was “complete, ratified, and binding”. However, the US cannot compel Canada – or any other country – to also change the name.Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalatesRead moreThe US president officially unveiled the name swap last week. He did not mention his escalating trade feud with the US’s northern neighbors in the order, but the timing suggested a retaliatory move after Canadian officials denounced Trump’s new sweeping tariffs and promised to instate tariffs of their own.Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, rejected the attempt to rename the body of water, saying in apost on social mediathat the lake’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.Late last month, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed, with the US subsequently imposing a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports. Trump additionally threatened another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney retaliated with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.Rather than mention any of this, Trump instead said inthe orderthat the purpose of the renaming is to honor “the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements”.Earlier this week, Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, said in an interview with Fox Business that “the president has reached out to Apple directly” and predicted with confidence that US users would “be seeing that change coming up soon”.Apple’s competitor, Google, alreadymade the changeover the weekend, with Google Maps now showing the Lake America branding. Google cited Trump’s order and its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).In ablogpostissued on Saturday, Google said US users would see the Lake America name while users in Canada will see Lake Ontario, and “those outside of the US and Canada will see both names.”The digital name change is unsurprising considering Google Maps was anearly adopterof the Gulf of America moniker and still currently displays the title, despite the renaminghardlybeing a success outside US government lingo.On Tuesday, it was reported that MapQuest, the pioneering online mapping app,reached the No 1 spoton Apple’s App Store after openly rejecting Trump’s request to rename the lake. The app simplyposteda screenshot of Lake Ontario on social media last Thursday along with the caption: “We’re not changing it.”The act of defiance was enough to catapult the app into becoming the most in-demand navigation tool in the US.Explore more on these topicsAppleDonald TrumpCanadaMark CarneyAmericasTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticism | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: Energy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeks to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is transformation of relations
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Energy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeks to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is transformation of relations
Content: Chris Wright and Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s interim president, during a meeting over an oil agreement at the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChris Wright and Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s interim president, during a meeting over an oil agreement at the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesVenezuelaTrump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticismEnergy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeks to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is transformation of relationsTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroWed 2 Sep 2026 15.44 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.23 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking to commandeer huge quantities of Venezuelan oil, amid growing criticism of Donald Trump’senergy dealwith the country’s interim leaders.“Absolutely not,” Wright replied when asked by a CNBC journalist if the US was engaged in a “heavy-handed” attempt to “take” Venezuelan oil in violation of the South American country’s constitution.Wright landed in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Tuesday night, four days after Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.“I think we are seeing an absolutely historic transformation of both Venezuela and the relations between Venezuela and the US,”Wright saidof the deal, which Trump has claimed will give the US control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil. “This is President Trump’s grand plan to replace conflict with commerce,” Wright said.The White Housesaysthe deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves. But there has been criticism from across the political spectrum.The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Trump’s deal with Venezuela’s unelected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, “looks less like a normal commercial transaction than it doesthe famous sceneof US businessmen meeting with the Cuban strongman in The Godfather Part II”.“The US government is essentially getting in bed with a foreign dictator and her favored capitalist,” the newspaper complained, in reference to Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan tycoon at the centre of the deal.View image in fullscreenDelcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s unelected interim president, has said the deal had ‘endless’ benefits.Photograph: Venezuelan Presidency/AFP/Getty ImagesThe economist Francisco Rodrígueztold Democracy Now: “It’s clear that this is not a deal that any Venezuelan government would have entered into unless this country had been subject to an invasion, and unless its authorities had been held at gunpoint. So I think we’ve replaced gunboat diplomacy now for gunpoint diplomacy.”Delcy Rodríguez was installed as interim president on 5 January, two days after the president, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces during a predawn raid on Caracas.Trump warned Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president, she would face an even worse fate if she did not toe the US line.Since Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez has made a series of once unthinkable concessions to US officials who their nominally socialist political movement, Chavismo, had spent years denouncing as predatory imperialists bent on stealing Venezuela’s natural resources.On Saturday,Rodríguez claimedthe oil deal had “endless” benefits and would help produce more than $209bn in revenues that could be used to improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said during a televised broadcast to the nation.The deal has dealt a body blow to Venezuela’s political opposition, who fear Trump is unlikely to push for a democratic transition or fresh presidential elections given his lucrative arrangement with Rodríguez.“This is a game between theTrump administrationand Delcy and her people,” one opposition figure lamented after the deal was unveiled.Speaking at a signing ceremony in the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday, Rodríguez thanked the Trump administration for its part in what she called a “win-win deal”. She said: “I have faith in the future of Venezuela. What we are doing today represents the future and the hope of the people of Venezuela.”Explore more on these topicsVenezuelaUS foreign policyTrump administrationDelcy RodríguezOilAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pete Hegseth criticized for body-shaming Canadian cadets: ‘Literally they’re kids’ | Pete Hegseth | The Guardian
description: US defense secretary faces backlash for attempting to mock Canada’s armed forces amid trade war
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: US defense secretary faces backlash for attempting to mock Canada’s armed forces amid trade war
Content: Pete Hegseth attends a ceremony at the Pentagon in Washington DC, on 27 July 2026.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPete Hegseth attends a ceremony at the Pentagon in Washington DC, on 27 July 2026.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/AFP/Getty ImagesPete HegsethPete Hegseth criticized for body-shaming Canadian cadets: ‘Literally they’re kids’US defense secretary faces backlash for attempting to mock Canada’s armed forces amid trade warRichard LuscombeWed 2 Sep 2026 15.44 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.51 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA social media post byPete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members of a Canadian youth development program remained online on Wednesday despite a furious backlash on both sides of the border.On Monday night, Hegsethposted on Xa photograph of two people in uniform with a Canadian flag and the caption “this is real”, an apparent attempt at mocking the country’s armed forces amid the Trump administration’s trade spat with its northern neighbor.However, the photograph was reproduced from an Instagram post by the Vernon Cadet Training Centre in British Columbia, which hosted asummer campin July for teenagers learning adult skills on the military base.Democrats warn of ‘hollowed out’ leadership after army chief resigns amid clashes with HegsethRead moreIts subjects are not members of Canada’s frontline military, and the person whose appearance Hegseth was attempting to ridicule is likely a volunteer instructor, critics said. The girl receiving a medal is a teenager no older than 18.The post, widely seen as part of a Trump administration “bullying campaign” over the trade war, was immediately condemned by officials in Canada and in the US. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, called it “beneath the office” of the secretary of defense.Responding on Tuesday to attacks on his country by US government officials, including Donald Trump’s attempt torenameLake Ontario by executive order, Carneytold reportersit was time for Washington to “start being serious” about efforts to de-escalate trade tensions.“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said.David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, echoed Carney’s sentiment. “It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to,” he said.The civilian Army Cadet League of Canada accused Hegseth of online harassment. “Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable,” the group said in a statement.Adam Kinzinger, the former Republican US congressman and a military veteran, was even more outspoken in a poston X.“Literally they’re kids. This is a cadet program and our ass hat of a Secdef is making fun of children,” he wrote. “MAGA [Make America Great Again] males are betas who have to punch down to feel big.”Ruben Gallego, the Democratic Arizona senator and a former marine, called the post “stupid” and “disrespectful”.Danny O’Regan, a Canadian veteran writingon X, also criticized the post. “The Secretary of Defence is body shaming cadet groups,” he said. “This is not a military unit. They are kids looking for adventure, test themselves and align themselves with the values of service. Don’t be a Pete.”US army secretary Dan Driscoll resigns over reported friction with Pete HegsethRead moreThe Pentagon, meanwhile, defended Hegseth. On Tuesday, Jacob Bliss, the defense department’s deputy press secretary, said: “The X post speaks for itself.”The incident comes as Hegseth faces increasing pressure on several fronts. The US army chief Dan Driscoll resigned this week, reportedly after months of internal clashes with Hegseth. Democrats have accused the defense secretary of having “hollowed out” the military’s senior ranks.On Wednesday, Iranaccusedthe US of a “war crime” after four people were killed, including a four-year-old child, and dozens injured in a reported missile strike on a wedding at a home in the south of the country.The ongoing Iran war has also left the US with a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors, the Associated Pressreported, sparking fears among Nato allies of increasing vulnerability to a potential Russian military attack.Hegseth has previously been critical of body shapes in the US military,telling senior commandersin Virginia last year that “fat troops are tiring to look at”.Ordering military officials to crack down on a lack of physical fitness, he said: “It’s tiring to look out at combat formations, or really any formation, and see fat troops.”Explore more on these topicsPete HegsethCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI | Canada | The Guardian
description: The company says it prioritizes safety, but suits allege its ChatGPT bot induced shooter to carry out attack in Canada
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: The company says it prioritizes safety, but suits allege its ChatGPT bot induced shooter to carry out attack in Canada
Content: A mother and son pay their respects at a memorial for the victims of a mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, on 14 February 2026.Photograph: Christinne Muschi/APView image in fullscreenA mother and son pay their respects at a memorial for the victims of a mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, on 14 February 2026.Photograph: Christinne Muschi/APCanadaTumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAIThe company says it prioritizes safety, but suits allege its ChatGPT bot induced  shooter to carry out attack in CanadaDara KerrWed 2 Sep 2026 14.22 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 16.40 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAIfaces 30 new lawsuits filed on behalf of victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.The suits, filed on Wednesday, allege the company’sChatGPTchatbot induced the shooter to carry out the attack in rural Canada in February, in which eight people were killed and dozens more wounded – most of them children.Family of Tumbler Ridge shooting victim sues OpenAI alleging it could have prevented attackRead more“These were people who really endured just total hell that day,” Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said in an interview. “Young kids who watched their teachers die, watched friends die and thought they were going to get shot and killed.”These new lawsuits, filed in federal court for the northern district of California, come after Edelsonfiled seven initial suitsin April – bringing the total number of cases against OpenAI for the Tumbler Ridge shooting to 37. All of the suits allege that the violent intentions of the shooter, identified as 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, were well-known to the senior leadership of OpenAI, which failed to report her to the authorities.Employees on the company’s safety team hadflagged the shooter’s accountto executives eight months before the attack, describing her in internal messages as “a credible and specific threat of gun violence against real people”, according to court filings. OpenAI banned her account, but she was able to quickly create a new one, the suits claim.The lawsuits accuse OpenAI and its CEO,Sam Altman, of negligence, aiding and abetting a mass shooting and product liability.Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, said in a statement that he thinks about what happened at Tumbler Ridge every day and that the company works hard to create standards for reporting cases to law enforcement.“The professionals working on these teams choose to do this incredibly difficult work because they care so deeply about keeping people safe,” Kwon said. “They come to work every day knowing that they may have to make a decision that they’ll think about for the rest of their lives.”A groundswell of cases have been brought against OpenAI andother tech companiesalleging that their chatbots exacerbate mental health crises and provoke violent acts. OpenAI has beensued in seven separate casesthat blame ChatGPT for acting as a “suicide coach”. A criminal investigation and civil lawsuit, brought by the attorney general of Florida, accuses OpenAI ofconcealing safety risksafter a mass shooting at Florida State University.The shooting in Tumbler Ridgetook place in a secondary school, shortly after Van Rootselaar killed her mother and 11-year-old brother in their family home. The new tranche of lawsuits includes cases from the family of one girl who was shot, along with the principal, teachers and students.The attack was one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history. In the aftermath, questionsswirled in the small British Columbia townabout how it could have happened.Edelson singled out Chris Lehane, who is OpenAI’s head of global affairs and a former member of Bill Clinton’s administration whospecialized in opposition research. He said Lehane was one of the people who received warnings from the company’s safety team but overruled repeated appeals to alert the authorities. That decision was also sanctioned by Altman, the lawsuits allege.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“What’s clear is that OpenAI over and over has made decisions to hide how dangerous their platform is because they’re worried about regulation and public pushback,” Edelson said.In response, OpenAI’s Kwon said: “It is absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision … It’s also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.”When the first seven lawsuits were filed against OpenAI in April, the company published ablogpostabout its “commitment to safety”. Altman alsosent a letterto the Tumbler Ridge community apologizing for not notifying Canadian police about what OpenAI knew regarding the shooter’s potential threat.“While I know words can never be enough, I believe an apology is necessary to recognize the harm and irreversible loss your community has suffered,” Altman wrote.David Eby, the British Columbia premier,postedthe letter to social media with the comment: “The apology is necessary, and yet grossly insufficient for the devastation done to the families of Tumbler Ridge.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIChatGPTAmericasCalifornianewsShareReuse this content

title: China’s falling emissions amid Iran war spark hope of decarbonisation watershed | Greenhouse gas emissions | The Guardian
description: Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls
Content: An aquaculture-photovoltaic hybrid project in Fengdu County, China. Clean energy use cushioned the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAn aquaculture-photovoltaic hybrid project in Fengdu County, China. Clean energy use cushioned the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockGreenhouse gas emissionsChina’s falling emissions amid Iran war spark hope of decarbonisation watershedOil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price fallsJonathan WattsThu 3 Sep 2026 00.01 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 00.08 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.The reportreveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by thestrait of Hormuzcrisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed forCarbon Briefby theCentre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months afterthe first US airstrikes in late February.How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.View image in fullscreenWind turbines on the Yellow Sea coast of Yancheng, China.Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPAThe country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.Thiselectrifying trendhad begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic andstrategic imperativeof reducing petro-dependence.In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChina has been preparing for a global energy crisis for years. It is paying off nowRead moreAnalysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” saidLauri Myllyvirta, the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.”Myllyvirta noted this was the first timeChina’s overall emissionshad fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption.In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels.Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst atEmber, which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further.“The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”Explore more on these topicsGreenhouse gas emissionsClimate crisisChinaStrait of HormuzUS-Israel war on IranAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Japan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streets | Japan | The Guardian
description: Speed limit dropped from 60km/h for around 70% of general roads in the hope of making narrow streets of crowded cities safer
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Speed limit dropped from 60km/h for around 70% of general roads in the hope of making narrow streets of crowded cities safer
Content: Narrow roads with no pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in serious accidents.Photograph: imagenavi/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNarrow roads with no pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in serious accidents.Photograph: imagenavi/Getty ImagesJapanJapan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streetsSpeed limit dropped from 60km/h for around 70% of general roads in the hope of making narrow streets of crowded cities saferJustin McCurryin TokyoWed 2 Sep 2026 06.15 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrivers on residential roads inJapanhave been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.Please don’t rearrange our shoes when we turn up, paramedics in Japan urgeRead moreThe measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements insafetyseen on larger roads.While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.Explore more on these topicsJapanAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in second national security case  | Hong Kong | The Guardian
description: Wong, 29, is accused of urging foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against China
Author: Danny Vincent
Headline: Wong, 29, is accused of urging foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against China
Content: Hong Kong teenage student leader Joshua Wong, left, pictured outside the Hong Kong magistrates' court in   2015.Photograph: Vincent Yu/APView image in fullscreenHong Kong teenage student leader Joshua Wong, left, pictured outside the Hong Kong magistrates' court in   2015.Photograph: Vincent Yu/APHong KongHong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in second national security caseWong, 29, is accused of urging foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against ChinaDanny Vincentin Hong KongWed 2 Sep 2026 05.57 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.23 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoshua Wong, one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence.Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activistNathan Lawto urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions againstHong Kongand China.The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong andChinaafter the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts.Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.‘Hong Kong is at a crossroads’: inside prison with the student who took on BeijingRead moreIn 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison.Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges.Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing.One supporter who attended the court criticised the proceedings.“Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong’s plea is a forced reality,” they said, asking not to be named. “This is not justice, but Beijing’s absolute eradication of Hong Kong’s dissident voices.”View image in fullscreenHong Kong activist and supporters hold signs during a press event to support pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong in Taipei, Taiwan, on Wednesday.Photograph: Chiang Ying-ying/APIn 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn.In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope.Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before thenational security lawwas enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively.“It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations.“By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.“Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate.On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.”With Associated PressExplore more on these topicsHong KongChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thai port after gruelling 270 days at sea | Thailand | The Guardian
description: Ship has been plagued by reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health because of lengthy deployment
Author: Natasha May
Headline: Ship has been plagued by reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health because of lengthy deployment
Content: Waiting journalists take photos of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier off Laem Chabang port, near the city of Pattaya in Thailand after more than 270 days at sea.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWaiting journalists take photos of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier off Laem Chabang port, near the city of Pattaya in Thailand after more than 270 days at sea.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesThailandUSS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thai port after gruelling 270 days at seaShip has been plagued by reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health because of lengthy deploymentNatasha Mayin Pattaya, and agenciesWed 2 Sep 2026 04.59 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 09.55 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USS Abraham Lincoln, a US aircraft carrier at the centre of a row over conditions on board after months at sea as part of Donald Trump’s war against Iran, has arrived off a Thai port.Reports ofdeteriorating living conditionsand poor mental health on the vessel, includingattempted suicides, have made headlines around the world, provoking criticism of the president’s actions in the Middle East.A heavy security presence was in force at Laem Chabang port near Pattaya, south of Bangkok, where the 5,000-strong crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln arrived on Wednesday morning after more than 270 days at sea.The huge nuclear-powered ship left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.Thai resort prepares to host USS Abraham Lincoln sailors after more than 270 days at seaRead moreThe resort city of Pattaya, a rest-and-recreation destination for US troops since the Vietnam war, has stepped up security as it prepares to welcome the sailors and Marines.View image in fullscreenA tug boat greets the USS Abraham Lincoln as it arrives at the port in Laem Chabang, Chonburi, Thailand.Photograph: Sakchai Lalit/APThe sailors will disembark in groups of approximately 50, according to police colonel Anek Srathongyoo, a superintendent of Pattaya city police station.Once a quiet fishing village, Pattaya was transformed into one of the most infamous red light districts in the world with the arrival of American troops using military bases inThailandduring the Vietnam war.At its peak, tens of thousands ofUS militarypersonnel came through each year, said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor specialising in tourism at Bangkok University.“In my opinion, it’s really the founding influence for the town. The US military turned a quiet fishing village into a global destination for an international nightlife and entertainment hub in about 15 years,” he said.Pattaya is now hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.Although the American troops left by the mid-70s, the sex industry infrastructure continued to grow, with European tourists taking their place, and more recently waves of Chinese and Russian visitors, Pipatpong said.View image in fullscreenThe USS Abraham Lincoln has 5,000 sailors aboard.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesSex work is illegal in Thailand, but authorities often turn a blind eye, said Pattarachit Gozzoli, a sociologist at Mahidol University in Bangkok.Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, has downplayed the city’s past, saying there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied it was linked to the US arrivals. Local police arrested 25 women for soliciting on the beachfront promenade a week before the ship arrived.The mayor said buses had been arranged to transport the sailors between the ship and Pattaya until the carrier departs on Sunday.Outside one bar, a sign said: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.”Poramase said in a Facebook post: “They come to relax. Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don’t take advantage of them.”He said they had been banned from water sports such as jetskis, and from taking advantage of Thailand’s lax cannabis laws, but encouraged them to enjoy the city’s many other attractions, from malls to religious sites.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsThailandAsia PacificUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t go looking for trouble’: Protester sues NSW after allegedly being punched by police at Herzog rally | Australian police and policing | The Guardian
description: Eyad Shadid launches civil case in district court after charges against him dropped, alleging he was ‘battered’ near Sydney’s town hall in February
Author: Jordyn Beazley
Headline: Eyad Shadid launches civil case in district court after charges against him dropped, alleging he was ‘battered’ near Sydney’s town hall in February
Content: Eyad Shadid at Sydney’s town hall in Sydney. He is suing NSW police.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEyad Shadid at Sydney’s town hall in Sydney. He is suing NSW police.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianAustralian police and policing‘I didn’t go looking for trouble’: Protester sues NSW after allegedly being punched by police at Herzog rallyExclusive: Eyad Shadid launches civil case in district court after charges against him dropped, alleging he was ‘battered’ near Sydney’s town hall in FebruaryFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJordyn BeazleyWed 2 Sep 2026 16.00 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 01.17 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Palestinian Australian man who alleges he was punched in the face when trying to stop police from harassing Muslim men praying during an anti–Isaac Herzog protest is suing New South Wales over “a series of false accusations”.Eyad Shadid has launched a civil case in the NSW district court, alleging he was assaulted, battered and falsely imprisoned by police near Sydney’s town hall.ThePalestineAction Group member, in his statement of claim, says NSW police committed misfeasance in public office and subjected him to a malicious prosecution.“I attended the protest to object to our governmentrolling out the red carpet for Isaac Herzog, president of a state that has been found by United Nations commissioners and most major human rights organisations to be perpetrating a genocide,” Shadid told Guardian Australia.Footage of police officer boasting about punching Sydney anti-Herzog protester raises questions about conductRead more“The right to protest in this state must mean more than words on paper and, if we must go to court to prove that, then so be it. I did not go to town hall looking for trouble. I went to be counted.”Shadid, 26, was looking for his mother – who, like his father, is from Palestine – after they became separated during the protest on the evening of 9 February.He found himself betweena group of Muslim men prayingand advancing police when, according to his statement of claim, he told officers: “Stop, they are praying.”Const Daniel Stewart then allegedly dragged Shadid, who had travelled from Parramatta, to the ground and punched him in the face and twisted his wrist. Another officer kneeled on his head, the documents allege.Shadid alleges that when on the ground another officer handcuffed him and he was taken into custody. He was charged with failing to comply with a police direction and resisting arrest.In May, NSW police dropped the charges. Since then, three others charged after the protest have had their charges withdrawn. More than 20 protesters aredue to face a joint trialin mid-2027.View image in fullscreenEyad Shadid returns to Sydney’s town hall.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianShadid alleges in court documents that Stewart failed to tell another officer deciding whether to charge him that the police line had been advancing towards people praying – and he’d requested the police stop because of that.He claimed the omission was “deliberate” and that Stewart falsely alleged Shadid threatened him with words to the effect of: “Mate, I’d fuckin’ drop you.”In his police statement, Stewart wrote the group of men “began” to pray as the police line moved forward and he was acting in the lawful execution of his duty when he arrested Shadid.Shadid claims that allegation was “dishonest” and designed to make it look like the prayer was a “cynical ploy” to frustrate officers.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailNSW police issued a statement three days after the protest confirming the prayer had been authorised, but claimed thatmessage was not passed on to officers. The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, apologised “for any offence that may have been taken” after officers dragged away those praying.After Shadid’s charges were dropped, the police prosecutor agreed officers had not given him a move-on direction. The 26-year-old was awarded costs.“As a consequence of the matters pleaded herein, the plaintiff was assaulted, battered, falsely imprisoned, subjected to a misfeasance in public office, and maliciously prosecuted,” his statement of claim argues.Shadid, a social services worker, is seeking aggravated and exemplary damages, arguing there was an “oppressive abuse of police powers” and he was prosecuted for “exercising a lawful democratic right to engage in peaceful protest”.Shadid said after he was charged his name was published in media reports and he lost business clients.View image in fullscreenEyad Shadid’s lawyer, Nick Hanna.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianShadid’s lawyer, Nick Hanna, said the case involved “very troubling allegations of police misconduct”.“We claim that Mr Shadid was violently assaulted and arrested without any lawful basis and then charged and prosecuted on the basis of a series of false accusations and misleading omissions,” Hanna said.The defence is yet to file its response to Shadid’s statement of claim. The NSW premier,Chris Minns, and NSW police declined to comment while the matter was before the court.Minns said after the rally that police were “put in an impossible situation” after protesters attempted to defy the public assembly restriction declaration (Pard) law. He refused to apologise to the prayer group or for the police’s conduct.In April, the state’scourt of appealfound that law unconstitutional, ruling in favour of the Palestine Action Group and Blak Caucus.Derek Jones, who becameknown as “white shirt guy”, said in May he intended to launch legal action in the supreme court against police regarding their conduct at the Herzog rally.“It was completely unprovoked, unwarranted, excessive, crazy,” the 56-year-old finance worker told Guardian Australia at the time.The February protest is the subject of a police watchdog investigation after allegations of widespread police brutality.Footage emerged earlier this weekof a separate incident in which an officer boasted about punching a protester.The police commissioner, when asked about the video on Wednesday, said: “The language is something that I don’t condone, but I need to understand the context of it.”Herzog was invited to Australia by the federal government after the antisemitic massacre in Bondi when 15 people were killed by two allegedly Islamic State-inspired gunmen.Explore more on these topicsAustralian police and policingIsraelPalestineGazaChris MinnsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Timidity is a virus’: Paul Keating fights the fading of the light as he seeks to enshrine his legacy | Paul Keating | The Guardian
description: As a major new biography of the former prime minister goes on sale, he talks about meeting the Queen, Trump’s aims, and why his big vision will never fade
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: As a major new biography of the former prime minister goes on sale, he talks about meeting the Queen, Trump’s aims, and why his big vision will never fade
Content: Paul Keating: ‘My view of the country was bigger than the country’s view of itself, but the vision will never deteriorate.’Photograph: Sitthixay Ditthavong/AAPView image in fullscreenPaul Keating: ‘My view of the country was bigger than the country’s view of itself, but the vision will never deteriorate.’Photograph: Sitthixay Ditthavong/AAPPaul Keating‘Timidity is a virus’: Paul Keating fights the fading of the light as he seeks to enshrine his legacyAs a major new biography of the former prime minister goes on sale, he talks about meeting the Queen, Trump’s aims, and why his big vision will never fadeFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBen DohertyWed 2 Sep 2026 14.24 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 22.42 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQueen Elizabeth II metPaul Keating“alone, to her credit” in what the prime minister was informed was her great-great-grandmother Queen Victoria’s favourite room at Balmoral Castle.“And I took some pleasure in explaining the furniture to her,” Keating recalls, an old elan breaking through.“It was made of Karelian, Russian Karelian birchwood. She had kept all the green-and-blue tartan carpets, all worn, so the room had something going for it. But the thing is, what had nothing going for it was any relativity to Australia.”Keating was in the UK to deliver his monarch a message, that Australia, Australians, “did not need her any more”. Australia should, must become a republic.“She said to me in this conversation, rather plaintively, ‘my family and I do our best for Australia’, whereas what I was really offering was a way out.”View image in fullscreenQueen Elizabeth and Paul Keating in 1992.Photograph: Stephen Dupont/AFPA file note written by Keating after the meeting reaffirmed his belief in Australia’s independent future.“The hereditary nature of the queen’s position, the remoteness from any contemporary mandate, struck me at that moment, at that proximity, as so banal, even sad.”Keating, Australia’s 24th prime minister, was in conversation on Wednesday night at a Sydney writers’ festival event with Sydney University professor of modern history James Curran, author ofGrand Ambition: Paul Keating’s Global Vision for Australia.It is an adroitly drawn portrait of a past leader – Keating lost power 30 years ago – who remains firmly convinced his vision is still very much this country’s future. An Australia that finds its securityin, rather thanfrom, Asia, that will be a republic, that will finally walk the path to reconciliation with its Indigenous history.‘Timidity is like a virus’“My view of the country was bigger than the country’s view of itself, but the vision will never deteriorate,” Keating said.‘If he can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine by him’: Francis Fukuyama on Trump, democracy - and changing his mindRead moreCurran reminded his audience (gently) that his interlocutor is no longer a young man, a child of the second world war (born 1944), who was just 25 years old when he entered parliament in 1969. Who cut his political teeth during the height of the cold war, and whose time as leader coincided with its end (once held up as the “end of history”).Keating’s first remarkable month as prime minister took in the fall of the Soviet Union; the arrival on Australian shores for the first time in three decades of a US president (George HW Bush, whom Keating wanted to “put in a headlock” to get something from him – the result was Apec, now still a key leaders’ meeting on the multilateral calendar, deep in its fourth decade); and a visit from Her Majesty (still yet a couple of years from their awkward meeting at Balmoral).Keating’s age was apparent on Wednesday.The voice was a little weaker, raspier; the pauses – formerly used to such dramatic effect on the floor of the Reps – a little longer; the quotes once-remembered now through an aide-memoire.But there was still the killer line, the rapier wit, blunted a little, but still penetrating.“Timidity,” he told Curran in their interviews for the book, “is like a virus in the bloodstream.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailCurran writes: “Keating’s central theme over the years is that the country has become afraid, and that its leaders have refrained from articulating a bigger idea of the place.“Instead of long-term strategic thinking about the kinds of issues coming down the national and international track, he sees frenzied activity. His retort? ‘Busyness is not substance.’”Australia suffers no shortage of political autobiography, for better or worse. Keating, famously/notoriously, has never put pen to paper in his own defence.Recollections of a Bleeding Heart, a memoir by his speechwriter, Don Watson, was said to have wounded him. He saw it as a betrayal. In response to what he saw as yet another Hawke biography, Keating delivered a veiled threat: “If I get around to writing a book, I will be telling the truth; the whole truth.”It never eventuated.But throughout this conversation, and throughout Grand Ambition, it was apparent that Keating has always kept an eye on legacy, on his place in history, and on grand ambition – his own and the country’s.Trump wants to ‘avoid world war three’He keeps, Curran writes, meticulous records of the policies he considers the signal markers of his time in office, “the pillars of his political legacy”.For a historian of Curran’s forensic eye, exclusive access to these files is manna from heaven.“Each folder contains the relevant primary cabinet documents and diplomatic cables and, where applicable, briefings to and from his advisers and department, records of what other ministers thought or wrote, details of critical conversations with other leaders, and a carefully selected array of newspaper articles.“They are all stamped ‘PJ KEATING PERSONAL COLLECTION’, arranged in precise chronological order and stapled at top left. The stamp itself is a statement about more than just the provenance of the documentary record; it is asserting, in its own way, Keating’s ownership of that past.”Populist One Nation’s latest victory points to a thirst for unity. But there are better ways to feel connected | Peter LewisRead moreTo end the evening, Keating was asked for his message for young Australians, and the future they will encounter and make. The key themes were still there: a republic, Indigenous reconciliation, a fairer Australia “making housing more affordable is a great thing to be doing. And if we’ve lost10 or 15% in house values, so what?”But there were still surprises. Keating’s proclaimed support for the foreign policy of the current occupant of the White House – “what Trump wants to do is avoid world war three” – his existential concern over the rise of artificial intelligence: “which I think is going to be the greatest agency of change since the discovery of electricity”.Keating was taken to a speech he gave at Kokoda. On Anzac Day in 1992, as prime minister, he had fallen to his knees and kissed the base of the memorial to fallen Australian soldiers, describing the Papua New Guinean highlands village as “the place where the depth of the soul of the Australian nation was confirmed”.“It is important for all of us, but particularly and especially young Australians,” Keating said that day, “to believe in an independent Australia, beholden to nobody. We can’t deny young Australians their birthright to a past with meaning for them and a future without meaning: it has to be a future with meaning.”Explore more on these topicsPaul KeatingAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fatal Sydney shooting could be another case of mistaken identity, police say | Sydney | The Guardian
description: A man shot dead in Merrylands West was not known to police, in a case with similarities to Tuesday’s killing in Campbelltown
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: A man shot dead in Merrylands West was not known to police, in a case with similarities to Tuesday’s killing in Campbelltown
Content: Police officers at the scene of a fatal shooting in Merrylands West.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenPolice officers at the scene of a fatal shooting in Merrylands West.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPSydneyFatal Sydney shooting could be another case of mistaken identity, police sayA man shot dead in Merrylands West was not known to police, in a case with similarities to Tuesday’s killing in CampbelltownGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAchol ArokWed 2 Sep 2026 11.32 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 12.05 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew South Wales police are investigating the shooting death of a man in Sydney’s west as a potential case of mistaken identity, marking the second fatal shooting incident in as many days.Emergency services responded to reports of a shooting at a home in Merrylands West at about 3.15pm on Wednesday, where a man believed to be in his 30s sustained a gunshot wound.The victim, who was yet to be formally identified, was treated by paramedics but died at the scene.Police said the property was a location known to police for organised crime, but said “the victim has no links that we’re aware of to organised crime”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAt a press conference, Supt Simon Glasser said it was unclear what the man who was shot was doing at the location or his connection to the residents.“The person who we believe has been shot has no adverse holdings with police. People that are linked to this address are known to … organised crime,” he said.“It’s very early on in the investigation, however, there is a possibility that the wrong person has been shot by these offenders.”The alleged shooting marks the second incident of its kind this week.Sydney home invasion during which man shot and killed a ‘targeted attack’, police believeRead moreOn Tuesday, 23-year-old Marco Tapiawas shot deadin his bed as his family slept at about 3.40am after multiple attackers were believed to have forced their way into a two-storey home in Glen Alpine, near Campbelltown, in south-west Sydney.That case was being investigated as a case of mistaken identity, police said, because Tapia was not known to authorities and had nothing more than a traffic offence on his record.His martial arts gym remembered him in a public tribute overnight.“We lost a real one today,” they wrote, adding: “Rest easy Marco, one of us forever.”The Alameddine network, a notorious
