crime family, and the Coconut Cartel, an emerging crime-for-hire network, have allegedly become embroiled in a feud, spilling into shootings acrossSydneyin recent months.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionActing Supt Gretchen Atkins of Campbelltown police said on Tuesday she was aware of online posts about the Glen Alpine case and said everything was under consideration.The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said the incidents showed gangland violence was out of control.“We need to be very clear about the threat on our streets and that is dangerous organised criminals … innocent people have been in the firing line way too often,” she said.“Whether it is a young man, a student sleeping in his bed at night [or] a grandfather who’s kidnapped and murdered,” referring to the Sydney grandfatherChris Baghsarian, who was taken from his home on 13 February and later found dead.She suggested the government was not doing enough to stop the shootings.But the police minister, Yasmin Catley, criticised Sloane, whose electorate is in Sydney’s eastern suburbs, over her position on the state’s gun buyback scheme, launched after December’s Bondi massacre.“The member for Vaucluse, we must remember, is also the same person that wants to squash [national gun buyback reform],” Catley said.“She wants more guns on the street and wants to blame the police for not doing their job … I’m not tolerating that, I won’t have a bar of that.”Explore more on these topicsSydneyNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dutch central bank moves 86 tonnes of gold to UK from US and Canada, citing ‘geopolitical unrest’ | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: Bank says gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily and the move will allow it to respond more rapidly in a ‘crisis situation’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bank says gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily and the move will allow it to respond more rapidly in a ‘crisis situation’
Content: The Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US and Canada.Photograph: Mike Groll/APView image in fullscreenThe Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US and Canada.Photograph: Mike Groll/APNetherlandsDutch central bank moves 86 tonnes of gold to UK from US and Canada, citing ‘geopolitical unrest’Bank says gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily and the move will allow it to respond more rapidly in a ‘crisis situation’Agence France-PresseThu 3 Sep 2026 00.47 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 01.09 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US andCanadato London, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest”.De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) said gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily than those held in New York and Ottawa.“This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation,” the bank said in a statement on Wednesday.“With this step, we have improved the deployability of the gold reserves. We assume that we will never need to deploy the gold, but it is nevertheless necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” said DNB’s president, Olaf Sleijpen.Gold price hits three-month high amid fears over Iran war and Trump economyRead moreThe total Dutchgold stockamounted to 612.4 tonnes and was valued at €72.2bn ($83.7bn) at the end of 2025, said the DNB.Before the deployment, the Dutch bank held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa.After the move, each country accounted for 18.5% of the Dutch gold reserve.The share of gold held in London increased from 18.1% to 32.1%. The bank still holds 30.8% of its gold inthe Netherlands.The transfer was carried out partially by buying and selling and partly by physically transferring gold, the bank said.The bank moved more than 27 tonnes of physical gold from the US and Canada to Zeist.The same quantity of gold was moved from Zeist to London, preventing the melting down of gold bars.“By combining buying and selling and physical transport, the risks associated with physically moving a large quantity of gold have been spread,” the DNB said.The operation took place between March and August of this year, it said.Laurent Schwartz, president of the Paris-based NationalGoldCounter, which facilitates gold trading in France, said central banks had been moving their reserves around for about a decade.“The current political context in the United States might also push certain central banks into favouring other storage locations,” he said.The London market was the deepest and most liquid, Schwartz said, making it easier to deploy in times of crisis.“Central banks can more easily lend their gold there to other banking institutions.”John Plassard, an analyst at Cite Gestion Private Bank, said the Dutch move was intended “for there to be more immediate availability in the event of a crisis”.For the moment, it was a “fairly one-off move”, but he warned that if other central banks followed suit, it could damage confidence in the US.At the beginning of the year, there were concerns raised in Germany about the security of its central bank’s reserves in New York.However, the powerful Bundesbank has decided for the moment not to shift its reserves away from New York.“The New York Fed is and remains an important storage site for our gold,” the bank told public TV station ARD in January.Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsEconomicsGoldCommoditiesBankingTrump administrationCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham targets migrant crisis ahead of Macron’s visit to No 10 | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: PM will aim to centre talks with French president on key foreign policy issues such as Iran, smuggling gangs and EU relations
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: PM will aim to centre talks with French president on key foreign policy issues such as Iran, smuggling gangs and EU relations
Content: Andy Burnham and Emmanuel Macron at a preview event for the Bayeux tapestry exhibition at the British Museum.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Emmanuel Macron at a preview event for the Bayeux tapestry exhibition at the British Museum.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham targets migrant crisis ahead of Macron’s visit to No 10PM will aim to centre talks with French president on key foreign policy issues such as Iran, smuggling gangs and EU relationsKiran StaceyPolicy editorWed 2 Sep 2026 22.30 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 22.31 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will begin the process of courting European leaders when he welcomesEmmanuel Macronas the first foreign head of state to visit him in Downing Street.The prime minister will meet the French president at No 10 on Thursday as he looks to make inroads on a number of foreign policy objectives, including curbing irregular migration and sealing a new deal with the EU.The meeting marks one of Burnham’s first forays into foreign policy, having previously promised to remain mostly focused on domestic issues, and comes weeks before a crunch EU summit that could shape much of his future economic strategy.Labour seeking ‘deeper relationship’ with EU under Burnham, new minister saysRead moreBurnham said in a statement on Wednesday: “The progress we have seen this summer [in bringing down the number of small boat crossings] shows what can be achieved when the UK andFrancework together.“But I am clear that we cannot be complacent. Smuggling gangs are constantly adapting their tactics, and the UK and France need to respond quickly and stay one step ahead of the criminals facilitating the dangerous crossings.“The small boats crisis is a shared European challenge, and no country can solve it alone. Working with France and our international partners, we will restore order and control to our borders and prevent smugglers exploiting vulnerable migrants.”While Burnham has talked almost exclusively about domestic issues such as the cost of living since becoming prime minister, he is quickly finding himself having to deal with international crises as well.Last monthhe metthe Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to help celebrate the country’s independence day, when he announced he would declassify sensitive military information to allow Ukraine to build more cruise missiles.On Thursday he will discuss migration, EU relations,Ukraineand the war in Iran with Macron.The two leaders will announce additional resources for French police to help stop small boats being launched from the country’s north coast and larger “mega-dinghies” departing from the west.Downing Street said on Wednesday that the number of French officers dealing with small boat crossings in northern France would soon rise to nearly 1,050 officers – up by roughly a quarter in four months.The teams will include a specialist 75-person team to seize equipment and arrest smugglers on land. A separate intelligence unit will be expanded from 18 to 30, while another 45 officers will be deployed to the west coast.Irregular migration has fallen down the political agenda in recent weeks thanks to a drop in the number of small boat crossings.This week, Burnham said the drop in numbers to a seven-year low was a result of efforts by his predecessor Keir Starmer to tackle smuggling gangs – thoughexperts sayexternal factors such as an improvement in Syria’s security situation have also played a role.The prime minister will also use the meeting to press Macron to support his efforts to renegotiate Britain’s treaty with the EU.Brussels postponed a planned summit from July to allow the new prime minister time to review tentative agreements made by Starmer, with a new one expected in early November.European countries have been pushing hard for Britain to agree a new youth mobility scheme and to allow their students to pay home fees at British universities – both concessions that Starmer was ready to make, according torecent reports.However, Burnham may take a tougher line on the number of young people he is willing to admit as part of the scheme, having promised to pass all government policies through a “Makerfield test” to measure them against the views of his constituents.In return, Britain wants new agreements to ease trade in electricity and agricultural products, which officials hope will give a timely boost to the UK economy.The prime ministertold the Guardianlast year he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU, but has since said this would not be something he would actively pursue as prime minister.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamFranceEuropeEmmanuel MacronForeign policyUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: Maltese tycoon found not guilty of involvement in Daphne Caruana Galizia murder | Daphne Caruana Galizia | The Guardian
description: Yorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrage
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Yorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrage
Content: Yorgen Fenech leaving court in Valletta after he was found not guilty of involvement in the 2017 murder of Maltese journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersView image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech leaving court in Valletta after he was found not guilty of involvement in the 2017 murder of Maltese journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltese tycoon found not guilty of involvement in Daphne Caruana Galizia murderYorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrageJuliette Garsidein VallettaWed 2 Sep 2026 20.26 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.49 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Malta’s richest men has been found not guilty of involvement in the murder of the anti-corruption journalistDaphne Caruana Galizia.The verdict, which is expected to be appealed against by the prosecution, came as a blow not only to the victim’s family, but to the politicians and campaigners who regard the case as a landmark action in the fight to protect press freedom inEurope.Nearly nine years after Caruana Galizia’s death in acar bombing in October 2017, a jury of six women and three men found Yorgen Fenech, 44, not guilty of both counts with which he had been charged: complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, and association with the intention of committing a crime.Delivered at 7.30pm, the verdict was decisive. To gasps from the gallery and cheers from Fenech’s relatives, the forewoman announced jurors had voted to dismiss both counts by an eight-to-one majority.View image in fullscreenCaruana Galizia’s sister Corinne Vella said: ‘Everybody is much more at risk now, because this signals you can kill journalists with impunity.’Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersAs Caruana Galizia’s family listened in shock, with some relatives in tears, the judge, Edwina Grima, immediately ordered Fenech’s release from custody. If convicted, he would have faced a life sentence. He left court through the front entrance, without responding to requests for comment.“Everybody is much more at risk now, because this signals you can kill journalists with impunity,” Caruana Galizia’s sister, Corinne Vella, said. “We knew an acquittal was a huge possibility. But it’s like when someone dies, it still shocks you.”In a message on Facebook, the journalist’s eldest son decried a “terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from. They had a great responsibility to deliver justice. And washed their hands of it”.The leader of the opposition Nationalist party, Alex Borg, requested the urgent reopening of parliament, which is currently in recess, to discuss the verdict. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” said Borg, speaking to a crowd of demonstrators that had assembled on Wednesday night outside parliament. He described the verdict as a black spot on the Labour government, and said the press should be free to do its work “independently and without undue pressure”.Fenech, an influential businessman and property developer whose family owns two Hilton hotels and has a share in a power station inMalta, had been accused by prosecutors of paying €150,000 (£129,000) via a middleman, Melvin Theuma, to have the journalist killed.The murder of Caruana Galizia, who targeted Fenech and leading political figures in her reporting, triggered the most consequential political scandal in Malta’s postwar history, becoming a rallying point for anti-corruption and press freedom activism.View image in fullscreenA person holds up an image of Caruana Galizia at a protest in Valletta in 2019.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersThe fallout resulted in Joseph Muscat, the then prime minister of the EU’s smallest member state, being forced out of office along with two of his ministers and his chief of staff.While Muscat left office, the party he led remains in power. In a statement, the government noted the verdict and appealed for prudence in public comments at a delicate moment, insisting: “The government remains committed to seeing justice served by its institutions.”The two-month trial laid bare the extent of Fenech’s network of political contacts, and raised questions about attempts to sabotage and interfere with the police investigation. Key witnesses, and the defendant himself, claimed the prime minister’s chief of staff had repeatedly leaked sensitive information to Fenech.Summing up the case against him, prosecutor Anthony Vella said Fenech believed he could “buy justice”, telling the jury: “You are being asked to decide whether a man who had extensive contacts in politics and among the heads of public entities had enough power to pay for Daphne to be killed.”The defence argued that the chain of command went higher, with suggestions from Fenech and his lawyers that the person who had ordered the killing was Muscat’s former chief of staff Keith Schembri. They said police had not done enough to investigate allegations about his involvement.“All roads lead to Keith, and all bridges to Keith were burned,” the defence lawyer Charles Mercieca said in his summing up.In his testimony, Fenech told the jury: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.” He said he had merely acted as a messenger between Schembri and Theuma, and that the taxi-driver had blackmailed him.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSchembri, who gave evidence at the trial, denied all wrongdoing, saying he had no involvement in leaks and no knowledge of the murder.Fenech’s defence lawyer, Giannella de Marco, said Schembri and others should have been investigated. She said the prosecution’s chief witness had not been believed.“The jurors did not believe Melvin Theuma. It was an eight-one verdict, which means unanimous … don’t you think jurors saw who the real masterminds were?” she said.The vote was effectively unanimous because juries in Malta rarely convict 9-0, as this would allow the public to know for certain which way individual members voted.Repubblika, a Maltese campaign group, called for a “national reckoning” in which the corruption investigated by Caruana Galizia, who was 59 when she died and one of Malta’s best-known journalists, is prosecuted.View image in fullscreenDaphne Caruana Galizia’s sons, Matthew, Andrew and Paul, step out of court after Yorgen Fenech was acquitted of conspiracy to murder her in 2017.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters“Those politically responsible for the culture of impunity of the Muscat years must not be rehabilitated into public life. The state must sincerely accept its responsibility and apologise to Daphne’s family,” a spokesperson said.Occupy Justice, meanwhile, described the verdict as “deeply painful and disappointing”, saying Malta remained “without full accountability for the person or people who ordered her murder”.An independent public inquiry, for which the family fought, concluded in 2021 that the state had to shoulder responsibility for the killing because it “created an atmosphere of impunity, generated from the highest levels”. It made a number of recommendations, many of which have yet to be implemented.In a statement, the Daphne Foundation said: “Nine years after Daphne’s brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed. Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne’s life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost.”Tom Gibson, the deputy advocacy director of the Committee to Protect Journalists, was in the courtroom for the verdict. In a statement, he said: “This is a heartbreaking verdict for the family after years of waiting for justice. We will continue to stand by them while they seek accountability for all of those involved in the murder.”Explore more on these topicsDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltaEuropeJournalist safetyPress freedomNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gun found in French lake is analysed by 2012 Alps killings investigators | France | The Guardian
description: British tourists reportedly discovered Luger pistol that is latest in long line of potential leads in mystery of al-Hilli deaths
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: British tourists reportedly discovered Luger pistol that is latest in long line of potential leads in mystery of al-Hilli deaths
Content: Investigators in 2012 at the campsite where Saad al-Hilli and his family had been staying near Annecy.Photograph: Lionel Cironneau/APView image in fullscreenInvestigators in 2012 at the campsite where Saad al-Hilli and his family had been staying near Annecy.Photograph: Lionel Cironneau/APFranceGun found in French lake is analysed by 2012 Alps killings investigatorsBritish tourists reportedly discovered Luger pistol that is latest in long line of potential leads in mystery of al-Hilli deathsPatrick DalyWed 2 Sep 2026 20.03 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExperts are examining a gun found by tourists to determine whether it might have been used to kill a British family in the French Alps 14 years ago.In what remains an unsolved murder case, Saad al-Hilli, 50, his wife, Ikbal, 47, and her mother, Suhaila al-Allaf, 74, were shot dead on a road near Annecy, a remote Alpine village in easternFrancein September 2012.The couple’s two young daughters, then four and seven, survived but a passing cyclist, 45-year-old Sylvain Mollier, was also killed.The French prosecutor Marie-Céline Lawrysz confirmed that a pistol, thought to be a Luger, was uncovered on 20 August by two tourists swimming in Lake Annecy. The weapon is currently being analysed by ballistics experts in France in connection with the al-Hilli cold case.During the initial investigation, pieces from the butt of the weapon used in the killings, a vintage Luger P06-29 pistol, were found on the ground near the British-registered BMW estate car that the family had been driving at the time of the attack. The gun was identified as a model used by the Swiss army in the 1930s, but its owner has never been traced.In a statement, Lawrysz said a semi-automatic pistol had been found by the tourists, reported to be British, at a depth of about five feet, a few dozen metres away from the shore of Lake Annecy.She said: “They kept the weapon for 24 hours and conducted online research to identify its type.“They subsequently drew a link between the discovered weapon and the one believed to have been used in the Chevaline [near Annecy] killing on September 5, 2012.“On August 21 2026, they handed the weapon over to gendarmes from the local Saint-Jorioz brigade.”Detectives have so far ruled out the possibility of a contract killing, saying a professional killer would not have used such a vintage weapon as the Luger.The discovery of the pistol is the latest in a long line of leads that investigators have followed in an effort to unravel the mystery that has surrounded the four deaths.Suspects previously arrested in connection with the case include an Iraqi prisoner known as Mr S who was claimed to have said he had been offered “a large sum of money” to kill Iraqis living in the UK.Mr al-Hilli’s brother Zaid was also arrested on suspicion of murder in 2013, but was later told he would face no further action after police found there was insufficient evidence to charge him with a crime.In 2022, another suspect was questioned but released without charge. Two years ago,DNA analysis was orderedby detectives in France’s cold case unit on clothes belonging to the victims, as well as on the pieces of the gun and cigarette butts found at the scene. No arrests were made following the tests.Explore more on these topicsFranceCrimeEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Bayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King Charles | Bayeux tapestry | The Guardian
description: Monarch tells Emmanuel Macron at the British Museum in London that the two nations will share a future ‘woven together’ by history and shared values
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Monarch tells Emmanuel Macron at the British Museum in London that the two nations will share a future ‘woven together’ by history and shared values
Content: King Charles and Queen Camilla examine the Bayeux tapestry during a visit to the exhibition at the British Museum.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKing Charles and Queen Camilla examine the Bayeux tapestry during a visit to the exhibition at the British Museum.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesBayeux tapestryBayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King CharlesMonarch tells Emmanuel Macron at the British Museum in London that the two nations will share a future ‘woven together’ by history and shared valuesCaroline DaviesWed 2 Sep 2026 19.58 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.23 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe loan of theBayeux tapestrywas “the best possible symbol” of the “entente amicale” between France and the UK, King Charles said, as he visited the famous embroidered masterpiece at the British Museum in London.Though the tapestry recounts a conflict, “here it is today, nearly 1,000 years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations,” he said.The “70 metres of memory and artistry” were a reminder “that our two nations have been bound together for almost a millennium”, added Charles, speaking at the new exhibition and accompanied by the French president,Emmanuel Macron, and UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.In a speech partly delivered in French, he said: “We have defended our values together in times of peril; we continue to do so today across the world.”He continued: “May this tapestry – and the treasures that will travel in return – stand as symbols not only of our shared past, but our shared future: a future woven, as it should be, by Britain andFrancetogether.”Macron, also speaking in French and English, said that the return of the tapestry “had required a little patience” , since he first spoke of it in 2018.“Since the first British request dates back to 1931, I choose to regard eight years as something of a speed record,” he said.He added that, with the tapestry in Britain, his hopes were that the two countries could “forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery”.The tapestry – the woven record of the Norman conquest – has returned to the UK for the first time in almost 1,000 years, and is on loan until September 2027 as part of a special trilateral agreement between the UK, France and the museum.Charles’s reference to entente amicale followed his use of the phrase to rebrand the famous “entente cordiale” between the two nations in his banquet speech at Windsor Castle when hehosted the Macronsin July last year.During Wednesday’s visit, he expressed his “deepest appreciation” to Macron and the French people “for the trust you have placed in the United Kingdom by agreeing to this unprecedented loan”.He said: “It once depicted warriors crossing the Channel; yet today it forms part of a cultural exchange that will see some of the British Museum’s own precious artefacts travel to France in return, in a spirit of friendship.”Thanking all those who made the loan possible, he added: “Anyone studying the tapestry’s scenes in detail will notice that, even in the 11th century, historic events rarely happened without extensive discussion, careful planning and a great deal of organisation beforehand.”The party, which also included Queen Camilla, France’s first lady, Brigitte Macron, and Burnham’s wife, Marie-France van Heel, stopped at key moments along the 11th-century artwork to hear from curators about historic events such as the coronation of Harold Godwinson and the much-disputed depiction of his death by an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.At hisfirst prime minister’s questionsearlier on Wednesday, Burnham said: “The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation, the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low.”The Labour leader also said the Bayeux Around Britain programme, which will see the digital exhibition displayed in museums, galleries and castles in all four nations, would “give communities across the UK the opportunity to learn about one of the defining stories of our past”.In exchange, Britain will loan the Sutton Hoo treasures – an assemblage of gold and other historic objects dating from the 7th century AD – and a selection of Lewis ‌chess pieces and other masterpieces owned by the trustees of the British Museum to museums in France.Explore more on these topicsBayeux tapestryKing Charles IIIEmmanuel MacronAndy BurnhamMonarchyFranceBritish MuseumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’ | Israel | The Guardian
description: Defence minister says he believes US backing could tip regional balance in favour of forced resettlement
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Defence minister says he believes US backing could tip regional balance in favour of forced resettlement
Content: Palestinian children queue to have their faces painted before an outdoor cartoon screening at a displacement camp in Gaza City.Photograph: Bilal Osama/APAImages/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPalestinian children queue to have their faces painted before an outdoor cartoon screening at a displacement camp in Gaza City.Photograph: Bilal Osama/APAImages/ShutterstockIsraelIsrael ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’Defence minister says he believes US backing could tip regional balance in favour of forced resettlementAndrew RothGlobal affairs correspondentWed 2 Sep 2026 19.20 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s defence minister has said his country is seeking Donald Trump’s support to approve plans to expel Palestinians from the Gaza Strip in what has widely been condemned as a potential war crime.Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza in the end without thismigration” during a conference hosted by the Israeli news site Ynet and the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth. He said the Israeli government was “organised and prepared to get them out by sea, by air, by every way possible”.Trump discussed a US takeover of theGazaStrip in early 2025 that would have involved removing Palestinians from the territory, but has since pulled back from the idea. A 20-point peace plan the White House drew up last year did not call for Palestinians’ deportation, an act that would be widely seen as ethnic cleansing.View image in fullscreenIsrael’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said removal of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip was ‘being discussed all the time’.Photograph: Israeli Defence Ministry/ReutersKatz, however, said on Wednesday that he believed US support could tip regional opinion in favour of the forced resettlement of Palestinians from Gaza. He said Trump’s approval was crucial to convince neighbouring countries to accept Palestinian refugees.“Every country that is willing to take them in wants American backing,” he said. “Trump has not cancelled this at the moment. He has frozen it.”The White House did not immediately respond to a request from the Guardian for comment on whether Trump was continuing to hold discussions on Israel’s proposals to forcibly depopulate the Gaza Strip.Ed Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward IsraelRead moreKatz pointed in particular to Egypt, which he said had lobbied Washington to oppose the forced removal of the Palestinian population. “It has not been cancelled,” he said. “It is being discussed all the time, including now, and I think there is no other solution in the end that is in everyone’s interest.”The remarks come during a competitive election season in Israel in which the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his rightwing allies have appealed to voters by calling for more aggressive measures against Palestinians.Some have been openly inflammatory and cruel. The far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, posted footage on X from a women’s prison where he said he was responsible for the dire conditions in the facility.When one prisoner told him they were not receiving medical care, showering or receiving clean clothing, Ben-Gvir said: “The good conditions in the prisons are over. This is the current situation, and I am directly responsible for everything. I am pleased with these conditions.”Netanyahu visited an Israeli military post close to the yellow line in the Gaza Strip on Wednesday. Israel has said it would not pull back from that line until Hamas disarmed, despite calls for a phased withdrawal to facilitate a recent ceasefire with the group.“We control the territory and are staying on this line,” Netanyahu said. “We are doing everything to achieve our goal – disarming Hamas and demilitarising Gaza. Gaza will no longer pose a threat to Israel.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities
Author: William Christou
Headline: Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities
Content: 1:28Iran retaliates after US missile strike reportedly hits wedding – videoUS-Israel war on IranIran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at weddingBlast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilitiesWilliam Christouin BeirutWed 2 Sep 2026 16.19 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 12.56 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has accused the US of a war crime after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikesprompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities.Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people.Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi.“It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride,told Mehr News.8:08Iran retaliates after US strikes reportedly kill wedding guests - The LatestA video of the aftermath shows colourful wedding streamers and decorations strewn across the ground, and shoes abandoned in the rush to escape the attack.“You wicked people have attacked people’s homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral,” said a man filming the aftermath of the strike, shared by Fars news agency.The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals.Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”.The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”.“If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.View image in fullscreenFootage of the aftermath of the strike shows a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris.Photograph: Iranian Red Crescent/AFP/Getty ImagesThe US attacksfollowed strikes on Sunday, endinga month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran, and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets.Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devastating” retaliation.Videos of the aftermath of the strikeshow a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watchingas injured children were being treated.“When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency.View image in fullscreenThe strike on Kuhestak appeared to signal another cycle of escalation in the US-Iran conflict.Photograph: Masoud Mohamadi/Tasnim News/AFP/Getty ImagesA woman with her hands decorated in henna for the nuptials posted a video on Instagram after the attack, saying “my hands and feet are still shaking”.A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”.‘Her head was broken’: parents at Iranian school bombed by US describe their worst dayRead moreIn February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation.Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to showthe internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst,identified some of the remnantsas belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missiletouted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate”.It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footagecaptured at least six strikesin the area within a minute. A separate strikeappeared to hit a communications towerabout 150 metres away from the home.Authorities said that several “telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged in the latest strikes”.View image in fullscreenA separate strike on Kuhestak hit a communications tower about 150 metres from the home where the wedding was being held.Photograph: Masoud Mohammadi/APThe US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply.Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board.In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: UK must end all trade with Israel, says co-founder of BDS movement  | Israel | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: sanctions against ministers and settler groups are ‘smoke and mirrors cop-out’ says Omar Barghouti
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Exclusive: sanctions against ministers and settler groups are ‘smoke and mirrors cop-out’ says Omar Barghouti
Content: Omar Barghouti said international law requires the UK to end all trade, diplomatic and economic relations with Israel.Photograph: George Sweeney/AlamyView image in fullscreenOmar Barghouti said international law requires the UK to end all trade, diplomatic and economic relations with Israel.Photograph: George Sweeney/AlamyIsraelUK must end all trade with Israel, says co-founder of BDS movementExclusive: sanctions against ministers and settler groups are ‘smoke and mirrors cop-out’ says Omar BarghoutiPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to take bigger steps than halting trade with illegal Israeli settlements or imposing further sanctions, Omar Barghouti, the co-founder of the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement has said.He described sanctions against individual settler groups or extremist ministers as a “smoke and mirrors cop-out and distraction” from the UK’s legal obligation under international law to end all support for Israel, including arms exports, trade deals and academic relations that “may directly or indirectly enable Israel’s illegal occupation” of Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem.The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised on Tuesday to introduce a “comprehensive reset” of the UK’s policy on Israel in the coming weeks.It has been reported that the UK is preparing to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Miliband told the Commons the government was looking at how to stop British companies “financing, constructing or advertising new settlements”.Ed Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward IsraelRead moreMiliband has calledplans for the E1 settlement, which would involve the construction of 3,400 houses through the heart of the West Bank, unacceptable and destructive, adding that, by cutting across the territory, critics say it will render a two-state solution impossible.Tenders for the settlements are due to be handed out, potentially irreversibly, days before the Israeli elections on 27 October.The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council have warned Miliband that a UK ban on trade with settlements may fuel antisemitism in the UK.A third group of British Jews, Yachad, also met Miliband to highlight “the growing concerns of many British Jews about the entrenchment of occupation and effective annexation of the West Bank”.Barghouti, an influential advocate for Palestinian rights for more than 20 years, said the litmus test for human rights law and the west still lay in Palestine.He said: “In July 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Israel’s entire occupation of Gaza, and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is illegal and amounts to a violation of the racial segregation and apartheid prohibitions under international law.“Dozens of UN human rights experts have said to fulfil those obligations a set of minimal steps are required: a full military embargo, export import, dual-use transfer and transit.“They also said you have to end all trade, diplomatic and economic relations and academic relations that enable Israel’s illegal occupation.”Barghouti added: “Further in January 2024, the ICJ said there is a plausible case of the violation of Palestinian rights under the Genocide Convention.“The ICJ decided there is a plausible risk of genocide that is sufficient to trigger third state responsibilities. But UK government lawyers seem to ignore that part of the ruling and say the court has not ruled on genocide.“But the genocide convention is very clear – where there is a risk, the obligation to prevent is triggered, and how do you prevent a genocide? You stop enabling it. You end all forms of complicity.”The Israeli embassy referred to the warning by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools.” He added: “The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham to face pressure at Labour conference to recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocideRead moreExplaining why he regards UK sanctions as “totally performative”, Barghouti said: “They have no concrete effect in holding Israel to account or pressuring it to comply with international law.”He added: “Israel has de facto annexed the occupied Palestinian territory, making it near impossible [to] differentiate so-called settlement goods and services.”Pressed whether the BDS movement is trying to change the minds of Israelis through economic force, Barghouti insisted sanctions have to be legal and ethical.“They have to target the perpetrators, whether entities or individuals that are involved in crimes, especially international crimes. They are actually measures of accountability, not sanctions that simply say settlers shall not have vacations in London.”Despite South Africa feeling forced to return to the ICJ to point out Israel is not complying with court orders, he said he retained his faith in international law – for all its colonial origins – arguing it was not something engraved in stone, but dynamic.“Humanity has agency to evolve and expand international law. We in the BDS movement have been pushing the envelope of its interpretation.”Barghouti added: “So, in the BDS movement, we try to hold states, corporations and institutions accountable to end their own complicity in genocide rather than just wait for the messiah of international law to come and save us.“We definitely need international law, just as we need to maintain the ethical high ground. Both are necessary, but not sufficient. We need people power to achieve liberation. There is no other way.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: US and Iran exchange more airstrikes, fuelling fears of wider return to hostilities | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Attacks on Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and reprisals against US bases in Middle East quash hopes that flare-up last weekend was limited in nature
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Attacks on Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and reprisals against US bases in Middle East quash hopes that flare-up last weekend was limited in nature
Content: A small boat sails past cargo ships and other commercial vessels anchored in the strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, on 5 August 2026.Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA via APView image in fullscreenA small boat sails past cargo ships and other commercial vessels anchored in the strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, on 5 August 2026.Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA via APUS-Israel war on IranUS and Iran exchange more airstrikes, fuelling fears of wider return to hostilitiesAttacks on Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and reprisals against US bases in Middle East quash hopes that flare-up last weekend was limited in natureLucy Campbelland agenciesWed 2 Sep 2026 02.06 BSTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 18.46 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets, prompting counter strikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan and Iraq, and fuelling concerns about a ⁠wider renewal of hostilities.The US Marine Corps base Camp Titin in Jordan was targeted for an “intense ballistic missile attack”, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said early on Wednesday, according to Iranian news outlet Tasnim.The Jordanian army said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired from Iran, and did not confirm any injuries or hits on the US training camp located on the Gulf of Aqaba, near the borders with Israel and Saudi Arabia. Three other missiles landed in remote areas, it said.Missile and drone attacks were also reported in Kuwait, where the army said it was responding to Iranian hostilities. Agence France-Presse reporters in Bahrain heard alert sirens for airborne attacks go off early on Wednesday. The IRGC also claimed it struck a US base in Erbil, Iraq.US central command (CentCom) said it had completed a new wave of strikes that targeted the IRGC. It said the strikes were in response to attempted attacks on commercial shipping in the strait of Hormuz and against American service members.The Iranian Red Crescent said four people, including a child, were killed and more than 50 were wounded when shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a home where a wedding celebration was taking place in the city of Kuhestak.Asked if theUS militaryhad received any credible reports of civilian casualties, a US CentCom spokesperson, Capt Tim Hawkins, said “the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC”.Iran’s state broadcaster reported explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait, and state-linked news agency Nour ‌News reported explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast.Oil prices are ​already on the rise after an exchange of attacks by the US and Iran at the weekend, the first since July, and after reports that two tankers had been hit in the strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping.Tehran warned ⁠that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat byDonald Trumpto hit Iran “hard” in response to the Iranian strikes, and a warning from Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, that Washington was about to ⁠impose new sanctions.The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US airbases in Jordan.On Tuesday, Trump warned that if Iran retaliated against the US’s latest strikes, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.The US president has in the past made threats thatcould amount to war crimesif carried out, including threatening to destroy critical civilian infrastructure, bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages”, and an April threat that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if a peace deal wasn’t reached.In Iran, the Fars news agency quoted an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks”. The IRGC later said it had begun a “regretful response to the aggressors”, state broadcaster IRIB reported.In its statement, the IRGC said that “in blind and desperate attacks”, the US had bombed several locations, including civilian areas. It described them as “attacks that tightened the blockade of the strait of Hormuz and strengthened the determination of the fighters to suppress the foreign forces interfering in the strait of Hormuz”.Recent pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, had said early on Tuesday ​that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was intended to halt the conflict.The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on 28 February. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period – which passed without further agreement.“I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the ⁠memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, at ​a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which includes Russia ​and China.But Iranian officials have shown no public ​sign of bowing to pressure.“If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be ​able to export oil,” Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker, was ​quoted as saying by Iranian media. If ​the US intensified its “siege”, he said Tehran would respond militarily.Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was “addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”.“As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far,” he added, warning that Tehran would “use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus”.Reuters contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranUS militaryDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest | Global development | The Guardian
description: Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site
Content: Rampal power plant on the Pasur River. A study found high levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples in the nearby Sundarbans wetlands.Photograph: NurPhoto/GettyView image in fullscreenRampal power plant on the Pasur River. A study found high levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples in the nearby Sundarbans wetlands.Photograph: NurPhoto/GettyGlobal developmentBarclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forestBangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage siteSupported byAbout this contentMatthew PearceWed 2 Sep 2026 11.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.02 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people inBangladeshand India.Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, aUnesco world heritage sitemade up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supportshundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”Last November, astudy found elevated levels of mercury and arsenicin water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.View image in fullscreenThe Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people.Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/AlamyMillions of people live in the Sundarbans, and manydepend on the riverand forests for food and other resources.The claimants allege thatBarclaysfailed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank ofIndiabetween 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, includingconcerns raised by Unescoin a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France,refused to support the projectbecause of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentClimate crisisBangladeshIndiaFossil fuelsEnergySouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Relief as five Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood disaster found alive | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Several missing Australians have been found since Tuesday morning, bringing the total citizens unaccounted for to 38
Author: Kat Wong
Headline: Several missing Australians have been found since Tuesday morning, bringing the total citizens unaccounted for to 38
Content: An aerial view shows the aftermath of flooding along the Bhotekoshi River, near Syabrubesi Bazar, Rasuwa, Nepal.Photograph: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAn aerial view shows the aftermath of flooding along the Bhotekoshi River, near Syabrubesi Bazar, Rasuwa, Nepal.Photograph: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNepal-Tibet flood disasterRelief as five Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood disaster found aliveSeveral missing Australians have been found since Tuesday morning, bringing the total citizens unaccounted for to 38Australians missing in the Nepal floods: what we know so farKat WongWed 2 Sep 2026 02.59 BSTFirst published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 06.43 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA total of five Australians missing after devastating floodsravaged the Nepal-Tibet borderlast week have been found.Of the five Australians confirmed safe, one was found in Nepal, one inTibet, and three outside the crisis-hit area. The total number still missing is 38.These Australians had not spoken to families and next of kin since the disaster struck seven days ago.There were “grave concerns” for the dozens of citizens still missing in the disaster, the minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, told the ABC on Wednesday morning.“There are real logistic issues, including communications to find out where people are,” she said.How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideRead more“For those families that are still waiting, those 38 individuals unaccounted for, we understand that it’s a really concerning time, and we’ll continue to do what we can to try and locate those people.”Earlier, the minister for the Pacific, Pat Conroy, told Radio National the government was “focused on establishing their whereabouts and supporting their families”.The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) has received nearly 800 calls in relation to the floods, with 18 Australian personnel having travelled toNepalto join staff on the ground.More humanitarian and disaster relief from Australia was due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday afternoon.Another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino,was safely locatedlast week.After an Australian in Tibet made contact with family and Dfat yesterday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “incredibly thankful”.“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”A map of the flood affected areaThe death toll from the ⁠unprecedenteddeluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debrison Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.More than 4,400 people are missing.Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead.“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said.Nepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnelsRead more“As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.“Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.”Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet.Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed.This story was amended on 2 September 2026. An earlier version misstated the number of people who had been found.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump ‘happy’ about Harry and Meghan UK return: ‘I was not a fan’ | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President praises late queen and King Charles but says duke and duchess treated royal family ‘with great disrespect’
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: President praises late queen and King Charles but says duke and duchess treated royal family ‘with great disrespect’
Content: Harry and Meghan visit Bondi Beach in Sydney in April.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA/APView image in fullscreenHarry and Meghan visit Bondi Beach in Sydney in April.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA/APDonald TrumpTrump ‘happy’ about Harry and Meghan UK return: ‘I was not a fan’President praises late queen and King Charles but says duke and duchess treated royal family ‘with great disrespect’Victoria Bekiempisand Guardian staffWed 2 Sep 2026 21.01 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has weighed in on the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s move back to Britain, declaring: “I’m happy about it.”“I was not a fan,” the US president told reporters during a question-and-answer session after a press conference with travel executives on Wednesday. “I had a very good relationship with the queen, really good. I got to know her very well. A really good relationship with King Charles – I knew him as Prince Charles and King Charles. I’ve known him for a long time.”Harry and Meghan: the key moments, conflicts and controversies since their US moveRead moreTrump, describing Charles as a “great, great guy”, said he thought Harry and Meghan “treated the royal family with great disrespect”.“I didn’t like it,” he also said, adding, “If I were the royal family, I would not have taken them back.”The couple moved back to the UK last week, six years after they left for the US. They had lived in California since 2020. They have yet to speak publicly about their plans, are said to be settling for an “extended period” of time amid speculation as to how long they will stay, and where they will live.Trump has a longstanding fascination and admiration for the royal family, which he traces back to a childhood memory of watching Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation on TV in 1953 with his mother, Mary Anne Trump, who was born in Scotland. Trump adored the late queen, whom he described as a “great woman” who had “really never made a mistake” during her decades on the throne.The king is reportedly looking forward to spending more time with the duke and duchess in a personal capacity, but Harry, 41, and Meghan, 45, will remain private individuals. They previously gave up their official royal duties.The couple is not expected to be offered a “half-in half-out” option, after that was firmly rejected by Queen Elizabeth II.Questions remain unanswered, including whether British taxpayers will foot the bill for the pair’s security detail after their return to the UK.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpMeghan, the Duchess of SussexPrince HarryMonarchyKing Charles IIIQueen Elizabeth IInewsShareReuse this content

title: Green party members back Zack Polanski to stand in London byelection | Green party | The Guardian
description: Party leader in England and Wales seen as favourite to contest Holborn and St Pancras after Starmer’s resignation
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Party leader in England and Wales seen as favourite to contest Holborn and St Pancras after Starmer’s resignation
Content: The Green party’s Zack Polanski is not a member of parliament at present.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenThe Green party’s Zack Polanski is not a member of parliament at present.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAGreen partyGreen party members back Zack Polanski to stand in London byelectionParty leader in England and Wales seen as favourite to contest Holborn and St Pancras after Starmer’s resignationAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentWed 2 Sep 2026 19.11 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski moved a step closer in his quest to become an MP on Wednesday, with local Green party members supporting him to become the party’s candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.The party leader in England and Wales started campaigning alongside his fellow Green, Hannah Spencer, the MP for Gorton and Denton, in the Holborn area on Tuesday, and is seriously considering putting himself forward as the party’s candidate in the seatvacated by Keir Starmer on Monday.Green party sources said local party members would have the final say on the selected candidate, but the Guardian understands local members are supportive of Polanski running, with no clear local activist with significant support expected to oppose him. It is understood nominations will open soon and candidates will be selected by the end of next week.Lorna Jane Russell, the leader of the Greens on the local Camden council, will not stand, having previously expressed a desire to focus on her role as the leader of the opposition at Camden Town Hall and her pregnancy.On the anniversary of his election on 2 September 2025, Polanski said the byelection would be a “referendum on ending rip-off Britain”, adding: “I am very excited for the next chapter for myself, for the Greens and for people across the country.”Sources inside the party in London said that therise in membership since Polanski became leadermade him the favourite for the role.“There would be a lot of excitement about him standing,” said one Green party source. “This is the kind of seat that has always had high-profile figures and I think having someone with Zack’s profile would play very well with local party members.”The move is not without risk for Polanski, with the former prime minister’s seat traditionally considered to be safe for Labour. The Green party leader may prefer to contest a seat in Hackney, wherethe party has recently won the mayoralty, if a sitting MP such as Diane Abbott were to step down. In a difficult political climate in the May local elections, Labour lost seats but held on to Camden council. “This is not Gorton and Denton,” said one Labour source. “The Burnham bounce will help.”Tulip Siddiq, the Labour MP for Hampstead and Highgate, said party members were already out campaigning and were confident they could retain the seat. “I know Camden through and through and I do believe that we can win this,” she said.Siddiq added: “I think theLabourvote is resilient and I think Andy Burnham’s pledges on the doorstep are being gratefully received by people in Camden. Certainly I’ll be out campaigning every day and giving it my best shot.”Labour will not run an all-women shortlist and will announce their candidate by next Wednesday, with applications closing on Friday and shortlisting expected by the start of next week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReform UK bans three journalists from its conference after critical reportingRead moreThe frontrunner is thought to be Sagal Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia and has been theleader of Camden council since May. “She’s got a compelling personal story and can reach people from all faiths and backgrounds in Camden,” said one Labour source. “She’s also been really active in the local party for a long time. Lots of people know her and like her.”Adam Hug, the former leader of Westminster council who lost his job leading the council when the Conservatives took control of itin May’s local election, is also a mooted name. Other possible candidates are Nash Ali, the former mayor of Camden, and Rishi Madlani, a former Camden councillor.Abdi-Wali is close to Starmer and local Labour sources said any attempts to bring in a candidate not from the area would be met with fierce criticism. “It will be interesting to see if Burnham has the same appeal in northLondonas Makerfield,” said one. “A lot of the policies he’s been talking about feel more geared towards the rest of the country, not really London.”Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiHannah SpencerKeir StarmerByelectionsLabourTulip SiddiqnewsShareReuse this content

title: Female film-makers still being squeezed out of industry, London film festival director says | London film festival | The Guardian
description: Over 40% of films in LFF programme are female-made, but only two of 21 gala films are directed by women
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Over 40% of films in LFF programme are female-made, but only two of 21 gala films are directed by women
Content: Kristy Matheson, the director of the BFI London film festival, said programmers had no problem finding strong female-made debut films, but the numbers dropped off after that.Photograph: Simon Ackerman/Getty Images for BFIView image in fullscreenKristy Matheson, the director of the BFI London film festival, said programmers had no problem finding strong female-made debut films, but the numbers dropped off after that.Photograph: Simon Ackerman/Getty Images for BFILondon film festivalFemale film-makers still being squeezed out of industry, London film festival director saysOver 40% of films in LFF programme are female-made, but only two of 21 gala films are directed by womenNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 2 Sep 2026 19.00 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFemale film-makers are still being squeezed out of the industry as they progress beyond their debut films, the director of theLondon film festivalhas said, adding that “the dial does not seem to be moving”.Kristy Matheson’s comments came as LFF announced its full programme for this year’s event, which runs from 7 to 19 October. Of the 251 titles, 109 (43%) are made by female film-makers, but only two of the 21 gala films are directed by women.The figure comes as theVenice film festivalfaces renewed scrutiny over its lack of female directors in the competition. Maggie Gyllenhaal, the president of the Venice jury, said on Wednesday that there was a “systemic problem” preventing women from getting opportunities, including access to financing.Speaking aboutLFF, Matheson said programmers had no difficulty finding strong films by women at the beginning of their careers, but numbers declined sharply thereafter.“The statistics are not where you would want them to be,” she said. “We have no problem finding incredible films by female directors. We could make a whole Sutherland competition [recognising directorial debut] easily and have only female directors.“Then it really drops off. So short films, first films, you’re just seeing all of this incredible talent. Second films, it starts to drop off. This is not something new to this year. It seems the dial does not seem to be moving.”Matheson said the disparity was particularly visible in the festival’s higher-profile sections.“You’ll find less female film-makers in the gala section, for example,” she said. “How many female directors get to make big-budget films? How many get to make fourth films, fifth films?”The festival will also feature screen talks withAndrew Scott, Ava DuVernay, Cynthia Erivo, Jesse Eisenberg, John Malkovich, Sofia Coppola, Brad Bird, James Gray, Mahershala Ali, Naomi Ackie and Danny Boyle.View image in fullscreenAndrew Scott in Elsinore, which will open the festival.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/Focus FeaturesOpening and closing this year’s festival are films about theatre, creativity and the communities people build around them.Simon Stone’s Elsinore, receiving its European premiere, will open the festival with the story of the actor Ian Charleson and stars Andrew Scott andOlivia Colman. Jesse Eisenberg’s comedy The Debut, a love letter to community theatre, will close it with its UK premiere, starring Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti.“To make theatre is to be with others. It’s an act of community,” Matheson said.“Elsinore and The Debut are two very different films in tone. But in both, you get a sense of what creative community means, and how nourishing and enriching that can be. What they share is this idea of transformation. They’re both films about people on the precipice of something.”Labour emerged as another theme, Matheson said, with films showing people at work opening up bigger questions about society. Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care follows two flatmates working in social care, while Boots Riley’s I Love Boosters, starring Keke Palmer and Demi Moore, turns a confrontation between professional shoplifters and a ruthless fashion mogul into a story about unionising.Other films focus more explicitly on community and “radical care”, Matheson said. All of a Sudden, set in a nursing home, uses the relationship between two women to explore friendship and what it means to belong.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKate O’Flynn, Marion Bailey and Alice Bailey Johnson in Tender Loving Care, directed by Mike Leigh.Photograph: International Film FestivalElsewhere, the programme explores political themes. Boyle’s Ink, premiering at the Mayor of London’s Gala, revisits Rupert Murdoch’s acquisition of the Sun and its impact on British politics and western democracy. Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine returns to the eve of Pinochet’s 1973 coup in Chile, while Sergei Loznitsa’s Imperium reworks footage shot in Russia in the early 1970s into a meditation on empire.“They’re using history to process now,” Matheson said.The Match, a documentary about the 1986 England-Argentina World Cup quarter-final, is structured like a thriller while examining politics, colonialism and ownership. Josephine, which premiered atSundance, uses thriller conventions to explore trauma after a violent sexual assault witnessed by a young girl.“There are films that are not usually the subject matter of a thriller, but are using this genre to explore topics in an engaging and enticing way,” Matheson said.View image in fullscreenBoots Riley’s I Love Boosters.Photograph: NeonAmong the festival’s international premieres is Tony Gilroy’s Behemoth!, starring Pedro Pascal, Olivia Wilde and Will Arnett, and set in the world of classical music.World premieres include Anthony Wonke’s British boxing biopic In the Shadows and Michael Winterbottom’s The Trip to the Northern Lights, starring Rob Brydon and Steve Coogan.Additional galas include Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s The Beloved, Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland, Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord – winner of the Palme d’Or in Cannes in May – Taika Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun, and Susanna White’s adaptation of Suzie Miller’s acclaimed play Prima Facie.There is also Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, Jordan Firstman’s Cannes breakout Club Kid, James Gray’s Paper Tiger, and Andrew Haigh’s adaptation of Colm Tóibín’s short story A Long Winter.Explore more on these topicsLondon film festivalBFILondonFestivalsAndrew ScottOlivia ColmanBoots RileynewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Fair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s status
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Fair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s status
Content: Andy Burnham (right) and his chancellor, John Healey, could face an even uglier bond market if they defer hard decisions in the October budget.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham (right) and his chancellor, John Healey, could face an even uglier bond market if they defer hard decisions in the October budget.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesNils Pratley on financeGiltsBurnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budgetNils PratleyFair to say the current sell-off is international, but the PM has said little yet to make investors rethink the UK’s statusWed 2 Sep 2026 18.14 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTShareIt’s too soon to say the bond markets have turned on Andy Burnham.
