Needing to assert his dominance, Trump has now started atrade warwith our northern neighbor, friend, second-largest trading partner (after Mexico) and, at least until now, reliable ally.He’s hammering Canada on his Truth Social and in media appearances, saying Canada has “ripped off” the US for years, andsigningan order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”.This is pure bunk, of course – more empty Trump bravado and ignorant belligerence.Canada?Really? If Mel Brooks were still making movies, this would be a comedy. But as all else with Trump, it’s no laughing matter.The rebranding of ‘Lake America’ is Trump’s desperate attempt to distract us | Arwa MahdawiRead moreTrump apparently assumed that Canada would quickly surrender because it had more to lose. ThetariffsTrump has imposed on Canada – along with those he’s threatening if Canada retaliates –affecta tiny portion of the US’s total imports but a huge portion of Canada’s total exports.Jamieson Greer, Trump’s US trade representative,saysthe duties are too small to pose a problem for the US and are “more [Canada’s] emergency than ours”.But bullies like Trump rarely think about the effects of their bullying on the thinking and attitudes of their targets.Trump’s bullying ofIranhas not only reinforced its hardline regime but shown them that control over the strait of Hormuz is an effective means of gaining concessions from other Gulf states as well as the US, and likely strengthened their resolve to build a nuclear weapon.Trump’s bullying of Canada, meanwhile, is igniting a patriotism that has often eluded that nation, which separatist factions have long threatened to pull apart.Mark Carney’s decision to stand up to Trump – through “dollar for dollar”retaliationon goods coming from key industries in states including Ohio and Texas with competitive Senate elections – has led to a surge of support for the prime minister’s Liberal party. Liberalswonthree special by-elections on Monday.Trump’s trade war with Canada has also dimmed the prospects of Canada’s separatist movements, at least in the short term. A candidate from Carney’s Liberal party edged out a Quebec separatist in one of Monday’s special by-elections, in a district hit hard by US tariffs.This is a good omen for Canada before 5 October’s vote in Quebec on whether the province’s secessionist party, Parti Québécois, gains additional seats in the province’s legislative body, and 19 October’s vote in Alberta on whether to hold a referendum to secede from the rest of Canada.Trump may also have underestimated the negative reactions to his trade war at home. According to a newReuters/Ipsos poll, 57% of Americans ‌oppose Trump’s moves to impose tariffs on Canadian imports. About 63% oppose his peevish order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”. Only 20% support the higher tariffs on Canadian goods.Canadians do not seek a trade war – but nor will we be bullied by Donald Trump | Jen GersonRead moreThe negative response is especially pronounced in border states whose economies are tightly interconnected with Canada.In Michigan, for example, where overwhelming majoritiesopposeTrump’s tariffs on Canada, Democrats have launched new attack ads on the Republican Senate candidateMike Rogersfor refusing to denounce the tariffs. The Democratic Senate candidateAbdul El-Sayedcalled Trump an “asshole”for launching the trade war.There’s still time for the US and Canada to avoid the worst of the economic and political fallout from this. Carney’s “dollar for dollar” retaliation goes into effect on 8 September but Trump’s counter-counter measure –threatened50% tariffs on autos and auto parts – won’t go into effect until New Year’s Day.Still, no one should expect an easy resolution to what may go down in history as the stupidest of all the stupid foreign policies Trump has initiated. And given the extent of Trump’s dumb international moves, that is saying something.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKThis article was amended on 2 September 2026. An earlier version said the provincial election in Quebec is on 8 October, but it will be on 5 October.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS foreign policyCanadaTariffsIranUS-Israel war on IranAmericascommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Kemi Badenoch and the economy: a plan stuck in the Tory comfort zone  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election
Content: Kemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons on 1 September.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons on 1 September.Photograph: House of CommonsOpinionConservativesThe Guardian view on Kemi Badenoch and the economy: a plan stuck in the Tory comfort zoneEditorialThe Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last electionWed 2 Sep 2026 18.29 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.08 BSTShareTo outlast a prime minister always counts as some kind of achievement for an opposition leader, although Kemi Badenoch cannot claim credit for Sir Keir Starmer’sdownfall. Sir Keir’s wounds were mostly self-inflicted. To the extent that opposition pressure was involved, it waselectoral threatsfrom Reform UK and the Green party that stoked Labour party frustration to a regicidal pitch. The Tory leader’s role was largely as a spectator.Mrs Badenoch still hopes to use regime change to her advantage. She thinks the economy, and fiscal discipline in particular, will be her most fruitful line of attack. In their first confrontation atprime minister’s questionson Wednesday, the Conservative leader called Mr Burnham a “spendthrift” and “people pleaser” who will dodge the tough decisions required to prove Britain’s creditworthiness on international markets. She expects him to yield to Labour MPs’ demands for budget increases, which will then have to be financed with tax rises.View image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersIn that scenario, Mrs Badenoch imagines a vacancy for a rehabilitated small-state Conservative party offering hard-headed budget management, less profligate than Labour; more sober and respectable than Reform UK. That message would unite what remains of her depleted party. She can’t compete with Nigel Farage on the terrain of anti-immigrant rhetoric (although that doesn’t stop heraping his stances). She shows no interest in finding political accommodation for socially liberal, pro-European one-nation Tories who now have more in common with the Liberal Democrats than the modern Conservative party.This leaves the Tories with a narrow focus on tax cuts, reining in welfare spending and deregulation as a spur to enterprise. Mr Farage supports those things too, but Mrs Badenoch believes that Reform UK’s maverick style and the whiff of impropriety around its financial dealings make it an unreliable vehicle for a classically Thatcherite agenda that belongs, by rights, to Lady Thatcher’s own party.The claim to be the truekeeper of the Thatcherite flamehas become a ritual for Tory leaders. The mantle has passed through so many hands, it is threadbare as a political definition in 2026. It was worn most preposterously by Liz Truss, who posted photos of herself on social media recreating iconic images of the Iron Lady in her pomp. She then detonated her government with a “mini-budget” that was a crass pastiche of the economic ideas she claimed to venerate – a wild foray into fiscal irresponsibility masquerading as free-market radicalism.One of the Treasury ministers who enthusiastically endorsed Ms Truss’s plan, Andrew Griffith, wasthis week appointedMrs Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor. He replaces Mel Stride, a lower-octane performer who was deemed not to have made sufficient impact in the role. It is a revealing choice that undermines the Tory leader’s plan to make economic competence the centrepiece of her pitch to lead the nation. When considering a potential chancellor, she clearly values the ability to grab attention over economic judgment.This is consistent with a pattern of failure to engage with the full spectrum of failures over many years that accounts for the scale of Tory defeat at the last election. What Mrs Badenoch imagines to be a political strategy looks more like retreat to an ideological comfort zone in the hope that a second prime minister will self-destruct while she watches from the sidelines.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsConservativesOpinionKemi BadenochAndy BurnhamKeir StarmerLabourEconomicsTaxeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Thames Water, I refuse to pay the sewage charge in my bill while you pollute Britain’s rivers and coastlines | Jenny Jones | The Guardian
description: I will calmly read all the threatening letters and await the court case against me. But I will take a stand even if our government won’t, says Jenny Jones, a Green party peer
Author: Jenny Jones
Headline: I will calmly read all the threatening letters and await the court case against me. But I will take a stand even if our government won’t, says Jenny Jones, a Green party peer
Content: Surfers Against Sewage stage a paddle out protest against sewage pollution in Falmouth, 17 May 2025.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSurfers Against Sewage stage a paddle out protest against sewage pollution in Falmouth, 17 May 2025.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty ImagesOpinionThames WaterThames Water, I refuse to pay the sewage charge in my bill while you pollute Britain’s rivers and coastlinesJenny JonesI will calmly read all the threatening letters and await the court case against me. But I will take a stand even if our government won’tWed 2 Sep 2026 11.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.07 BSTShareIcan’t even remember when I decided to stop paying the sewage element of my Thames Water bill. It might have been after reading this headline from the Guardian in July 2025: “Serious pollution incidents by English water companies rose 60% last year,” with the subheading: “Environment Agency records 75 serious incidents among total of 2,800, with Thames Water being worst offender.”Living in London means that my supplier isThames Water, which makes a profit out of pollution. I decided that if the government wouldn’t act, I could at least do my part and not pay for this travesty.The case for not paying these outrageous charges is clear. The water companies are not fulfilling their duties and instead they are discharging raw sewage into our waterways and lives. Beyond that, they have brought in hosepipe bans, despite last winter beingone of the wetteston record, because they haven’t built enough reservoirs to store water for use in the summer.They ask us to use water wisely, and send us advice on how to cut our usage, and to consider dynamic pricing, while at the same time failing to fix the leaks thatlose about a fifthof all public supply in England and Wales. My final gripe is that a huge chunk of my bill doesn’t even get spent on fixing these problems; insteadit is spent on interest paymentsfor debts that enable Thames Water to pay shareholders billions of pounds.Nothing will change until these companies go officially bankrupt and the quickest way of ensuring that happens is if people stop paying their bills. A few decades ago millions of people did exactly that with the poll tax and the governmentbacked down. (I was taken to court over that.) So why not use the same nonpayment tactic to end water privatisation? Even a few million of us delaying the payment of our bills by several months would threaten the viability of these water companies.As a ThamesWaterbill-payer, I felt that it was hypocritical of me to be constantly campaigning on the issue and then meekly paying up. As a Green party member since 1988, and green-minded since my teens, it just seemed wrong not to take a stand.When I decided I had to do more than just speak out, I wrote to Thames Water and explained that I was very happy to pay the proportion of the bill related to their supplying me with water, but not to the proportion for their dealing with sewage. They wrote back saying that they don’t work out the proportions like that between water and sewage. And followed it up with a threatening letter and a vastly increased bill with penalty charges.Of course the real solution to this problem would be nationalising these companies. Public opinion isfirmly in favour of renationalisation, yet the government keeps trotting out a fictitious number of£100bn as the cost of taking companies over. That figure is bogus because it includes the companies’ debt as part of its value. Many argue that thenationalisation costis actuallyfar lower, possibly even zero.The government has also talked about “public control”, which is of course not public ownership, but would allow oversight of how companies are run and the ability to impose penalty charges. But if laws and oversight worked, we wouldn’t be in this mess.We aren’t holding the bosses to account for their failures. We aren’t prosecuting them, finding them guilty of illegal dumping of effluent. No need to send them to our overcrowded prisons. They can be sentenced to community service of 20 hours a week cleaning up the filth they’ve allowed into in our streams and rivers and on our seashore.None of this is new. We’ve had a Labour government for more than two years, but nothing has really changed and the bills are getting bigger while our preciouschalk streams are dying, river ecosystemsare collapsingand swimmers are beingmade ill by sewagefloating near beaches.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI will continue my own protest. The letters are unpleasant, and there has been mention of bailiffs, so I don’t recommend anyone else going into this lightly. I will calmly read all the threatening letters and await the court case against me. Despite having a seat in the House of Lords, I don’t have a lot of assets but, win or lose in court, by taking on Thames Water I know I can only win in terms of my own self-respect.I have drawn a line in the sand. And I hope to win this particular battle.Jenny Jones is a Green party peerExplore more on these topicsThames WaterOpinionWater billsWater industryNationalisationUtilitiesRiversPollutioncommentShareReuse this content

title: The $1 Trump coin: legal tender, depending on what you mean by legal | US news | The Guardian
description: Various laws and 250 years of tradition prevent the likeness of living people from appearing on currency. Donald Trump and Scott Bessent don’t want you to worry about that
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: Various laws and 250 years of tradition prevent the likeness of living people from appearing on currency. Donald Trump and Scott Bessent don’t want you to worry about that
Content: The new Trump $1 coin – yours for roughly $2.44.Photograph: Department of Treasury/United States Mint/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe new Trump $1 coin – yours for roughly $2.44.Photograph: Department of Treasury/United States Mint/ReutersThis Week in TrumplandUS newsAnalysisThe $1 Trump coin: legal tender, depending on what you mean by legalAdam GabbattVarious laws and 250 years of tradition prevent the likeness of living people from appearing on currency. Donald Trump and Scott Bessent don’t want you to worry about thatThis was originally published in This Week in Trumpland.Sign up to receive it in your inbox every WednesdayWed 2 Sep 2026 17.50 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.10 BSTShareTwo hallmarks ofDonald Trump’s second-term: the president’s enthusiasm for putting his name and face on things, and his cavalier approach to established law.Today the president is once again combining both those interests, as the government releases a$1 coin bearing his image, an item of currency that scholars say should be illegal, but which is happening anyway. How many times have you heard that in the last 18 months?The US has had a long tradition of not putting living people on US currencybeginning in the late 1700s when the US Mint, which manufactures and distributes currency, wanted to put an image of George Washington on US money. Washington declined, saying it would be too much like a monarchy putting its rulers on money. In 1866, Congress passed an amendment barring the “portrait or likeness” of living people from appearing on currency.That doesn’t appear to have bothered Trump. His scowling face dominates the new $1 coin, which is legal tender, and looks gold but is actually made from zinc, manganese, nickel and copper. It costs $61 to buy 25 one-dollar coins – you do the math – and about 9m of the coins are being made. They will, according to the US Mint, “honor 250 years of great American heritage”.That all sounds great, if you’re into that sort of thing, but what about the law?.How to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticksRead moreScott Bessent, the treasury secretary, has argued that during the 150th celebration of America’s “birthday”, the face of then president Calvin Coolidge appeared on a coin, so during the 250th, the Trump coin is fine.The main problem seems to be that there’s a hodge-podge of laws which govern what can and cannot go on a coin. The 1866 ban on featuring living people arose from an impressively creative act of vanity. An incoming five-cent note was supposed to feature an image of the deceased explorer William Clark, but a treasury official called Spencer M Clark took advantage of the pair sharing a last name to insteadprint his own faceon the note.The problem was that members of Congress a) noticed and b) were unamused. They passed an amendment which ruled that US money can only feature dead individuals – but it only applied to paper money.“For me, I would consider it illegal,” Gabriel Mathy, an associate professor of economics at American University who has studied American currency, said of the Trump coin.“But the United States has all these laws, which really are norms because they’re not really enforceable.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis Week in TrumplandA deep dive into the policies, controversies and oddities surrounding the Trump administrationEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe coin hasn’t been produced without a fight. In May, a group of Democratic members of Congress wrote to the treasury department in May, urging them to desist with the coin, pointing to a 2005 law which further restricted which presidents could appear on coins.And in March, James Rickher, a retired attorney in Portland, filed a request to block the coin, arguing it was illegal, but in June a federal judge denied that motion, writing that Rickher had “failed to present evidence that clearly shows he will personally suffer concrete harm from issuance of the challenged coin”, Fox 12reported. The judge noted, however, that his ruling did not determine whether the coin is illegal or legal.And so today, Americans will be able to honor 250 years of great American heritage by buying a questionably legal one-dollar coin for roughly $2.44. If you’d like to know who came up with such a brilliant plan, just look at the coin.Explore more on these topicsUS newsThis Week in TrumplandUS politicsDonald TrumpCurrenciesanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: Being subservient to the interests of the wealthy now means that his hands are tied, and he will be unable to tackle Britain’s most pressing issues, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: Being subservient to the interests of the wealthy now means that his hands are tied, and he will be unable to tackle Britain’s most pressing issues, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Alamy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Alamy/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donationsGeorge MonbiotBeing subservient to the interests of the wealthy now means that his hands are tied, and he will be unable to tackle Britain’s most pressing issuesWed 2 Sep 2026 06.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.06 BSTShareDamn the electorate. They’reso impatient. No sooner do they get a new leader than they want another one. Those ingrates arealreadystarting to grumble about Andy Burnham. Maybe the country isbecoming ungovernable. Perhapsit’s social media. Or a consumerist culture, always picking the next shiny thing. Perhaps we’readdicted to drama. As we’re on our sixth prime minister in 10 years, and as similar levels of discontent surface in many other countries, these claims are recited across the media. What’s wrong with us?Yet our disgruntlement is entirely rational. We give up so quickly on our prime ministers because they give up so quickly on us. Though it may involve different issues, it is always the same betrayal: the public interest is sacrificed for the sake of a tiny number of immensely wealthy people. And it tends to happen almost immediately.The latest example, which has triggered both fury and grim resignation, isBurnham’s backtrackingon his intention to cap political donations. It was hardly a radical policy: he proposed that no person would be able to give more than £500,000 to a political party in one year. That would still have granted the very wealthy disproportionate influence over our politics. I have long believed that the only fair system is one in which there should beno private donations at allbeyond a standard, fixed membership fee. Otherwise voters will always take second place to money. But at the moment there is no cap, which ensures that billionaires can buy political parties and their platforms. So a £500,000 maximum, pathetic as it is, is at least a start. In asubsequent pledge, Burnham suggested that it could gradually be lowered.Now, we are told, even this high cap has been abandoned: therepresentation of the people billwill concentrate instead on introducing Keir Starmer’s risible proposals, which are intended to limit donations sent from abroad but not from within the UK: as if billionaire donors and their wealth managers have no expertise in transferring money from one account to another. The loopholes are designed in.Burnham’s buckling on this issue is not a small matter. It cuts to the quick of what this country is and how it works. It has immense implications for democracy, for policy formation and for every other aspect of civic life. What it means is that the ultra-rich will continue to own our politics and our country. Succumb to the power of money and you will find yourself, like Starmer, tongue-tied and immobilised, unable to rise to any challenge that requires a confrontation with oligarchic might. In other words, get this wrong andevery other wrong thing follows.The official reason for Burnham’s U-turn is that trade unions objected: they have long channelled large sums into the Labour party. I doubt this is the real explanation; most of the donations Burnham received for his leadership campaigncame from large private donors. Almost half was supplied by Lord Sainsbury, who was also a major funder of the Starmer project. Union money scarcely featured.But even if Burnhamhasretreated from his promise for the sake of the unions, I believe trade union funding is also problematic. It ensures that sectoral interests are elevated above the general interest. For example, Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers. And if the unions believe that an uncapped system works for them, they are deluded. They can never match thespending power of billionaires, whose interests in most cases are diametrically opposed to those of their members.The power of the ultra-rich is now manifest in every policy governments do adopt and the policies they don’t. We see it in the new protest laws and their applications, which become more absurd by the week. Labelling protesters “terrorists” is part of a long-running programme to ensure thatno one dares protest about anythingany more. This programme has beenrolled out across the world, through model legislation drawn up by junktanks funded by some of the richest people on Earth. Just as itdid in the 18th century, an ever more extreme defence of property keeps pace with agrowing concentration of wealth.We see it in the way that datacentres have been labelled “critical national infrastructure”, enabling the government tobypass the usual planning processand impose them on communities, regardless of their impacts onlocal people’s quality of life, on water resources, energy supply and climate breakdown. Again,similar measures are being imposedin other countries at the behest of the same billionaire-funded groups. The role of governments appears to have been reduced to nodding them through.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham accused of U-turn after initially backing political donations cap to fall below £500kRead moreWe see it in the Burnham government’s insistence this summer, in the midst of shattering droughts, heatwaves and fires, onlaunching a consultationthat proposesradically curtailingthe transition to electric vehicles. I believe there is only one possible explanation for this policy: lobbying by corporations and their shareholders. Their interests appear to outweigh those of the living planet and its 8 billion people.If our country and many others are becoming ungovernable, it is not because of the people. It is because the ultra-rich have smashed the system. The electorate and the MPs who might seek to represent us pull the political levers, but nothing happens. They might replace the leader, but the new one promptly repeats the “mistakes” that caused the eviction of the old one. It makes you wonder: what threat do the oligarchs present that outweighs even the threat of losing power?Whatever the reason may be, disillusionment is an inevitable result of such betrayals. I think most people want stability. I think most people want to be able to trust their governments. We don’t like in-built obsolescence in our leaders any more than like it in our phones. I don’t want to see Burnham go the way of Starmer. But I know he will succeed only if he defends the public interest against the power of money. So what’s stopping him?George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionParty fundingKeir StarmerLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Fake 10 Downing Street listing on Booking.com highlights security failures | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: Consumer watchdog Which? set up and accepted payment for fake listing for ‘1 bed apartment in heart of London’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Consumer watchdog Which? set up and accepted payment for fake listing for ‘1 bed apartment in heart of London’
Content: A fake review was also uploaded, describing enjoying the experience of ‘hanging out with Larry the cat’.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenA fake review was also uploaded, describing enjoying the experience of ‘hanging out with Larry the cat’.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAConsumer affairsFake 10 Downing Street listing on Booking.com highlights security failuresConsumer watchdog Which? set up and accepted payment for fake listing for ‘1 bed apartment in heart of London’Ben QuinnWed 2 Sep 2026 08.45 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuccessive politicians have clawed their way past colleagues over the years to call the residence home. Yet in an offer that probably seemed too good to be true, the property site Booking.com has been accused of “systemic security failures” after it was able to set up and accept payment for a fake listing for 10 Downing Street.A property listed as a “1 bedroom apartment in the heart of London” – with the exact address and a picture of the prime minister’s home – was listed on 18 June by researchers from the consumer watchdog Which?.The listing, which promised a four-minute walk to the Houses of Parliament, was set up so that users had to request a stay and were unable to reserve and pay automatically.The booking window opened briefly and closed so that a test could be carried out by a researcher from Which?. The consumer watchdog said a payment for a week-long stay had been processed by the digital travel site that enables users to book hotels and other accommodation as well as flights and car rentals.View image in fullscreenPolice officers patrol outside 10 Downing Street after a cabinet meeting in July.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesThe money had stillnot been refundedmore than six weeks after it had been set up, according to Which?, which is associated with the Consumers Association charity.A fake review was also uploaded to the site, describing the stay as “exceptional” and enjoying the experience of “hanging out with Larry the cat”, in a reference to Downing Street’s resident feline.Despite Booking.com sending a message saying the review would be checked by a team of moderators, the consumer watchdog said it had been added almost immediately.The team of researchers were also said to have used Booking.com’s mailing system to send an external URL asking the representative for credit card details to confirm the booking, Which? said.The watchdog claimed the travel site had told them it had the ability to block URLs being sent through the messaging system if it suspected fraudulent activity, but it had not done so.The listing was finally removed on 27 August, six weeks after it went live.Rory Boland, the editor of Which? Travel, said: “If Booking.com’s so-called sophisticated AI systems can’t spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it’s no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily.”The watchdog said its investigation had “uncovered systemic security failures across the platform” and urged Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, to investigate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Booking.com spokesperson said: “This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings on our platform. The property added by Which? was not visible to customers or ‘live’ for the time period referenced.‘We didn’t feel safe’: Booking.com users face battle to get money backRead more“We use a range of checks, verification measures and artificial intelligence, which help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours.”It said that as the property was not open and bookable, some of its automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the fraud listing.An Ofcom spokesperson said platforms have legal duties obliging them to take down illegal content generated by users once it is known. “Booking.com is not in scope of future rules that will apply to paid-for fraudulent advertising, and any change to that would be a matter for government,” they said.Get in touchContact Ben Quinn about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Ben using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. When asked to choose a recipient please switch to the Journalists list and select Ben Quinn.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailben.quinn@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsConsumer affairsTravel & leisureConsumer rightsPropertyLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sadiq Khan fined over untaxed car falsely registered in his name | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: London mayor’s office says he is ‘victim of a scam’ after conviction under fast-track system where magistrates can decide outcomes in seconds
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: London mayor’s office says he is ‘victim of a scam’ after conviction under fast-track system where magistrates can decide outcomes in seconds
Content: Khan has been the focus of protests by motorists angry at the Ulez expansion scheme.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKhan has been the focus of protests by motorists angry at the Ulez expansion scheme.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockSadiq KhanSadiq Khan fined over untaxed car falsely registered in his nameLondon mayor’s office says he is ‘victim of a scam’ after conviction under fast-track system where magistrates can decide outcomes in secondsBen QuinnPolitical correspondentWed 2 Sep 2026 18.08 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 09.28 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSadiq Khan’s office has revealed he was the victim of a scam that led to him being fined for failing to tax a car that did not belong to him.TheLondonmayor was found guilty last month under a system of “conveyor-belt justice”, in which magistrates decide on hundreds of cases a day, sometimes spending less than a minute on each.City Hall officials say the 24-year-old Nissan Micra did not belong to Khan orTransportfor London.The mayor has been the focus of protests by motorists angry at the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone in London. Some said they planned to register cars in Khan’s name to make him liable for the £12.50 daily charge.The prosecution was undertaken by the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, which accused Khan of being the keeper of the vehicle when it was spotted as being untaxed on 24 January. In a move that paves the way for the conviction to be erased after a court hearing on Thursday, theDVLAsaid on Wednesday evening that the case had been withdrawn after a review and it was investigating the circumstances.“This is a scam, which is a crime,” said a spokesperson for Khan.“It’s not the first time the mayor has been the victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle. Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware.”A magistrate, sitting in a private hearing of thesingle justice procedurein Herefordshire, convicted Khan in his absence and ordered that he pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs and settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.PA Media alerted the DVLA to the criminal conviction on Tuesday and its officials confirmed they were reviewing the case and investigating the circumstances of the prosecution.Court documents show that DVLA letters addressed to the mayor about the unpaid tax bill were sent to a Gordon Ramsay restaurant in east London instead of the nearby TfL offices.The mayor faces the possibility of having to appear in court to try to overturn the conviction.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUlez has been a breath of fresh air for London | LettersRead moreThe single justice procedure was introduced in 2015 as a cheaper method of dealing with low-level criminal cases, allowing magistrates to sit alone and in private.The system, which is under government review, was criticised in 2024 when about 59,000 train-fare evasion convictions were overturned for being unlawful. It also emerged that children had been wrongly convicted in the secretive courts.More scrutiny has come over repeated incidents of sick and incapacitated pensioners being convicted for not paying their household bills.In Khan’s case, court records show he was prosecuted by the DVLA after the annual tax on the Micra, which was first registered in 2002, ran out last September.Explore more on these topicsSadiq KhanLondonLow emission zonesUK criminal justiceTransportTransport policyDVLAnewsShareReuse this content

title: Architect of UK’s AI strategy joins Anthropic amid conflict of interest warning | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Matt Clifford will stay as chair of government funding body for tech projects alongside his senior role at US firm
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Matt Clifford will stay as chair of government funding body for tech projects alongside his senior role at US firm
Content: From Downing Street to Silicon Valley: Matt Clifford played a key role in helping create the UK’s AI Security Institute.Photograph: Tayfun Salci/Zuma Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenFrom Downing Street to Silicon Valley: Matt Clifford played a key role in helping create the UK’s AI Security Institute.Photograph: Tayfun Salci/Zuma Press/AlamyAnthropicArchitect of UK’s AI strategy joins Anthropic amid conflict of interest warningMatt Clifford will stay as chair of government funding body for tech projects alongside his senior role at US firmDan Milmo,Robert BoothandKiran StaceyWed 2 Sep 2026 15.29 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe architect of the UK government’s AI strategy has joined the US startupAnthropicin a senior role a year after stepping down from his Downing Street post.Matt Clifford, a successful tech investor, was appointed as AI opportunities adviser by Keir Starmer last year but resigned from the unpaid role six months later for personal reasons.His move to the company behind the Claude chatbot has raised concern, with the head of the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committee, Chi Onwurah, saying that his decision to remain as chair of the government-backed Aria funding body represented a “clear conflict of interest”.Clifford will be Anthropic’s managing director, international affairs, and will lead the company’s engagement with governments outside the US including in the UK, Europe, Asia-Pacific and India.Anthropic said Clifford would remain as the chair of Aria, the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency, whichfunds “moonshot” science and tech projects. He will also maintain his chair role at Entrepreneurs First, the tech venture capital firm he co-founded.He was appointed chair of Aria in 2022. Anthropic said Clifford would step back from any matter involving the company at Aria. But Onwurah said the roles clashed and she called on the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, to intervene.“His intention to remain as chair of Aria, which spends taxpayer money on cutting-edge research, much of it related to or driven by AI, is a clear conflict of interest and I look forward to the AI minister setting out clear boundaries,” Onwurah said.View image in fullscreenChi Onwurah said Clifford’s intention to remain as the chair of Aria was ‘a clear conflict of interest’.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesAnthropic said its commercial relationship with Aria was handled by a separate team to Clifford’s and he did not make procurement or programme-level spending decision at Aria anyway.“Matt has no involvement in any decision touching Anthropic, and that arrangement has been agreed with Aria and the Department of Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, which is responsible for appointing Aria’s chair,” the company said.The UK government has been approached for comment.Several senior politicians have taken roles at Silicon Valley firms in recent years. The former deputy prime ministerNick Clegg took a senior postat Meta in 2018. Last year the former prime ministerRishi Sunak took advisory rolesat Microsoft and Anthropic, and theex-chancellor George Osborne joined OpenAI.Commenting on his role at Anthropic, Clifford said the most important decisions about AI would be made by companies and governments together. He said: “Countries everywhere want real agency over how this technology is built and used, and my job is to make Anthropic a genuine partner in that – in Europe, Asia and beyond.”Anthropic is preparing for a stock exchange flotation that could value the business at $2tn (£1.5tn).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTom Brake, the chief executive ofUnlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group, said the move showed that “the revolving door is a problem for advisers as much as it is for ministers”.“Taking extensive knowledge obtained within government, about a policy as sensitive as AI, to a private sector company shortly after leaving government gives that company a huge advantage,” said Brake, a Liberal Democrat MP from 1997 to 2019. “Regardless of any safeguards, this weakens the government’s hand when pushing for a precautionary approach towards AI development.”Beeban Kidron, a crossbench peer and prominent critic of the government’s AI policy, said: “We need more independent politics which puts the interests of workers, citizens and society at the forefront of our relationship with the tech sector.”An Anthropic spokesperson said the UK was “one of dozens” of governments Clifford’s team would engage with. “We hire people with expertise and who understand how government works because our work requires it – in every market, not just the UK,” they said.Clifford began his tech career in the private sector. Prior to his government work, he was an established figure on the UK tech scene as a co-founder of Entrepreneurs First, which has helped build tech companies with a combined worth of more than $20bn.Clifford worked with Sunak’s government as his representative to the 2023 AI Safety Summit in the UK, and helped create the organisation that later became the world-leading AI Security Institute.He was appointed as Starmer’s AI adviser after drafting thegovernment’s AI action plan, which supports the creation of AI growth zones to host datacentres and the building of the UK’s own AI models.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest | Global development | The Guardian
description: Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site
Content: Rampal power plant on the Pasur River. A study found high levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples in the nearby Sundarbans wetlands.Photograph: NurPhoto/GettyView image in fullscreenRampal power plant on the Pasur River. A study found high levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples in the nearby Sundarbans wetlands.Photograph: NurPhoto/GettyGlobal developmentBarclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forestBangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage siteSupported byAbout this contentMatthew PearceWed 2 Sep 2026 11.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.02 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people inBangladeshand India.Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, aUnesco world heritage sitemade up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supportshundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”Last November, astudy found elevated levels of mercury and arsenicin water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.View image in fullscreenThe Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people.Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/AlamyMillions of people live in the Sundarbans, and manydepend on the riverand forests for food and other resources.The claimants allege thatBarclaysfailed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank ofIndiabetween 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, includingconcerns raised by Unescoin a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France,refused to support the projectbecause of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentClimate crisisBangladeshIndiaFossil fuelsEnergySouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find | Pesticides | The Guardian
description: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities
Content: A farmer sprays pesticide on sesame fields in Burkina Faso, west Africa.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenA farmer sprays pesticide on sesame fields in Burkina Faso, west Africa.Photograph: AlamyPesticidesAlmost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts findStudy reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalitiesPippa NeillEnvironment reporterWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 22.43 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, astudyhas found.Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned byPesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and eastAfrica.The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was inBurkina Fasoin west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.View image in fullscreenYoung farm workers harvesting cotton in a field near Boromo in Burkina Faso.Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/GettyThe study,publishedin the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action NetworkIndia, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCalifornia bans paraquat, highly toxic herbicide outlawed in more than 70 countriesRead moreGénon Jensen, the executive director of theHealthand Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, withgrowing evidencelinking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it asan occupational disease for farmers.Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the EarthEuropeearlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.Explore more on these topicsPesticidesAgricultureFarmingParkinson's diseasePoisonHealthEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Blackout risk rises as heatwave stresses largest US electric grids | US weather | The Guardian
description: US energy department warns of potential for outages in PJM Interconnection, serving 67 million from DC to Chicago
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US energy department warns of potential for outages in PJM Interconnection, serving 67 million from DC to Chicago
Content: Electrical workers on the street repairing power in Gary, Indiana, on 20 August, more than a week after a deadly storm passes through the area.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APView image in fullscreenElectrical workers on the street repairing power in Gary, Indiana, on 20 August, more than a week after a deadly storm passes through the area.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APUS weatherBlackout risk rises as heatwave stresses largest US electric gridsUS energy department warns of potential for outages in PJM Interconnection, serving 67 million from DC to ChicagoReutersWed 2 Sep 2026 13.16 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe risk ⁠of power outages ⁠is expected to ​escalate across a broad swath of the United States on Wednesday as intense heat will test the capacity of electricity supplies ⁠serving millions of homes and businesses from the midwest through the mid-Atlantic.The US Department of Energy warned of the potential for heightened blackout risks in ⁠the PJM Interconnection, the largest US electric grid, which serves 67 million people in ​a territory stretching fromWashington DCto ‌Chicago.Late on Tuesday night, ‌Chris Wright, the energy secretary, authorized PJM to direct backup generation resources to operate as a ‌last resort before declaring a level three energy emergency alert, which can be one of the last steps before rotating blackouts are ordered.The energy department said the move was part of a plan “to stabilize the Mid-Atlantic grid and mitigate the risk of blackouts”.Tropical Storm Edouard strengthens as it bears down on Texas and LouisianaRead more“Maintaining affordable, reliable, and secure power for hardworking American families and businesses during ‌periods of hot weather is non-negotiable,” Wright said in a statement.Temperatures inChicago, St Louis and Washington DC were expected to rise above 90F (32C) during peak electricity demand.PJM’s “maximum generation emergency” alert in effect early on Wednesday directed generators on planned outages to report how quickly they could return units to service.Meanwhile, the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (Miso), the regional grid operator for 15 US states ⁠in the midwest and the south, predicted peak demand on Wednesday would approach ​record territory at ​about 121 gigawatts. Miso’s all-time high ​is 127.1 GW.Miso warned of tight conditions and increased its normal reserve ​requirement as a ‌buffer against unexpected ​power plant outages and ​transmission line congestion.In the Ozark region of ruralMissouri, the Howell-Oregon Electric Cooperative advised customers to unplug unused chargers and appliances due to the continued extreme heat. Customers also were asked to consider raising their thermostats to reduce air conditioning use.Explore more on these topicsUS weatherEnergyTrump administrationExtreme heatWashington DCChicagoMissourinewsShareReuse this content

title: Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original work
Author: Aaron Mok
Headline: As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original work
Content: Guardian DesignGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.ReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original workSupported byAbout this contentAaron MokWed 2 Sep 2026 13.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.24 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release ofChatGPTin 2022. She went from receiving slow one-off jobs creating logos and packaging to an onslaught of requests asking her to fix versions that were generated by artificial intelligence – from sharpening fuzzy images for printing to turning flawed designs into usable files.By 2025, Lisa, who asked not to be fully named to avoid solicitations, said 90% of her incoming logo and packaging design requests required cleaning up AI-generated content, work that accounted for 60% to 70% of her annual income. But the grind was exhausting. Clients lowballed her;' some AI-generated designs were so flawed that she had to recreate them from scratch and she worried about being complicit in AI-driven copyright infringement. By the end of the year, she began turning those jobs down.“It was just so soulless,” said Lisa, who now focuses on “human-made designs”.Lisa is part of a growing group of creative freelancers being hired to clean up AI slop, a term used to characterize low-quality, AI-generated output. As businesses use tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude to produce marketing copy, illustrations, books and videos, they are hiring creative professionals to humanize AI-generated copy, repair botched images and salvage flawed footage.The work serves as a stopgap in an increasingly challenging job market, supplementing income for those who freelance full-time or on the side. But clients often underestimate the time and skill involved, expecting cleanup to be quick and cheap when it can require as much work as creating something original, freelancers said. And while the high volume of cleanup gigs can be lucrative, freelancers are divided over the trade-off. Some find it tedious and creatively unfulfilling, while others enjoy the challenge. As AI improves, freelancers question how long the demand will last and where they’ll turn once the jobs dry up.For now, demand for AI cleanup work is growing.On Freelancer.com, a contract work platform with more than 88 million users, job listings tagged with phrases such as “correct AI”, “AI hallucination” and “AI error” rose 87% to 10,760 globally between August 2025 and June 2026, according to internal data shared with the Guardian. The jobs were concentrated in graphic design, followed by video editing, proofreading and content writing. Upwork saw AI remediationgigs jump 70%year over year, and Fiverr saw keyword searches for “AI cleanup” services grow more than 20 times between 2023 and 2026, according to data shared with the Guardian.The specter of AI could spell trouble for the creative freelance labor market. Listings for freelance jobs exposed to automation fell 21% in the eight months after ChatGPT launched and image-creation gigs dropped 17% after AI image generators arrived, according to a2025 studypublished in the academic journal Management Science. And those losses have continued, according to a2026 study.Meanwhile, more workers are turning to freelance work as companies cut staff and hire less, intensifying competition. The average project on Freelancer.com drew 54 bids in 2025, up 8% from the year before, according to the site’sannual report.But as companies cut costs, they’re changing the nature of freelance assignments, from requests for creative work to sprucing up AI output. Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, said the cleanup work is often commissioned by small companies and entrepreneurs using AI to produce a first pass, only to run into problems they don’t have the expertise to solve.“[AI output] needs a human to turn it into something polished that can actually be used,” he said. The time and money saved on the first draft can be eaten up by the “incredibly time-consuming” work of preparing it for commercial use.The rise of the AI cleanup crewsFor some freelancers, cleanup is taking up a growing share of their workload and traditional creative projects are becoming harder to find.Todd Van Linda, a full-time freelance illustrator in Florida, began taking AI cleanup gigs in 2023 as his usual work drawing illustrations, video game art and architectural plans became less steady. The work typically involves filtering out visual noise, improving resolution, and hunting for glitches like an extra toe.“Money”, Van Linda said of his motivation. “The jobs were there to be done.”Though some clients expect AI cleanup to cost less than original work, Van Linda won’t lower his rates. When one prospective client offered about $500 to repair 13 to 15 AI-generated illustrations for a children’s book, with the expectation that each should take about 15 minutes, he turned it down. He said projects can take between a few hours of work to days depending on the scope. His rate is $65 an hour and “doesn’t go down from there”, he said.For Kym Dunbar, a freelance writer and editor based in Australia, AI cleanup now accounts for about 60% of her workload, as writing work like blogs and website copy have dwindled. As a result, Dunbar said her monthly earnings from writing original content have fallen to roughly a third of what she made during the pandemic.Dunbar stumbled into cleanup work in 2024, when a client asked her to revise an AI-generated article. She quickly learned to spot recurring problems, from repetitive language and awkward paragraph structures to a lack of emotional nuance. Since then, she has worked on about 40 AI-generated nonfiction books, longform articles and technical papers.“There’s a lot less good projects available for writers and editors these days,” Dunbar said.But “cleanup” can understate how much work is involved.Nathan McConnell, a multimedia editor who freelances on top of his full-time job, started editing AI-generated videos in 2023. His work has ranged from removing reflections from AI real estate videos to fixing robotic voiceovers and malformed 3D models. The requests have increased from two or three projects in 2023 to eight to 10 so far this year, he said.One client brought him roughly 100 AI-generated images of humanoid animals for a tarot deck riddled with extra fingers, two left feet and other mistakes. McConnell spent two to three hours repairing each image in Photoshop, expecting the project to take nearly two weeks to finish. But after making the first 10 cards, he called the project off because of health issues and constant changes requested from his “persnickety” client.Not everything that lands in McConnell’s inbox can be saved, he said. That could look like videos where the physics feel off, like shadows falling the wrong way, or animations that repurpose another creator’s work without permission.“I’ve told a client before that it’s ‘too’ slop,” McConnell said. “There’s no way I can fix this.”While McConnell and Van Linda would rather make original work, not everyone finds fixing AI outputs dispiriting. Dunbar considers it “interesting” and “challenging”, and takes satisfaction in turning a weak draft into polished prose.What troubles her is that people increasingly see AI not as a tool, but as the “be-all and end-all” of the creative process.“I just feel it’s a shame we need to do it,” Dunbar said.Slop cleanup jobs may not lastIt’s unclear whether cleaning up AI-generated slop will remain a viable source of work.Dunbar isn’t convinced it will. She believes much of the work humanizing AI could dry up within five to 10 years as models improve and allow businesses to generate usable content themselves.McConnell sees it differently, arguing that AI still needs to be “babysat” to catch mistakes an untrained eye might miss, from logos that violate brand guidelines to objects that appear and disappear in videos. “We need people [to fix] problems that AI is creating,” he said.But Van Linda is already creating a different path. After he stopped taking AI cleanup gigs late last year, he has seen more clients, some of whom have been dissatisfied with AI, seeking original, hand-drawn work.“Quite frankly, this kind of thing has gotten extremely distasteful to me,” he said about AI cleanup work.Though Lisa, the freelance graphic designer, updated her profile to say she no longer works with AI-generated images, she still gets requests to edit them. She occasionally takes cleanup gigs for clients who come to her after getting poor results with AI. But some clients “straight up lie” and pass off the images as original creations.“They say ‘I don’t use AI,’ but there’s a “[Google] Gemini logo on the bottom,” she said.But just in case AI makes her job obsolete, she has a plan. Lisa has begun returning to the canvases, watercolors and other physical art she practiced before she pursued a career in graphic design. She predicts that within “another year or two”, AI will be able to do logo and packaging design as well as she can, leaving only “the best of the best” able to make a living.“I don’t know if I’m good enough to survive the digital stuff,” she said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedChatGPTOpenAIfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Britain is OK with public ownership, but only by foreign powers. Why? | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: Arthur Downing, author of Power and the People: A History of British Energy, says all-encompassing rapid transition will need a mutualised system
Author: Maya Goodfellow
Headline: Arthur Downing, author of Power and the People: A History of British Energy, says all-encompassing rapid transition will need a mutualised system
Content: A British Gas engineer services a gas-powered lamp near the Houses of Parliament, London.Photograph: Daniel Leal/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA British Gas engineer services a gas-powered lamp near the Houses of Parliament, London.Photograph: Daniel Leal/AFP/Getty ImagesEnergy industryBritain is OK with public ownership, but only by foreign powers. Why?Arthur Downing, author of Power and the People: A History of British Energy, says all-encompassing rapid transition will need a mutualised systemMaya GoodfellowWed 2 Sep 2026 08.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 16.37 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHave you ever wondered why it is that most houses in the UK are reliant on gas boilers? Not what’s stopping more people from replacing them with heat pumps, but instead why and how the gas boiler became so ubiquitous in the first place?Arthur Downing, the author of thenew bookPower and the People: A History of British Energy, can tell you exactly why. “We only have boilers in our houses because of a state-owned enterprise that went into everybody’s home and installed natural gas-suitable appliances at no direct cost,” he says. The nationalised gas industry of the 1940s to the 1980s, which oversaw this huge project, was for three decades one of the “most dynamic, innovative, efficient industries in Britain”, Downing says. Yet few of us would use these terms to describe it as such now.Instead, Britain’s electricity and gas industries are “fragile, fragmented, comically complicated and hopelessly dependent on imported fossil fuels”, Downing writes. On top of that, as consumers, we are facingsoaring energy billsamid a cost of living crisis.View image in fullscreenCrowds admiring the electric lights on Victoria Docks, London, in the 19th century. From El Museo Popular, published 1887.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesUnearthing how this happened, by exploring the history of Britain’s energy industry, is the subject of Downing’s book. It’s one he lives and breathes – by day, Downing works as the director of strategy at OctopusEnergy, the UK’s largest supplier of energy, but the book itself is written in a personal capacity.Central to his argument is that this is a history a lot of us, even people working in the industry now, know little to nothing about. Yet it is instructive for the present, Downing argues, showing why we have the system we do – and, importantly, how we might change it for the better.This summer’s string of climate crisis-drivenheatwavesmakes his book feel even more urgent. Although the UK has reducedgreenhouse gas emissionsby 50% compared with 1990 levels, Downing explains: “The second half of the journey will be much harder than the first. All the low-hanging fruits have been picked, like deindustrialising and switching from coal to gas.”View image in fullscreenThe wind turbines of the Burbo Bank windfarm in Liverpool Bay, off New Brighton beach.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesYet debates about the energy system often happen behind closed doors, and part of his aim was to make it more intelligible. An economic historian by training and with encyclopaedic knowledge about energy, both shine through in the book, which charts how the crisis came into being.His argument is straightforward: ownership matters. “Who owned and controlled the means of making, moving, and selling energy shaped which technologies were developed, what infrastructure got built and the extent to which citizens and consumers benefited,” he writes. Between 1926 and 1979, for instance, state-owned enterprises built huge infrastructure – from hydroelectric plants to power stations inside mountains – faster and cheaper than Britain’s private sector companies today. The system has been privatised since the start of the 1980s, and despite the mess it’s currently in, the orthodoxy tends to still be that private is always better than public ownership – cheaper, more efficient and more creative. Downing does not agree.“I tend to view things from the perspective of political economy – the institutions, the ownership models, the organisations and the people make the system,” says Downing, who speaks with energising enthusiasm and expertise. “For me, the technology is interesting, but it is very strange to think of the [energy] system composed of inanimate objects, as if these things have agency and they don’t. They’re only there because of [human decisions].”View image in fullscreenThe work of the Central Electricity Board: a general view of a power station control room, 1945.Photograph: piemags/archive/military/AlamyDowning’s book charts four phases over the last 200 years, each given a chapter of its own. In the first phase, from the late 1880s to the 1920s, ownership of Britain’s energy system was overwhelmingly public and municipal. This meant that even where private companies were involved, they were highly local, embedded in regional networks, and with municipal authorities making the decisions about how to plan and coordinate the gas and electricity system. The second phase, 1920-1945, saw government become a major owner and operator of some energy infrastructure. The third, from 1945-1979, saw energy nearly completely nationalised. And the final, before the mess of the system we have today, was characterised by almost total privatisation between 1979 and 2010.View image in fullscreenArthur Downing says the British energy system is now a ‘dysfunctional hybrid’ of public and private.Photograph: Verso BooksAlthough 1,500 energy entities were brought into two state-owned enterprises after the second world war, nationalisation didn’t begin in the 1940s but rather started in that second phase. In fact, in 1926, it was the Conservative prime minister, Stanley Baldwin, who set up the Central Electricity Board (CEB) – a state-owned public corporation that built the first National Grid. Unlike now, this was done on time and at cost.Downing says the energy system we have now is a zombie – a “dysfunctional hybrid” of public and private. For example, it remains privately owned but feeds off state subsidies, meaning few benefits of either model but most of the costs in that it is expensive and inefficient.In February, Engie, the electric utility company in which the French government is the largest shareholder,bought UK Power Networks(UKPN), which owns and maintains electricity cables in the south and east of England, from a conglomerate. On that very day, Downing points out, 10-year bond borrowing rates of the French state went down and the stock value of Engie went up, meaning every French citizen got a bit richer. It didn’t play out the way the British media often claims – the bond markets didn’t blink and the government didn’t collapse.Downing suggests Andy Burnham’s early announcement of aVAT cut on energy billswas a good first move. But if he could ask Burnham to do anything else, what would it be? “Shift the focus from producers to consumers, from investors to citizens,” he says. This would include getting bills down by taking off levies, which are added to fund environmental and social programmes. But it would also mean looking at questions of ownership.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Public ownership was an extraordinary tool for building infrastructure at pace while delivering benefits for citizens,” Downing says. “It can be again.”View image in fullscreenElectric signs outside the London Pavilion in Piccadilly Circus, July 1929.Photograph: J Gaiger/Getty ImagesDowning doesn’t want a return to a 1940s-style system. Instead, he advocates for a mutualised system, meaning neither nationalised nor privatised. “The old labels don’t fit,” he explains. “The principle is that energy should be built around mutually beneficial relationships between capital, citizens and the state, with ownership and decision-making spread out rather than concentrated.” What does that look like in practice? “Public corporations owning the networks and part of generation, councils and community schemes taking real ownership stakes in local infrastructure, and households owning solar, batteries and electric vehicles and being paid properly for the flexibility those provide. Citizens as owners of the system, not only customers of it.”The state would become even more involved in regulation, because regulatory institutions make the system more complex. For example, Ofgem is tasked with setting the price cap and assessing the components of bills but in many instances it doesn’t actually control the costs that are accruing.View image in fullscreenAn all-electric signal box depicted on a Churchman’s cigarette card, from a series titled Modern Wonders, 1938.Photograph: Print Collector/Getty ImagesMarkets would still be involved. Natural monopolies – in networks and onshore transmission, for instance – would be publicly owned, while markets would stay for retail, electrical vehicle charging, home solar and batteries. “Public ownership and markets are not opposites,” Downing says. “The Nordic countries introduced competition in [power] generation and retail shortly after Britain and kept extensive public ownership. China is running markets at huge scale within a publicly owned system. The US has the longest tradition of private ownership and some of the least competitive markets in the world.”To make such a change would require bold political intervention. Maybe the local aspect, which is a big part of Downing’s proposal, appeals to Burnham’s talk ofdevolution, nationalisation and reindustrialisation.Energy transitions are rare and protracted, usually taking around a century, Downing says, and if this were to happen, it would be the “first all-encompassing rapid energy transition in human history”. His book suggests it is possible. We just have to reject the British orthodoxy that says the state is useless in a way private companies never are.“We have a strange situation where we are OK with public ownership, just not by our own state,” he says.Power and the People by Arthur Downing (Verso Books, £25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.View image in fullscreenParliament Square, London, circa 1906, showing early electric lamps.Photograph: Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsEnergy industryEnergyEnergy billsConsumer affairsOil and gas companiesGasHousehold billsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This data has helped fight workplace discrimination for 60 years. The Trump administration plans to delete it | Trump administration | The Guardian
