The 19-year-old American was later seriously injured in a crash during the race.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEzra Caudell (left) rides past the Philadelphia Museum of Art during the men’s Philadelphia Cycling Classic on Sunday. The 19-year-old American was later seriously injured in a crash during the race.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesCyclingUS cyclist Ezra Caudell hospitalized with ‘multi-system trauma’ after Philadelphia crash19-year-old remains hospitalized after Sunday crashCaudell receiving care for ‘multi-system trauma’Lotto-Intermarché yet to update on Milan MentenGuardian sportWed 2 Sep 2026 18.50 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.56 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmerican cyclist Ezra Caudell remains hospitalized with “multi-system trauma” after being seriously injured in a crash during Sunday’sPhiladelphia Cycling Classic, his team said on Tuesday.The 19-year-old Modern Adventure Pro Cycling rider was involved in a collision with Belgium’s Milan Menten of Lotto-Intermarché early in the men’s race. Caudell was knocked unconscious in the crash and both riders were taken to local hospitals for treatment, accordingto the Philadelphia Inquirer.Modern Adventureposted an updateon Caudell’s condition to social media on Tuesday evening, two days after the accident.Can the Philly Classic ignite another golden age of US road cycling?Read more“Ezra remains hospitalized and is actively receiving care for multi-system trauma he sustained as a result of his crash at thePhiladelphiaCycling Classic,” the team said.“He has an incredible team working diligently and family at his bedside. We are grateful for the thoughts and ongoing outpouring of support.”No further details were provided about the nature of Caudell’s injuries or his prognosis.Philadelphia mayor Cherelle Parkersaid after Sunday’s racethat city officials were monitoring the condition of two cyclists who had required hospital treatment after the crash.“City first responders, including our Fire Department, on-site medical personnel, and my leadership team responded immediately to the incident, and I am grateful for their service,” Parker said. “Our thoughts and prayers are with both cyclists, their families and teams.”Lotto-Intermarché have not publicly provided details about Menten’s condition.Caudell has emerged as one of the most promising young American road cyclists. The Georgia native finished fourth in the under-23 road race at the US national championships in June before placing seventh against the country’s leading professionals in the elite men’s road race the following day.The teenager has also gained experience in Europe this season. He was the youngest rider in the field at Paris-Roubaix in April, finishing 121st in his debut at the celebrated one-day classic, and also competed at the Arctic Race of Norway and Tour of Denmark.Caudell rides for Modern Adventure ProCycling, the American team founded by former Tour de France stage winner George Hincapie. His teammate Ben Oliver finished seventh in Philadelphia on Sunday.The Philadelphia Cycling Classicreturned last weekendafter a decade-long absence, reviving one of the best known races in American cycling. The course took riders through central Philadelphia and along the Schuylkill river beforethe traditional climb through Manayunk.Explore more on these topicsCyclingPhiladelphiaShareReuse this content

title: Somerset dominate Glamorgan; Yorkshire struggle against Surrey: county cricket, day one – as it happened | County Championship | The Guardian
description: Hampshire make U-turn over Scott Kuggeleijn signing after fan backlash as Warwickshire add to their troubles
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: Hampshire make U-turn over Scott Kuggeleijn signing after fan backlash as Warwickshire add to their troubles
Content: 5h ago20.42 BSTRoundup: Somerset steal a march on rivalsTanya AldredIt was slip-catching heaven at Taunton, withSomerset’sfielders gobbling seven inGlamorgan’s first innings, and James Rew scooping up the rest. Ben Kellaway was the only man to pass 50. Somerset’s innings started under lights, but a milky sun eventually emerged to light the way and allow Somerset to steal a march on their Championship rivals, whose matches were curtailed by rain.Charlie Bennett’s pain was Jamie Porter’s gain at Chelmsford after the young seamer limped off after three overs. To a background of autumnal slate, Porter then grabbed three for 32 forEssexagainstSussex, who chose to bat and progressed in fits and starts. Sam Cook pocketed the 500th dismissal of his professional career.At the Oval,Yorkshirelimped along from the ignominy of one for three, which included an elegant flying catch by Ben Foakes to dismiss Will Luxton for a duck. James Wharton and Matthew Revis added 89, butYorkshirethen lost four for 21, including Jonny Bairstow, who stamped and delivered a pitch-perfect slip catch to Ollie Pope. Dan Worrall bowled beautifully for three for 24.After making a sudden U-turn on the selection of Scott Kuggeleijn, relegation-threatenedHampshirewere in trouble on the field as well. Rob Yates and Dan Mousley both embroidered half-centuries as Warwickshire piled on 141 for one between the showers.David Bedingham passed 1,000 runs for the season in the process of an elegant fifty againstNorthants. There had been rebuilding to do afterDurhamslumped to 16 for two, a wonder ball by Luke Procter plucking out Ben McKinney’s middle and off stumps and pinging them in different directions, while Will Rhodes was brilliantly run out by James Sales. Meanwhile, Division Two promotion rivalsKenthad a so-so day againstWorcestershire, losing five for 25 in the evening session. Daniel Bell-Drummond pinged 52.After two months on the sidelines with a dodgy calf, Jimmy Anderson showedLancashirewhat they’d been missing by reducingMiddlesexto 20 for two. But Max Holden and Leus du Plooy steadied the ship on a damp, dark day at Merchant Taylors’ School.Gloucestershire’sdismal season continued, after choosing to bat and being reduced to 62 for five againstDerbyshire. Only James Bracey, flameproof boots on the burning deck, made more than 10. There were two wickets for Shoaib Bashir. Only 10.3 overs were possible at Trent Bridge, butNottscaptain Haseeb Hameed, who has struggled for form this season, stroked six morale-boosting fours.ShareUpdated at20.43 BST

title: Dream team or stuff of nightmares? Rams’ bold moves could go either way | Los Angeles Rams | The Guardian
description: LA added Myles Garrett and brought Aaron Donald out of retirement to create the NFL’s most menacing defense. A Super Bowl trip still isn’t a guarantee
Author: Doug Farrar
Headline: LA added Myles Garrett and brought Aaron Donald out of retirement to create the NFL’s most menacing defense. A Super Bowl trip still isn’t a guarantee
Content: Aaron Donald signed a one-year deal to return to the Los Angeles Rams.Photograph: Elaine Thompson/APView image in fullscreenAaron Donald signed a one-year deal to return to the Los Angeles Rams.Photograph: Elaine Thompson/APLos Angeles RamsDream team or stuff of nightmares? Rams’ bold moves could go either wayLA added Myles Garrett and brought Aaron Donald out of retirement to create the NFL’s most menacing defense. A Super Bowl trip still isn’t a guaranteeDoug FarrarWed 2 Sep 2026 10.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 10.03 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast Saturday night,NFLNetwork premiered the 2025 edition of America’s Game, the annual NFL Films-produced documentary on the reigning Super Bowl champions, this time starring the Seattle Seahawks.Less than 24 hours later, the Los Angeles Rams announced thatthey had lured Aaron Donaldout of retirement and signed him to a one-year, $20m contract that could reach $30m with incentives.This may or may not be a coincidence.All-time great Aaron Donald comes out of retirement to rejoin stacked LA RamsRead moreThe Seahawks and the Rams were the NFL’s two best teams in the 2025 season; of that there is little doubt. They faced each other three times – twice in the regular season and then, in the NFC championship game – and the final point total in those three games was 88-85 in Seattle’s favor. Seattle’s 31-27 NFC championship win was far more competitive than Super Bowl LX, which saw the Seahawksbeat upon the New England Patriots 29-13 in a game less competitive than the score indicates.While the Seahawks spent the offseason celebrating their championship and, in the words of head coach Mike Macdonald, “running it forward”, the Rams underwent a defensive transformation the likes of which you rarely see in one year – if ever. They traded multiple draft picks, including a 2026 first-round selection, for Kansas City Chiefs cornerback Trent McDuffie, and signed him to a four-year, $124m contract extension with $100m guaranteed. To finish a much-needed makeover of a vulnerable cornerback group, they signed free agent Jaylen Watson, McDuffie’s estimable bookend in Kansas City, to a three-year, $51m contract.As if that wasn’t enough, on 1 June, the Ramstradedtheir 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 second-round pick and a 2029 third-round pick, plus edge-rusher Jared Verse, to the Cleveland Browns for edge-rusher Myles Garrett. The 30-year-old is the best pass rusher of his era; he’s coming off a 2025 campaign in which he set pro football’s official single-season sack record at 23.Donald’s subsequent return seems like overkill. And the effect on opposing offenses could be severe. PerESPN Analytics/NFL Next Gen Stats, Garrett and Donald rank first and second in pass rush win rate since 2017, and that’swithDonald missing the last two seasons. Add these future first-ballot Hall of Famers to a Rams defensive line that already rebuilt itself after Donald’s retirement, and those poor opposing offenses may have no way to counter the formidable combination of pressure and coverage.View image in fullscreenMyles Garrett joined the Rams this offseason in a blockbuster trade after a lengthy stint with the Browns.Photograph: Jeff Dean/APGarrett and Donald have been among the most double-teamed defenders throughout their careers. Now, who do you double, and who do you leave on an island, putting your quarterback at severe risk? There is no right answer. Even if you double both players, that leaves openings for Byron Young, Kobie Turner and Braden Fiske – all great quarterback disruptors the Rams developed Moneyball-style after Donald’s first retirement, when they had toreplaceone irreplaceable player in the aggregate.That’s the idealized version of the story.The less palatable version for the Rams is … well, more like a nightmare. What if this “Dream Team” goes the way of the 2004 New York Yankees, the 2007 New England Patriots, the 2011 Philadelphia Eagles, the 2011–12/2012–13 Los Angeles Lakers, or other “perfectly assembled” teams who ultimately fell short of their goals?The Rams’ biggest potential speedbump is not on defense. It’s the health of quarterback Matthew Stafford, who will turn 39 a week before this season’s Super Bowl. Stafford was healthy and at his best in 2025; that’s how he bagged his first NFLMVPaward.Including the playoffs, Stafford threw 52 touchdown passes last season. But in the previous three seasons from 2022 to 2024, as he dealt with injuries that had him thinking of retirement more than once, he totalled 60 combined. With Stetson Bennett and rookie Ty Simpson, the Rams do not have a backup plan that is Super Bowl-conversant.Per Sumer Sports, since 2022, the Rams’ on/off splits regarding Stafford are terrifying.With Stafford on the field (3,517 plays):5.69 yards per play+0.035 EPA per play155 offensive touchdowns35 interceptions on 1,940 pass attemptsWithout Stafford on the field (703 plays):4.56 yards per play-0.106 EPA per play20 offensive touchdowns10 interceptions on 330 pass attemptsThere’s also the possibility that receiverPuka Nacuaand left tackle Alaric Jackson, two of the offense’s most important players not named Matthew Stafford, could face suspensions this season for off-field transgressions.NFL preseason storylines: are the Rams inevitable and will the Pats survive scandal?Read moreWhile Donald may be the best defensive tackle in the history of professional football, coming back after two full seasons away from the game – at the age of 35 – is an outlier of outliers.Donald has become famousfor keeping himself in amazing shape during his hiatus, but gym-shape and football-shape are two entirely different things.“I’ve kind of been in a football mindset the last 14 weeks,” Donald said in the press conference officially announcing his return. “If anything, it’s just getting back on that grass and knocking the rust off as far as playing football again … working my eyes, getting a feel for the game, certain reaction things that made me who I am.“But do I feel like I can play at a high level? Yes. Do I feel like I can still be myself? 100%. If I didn’t feel like that, I wouldn’t be here.”That’s all well and good, but history has not been kind to 35-year-old defensive tackles. The only such player who amassed more than 10 sacks in a seasonwasSteve McMichael for the 1992 Chicago Bears, and McMichael wasn’t coming off a long layoff – he had nine sacks the year before. Donald was above McMichael’s level at his peak, but this is still no sure thing. “Mean” Joe Greene of the legendary Pittsburgh Steelers dynasty teams of the 1970s, the rare individual who could knock Donald off the “Greatest DT of All Time” mountain,started seven games and had just 4.5 sacks in his age 35 year of 1981. Again, without that two-year layoff.When you’re relying on gamechangers on the wrong end of the age curve, any regression can hit with the force of a Donald/Garrett combined quarterback sack.On paper, there are all kinds of reasons to think of the Rams as the prohibitive favorite to win the Super Bowl. But as the old cliche tells us, games are not played on paper – they’re played on the field. And there’s a lot of football to be played before we’ll know how all this activity actually works. Ask the other Dream Teams who never quite made their dreams come true.Explore more on these topicsLos Angeles RamsNFLUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Deadline-day shambles leaves Everton and David Moyes fighting the odds again | Everton | The Guardian
description: From accepting a bid for Armstrong to Balogun walking away, TFG has shown an amateurish and unambitious approach
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: From accepting a bid for Armstrong to Balogun walking away, TFG has shown an amateurish and unambitious approach
Content: Everton’s owners have challenged David Moyes to go further with fewer resources.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEverton’s owners have challenged David Moyes to go further with fewer resources.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockEvertonDeadline-day shambles leaves Everton and David Moyes fighting the odds againFrom accepting a bid for Armstrong to collapse of Balogun deal, TFG has shown an amateurish and unambitious approachAndy HunterWed 2 Sep 2026 19.02 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 21.16 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo be placed in the same bracket as owners whose lack of ambition, lack of resources and/or incompetence has contributed to the longest trophy drought in Everton’s history, particularly 20 months into a reign that has accompanied the move to a glittering new stadium and the clearing of onerous debt, should be cause for considerable discomfort and embarrassment at The Friedkin Group (TFG) on Wednesday. The slight on Everton’s owner is neither unkind nor unfair. At least Farhad Moshiri had a go before the taps were turned off.TFG may have restored financial stability to Everton after the near-ruinous chaos of Moshiri’s final years and his attempts to sell to 777 Partners but its reputation as “winners” – as the club’s chief executive, Angus Kinnear, labelled his American employers – has been shredded in the space of four days. The description always appeared generous given its approach to the summer transfer window, part two of Everton’s strategic rebuild according to Kinnear. But from accepting Nottingham Forest’s £35m bid for Harrison Armstrong on Saturday morning to Folarin Balogun walking away from a £40m move from Monaco on Tuesday night, and more in between, TFG has positioned itself as just another Everton owner unable or unwilling to realise the club’s potential and to give an expectant fanbase grounds for optimism.Balogun pulled out of Everton move over handling of his medical, claim MonacoRead moreEvertonians hoped for an overdue departure when TFG acquired the club in December 2024 and proceeded to refinance damaging loans and the long-term repayment costs of Hill Dickinson Stadium. The shambles of deadline day, however, was all too familiar and has caused serious damage to its standing among supporters.David Moyes kept his counsel throughout pre-season as Everton spent £16.5m on Hayden Hackney, rising to £25m for last season’s Championship player of the year, £18m on each of Merlin Röhl and Tyrique George, who he had on loan last season, £7m on Christian Nørgaard and swapped Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. The most Everton paid up front for a player all summer would prove to be £18m.When Moyes did eventually speak in public it was to stress, repeatedly, the need for Everton to sign more players, more quality and to keep their best talents. At the end of last season he had 22 outfield players at his disposal. At the start of deadline day he had 20 outfield players. By the end of transfer deadline day he had 18.That total includes one striker, Thierno Barry, no back-up for either full-back and, strictly speaking given that Ainsley Maitland-Niles did not start out in the position, no natural right-back. Evertonsold their most creative asset, Iliman Ndiaye, to Manchester City in a below-market price £65m deal despite the Senegal international having three years on his contract. They sold Beto, their only striking alternative to Barry, before securing a replacement and were left desperately scrambling around for one when Balogun’s medical went awry.View image in fullscreenEverton have sold Iliman Ndiaye (left) and brought in Merlin Röhl (right) for £18m in the summer transfer window.Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty ImagesManchester United said no to a loan offer for Joshua Zirkzee that arrived a few hours before the deadline. Tammy Abraham said no to leaving Aston Villa. Finally Balogun, having arrived later than scheduled for his medical and seen Everton renegotiate the terms of his fee with Monaco, compounded the chaos by also saying no despite signing a deal sheet shortly before 11pm. Barry looked out of his depth for much of his debut season in the Premier League. Now he is the precious commodity that Everton cannot afford to lose.Kinnear, perhaps in response to Moyes raising concerns over Everton’s business for the first time, gave several local interviews two weeks ago that painted a rosy picture of the club’s finances, transfer strategy and ambition. Subsequent events have cost him credibility on every count. The chief executive also got his manager’s back up by claiming TFG regarded not qualifying for Europe last season as “a failure” and that the squad is better placed to sustain a European challenge while striving to end Everton’s 31-year wait for a trophy.Moyes’s team face-planted during last season’s run-in, failing to win any of their last seven games when Europe was in reach. He has been challenged to go further with fewer resources. An added annoyance for Moyes and supporters is that Everton have started this season brightly, only to be surrounded by problems entirely of the hierarchy’s making.It was Kinnear who implemented a new “senior leadership team” at Everton and the move away from a director of football model. The team consists of the technical director, Nick Cox, director of scouting and recruitment, James Smith, director of football strategy and analytics, Chris Howarth and head of player trading, Nick Hammond. Moyes is also part of the leadership team, although he has appeared to be on a different page this summer. There has been sensible, cost-effective recruitment for Hackney, Röhl and Johnson but the end to the window invites criticism of the leadership team’s effectiveness and expertise. It resembles a case of too many chiefs and no clear direction, especially given some of the targets Everton went for in the final days.View image in fullscreenHarrison Armstrong is Everton’s first academy prospect to establish himself in the first team since Anthony Gordon.Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty ImagesThecollapse of the Balogun dealhas caused turmoil at Everton but a player getting cold feet over a move or a medical jeopardising a deal can happen. It is events under Everton’s control, and decisions they have taken, that are of greater concern. TFG’s decision to accept Forest’s offer for Armstrong, the first academy prospect to graduate through the ranks and establish himself since Anthony Gordon six years ago, was the first indication that Everton were struggling to meet the new squad cost ratios. So much for a new financial era at Hill Dickinson.TFG merits some credit for listening to supporters over theproposed sale of Armstrongand pulling the plug. To then consider selling Ndiaye to Tottenham for £60m and spending £35m on Richarlison, however, was another alarming sign.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEverton have been looking for a right-back since Moyes returned to the club in January 2025, and needed one before then. Moyes wanted Guéla Doué from Strasbourg but the 23-year-old was deemed too expensive. Doué joined Bayer Leverkusen on deadline day for £25.7m. At least five alternatives were explored before Everton, their £9m deal for Fulham’s Kenny Tete having fallen through, signed Maitland-Niles as the £4.3m answer to one glaring problem.A bigger weakness lay up front. No Premier League club of serious intent would enter a second season with their striking options limited to Beto and Barry. An upgrade was essential. Instead, Everton downgraded. So much for the leadership team’s vision and the owner’s ambition.Everton are the lowest net spenders in the Premier League over the past five years and, more by accident than design, ended this summer making a net profit of £25m on transfers. TFG committed £78m on signings in a summer where, by the calculations of the football finance expert Kieran Maguire, the average spend per Premier League club was £181m. Everton’s outlay does not include the significant cost of re-signing Jack Grealish on loan.TFG’s frugal spending and efficiency drive – redundancies were made behind the scenes at Everton this summer – has fuelled talk of Dan Friedkin and co looking to sell the club. However, the owners have allocated £40m to cover the compensation payable to Burnley should Everton fail in their appeal against the outcome of a profitability and sustainability breach case, and are investing almost £14m in infrastructure projects at Hill Dickinson, Goodison Park and Finch Farm training ground.What is certain is the anger TFG would face if they attended Sunday’s home game against Manchester United. Dan Friedkin has yet to attend a match at Hill Dickinson, where some season ticket prices were increased by up to 10% this season.The Everton fans’ forum and Everton fan advisory board issued statements on Wednesday criticising the club’s amateurish, unambitious approach to the transfer window. The 1878s, the group of volunteers responsible for the impressive tifos and banners at the stadium, has withdrawn its support for the foreseeable future. “We do not feel that our fanbase’s ambitions and the club’s ambitions align right now – what happened yesterday has proved that even more,” the group said.It looks a long road back to acceptance for TFG, Kinnear and Everton’s senior leadership team.Explore more on these topicsEvertonDavid MoyesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Premier League transfer talking points: three things we learned from the data | Premier League | The Guardian
description: After record spending in the transfer market, England’s top clubs have widened the gap to their European counterparts
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: After record spending in the transfer market, England’s top clubs have widened the gap to their European counterparts
Content: Clockwise from top left: Elliot Anderson, Bradley Barcola, Ezri Konsa, Johan Manzambi.Composite: GettyView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: Elliot Anderson, Bradley Barcola, Ezri Konsa, Johan Manzambi.Composite: GettyPremier LeagueAnalysisPremier League transfer talking points: three things we learned from the dataAndrew BeasleyAfter record spending in the transfer market, England’s top clubs have widened the gap to their European counterpartsWed 2 Sep 2026 16.29 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePremier League clubs have invested more than £3.4bn in players this summer, an increase of 11.9% on last year. There are three aspects of this enormous spending worthy of closer scrutiny.Priorities on player age have changedPremier League clubs are spending less on players in the peak 24-27 age band even though those players are increasingly the core of their selections.As recently as 2021-22, 40% of minutes were taken by players at least 28 years old at the start of the season. That proportion has dropped each year, reaching 26.6% in 2025-26. The reliance on veterans has declined. The bulk of their lost minutes went to players aged between 24 and 27, which is now the dominant age band.Chart showing percentage of Premier League minutes played by different age ranges since 2021-22The spend on that key demographic has fallen by 23% since last summer though. Without Manchester Citysigning the 25-year-old Enzo Fernández for a British transfer record-equalling £125mshortly before the window closed, the drop would have been even greater.Younger players account for some of the shortfall but a surprisingly high slice of it has gone towards older footballers. The Premier League has invested £323.3m in players aged at least 28, only around £50m shy of the outlay on this age range in the previous three summers combined (£370.5m). Their proportion of the total has not been as high for four years.Chart showing percentage of Premier League summer transfer spend by different age ranges since 2022How much this increased spending on veterans affects the playing time figures depends in part on the selection decisions of Mikel Arteta. Arsenal signed two 28-year-olds for a combined £126m:Bruno Guimarães (£75m)andEzri Konsa (£51m). Transfermarkt considers them to be the most expensive central midfielder and centre-back respectively aged over 27 in history.The three most expensive Premier League signings of the summer before Fernández – Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson and Bradley Barcola – were 23 when their deals were completed. With only slightly less spent collectively on footballers who are 22, clubs have gone hard for players on the verge of entering their peak years rather than those in them.Chart showing Premier League summer spending by player age in 2025 and 2026The Premier League is becoming a closed shopPerhaps the most notable aspect of transfer spending this summer is how much of it has remained within English football. Fourteen of the 19 signings that cost Premier League clubs at least £50m were made from within the division or from relegated West Ham. Where 30.2% of spending remained in the Premier League in summer 2022, the figure hit 39.3% this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTransfer window verdict: how every Premier League club faredRead moreWith the combined outlay growing by almost £1.5bn in that period, what appears a relatively small percentage shift becomes a significant figure in the accounts. The squad cost ratio rules are unlikely to stem this flow either, because clubs will be happy to sell for inflated fees that can almost only come from within the division.Barcola was the oldest of the five costliest signings from overseas, with Matias Fernandez-Pardo and Jérémy Jacquet (aged 21), Johan Manzambi (aged 20) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (aged 18) completing the set. The Premier League is able to retain its top stars, its clubs exchanging them among themselves, while having the funds to hoover up the most exciting young talent from elsewhere.Squad-building trends may be evolving in the Premier League, but the money is here and a significant portion of it is not going anywhere else. English football is starting to become an enclosed ecosystem.The rest of Europe cannot keep upVery few clubs across Europe come close to competing financially. The Premier League features a match this weekend between the top two teams in Europe for net spend and it isn’t Arsenal v Chelsea. Liverpool’s trip to Ipswich takes the honour.The promoted sides have invested enormous sums to try to be competitive. They have all played League One football within the previous eight seasons, yet Real Madrid are the only club from another country with a higher net spend than Hull or Coventry.Chart showing the top 10 clubs for net spend in summer 2026. Nine of them are from the Premier LeagueThe cream of the Premier League crop can probably only move within England. The transfer fee for Rogers (£117m) or Anderson (£116m) was above the net spend of 75 of the 76 top-flight clubs in France, Germany, Italy and Spain. Milan narrowly spent more than the cost of Sandro Tonali (£92.5m) net, but no other side beyond Madrid from mainland Europe did. Most non-English sides would have to have a clearout of talent to raise funds for a single elite player from the Premier League, which isn’t practical.This financial dominance can be seen in continental competitions. Five English clubs have featured in the past eight Champions League finals, as many teams as the rest of Europe has provided in that time. The Premier League has supplied three of the past four Europa League finalists and three of the past four Conference League winners. This is unlikely to change when relegation favourites in England can outspend all but the very richest clubs overseas.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTransfer windowanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Nate Boyer, the Green Beret who stood beside Kaepernick: ‘The vitriol was more disrespectful than the protest’ | Colin Kaepernick | The Guardian
description: Ten years after he helped shape the quarterback’s anthem protest, the former NFL player and Army veteran says he still sees it as an act of patriotism
Author: Melissa Jacobs
Headline: Ten years after he helped shape the quarterback’s anthem protest, the former NFL player and Army veteran says he still sees it as an act of patriotism
Content: Nate Boyer (right) stands alongside the kneeling Eric Reid and Colin Kaepernick before a game in San Diego in 2016.Photograph: Michael Zagaris/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNate Boyer (right) stands alongside the kneeling Eric Reid and Colin Kaepernick before a game in San Diego in 2016.Photograph: Michael Zagaris/Getty ImagesColin KaepernickNate Boyer, the Green Beret who stood beside Kaepernick: ‘The vitriol was more disrespectful than the protest’Ten years after he helped shape the quarterback’s anthem protest, the former NFL player and Army veteran says he still sees it as an act of patriotismMelissa JacobsWed 2 Sep 2026 10.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 10.01 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNate Boyer was stunned. The formerNFLlong snapper and United States Army Green Beret had big plans for his MVP (Merging Vets and Players) foundation, an organization that helps veterans and NFL players address the challenges that await once they take the uniform off for good. MVP was all set for a season-long college football activation tour thanks to a five-figure sponsorship from a well-known brand that happens to be one of the NFL’s longstanding partners. Boyer and his team were prepping for their trip to Columbus for Ohio State’s home opener. Everything was ready to go. Thousands in upfront costs had been spent. Then the company pulled out.Colin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black people | Howard BryantRead more“They suddenly stopped replying to emails,” Boyer says. “Finally, on that Thursday, when I was at the airport en route, I called our point person, also a veteran, who begrudgingly told me what was going on.”It turns out the company’s legal department discovered that Boyer had met withColin Kaepernickwhen the former 49ers quarterback began protesting during the national anthem. When Boyer attempted to get a deeper explanation from the company, he was ghosted.This happenedlastAugust,nine yearsafter Kaepernick’s protests.“I just couldn’t believe that all those years later there were still people upset about something I was such a small part of that had nothing but intentions of unity and understanding,” Boyer says.“What the heck? Why is he protesting the anthem?” That was Boyer’s first reaction when he saw Kaepernick sitting on the bench during a preseason game against the Green Bay Packers in August 2016. For a second, Boyer – who had been part of the Seahawks in 2015 after six years in the military – bought into the initial buzz that Kaepernick was specifically protesting the anthem and disrespecting the American flag.He was disappointed because, as a former Green Beret, the flag represented to him honor, sacrifice, and freedom. But Boyer also happened to be a lifelong 49ers fan, and Kaepernick was his favorite player at the time.“He brought us out of a time of mediocrity as far as football goes,” he says. Adding to Boyer’s conflicting feelings was the fact that Kaepernick had donated an inscribed football to Boyer’s MVP foundation with the message, “God Bless Our Troops.”​​​ The narrative that Kaepernick was somehow anti-military didn’t really make sense to Boyer.Then Boyer did something increasingly rare in modern times. He tabled his snap judgment and listened to the full 18-minute interview Kaepernick gave explaining the reasons for his protest.“He talks about a lot of things, and one of the things he mentioned was that he had a lot of support for people in the military,” Boyer says. “And then he said, ‘I’m not going to stand for the flag of a country that oppresses people of color.’ He just felt that we were not living up to the promises of what the flag was supposed to represent. I didn’t necessarily disagree with that.”Boyer says he understood Kaepernick’s sentiments when the quarterback said “I am not going to stand up to show pride in a flag for a country that oppresses Black people and people of color. To me, this is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way. There are bodies in the street and people getting paid leave and getting away with murder.”And while Boyer acknowledged an anthem protest could hurt his feelings, he was proud to have taken the oath to defend an American’s right to freedom of speech. At the time, Boyer viewed Kaepernick’s act as a chance to have a balanced societal discourse.“I thought it was potentially a pretty powerful thing and something that could really bring people together,” he says.Unfortunately, Boyer’s hopes for unity did not come to fruition.The story quickly became a lightning rod, culturally and politically. Boyer, with his unique military and football experience, was asked to join roundtable conversations on several major networks. Certain that they had a preconceived notion of his views, Boyer turned them down.“We just assume if somebody wears a certain uniform or is a certain color, that they feel a certain way. That just wasn’t true,” he says.Instead Boyer, who proudly considers himself apolitical, wrote anopen letterin the Army Timessharing his nuanced opinion of Kaepernick’s protest. He woke up to a full mailbox, endless texts and social media messages. Boyer calls his letter a reasonable stance that was intended “not for the 10% of people on both ends of the fringes, but for the 80% of us that usually don’t have a voice.”Among the multitude of people who read Boyer’s open letter was Kaepernick, who was suddenly the most prominent NFL player in the world. Boyer was in the NFL Network green room when he received a call from an unknown number which he serendipitously picked up. It was a representative from Kaepernick’s agency informing him that the quarterback had requested to meet with him in San Diego ahead of the 49ers preseason game the next day.Once in San Diego, Boyer was shepherded into the lobby of the 49ers’ team hotel where he chatted with Kaepernick for about 90 minutes. 49ers safety Eric Reid, who was aligned with Kaepernick’s stance, was also in attendance.Boyer says that the three of them were nervous given the new and fiery nature of the situation. But he says they were comfortable fast and that it was ultimately like we were talking in a locker room.View image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick became the focus of huge media attention after his protests.Photograph: Troy Wayrynen/USA Today SportsBoyer relishes the complexity of the conversation. Kaepernick and Reid said they didn’t want to stand for the anthem until there was real change in America. When pressed by Boyer on what change looks like, they said they wanted to see a day when zero people of color being unfairly targeted. Boyer talked about how he wanted zero military suicides each day instead of the current number of 22. Neither objective was likely to be achieved anytime soon but they agreed that it was important to try.It was an extremely respectful conversation from Boyer’s perspective, and he especially appreciated the question that changed everything. Kaepernick asked if there was a way he and Reid could protest and not offend people in the military.“I was like, no. I think no matter what, no matter what you do, some people are gonna be offended because we’re a very diverse microcosm,” Boyer says. “That’s when I told him that sitting on the bench by himself wasn’t the most inspiring look and the only other thing that maybe made sense logistically was to take a knee.”Boyer pointed out the respect and symbolism synonymous with kneeling. People kneel to pray. They kneel to propose marriage. Boyer says Kaepernick and Reid nodded as he was talking and decided that taking a knee was the perfect compromise (Kaepernick sayskneeling was Reid’s idea and Boyer endorsed it).They briefly talked about Boyer taking a knee beside them during the 49ers-Chargers game, but Boyer said he felt more comfortable standing next to them in support.The military fanfare was particularly strong that night. After all, San Diego is home to one of the country’s largest military communities. The pregame festivities included a flyover with Navy Seals parachuting on to the field. A Black member of the Navy sang the anthem. And there was Boyer standing next to the kneeling Kaepernick and Reid in a show of support that he considered patriotic.Then came the deafening boos. A stunned and frustrated Boyer couldn’t believe a crowd would boo during the anthem because a couple of guys were kneeling for social justice.“That was just crazy to me,” he said. “I understand not being on board with it, but I didn’t understand the vitriol. It was sad and I thought that was way more disrespectful than any protests.”Discourse about the protests quickly became omnipresent. Boyer heard from all sides. One of his military buddies told Boyer he had read his letter in the Army Times and was in support even though one of their brothers had just returned from battle, his coffin draped in the American flag. Boyer’s friend said he was filled with rage at anybody that disrespects the flag. But he didn’t think Kaepernick’s intent was to disrespect it at all.Another military brother, an amputee, told Boyer, “Even though I don’t have legs, I’ll stand with enough pride for both of us.”Then there was a veteran who had been shot a couple of times and called Boyer, “a disgrace to the Green Berets.” This is a man Boyer says he looked up to and still does to this day. Given his disappointment with some of the reactions he received, Boyer could only imagine what was coming for Kaepernick.Kaepernick received a level of animosity rarely seen in America. Donald Trump stoked the flames on a daily basis, spreading the black or white notion that Kaepernick’s protests were solely about disrespecting the military and that the quarterback was un-American. The unity that Boyer hoped for was nowhere in sight.Boyer and Kaepernick remained in touch for several months after their first meeting. Nothing traumatic, just regular check-ins with Boyer offering support. Kaepernick’s football career, meanwhile, quickly took a nosedive and he never played in the league again after the 2016 season. Boyer is unwilling to say Kaepernick was blackballed by the league, a notion that became a common narrative.“It’s not that cut and dry,” he said. Boyer points out that after Kaepernick left the 49ers, Denver gave him a look. Baltimore and Seattle supposedly considered him for their rosters.In fact, Boyer says the Seahawks reached out to him for a scouting report. He told them that he thought Kaepernick was a good guy and genuine. He also shared how he appreciated that Kaepernick (along with Reid) did the 22 push-up challenge to raise awareness for the 22 veterans who take their lives on a daily basis.“I’m not sure the reason why it didn’t work out. Who knows?,” Boyer says of Kaepernick’s career. “Could have been totally football related. I have no idea. I know he had some injuries and stuff like that. I would imagine there’s probably certain politics that did play a role as well.”An NFL coach later told Boyer why his team decided to steer clear of Kaepernick. He said Kaepernick had lost a step and wasn’t the same player that took the 49ers to the Super Bowl at the end of the 2012 season. But that was just part of the coach’s rationale.He told Boyer, “If we bring him in to be the backup, and all of a sudden, you got all these people who maybe they’re fans, maybe they’re not, are saying, ‘Why don’t you start Kaepernick?’ Why don’t you give him a chance?’ The starting quarterback has one bad game, and everyone’s up in arms, and then you’re potentially dividing the locker room. It quickly becomes a circus.”Kaepernick’s final NFL game was on 1 January 2017, against Boyer’s former team, the Seahawks. He became immersed in social justice causes, including his ownKnow Your Rights Camp, while suing the NFL for collusion. The case was settled in 2019.Meanwhile, Boyer’s MVP foundation is going strong and he’s added the title of film-maker to his unique resume. Boyer is working on a D-day documentary about a 102-year-old Black soldier whose grandparents were born into slavery.Though Boyer’s dialogue with Kaepernick only lasted a few months, they will forever be entwined as evidenced by the company that pulled its sponsorship just a year ago.Despite the continued hostility by some, Boyer is grateful for the link with Kaepernick and all the intellectual powerhouses such as Dr Harry Edwards, Tommie Smith and John Carlos, he’s met along the way.Boyer hopes that historians will view Kaepernick’s protest as an act of patriotism and that his legacy will be taught through a balanced lens.“I hope they will think about being courageous and doing the right thing, even when it’s not popular, and even when you know that a lot of people are going to be upset with you,” he says. “As long as you do it, whatever you do, do it with utmost respect, and try to honor those people that you know are going to disagree with you.”Explore more on these topicsColin KaepernickNFLUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Football connects communities but can pull them apart if governed carelessly | Sport | The Guardian
description: Sport is a space to help youngsters to develop character, resilience and confidence, but we need stronger leadership and safer environments to make this happen
Author: Cath Bishop
Headline: Sport is a space to help youngsters to develop character, resilience and confidence, but we need stronger leadership and safer environments to make this happen
Content: Games of football for 750 children in Scotland were cancelled last weekend because of severe behavioural issues by adults.Photograph: FatCamera/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGames of football for 750 children in Scotland were cancelled last weekend because of severe behavioural issues by adults.Photograph: FatCamera/Getty ImagesSportFootball connects communities but can pull them apart if governed carelesslyCath BishopSport is a space to help youngsters to develop character, resilience and confidence, but we need stronger leadership and safer environments to make this happenWed 2 Sep 2026 08.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.02 BSTShareThe fight for the soul of football isn’t just happening in the offices of Uefa and Fifa, it’s taking place on pitches much closer to home. At the weekend games of football for 750 children aged five to six in Scotlandwere cancelledbecause of severe behavioural issues within the ironically named “Fun 4s” programme. Seventy-two red cards were handed out in the first week of the season. Accounts describe adults displaying aggression, intimidation and head-butting as if it’s the “wild west”.This isn’t just a Scottish problem. Contacts I speak to in different roles around football confirm and almost accept that “youth football is atrocious”. This should be sounding major alarm bells, for the consequences go way beyond the pitch. The existing disciplinary systems and PR campaigns are not nearly enough to address and change the situation.Lionel Messi in his 30s was one of the best international players ever | Jeff RueterRead moreIt’s incredibly selfish and socially corrosive for an adult to intervene and spoil the experience of kids playing football. There are no good outcomes. For the children, they learn to associate football, and potentially life more broadly, with violence and aggression. They are robbed of a space to be free, to play and develop and have fun alongside their friends. They see adults role-modelling a dog-eat-dog, win-at-all-costs mentality that is not laying the foundations for them to become good team players, school pupils or later civic-minded citizens. It also prevents young people from developing a love of being active and working positively in a team, perhaps one of the most powerful elements for a healthy life. It’s not a great way to develop parenting skills, either.There is no shortage of evidence about how important it is – whether you are trying to develop skilful football players or healthy young people – that children need space to play, try stuff out and thrive. We also know that it’s what children want from sport.Research by Amanda Visekat the Milken Institute of Public Health at George Washington University, confirms that when it comes to organised sport, kids just want to have fun. What counts for girls and boys are things such as trying your best, working hard, playing well together as a team. When mapping 81 determinants of fun, “winning” ranked 40th in importance.The Campaign for Children’s Rights in Football is an independent and impartial organisation. It’s preparing to launch and trying to create a greater platform for its work in the sport internationally. It’s needed more than ever.The Centre for Young Lives set up the Raising the Nation Play Commission thatpublished its report last yearas part of a campaign for a national strategy to put play back into children’s lives. Last year the Scottish government published Scotland’sPlay Vision Statement and Action Plan 2025-2030to ensure that “every child is able to play across all stages and aspects of their life to support their social development, resilience, language and communication development, health, physical and mental wellbeing”. The Scottish FA had a “Let Them Play” campaign. But events playing out in Scotland show just how gaping the void is between government strategies, research and reality. This is going to take more than a communications campaign and a swathe of disciplinary proceedings. But investing in what is required for a deeper cultural change could create many positive ripples across our communities if the governing bodies get serious about making this their priority.Creating thriving environments, ethics and focusing on the experience of those around you must become the first lesson in coaching training courses whether beginner or advanced. This needs to be the first part of training to be an official, or the conversation when your offer to volunteer is accepted by a local club. For any parents bringing their children to a club, clear standards, expectations and clarity on behaviours on and off the pitch should be integrated from the very first moment.There is a bigger issue here. Sport is cited rightly as a great space to develop character, resilience, confidence. But that only happens in sports environments set up to develop those things. That wasn’t what was on offer on these Scottish youth football pitches. More sport may not help young people. Better experiences and environments will. That’s a crucial difference that has been missed when metrics have simply focused on growing participation and levels of activity.Leadership is needed at the highest level. There’s a gap for our prime minister to call for sport to change itself in order to offer more to children and adults across the UK. When Andy Burnham called for “care to be at the heart of everything we do” that should include youth football and other sports experiences.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionElite football clubs have a responsibility, too, as key role models for how to play football. If there are things that happen in the Premier League that we wouldn’t want our children to emulate, we have to stop and ask why these things are happening at all. This question opens up a greater space for football to be a force for good. From their own talent-scouting interests, it’s also vital that future players are able to build on strong foundations of creativity, connection and strong intrinsic motivation – ie the love of the game, not just a love of winning.Football and sport more widely have the power to unite a nation, to connect communities, to build positive solidarity. But we must also acknowledge, admit and understand that done poorly, without care, without strong leadership and clear cultural principles based on the experiences of all involved, it can pull apart the civic fabric we so desperately need to strengthen.Explore more on these topicsSportScotlandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Premiership: Durán inspires Celtic to convincing victory after Dalglish ovation | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: The Colombian opened the 3-0 win against Aberdeen, while Falkirk lost 1-2 to Rangers and Kilmarnock lost 0-1 to St Mirren
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Colombian opened the 3-0 win against Aberdeen, while Falkirk lost 1-2 to Rangers and Kilmarnock lost 0-1 to St Mirren
Content: Camilo Durán starred again as Celtic swept aside Aberdeen.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCamilo Durán starred again as Celtic swept aside Aberdeen.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesScottish PremiershipScottish Premiership: Durán inspires Celtic to convincing victory after Dalglish ovationColombian opens scoring in 3-0 win against AberdeenFalkirk 1-2 Rangers; Kilmarnock 0-1 St MirrenAgence France-PresseWed 2 Sep 2026 23.09 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 00.18 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheCelticstriker Camilo Durán inspired the Scottish champions’ 3-0 win overAberdeen, whileRangerssnatched a 2-1 victory againstFalkirkon Wednesday.Durán has scored six goals in five matches for Martin O’Neill’s side after his latest eye-catching contribution at Parkhead. The Colombian netted in the 14th minute with the latest in his series of spectacular strikes since joining from Qarabag in the close-season. Durán collected Benjamin Nygren’s pass and unleashed a long-range drive that cannoned in off the crossbar.Scottish Premiership: Shankland on the spot to ease pressure on McInnes and RangersRead moreO’Neill may find it difficult to put the winger back on the flanks when the striker Kasper Høgh recovers from a thigh injury. Nygren and Yang Hyun-jun were also on target asCeltickilled off the game before the break.Although they suffered a humiliating Champions League exit against Lask, Celtic have made a perfect start to their title defence with four successive wins. It was an emotional night in Glasgow as Kenny Dalglish was given a warm ovation on the pitch before the match. Dalglish launched his iconic career with Celtic before joining Liverpool in 1977. The 75-year-old revealed earlier this year that he was receiving treatment for cancer.Celtic are two points clear of second-placeSt Mirren, whose 1-0 win atKilmarnock– their first at Rugby Park for 13 years – was secured by Fraser Taylor’s maiden goal for the club in the third minute.Lawrence Shankland’s double gave Rangers a dramatic win over Falkirk to ease the pressure on theirmanager, Derek McInnes. With McInnes serving the first of a two-matchtouchline ban(reduced from four matches) for comments made as Hearts manager last season, he watched from the stands as Shankland saved him from another chastening result.View image in fullscreenRangers’ captain, Lawrence Shankland, celebrates his second goal against Falkirk.Photograph: Kirk O’Rourke/Rangers FC/ShutterstockShankland, who scored from the spot in the 1-0 win at Aberdeen on Sunday, fired Rangers ahead with a fine strike in the seventh minute. Kosta Nedeljkovic, making his first Rangers start since signing on loan from Aston Villa, turned an Ethan Ross cross into his own net to giveFalkirkan unexpected equaliser just before the break. But Scotland star Shankland, who signed from Hearts in the close-season, reduced Rangers’ anxiety when he curled in the winner after 79 minutes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMotherwellare third after Seb Palmer-Houlden, Alex Lowry and Dylan Levitt scored their first goals for the club in a 3-0 win againstDundee United.St Johnstonesalvaged a 1-1 draw in the Tayside derby againstDundee. Dundee seemed to have sealed the points when Charlie Reilly scored in the 87th minute, but St Johnstone’s Josh Fowler levelled in the 90th minute.Explore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipCelticRangersAberdeenFalkirkSt MirrenKilmarnocknewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A commodity’: Ismaïla Sarr’s agent wants respect for African players in transfer deals | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Diomansy Kamara says African players feel like “a commodity’ after Crystal Palace turned down an approach from Liverpool for their forward
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Diomansy Kamara says African players feel like “a commodity’ after Crystal Palace turned down an approach from Liverpool for their forward
Content: Ismaïla Sarr won the Conference League with Crystal Palace last season but is yet to feature in the current campaign.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenIsmaïla Sarr won the Conference League with Crystal Palace last season but is yet to feature in the current campaign.Photograph: Adam Davy/PATransfer window‘A commodity’: Ismaïla Sarr’s agent wants respect for African players in transfer dealsDiomansy Kamara says players must ‘be heard’Monaco defend halting Lamine Camara’s Chelsea moveEd AaronsWed 2 Sep 2026 20.29 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 23.04 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsmaïla Sarr’s agent has claimed some African players are treated like “a commodity” afterCrystal Palaceturned down Liverpool’s approach for the Senegal forward and Lamine Camara’s move from Monaco to Chelsea broke down on deadline day.Palace are understood to have rejected a bid from Liverpool for Sarr last week and insisted last season’s top scorer was not for sale. The 28-year-old, who missed the opening two matches against Everton and Manchester City after the manager, Pierre Sage, said he had picked up an injury, subsequently deleted all references to the Conference League winners from his social media accounts and is thought to have been disappointed by Palace’s stance.Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club faredRead moreLiverpool did not return with a bid on deadline day after deciding to keep Cody Gakpo, who was wanted by City.Sarr’s Senegal teammate Camara was poised for a £47m move until Monaco backtracked on a club-to-club written agreement, leaving Chelsea fuming. The Ligue 1 side have said they pulled the plug on Camara’s transfer because they thought Folarin Balogun’s £40m move to Everton was back on after doubts over his medical.Sarr’s agent, Diomansy Kamara, who won 50 caps for Senegal and played for Portsmouth, West Brom and Fulham, released a statement on Wednesday questioning the treatment of his compatriots.View image in fullscreenThe Senegalese midfielder Lamine Camara saw a move from Monaco to Chelsea fall through on transfer deadline day.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty Images“The cases of Ismaïla Sarr and Lamine Camara must all interrogate us,” he said. “We have to get out of this logic where the African player can sometimes give the feeling that he is just a commodity: you buy it, you set its price, you negotiate its future and, too often, your will seems to go to the background. Our African players deserve respect. The respect of their work. The respect of their career. Respecting their ambitions. The respect of their voices.”Kamara added: “The fact that clubs can sometimes have the final word is a reality of professional football. But one question remains: what about the career and the will of the player? The player must be able to be heard and respected in the decisions that determine his future. ‘Let’s never forget what’s important: behind every success, it’s the players who write history first.’”Palace were contacted for comment. Monaco’s sporting director, Thiago Scuro, defended the Ligue 1 side’s actions in a press conference on Wednesday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said: “Around 10pm, in our time here, maybe a bit earlier, Everton realised that OK there is no problem: ‘We are ready to do it. Let’s sign the contract.’ As soon as we got the information, yes, we did come back to Chelsea and told [them]: ‘OK, we have our deal there. There is no deal on Lamine.’ Because it’s also fair to do this. It’s also part of the game.”He said it was unfair to portray Monaco as “the bad guys in the room”: “Everybody is very fair and nice in the football industry, just Monaco is not. Too much.”Everton were left with only one recognised striker after Balogun changed his mind over the move to Merseyside and Scuro suggested the US forward wasunhappy with how Everton had treated himover his medical.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowCrystal PalacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Balogun pulled out of Everton move over handling of his medical, claim Monaco | Everton | The Guardian
description: Thiago Scuro, Monaco’s chief executive, has suggested Everton are responsible for the collapse of Folarin Balogun’s deadline-day move, while also defending his club’s decision not to sell Lamine Camara to Chelsea
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Thiago Scuro, Monaco’s chief executive, has suggested Everton are responsible for the collapse of Folarin Balogun’s deadline-day move, while also defending his club’s decision not to sell Lamine Camara to Chelsea
Content: Folarin Balogun was not happy with the way his Everton medical was conducted, according to Monaco’s chief executive.Photograph: Soccrates Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFolarin Balogun was not happy with the way his Everton medical was conducted, according to Monaco’s chief executive.Photograph: Soccrates Images/Getty ImagesEvertonBalogun pulled out of Everton move over handling of his medical, claim MonacoThiago Scuro suggests Merseyside club responsibleMonaco chief executive defends keeping CamaraAndy HunterWed 2 Sep 2026 18.46 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFolarin Balogunpulled out of a £40m move to Evertonbecause of how he was treated over his medical, according to Monaco’s chief executive, Thiago Scuro, who also defended the late decision not to sell Lamine Camara to Chelsea.Balogun signed a deal sheet shortly before 11pm on deadline day to allowEvertonto complete his transfer only to reject the move shortly after. Everton had renegotiated the structure of the fee with Monaco after discovering an issue with the USA international’s medical and failing in attempts to sign Joshua Zirkzee or Tammy Abraham on loan.Deadline-day shambles leaves Everton and Moyes fighting the odds again | Andy HunterRead moreEverton sources have claimed the 25-year-old arrived later than scheduled from France and thatMonacowere slow in sharing the appropriate medical records, giving them less time to resolve the problem. But at a press conference in Monaco on Wednesday, Scuro insisted it was Everton’s treatment of the striker that caused the deal to collapse.“The Premier League has a mechanism where you can request one extra hour to finish the paperwork,” he said. “This was done five minutes to the close of the transfer window there. I signed the contract, Everton signed the contract. At the last moment, the player decided not to sign. And basically, the allegation of Balogun is that: ‘I’m not feeling well by the way the club treated me. I’m not feeling well by the way the medical department of Everton brought doubts about my future or my health. I have nothing [wrong with me], so I’m not comfortable to sign a long contract here.’ And that’s the way we finished our transfer window.”Scuro insisted he did not want to “create war” with Everton orChelseaover their failed deadline-day deals but disputed the former’s concerns over Balogun’s medical results. He said: “At four o’clock Balo was in Liverpool making his medicals. Everything was going pretty well. Around 7pm we were contacted by Everton, raising questions on the medicals of Balo, which for our medical staff, [and] for the personal medical staff of the player, made totally no sense. The explanations were not enough to justify or bring concerns of the future of the player. Which there isn’t.“This discussion started between the medical departments here and there. It took Everton around two, three hours to go deep on the assessment, check with other doctors; this is a normal situation when the doctor of the club raises concerns … meanwhile, as everything on the last days, this was in the press quite quickly. I would say around half an hour after we were contacted, it was already in the media that Balogun is failing the medicals. And then of course Chelsea saw the opportunity.”Chelsea struck a £47m deal to sign Camara as they lookedto replace the Manchester City-bound Enzo Fernández, with a written agreement believed to have been in place.However Monaco, who wanted to raise funds but preferred to sell Balogun, reneged on the Camara deal with Chelsea once Everton decided to proceed with their move for Balogun.Scuro said: “Around 10pm, in our time here, maybe a bit earlier, Everton realised that OK there is no problem: ‘We are ready to do it. Let’s sign the contract.’ As soon as we got the information, yes, we did come back to Chelsea and told [them]: ‘OK, we have our deal there. There is no deal on Lamine.’ Because it’s also fair to do this. It’s also part of the game.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTransfer window verdict: how every Premier League club faredRead more“There is no reason that this kind of discussions or dynamic on the last day of the transfer window, which all of us decided to be on the last day, trying to find solutions, with the clock ticking on our neck, [makes Monaco] the bad guys in the room; that Monaco is not fair, Monaco is not right. title: Richarlison could still leave Tottenham as Trabzonspor weigh up bid for striker | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: Richarlison is the subject of firm interest from Trabzonspor and could move there from Tottenham before the closure of the transfer window in Turkey on Friday night
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Richarlison is the subject of firm interest from Trabzonspor and could move there from Tottenham before the closure of the transfer window in Turkey on Friday night
Content: Richarlison has asked to leave Spurs and could get his wish and join Mo Salah at Trabzonspor.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRicharlison has asked to leave Spurs and could get his wish and join Mo Salah at Trabzonspor.Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty ImagesTottenham HotspurRicharlison could still leave Tottenham as Trabzonspor weigh up bid for strikerTurkish transfer window closes on Friday nightBrazilian refused a return to Everton on TuesdayDavid HytnerWed 2 Sep 2026 18.11 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.46 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRicharlison is the subject of firm interest fromTrabzonsporand could move there from Tottenham before the closure of the transfer window in Turkey on Friday night.The striker has asked to leave, according to the Spurs manager, Roberto De Zerbi, who did not stand in the way of two of his other players who did so before the deadline in England on Tuesday night: Kevin Danso and Pape Sarr. They were allowed to join Sunderland and Juventus respectively on loans with purchase clauses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPremier League transfer talking points: three things we learned from the dataRead moreDe Zerbi said on Saturday after his team’s home loss to Newcastle that Richarlison had requested to leave “too many times” this summer. It looked as if the Brazilian might return to his former club Everton, as Spurs tried to sign Iliman Ndiaye,only for that not to happen. Ndiaye ended up going to Manchester City for £60m plus £5m in add-ons.Richarlison was emotional when he used social media on Monday evening to say, in essence, that he would not be forced into a move he did not want. Xavi Simons, however, is out until March or April, according to De Zerbi, with an anterior cruciate ligament injury.
