title: Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original work
Author: Aaron Mok
Headline: As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original work
Content: Guardian DesignGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.ReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original workSupported byAbout this contentAaron MokWed 2 Sep 2026 13.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.24 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release ofChatGPTin 2022. She went from receiving slow one-off jobs creating logos and packaging to an onslaught of requests asking her to fix versions that were generated by artificial intelligence – from sharpening fuzzy images for printing to turning flawed designs into usable files.By 2025, Lisa, who asked not to be fully named to avoid solicitations, said 90% of her incoming logo and packaging design requests required cleaning up AI-generated content, work that accounted for 60% to 70% of her annual income. But the grind was exhausting. Clients lowballed her;' some AI-generated designs were so flawed that she had to recreate them from scratch and she worried about being complicit in AI-driven copyright infringement. By the end of the year, she began turning those jobs down.“It was just so soulless,” said Lisa, who now focuses on “human-made designs”.Lisa is part of a growing group of creative freelancers being hired to clean up AI slop, a term used to characterize low-quality, AI-generated output. As businesses use tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude to produce marketing copy, illustrations, books and videos, they are hiring creative professionals to humanize AI-generated copy, repair botched images and salvage flawed footage.The work serves as a stopgap in an increasingly challenging job market, supplementing income for those who freelance full-time or on the side. But clients often underestimate the time and skill involved, expecting cleanup to be quick and cheap when it can require as much work as creating something original, freelancers said. And while the high volume of cleanup gigs can be lucrative, freelancers are divided over the trade-off. Some find it tedious and creatively unfulfilling, while others enjoy the challenge. As AI improves, freelancers question how long the demand will last and where they’ll turn once the jobs dry up.For now, demand for AI cleanup work is growing.On Freelancer.com, a contract work platform with more than 88 million users, job listings tagged with phrases such as “correct AI”, “AI hallucination” and “AI error” rose 87% to 10,760 globally between August 2025 and June 2026, according to internal data shared with the Guardian. The jobs were concentrated in graphic design, followed by video editing, proofreading and content writing. Upwork saw AI remediationgigs jump 70%year over year, and Fiverr saw keyword searches for “AI cleanup” services grow more than 20 times between 2023 and 2026, according to data shared with the Guardian.The specter of AI could spell trouble for the creative freelance labor market. Listings for freelance jobs exposed to automation fell 21% in the eight months after ChatGPT launched and image-creation gigs dropped 17% after AI image generators arrived, according to a2025 studypublished in the academic journal Management Science. And those losses have continued, according to a2026 study.Meanwhile, more workers are turning to freelance work as companies cut staff and hire less, intensifying competition. The average project on Freelancer.com drew 54 bids in 2025, up 8% from the year before, according to the site’sannual report.But as companies cut costs, they’re changing the nature of freelance assignments, from requests for creative work to sprucing up AI output. Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, said the cleanup work is often commissioned by small companies and entrepreneurs using AI to produce a first pass, only to run into problems they don’t have the expertise to solve.“[AI output] needs a human to turn it into something polished that can actually be used,” he said. The time and money saved on the first draft can be eaten up by the “incredibly time-consuming” work of preparing it for commercial use.The rise of the AI cleanup crewsFor some freelancers, cleanup is taking up a growing share of their workload and traditional creative projects are becoming harder to find.Todd Van Linda, a full-time freelance illustrator in Florida, began taking AI cleanup gigs in 2023 as his usual work drawing illustrations, video game art and architectural plans became less steady. The work typically involves filtering out visual noise, improving resolution, and hunting for glitches like an extra toe.“Money”, Van Linda said of his motivation. “The jobs were there to be done.”Though some clients expect AI cleanup to cost less than original work, Van Linda won’t lower his rates. When one prospective client offered about $500 to repair 13 to 15 AI-generated illustrations for a children’s book, with the expectation that each should take about 15 minutes, he turned it down. He said projects can take between a few hours of work to days depending on the scope. His rate is $65 an hour and “doesn’t go down from there”, he said.For Kym Dunbar, a freelance writer and editor based in Australia, AI cleanup now accounts for about 60% of her workload, as writing work like blogs and website copy have dwindled. As a result, Dunbar said her monthly earnings from writing original content have fallen to roughly a third of what she made during the pandemic.Dunbar stumbled into cleanup work in 2024, when a client asked her to revise an AI-generated article. She quickly learned to spot recurring problems, from repetitive language and awkward paragraph structures to a lack of emotional nuance. Since then, she has worked on about 40 AI-generated nonfiction books, longform articles and technical papers.“There’s a lot less good projects available for writers and editors these days,” Dunbar said.But “cleanup” can understate how much work is involved.Nathan McConnell, a multimedia editor who freelances on top of his full-time job, started editing AI-generated videos in 2023. His work has ranged from removing reflections from AI real estate videos to fixing robotic voiceovers and malformed 3D models. The requests have increased from two or three projects in 2023 to eight to 10 so far this year, he said.One client brought him roughly 100 AI-generated images of humanoid animals for a tarot deck riddled with extra fingers, two left feet and other mistakes. McConnell spent two to three hours repairing each image in Photoshop, expecting the project to take nearly two weeks to finish. But after making the first 10 cards, he called the project off because of health issues and constant changes requested from his “persnickety” client.Not everything that lands in McConnell’s inbox can be saved, he said. That could look like videos where the physics feel off, like shadows falling the wrong way, or animations that repurpose another creator’s work without permission.“I’ve told a client before that it’s ‘too’ slop,” McConnell said. “There’s no way I can fix this.”While McConnell and Van Linda would rather make original work, not everyone finds fixing AI outputs dispiriting. Dunbar considers it “interesting” and “challenging”, and takes satisfaction in turning a weak draft into polished prose.What troubles her is that people increasingly see AI not as a tool, but as the “be-all and end-all” of the creative process.“I just feel it’s a shame we need to do it,” Dunbar said.Slop cleanup jobs may not lastIt’s unclear whether cleaning up AI-generated slop will remain a viable source of work.Dunbar isn’t convinced it will. She believes much of the work humanizing AI could dry up within five to 10 years as models improve and allow businesses to generate usable content themselves.McConnell sees it differently, arguing that AI still needs to be “babysat” to catch mistakes an untrained eye might miss, from logos that violate brand guidelines to objects that appear and disappear in videos. “We need people [to fix] problems that AI is creating,” he said.But Van Linda is already creating a different path. After he stopped taking AI cleanup gigs late last year, he has seen more clients, some of whom have been dissatisfied with AI, seeking original, hand-drawn work.“Quite frankly, this kind of thing has gotten extremely distasteful to me,” he said about AI cleanup work.Though Lisa, the freelance graphic designer, updated her profile to say she no longer works with AI-generated images, she still gets requests to edit them. She occasionally takes cleanup gigs for clients who come to her after getting poor results with AI. But some clients “straight up lie” and pass off the images as original creations.“They say ‘I don’t use AI,’ but there’s a “[Google] Gemini logo on the bottom,” she said.But just in case AI makes her job obsolete, she has a plan. Lisa has begun returning to the canvases, watercolors and other physical art she practiced before she pursued a career in graphic design. She predicts that within “another year or two”, AI will be able to do logo and packaging design as well as she can, leaving only “the best of the best” able to make a living.“I don’t know if I’m good enough to survive the digital stuff,” she said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedChatGPTOpenAIfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Cook handed $47m package for new role as executive chair of Apple | Apple | The Guardian
description: Pay and shares deal nearly matches $58m award to John Ternus, his successor as CEO at the $4.7tn tech company
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Pay and shares deal nearly matches $58m award to John Ternus, his successor as CEO at the $4.7tn tech company
Content: John Ternus, left, is taking over as Apple’s chief executive from Tim Cook, who spent 15 years in the role.Composite: Bloomberg, AFP, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Ternus, left, is taking over as Apple’s chief executive from Tim Cook, who spent 15 years in the role.Composite: Bloomberg, AFP, Getty ImagesAppleTim Cook handed $47m package for new role as executive chair of ApplePay and shares deal nearly matches $58m award to John Ternus, his successor as CEO at the $4.7tn tech companyDan MilmoGlobal technology editorWed 2 Sep 2026 15.46 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.28 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTim Cook has received a $47m (£35m) pay deal as Apple’s executive chair, a remuneration package that nears the level set for his successor as chief executive.Cook, who handed over toJohn Ternuson Tuesday, will be paid a base salary of $2m and$45m worth of shares. Half of the share award will be based on performance targets being met, while the remaining half will be paid out over four years.Ternus will receive a base salary of $3m and a $55m share award, with the latter more weighted to performance.Cook’s total compensation as chief executive for 2025 exceeded $74m. Cook, who owns more than 3m shares inApple, has been placed in the multi-billionaire category by Forbes, which estimates his wealth at $3bn.His predecessor, the Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, was paid a symbolic $1 a year but was worth $7bn when he died, including a sizeable shareholding in Disney he acquired after selling the Pixar animation studio to the entertainment conglomerate.Cooktook over from Jobsin 2011 having impressed as an operations specialist. The stock has risen 2,200% since he took charge, with Apple now valued at about $4.7tn – compared with about $350bn when he became chief executive.He built the tech company’s sophisticated supply chain and is succeeded by a 51-year-old engineer and longstanding Apple employee, who built products as senior vice-president of hardware engineering.View image in fullscreenJohn Ternus speaks during Apple's annual developer conference in San Jose in 2017. He has run the engineering teams behind Apple’s product lineup.Photograph: Stephen Lam/ReutersTernus’s role meant he ran the engineering teams behind Apple’s entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company’s revenue. Analysts are not only anticipating new products but also further progress on integrating AI into Apple hardware.Ternus’s first big public moment at Apple will be at its annual iPhone event on 9 September, where a foldable handset is expected to be revealed. New iterations of the Apple Watch and AirPods are also anticipated, although Bloomberg reported last week that AirPods with cameras – another big product rumour – “aren’t launching anytime soon”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCook’s new mandate includes engaging with policymakers around the world and will involve maintaining the company’s relationship with Donald Trump, as well as overseeing the company’s diplomatic ties with China – a key production hub. In a final memo to employees on Monday, he focused on Apple’s products.“I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” he said. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.”Explore more on these topicsAppleTim CookiPhoneComputingMobile phonesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration sides with OpenAI in lawsuit against New York Times | Technology | The Guardian
description: The Times and many companies are accusing OpenAI of misusing their material to train AI systems without compensation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Times and many companies are accusing OpenAI of misusing their material to train AI systems without compensation
Content: OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman speaks at the G20 innovation ministerial summit in North Carolina on Wednesday.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman speaks at the G20 innovation ministerial summit in North Carolina on Wednesday.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersTechnologyTrump administration sides with OpenAI in lawsuit against New York TimesThe Times and many companies are accusing OpenAI of misusing their material to train AI systems without compensationGuardian staff and agenciesWed 2 Sep 2026 21.39 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 21.52 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administrationis supporting OpenAI in ⁠a lawsuit against the New York Times, arguing in favor of the use of copyrighted writing to train artificial intelligence.The Times accusesOpenAIand its largest financial backer, Microsoft, of using millions of newspaper articles without permission to train OpenAI’s popular chatbot. Other newspapers have joined in the suit, first filed in 2023.In a brief filed in Manhattan federal court on Tuesday, the US government weighed in for the first time on lawsuits over the tense battle over AI and copyright. A brief has advisory rather than legal weight but could bolster tech ⁠companies as they fight the claims.“The United States has a strong interest in continuing to develop a robust and competitive artificial intelligence industry that sets the standard for the practice and procedure of AI use globally … As such, it is critical for the United States to ‘retain global leadership in artificial intelligence’,” the brief said.Copyright owners, including authors, publishers, music labels and news outlets, have filed dozens of lawsuits over AI training against tech companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms. They say the companies ⁠misuse their material to train AI systems and do so without compensation.For AI chatbots to generate responses, machine learning systems are first fed billions of lines of text. The bots produce their output by statistical analysis of what the next word should be by matching a user’s query to parts of the database.Spokespeople for the Times and OpenAI did not immediately respond ‌to requests for comment on the filing on Wednesday.“AI dominance is critical to promote national security, prosperity, and economic mobility for all Americans,” US associate attorney general Stanley Woodward Jr said in a statement posted to X. “This Administration will never let our Nation be at a disadvantage relative to our foreign adversaries based on a plainly incorrect understanding of copyright law.”The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, separately told G20 officials ‌at a meeting in North Carolina on Wednesday that their countries should embrace fair use and allow AI companies to train their models on creators’ work while finding ​a way to “protect artists”.All of the pending cases will probably ​revolve around whether AI systems make ​fair use of copyrighted material by ​using it to create new, transformative content. The first two judges to consider the ​question issued diverging rulings ‌last year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government ​agreed with ​tech companies in Tuesday’s brief that AI training is “extraordinarily” transformative.“Beyond the subject matter of this litigation, LLMs are already helping researchers across fields achieve major breakthroughs,” the brief said. “Constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAINew York TimesTrump administrationNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Google defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech sale | Google | The Guardian
description: Judge declines to make Google sell AdX in win for firm against US antitrust enforcers’ attempts to break up big tech
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Judge declines to make Google sell AdX in win for firm against US antitrust enforcers’ attempts to break up big tech
Content: Google’s office on 19 May 2025 in New York City.Photograph: Gary Hershorn/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGoogle’s office on 19 May 2025 in New York City.Photograph: Gary Hershorn/Corbis/Getty ImagesGoogleGoogle defeats US justice department bid to force ad tech saleJudge declines to make Google sell AdX in win for firm against US antitrust enforcers’ attempts to break up big techReutersWed 2 Sep 2026 19.37 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 21.03 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlphabet’s Google escaped a breakup of its advertising technology business on Wednesday, when a judge in Virginia ⁠rejected US antitrust enforcers’ attempt to force a sale of Google’s online advertising exchange.While the ad exchange is a small part of Google’s business, the ruling is the second powerful ⁠symbolic victory against the US Department ⁠of Justice in ​its efforts to forceGoogleto sell assets to address illegal monopolies.US judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, declined to make Google sell AdX, where publishers pay Google a ⁠20% fee to sell ads in auctions that happen instantly when users load websites. She accepted most of the parties’ proposed behavioral remedies.The justice department and a broad coalition of states sued Google in 2023 over ⁠its dominance in markets for advertising technology used by online publishers and websites.In April 2025, Brinkema ruled that Google holds ​illegal monopolies on servers that host publisher ads and ad ‌exchanges which sit between buyers and ‌sellers. Google unlawfully locked publishers on its ad server into using its AdX, the judge found.The tech company’s anticompetitive conduct “substantially harmed ‌Google’s publisher customers, the competitive process, and, ultimately, consumers of information on the open web”, Brinkema said at the time.At a trial last year on remedies in the case, the justice department argued that Google cannot be trusted to run AdX, given its past behavior.Google argued that a forced sale would be technically difficult and result in a long and painful transition that would hurt customers. The company also sought to show the justice department’s demand was different from Google’s own previous offer ‌to sell AdX to end an EU antitrust investigation, which Reuters reported in 2024.Ad Manager represented 4.1% of Google’s overall revenue and 1.5% of operating profit in 2020, according to Wedbush research and analysis of ​court documents. More recent figures were redacted from court documents.The ruling is the third time in a row that a judge has rejected a bid by US antitrust enforcers to break up big tech in a crackdown that started during Donald Trump’s first term. It is likely to fuel questions about whether courts are up to the task of checking ⁠the industry’s unprecedented power over the US economy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA federal judge in Washington last year rejected the ​Federal Trade Commission’s attempt to make Meta ​Platforms sell off Instagram and WhatsApp, saying the ​agency failed to prove that Meta holds a monopoly in a social media landscape that has shifted ​drastically since the case ‌was brought in 2020.Likewise, ​another judge in Washington, ​who previously ruled that Google holds an illegal monopoly in online search, rejected the justice department’s attempt to make the company sell its Chrome browser, citing rising competition from generative artificial intelligence companies such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT.US antitrust cases against Amazon and Apple, which involve big smartphone and online retail markets, will not go to trial until 2027 at the earliest.Explore more on these topicsGoogleAlphabetLaw (US)AI (artificial intelligence)AdvertisingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Uber drivers launch European class action over ‘soulless’ and ‘scary’ AI algorithm | Uber | The Guardian
description: Landmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earnings
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Landmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earnings
Content: Mohammed Shirwa, an Uber driver from Rotterdam, claims Uber’s pay-setting mechanism preys on weakness.Photograph: Judith Jockel/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMohammed Shirwa, an Uber driver from Rotterdam, claims Uber’s pay-setting mechanism preys on weakness.Photograph: Judith Jockel/The GuardianUberUber drivers launch European class action over ‘soulless’ and ‘scary’ AI algorithmLandmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earningsRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 2 Sep 2026 16.37 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUber drivers have launched a landmark legal action against the ride-hailing company claiming they live in “constant fear” of a “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs.Drivers from the UK, theNetherlandsand other countries have joined the compensation claim that could run into billions of dollars. It alleges an AI-powered pay-setting system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings.The claim has been filed at Amsterdam’s district court, where the $150bn (£111bn) San Francisco tech company has its European HQ. It is the first collective legal move of its kind, according to the European Trade Union Confederation.The case centres on an opaque “black box” algorithm fed on information about drivers, which sets a personalised rate for each ride. Drivers fear it pushes down fares to the minimum they are willing to accept.Drivers have told the Guardian the algorithm has offered the same job to different people at different pay rates and offers them less for a return journey after a long trip because it calculates they will not want to come home empty.“It is like someone watching you all the time and knowing about your weakness – the boss is the algorithm,” said Mohammed Shirwa, a 41-year-old Uber driver in Rotterdam. “All the time the algorithm is learning about you and what you are willing to accept. So the prices go low but you are stuck. It knows you need the job.”View image in fullscreenKola Oba, from Tottenham in north London, claims Uber exploits information it collects about him to push down fares.Kola Oba, who calls the algorithm “soulless”, was taking a break in Tottenham, north London, with another driver when they were offered the same job.The other driver was offered £27 and Oba was offered £23. The pair suspected it was because Oba, 48, had taken several cheap jobs and the AI assumed he would accept a lower price. Uber has previouslysaidsuch discrepancies were down to other features of its system including GPS, surge pricing, promotions and testing.“It’s scary – they have all my information and they are using it against my own wellbeing,” Oba said. “It defines how much I earn, how long I have to work, my time with my family, my resting time.”AI models take an increasing role in assigning work to humans by using their rapidly increasing power to learn about a business’s needs and staff behaviour and then acting as a “synthetic manager”.The Dutch data protection authorityfined⁠Uber €825m (£708m) last month for deactivating driver ⁠accounts through automated systems without ​adequate notice. Uber said it would appeal. The company is also planning to roll out driverless cars in European cities from London to Zagreb, initially with human supervisions.The legal case is being led by the Worker Info Exchange, a campaign group whose founder, James Farrar,secureda UK supreme court ruling that Uber drivers should have worker rights.Relating to about 241,000 drivers across the EU and the UK, the claim alleges that Uber has unlawfully used automated decision-making, including profiling, in dynamically setting pay and allocating work.The lawsuit, which also claims the company unlawfully used driver data to train its AI models, is seeking damages for affected drivers and an injunction to halt the conduct which it claims breachesGDPRdata regulations.The drivers claim Uber has operated dynamic pay-setting in the UK since 2023, pushing down their annual incomes by about £5,000. The system was introduced in the Netherlands this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUber’s chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi,said in 2023: “I think that what we can do better is targeting of different trips to different drivers based on their preferences or based on behavioural patterns that they’re showing us.”View image in fullscreenUber, which has its headquarters in San Francisco, said it categorically rejected the allegations.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUber said it did not adjust the price offered for a trip based on an individual driver’s behaviour and that a history of accepting or rejecting trips was not used to personalise pay offers. Instead, it said, dynamic pricing allowed it to increase pay on less attractive trips, boosting a driver’s earning potential.“While we haven’t seen the claim yet, we categorically reject the allegations,” an Uber spokesperson said. “The Uber app uses real-time information about the trip such as journey, duration and destination to calculate fares.“Drivers see their earnings and where a trip is going before they decide whether to accept it. The vast majority of total fares continue to go where they belong: into drivers’ pockets, and the percentage that Uber keeps from fares has remained relativelyflat.”A 2025studyby academics at the University of Oxford, which Uber said relied on incomplete and selective data,foundthere had been substantial cuts in driver earnings after the “dynamic” algorithm was introduced.Farrar said: “It’s bad enough that Uber’s dynamic pay algorithms have squeezed driver pay for years now but the intrusive and underhanded way in which Uber uses its technology to monitor and influence drivers’ behaviour is an affront to their dignity as workers and as human beings.”Anton Ekker, a Dutch lawyer leading the case, said: “A computer algorithm should not independently make decisions that strip individuals of their livelihood. Like so many other online platforms, it should be held accountable for the large-scale exploitation of vulnerabilities of European citizens.”Explore more on these topicsUberAI (artificial intelligence)TransportGig economyEuropeNetherlandsGDPRnewsShareReuse this content

title: New York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high school | Technology | The Guardian
description: Teachers and parents have warned against AI use in schools over concerns of ‘cognitive surrender’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Teachers and parents have warned against AI use in schools over concerns of ‘cognitive surrender’
Content: Parents and students flock to PS 151-Yorkville community school on 7 September 2023 in Manhattan, New York.Photograph: Barry Williams for NY Daily News via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenParents and students flock to PS 151-Yorkville community school on 7 September 2023 in Manhattan, New York.Photograph: Barry Williams for NY Daily News via Getty ImagesTechnologyNew York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high schoolTeachers and parents have warned against AI use in schools over concerns of ‘cognitive surrender’Guardian staff and agenciesWed 2 Sep 2026 16.22 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 16.36 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew YorkCity will ban students’ use ofartificial intelligencein public schools through eighth grade, typically age 13 or 14. The prohibition is scheduled to be announced on Wednesday and will go into effect next week.The change is part of a sweeping overhaul of the use of technology in the US’s largest school district, which enrolls roughly 900,000 students a year. In another policy shift, classrooms will keep students off laptops or tablets through the third grade, age nine or 10. The city’s public school technology policies are closely watched by the rest of the United States.Teachers and parents have warned against the use of AI instructional software in schools over concerns about harming children’s mental health and cognitive development, in particular an abdication of reasoning to software, a phenomenon researchers have dubbed “cognitive surrender”, as well as environmental damage.AI use will only be allowed in high school, which begins in the ninth grade in the US school system. Even then, it will be limited to specific uses, such as learning about the technology itself.AI “companion chatbots” offering psychological support will also be banned. The rules allow teachers to use AI for tasks including preparing lessons or writing messages, but they are forbidden from asking AI to grade assignments.The city’s education department recommends limiting screen time to 45 minutes in class for middle schoolers – sixth through eighth grade – and 30 minutes for elementary school students. But the question remains of how to monitor AI use, since it often takes place outside the school environment.The new rules follow an initial framework published in March, which used a traffic light system to determine which tasks AI would be used for. In 2023, the school system forbade students’ use of ChatGPT, though the ban was reversed less than a year later.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNew York City schools ban AI chatbot that writes essays and answers promptsRead moreThe 2026 framework, which allowed students to use AI for research, exploration and creative projects, sparked fury among many parents and teachers who considered it too lenient.In response, the city’s schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, said that leaders had “missed the mark” in their communications, adding his office would carefully review parents’ feedback for incorporation into future rules.The city had long planned to follow the March framework with a more comprehensive “guidebook” to take feedback into account, the education department has said.The department will set up a taskforce made up of teachers, elected officials, experts and union representatives. The taskforce is to produce a report in April, intended to serve as the basis for New York’s AI-in-schools policy.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)US educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: The best kettles in the UK to save energy and speed up your cuppa, tested | Tea | The Guardian
description: We boiled litres of water to find the best electric kettles, from hard-water heroes to vintage-style, repairable and wifi-connected models
Author: Rachel Ogden
Headline: We boiled litres of water to find the best electric kettles, from hard-water heroes to vintage-style, repairable and wifi-connected models
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. It’s what we turn to in times of strife, when spirits are flagging, or to start our day. When a visitor calls, one of the first things we often do is put the kettle on.Many small appliances have evolved beyond their original form, but the kettle’s basic principles remain largely unchanged. Water goes in and heats until a thermostat switches it off; the water then pours out, and we enjoy a cuppa. However, the technology that goes into a kettle has been slowly improving: better insulation to keep water hotter for longer and reduce reboils; different temperature settings to suit every drink from green tea to herbal brews; and more features such as filters and concealed elements to keep scale out of our cups.When your existing kettle makes its last brew and must be taken to the big recycling centre in the sky, it pays to check out what’s on offer to replace it. The next one you buy may make more of a difference to your day than you might think.At a glanceBest kettle overallBoschSky kettle£100 at John LewisBest budget kettleKenwoodRipple kettle£39 at John LewisThe forever kettleDualitClassic kettle£164.99 at CurrysThe fastest-boiling kettleNinjaPerfect Temperature kettle£79.99 at NinjaBest budget variable temperature kettleLakelandDigital double-walled kettle£49.99 at LakelandWhy you should trust meWhen a friend heard I was writing this, she asked me, “Aren’t all kettles the same? They all boil water, don’t they?” And while she’s right about the second part, it took me at least 15 minutes to explain why she was wrong about the first. I’ve been testing kettles for years, and they vary greatly – in design, weight, ease of maintenance, ease of use and build quality. Some will last for decades while others will barely make it past the basic guarantee period. In short, yes, all kettles boil water – but they are far from being all the same.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach kettle was hooked up to a power meter to assess electricity consumption.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianAs you can imagine, I boiled a lot of water. Litres upon litres of the stuff. Enough to turn my kitchen into the steamiest hammam and clear my pores of blackheads I’ve had since I was a teenager.Testing wasn’t just about making gallons of tea and having a deep skin cleanse on the cheap, though. I also brought a lot of gadgets to the party: a power meter to assess electricity use for each kettle when boiling exactly one litre of water from cold; a timer to measure how long that took; and a probe thermometer to gauge how long it took for the kettle to click off once it had reached boiling point.Fancy a cuppa? My epic kettle showdown – and what I learnedRead moreExternal temperature was measured using an infrared thermometer and the highest reading noted, while maximum noise levels were recorded with the Decibel X app. After boiling, water temperature was checked at the 30-minute, one- and two-hour points to see how much it had cooled.I tested 13 kettles in total. The ones that made the cut were selected on the basis of good energy efficiency or low minimum fill, plus ease of use or maintenance. Value for money has also been considered, as have longer guarantees and durable build quality that should translate into a lengthy lifespan for the appliance. Energy costs below have been calculated based on the 1 October to 31 December 2026 price cap in Great Britain. All samples have been returned to their supplier or donated toCaterham Round Tableto raise funds for local causes and charity projects.The best kettles in 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianBest kettle overall:Bosch Sky kettleBoschSky kettlefrom£100£100 at John Lewis£100 at AmazonWhat we loveLower temperatures ideal for green tea drinkersWhat we don’t loveNot the priciest here but it’s still an investmentView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£100 at John Lewis£100 at AmazonOffering variable temperatures and a double-walled stainless-steel housing, the 3kW Sky is a brilliant blend of robust form and function. It boasts a low minimum boil (300ml, which is just over a cup), a keep-warm setting and touch controls.Why we love itI found it difficult to select a best kettle from so many that performed well, but the Bosch Sky clinched it because it’s such a good all-rounder that will suit most people. It pours well, has a button that’s within easy reach of the handle so it’s simple to open the lid without touching it, and it’s insulated so the exterior doesn’t become too hot to touch. From a design perspective, it has a more industrial feel than many others – no frippery here – but not too modern that it wouldn’t fit into most kitchens. Its display is thoughtfully designed, easy to keep clean and lights up as it heats.The exterior doesn’t get too hot (up to 40C), and while it wasn’t the fastest to boil in testing, it was only seconds behind the Dualit below. It clicked off at boiling point, and the water was still a toasty 78C 30 minutes later. At the hour point, it was 66C, and after two hours 52C, meaning you’ll spend less time and energy reboiling.It’s a shame that …its premium look ends at the handle, which seems cheap and plasticky next to the sleek aesthetic of the rest of it.Time to boil one litre:2mins 22secsMinimum fill:300mlMaximum fill:1.7lDimensions:15.8 x 23.8 x 25.8cm (WDH, inc base unit)Total weight:1.5kgPower use:0.112kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWhMatching toaster?YesMaximumnoise recorded:59dBTemperature settings:70C, 75C, 80C, 85C, 90C, 95C, 100C, keep warmWarranty:two yearsBoschSky kettlefrom£100£100 at John Lewis£100 at AmazonWhat we loveLower temperatures ideal for green tea drinkersWhat we don’t loveNot the priciest here but it’s still an investmentBest budget kettle:Kenwood Ripple kettleKenwoodRipple kettlefrom£26.10£39 at John Lewis£26.10 at AmazonWhat we loveSingle cup marking is great for a solo householdWhat we don’t loveIts base is light but also feels flimsyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£39 at John LewisFrom £26.10 at AmazonAvailable in four “ocean-inspired” shades – eggshell blue, storm blue, pure white and midnight black – Kenwood’s Ripple kettle has a subtle design that belies its affordable price. Heat retention was decent at first – 70C after 30 minutes – but after two hours, it had reduced to a tepid 41C, meaning more energy is required for a reboil.Time to boil one litre:2mins 17secs;minimum fill:500ml;maximum fill:1.7l;dimensions:22.6 x 17.1 x 24.8cm (WDH);total weight:1.6kgpower use:0.114kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWh;matching toaster?Yes;maximum noise recorded:60dB;temperature settings:100C;warranty:two yearsSmeg50s-style kettlefrom£149£149 at John Lewis£159.95 at SmegWhat we loveFeels robust while oozing styleWhat we don’t loveHigh minimum fill so you’re always boiling for twoTower Scandi kettleTowerScandi kettlefrom£25.99£25.99 at Wayfair£29.99 at TowerWhat we loveA bargain; frees up money for luxe tea and coffeeWhat we don’t loveLooks lovely but feels a bit plastickyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rachel Ogden/The Guardian£25.99 at Wayfair£29.99 at TowerBest for:an affordable luxury kettleIf the price of the two stylish kettles above has you wincing, fear not: you can bag an attractive kettle for less than £30. There’s good stuff besides the design, too: it’s lightweight (940g), has a speedy boiling 3kW element, and water windows on both sides that are marked with cups and litres.It didn’t make the final cut because …the minimum fill is 500ml, and it took six seconds to click off after reaching 100C. It’s also not very well insulated: the exterior reached 84C after boiling, and while the water temperature was 72C 30 minutes after boiling, it registered at only 44C two hours later.Time to boil one litre:2mins 21secs;minimum fill:500mll;maximum fill:1.7l;dimensions:16.5 x 25.5 x 24cm (WDH);total weight:0.9kg;power use:0.117kWh = 3p at 26.32p per kWh;matching toaster?Yes;maximum noise recorded:59dB;temperature settings:100C;warranty:one yearTowerScandi kettlefrom£25.99£25.99 at Wayfair£29.99 at TowerWhat we loveA bargain; frees up money for luxe tea and coffeeWhat we don’t loveLooks lovely but feels a bit plastickyWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenWhat key features should I look out for?How you use your kettle will probably dictate which functions you’ll find the most useful, but generally, any feature that helps to save energy is valuable. For example, kettles that are dual-walled help to trap heat inside, so the water stays warmer for longer while the outside stays cool to the touch.Those with low minimum fills enable you to boil just enough water for a single cup, so you don’t waste energy heating more than you need. Some kettles also have a keep-warm function that stops the water cooling below a certain temperature, which is ideal for those who become distracted after boiling or drink consecutive cuppas. It’s a good idea to check for safety features too, such as an auto shut-off to prevent it from boiling dry if there’s not enough water.Other features are more “nice to haves”: variable temperature models enable you to choose water heated to lower temperatures than boiling, such as 70C or 80C, for other types of tea or for filling a hot-water bottle. Concealed elements, which are easier to keep scale-free, and removable, washable limescale filters will be useful for those who live in hard-water areas. Then there’s connectivity. While wifi-enabled and voice-controlled kettles can feel a little gimmicky, they can be a gift for busy parents who usually have their hands full.Are rapid-boiling kettles faster than normal ones?Rapid-boil kettles don’t have a strict industry definition, so while a rapid-boil kettle should boil water quickly, it may not differ much from one that’s not labelled as such.A more reliable indicator of how fast a kettle will boil is its power rating: this is listed either in watts (eg 3,000W) or kilowatts (eg 2.2kW). The higher the number, the more power its element can use to heat water quickly. However, this isn’t the whole story: boiling times can also be quicker in double-walled kettles (as they lose less heat to their surroundings) and those with concealed or flat elements (which provide more surface area to heat the water than a coil).How to descale your kettleLimescale reduces your kettle’s efficiency, costing you more to boil each time, and shortening the appliance’s lifespan. Descale it monthly, especially if you live in a hard-water area. Standing water encourages the buildup of limescale, so try not to leave water in the kettle after use.While you can buy descaler in the supermarket, a lower-cost and more eco-friendly option is to combine a weak food-safe acid, such as white vinegar or lemon juice, with water. Fill the kettle three-quarters with either water and the juice of one lemon or equal parts water and vinegar. Let it soak for an hour, then boil the kettle (once for vinegar, three times for lemon). Once it’s cooled, rinse thoroughly. If your kettle has a removable filter, take it out and rinse it under running water at the same time.What material is best for a kettle?The material a kettle’s body and lid are made from can make a difference to the appliance’s durability, daily use and even the taste of your drink. The most common materials for electric kettles are plastic, stainless steel and glass.Plasticis probably the one you’ll encounter the most. It allows kettles to be affordable, lightweight – crucial if you have difficulty lifting or pouring when it’s full – and can be almost any colour or texture.Over time, though, plastic can be prone to damage, such as cracks or scratches, and can absorb odours. This means a plastic kettle will usually need to be replaced more frequently than others. Most modern models are made using food-grade plastic, are BPA-free (check websites and labels to be sure), and meet current safety standards: research remains inconclusive about health risks from using a plastic kettle.Stainless steelis another popular material for kettles. It’s hard-wearing, hygienic and resistant to corrosion, scratches and damage. Stainless steel is also a recyclable material (although the recyclability of your kettle will also depend on its construction and how easily its different materials can be separated). In terms of everyday use, good-quality stainless steel is considered to be taste neutral (although a new kettle may impart a slight metallic flavour at first).Kettles made from stainless steel tend to be heavier overall, and will become hot on the outside when boiling and for some time afterwards. They may also be louder when boiling and can stain over time.Glass kettleshave been steadily gaining in popularity – for many, watching the bubbles rise during a boil is part of the ritual. Taste-neutral – a must for tea lovers who want their blends to shine – glass kettles are usually made from borosilicate glass, just like the glassware in laboratories, which is resistant to thermal shock and rapid temperature changes. The material is also non-toxic, non-reactive and won’t corrode – plus, you can always see how much water is left.A glass kettle tends to be heavier than plastic but lighter than stainless steel. However, while glass kettles are tough enough to withstand daily use, they can still break on impact. You may also find they don’t retain heat as well as other materials, and if you live in a hard-water area, the visible limescale may lead to a more frequent need for descaling.How to know when to replace your kettleAccording to various estimates, the average kettle lasts aroundsixtoeightyears. The higher quality the kettle, the better you maintain it and how often you use it will all determine its lifespan.However, while this is a general guide, you should stop using your kettle if you notice damage, discoloration, leaks or any electrical safety issues – such as burning smells, rattling or buzzing sounds, scorch marks, sparks or exposed wires. A kettle that trips your electrics should be replaced immediately. Contact the manufacturer if you are still within warranty or to explore repairability options.Performance issues are also a sign that your kettle is failing. These can include a kettle that’s taking longer to boil, or that switches off before boiling point is reached (indicative of a faulty thermostat). Even if everything looks fine inside, if water begins to taste different, looks cloudy or has a smell, it’s time for a new kettle. Limescale that is hard to shift is another sign your kettle has to go: this points to deteriorating surfaces.What to do with your old kettleIf the kettle still works, some charities accept unwanted electrical items as donations, or you could give it to a friend. Some kettles can be repaired by the manufacturer, such as theDualit modelreviewed above, or repaired locally, so check if there’s a repair cafe or other repair resource near you.If your kettle is broken or past its best, recycling is the best option. Take it to a recycling centre, drop-off point or a store that offers a retailer take-back scheme if you’re buying a new one. Your council may also be able to pick it up at the kerbside. title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a phenomenon – but there is much more to the gaming world | Games | The Guardian
description: As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining
Content: Grand Theft Auto VI’s star-crossed lovers, Jason and Lucia, on a motorcyle.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto VI’s star-crossed lovers, Jason and Lucia, on a motorcyle.Photograph: Rockstar GamesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesGrand Theft Auto VI is a phenomenon – but there is much more to the gaming worldAs Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explainingKeith StuartWed 2 Sep 2026 15.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.04 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePredictably, the Grand Theft Auto VI “extended look” which premiered on Netflix last weekwas a success for all involved. The 30-minute preview scorched to No 1 on the viewing chart and even brought the site down for a few minutes as millions of gamers tried to watch what was, effectively, a very long teaser trailer. According to datacollated by Eurogamer, more than 9,000 Twitch streamers covered the show leading to 5,227,798 hours of viewing there alone. And this was just the beginning of what will surely be two months of escalating hype – and unprecedented media attention.Call me cynical, but I suspect the coverage of GTA VI in the media over the next few weeks will follow a familiar pattern. Mostly, it will be five-minute slots wedged in near the end of news bulletins in which games journalists, industry analysts and other pundits will be asked why the game is such a big deal, how much it cost to make and how much revenue it will generate. Perhaps a few will try to reignite the hoary old “violence in video games” debate, there will be presenters laughingly admitting they’ve not touched a game since Pac-Man, rolling their eyes and wallowing in their ignorance, in a way they never would while discussing any other art form. Somebody will venture the subversive view that “games are no longer just for kids”; somebody else will say “games make more money than films and music put together”. And that will be that, job done for another decade … or until there’s a funny story about Pokémon.I hope I’m wrong. I hope, at least, the BBC, which employs plenty of staff who understand video games, will make time in its schedule to take a good look at GTA VI – its themes and influences, its creators, its place in the wider culture of games and entertainment. Sure, arts coverage on BBC televisionhas been in declinefor years, with the broadcaster shifting this content to digital platforms, but I saw plenty of in-depth analysis of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, looking at the quality of its translation, its depiction of female characters, its use of practical effects. I didn’t see a single presenter shrugging, looking comedically bewildered and admitting they’d not read Homer since secondary school.View image in fullscreenLost Records: Bloom and Rage is one of the games that deserves a least a portion of the attention GTA gets.Photograph: Don't Nod Entertainment SAOn top of this, whatever mainstream media attention GTA VI does get it will come at the expense of covering other titles. Because, when the next video game story comes up in the wake of Rockstar’s behemoth, TV and radio editors and producers will be thinking, “Oh, we covered games last month.”The thing is, GTAisa phenomenon – it looks gorgeous, it looks vast, and it will sell many millions of copies. The series’ notoriety transcends the medium. But is it the most interesting video game since GTA V? So much has changed since then. We’ve explored the fascinating, innovative open worlds of Elden Ring, Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and No Man’s Sky (an open galaxy!); we’ve seen brutal adult themes explored in The Last of Us: Part 2 and Silent Hill; we’ve experienced dizzying narrative innovations via Disco Elysium, Split Fiction and Lost Records: Bloom & Rage. All of these deserved at least a portion of that GTA screen and radio time.True, some gameshavedrawn similar levels of media attention. Minecraft and Fortnite receive regular coverage, but almost always because of concerns over children and games addiction, or because of how they intersect with other media: Minecraft through its hit movie, Fortnite through its many collaborations with music artists. And this is the key problem. Mainstream media is still at the stage where every single games story that does make it to TV or radio has to do the job of explaining and justifying the whole industry. It’s time for programme-makers to understand that video games are a mass cultural phenomenon. Enough people play them and understand them so that they don’t have to be re-introduced every time they’re covered. And most importantly, there is life, love, art and brilliance beyondGrand Theft Autoand beyond the coming storm of hype.What to playView image in fullscreenWhat The Dub?! will definitely be revived at future family celebrations.Photograph: Wide Right InteractiveIt was my birthday a couple of weeks ago, so I set out to find a simple, fun video game that the whole family could enjoy – and I wanted to share my discovery.Inspired by Dominik Diamond’srecent columnon this very subject, I downloaded the party gameWhat The Dub?!, in which players watch old film clips with portions of the sound dubbed out and then enter their own amusing dialogue to fill the gap. The clips are then re-shown with each player’s text added to the soundtrack via a stilted robotic voice – then everyone votes on the funniest entry. It was hilarious, especially because the clips are from weird old public domain films and TV shows, so everything feels stilted and ridiculous. It’s also simple to take part, with each player using their phone to enter their dialogue choices. Apparently, it’s possible to add new clips via the Steam Workshop, the digital store’s user-generated content feature, but we didn’t figure that out. Regardless, What the Dub?! will definitely be revived at future family celebrations.Available on:PCEstimated playtime:All evening!What to readView image in fullscreenThe Sims 4 from EA, which declined to comment on reports of staff concerns.Photograph: EA GamesEA staff have beenspeaking anonymouslyto the industry-news site Game Developer about their concerns after the Saudi-led buyout ofElectronic Arts. Some are troubled by the prospect of popular games such as EA Sports FC, Madden and Battlefield being used by Saudi Arabia to distract from its poor human rights record. There are also worries about the company’s culture and job security.TV producers looking for interesting game stories that don’t involve GTA could check out Eurogamer’sexcellent articleon theNo Man’s Sky’s Galactic Hub project. It’s a community of players exploring and scientifically cataloguing specific regions of the long-running space adventure sim, like a sort of ragtag Starfleet mission. Live long and prosper, lads.As if making and marketing independent video games isn’t hard enough, several developers have reported thefts at this year’sGamescomevent in Cologne.Posting on X, Mimic creator Ryan Laley said: “Our equipment was stolen last night from the booth. Police reports have been filed. At a loss for words to describe the feeling. Just defeated. Gonna do my best with what’s left of the week. But a huge blow financially and mentally.”According to VGC, others affected included publisher iam8bit and Tessera Studios.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickGems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past – Geralt of Rivia returns after a decade in the sunHelp! I have disappeared down a rabbithole of horrible mobile gaming advertsTrainwatch – alone with your thoughts on a railway line to nowhereStar Wars Zero Company – joyfully absurd heroics with a tight-knit team of misfits | ★★★★☆Vholume – a headlong rush of parkour perfection in a brutalist wonderland | ★★★★☆Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan myth | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenA game that soars … Microsoft Flight Simulator.Photograph: MicrosoftA question fromRichardvia email:“My son, aged 6, is a big fan of aeroplanes and is really interested in flight. What games are there that could be used to entertain him, as a thing to do with me. I have (ridiculously) a PS5 and Xbox Series X – is Flight Simulator right? How about Ace Combat? Anything else?”I’d definitely recommendMicrosoft Flight Simulator, which is available on PS5 and Xbox. It can be controlled with just a joypad and you can switch off all the technical elements for your son so he’s basically just steering the craft like in an arcade game. There are lots of aircraft to fly, from tiny prop planes to passenger jets, and you can choose anywhere on Earth to explore. I love simply zooming over cities and scenic highlights, taking it all in.If you’re ok with him doing a bit of shooting,Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theveis out in October, promising highly detailed visuals and exciting dogfighting. Fans say it looks to be a highlight for the series. I’d also recommend No Man’s Sky, which is a space exploration game, but the flight feels lovely, whether you’re scorching over the surface of a planet or out in the depths of the cosmos. The controls are extremely intuitive too. If he gets into space flight, the slightly more involvedEliteDangerousis worth a look, and for an accessible combination of space flight and shooting,Everspace: Stellar Editionis a really nice option on PS5.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterGrand Theft AutoGrand Theft Auto VINetflixFilm adaptationsTwitchfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Star Wars Zero Company review – joyfully absurd heroics with a tight-knit team of misfits | Games | The Guardian
description: Split priorities between scripted and emergent story moments hamper an otherwise brilliant Star Wars-themed successor to XCOM
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Split priorities between scripted and emergent story moments hamper an otherwise brilliant Star Wars-themed successor to XCOM
Content: Star Wars Zero Company.Photograph: Bit Reactor/EAView image in fullscreenStar Wars Zero Company.Photograph: Bit Reactor/EAGamesReviewStar Wars Zero Company review – joyfully absurd heroics with a tight-knit team of misfitsPlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Bit ReactorSplit priorities between scripted and emergent story moments hamper an otherwise brilliant Star Wars-themed successor to XCOMNic ReubenWed 2 Sep 2026 10.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.10 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven if you’re unfamiliar with the term “emergent storytelling”, you’ve likely experienced some of the unscripted tales that can bubble up out of a game’s systems. Perhaps you’ve led a scheming dynasty in Crusader Kings, or watched a favourite hero succumb to madness inDarkest Dungeon. Maybe you’ve surrendered yourself to the infinite yarn-spinner that isDwarf Fortress– or read about it from the mid-00s forums where users helped popularise the term “Let’s Play” bychronicling their gamesin descriptive posts. Or perhaps you’ve played Firaxis’XCOM, the alien invasion tactics hit that several key members of Zero Company studio Bit Reactor had a hand in.Zero Company hinges on a concept as simple as it is perfect: take the complementary class abilities, tough dice rolls, and permanent character deaths of XCOM, and house them in a sci-fi setting known for spaghetti western blaster duels, last stands and heroic sacrifices. As creative director Greg Foertschputs it, “Star Wars is about loss.” Which losses you end up mourning in Zero Company depends on you.In theory, anyway. The game echoes Rogue One in its titular company of doomed misfits, but despite selling permadeath as a looming threat in the scripted tutorial, things rarely get dicey enough to put your squad in real danger. Even on its toughest difficulty, Zero Company feels reluctant to let a stray thermal detonator cut your companions’ stories short, blunting much of its potential for unscripted drama.But in lieu of heroic sacrifices, Zcom (as I like to call it) is exceptional at telling a different kind of emergent story. Ones about iron-clad camaraderie and uneasy alliances. About the time your Mandalorian medic jetted in to heal your Jedi right on time, or the begrudging “nice shot” your clone trooper paid a former enemy sniper. The script feels designed to sell your mercenaries as an inseparable, dysfunctional family. Unironically, this one really is about the friends you make along the way.Each fight is a reminder that Zero Company have each other’s backs. After an opening shot at enemy droids, you might have Kabb – a squat, bulbous alien scoundrel who speaks entirely in cutesy anastrophes – rush over and punch a hulking robot straight down a ravine. “What’s for supper? Cutty-upper!”, he declares for the third time in 15 minutes, met by some variations of “nicely done” from a random squadmate. Kabb’s still in bad shape from last turn, so you have your Astromech launch over healing stim. Kabb grabs it mid-air, slams it into his bicep, thanks the droid, and a notification tells you their bond has gotten stronger. That’ll mean a nice stat bump for them both later.As all this happens, the battlefield buzzes with noise and motion. Idle combatants trade harmless potshots, ducking behind cover. Blaster holes sizzle through steel barriers. Battle Droids mock your missed shots, babbling “oh no!” like exploding lemmings when their comrades fall. There is so much personality in the different ways characters move. Gangers scramble down ladders. Astromechs bump into crates, then jump-jet over. Jedi leap and flip, and droids curl and spin like chrome woodlice. Through it all, veteranStar Warscomposer Gordy Haab underscores every peril and triumph, paying pitch-perfect tribute to the textures of John Williams’ original score.View image in fullscreenStar Wars Zero Company.Photograph: Bit Reactor/EABetween missions, you’ll return to the Den: a streamlined but engaging take on the customisation and upgrades of XCOM’s command centre, with the hangout space of Mass Effect’s Normandy. Via a galaxy map, you’ll spend intel, collect rewards, and make tough choices about which upgrades to deny your foes. It’s also here you’ll learn about your crew’s pasts. If you’ve got the time, you can even join them on personal quests.I haven’t mentioned Zero Company’s overarching plot so far, mainly because there’s little worth mentioning. Its central threat, the Infinite Coil, are a tiresomely exoticised, first-draft cult with ill-defined goals, evidently concocted because the combat needed an enemy faction with some flavour of space magic for variety’s sake. The enemy’s reliance on healing and damage negation – a clumsy workaround for AI that can’t keep up with your team’s escalating stats and skills – results in some laborious late-game encounters.These are by far the weakest parts of an otherwise brilliant debut from Bit Reactor, however. And even when the plot falters, touching character moments join digestible, deeply human explorations of this era of Star Wars’ byzantine factional politics. XCOM’s success has influenced countless turn-based tactics games. Few have made squeezing joyfully absurd heroics out of a handful of action points feel this good. Fewer have made me grin so hard at a final lucky shot during a last-second evacuation. That’smysquad down there, after all.Star Wars: Zero Company is out now: £39.99Explore more on these topicsGamesStrategy gamesStar WarsPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XPCreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Farewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something more | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: ‘U-turn’ doesn’t do justice to the myriad ways he found to break a pledge. Now the former PM is resigning as an MP, why did I have such high hopes? asks Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: ‘U-turn’ doesn’t do justice to the myriad ways he found to break a pledge. Now the former PM is resigning as an MP, why did I have such high hopes? asks Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Keir Starmer delivers a speech in Gateshead, England, July 2022.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKeir Starmer delivers a speech in Gateshead, England, July 2022.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesOpinionKeir StarmerFarewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something moreZoe Williams‘U-turn’ doesn’t do justice to the myriad ways he found to break a pledge. Now the former PM is resigning as an MP, why did I have such high hopes?Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.02 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTShareKeir Starmer exits the British political stage as he entered it: doing the exact opposite of the thing he said he was going to do. It’s only 10 weeks since hepledged to remainas MP for Holborn and St Pancras until the next election, despite stepping down as prime minister. That’s plainly the decent course of action: a dedicated Labour man wouldn’t want to force a byelection. Even if it’s a slam dunk for the party, it inevitably draws focus and resources from more important matters. Someone who takes the business of representing constituents even a 10th as seriously as all MPs say they do would feel that the honour of those votes should be repaid.It’s a pretty boring life for an ex-PM turned backbencher. You have to keep your counsel as a large amount of blame is tacitly shovelled your way, while keeping your opinions to yourself. But that second requirement was the one thing Starmer was really good at. Once it transpired that the opinions he said out loud were open to endless revision and denial, I was never able to figure out what the real ones were.The Tories are crying U-turn atthis resignation, and technically it is – but the category needs more subdivisions to properly describe all the different ways Starmer found to break a pledge. There were the grand statements with which he came armed when he was initiallyseeking the Labour leadership: economic justice, social justice, climate justice, migrants’ rights, putting human rights at the heart of foreign policy. It would be tedious and a little depressing to track the moment at which each aim was jettisoned. Suffice it to say, these did not describe the politician he was. In fact, to be a Starmerite Version 2020 – Corbyn in a tie, basically – was enough to get you kicked out of the Labour party by 2024, and to vote in favour of policies he had once championed (ending the two-child benefit limit, for instance) was enough tohave the whip suspended. “U-turn” doesn’t really cover a deception so kaleidoscopic.There were specific reversals on policy, of course, forced by backbench rebellion (on welfare) or the first disastrous local election results (winter fuel allowance). But those didn’t feel like Starmer’s decisions so much as his having been backed into a corner. Then there were statements he made that he later claimed not to have meant. In October 2023 hetold Nick Ferrarithat Israel had a right to defend itself – even, when pressed, if that meant cutting off power and water to Gaza – thena few days latersaid: “I was saying Israel had the right to self-defence and when I said ‘that right’, it was that right to self-defence. I was not saying that Israel had the right to cut off water, food, fuel or medicines.” Not really a volte-face, more of a squirm.View image in fullscreenLabour candidate Keir Starmer canvasses in Holborn and St Pancras, London, in April 2015.Photograph: Frantzesco Kangaris/Frantzesco Kangaris for The GuardianStarmer, in short, was bad at politics in so many ways, and in ways that oughtn’t to coexist within the same politician. He wasn’t a communicator, but nor was he a meticulous or far-sighted planner. He had no backbone, and yet was incredibly rigid. He was extremely tribal in his determination to extinguish the left of his party, and yet he didn’t seem to have his own loyal tribe. None of that really matters, since he’s unlikely to trouble parliament again, but it matters what we thought we saw in him, and why.Sorry, scratch that: I have lately come to abhor the journalistic formulation “we made the following mistakes”, which I hope isn’t the start of any deeper self-reflection. These are simply mistakes I made on my own.I always claim to wantLabourto be truly pluralistic; to discuss its project and purpose meaningfully between the constituency and parliamentary levels; to vote at party conference as if it matters, rather than have its values handed to it on the last day in a carefully manicured, ultimately meaningless speech. When it came to it, though, the promise of a candidate who obviated the messiness of pluralism by satisfying every wing just enough was too appealing.There was also an internalised patriarchalism. I dismissed way too readily the voices that said it was ridiculous, in the year 2020, for the party of equality tohave never had a female leader. That absurdity wasn’t really about whether any woman in the party was better suited to the job. It was about a failure, over decades, to reflect on where that preference for a middle-class white guy was actually coming from. What qualities of steadiness, credibility and intelligence was I projecting on to him? What cosplayed status quo-ism was I hoping would be sold to the rest of the voting public?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s funny to be returning to the saying thatGeorge W Bush famously mangledin a very different political age: “Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me”. The Keir Starmer who fought the general election had already fooled his original supporters more times than they could count. It was obvious by the time he had his core team in place, with Morgan McSweeney at their helm, that it wasn’t even technocracy he was promising, it was a Blairite/Mandelsonian project much further to the right of what those politicians were flogging in the 90s. Perhaps I was hoping it was all just a feint to get into power, after which he’d rediscover his radicalism, or perhaps “hope” is just a pretty word for “I would prefer to believe than to participate”. So I’ll go along with Andy Burnham’s “hope in every heart” – it would be churlish not to – but it will be as well as, not instead of, comparing his actions with his promises.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsKeir StarmerOpinionLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: I inadvertently misled parliament over a British nuclear scandal. Now I’m calling for justice | Tobias Ellwood | The Guardian
description: Thousands of service personnel took part in dangerous cold war-era nuclear tests. The government owes them the truth – and compensation, says former defence minister Tobias Ellwood
Author: Tobias Ellwood
Headline: Thousands of service personnel took part in dangerous cold war-era nuclear tests. The government owes them the truth – and compensation, says former defence minister Tobias Ellwood
Content: A British H-bomb is tested at Christmas Island in 1957.Photograph: Christmas Island/PopperfotoView image in fullscreenA British H-bomb is tested at Christmas Island in 1957.Photograph: Christmas Island/PopperfotoOpinionMinistry of DefenceI inadvertently misled parliament over a British nuclear scandal. Now I’m calling for justiceTobias EllwoodThousands of service personnel took part in dangerous cold war-era nuclear tests. The government owes them the truth – and compensationWed 2 Sep 2026 22.30 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.07 BSTShareIn December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament. Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was “unable to locate any information” suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them. This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.More than 20,000 armed forces personnel took part in dozens of nuclear tests and nearly 600 radiation experiments, the majority between 1952 and 1967. This was for the entirety of the cold war. The science was deemed necessary. How effective were our own bombs and, just as importantly, how well could our military function if the Soviet Union used theirs against us? Test after test was conducted in the Australian desert, at Christmas Island in the Pacific, and we also sent service personnel into the atomic clouds of allies and enemies. Yet their medical records for the period are missing.Other nuclear nations, such as the US, France and the Soviet Union, did the same. Yet they acknowledged that it happened and created dedicated compensation schemes for nuclear test veterans who subsequently developed serious illnesses. Britain stands apart here. In Britain, the burden was placed on veterans to prove their case. But how do you claim what happened decades earlier when potentially vital records are missing or inaccessible?In 2007, about 1,000 nuclear test veterans and familiestook the MoD to courtseeking compensation. Pilots had been instructed to fly through mushroom clouds. Service personnel sailed and crawled through fallout. Others witnessed nuclear explosions, in some cases just two miles from ground zero. Surely our service personnel deserved better?This is where the scandal turns ugly. To deal with the veterans’ litigation, the MoD instructed the Atomic Weapons Establishment (AWE) to collate relevant documentation into a searchable database called Merlin. More than 28,000 documents were eventually assembled, covering radiation, precautions, health monitoring and what was known about the possible biological effects of the tests. Yet the veterans’ lawyers had no practical access to this vast archive. Thanks to the extraordinary investigative journalism of Susie Boniface, historical documents began emerging referring to blood and urine testing.When I saw the evidence, I raised it in November 2022 as chair of the defence committee. The MoD finally acknowledged that the AWE held copies of blood-test results and urine-radioactivity measurements for “a small number of individuals”. That took me straight back to my parliamentary answer four years earlier.I challenged the then defence secretary,Ben Wallace. If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture? He agreed that withholding relevant medical information would be “deeply wrong” and undertook to investigate.The dam was beginning to burst. Searches of Merlin for “blood” and “urine” subsequently identified 151 documents. Then another extraordinary twist. A software change meant the AWE could no longer provide a historical audit trail showing who had accessed Merlin.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlutonium levels at nuclear test site in WA up to 4,500 times higher than rest of coast, study findsRead moreIn 2024 (after the general election), the government finally ordered a discovery exercise into what blood and urine testing had taken place.Its findings, published this July, are damning. Evidence indicates that medical examinations or blood testing were required for “the majority, if not all” of Britain’s nuclear-testing period, across all three armed services. Bizarrely, the review says it found no evidence of intentional concealment.But after seven decades of incomplete answers and ministers kept in the dark, this cannot be where the story ends. Had veterans and their doctors known the full picture decades ago, cancers and other illnesses could have been diagnosed earlier. Lives could have been saved.Merlin is now being transferred to the National Archives. But declassifying 28,000 documents into the public domain will take time and is not the same as giving veterans answers. Many are now in their 80s and 90s.Given the numbers of veterans involved and the decades this has been allowed to drag on, this is arguably one of Britain’s biggest scandals – alongside infected blood, Windrush and the Post Office. It demands an apology to the nation from the prime minister, an independent tribunal to establish the truth, and a compensation scheme for veterans and widows similar to that provided in the US.These men served their country. Their country failed them. Seventy years on, veterans should not still be fighting their own government for the truth.Tobias Ellwood is a former defence minister and the author of Ten Steps to Prevent World War ThreeDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
