title: Thames Water, I refuse to pay the sewage charge in my bill while you pollute Britain’s rivers and coastlines | Jenny Jones | The Guardian
description: I will calmly read all the threatening letters and await the court case against me. But I will take a stand even if our government won’t, says Jenny Jones, a Green party peer
Author: Jenny Jones
Headline: I will calmly read all the threatening letters and await the court case against me. But I will take a stand even if our government won’t, says Jenny Jones, a Green party peer
Content: Surfers Against Sewage stage a paddle out protest against sewage pollution in Falmouth, 17 May 2025.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSurfers Against Sewage stage a paddle out protest against sewage pollution in Falmouth, 17 May 2025.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty ImagesOpinionThames WaterThames Water, I refuse to pay the sewage charge in my bill while you pollute Britain’s rivers and coastlinesJenny JonesI will calmly read all the threatening letters and await the court case against me. But I will take a stand even if our government won’tWed 2 Sep 2026 11.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.07 BSTShareIcan’t even remember when I decided to stop paying the sewage element of my Thames Water bill. It might have been after reading this headline from the Guardian in July 2025: “Serious pollution incidents by English water companies rose 60% last year,” with the subheading: “Environment Agency records 75 serious incidents among total of 2,800, with Thames Water being worst offender.”Living in London means that my supplier isThames Water, which makes a profit out of pollution. I decided that if the government wouldn’t act, I could at least do my part and not pay for this travesty.The case for not paying these outrageous charges is clear. The water companies are not fulfilling their duties and instead they are discharging raw sewage into our waterways and lives. Beyond that, they have brought in hosepipe bans, despite last winter beingone of the wetteston record, because they haven’t built enough reservoirs to store water for use in the summer.They ask us to use water wisely, and send us advice on how to cut our usage, and to consider dynamic pricing, while at the same time failing to fix the leaks thatlose about a fifthof all public supply in England and Wales. My final gripe is that a huge chunk of my bill doesn’t even get spent on fixing these problems; insteadit is spent on interest paymentsfor debts that enable Thames Water to pay shareholders billions of pounds.Nothing will change until these companies go officially bankrupt and the quickest way of ensuring that happens is if people stop paying their bills. A few decades ago millions of people did exactly that with the poll tax and the governmentbacked down. (I was taken to court over that.) So why not use the same nonpayment tactic to end water privatisation? Even a few million of us delaying the payment of our bills by several months would threaten the viability of these water companies.As a ThamesWaterbill-payer, I felt that it was hypocritical of me to be constantly campaigning on the issue and then meekly paying up. As a Green party member since 1988, and green-minded since my teens, it just seemed wrong not to take a stand.When I decided I had to do more than just speak out, I wrote to Thames Water and explained that I was very happy to pay the proportion of the bill related to their supplying me with water, but not to the proportion for their dealing with sewage. They wrote back saying that they don’t work out the proportions like that between water and sewage. And followed it up with a threatening letter and a vastly increased bill with penalty charges.Of course the real solution to this problem would be nationalising these companies. Public opinion isfirmly in favour of renationalisation, yet the government keeps trotting out a fictitious number of£100bn as the cost of taking companies over. That figure is bogus because it includes the companies’ debt as part of its value. Many argue that thenationalisation costis actuallyfar lower, possibly even zero.The government has also talked about “public control”, which is of course not public ownership, but would allow oversight of how companies are run and the ability to impose penalty charges. But if laws and oversight worked, we wouldn’t be in this mess.We aren’t holding the bosses to account for their failures. We aren’t prosecuting them, finding them guilty of illegal dumping of effluent. No need to send them to our overcrowded prisons. They can be sentenced to community service of 20 hours a week cleaning up the filth they’ve allowed into in our streams and rivers and on our seashore.None of this is new. We’ve had a Labour government for more than two years, but nothing has really changed and the bills are getting bigger while our preciouschalk streams are dying, river ecosystemsare collapsingand swimmers are beingmade ill by sewagefloating near beaches.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI will continue my own protest. The letters are unpleasant, and there has been mention of bailiffs, so I don’t recommend anyone else going into this lightly. I will calmly read all the threatening letters and await the court case against me. Despite having a seat in the House of Lords, I don’t have a lot of assets but, win or lose in court, by taking on Thames Water I know I can only win in terms of my own self-respect.I have drawn a line in the sand. And I hope to win this particular battle.Jenny Jones is a Green party peerExplore more on these topicsThames WaterOpinionWater billsWater industryNationalisationUtilitiesRiversPollutioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: Being subservient to the interests of the wealthy now means that his hands are tied, and he will be unable to tackle Britain’s most pressing issues, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: Being subservient to the interests of the wealthy now means that his hands are tied, and he will be unable to tackle Britain’s most pressing issues, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Alamy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Alamy/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donationsGeorge MonbiotBeing subservient to the interests of the wealthy now means that his hands are tied, and he will be unable to tackle Britain’s most pressing issuesWed 2 Sep 2026 06.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.06 BSTShareDamn the electorate. They’reso impatient. No sooner do they get a new leader than they want another one. Those ingrates arealreadystarting to grumble about Andy Burnham. Maybe the country isbecoming ungovernable. Perhapsit’s social media. Or a consumerist culture, always picking the next shiny thing. Perhaps we’readdicted to drama. As we’re on our sixth prime minister in 10 years, and as similar levels of discontent surface in many other countries, these claims are recited across the media. What’s wrong with us?Yet our disgruntlement is entirely rational. We give up so quickly on our prime ministers because they give up so quickly on us. Though it may involve different issues, it is always the same betrayal: the public interest is sacrificed for the sake of a tiny number of immensely wealthy people. And it tends to happen almost immediately.The latest example, which has triggered both fury and grim resignation, isBurnham’s backtrackingon his intention to cap political donations. It was hardly a radical policy: he proposed that no person would be able to give more than £500,000 to a political party in one year. That would still have granted the very wealthy disproportionate influence over our politics. I have long believed that the only fair system is one in which there should beno private donations at allbeyond a standard, fixed membership fee. Otherwise voters will always take second place to money. But at the moment there is no cap, which ensures that billionaires can buy political parties and their platforms. So a £500,000 maximum, pathetic as it is, is at least a start. In asubsequent pledge, Burnham suggested that it could gradually be lowered.Now, we are told, even this high cap has been abandoned: therepresentation of the people billwill concentrate instead on introducing Keir Starmer’s risible proposals, which are intended to limit donations sent from abroad but not from within the UK: as if billionaire donors and their wealth managers have no expertise in transferring money from one account to another. The loopholes are designed in.Burnham’s buckling on this issue is not a small matter. It cuts to the quick of what this country is and how it works. It has immense implications for democracy, for policy formation and for every other aspect of civic life. What it means is that the ultra-rich will continue to own our politics and our country. Succumb to the power of money and you will find yourself, like Starmer, tongue-tied and immobilised, unable to rise to any challenge that requires a confrontation with oligarchic might. In other words, get this wrong andevery other wrong thing follows.The official reason for Burnham’s U-turn is that trade unions objected: they have long channelled large sums into the Labour party. I doubt this is the real explanation; most of the donations Burnham received for his leadership campaigncame from large private donors. Almost half was supplied by Lord Sainsbury, who was also a major funder of the Starmer project. Union money scarcely featured.But even if Burnhamhasretreated from his promise for the sake of the unions, I believe trade union funding is also problematic. It ensures that sectoral interests are elevated above the general interest. For example, Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers. And if the unions believe that an uncapped system works for them, they are deluded. They can never match thespending power of billionaires, whose interests in most cases are diametrically opposed to those of their members.The power of the ultra-rich is now manifest in every policy governments do adopt and the policies they don’t. We see it in the new protest laws and their applications, which become more absurd by the week. Labelling protesters “terrorists” is part of a long-running programme to ensure thatno one dares protest about anythingany more. This programme has beenrolled out across the world, through model legislation drawn up by junktanks funded by some of the richest people on Earth. Just as itdid in the 18th century, an ever more extreme defence of property keeps pace with agrowing concentration of wealth.We see it in the way that datacentres have been labelled “critical national infrastructure”, enabling the government tobypass the usual planning processand impose them on communities, regardless of their impacts onlocal people’s quality of life, on water resources, energy supply and climate breakdown. Again,similar measures are being imposedin other countries at the behest of the same billionaire-funded groups. The role of governments appears to have been reduced to nodding them through.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham accused of U-turn after initially backing political donations cap to fall below £500kRead moreWe see it in the Burnham government’s insistence this summer, in the midst of shattering droughts, heatwaves and fires, onlaunching a consultationthat proposesradically curtailingthe transition to electric vehicles. I believe there is only one possible explanation for this policy: lobbying by corporations and their shareholders. Their interests appear to outweigh those of the living planet and its 8 billion people.If our country and many others are becoming ungovernable, it is not because of the people. It is because the ultra-rich have smashed the system. The electorate and the MPs who might seek to represent us pull the political levers, but nothing happens. They might replace the leader, but the new one promptly repeats the “mistakes” that caused the eviction of the old one. It makes you wonder: what threat do the oligarchs present that outweighs even the threat of losing power?Whatever the reason may be, disillusionment is an inevitable result of such betrayals. I think most people want stability. I think most people want to be able to trust their governments. We don’t like in-built obsolescence in our leaders any more than like it in our phones. I don’t want to see Burnham go the way of Starmer. But I know he will succeed only if he defends the public interest against the power of money. So what’s stopping him?George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionParty fundingKeir StarmerLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Free cholesterol tests on the NHS are great – but here’s the five-point health MOT I’d really like to see  | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: You could be walking around symptom-free and not know you’re pre-diabetic, living with hypertension or at a high risk of a heart attack, says public health academic Prof Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: You could be walking around symptom-free and not know you’re pre-diabetic, living with hypertension or at a high risk of a heart attack, says public health academic Prof Devi Sridhar
Content: A finger-prick cholesterol blood test is be offered in participating pharmacies in England.Photograph: Frederick Florin/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA finger-prick cholesterol blood test is be offered in participating pharmacies in England.Photograph: Frederick Florin/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionHealthFree cholesterol tests on the NHS are great – but here’s the five-point health MOT I’d really like to seeDevi SridharYou could be walking around symptom-free and not know you’re pre-diabetic, living with hypertension or at a high risk of a heart attackProf Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghWed 2 Sep 2026 08.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 16.46 BSTShare“An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,” Benjamin Franklin’s adage goes. Yet that simple prescription has been hard to follow in the current NHS. As has been frequentlyhighlighted, one of the biggest challenges for the health system is not just how much we spend per capita, but where and when it is spent. In England, there has been an ongoing shift within the NHS budgettowards acute hospital care– treating people in hospitals, often after they are already quite ill – while funding for primary care such as GPs has fallen.The consequence is that theNHSis increasingly paying for serious and expensive disease treatment, rather than investing upstream to prevent disease in the first place. We spend heavily on dealing with heart attacks, strokes and other life-threatening conditions, rather than identifying those who are at higher risk and intervening earlier to reduce their chances of getting ill.So, it’s excellent news that theNHS in Englandwill begin to offer free cholesterol tests, and the offer of a blood pressure check, in participating high street pharmacies for those aged 40 to 84. The nationwide phased rollout follows a pilot study in north London in which close to 2,500 patients were checked across 61 community pharmacies. Nineteen percent were found to be at high risk of a heart attack or stroke and were offered advice or referred for medical treatment.I think it’s a brilliant policy move: it is convenient, relatively inexpensive, takes pressure off GPs and hospitalsand, most importantly, can reduce preventable suffering and deaths. From decades of population-level studies, we have solid data on the factors that can help us predict the risk of serious conditions such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.There are a staggering number of health tests available (and many that are advertised to us by private companies touting “health checkups”). But I’d say (combining my public health and personal trainer backgrounds) that a small number of low-cost, simple measurements and tests are enough to provide a really useful snapshot of health status and indicate whether intervention is required, either through lifestyle change or medical support. It wouldn’t take much to offer an annual health MOT in community pharmacies.I’d start with blood pressure: a simple test reveals how much pressure circulating blood is putting on the walls of the arteries and the cardiovascular system. Hypertension (high blood pressure) is often called the silent killer because you can feel perfectly fine while internal damage is accumulating.Next I’d say a simple waist circumference measurement. This isn’t anything to do with how you look, but rather that where we store fat matters for our health, perhaps more than how much we weigh. Visceral fat, fat around our organs in the abdomen, is associated with high blood pressure, insulin resistance (linked to type 2 diabetes) and heart disease. For good health, waist measurements should stay under 50% of height.View image in fullscreenA brisk one-mile walk on a treadmill is a simple fitness test.Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty ImagesAlso a cholesterol finger-prick test, like that one now being offered. Knowing the cholesterol makeup in our blood can indicate longer term cardiovascular risk and whether dietary change or further medication, such as statins, are necessary to lower LDL (the bad) cholesterol. And while we’re pricking our fingers for blood, we could add a glucose/HbA1c finger-prick test. HbA1c measures average blood glucose over the previous two to three months and can identify those with increased risk of diabetes. Similar to hypertension, pre-diabetes and even early type 2 diabetes can be symptom-free, so tests are really useful to detect them early.Finally, I’d like to see a simple fitness test. There are many ways to measure fitness, and no quick test is perfect, but you can learn a lot from just a one-mile brisk walk on a treadmill, and checking how many press-up can be completed in a minute. The walk shows cardiovascular fitness – how effectively our lungs, heart, blood vessels and muscles work together to deliver oxygen during exercise. The press-ups check strength and muscular capacity, both of which can give a sense of overall risk of disease, as well as life expectancy.Knowing these results, plus whether someone smokes, how much they drink, their age and relevant family history, would give a rough, but pretty good, snapshot of health status in an inexpensive and accessible way. There would be some costs to roll out such tests in pharmacies, but it would surely save money for the entire system in the longer term by preventing illness and thus expensive treatments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAside from the economics, you could be walking around symptom-free and not know you’re pre-diabetic, living with hypertension or at a high risk of a heart attack. You may only find out once you’re admitted to hospital or when a disease has progressed far enough to cause symptoms and pain.That is precisely what prevention is all about. We already have annual car MOTs by trained professionals to prevent a dangerous breakdown on the highway. Doesn’t it make sense to do the same for our bodies?Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionNHScommentShareReuse this content

title: The shadow of the AfD hangs over German democracy – but I still have faith in my adopted country | John Kampfner | The Guardian
description: As I celebrate five years of citizenship, the far right is poised to take control in Saxony-Anhalt. Courage is needed to defeat it, says author John Kampfner
Author: John Kampfner
Headline: As I celebrate five years of citizenship, the far right is poised to take control in Saxony-Anhalt. Courage is needed to defeat it, says author John Kampfner
Content: Demonstration against the far-right Alternative für Deutschland in Halle, Saxony-Anhalt, 29 August 2026.Photograph: Maria Castro/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDemonstration against the far-right Alternative für Deutschland in Halle, Saxony-Anhalt, 29 August 2026.Photograph: Maria Castro/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionGermanyThe shadow of the AfD hangs over German democracy – but I still have faith in my adopted countryJohn KampfnerAs I celebrate five years of citizenship, the far right is poised to take control in Saxony-Anhalt. Courage is needed to defeat itWed 2 Sep 2026 05.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 16.36 BSTShareTwo events take place in coming days that will affect my relationship withGermany. One, which will be splashed across the media, is dark and forbidding. The other, which will pass unnoticed except by me and my close family, should have brought me joy. Now that feeling is tempered with confusion.On 6 September, voters in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt areexpectedto give Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) a resounding victory. If the arithmetic falls in a certain way, a German far-right party could assume power for the first time since the Nazis.It is possible the AfD could just fall short. That would depend on whether enough centrist parties make it over the 5% hurdle to enter the legislature. If that happens, the mainstream assortment of centre right to centre left might cobble together an unwieldy coalition.Two days after the election, I will celebrate my fifth anniversary as a German citizen. I remember the pride I felt that day in 2021. To most Britons shopping desperately around for a passport to a European Union country, it was about regaining free movement. For me it was that too, but then, as it is now, it was also emotional.Having a Jewish, German-speaking father, I had always felt a sense of unfinished business. As a young newspaper correspondent in 1988-1990 in then East Berlin, I had reported with admiration on the peaceful revolution that led to the fall of the Wall and reunification. In the ensuing years, I was drawn to a Germany that earnestly took its responsibilities towards liberal democracy. I admired the sobriety and seriousness of German society, the consensual nature of its politics, the emphasis on communitarianism. Later, I juxtaposed it with the UK of the post-Brexit years, which my German friends used to call “clown country”. I felt humiliated by Britain.When my bookWhy the Germans Do It Betterwas published in 2020, many Germans seemed bewildered. On the main morning radio programme,Deutschlandfunk, the presenter repeatedly asked me: “How could you possibly write that?” I have rarely known Germans to have much good to say about their country, even when things were going well. In recent years, amid economic stagnation and stuttering mainstream governments, the default to gloom has increased.Some of it is justified. The AfD is at the extreme end of the spectrum of European rightwing groupings, its organisation in Saxony-Anhalt and nearby Thuringiaformally labelled as extremist by domestic intelligence.The AfD’spledges on “remigration”, its downplaying of Nazi history and its warmness towards the Kremlin are but three of many alarming positions. It is also a poster child of the Trump administration, which in itsnational security strategypledged to support “patriotic” parties across Europe to help prevent “civilisational erasure”.The consequences of its rise are already evident. The coalition of centre-right Christian Democrats and Social Democrats is fractious, its reform programme from pensions to healthcare to welfare stumbling and delayed. Friedrich Merz is widelyseen to be on his last legsas chancellor, and yet his likely successor, Hendrik Wüst, premier of the most populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia, is reluctant to take on the mantle at such a bleak moment. The problems go beyond the makeup or policies of the present government (or its predecessor under Olaf Scholz). Many of the characteristics of postwar Germany long hailed as positives – coalitions, consensus, compromise – are now denounced.Public opinion is further poisoned by disinformation, aided and abetted by the Kremlin and Silicon Valley. Merz’s disappointing tenure and often acerbic manner would in a previous media environment have invited strong criticism; now the tone ranges from contempt to bile.So how do I justify my continued, if bruised, optimism? In the short term, the best to be expected is survival of the existing order: the AfD just about held off (I’d give that 50/50) in Saxony-Anhalt and in other forthcoming regional elections. Yet that’s just a sticking plaster. Longer term, rather than generalised exhortations to democracy, what is needed is a much more pugnacious approach to policymaking from the political centre, a willingness to be bolder, to take more risks.Germany was written offas the “sick man of Europe” in the late 1990s, only to restructure its economy; it was widely seen as the paralysed pacificist, only in just a few years to hike defence spending from barely 1% of GDP to be on course to hit its target of 3.5% by 2029 – streets ahead of the UK.Public opinion has been impressively robust in supporting the increase, though much less so in the former Communist east. The sacrifices required are immense: hospitals and schools could do with that money. But a vigorous public debate has transformed perceptions of the dangers posed by Russia. That’s courage, and more of that is needed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy home state is set to hand a breakthrough to the German far right. It’s a disaster decades in the making | Marcus BöickRead moreThe AfD is dominating discourse, with good reason; positives go largely unreported, because they don’t conform to the narrative of unstoppable decline. After a decade and a half of underinvestment in infrastructure,a half-trillion-eurospending spree is starting to make a difference. A strong engineering base is being redeployed in new industries,such as aeronautics.Most of all, in so many areas, community cohesion and solidarity remain strong. I’m reminded of something Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the president, said five years ago, while talking of the good Germany: “The alien, the different, the new are not rejected or excluded; they are curiously and hungrily embraced and absorbed.”Avariety of surveysshow public alarm at democratic backsliding accompanied by a determination to reinforce it, particularlyamong the young. With the AfD at the door, with the far right on the rampage in France, across Europe, and still not slain in Britain, Germany has a choice – to succumb to these forces, or to find in adversity a commitment to something better.John Kampfner is a Berlin-based author and broadcaster. His latest book, Braver New World, is published by AtlanticBraver New World by John Kampfner (Atlantic Books, £12.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)EuropeThe far rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Kemi Badenoch and the economy: a plan stuck in the Tory comfort zone  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election
Content: Kemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons on 1 September.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons on 1 September.Photograph: House of CommonsOpinionConservativesThe Guardian view on Kemi Badenoch and the economy: a plan stuck in the Tory comfort zoneEditorialThe Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last electionWed 2 Sep 2026 18.29 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.08 BSTShareTo outlast a prime minister always counts as some kind of achievement for an opposition leader, although Kemi Badenoch cannot claim credit for Sir Keir Starmer’sdownfall. Sir Keir’s wounds were mostly self-inflicted. To the extent that opposition pressure was involved, it waselectoral threatsfrom Reform UK and the Green party that stoked Labour party frustration to a regicidal pitch. The Tory leader’s role was largely as a spectator.Mrs Badenoch still hopes to use regime change to her advantage. She thinks the economy, and fiscal discipline in particular, will be her most fruitful line of attack. In their first confrontation atprime minister’s questionson Wednesday, the Conservative leader called Mr Burnham a “spendthrift” and “people pleaser” who will dodge the tough decisions required to prove Britain’s creditworthiness on international markets. She expects him to yield to Labour MPs’ demands for budget increases, which will then have to be financed with tax rises.View image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersIn that scenario, Mrs Badenoch imagines a vacancy for a rehabilitated small-state Conservative party offering hard-headed budget management, less profligate than Labour; more sober and respectable than Reform UK. That message would unite what remains of her depleted party. She can’t compete with Nigel Farage on the terrain of anti-immigrant rhetoric (although that doesn’t stop heraping his stances). She shows no interest in finding political accommodation for socially liberal, pro-European one-nation Tories who now have more in common with the Liberal Democrats than the modern Conservative party.This leaves the Tories with a narrow focus on tax cuts, reining in welfare spending and deregulation as a spur to enterprise. Mr Farage supports those things too, but Mrs Badenoch believes that Reform UK’s maverick style and the whiff of impropriety around its financial dealings make it an unreliable vehicle for a classically Thatcherite agenda that belongs, by rights, to Lady Thatcher’s own party.The claim to be the truekeeper of the Thatcherite flamehas become a ritual for Tory leaders. The mantle has passed through so many hands, it is threadbare as a political definition in 2026. It was worn most preposterously by Liz Truss, who posted photos of herself on social media recreating iconic images of the Iron Lady in her pomp. She then detonated her government with a “mini-budget” that was a crass pastiche of the economic ideas she claimed to venerate – a wild foray into fiscal irresponsibility masquerading as free-market radicalism.One of the Treasury ministers who enthusiastically endorsed Ms Truss’s plan, Andrew Griffith, wasthis week appointedMrs Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor. He replaces Mel Stride, a lower-octane performer who was deemed not to have made sufficient impact in the role. It is a revealing choice that undermines the Tory leader’s plan to make economic competence the centrepiece of her pitch to lead the nation. When considering a potential chancellor, she clearly values the ability to grab attention over economic judgment.This is consistent with a pattern of failure to engage with the full spectrum of failures over many years that accounts for the scale of Tory defeat at the last election. What Mrs Badenoch imagines to be a political strategy looks more like retreat to an ideological comfort zone in the hope that a second prime minister will self-destruct while she watches from the sidelines.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Israeli settlements: Britain can no longer look away | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: International law, European action and UK public opinion point the same way. Britain should stop helping to sustain Israeli settlements economically
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: International law, European action and UK public opinion point the same way. Britain should stop helping to sustain Israeli settlements economically
Content: An Israeli settler attacks a leftwing activist in the Israeli-occupied Palestinian village of Jannatah.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn Israeli settler attacks a leftwing activist in the Israeli-occupied Palestinian village of Jannatah.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionIsraelThe Guardian view on Israeli settlements: Britain can no longer look awayEditorialInternational law, European action and UK public opinion point the same way. Britain should stop helping to sustain Israeli settlements economicallyWed 2 Sep 2026 18.29 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.07 BSTShareIn the Commons this week, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, appeared to have accepted the principle of a trade ban between the UK and Israeli settlements, which Britain says are illegal under international law. This is long overdue. The test now is whether his promised “comprehensive reset” deserves the name. Stopping settlement-produced goods at the border is not enough. Britain should prohibit its companies fromsustainingsettlement activity – by financing, constructing, insuring, advertising – in territory whose occupation it regards as unlawful. The ban must have teeth.The UK can no longer ignore theviolence and pressureexerted on Palestinians in the West Bank by Israel’s government, military and settlers. There have been more than 1,400 settler attacks so far this year, according to the UN, against a record 1,800 registered in 2025. An election campaign has only made matters worse. Last month, Israel issued tenders for1,234 homes in the 3,401-unit E1 development east of Jerusalem. The country’s ministers gave the green light for the controversial settlement – long condemned for effectively bisecting the West Bank – expressly to “erase” the idea of a Palestinian state, the creation of which the UK officially supports.Israeli ministers havereactedwith fury, threatening retaliation if Britain imposes sanctions over settlement expansion. This is disappointing, but hardly surprising. Benjamin Netanyahu has accused countries imposing sanctions of “moral bankruptcy”. Yet Britain would be following several comparableEuropeanstates that increasingly regard such bans as a consequence of international law. Spain has banned settlement imports; Norway is legislating against trade and services linked to settlements; nine EU governments have demanded action from Brussels.View image in fullscreenEd MilibandPhotograph: Ian Davidson/SOPA Images/ShutterstockSince 1967, Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jewish people among 3.3 million Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem. There are now calls tosuspendthe EU’s trade agreement with Israel. Britain has such adealand, under Sir Keir Starmer, Labourwantedto “distinguish and protect trade with people and businesses across the state of Israel”. This gave critics reason to warn that targeting settlements could end up as a “de facto” boycott of Israel. But that gets the argument backwards: Israel cannot make the settlements part of its economy and then argue that other nations must treat them as part of the country.Mr Miliband has political room to manoeuvre. Pollingsuggeststhat even Reform UK and Conservative voters are more likely to support than oppose a settlement trade ban. In parliament there wasagreementstretching from the Greens to Labour to Tory MPs that something has to be done.Settlement expansion accelerated after Mr Netanyahu’s far-right coalition took power in 2022 and then again after Hamas’s murderous attack sparked the Gaza war in 2023. The legal case is clear: other nations are acting and the political space is opening up – all while creeping annexation becomes a reality. Israel isextendingcivilian control over occupied territory as settlements expand. Gaza, where more than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed, has understandably commanded the world’s attention. No one disputes that Israel exists in a violent and unstable neighbourhood, though its actions aggravate, rather than alleviate, that instability. But the West Bank and Jerusalem cannot be ignored. Security cannot justify an ideological land grab.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Andy Burnham must face down unions over donation cap | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Letters: It is no use promising to reform politics and return power to the people without addressing the power of the big beasts, writes Paul Sawbridge. Plus letters from Marcus Hallside and Martin Knott
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: It is no use promising to reform politics and return power to the people without addressing the power of the big beasts, writes Paul Sawbridge.  Plus letters from Marcus Hallside and Martin Knott
Content: ‘It is no use promising to return power to the people and then refuse to address the power of the big beasts of the politics of yesteryear.’Photograph: Andrzej Rostek/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It is no use promising to return power to the people and then refuse to address the power of the big beasts of the politics of yesteryear.’Photograph: Andrzej Rostek/AlamyParty fundingLettersAndy Burnham must face down unions over donation capIt is no use promising to reform politics and return power to the people without addressing the power of the big beasts, writesPaul Sawbridge.Plus letters fromMarcus HallsideandMartin KnottWed 2 Sep 2026 18.04 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTShareSo much for a new way of doing politics. Even before parliament had convened under his premiership, Andy Burnham had already stumbled at the first hurdle (Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donors, 26 August).Despite widespread support for hard caps to political donations, and despite years of affirming support for such measures, a whisper of opposition from the union lobby has produced a screeching U-turn.It is no use promising to return power to the people via devolution, employee ownership and so on, and then refusing to address the power of the big beasts of the politics of yesteryear. Come on, Andy! If you are to make any impact on reversing the appalling effects of Thatcherite neoliberalism, you are going to need to show more bottle than this. You should immediately supportStella Creasy’s amendment– and throw in a commitment to a national commission on electoral reform.Paul SawbridgeEaling, LondonThe GMB union’s opposition to a cap on political donations raises a question that goes beyond the immediate dispute: when does legitimate defence of an organisation’s interests become defence of a political system that gives that organisation disproportionate influence?Trade unionshave a legitimate role in politics. But political finance should ultimately be governed by the democratic interests of citizens, not those of organisations. The same principle must apply to wealthy individuals and corporations.There is a troubling historical precedent. In the 2010 Labour leadership election, the GMB was one of the unions that backed Ed Miliband against his brother, David. David led decisively among Labour MPs and party members, but Ed won overwhelmingly in the union section and ultimately became leaderby just 50.65% to 49.35%. The unions did not single-handedly determine that result, but their mobilisation was crucial. It is therefore reasonable to ask whether the GMB has reflected on the consequences of using its organisational power to influence Labour’s political direction.Ed Miliband’s leadership was followed by Labour’s defeat in 2015, the return of Conservative government and years of austerity. His defeat also formed part of the political sequence that culminated in the Brexit referendum. To say the unions “caused” these outcomes would be simplistic. But to pretend that their intervention had no consequences would be equally misleading.The GMB argues that a cap on donations could damage Labour’s ability to raise funds from affiliated organisations. That is institutional self-interest. But it should not be confused with the national interest. Britain needs political finance rules that reduce the influence of money and organised interests, whoever they are.Marcus HallsideRadlett, HertfordshireI am in favour of both empowering unions and capping donations. The objectives of union donors are widely different to those of the mega-rich donors. While the latter seek self-enrichment, the unions’ only aim is to enable a society where workers’ rights are upheld and a fair wage is earned, and to increase employment rates. This fits perfectly with the aims of the Labour party: to support everyday working people and provide for those who cannot work. So I say: cap at around £1m to enable unions to donate and to curb the excessive influence of the mega-rich.Martin KnottEdinburghHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: An autism or ADHD diagnosis without access to treatment is a hollow outcome | Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder | The Guardian
description: Letters: Helen Macdonald responds to a report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsman
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Helen Macdonald responds to a report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsman
Content: ‘Too many people with ADHD and autism receive a diagnosis only to find there is no evidence-based treatment pathway attached to it.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Too many people with ADHD and autism receive a diagnosis only to find there is no evidence-based treatment pathway attached to it.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderLettersAn autism or ADHD diagnosis without access to treatment is a hollow outcomeHelen Macdonaldresponds to a report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsmanWed 2 Sep 2026 18.03 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTShareThe parliamentary and health service ombudsman’s findings are stark and sadly familiar (Autism and ADHD care complaints more than triple in five years in England, 26 August). A more than 200% rise in complaints, years-long waits, patients paying thousands of pounds for private care when the NHS fails them, and a system so complex that people are routinely denied rights they are legally entitled to – these are exactly the issues that the British Association for Behavioural and Cognitive Psychotherapies (BABCP) has been documenting and raising for years.What the ombudsman’s report does not fully address is what happens once people are assessed and diagnosed. Too many people with ADHD and autism receive a diagnosis only to find that there is no evidence-based treatment pathway attached to it. Cognitive behavioural therapy is recommended by the National Institute forHealthand Care Excellence for the anxiety and depression that commonly accompany neurodevelopmental conditions, and in specific contexts for adults with ADHD itself. Yet workforce shortages mean that even where the clinical will exists, the capacity often does not. A diagnosis without access to appropriate treatment is a hollow outcome.A final report by the clinical psychologist Prof Peter Fonagy is expected soon and will inform a new national approach. It must go beyond assessment waiting times and address the full pathway, from recognition to diagnosis, treatment and ongoing support. Closing the regulatory gap that the ombudsman identifies is important. Equally important is ensuring that the services people eventually reach are staffed by clinicians with the specialist training to deliver the care that neurodivergent people need.Helen MacdonaldSenior clinical adviser,BABCPHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Banning nuts from the skies would not keep people with allergies safe | Allergies | The Guardian
description: Letter: Alison Smith says food bans do not improve compliance, they create a false sense of security in patients
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Alison Smith says food bans do not improve compliance, they create a false sense of security in patients
Content: ‘Last summer I spent six hours compulsively cleaning on a demonstrably filthy flight.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Last summer I spent six hours compulsively cleaning on a demonstrably filthy flight.’Photograph: AlamyAllergiesLettersBanning nuts from the skies would not keep people with allergies safeAlison Smithsays food bans do not improve compliance, they create a false sense of security in patientsWed 2 Sep 2026 18.03 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTShareAs the mother of a child with anaphylactic allergies, I am sympathetic to the terror that Lucy Pasha-Robinson describes (Food allergies when flying are no joke. That’s why nuts should be banned on planes, 27 August). Indeed, last summer I spent six hours compulsively cleaning on a demonstrably filthy flight. Flight crew handed out wipes to passengers “to clean your tray tables”, then proceeded to serve packets of cashews (my child’s anaphylactic nut) with drinks. My nerves were shredded by the time we arrived in Chicago.However, I am firmly against the banning of nuts from the skies.Foodbans do not improve compliance, and they create a false sense of security in patients.Because my son’s most severe anaphylactic allergy is not nuts but lentils (which, like peanuts, can be airborne and serious from the tiniest quantities), we have had to learn to live with risk. Time and again, I note his allergies on intake forms, only to be blithely reassured that “we are a nut-free setting”, as if that constituted a proper allergy-protection policy. Instead, I am the helicopter parent boarding flights early with gloves and wipes, deep cleaning our entire row before we sit down.My son knows not to accept food from others and to touch nothing on board until I give the all-clear; we pack meals, pillows and blankets for every flight; brief every flight crew on his allergies and the location of our EpiPens; and, from the age of three, practised administering Epi at least once a month. We will never travel fear-free, but we feel the fear and travel anyway.Alison SmithWorcester Park, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Content: Daffodils in churchyard at Holt in Norfolk.Photograph: David Burton/AlamyView image in fullscreenDaffodils in churchyard at Holt in Norfolk.Photograph: David Burton/AlamyBrief lettersDeath and dyingLettersDon’t shy away from the language of lossWords of condolence | Autumn versus winter | More fitting namesWed 2 Sep 2026 18.03 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 19.08 BSTSharePolly Hudson writes about how people don’t know what to say to the bereaved (26 August). Trust me, the bereaved don’t either. My parents died in a car crash. I watched people sheer away in absolute mind-numbing embarrassment, not because they didn’t care, but because they were afraid they would make it worse. Well, you can’t make it worse, trust me. And we’re not looking for poetry. A simple “I’m sorry for your loss” is perfect.Isobel CassidyArdtrasna, County Sligo, IrelandIt seems appropriate to write about grief following a bereavement to thank the fellow Guardian letter writers who have contacted me via the letters editor. Their kind words have really helped me over the last few weeks, and are read and reread on a regular basis.Ian GrieveGordon Bennett, Llangollen canalMy husband, Bob, who died in 2017 from motor neurone disease 20 months after diagnosis, said he found that people who asked “How are you today?” were aware that some days are less shit than others.Helen KeatsBrighstone, Isle of WightAutumn is a wonderful season, but it’s even better in the bleak midwinter (Letters, 31 August).Andrew CarrollCastletimon, County Wicklow, IrelandI used to resist the temptation to read any letter about nominative determinism. title: Joey Ramone smiling! And having fun! At the beach! Roberta Bayley’s best photograph  | Photography | The Guardian
description: ‘Joey didn’t surf. And he didn’t like this photo. He said, “You made my legs look thin.” Like it was my fault he had skinny legs’
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: ‘Joey didn’t surf. And he didn’t like this photo. He said, “You made my legs look thin.” Like it was my fault he had skinny legs’
Content: ‘Eddie Vedder has a copy’ … Joey Ramone, Coney Island, 1977.Photograph: Roberta BayleyView image in fullscreen‘Eddie Vedder has a copy’ … Joey Ramone, Coney Island, 1977.Photograph: Roberta BayleyMy best shotPhotographyJoey Ramone smiling! And having fun! At the beach! Roberta Bayley’s best photograph‘Joey didn’t surf. And he didn’t like this photo. He said, “You made my legs look thin.” Like it was my fault he had skinny legs’Interview byDave SimpsonWed 2 Sep 2026 14.46 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.07 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first band I ever saw were the Beatles, on 19 August 1964 at the Cow Palace Arena near San Francisco. I was 13. I remember every 29 minutes of it: 17,000 screaming girls making a deafening din and thousands of flashbulbs going off at once, lighting up the entire stadium. I’d been a Beatlemaniac since seeing a clip of them at the London Palladium on the Jack Paar show, then live on the Ed Sullivan show. I bought magazines with them in and wondered what kind of person took the photographs. So my first forays into photography were taking photographs of photographs of the Beatles with the primitive family Kodak.When I was 15 I took a very basic photography class, but later, after three years of college, I dropped out, sold my Nikon and went to England. I started dating Ian Dury, then after we broke up, a friend gave me a one-way ticket to New York where I started going out withRichard Hell, whose band Televisionplayed CBGBsevery Sunday night. Richard and I split up on good terms, and he asked me to take pictures of him. My first was the famousfake blood photo of the Heartbreakers, the band he formed with Johnny Thunders and Jerry Nolan from the New York Dolls. Richard suggested captioning the poster “Catch them while they’re still alive” because they had a nefarious reputation.double quotation markBuried to the right is a Schaefer beer can, a New York drink that’s no longer made, which is a cool touchIn January 1976, I started taking pictures for Punk magazine. I was working the door at CBGBs by that point, so I was always in a position to take photos of the bands playing there: Television, Talking Heads, Blondie and, of course, the Ramones. Sire Records paid me $125 to shoot them against a wall fortheir first album cover. We were friends, so there was no hair or makeup and I wasn’t telling them how to pose. I shot three rolls of film and one shot happened to be perfect, but my most popular photo is this one of Joey on the beach at Coney Island.Snapshots: the covers of Punk magazineRead morePunk magazine did a “fumetti” – an Italian style of comic strip – starring Joey and Debbie Harry as star-crossed lovers, with speech bubbles in their photos. Andy Warhol was the mad scientist and [music journalist] Lester Bangs played a biker. John Holmstrom dida drawing of Joey for the cover. This Joey photo wasn’t used because he was smiling at the camera – breaking the fourth wall – but it’s just kind of a perfect picture. It’s unusual because he’s carrying a surfboard and Joey didn’t surf! We were just having fun at the beach. There’s a childlike aspect because he was shy. Looking like that, he knew there was no other path for him than rock’n’roll, so he’d got in a band as soon as he could.I’d read that for shooting outside you should use Plus-X film, but this session is the only time I ever used it. Most photographers used Tri-X, because you got a better range of light and dark. Buried to the right of Joey is a Schaefer beer can, a New York beer that’s no longer made, which is a cool touch. Joey didn’t like the photo – he said, “You made my legs look thin.” Like it was my fault he had skinny legs.Summer and smoke: rock’n’roll in the warmer months – in picturesRead moreAlso, the Ramones never smiled. Sire used a vertical shot from my album session where they’re smiling, with the caption: “The Ramones: they’re so punky, you’re gonna love them.” They wanted them to be this cute band that would appeal to Bay City Rollers fans, but Joey went, “No way. Bury that picture. Never use it again.” After that they never smiled in photographs again, but I have this one on top of my bookshelf and it makes me very happy. I think other people like it for the same reason.I sell more of it than the album cover photo. Eddie Vedder has a copy. Karen O has one in her kitchen. Andrew Watt, the superstar producer of Paul McCartney and the Rolling Stones, has it. I never wanted to become a professional photographer taking pictures of people I don’t know. For 98% of my career I never got paid but I had a lot of fun. I was just taking photographs of my friends.Roberta Bayley is the recipient of the Icon award at the2026 Abbey Road music photography awards. This year’s winners will be revealed at the awards celebration on 24 September at Abbey Road Studios, LondonView image in fullscreenRoberta Bayley’s CVBorn:Pasadena, California, 1950High point:Maybe taking the Ramones’ album coverTop tip:Photograph what you really like, because then if you’re not successful, at least you’ll have photographs of what you loveExplore more on these topicsPhotographyMy best shotThe RamonesPop and rockPunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From petrol pump attendant to Dylan-feted rocker and Judd Apatow muse: the delightfully unlikely life of Graham Parker | Music | The Guardian
description: Fifty years ago Parker was hailed as rock’s next big thing, but he picked a different path: cult records, a Hollywood diversion, an aversion to stardom. Ahead of a UK tour, he looks back at his strange trajectory
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Fifty years ago Parker was hailed as rock’s next big thing, but he picked a different path: cult records, a Hollywood diversion, an aversion to stardom. Ahead of a UK tour, he looks back at his strange trajectory
Content: ‘I realised I don’t have to go out and grab the audience by the lapels, I can talk to them’ … Graham Parker.Photograph: Dion OgustView image in fullscreen‘I realised I don’t have to go out and grab the audience by the lapels, I can talk to them’ … Graham Parker.Photograph: Dion OgustMusicInterviewFrom petrol pump attendant to Dylan-feted rocker and Judd Apatow muse: the delightfully unlikely life of Graham ParkerAlexis PetridisFifty years ago Parker was hailed as rock’s next big thing, but he picked a different path: cult records, a Hollywood diversion, an aversion to stardom. Ahead of a UK tour, he looks back at his strange trajectoryWed 2 Sep 2026 15.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo say Graham Parker enjoyed a swift rise to fame is an understatement. He played his first live show with his most famous backing band, the Rumour, in October 1975, at the Newlands Tavern, a pub in Nunhead, south-east London. By the start of the following year, he had a record deal and was in the studio recording his debut album, Howlin’ Wind. The buzz around him was such that the sessions were interrupted by the arrival of a succession of stars – Thin Lizzy’s Phil Lynott among them – intrigued to hear what the fuss was about: a petrol pump attendant from Surrey who sang like Van Morrison and had written a set of smart, sharp, literate songs in between filling up cars.The record arrived in April 1976 to vast critical excitement, a lot of it occasioned by the album’s closing track, the reggae-influenced, attitude-laden Don’t Ask Me Questions. After Howlin’ Wind came out, followed in October by Heat Treatment, things ratcheted up another notch. Parker turned up in Australia to discover the media waiting for him and a press conference arranged in the airport: they had taken the amount of music press coverage Parker was receiving to mean he was “as big as Bruce Springsteen, which was insane”. Low down on a festival bill topped by Bob Dylan, he found himself backstage collared by the headline act, eager to tell Parker how much he loved his work. There also exists a photo of Parker in Los Angeles, with, of all people, Michael Jackson, but their meeting was apparently less successful. “I said to him: ‘Michael, great to meet you, I did a version of [Jackson 5 hit] I Want You Back recently.’ And he just sort of said: ‘Ooh.’ So that,” he laughs, “was the full extent of my conversation with Michael Jackson.”View image in fullscreen‘I’d infused myself with this rather melodramatic idea that I was the kiddy’ … Graham Parker in January 1976.Photograph: Ian Dickson/RedfernsIn truth, Parker seemed an unlikely candidate for a saviour of rock. He was short and wiry, a former hippy who had taken himself off to Morocco in his teens and served time in a band called Terry Burbot’s Magic Mud: “My idea,” he sighs, “a burbot being a fish that I knew had become extinct in England because Angling Times offered £100 to anyone who could prove they’d caught one.” On returning, he went back home to Deepcut in Surrey, shorn of his “arse-length” hair, writing songs influenced not by prevalent trends (“I thought progressive rock needed to be destroyed thoroughly”), but the music he’d loved in his youth: Motown, soul, ska, “pop hits on the radio”.On today’s video call from his home in upstate New York, ahead of a UK tour, Parker’s eyes are shielded by tinted sunglasses. Decades ago, dark glasses were his permanent look, which helped give Parker the air of a man who was almost disproportionately angry, or at least a lot angrier than his songs suggested he was. On Howlin’ Wind, he spat out the lyrics of Lady Doctor as if they were a ferocious broadside against the establishment, rather than about fancying a female GP. “Correct,” he nods. “If you went to see a band in the suburbs back then, the audience sat cross-legged, so I thought, we’ve got to do the opposite, get people up and dancing instead of sitting. So I just went out and yelled.”The thing was, Parker didn’t seem to think his sudden rise to fame was at all unlikely. He may have looked a little incredulous in the photo of himself backstage with Dylan, but that was the exception. “Oh no, I was brimming with confidence,” he says, smiling. “I’d infused myself with this rather melodramatic idea that I was the kiddy, you know: I’m going to be the one who shows people something that can be done – attitude, great lyrics that say something, a tight band. I got an instant record deal, I was getting all this attention and none of these people who’d been slogging around the pubs for years were. I remember one of the early gigs we did, the great Ian Dury and his minder, Fred ‘Spider’ Rowe, standing in front of the stage wearing sunglasses, trying to put the mockers on me. I thought: I’m having a great effect here. This is good! I can’t help being this good, you know!” He suddenly looks a bit concerned at revealing his youthful cockiness. “I hope,” he says quietly, “you can write this up with some humour in it. I do know I was being an idiot.”Graham Parker and the Rumour: Hey Lord, Don’t Ask Me Questions – videoOf course, Parker never quite became the huge star everyone seemed to think he would be in 1976. Instead, he carved out a fascinating 50-year career as a critically lauded, cult singer-songwriter whose work has ranged wildly. He recorded an album of obscure Lennon and McCartney songs with Kate Pierson of the B-52s; published novels and short stories; and maintained a pretty startling level of quality control over the course of 47 albums, despite his belief that “you should press the reset button” with every new release. His most recent, 2023’s Last Chance to Learn the Twist, was a delight, a live-sounding collection of songs that range in style from soul to prewar pop.His career has also regularly involved Parker doing the exact opposite of what one might have expected under the circumstances. In the late 70s, dissatisfied with his then record label, Mercury, he terminated their relationship by releasing Mercury Poisoning, a spectacularly withering song that, among other accusations, suggested the label “couldn’t sell kebabs to the Greeks” (“a bit literal,” he concedes today). His commercial stock rising in the 80s US, thanks to 1979’s superb Squeezing Out Sparks album, he signed a deal with Atlantic Records, whose chair Ahmet Ertegun suggested he make his next album sound “like Phil Collins”. Parker proceeded to make the deliberately rough-hewn The Mona Lisa’s Sister: a wonderful collection of songs utterly out of step with mainstream 80s rock trends, that, one can’t help but notice, has aged rather better than most mainstream 80s rock.View image in fullscreenStardom … Graham Parker and the Rumour performing at Reading festival in 1977.Photograph: Odile Noel/AlamyIn 2012, he unexpectedly found himself in Hollywood at the behest of Judd Apatow, a long-term fan: a golden opportunity that might nevertheless have given another artist pause, given that Parker was required to play himself in This Is 40, one of a plethora of underperforming artists who Paul Rudd’s record label honcho character has put his faith in. “He’s signing all these losers from the 70s and 80s. He’s got Haircut 100, and Frank Black without the Pixies, and me,” Parker says, chuckling. “When Judd told me, I said: I can do this, I could destroy his record company instantly, mate. I’m in.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I knew it was over for us’: the bands who got left behind when punk explodedRead moreHollywood was another entirely unexpected state of affairs. “For me, small timer, quite happy with his little career – playing grungy little solo gigs, doing records my way with no one interfering – to suddenly become this actor, pop singer thing, I didn’t see that coming. I ended up sitting in a dressing room with John Lithgow and Paul Rudd and Megan Fox, thinking, I should call a cab, I don’t belong here. But I sank into it pretty good. Being flown to Hollywood to do talks, first class, put up in these amazing hotels … I’m suddenly somebody, for five minutes. But it was a long five minutes, because the film went on and on in America, it was shown for months.”Parker does, indeed, seem perfectly contented with his little career, grungy solo gigs and all: that’s exactly what he’s doing in the UK this month. For all his vaulting ambition in his early 20s, he is not sure that he was really cut out for fame. “The little bit of stardom I had, when everyone’s after you, everyone’s trying to grab you, that crept in and it was quite unpleasant really. Record labels start giving you too much money for music that I knew wasn’t for everybody and probably wasn’t going to burst out in platinum sales. I ended up telling my manager, tell them to pay me half what they’re offering. Which is weird, I know, but I think I did the best thing.”View image in fullscreenFar from the end … Parker performing in New Jersey in 2019.Photograph: Lisa Piernot/Zuma Wire/ShutterstockIndeed, he is a vociferous advocate for keeping things small-scale. “I can pull a crowd, I can do it without the costs of a band, and it taught me to sing – I realised I don’t have to go out and grab the audience by the lapels, I can talk to them.” Although he has caveats. His mordantly funny 2001 song I’ll Never Play Jacksonville Again details the true story of a gig at which Parker ended up playing to “two couples, two barmen who looked like Ted Nugent, and a guy who looked a bit gormless and kept staring at one of the women’s legs until her boyfriend head-butted him. Five people in the audience and there’s a fight! How fucking often does that happen, man? I thought, this is the end.”He says he’s been true to the song’s title and never played Jacksonville again. “But only because nobody’s offered me a gig there. If the money’s good enough and there’s two other gigs nearby, maybe I’ll do it. And I’ll do that song. It’ll be fun.”Graham Parker is atWaterside Arts, Sale, on 8 September,then touringuntil 1 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Everything countercultural is doomed, isn’t it?’​ Sofie Royer, the bracingly brilliant pop star pondering life’s big questions | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Referencing Tarkovsky and French theory, the Austrian-Iranian singer is writing some of today’s wittiest music – though she’s ‘too pop for the art world, too indie-darling for the mainstream’
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Referencing Tarkovsky and French theory, the Austrian-Iranian singer is writing some of today’s wittiest music – though she’s ‘too pop for the art world, too indie-darling for the mainstream’
Content: ‘I don’t have a lot of stage fright’ … Sofie RoyerView image in fullscreen‘I don’t have a lot of stage fright’ … Sofie RoyerPop and rockInterview‘Everything countercultural is doomed, isn’t it?’​ Sofie Royer, the bracingly brilliant pop star pondering life’s big questionsBen Beaumont-ThomasReferencing Tarkovsky and French theory, the Austrian-Iranian singer is writing some of today’s wittiest music – though she’s ‘too pop for the art world, too indie-darling for the mainstream’Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.08 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.51 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou wait ages for a brilliant pop song about film-making and then two come along at once. Following on from Charli xcx’sCameracomes Actress by Sofie Royer, with lyrics referencing rotoscoping, call sheets, screenplays, establishing shots, cinéma verité and more. “When the dust settles on your heart / I’d like to audition for the leading part,” she purrs over pumping disco, screwball-funny as she stacks up the metaphors to woo some Letterboxd-brained beau. “My mise-en-scène is flawless, don’t you know I’m quite adored / I’ll win you over in 35mm 4K-restored.”It’s a typically smart and witty number from a singer, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and, as it happens, aspiring actor, whose erudition and taste light up one of the best albums of the year, the forthcoming Before/After. Its lead singleCowboy Mouthis a recreation of a Sam Shepard play in song;another songmakes a catchy funk-pop chorus from the word “sesquicentennial”. Her music is cosmopolitan enough to sit Italo disco next to new wave and garage rock, and across her discography there’s a big cast of cultural figures from Andrei Tarkovsky to Kenneth Anger, Luigi Mangione to Ivy Wolk, knowingness offset by her keen sense of humour.“Maybe I’ve just spent too many years on [academic journal database] Jstor, but I love a good reference, right?” she says, having studied philosophy, psychology and English for a teaching degree. “Paying attention to references is one of the coolest things that you can do: a little keyhole into another piece of knowledge.”Royer seems to ask me as many questions as I ask her during a bracingly intellectual video call from her apartment in Vienna, where she smokes elegant slim cigarettes in front of a tasteful array of paintings and furniture. After an unusually itinerant life, she is relatively settled in the city.Now 35, she was born in the US to an Austrian mother and Iranian father, who were IT workers in California, then spent her high-school years in Vienna and attended a conservatoire thanks to her brilliance on violin. It left her with a musical mindset that is “very classically based”. She says she wouldn’t call herself a singer-songwriter. “I struggle with even calling myself a singer!” But, she says, “if you’re doing violin solos [as a child] you have to want to be on stage. So I don’t have a lot of stage fright – for all that I couldn’t really sing when I released my first record, I was just like, whatever, it’s like karaoke with my own songs.”Aged 19, still long before she started writing songs, Royer went back across the world to work in Los Angeles at record label Stones Throw. Did she feel American again? “That’s a really hard question. If you come from a mixed background, and then you’re socialised in a third country, you aren’t ever really belonging to one place. I’m always just ‘part-’, right?”View image in fullscreenOut of place … Sofie Royer.Photograph: Oskar BurgerShe’s also aware of how a mixed identity such as hers can be parcelled up and sold. She cites a recent sarcastic lyric she admires byCharli xcx– “My heritage could give me quite the USP” – and frowns at the concept of female-only DJ nights. “I think you want to be a musician regardless of gender and heritage. I know it’s not fully possible, but I would love for some of the arts to just remain, at least in some small essence, a rare apolitical kind of structure. I love the surreal; I love things that extend beyond the imaginable.”After LA came another move, to London, as one of the first employees at Boiler Room, which has since become one of the world’s biggest music startups thanks to its brand-partnered livestreams of DJ sets. Boiler Room ultimately took on major investment cash, and isseen as having sold outby many in the underground. “There just wasn’t a necessity to scale up in that way,” she says. “It’s a bummer because it makes you think: everything [countercultural] is kind of doomed, isn’t it?”While working there, Royer’s mother was diagnosed with cancer. An only child, Royer quit and moved back to Vienna to care for her and start her degree (plus another one, in painting, left incomplete). Alongside state-funded therapy, songwriting became a way to process. “I was singing a lot of karaoke around that time in the basement of my art university, and then one thing led to another. It was a real way for me to escape. When I’m monkey-cymbal-clapping brain, when every sense is kind of occupied, it’s when I’m playing something and singing to it.”View image in fullscreen‘Very few professions are as measured in metrics as people working in the arts’ … Sofie Royer in a still from the video for Actress.Photograph: Eliott FettweisHer debut album, Cult Survivor, was released in 2020, but performing it live “was like reopening an old wound”, so she started broadening her writing. She dressed up as a pierrot character for 2022’s Harlequin, “a different persona to help me get over the fear of being perceived as a singer on stage, maybe”, and based 2024’s Young-Girl Forever on a French philosophical tract about culture’s obsession with young women. “The beauty of age is that you care less and less about it. You couldn’t pay me to go back to my 20s.” She reconsiders. “I mean, you could pay me, because I’m self-employed, so I’m down for money.”She is much admired by her peers, with Lana Del Rey, Air and LCD Soundsystem all getting her to support them on tour, but she’s not headlining the same venues. She addresses that relative lack of financial success and fame uproariously on the new album. “Always a nominee, never a winner / The longer I keep this up the less I can afford dinner,” she sings on Sold Out the Jazz Club, just one of many references across the album to how Royer is, as that song’s chorus has it, “too pop for the art world, too indie-darling for the mainstream”.“Very few professions are as measured in metrics as people working in the arts,” she says, “specifically music, and these metrics are publicly available” – Spotify listeners, tickets sold. “And not only that, then you’re being interviewed: ‘Where do you see yourself in five years? What does success mean to you?’ That’s what I wanted to perhaps release when it came to these songs.”She has also released herself from therapy, singing “I spent five years on that couch, and I’m not ever going back again” on another new song, C’est la D. “I was actually in therapy for longer than five years, but it just sounded so cool to sing five instead of seven,” she deadpans.She says she certainly needed therapy to begin with, but when she reached the cap to her free hours from the Austrian state, her therapist said she could continue, but he didn’t think she needed it any more. She agreed with him: “We as humans have a certain semblance of resilience, but there’s a lot of financial value placed in today’s market of psychoanalysis. In a lot of other cultures, that maybe aren’t as socialist as the one I currently enjoy living in, there’s more value in keeping somebody unhappy and dependent on therapy for the rest of their life.”‘The beast inside me wants to move!’ The smart, slapstick world of Audrey Hobert, the Steve Martin of popRead moreFinally a full-time musician (“a lot of it is an email job”), she is also branching into acting after a cameo in the 2024 remake of erotic dramaEmmanuelle, playing a bar singer (though a scene opposite Naomi Watts, who was “an absolute delight”, didn’t make the final cut). She’s been making two films with Austrian director Jasmin Baumgartner, a former student of Michael Haneke: Too Hot to Die, a satirical comedy about a reality dating show, and the bigger-budget dramedy Sentimental Fail Club. “I’m not there for myself; I don’t have any demands or wishes when I’m acting,” she says of its appeal. “You’re just the paintbrush and the film is the canvas. You’re just an element in somebody else’s artistic vision.”For all the many-layered meanings and references in her multi-faceted career, she’s also a dab hand at a straightforward love song, such asOpium, in which she compares her affection for her boyfriend to the drug’s high: “A hundred years is nothing with it, I want more,” she sings. Even here, though, there’s a dash of art-historical analysis. “That one just felt like such a direct, honest song,” she says. “And also, like, structurally dadaist. So it made the cut.”Before/After is released via Stones Throw on 4 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsPop and rockCharli xcxfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Messy, clever and can barely conceal its rage: is Furious the most outstanding TV show of the year?  | Television | The Guardian
description: The story of a serial killer taking revenge on the rich predatory men who abused her just earned a fantastic finale. With career-defining acting, daring Epstein parallels and super dark comedy, it’s a total must-watch
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: The story of a serial killer taking revenge on the rich predatory men who abused her just earned a fantastic finale. With career-defining acting, daring Epstein parallels and super dark comedy, it’s a total must-watch
Content: ‘Five feet tall with her fuckin’ socks on’ … Lola Petticrew as revenge killer Catherine Grace.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyView image in fullscreen‘Five feet tall with her fuckin’ socks on’ … Lola Petticrew as revenge killer Catherine Grace.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyTelevisionMessy, clever and can barely conceal its rage: is Furious the most outstanding TV show of the year?The story of a serial killer taking revenge on the rich predatory men who abused her just earned a fantastic finale. With career-defining acting, daring Epstein parallels and super dark comedy, it’s a total must-watchRebecca NicholsonWed 2 Sep 2026 15.17 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.21 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou could easily watch the first few minutes of Furious without knowing that it would turn out to be so special. It opens with a scene of pure horror: it’s Halloween night and a real monster is hiding among the pretend ones. A woman we come to know as Catherine Grace (an astonishingly good Lola Petticrew) is inside a man’s house, wearing a creepy kitten mask. The man is in bad shape, crawling on the floor, gasping for air and begging for his life. Catherine is alternately chirpy and tender with him, but eventually, she loses her patience with his pleading. She takes a syringe filled with fentanyl out of a pencil case decorated with sparkly stickers and jewels and finishes the job.So far, so creepy crime drama, but Furious is already hiding in plain sight, because the monster is not who we think it is. What looks as if it will be a cat-and-mouse story, in which a tenacious FBI agent hunts a twisted serial killer, quickly rips up any expectations. We learn that Catherine was trafficked into sex work as a teenager, and is now making her way through a kill list of predatory and powerful men. Her life has been shaped by a conspiracy of abuse, violence, neglect and indifference. She has decided to take matters into her own broken hands.View image in fullscreenThe role of her life … Emmy Rossum as FBI agent Alice Black.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyThe case finds its way to the desk of Alice Black (Emmy Rossum, in the role of her life), a tough former NYPD homicide detective turned recent FBI recruit. Her boss, Nora Washington (an equally excellent Quincy Tyler Bernstine), is the head of the sex crimes and crimes against children unit. She drinks to cope with the horrors she has to witness on a daily basis and is in possession of the darkest sense of humour on TV. She sees the potential, and pain, in Alice, and puts her to work. But as the series progresses, we see what it demands of them both to pursue justice, when they are repeatedly told to step back and stand down.View image in fullscreenExcellent … Quincy Tyler Bernstine as Nora Washington.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyIt is hard to think of a recent drama that has placed quite so much trust in the intelligence of its audience. Every character here is flawed. It has moral ambiguity baked into its core. Alice left the NYPD after being beaten by her cop ex-boyfriend Marshall Connelly (a truly sinister Jake Lacy). She has been ostracised by most of their former colleagues, who either do not believe her or, more likely, do not care. She is suffering from a complex response to trauma, and Furious does not shy away from depicting those complexities. It is a raw and unusually vivid portrait of women and PTSD.When Alice begins to investigate Catherine and her crimes, Furious becomes a big, bold examination of justice, and what that might look like for women who have no access to it. It can barely conceal its rage, and by the final episode, few would expect it to.
