Catherine, and countless other young girls like her, have had their lives stolen and destroyed by men who believed themselves to be invincible. “I didn’t get to decide a fucking thing about my life,” she shouts, in one of the series’ most devastating scenes.There is an obvious timeliness to this story, which may be one of the reasons why it is capable of landing such a blow. The Epstein parallels are not subtle, nor are they intended to be. The rich buy people off to cover up their terrible deeds. They operate in plain sight, daring people to catch them. There is an important photograph of trafficked teenage girls with older, wealthy men. One can only imagine if this show will pop up on the Mountbatten-Windsor streaming queue.View image in fullscreenPower reclaimed … Lola Petticrew’s Catherine poses as a waitress.Photograph: Sarah Shatz/DisneyBut what Furious provides is a fantasy of power, reclaimed and repurposed for the women who have had it taken away from them, if they ever had it at all. One cop describes Catherine as “five feet tall with her fuckin’ socks on”; that she can overpower her victims is something of a fantasy in itself. The finale has a near-impossible task in that it needs to maintain the bleak spirit of the story, while offering some sort of relief, or reward, for the women we have come to care so much about. It pulls it off by allowing for some magical thinking, while never veering too far from the grim reality of the situation. Some men pay for what they have done, whether formally or off the books. Some are given medals for their criminal behaviour. As messy as it is, the resolution is satisfying enough. Justice was never going to be clean.Furious is a clever show. It works as a straightforward thriller, gripping and tense, using a murder mystery and a manhunt to expose an institutional conspiracy. It is also an emotionally astute act of catharsis, and this fantasy of revenge can feel, at times, like a much-needed balm. It has been renewed for a second season already. No wonder. It is one of the year’s most outstanding shows, and, after all, there are plenty more monsters out there.Furious is on Disney+ in the UK and Australia and Hulu in the USExplore more on these topicsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a phenomenon – but there is much more to the gaming world | Games | The Guardian
description: As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining
Content: Grand Theft Auto VI’s star-crossed lovers, Jason and Lucia, on a motorcyle.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto VI’s star-crossed lovers, Jason and Lucia, on a motorcyle.Photograph: Rockstar GamesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesGrand Theft Auto VI is a phenomenon – but there is much more to the gaming worldAs Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explainingKeith StuartWed 2 Sep 2026 15.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.04 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePredictably, the Grand Theft Auto VI “extended look” which premiered on Netflix last weekwas a success for all involved. The 30-minute preview scorched to No 1 on the viewing chart and even brought the site down for a few minutes as millions of gamers tried to watch what was, effectively, a very long teaser trailer. According to datacollated by Eurogamer, more than 9,000 Twitch streamers covered the show leading to 5,227,798 hours of viewing there alone. And this was just the beginning of what will surely be two months of escalating hype – and unprecedented media attention.Call me cynical, but I suspect the coverage of GTA VI in the media over the next few weeks will follow a familiar pattern. Mostly, it will be five-minute slots wedged in near the end of news bulletins in which games journalists, industry analysts and other pundits will be asked why the game is such a big deal, how much it cost to make and how much revenue it will generate. Perhaps a few will try to reignite the hoary old “violence in video games” debate, there will be presenters laughingly admitting they’ve not touched a game since Pac-Man, rolling their eyes and wallowing in their ignorance, in a way they never would while discussing any other art form. Somebody will venture the subversive view that “games are no longer just for kids”; somebody else will say “games make more money than films and music put together”. And that will be that, job done for another decade … or until there’s a funny story about Pokémon.I hope I’m wrong. I hope, at least, the BBC, which employs plenty of staff who understand video games, will make time in its schedule to take a good look at GTA VI – its themes and influences, its creators, its place in the wider culture of games and entertainment. Sure, arts coverage on BBC televisionhas been in declinefor years, with the broadcaster shifting this content to digital platforms, but I saw plenty of in-depth analysis of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, looking at the quality of its translation, its depiction of female characters, its use of practical effects. I didn’t see a single presenter shrugging, looking comedically bewildered and admitting they’d not read Homer since secondary school.View image in fullscreenLost Records: Bloom and Rage is one of the games that deserves a least a portion of the attention GTA gets.Photograph: Don't Nod Entertainment SAOn top of this, whatever mainstream media attention GTA VI does get it will come at the expense of covering other titles. Because, when the next video game story comes up in the wake of Rockstar’s behemoth, TV and radio editors and producers will be thinking, “Oh, we covered games last month.”The thing is, GTAisa phenomenon – it looks gorgeous, it looks vast, and it will sell many millions of copies. The series’ notoriety transcends the medium. But is it the most interesting video game since GTA V? So much has changed since then. We’ve explored the fascinating, innovative open worlds of Elden Ring, Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and No Man’s Sky (an open galaxy!); we’ve seen brutal adult themes explored in The Last of Us: Part 2 and Silent Hill; we’ve experienced dizzying narrative innovations via Disco Elysium, Split Fiction and Lost Records: Bloom & Rage. All of these deserved at least a portion of that GTA screen and radio time.True, some gameshavedrawn similar levels of media attention. Minecraft and Fortnite receive regular coverage, but almost always because of concerns over children and games addiction, or because of how they intersect with other media: Minecraft through its hit movie, Fortnite through its many collaborations with music artists. And this is the key problem. Mainstream media is still at the stage where every single games story that does make it to TV or radio has to do the job of explaining and justifying the whole industry. It’s time for programme-makers to understand that video games are a mass cultural phenomenon. Enough people play them and understand them so that they don’t have to be re-introduced every time they’re covered. And most importantly, there is life, love, art and brilliance beyondGrand Theft Autoand beyond the coming storm of hype.What to playView image in fullscreenWhat The Dub?! will definitely be revived at future family celebrations.Photograph: Wide Right InteractiveIt was my birthday a couple of weeks ago, so I set out to find a simple, fun video game that the whole family could enjoy – and I wanted to share my discovery.Inspired by Dominik Diamond’srecent columnon this very subject, I downloaded the party gameWhat The Dub?!, in which players watch old film clips with portions of the sound dubbed out and then enter their own amusing dialogue to fill the gap. The clips are then re-shown with each player’s text added to the soundtrack via a stilted robotic voice – then everyone votes on the funniest entry. It was hilarious, especially because the clips are from weird old public domain films and TV shows, so everything feels stilted and ridiculous. It’s also simple to take part, with each player using their phone to enter their dialogue choices. Apparently, it’s possible to add new clips via the Steam Workshop, the digital store’s user-generated content feature, but we didn’t figure that out. Regardless, What the Dub?! will definitely be revived at future family celebrations.Available on:PCEstimated playtime:All evening!What to readView image in fullscreenThe Sims 4 from EA, which declined to comment on reports of staff concerns.Photograph: EA GamesEA staff have beenspeaking anonymouslyto the industry-news site Game Developer about their concerns after the Saudi-led buyout ofElectronic Arts. Some are troubled by the prospect of popular games such as EA Sports FC, Madden and Battlefield being used by Saudi Arabia to distract from its poor human rights record. There are also worries about the company’s culture and job security.TV producers looking for interesting game stories that don’t involve GTA could check out Eurogamer’sexcellent articleon theNo Man’s Sky’s Galactic Hub project. It’s a community of players exploring and scientifically cataloguing specific regions of the long-running space adventure sim, like a sort of ragtag Starfleet mission. Live long and prosper, lads.As if making and marketing independent video games isn’t hard enough, several developers have reported thefts at this year’sGamescomevent in Cologne.Posting on X, Mimic creator Ryan Laley said: “Our equipment was stolen last night from the booth. Police reports have been filed. At a loss for words to describe the feeling. Just defeated. Gonna do my best with what’s left of the week. But a huge blow financially and mentally.”According to VGC, others affected included publisher iam8bit and Tessera Studios.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickGems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past – Geralt of Rivia returns after a decade in the sunHelp! I have disappeared down a rabbithole of horrible mobile gaming advertsTrainwatch – alone with your thoughts on a railway line to nowhereStar Wars Zero Company – joyfully absurd heroics with a tight-knit team of misfits | ★★★★☆Vholume – a headlong rush of parkour perfection in a brutalist wonderland | ★★★★☆Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan myth | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenA game that soars … Microsoft Flight Simulator.Photograph: MicrosoftA question fromRichardvia email:“My son, aged 6, is a big fan of aeroplanes and is really interested in flight. What games are there that could be used to entertain him, as a thing to do with me. I have (ridiculously) a PS5 and Xbox Series X – is Flight Simulator right? How about Ace Combat? Anything else?”I’d definitely recommendMicrosoft Flight Simulator, which is available on PS5 and Xbox. It can be controlled with just a joypad and you can switch off all the technical elements for your son so he’s basically just steering the craft like in an arcade game. There are lots of aircraft to fly, from tiny prop planes to passenger jets, and you can choose anywhere on Earth to explore. I love simply zooming over cities and scenic highlights, taking it all in.If you’re ok with him doing a bit of shooting,Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theveis out in October, promising highly detailed visuals and exciting dogfighting. Fans say it looks to be a highlight for the series. I’d also recommend No Man’s Sky, which is a space exploration game, but the flight feels lovely, whether you’re scorching over the surface of a planet or out in the depths of the cosmos. The controls are extremely intuitive too. If he gets into space flight, the slightly more involvedEliteDangerousis worth a look, and for an accessible combination of space flight and shooting,Everspace: Stellar Editionis a really nice option on PS5.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterGrand Theft AutoGrand Theft Auto VINetflixFilm adaptationsTwitchfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘OK, fine. I’m a national treasure’: Joe Lycett on fatherhood, Celebrity Traitors – and his TV show live from a pub  | Television | The Guardian
description: The comedian’s new Friday night series will come live from a working pub, with his aunties working the bar and celebrities doing shifts as managers. Or it will be if he can only get his licence …
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The comedian’s new Friday night series will come live from a working pub, with his aunties working the bar and celebrities doing shifts as managers. Or it will be if he can only get his licence …
Content: ‘Let’s go and have a lock-in at mine’ … Lycett at the Lucky Saint in London.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Let’s go and have a lock-in at mine’ … Lycett at the Lucky Saint in London.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianTelevisionInterview‘OK, fine. I’m a national treasure’: Joe Lycett on fatherhood, Celebrity Traitors – and his TV show live from a pubStuart HeritageThe comedian’s new Friday night series will be set in a working pub, with his aunties working the bar and celebrities doing shifts as managers. Or it will be if he can only get his licence …Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.24 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe Lycett sits in a pub, an untouched pint in front of him. “Since I had my son, I’m not drinking anywhere near as much,” he laments. “Children do not respect hangovers, or tiredness in general.”His son is almost two, and Lycett has readjusted his life accordingly. “I’ve started going to bed when he does, which is about seven o’clock,” he explains. “I’ve seen a few nights where I’ve just gone: ‘Right, well, that’s me, then.’”However, this is all set to come to an end thanks to the comic’s new television programme, Live from the Lycett Arms, which will not only be broadcast live three hours after his new bedtime, but absolutely surround him with alcohol. The Lycett Arms is a continuation of what began with his previous live Friday night show,Late Night Lycett, only with a more ambitious premise. This time, Lycett will host while simultaneously operating a working pub. It sounds as if it has been specifically constructed to maximise impromptu chaos – more on that in a bit – but for now Lycett has a pair of larger anxieties to deal with.View image in fullscreen‘I took the licence exam but failed’ … Lycett in a publicity image for the show.Photograph: Matt Crockett/Channel 4/PAThe first is that, even though we’re meeting just a couple of weeks before the first episode, the pub isn’t ready. “It’s not fully constructed yet, so I’ve been to where it will be,” he explains. “It’s going to be in fashionable east London, and that’s everything I can say about it, because I don’t actually know the full address.”Nevertheless, he promises that the finished building will be “identifiably a pub. There’ll be an outdoor area and a cellar. There’s a bar. There’s a kind of back room. There’s a saloon bar. There’s a pool table. There’s darts. There’s karaoke. It should be really fun. That’s the goal. If it isn’t fun, there’s no point in doing it.”A bigger issue, though, is that, since the Lycett Arms will be a real pub, Lycett will be its licensed operator. This is a role that comes with a legal requirement: he needs to pass a mandatory exam to be accredited with a Level 2 Award for Personal Licence Holders. It is an accreditation he does not yet hold.“I took the exam but I failed,” he says. “I didn’t do any work, so that is a problem. I needed about 70% to pass, and I got something like 38%. I tried to use common sense, and I don’t have a lot of it apparently.”View image in fullscreenLycett … ‘If it isn’t fun, there’s no point in doing it.’Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianEager to help him out a little, I ask if he knows the four primary licensing objectives, as per section four of the Licensing Act 2003. The blood briefly drains from Lycett’s face. “Safe … safety … safe drinking environment to create … happy places, for people … to dwell?” he yammers.That isn’t what’s written on the test. The answer is: “Prevention of crime and disorder. Public safety. Protection of children from harm. Prevention of public nuisance.”“Yeah, that’s what I said, isn’t it?”No, not really.“Well, I think I paraphrased that. And I think that’s their problem that I didn’t get the licence because I did essentially paraphrase it right.”double quotation markI’m amazed they commissioned it because nobody’s commissioning anything. TV is in freefall. I don’t know if you’ve heardAfter strenuously assuring me that the show will go on, with a stand-in licensee if he continues to perform as disastrously as this, Lycett starts telling me how excited he is for people to see the show.“So, it’s my pub,” he says. “But from week one, there will be a celebrity manager who’s doing a trial shift. My aunties are going to be working the bar. There will be a weekly quiz and rotating regulars. I’m well up for weird and wonderful celebrities to just turn up, drink a pint and leave. I just want it to be constantly surprising and silly.”It’s also exciting that he gets to be the face of live, late-night television, I tell him. It’s a dying breed of show. “I’m kind of amazed they’ve commissioned it, because nobody’s commissioning anything at the moment,” he replies. “TV is in freefall – I don’t know if you’ve heard.”View image in fullscreenTailor made … Lycett getting involved as a host of The Great British Sewing Bee.Photograph: Mark Bourdillon/Love ProductionsSo in essence, running a pub could be a fallback career if the TV work ever dries up? “I mean, hospitality is in freefall as well,” he points out, not unreasonably. “Like most industries, it’s all just sort of fucked, isn’t it? Should I join the Guardian? Is that doing well?”Still, the thought of turning the Lycett Arms into a permanent nightspot is something that appeals to him. After all,if Jeremy Clarkson has proved anything, it’s that tourists love nothing more than a pub with a celebrity landlord.“I think lots of people feel like they could open up a pub or restaurant or whatever, and obviously it’s really hard,” he says. “But I do like the idea of it. I think it’s the cachet of being, like, ‘Let’s go and have a lock-in at mine.’ When the reality must be doing invoices and working out VAT.”This is a big year for Lycett. As well as Live from the Lycett Arms, he is returning to standup after stepping aside for a couple of years. This is something he is palpably excited about. “I’m touring next year, but since last October I’ve been trying to do one gig a week,” he says. “It took me a good few months to feel even close to like I knew what I was doing. I still don’t feel like I know what I’m doing. But I’m really enjoying being on stage, and I’m not panicked about it in the way I was when I had just come back from paternity leave.”Since his last tour, Lycett has become more recognisable and beloved in a way that nudges him towards national treasure status.“I dispute that,” he growls.Please agree for the sake of my question, I beg.“Fine, OK, I’m a national treasure, yes,” he says, rolling his eyes.View image in fullscreenClogs, gentlemen, please … Lycett.Photograph: Matt Crockett/Channel 4/PABecause people pay more attention to him now than when he last toured, does he feel a greater weight of responsibility for the topics he covers? “No,” he says. “If I started to change who I am on stage to fit what I think people want of me, I’d go mad. When you get reviewed, and the reviewer doesn’t like what you do, there’s this temptation to write the sort of show that the reviewer would like. But there are only about 10 comedy reviewers left in the whole country, and it wouldn’t be good to write something just so that 10 white men will like me.“I think the thing that has changed what I do most is being a father,” he continues. “I feel more risk averse, but I also want to stand up for things more than I used to. It’s like this weird tussle between not wanting to annoy the wrong people because I just want a calmer life, and also really wanting to annoy those people a lot more. But then a big part of this new show is also about swimming, so if you’re into swimming-based material, you’ll love it.”‘You don’t have to sell them on the idea’: how Celebrity Traitors has seduced the starsRead moreLycett will take part in The Celebrity Traitors later this year, which will almost certainly be 2026’s biggest show. He is sworn to such secrecy that he practically ties himself in a knot trying to give the blandest non-answers imaginable. “The production team were very nice, as was Claudia Winkleman. I can’t say anything about the other players, so I can’t say whether they’re nice or not,” he offers apologetically.But before that airs, Lycett has six episodes of Live from the Lycett Arms to deliver. As I leave, he is taking notes on the decor of the pub we are in, particularly the quality of the bar itself. “Apparently it’s been treated with Danish oil,” he says approvingly. “That might be a future requirement for any pub I go into. The bar must have been treated with Danish oil.”Live from the Lycett Arms is on Friday at 10pm on Channel 4Explore more on these topicsTelevisionJoe LycettinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Simply the best? Is the Berlin Philharmonic really better than all the rest?  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The orchestra – at the Proms this week – is hailed as among the best in the world, if not the best. For my money, that’s quite possibly right, but why?
Author: Tom Service
Headline: The orchestra – at the Proms this week – is hailed as among the best in the world, if not the best. For my money, that’s quite possibly right, but why?
Content: A thrilling festival close: the Berlin Philharmonic perform in Edinburgh’s Usher Hall on 26 August 2026.Photograph: Lena LaineView image in fullscreenA thrilling festival close: the Berlin Philharmonic perform in Edinburgh’s Usher Hall on 26 August 2026.Photograph: Lena LaineTom Service on musicClassical musicSimply the best? Is the Berlin Philharmonic really better than all the rest?Tom ServiceThe orchestra – at the Proms this week – is hailed as among the best in the world, if notthebest. For my money, that’s quite possibly right, but why?Wed 2 Sep 2026 14.02 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 14.05 BSTShareThe Berlin Philharmonic are in Londontonight and tomorrow at the Proms, days after closing theEdinburgh international festivalin thrilling style. It was their first visit to Scotland in over 20 years, but the orchestra and their chief conductor, Kirill Petrenko,are regular Proms visitors; their Royal Albert Hall concerts are always season highlights.“The best orchestra in the world”,as it is often hailed, brings programmes that offer the expected and – for them – the unexpected. Tonight there’s Tchaikovsky’s Fourth Symphony paired with Elgar’s Enigma Variations, a piece that’s still an astoundingly rare visitor to this orchestra’s concerts; and tomorrow, the safety-first repertoire warhorse is Beethoven’s Violin Concerto, but it’s paired with Scriabin’s brilliantly unhinged Third Symphony.But what does being the “best” mean? And how and why have the Berliners acquired, and held on to, their globe-topping orchestral reputation for so many decades, through changes of conductor and personnel, political upheaval and technological transformation?Their history is controversial. In 1933 the Berlin Philharmonic (founded in 1882) became the Nazi-sponsored Reichsorchester. Its four Jewish members, including the orchestra’s leader, Szymon Goldberg,were forced into exile. As Das Reichsorchester, its performances were used for flagrantly political ends on radio broadcasts and on film, at the opening of the 1936 Olympics and during the Nuremberg rallies. An aryanised Austro-German canon was favoured: Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Brahms, Bruckner and Wagner, while Jewish composers such as Mendelssohn, Mahler and Schoenberg were banned. Their conductor Wilhelm Furtwänglerwas a public critic of the Nazi regime(you can see himshake Joseph Goebbels’ handat the end of an apocalyptic performance of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony in 1942 with what looks like satanic disdain), but none of the orchestra of the time can escape the facts of how it was used to underpin the myths of German cultural supremacy as the public face of the Nazis’ fascism and genocide.View image in fullscreenApplause after a 1933 concert by the Berlin Philharmonic and Wilhelm Furtwängler. In the front row was Herman Goering, Adolf Hitler and Josef Goebbels (left to right).Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveWhat happened in the post-war years was nothing short of miraculous, in how conductorHerbert von Karajanwas able to present the Berlin Philharmonic as a vision of de-Nazified modernity. He shored up the idea of the orchestra as the sound of the freedom of West Berlin – something that was architecturally as well as musically unmissable whenHans Scharoun’s futuristic Philharmonieconcert hall was built for the orchestra in the early 1960s, just west of the Berlin Wall. Karajan used all the powers of technology to turn the Berlin Philharmonic into pioneers ofrecording and film, and put them at the vanguard of the digital age on CDs and on Laserdiscs. (Remember them? The 12-inch gold plates of the audio-visual future in the 1980s.) And the orchestra continues to outstrip its opponents technologically: itsDigital Concert Hallis today a model of how orchestras can stream concerts, widen access, and generate income.But if you’re looking for an index of exactly why this might be the best orchestra on the planet, that’s much harder to define. The Berlin Phil does not lead the orchestral world in terms of repertoire development – far from it.The coming seasonfeatures its former viola player Brett Dean as composer-in-residence, but a few other world premieres aside, there’s Mahler galore and programmes that don’t stray beyond their usual 19th and early 20th-century stomping grounds. The orchestra is also far behind others in terms of diversity of performers and programmes: just one female conductor, Elim Chan, leads it during the next season, and there’s music by a mere handful of female composers throughout the entire year. And with the exception of Maxim Emelyanychev playing a fortepiano in a Haydn concerto, they are miles behind other bands in the investigation of performance practice. So what are the Berlin Philharmonic “best” at?View image in fullscreenThe sound of freedom… the Berlin Philharmonic and Kirill Petrenko give a concert under the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, Germany, August 2019.Photograph: Omer Messinger/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockIt’s the alchemy that turns a collection of musicians, each and every one of incredible ability – all of whom think of themselves as individual musicians first and members of an orchestra second; many of them with egos of justifiably gigantic proportions – into a musical collective that speaks not with Hydra-headed confusion but with jaw-dropping power and precision, and with a delirious and fearless commitment to every moment of their music-making.Petrekno, their current music director, is the most consistently compelling conductor I’ve ever seen in how he’s able to harness these musical and sociological forces. He does it with forensic attention to detail: what seem like improvisatory flourishes of inspiration are, in reality, rehearsed to a point of fail-safe integrity. I remember a performance ofMahler’s Seventhsymphony at the Proms a few years ago that revealed the piece as the most adventurous symphony of pure orchestral sensation ever composed, in which the 100 and more musicians played with the subtlety and sensitivity of a chamber group and the effortless give-and-take of a big band.You can hear Petrenko and his players at their best on their recordings:their recent Schoenberg collectionis arguably the most important of the lot, reclaiming the sensuality of this music through a relentless focus on making Schoenberg’s manic counterpoint speak more clearly than any other performances I know of. Don’t just take my word for it – the recordingwas Andrew Clements’ best of 2025in what was sadly one of thefinal reviews he wrote.So yes: in music-making like this, the Berlin Phil really are the “best” that they can be, and they find dimensions in the music that have been there all along, it’s just taken these players and this conductor to find them. And it’s those ecstatic moments I’m hoping for at theirProms. Get there if you can; listen on Radio 3 if you can’t.View image in fullscreenMiraculous songs.. Elsa the Snow Queen in Disney’s Frozen.Photograph: APThis week Tom has been listening to:Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez’s songs for Disney’s Frozen on a never-ending loop – having lost control of the playlists to younger ears than mine while on a long drive. But these are miraculous songs: even on the 101st listen, there are still fractals of subtlety in these tunes and lyrics to discover.Let it Go-oo-ooo…Explore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicProms 2026PromsFestivalscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Bridge by Colm Tóibín review – betrayal and survival in the High Pyrenees | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Deep sorrow mingles with illicit desire in this potent novella, the follow-up to a 2006 story about an isolated family in the Catalan mountains
Author: Alexandra Harris
Headline: Deep sorrow mingles with illicit desire in this potent novella, the follow-up to a 2006 story about an isolated family in the Catalan mountains
Content: Austere worlds … The Catalan Pyrenees provide the setting for The Bridge.Photograph: Xavier Fores/Joana Roncero/AlamyView image in fullscreenAustere worlds … The Catalan Pyrenees provide the setting for The Bridge.Photograph: Xavier Fores/Joana Roncero/AlamyBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Bridge by Colm Tóibín review – betrayal and survival in the High PyreneesDeep sorrow mingles with illicit desire in this potent novella, the follow-up to a 2006 story about an isolated family in the Catalan mountainsAlexandra HarrisWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 07.31 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty years ago,Colm Tóibínpublished a steadily desolating novella set in the high villages of the Catalan Pyrenees. A woman walks out of her house and her life, starts along the mountain road and disappears in the snow. Her son Miquel, failing to find her body, waits through the dark months for the thaw. A Long Winter, which appeared in a standalone volume and then as the final story in the 2006 collection Mothers and Sons, followed Miquel through dramatically extreme circumstances and patient endurance. It was told with the most restrained prose ever likely to be employed for a son’s view of vultures circling a corpse.Now, in The Bridge, a single year has passed in Miquel’s life and he is eking out an existence with his hurtful, unyielding father. The sheep are grazing their high summer pastures; a side hustle smuggling contraband brings in a little much-needed cash. In the bare conditions of the lonely farm, any warmth of feeling is a kind of contraband smuggled in by night; love between men is doubly illicit. The grave tenderness that grows between Miquel and his father’s maltreated servant Manolo gives The Bridge its emotional centre. These young men salve the emptiness with a few quiet words and touches. We sense their youthful beauty and resilience, their suppleness in a place of fixity.In fact, and with a fullness that’s striking in this novella of watchfulness and withholding, Miquel enters into a varied erotic life. Visits to the local town bring assignations. A later relationship between cellmates is extraordinarily vivid as Miquel seeks to “assuage his hunger by biting Odo, chewing him”. But it’s the lost, interrupted love of Manolo that gives shape to the rest.double quotation markTóibín practises a sustained reticence, even as fate strikes so cruelly as to give this story an absurdist edgeA great alteration has come to the area in the form of a road bridge linking isolated settlements with the country beyond. Places “cut off and enclosed” for centuries are suddenly opened and connected. This central motif suggests a story concerned with social change, and certainly it could be described in those terms. There’s a potent scene in which dogs from both sides of the valley run wildly across the bridge, frenzied at the possibility of new mates. This is not the only moment of the feral, and the farcical. As for Miquel: the crossing should bring him a larger terrain for youthful exploration, but it casts him into peril and dire confinement. The Bridge stays in the mind less as a historically specific story of 20th-century development than as an ageless study of loss, betrayal and survival. Miquel himself comes to believe that “his isolation was nothing new, that he had always been far away even from those to whom he had been closest”.Tóibín’s relationship with Catalonia now spans five decades. His first novel was set in Barcelona; his latest collection,The News from Dublin, includes several fine Spanish stories. He spends part of each year in the mountains near Llavorsí, and in writing about Miquel he is thinking his way into lives that have unfolded in that long known yet hardly knowable place. The germ of Miquel’s story came in a particular glimpse of local history. Tóibín was told that a ruined building was all that remained of the house where a woman once grew desperate enough to walk away from her family. It was said that the snow came; it was said to be a terrible tale. A Long Winter and The Bridge have grown from that beginning.Tóibín responds powerfully to the qualities of exactitude and seriousness he finds in Catalan writing, in the work of Mercè Rodereda for instance, and these are very much qualities of The Bridge. We know that Miquel feels deeply, but nothing in his life has licensed or recommended the articulation of personal emotion. Tóibín practises a sustained reticence, even as fate strikes so cruelly as to give this story an absurdist edge.Readers of Brooklyn and its follow-upLong Islandwill know that Tóibín has careful ways of handling a sequel: those novels are both richly complete in themselves while opening depths in each other. The Bridge, too, works alone or as part of a pair. To read A Long Winter afterwards, meeting the past that crouches in the shadows of the later story, would be as absorbing as to read chronologically. A further instalment seems possible. Any change would be welcome to lift Miquel from stultifying conditions, though it’s unlikely to offer much relief.This is the kind of small volume temptingly piled by the checkouts at Christmas. I wouldn’t recommend it as a stocking-filler; the stocking would fall to the floor with the weight of sorrow. But this is a memorable short work in which Tóibín’s unsentimental prose is flawlessly matched to the austere worlds of people enduring, in their different ways, lives stripped back to the bone.The Bridge by Colm Tóibín is published by Picador (£12.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFictionBook of the dayColm TóibínreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Maggie Gyllenhaal says film industry has a ‘systemic problem’ with sexism | Film | The Guardian
description: Speaking at the opening of the Venice film festival, the actor-director addressed why the jury of which she is chair will only be shown two films made by female film-makers
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Speaking at the opening of the Venice film festival, the actor-director addressed why the jury of which she is chair will only be shown two films made by female film-makers
Content: ‘Who decides what’s good? Who decides what is valuable?’ … Venice jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal.Photograph: Fabio Frustaci/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Who decides what’s good? Who decides what is valuable?’ … Venice jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal.Photograph: Fabio Frustaci/EPAFilmMaggie Gyllenhaal says film industry has a ‘systemic problem’ with sexismSpeaking at the opening of the Venice film festival, the actor-director addressed why the jury of which she is chair will only be shown two films made by female film-makersPhilip Oltermannin VeniceWed 2 Sep 2026 15.26 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.45 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaggie Gyllenhaal said there is a “systemic problem” that explains why only two female directors are in the running for the Golden Lion at theVenice film festivalthis year.“It’s harder for women to get films financed,” said the actor-director, who is heading up the jury of the world’s oldest cinema showcase this year.“Could it be possible that the things that women, having had a different experience of being alive in the world, want to make movies about are not always deemed high art?” added Gyllenhaal, whose directing debut The Lost Daughter won a best screenplay prize at Venice in 2021. “Who decides what’s good? Who decides what is valuable?”The artistic directors of the film festival have faced criticism since the original lineup revealed that that only one of the 20 contenders for the top prize was by a female film-maker, Danish-Egyptian director May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown.Since then, the festival has boosted the main competition withNAZA, a new documentary film directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor– two of the four directors behind Oscar-winning No Other Land. The film is produced by the Guardian.At the 83rd edition of the festival, Gyllenhaal heads a seven-member jury that also includes Kaouther Ben Hania, the Tunisian film-maker behind The Voice of Hind Rajab, Hong Kong’s Johnnie To, Afghan director Shahrbanoo Sadat, French film-maker Xavier Giannoli, British composer Daniel Blumberg and Italian film scholar Francesco Casetti.In the run-up to the festival, there had been some uncertainty whether the jury would speak to the press ahead of the festival opening at all, supposedly due to a “scheduling conflict”.A lineup unusually packed with films touching politically sensitive issues – from Israel/Palestine and Russia/Ukraine to a feature film about Rupert Murdoch and a documentary about Elon Musk – meant that the jury members may also have felt nervous about facing the media on the opening day.At the jury press conference at this year’s Berlin film festival,jury president Wim Wenders faced a backlashwhen he said film-makers should “stay out of politics” while fielding questions about Israel and Palestine.Asked whether directors should wade into political debates or not, Gyllenhaal said what made cinema political was its ability to generate empathy, even for “the most corrupt, the most perverse people”.“I think that if movies really are an honest look into other people’s experience, then they are fundamentally, unavoidably political, as well as a lot of other things,” said the director, whose Marilyn Monroe-inspired short film Flesh Impact will screen out of competition later in the event.Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalMaggie GyllenhaalWomenFestivalsItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian film-maker criticises EU after it cuts Venice Biennale funding over Russia controversy | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Sergei Loznitsa likens removal of €2m grant to ‘a punishment in kindergarten’ on eve of Venice film festival
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Sergei Loznitsa likens removal of €2m grant to ‘a punishment in kindergarten’ on eve of Venice film festival
Content: Loznitsa’s new documentary Imperium uses archival footage from the early 1970s filmed in the former Soviet Union.Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMODView image in fullscreenLoznitsa’s new documentary Imperium uses archival footage from the early 1970s filmed in the former Soviet Union.Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMODVenice film festivalUkrainian film-maker criticises EU after it cuts Venice Biennale funding over Russia controversySergei Loznitsa likens removal of €2m grant to ‘a punishment in kindergarten’ on eve of Venice film festivalPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.43 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Ukraine’s most acclaimed film-makers has criticised the European Commission’s decision to cut off funds to theVenice Biennaleover the opening of Russia’s pavilion, likening it to “a punishment in kindergarten”.TheBiennale drew heavy criticism this springwhen it allowed Russia to use its pavilion for the first time since 2022, despite the ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Speaking on the eve of the Biennale’s cinematic branch, theVenice film festival, the director Sergei Loznitsa said that while he would “never ever” personally visit the Russian pavilion, the row was a distraction from the EU’s own failure to enforce more effective economic sanctions against Moscow.“The question I ask myself is this: can the existence of this Russian pavilion stop this war or not?” said Loznitsa, who won wide acclaim for his 2014 documentary Maidan and last year’s Soviet-set drama Two Prosecutors, and is showing his new film Imperium out of competition on the Lido this year.He added: “What I do know is that in the second quarter of this year, European companies imported gas from Russia at unprecedented levels, and all that money goes straight into bombs that fall onUkraine.”View image in fullscreenSergei Loznitsa at the Cannes film festival in May last year.Photograph: Kristy Sparow/Getty ImagesAccording to the EU’s Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators, European imports of Russian liquified fossil gasincreased by 17%compared with the same period in 2025, before a full EU-wide ban on Russian gas from 2027.Loznitsa said: “This is a much more serious issue than whether there is a Russian pavilion in Venice or not. Cutting off funding to the Biennale is like a punishment in kindergarten.”While the Russian pavilion’s exhibition The Tree is Rooted in the Sky was only accessible during the pre-opening vernissage dates and has been closed to the public since 9 May, the European Commissionconfirmedlast month that it was terminating its €2m (£1.7m) multiyear grant to the Biennale Foundation.The row is now also threatening to engulf the Venice film festival, which has a degree of institutional independence from the Biennale but will be directly affected by the funding cut.The Biennale’s management said the terminated grant used to co-finance the activities of the cinema department relating to Biennale College and the Venice Production Bridge affects “activities and a department that have nothing to do with Russia’s participation in the Biennale Arte”.In a confrontational speech before the announcement of this year’s lineup, the Biennale’s president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, accused the commission of “abandoning our journey”. The Biennale, he said, was not engaged in politics but “international research in the field of arts”.View image in fullscreenThe president of the Venice Biennale, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, has led the criticism of the commission’s decision.Photograph: Stefano Mazzola/Getty ImagesFor a festival that has in the past often looked more focused on attracting celebrity glitz than its competitors in Cannes and Berlin, this year’s programme is noteworthy for its political flavour and thematic focus on Russia and the countries in its sphere of influence.As well as Loznitsa’s Imperium, there is the French director Alexandre Smia’s geopolitical “disaster movie” Jupiter, in which the Russian president has survived an assassination attempt for which he blames Ukraine and seeks retribution. Andrei Kutsila’s partially animated documentary Letters from the Silenced Country focuses on political repression in Belarus, while the Russian-born American film-maker Julia Loktev’s five-hour documentary My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile follows a group of Russian dissident journalists working for the independent television channel TV Rain after they are forced to flee their country in the wake of the full-scale invasion.View image in fullscreenMy Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile stars Ksenia Mironova, left, and Valeria Ratnikova.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalLoktev’s film circles around the question of where art and journalism stops and propaganda begins. In one scene, the journalists working for TV Rain find themselves chastised for continuing to speak of “our army” after they have registered the network in Latvia. “It’s a film about when your country does terrible things, how to take accountability,” said Loktev. “How do you speak as a citizen of your country about the awful actions and the crimes your country is committing?”The inclusion of another Russian-themed film project, Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s Dau, has brought criticism from Ukrainian authorities. The Ukrainian ministry of foreign affairs raised “profound concern” over Khrzhanovsky’s film, which tells the story of the Soviet physicist who reluctantly contributed to the creation of the first atomic bomb.“Russia has long used culture as an instrument of state policy and hybrid warfare,” the ministry said in a statement. “For the Kremlin, culture is a way to restore to sanctioned figures the respectability that politics has taken from them; to legitimise its presence where tanks cannot reach; and to appropriate the history of the very lands it seeks to erase.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe ministry said that the multi-film Dau project, once described as a “Stalinist Truman Show”, has received funding from the Russian businessman Sergey Adonyev, who has been sanctioned by the US and Ukraine, and that its Greek-born protagonist Teodor Currentzis accepted Russian citizenship granted by Putin.View image in fullscreenA still from Imperium.Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMODBut in a social media post, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, Alberto Barbera, rejected the description of Dau, which was principally shot from 2008 to 2011, as a “Kremlin-financed project”: “[It] is not a Russian film; it is not pro-Putin propaganda,” he said. “It is a film that denounces totalitarian regimes and their intrusion into citizens’ lives to restrict their freedom.”Unlike at the Venice art biennial, directors showing their work at the film festival do not represent a country. Dau was funded by Germany, France and Sweden, while My Undesirable Friends was made in the US and Loznitsa’s Imperium has received financial support from Germany, Italy, France and Lithuania.The comments on the festival row by the Belarus-born, Ukraine-raised and now Germany-based Loznitsa are striking, not least because his own submission to the festival applies a strongly critical lens to the internal contradictions of Russian imperialism, the role of cultural propaganda and blindspots in how the Soviet Union used to be seen from the west – specifically from Italy.The three-hour film is solely based on archival footage shot by a group of Italian film-makers who, thanks to the blessing of the Italian Communist party, were allowed to make three filming expeditions to the Soviet Union between 1970 and 1973.View image in fullscreenThe footage used to make Imperium was shot by Italian film-makers on an officially sanctioned visit.Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMODWith filming strictly supervised by KGB handlers, the footage they amassed was meant to project the unity of the Soviet empire, showing a sea of red flags on Moscow streets as the patriotic anthem Wide is My Motherland blares from speakers.Yet the further the crew travels into the outer reaches of the Soviet Union, the more the ambiguous the images become. Local customs, from throat singing to reindeer racing to village wrestling competitions, emphasise the disparity rather than the unity of Soviet culture. In the Yakut Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, local people watch on with visible scepticism as a group of urban young Russians parade through the streets with guitars and fiddles.“I wanted to show that the Soviet Union collapsed not just for economic reasons, but also because it was impossible to keep so many different cultures under one roof,” said Loznitsa.Moscow’s much-mythologised propaganda arm – still detected by many behind the cultural policies of the Russian state today – appears largely ineffective in Loznitsa’s film. In one scene, the camera hovers over a small tractor parading portraits of members of the politburo through a muddy and forlorn landscape in Dagestan.“It’s a bit like the Russian pavilion in Venice now,” the film-maker said. “As propaganda, it’s just so ridiculous.”Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalFestivalsUkraineEuropeRussiaVenice BiennalenewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: the unmarried women who were forced to give up their babies | Television | The Guardian
description: An enraging documentary hears from women sent away for becoming pregnant outside marriage. Plus: the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: An enraging documentary hears from women sent away for becoming pregnant outside marriage. Plus: the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Blood-boiling … Stolen Babies on BBC Two.Photograph: Jaqui Adams c/o Finestripe ProductionsView image in fullscreenBlood-boiling … Stolen Babies on BBC Two.Photograph: Jaqui Adams c/o Finestripe ProductionsTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the unmarried women who were forced to give up their babiesAn enraging documentary hears from women sent away for becoming pregnant outside marriage. Plus: the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Here’s what to watch this eveningAli Catterall,Priya Elan,Phil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellWed 2 Sep 2026 06.20 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStolen Babies9pm, BBC TwoAnn in Wales was sent away by her parents when she became pregnant after being raped (“I didn’t blame them, I blamed myself”). Joan in Sunderland gave evidence in court against the teacher who raped and got her pregnant – but he was acquitted. They tell their stories in this blood-boiling documentary, along with other women who were unmarried, pregnant and sent to so-called “mother and baby homes” between 1949 and 1976. People who worked in those places also speak, as do some of the grown-up children who were adopted by mostly white, middle-class families. It brings their fight up to date as they demand an apology from the state. Remarkably, there are some joyful moments to hang on for.Hollie Richardson9/11: Days That Shocked the World10pm, Channel 4It is the 25th anniversary of one of this century’s defining geopolitical events and this two-part documentary offers a straightforward but still striking commemoration of that terrible day. It hears from rescue workers, witnesses and survivors of the attack on New York but also explores the assault on the Pentagon and the fate of the fourth airliner, which crashed into a field in Pennsylvania. The horror still startles but so does the courage of many of the initial responses.Phil HarrisonSurviving Earth8pm, Sky OneTwo mating dinosaurs in Antarctica take the spotlight in this week’s episode. How long before their time runs out and they feel the ripple effects of the seven-and-a-half-mile-long asteroid that has just landed in Mexico? Your enjoyment will very much depend on how much of the uncanny CGI you can stomach.Priya ElanBookish8pm, U&AlibiView image in fullscreenOn the case … Ruth Codd as India Flynn in Bookish.Photograph: UKTV/PAA suspicious death at a tailor’s emporium is the latest two-part whodunnit for Mark Gatiss’s tweedy postwar sleuth Gabriel Book. But why is the 75-year-old proprietor so keen to confess to murder? Meanwhile, Book’s rascally apprentice Jack (Connor Finch) just happens to have acquired a snazzy new suit.Graeme VirtueProfessor T9pm, ITV1After school inspector Tyrone Walsh is found murdered following a spate of burglaries, Professor T and co explore the possible motives: was Walsh’s “cultural bias against alternative education” a factor in his murder? Meanwhile, Miss Snares (Sarah Woodward) investigates whether or not Dean is Jasper’s (Ben Miller) biological father.Ali CatterallReading Festival Highlights 202610.40pm, BBC OneBeholdthe edited highlights of a star-studded and presumably quite messy weekend of music in a field just outside Reading. This year, the festival sees performances from Chase & Status, Dave, Florence + the Machine, Raye and, both touting excellent new material, Fontaines DC and Charli xcx.PHFilm choiceView image in fullscreenSurvivor story … Dustin Hoffman in Little Big Man.Photograph: Pictorial Press/AlamyLittle Big Man (Arthur Penn, 1970),11.45am, 5ActionArthur Penn’s revisionist western about the “sole white survivor of the Battle of the Little Bighorn” may have Dustin Hoffman as its hero, but it is the Native Americans he meets, befriends and lives with who are at the film’s warm, melancholy heart. Hoffman’s 121-year-old Jack Crabb relates his picaresque history, from being orphaned after a Pawnee attack and raised by Cheyenne tribal leader Old Lodge Skins (a deadpan Chief Dan George) to surviving in a “civilised” white world of adulterers, snake-oil salesmen and, most horrifically, genocidal soldiers led by the likes of Gen Custer.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Turning Point: Generation 9/11 review – nothing about that day has lost its power to shock or harrow the soul | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The attacks changed the world as we know it – and now, 25 years on, this heartbreaking Netflix film shares 9/11 recordings and memories from the bereaved that stop time in its tracks
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The attacks changed the world as we know it – and now, 25 years on, this heartbreaking Netflix film shares 9/11 recordings and memories from the bereaved that stop time in its tracks
Content: LeRoy Homer, the co-pilot of United Flight 93 … Turning Point: Generation 9/11.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenLeRoy Homer, the co-pilot of United Flight 93 … Turning Point: Generation 9/11.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewTurning Point: Generation 9/11 review – nothing about that day has lost its power to shock or harrow the soulThe attacks changed the world as we know it – and now, 25 years on, this heartbreaking Netflix film shares 9/11 recordings and memories from the bereaved that stop time in its tracksLucy ManganWed 2 Sep 2026 08.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 08.01 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is 25 years since two planes, sent by Osama bin Laden as the head of the terrorist organisation al-Qaida, flew into the North and South Towers that comprised the World Trade Center, killing almost 3,000 people and changing the world as we know it.I’m old enough to remember the day itself – I was a trainee lawyer in London and we watched the news unfold on a conference room television – which means I am also old enough to remember the world before it. But a quarter of a century on, it is taught in schools as a historical event. Can you believe it? No, because if you experience such a convulsive moment – even at the distance of being a television viewer in a different country – time bends around it and normal chronology becomes meaningless ever after. But that is only our perspective.The 90-minute documentary Turning Point: Generation 9/11 begins with the sights, sounds and some of the stories of that day, none of which have lost any of their power to shock or to harrow the soul. The beautiful, clear blue sky filling with smoke and fire. The 911 calls from people trapped in the burning buildings. “The only thing they can really say is, ‘Hang on – we’re coming for you,’” says the oral historian and curator of the museum that now houses those recordings. The photos of some of the people who tried and who died in the attempt. The memories of some who survived: “I heard ‘pop, pop, pop’. It was the sound of the floors pancaking.” Calls from those about to die to their families: “Mostly I just want to say I love you.” Recollections of the bereaved. “She worked on the 96th floor but I was hoping for the best.” “We talked about the happiness we shared during our lives together. He kept saying ‘I love you’. Then I heard a crack and a sound like an avalanche.”View image in fullscreenAn Nguyen with his dad Khang Ngoc Nguyen, who died on 9/11 … Turning Point: Generation 9/11.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixThe depth of the tragedy inescapably established, the film then moves on to the breadth of it, positing that the decisions made in the aftermath have inexorably shaped the US and helped to lead it into its current state of Trumpian chaos and division. The gamechanger, according to the film-makers with whom I suspect a lot of us will agree, was the Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) passed by Congress a few days after the attack. It was ostensibly to allow the US to use all necessary force against anything or anyone linked to 9/11, but has since been used to justify just about any strike against any perceived threat anywhere since, especially in the Middle East.Turning Point takes us through the invasion of Afghanistan, where Bin Laden and al-Qaida were known to be based, and where the citizens living under the tyranny of the Taliban-controlled government at first welcomed the US troops as liberators. Soldiers testify to the support they felt and their pride in the mission. An Afghan fighter pilot who had trained in the US and returned to fight the Taliban says they all felt like allies.Back home, however, public feeling was turning against Muslim citizens. “All of a sudden I’m a foreigner,” remembers Brooklyn businessman Mohammad Razvi. “I’d never felt that.” The Italian owners of the shop next to his asked how his people could do this. “These are not my people,” he told them, a microcosm of the national and international conversation that would continue to grow in intensity and irrationality.Soon Homeland Security and the “war on terror” emerge as concepts – nebulous concepts, but incredibly useful to the powers that be and in which you can see the seeds sown for the flourishing of ICE. The nascent internet supercharges the conspiracy theories and unites the theorists that terrible events always produce. It gives them unprecedented power that is harnessed and exploited by the people and institutions we once trusted to protect us fromsuch misinformation. For others, trust in them would be further eroded by the mission creep that AUMF had enabled. Was the invasion of Iraq anything to do with 9/11? The drone strikes and assassinations under the Obama administration? How do we know that the aggression of Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq and Syria (to defeat Islamic State) and its ilk don’t entrench anti-US sentiment and create more terrorists than they kill, as one expert asks.Turning Point avoids coming to any firm conclusions about what is next. On the one hand, it points to Trump’s US and all the potential for utter disaster it holds. The beneficiaries of the presidential freedoms and geopolitical divisions instigated by 9/11 appear few and dreadful. On the other, it points out that the old guard is – well, old. The people who have grown up distanced from events by time perhaps have a clearer, calmer view of what is needed now. And perhaps – perhaps – they will turn in the right direction.Turning Point: Generation 9/11 is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings by Jared Diamond review – how to change the course of history | Jared Diamond | The Guardian
description: The author of Guns, Germs and Steel falters in this flawed study of whether individuals really make a difference
Author: Steven Poole
Headline: The author of Guns, Germs and Steel falters in this flawed study of whether individuals really make a difference
Content: A performance of Hamlet at Shakespeare’s Globe, London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA performance of Hamlet at Shakespeare’s Globe, London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianJared DiamondReviewProfits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings by Jared Diamond review – how to change the course of historyThe author of Guns, Germs and Steel falters in this flawed study of whether individuals really make a differenceSteven PooleWed 2 Sep 2026 09.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 09.58 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly in this book, Jared Diamond proudly introduces “what I term ‘the Hamlet test’”, which helps decide whether prominent individuals really make a difference, or whether others might have done just as well. Among William Shakespeare’s contemporaries on the Elizabethan stage, he explains, were “Ben Jonson,Christopher Marloweand John Webster. But not even their best plays remotely approach in quality Hamlet and Shakespeare’s other masterpieces.” It follows, for Diamond, that Shakespeare was indeed “uniquely talented”: “We can be confident that no Elizabethan other than Shakespeare could have written a masterpiece like Hamlet if Shakespeare hadn’t done so.”One obvious problem with this is that Marlowe was stabbed to death in a pub in Deptford in 1593 at the age of 29, having already written the absolute bangers Doctor Faustus and Tamburlaine, as well as – so it is now thought – co-writing the Henry VI trilogy with the up-and-coming Shakespeare. Shakespeare himself did not begin to compose his major tragedies, including Hamlet, until he was a decade older. So we can’t rule out the possibility that, had Marlowe lived another 10 years, he would have matched or even exceeded his colleague’s genius. Scholars widely agree that Hamlet and Shakespeare’s other masterpieces were possible only thanks to the outsized influence of Marlowe.But Diamond is not interested in what literary scholars think, and is confident that his “Hamlet test” is a fine intellectual novelty. Indeed, he is not much interested in what scholars of history, or ethics, or business studies think either, because this is one of those books that pretends the subject is one nobody has thought rigorously about before.Diamond argues persuasively that at least the first president of independent Botswana, Seretse Khama, passes the Hamlet test: he made the country safe for democracy by “gut[ting] the power of the traditional chiefs”, for example, but only he could do that, “because he was the most powerful chief”. Much later in the book, we happily agree that only a particular couple of very rich Californians could have invented the pomegranate-juice industry – or, to generalise the lesson, you have to have lots of wealth already to go into a business with very high up-front costs and a lengthy startup period. No shit, Sherlock, as the reader will have cause to exclaim at numerous points throughout the book.As Diamond skips from politics to sport to business, the main interest is supplied by his concentration on the method of “natural experiments”: the statistical comparison of similar past events. In the 1990s, economists David Card and Alan Krueger analysed fast-food joints close together on either side of a state line: New Jersey had just passed a law to increase its minimum wage, while its neighbour Pennsylvania had not. In two celebrated papers, they proved that the increase in the minimum wage led tohigheremployment, contrary to the received economic wisdom. Similar analyses suggest that CEOs are responsible for between 6% and 29% of the variation in a company’s earnings, while sports coaches are on the hook for at most about 30% of a team’s performance. (Here I thought I could hear Thomas Tuchel breathing a sigh of relief.)Analysis of natural experiments is a fun tool, but obviously harder to make work the further you travel from objectively quantifiable things such as money or win/loss records. One Diamond cites used the amount of parking fines incurred by national staff at the UN’s New York headquarters as a proxy for their countries’ level of political corruption, which is already a stretch. Another took the preponderance of cousin marriage as a proxy for lower IQ (because of inbreeding effects), and so found that stupider European monarchs over the past four centuries were less successful in expanding their territory. (Not supplied here is any argument that expanding your territory is always good.)One of Diamond’s more striking examples also betrays some unreliability on his part. He writes that in their 2009 paper Hit or Miss? The Effect of Assassinations on Institutions and War, Benjamin F Jones and Benjamin A Olken showed that successful assassinations don’t make much difference to the outbreak of wars, and concludes that the killing of Franz Ferdinand didn’t cause the first world war. But the study itself explicitly cautions against that inference: Ferdinand is not included in their data, since he was not the “leader” of the Austro-Hungarian empire. Diamond also neglects to mention that paper’s more interesting finding, which is that, in autocracies, assassination can help make a transition to democracy more likely.The book ends by suggesting other questions that “natural experiments” of this kind might address, on the implicit grounds that only quantitative methods from the social sciences can provide satisfactory answers. One of them is “Under what circumstances do military leaders most make a difference?” On this topic, Diamond might have read with profit a book by a military historian, for example, Lawrence Freedman’s superbCommand. But from this book’s Olympian perspective, subject-matter experts in military affairs are as invisible as those in literary history.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionProfits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Make a Difference? by Jared Diamond is published by Allen Lane (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsJared DiamondHistory booksScience and nature booksWilliam ShakespeareChristopher MarlowereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He was always a bit of a groundbreaker’: David Bowie enters a new dimension in ‘extended reality’ documentary | Film | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of unseen images of the star feature at the Venice film festival, alongside virtual worlds exploring wildfires, wolves and the birth of stars
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Hundreds of unseen images of the star feature at the Venice film festival, alongside virtual worlds exploring wildfires, wolves and the birth of stars
Content: ‘He wasn’t just about the music’ … still from David Bowie: Unseen Unheard.Photograph: Venice film festivalView image in fullscreen‘He wasn’t just about the music’ … still from David Bowie: Unseen Unheard.Photograph: Venice film festivalFilm‘He was always a bit of a groundbreaker’: David Bowie enters a new dimension in ‘extended reality’ documentaryHundreds of unseen images of the star feature at the Venice film festival, alongside virtual worlds exploring wildfires, wolves and the birth of starsXan Brooksin VeniceWed 2 Sep 2026 11.36 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.58 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Bowie shares the bill with starmen, firefighters and Walt Disney wolves at the 10th anniversary edition of Venice Immersive, the film festival’s pioneering showcase for new forms of storytelling. David Bowie: Unseen Unheard – a 3D documentary featuring hundreds of previously unseen images – is among 69 XR (extended reality) pieces playing at the event’s regular base on Lazzaretto Vecchio, a repurposed small island off the Venice Lido.Venice Immersive’s 10th birthday marks a milestone for an event which aims to provide a bridge between emergent technology and traditional narrative cinema. But the programme’s organisers are at pains to emphasise the ongoing scope of a project that has in recent years prompted similar sections at the Cannes, Geneva and Toronto film festivals. “This is not a retrospective,” declares the official festival blurb that welcomes guests to the island. It almost sounds like a warning.“This is such a fast-evolving medium,” says Liz Rosenthal, Venice Immersive’s co-curator. “We’re basically witnessing new forms of art being crafted in real time. So we’re already looking forward to the next 10 years. I think we’re very much at a turning point in terms of the platforms and technology that’s available – and this in turn will shape the nature of the storytelling itself.”View image in fullscreenSound and vision … David Bowie on stage at the Serious Moonlight tour in 1983, a scene from David Bowie: Unseen Unheard.Photograph: Denis O’ReganBilled as an immersive spatial-sound documentary, David Bowie: Unseen Unheard is a personal portrait of the singer by Denis O’Regan, who worked as Bowie’s official photographer. The installation plays out across eight screens and 84 hidden speakers, folding 12 Bowie songs alongside O’Regan’s commentary and archive of nearly 800 photographs. Bowie died in 2016, but the project was conceived and developed with the full support and cooperation of the late singer’s estate.“David would have loved this, definitely,” O’Regan says. “And he would have loved it going into the Venice film festival. He was always a bit of a groundbreaker. David loved his technology. He loved making things happen and experimenting with new ideas, like his Bowie bonds orBowie.net. Listen to theAladdin Sane albumfrom 1973 and he’s already writing lyrics like, ‘Pour me out another phone, I’ll ring and see if your friends are home’. The thing about David is that he wasn’t just about the music. He was about mime, visuals, theatre, film.” It is this hybrid quality, O’Regan adds, that makes him a natural fit for Venice Immersive.Fittingly, David Bowie: Unseen Unheard rubs shoulders with a rogues’ gallery of genre-defying new work from around the globe. The climate crisis is a major focus at this year’s edition, with Felix Gaedtke and Gayatri Parameswaran’s Solomon Islands-set Solwata, Barthélemy Antoine-Loeff and Hugo Arcier’s interactive The White Saboteur and the LA wildfire documentary Out of the Ashes all tackling the issue of human-made climate change.Other potential highlights include the immersive nature documentaries Galápagos: The Last Eden and Disneynature’s Wolf, which conducts a virtual tour of Canada’s remote Ellesmere Island. James Elliott Mizroch’s VR installation Smithsonian Starstruck goes further still, inviting users to step inside the cosmos to watch a star being born.“The first years of Venice Immersive were more about experimentation,” says Rosenthal. “The pieces were either playing with the various formats or they were these small side projects of big media properties. Now we’re seeing big works that have a proper distribution strategy. That means that the work has a life that extends far beyond the island. They can be seen and enjoyed by people around the world.”Venice Immersive2026 runs until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalDavid BowieVirtual realityItalyEuropeFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Intoxicating mix of humour, high camp and danger’: Tim Curry remembered | Film | The Guardian
description: Guardian readers share memories of actor best known for roles in The Rocky Horror Show and Stephen King’s It
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: Guardian readers share memories of actor best known for roles in The Rocky Horror Show and Stephen King’s It
Content: Tim Curry gained wide acclaim as the extraterrestrial mad scientist Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarView image in fullscreenTim Curry gained wide acclaim as the extraterrestrial mad scientist Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarFilm‘Intoxicating mix of humour, high camp and danger’: Tim Curry rememberedGuardian readers share memories of actor best known for roles in The Rocky Horror Show and Stephen King’s ItGuardian readers andAlfie PackhamWed 2 Sep 2026 15.27 BSTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.49 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Always had a glorious glint in his eye’I first saw him in the 1978 series Will Shakespeare, where he played Shakespeare alongside Nicholas Clay. Two very classy actors who, whatever the value of the programme, made me want to know more about the man and his work.Tim Curryalways had a glorious glint in his eye which drew you in as if you were the only person who understood.Margaret Carradus, Lancaster‘A delightful exchange’My best friend lives down the street from the Dakota building [in Manhattan]. One night I was waiting for her outside and two nicely dressed, handsome gentlemen were walking together. I was holding my very sweet poodle, Honey, in my arms. One of the men, who I then realised was Mr Curry, placed his hand under Honey’s chin and said: “She looks like a delicious peppermint!” We all chuckled as they continued on their way. Quite a delightful exchange.Mary Donaghy, New YorkClowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in picturesRead more‘That intoxicating mix of humour, high camp, sex and danger’I’ve always loved Tim Curry. More than any other performer. That intoxicating mix of humour, high camp, sex and danger. So I was excited to spot him in a florist decades ago and told him I was a fan. He was very friendly and said he was buying flowers for the cast of a show he was in – first-night presents – and filled the back of his car with them.Jo Glanville, LondonView image in fullscreenTim Curry in The Rocky Horror Picture Show … ‘no words to describe how important [he was] to me and my freaky relationship with myself and my gender identity’.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Allstar‘No other actor could have pulled that role off’As a child, I remember being captivated and equally terrified seeing him as the grand wizard in The Worst Witch and ever since he has continued to do both. But my favourite character of his has to be Wadsworth in Clue. No other actor could have pulled that role off with its endless dialogue and frenzied physical comedy requirements. A legend in every sense.Robert E Moore, Los Angeles‘He played a role in my self-acceptance’One of the first films that stuck with me as a child was FernGully: The Last Rainforest. Tim Curry has been a part of so much of my life. The Rocky Horror Picture Show was so important to me as a queer person and there are no words to describe how important the role of Frank-N-Furter is to me and my freaky relationship with myself and my gender identity. Even at the end of his life, he played a role in my self acceptance. Since I was 10 years old, I have developed a disability that affects my ability to walk, talk, use my hands and arms, and to see and hear. As my mobility and speech declined, he showed me I can still be an icon and contribute to the world even though I’m different and can’t do what everyone else can.Lilly, 22, PenrithView image in fullscreenTim Curry performs in the musical Spamalot at the Broadway premiere in New York.Photograph: Stuart Ramson/AP‘He could embody the wildest characters’I first remember seeing the Rocky Horror Picture Show as a teenager in the Chicagoland area. It blew my mind. I had no idea what to make of it, nor of the costumed people attending. I saw it again several times and couldn’t get enough. After I moved to Japan, I found a copy of the DVD and shared it with friends, all of whom loved it. What always struck me was how he could embody the wildest characters and give them enough depth that you enjoyed them, even if you didn’t like them. The risks he took were admirable. His characters allowed me to explore who I am and appreciate being not the norm. He was a true thespian and a unique person. No one can replace him. Sayonara, Mr Curry, you will be missed and remembered.Joe Guzman, 63, Japan‘A lovely man’In 1982, I was Pamela Stephenson’s dresser on The Pirates of Penzance, which starred Tim Curry as the Pirate King. I got tickets for my sister and my nephew, who were seven or eight years old, to see the show. Neither had ever been to a West End production before. At one point during the performance, Tim Curry took a breath during a rousing speech and in that silence, my nephew, entirely carried away by the experience, very audibly shouted his support. Without missing a beat, Tim Curry replied: “Well said, my man!” A lovely man and I still have my “buckets of blood” badges he distributed to the cast and crew.Gill, East SussexView image in fullscreenTim Curry with Richard O’Brien and Patricia Quinn in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Allstar‘Charm personified’I briefly met him, twice, at the stage door of the Palace theatre when he was in Spamalot in 2006. Although clearly tired after his wonderful performance, he was charm personified – and very happy to sign not only my Spamalot pieces, but also some of my Rocky Horror memorabilia. His was the last of the four signatures I needed on my 8x10 of the famous throne scene during Sweet Transvestite in The Rocky Horror Picture Show – now one of the most precious artefacts in my collection. More importantly, I got to say thank you to him for his performances. I’m really glad I did. Speaking to such a hero can be an intimidating experience: there’s a risk they will disappoint. Curry never did. He was every bit as wonderful as he was when he first strode out on stage that night, looked out into the audience, and every one of us truly believed that he was “looking directly at me!”Edward Marlowe, 52, LondonExplore more on these topicsFilmTim CurryRocky Horror ShowActingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The year of Domhnall Gleeson: ‘No one talks about actors’ dedication. But I had a perm for five months!’ | Domhnall Gleeson | The Guardian
