description: He started in the Harry Potter films and has since become ubiquitous, playing every type of character: romcom leads, evil villains, comical idiots. He even starred in a Taylor Swift video. So how does he stay so under the radar?
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: He started in the Harry Potter films and has since become ubiquitous, playing every type of character: romcom leads, evil villains, comical idiots. He even starred in a Taylor Swift video. So how does he stay so under the radar?
Content: ‘I don’t believe in having a bad time at work’ … Domhnall Gleeson.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian. Photographer's assistant: Flora LunaView image in fullscreen‘I don’t believe in having a bad time at work’ … Domhnall Gleeson.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian. Photographer's assistant: Flora LunaDomhnall GleesonInterviewThe year of Domhnall Gleeson: ‘No one talks about actors’ dedication. But I had a perm for five months!’Steve RoseHe started in the Harry Potter films and has since become ubiquitous, playing every type of character: romcom leads, evil villains, comical idiots. He even starred in a Taylor Swift video. So how does he stay so under the radar?Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.33 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDomhnall Gleeson has got so much new stuff coming up, someone recently joked that this was the “summer of Domhnall”. Now the phrase is all over the internet, and Gleeson is mortified: “The worry is that somebody will say this to me now thinking that I believe it.” He doesn’t know where it came from – possibly his co-star Gayle Rankin on his new movie The Incomer. “It’s certainly not something I’m trying to push … but it would be great if it could be the headline.”He’s in a good mood when we meet at a London hotel on a hot afternoon. You could say he’s good at interviews – charming, funny, garrulous, the perfect chatshow guest. He could just beacting, admittedly, but he seems to be a genuinely good-natured, grounded sort of guy.The Incomer, an eccentric Scottish comedy, is one of three new projects Gleeson has coming out in a matter of weeks. The others are the second season of the US Office spin-off The Paper and Werner Herzog’s new film, Bucking Fastard, which is about to play at the Venice film festival. More of all this later, but first we must address Gleeson’s most prominent, and least probable, recent role: as the star of a Taylor Swift music video.View image in fullscreenGleeson as Daniel in The Incomer.Photograph: Universal Pictures. All Rights Reserved/PADirected by Swift herself, thevideo for Opaliteis a bizarrely goofy concoction with an equally bizarre origin story. It came about because the two of them appeared together on the Graham Norton show last October. Fellow guest Cillian Murphy joked that The Paper was worth watching for Gleeson’s dancing alone. “I’m hoping to get in a Taylor Swift music video,” he joked in reply.That was that, he thought. “Then two weeks later, we got an email. Like, wild!” Not just him: Swift asked every other guest on the show to be in the video – Murphy, Greta Lee, Jodie Turner-Smith, Lewis Capaldi,even Norton himself. “No one else in the world can come up with an idea like that and make it happen,” Gleeson says.View image in fullscreenWith Taylor Swift and Graham Norton, during the shoot for Swift’s music video Opalite.Photograph: SpotifyGleeson has the starring role, as a lonely man who gets an upgrade on his painful relationship with a cactus when he is magically matched with fellow loner Swift. Then they dance together joyfully in matching glittery turquoise tracksuits.“They told me the day before there was going to be a dance. I was like, are you fucking joking?” Gleeson recalls. Are you good at that kind of thing, I ask. “No. I’m terrible at it!” He spent all night practising in front of the mirror. But Swift’s direction did the rest: “She said ‘full send’, though I didn’t knowwhat that phrase meant. She was like, ‘The moves don’t matter. You just gotta go for and love it, and just trust in it and experience it.’” The first take after she said that was the one they used. “The believing in it and the joy of it helps you do it.”So did he go to her wedding?“Er …” He ums and ahs. “Can I plead the fifth?”Sociable as he is, Gleeson is also very good at protecting his privacy. He’d rather not answer questions about his immediate family (he has been married to the producer Juliette Bonass since 2023), and he’s not on social media at all, he says. “I think that’s just like a line in the sand that helps immediately in terms of the personal not being public.”In short, Gleeson does a fine job of staying under the radar while also being everywhere. He is not exactly an inconspicuous figure, with his bright red hair and striking features – his Italian co-worker in The Paper says to him: “Look at your eyes: scary, like goat” – but on screen Gleeson is remarkably adaptable. He doesn’t really have a type. He’s played romantic leads (Richard Curtis’s About Time, for example), evil villains (General Hux in the Star Wars movies, or terrorising Julianne Moore in last year’s Echo Valley), real-life characters (Bob Geldof, AA Milne), comical idiots (Frank of Ireland). Family films, period dramas, westerns, sci-fi – he just seems to fit in wherever you put him. Even his age is strangely malleable: he’s now 43 but looks barely any older than he did playing Bill Weasley in theHarry Potterfilms.View image in fullscreenGleeson: ‘I liked the buzz of hearing people laugh.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianWhat’s more, he’s so good at accents, I’d almost forgotten that he’s Irish. When I first met Gleeson a decade ago, it wason the set of Frank, the indie satire based on the outsider musician Frank Sidebottom. We were in a freezing cabin in rural Ireland but Gleeson was playing a middle-class English guy, and stayed flawlessly in accent throughout (but not in character). That’s the best way, he’s learned from experience: “One day when I was doing Harry Potter I kind of went Australian by accident and couldn’t retrieve it.” It has its disadvantages, though: “You don’t want to do any phone calls with anyone from home during your work day.”In The Incomer he’s passing as Scottish, which is more challenging: “Going to Scotland and doing a Scottish accent in front of an all-Scottish crew is a very different experience.” It was kind of fitting, though: Gleeson plays the unwelcome visitor of the title: a mainland bureaucrat who comes to a remote Scottish isle to evict its only residents, a pair of insular siblings (Rankin and Grant O’Rourke). Written and directed by Louis Paxton, and filmed right at the northern tip of Scotland, the film is a charming mix of surreal comedy, local folklore, rugged landscapes and tender companionship, plus a great deal of seagull action – catching them, eating them, being attacked by them, even pretending to be them.View image in fullscreenGleeson as Ned in The Paper, with (from left) Ramona Young as Nicole, Oscar Nuñez as Oscar Martinez and Alex Edelman as Adam.Photograph: Peacock/SkyAt heart it’s a film about isolation and acceptance, he says. His character is as lonely as the siblings: an awkward, underconfident middle-manager type. He cuts a pretty pathetic figure visually, too: geeky dress sense, feebly unassertive, his hair a mess. “I got a perm for that,” he says. “No one talks about the dedication of an actor any more. I lived with a perm for four or five months after I did that film!” But he wanted to have a “comedic silhouette”, he says. “So the perm made just my head bigger, like a big lollipop sort of thing.”He’s a slightly more dashing middle-manager type in The Paper: the almost naively idealistic editor of a once great Ohio newspaper. The show is a gentle mockumentary sitcom in the mould of co-creator Greg Daniels’ other hits, Parks and Recreation and The Office, but it touches on a serious issue: the decline of local news (the paper in question is an afterthought to the company’s primary business – manufacturing toilet paper). It’s not overtly political, but “making something that is pro-journalism speaks for itself in terms of protecting it and caring about it”, says Gleeson, who considers himself “very much on the left”.As always, Gleeson did his homework. Months before starting, he went and hung out with real journalists on some of Ohio’s surviving daily newspapers, shadowing them, attending editorial meetings, asking questions. It was eye-opening but also depressing. “By the time we were doing press for the first season, this person who I had shadowed a little bit, who was a very well-established journalist, was out of the job,” he says. She’d moved on because she could no longer make a living.View image in fullscreenGleeson in Frank, with Michael Fassbender.Photograph: Cinematic/Alamy“It’s harder than it should be to do good journalism. People don’t want to pay for it, and people who it’s against don’t want it to exist. So you can’t pretend that’s not happening, but the young people I met who were going into it, as well as those who were staying the course and fighting the good fight, I found overwhelmingly inspiring. So it gives me hope, even though maybe not optimism.”It’s a rare thing to interview an actor who actually sympathises with your profession, given how intrusive some of us can be: stalking their socials, ambushing their leisure time or even just asking questions about their lives, like I am now. But he knows the drill. “I’m trying to keep my personal life personal, just to talk about the work.”Having a famous dad may have coloured Gleeson’s stance towards celebrity – even if he was essentially a grownup before Brendan became well known outside Ireland in the late 90s. “He is much more intensely famous,” says Gleeson of his father. Back home, Brendan can no longer walk down the street without being stopped. Domhnall gets a little of that, he says, “but not to the same extent”. He goes into Dublin all the time and it’s usually fine. “I’m quite unusual or individual-looking, but I’m also quite different-looking in lots of things, so sometimes people don’t put them all together, which is great.” The perm drew some attention, though, he admits.View image in fullscreenGleeson with Clémence Poésy, Robbie Coltrane and Mark Williams in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 1.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyHis parents never encouraged or discouraged him, or his three younger brothers, from following in his father’s footsteps. “The only thing: they asked me not to be a standup comedian. Probably just because I wasn’t funny.” He’s not being entirely truthful here. His intention was to write and direct, but one day he agreed to accept an award on his father’s behalf. He was still at school at the time (a state secondary school just outside Dublin). “I was 16 and really shy, but weirdly it was like, ‘I could do that if he needs me to.’” This was going out live on Irish national television. “Right before I went up, they said, ‘You’ve got 30 seconds for your acceptance speech,’ and I had this three-page speech that my dad had written. I was like, ‘I’m not gonna be able to say that in 30 seconds,’ so I went up and sort of vamped, and made fun of it.”It turned out hewasfunny. “I quite liked the buzz of hearing people laugh,” he admits. His father’s agent, Teri Hayden, was watching, and called him in for a meeting.Three years later, in his first year at the Dublin Institute of Technology, he was cast in Martin McDonagh’s IRA black comedy The Lieutenant of Inishmore. That’s when he got hooked on acting: “I didn’t have a thing of, ‘I don’t want to be an actor because of my dad.’ It was just by doing it I went, ‘Idowant to be an actor.’ And the play was in London, so there was a bit of distance from my dad. It wasn’t like doing it in Dublin and feeling him looking over my shoulder the whole time.” Four years later the play transferred to Broadway, where Gleeson received a Tony nomination. His career was up and running.View image in fullscreenFamily affair … Gleeson (centre) with (right) his dad, Brendan, and brother Brian in The Walworth Farce, in Dublin.Photograph: Artur Widak/Nurphoto/ShutterstockHe has worked with his father and his brother Brian, who is also an actor, many times since: in McDonagh’s short film Six Shooter, which won an Oscar in 2006; in the Harry Potter movies (Brendan played Alastor “Mad-Eye” Moody); he and Brian fought to the death in Darren Aronofsky’s Mother! and were best buddies in the 2021 sitcom Frank of Ireland. And all three of them performed on stage together in 2006 in Enda Walsh’s The Walworth Farce.It’s not necessarily a jolly love-in when they work together. “It can be difficult at times, and I’m sure we all drive each other mad, but that happens with everybody you work with.” But then it’s not meant to be fun, he believes. “There’s no point being there to be nice to each other. The point is to change the other person’s performance with your own, the point is to bounce off each other and create sparks.” Not in a negative way, though. “I don’t believe in having a bad time at work. That’s all bullshit: to make good art, you have to have a bad time – fuck all that.”He’s now worked with some of the biggest names in the business – the Coen brothers, Tom Cruise, Leonardo DiCaprio, Jennifer Lawrence, Julianne Moore, Margot Robbie,Taylor Swift– but Gleeson still gets awed by people, he says. “When I met the Coen brothers I found it hard. I bumped into Paul Thomas Anderson at something once and I found that very difficult to keep my shit together.” That was almost the case with Werner Herzog, but luckily, their first meeting was over Zoom, “which is so depersonalising and demythologising, just because it’s all, ‘Sorry, can you hear me?’ There’s nothing fancy about it. After that I felt prepared to meet him.”View image in fullscreenGleeson: ‘You don’t know what the next challenge is going to be.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianGleeson only worked a few days on Bucking Fastard, but it was a memorable experience. Kate and Rooney Mara play twins who do everything together – speaking, living, dressing. They even fall for the same man. Gleeson plays their social worker. Unbelievably, it’s based on a true story. Herzog met the real-life twins, Freda and Greta Chaplin (the title is a spoonerism they both made, in unison, in court). “I think maybe he was interested in making a documentary about them,” says Gleeson. He began to suspect that although his character is Irish, he was based on Herzog himself. “He told me a couple of stories about meeting them and what it was like to be around them, then I realised my character in the film has some similar experiences. One of the scenes is basically something that happened to him, with them.”Herzog, of course, has one of the most famous and highly imitable accents in cinema. Was Gleeson tempted to try it? “When I realised that my character has aspects of him in it, for a second in your mind you’re like, ‘Should I do it?’ Then you’re like, ‘No. Absolutely not. No, no, no.’”What’s next for Gleeson? He doesn’t really know, he says, though he hopes The Paper will get another season. He’s always got stuff in the pipeline, he’s always in demand for all sorts of roles, genres, accents. Not having a “type” has proved to be a professional asset, and it keeps life interesting. “It’s where I’m happiest,” he says, “because you don’t know what the next job is going to be, you don’t know what the next challenge is going to be.”Before he goes, he apologises again for not answering some of the more personal questions I’d asked him, which really isn’t necessary at all. Maybe it’s the other side of the coin of his versatility. We don’t have to know everything about people just because we see them on screen – and often it helps that we don’t.Season two of The Paper launches on Sky and NOW in the UK on 10 September.The Incomer is in cinemas in the UK from 4 September.Explore more on these topicsDomhnall GleesonBrendan GleesonTelevisionHarry PotterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Runner review – Gal Gadot stumbles through derivative high-speed, low-rent thriller | Gal Gadot | The Guardian
description: A string of London locations can’t save Amazon’s overly familiar B-movie dragged down by another ineffective performance by the Wonder Woman star
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: A string of London locations can’t save Amazon’s overly familiar B-movie dragged down by another ineffective performance by the Wonder Woman star
Content: Gal Gadot in The RunnerPhotograph: Amazon MGM StudiosView image in fullscreenGal Gadot in The RunnerPhotograph: Amazon MGM StudiosGal GadotReviewThe Runner review – Gal Gadot stumbles through derivative high-speed, low-rent thrillerA string of London locations can’t save Amazon’s overly familiar B-movie dragged down by another ineffective performance by the Wonder Woman starBenjamin LeeWed 2 Sep 2026 05.05 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.12 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe’re propelled on to an extremely familiar journey in Amazon’s quickie action thriller The Runner, both in reheated premise and strategic aim. The film is yet another example of a real-time assassination nightmare as an ordinary citizen is placed in an extraordinary situation, forced to do something terrible by someone terrible. Think Johnny Depp in Nick of Time, Rachel McAdams in Red Eye, Shia LaBeouf in Eagle Eye, or more recently, Taron Egerton inCarry-Onand Meghann Fahy inDrop, with technology increasingly a key component. We’re also faced with what’s another strained attempt to turn Gal Gadot into a movie star, a mission that’s proved close to impossible after she broke out in Wonder Woman. Her streaming vehicles, likeRed NoticeandHeart of Stone, might have proved easy at-home hits (the latter was also surprisingly entertaining), but on the big screen, playing botha Disney villainandan Agatha Christie victimproved to be of little interest to audiences, who chosememe-ing her worst momentsover turning up to see them.Onslaught review – super soldier slasher doesn’t go hard enoughRead moreAn action-first film like The Runner, disposable and undemanding, might seem like the safest place for Gadot’s rather limited skill set, but even with a role that asks more of her physically than emotionally, it’s still a rather awkward stretch. Luckily, she’s paired with real on-the-ground London locations, from Kentish Town to Somerset House, the city proving to be a scene-stealing co-star. Gadot plays Maia, a single mother and lawyer, who says goodbye to her diabetic son at school and starts her run to work (surely her son’s diabetes will not become an important part of the plot,right?). But her day is soon interrupted by a nefarious “freelancer” working for a local crime boss, voiced byDamian Lewis. He has kidnapped her son and hacked his insulin dispenser, forcing him into a hypoglycemic coma, his life hanging in the balance until Maia agrees to murder a key witness she was supposed to be representing in court that morning. The film’s slight novelty is that Maia must run five miles to the hotel where he’s staying within an hour, no interruptions allowed. The slight 2026 update is that, in what’s increasingly becoming a lazy crutch for screenwriters, AI is an important weapon.It’s all as hopelessly cut-and-paste as one would expect – lead character with relevant personal trauma revealed to us as if it’s a surprise, sinister voice on the phone saying allegedly creepy things like: “There’s more blood in the human body than you can fathom!”, teary “I can’t do this” waterworks hardening into an inevitable turn of the tables – and given just how effective Carry-On was at freshening up this formula, The Runner just feels that much lazier in comparison.It’s directed byKevin Macdonald, the Oscar-winning documentarian behind Touching the Void whose narrative films have included State of Play and the very enjoyable submarine thriller Black Sea. He tries to make it all as frenetic and involving as possible, maniacally hurtling his camera around the city as we run alongside Gadot, but rather than immersing us in the chaos of London, his dated flourishes take us back to the 2000s instead. The action is cheap and unexciting, and the more he tries to insist a sense of style upon the film, the worse it ends up looking, with a misjudged slow shutter speed effect that, when coupled with Gadot’s hapless histrionics, borders on laughable.Her performance is once again athletically impressive (one believes she is actually running!) but entirely emotionally stiff and in essentially a one-woman showcase, with plentiful zoomed-in closeups, it crushes a film already limping its way to the finish line. The best version of this movie has us right there with her, agonising over what decisions she makes and nervously keeping an eye on the countdown clock but, crucially, Gadot just can’t get us on side enough to care about what happens. Mark Gibson’s script is far too plain, the rules of the game far too inconsistent and the dynamic between hero and villain far too generic (Carry-On found a fun mix of a boss/subordinate and dom/sub relationship to keep us involved) and an attempt at a smug switcheroo ending is far too clunky to prove as sneakily smart as those involved seem to think it is. Intelligence might not be what one would expect here, which is somewhat acceptable in B-movie territory such as this, but the lack of excitement is hard to forgive.The Runner is now available on Amazon Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsGal GadotThrillersDamian LewisAction and adventure filmsKevin MacdonaldreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Fall 2: Deadpoint review – silly seat-edge sequel can’t reach heights of the original | Thrillers | The Guardian
description: There are just about enough hand-over-mouth moments to please thrill-seekers in this B-movie follow-up but eyerolls soon prevail
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: There are just about enough hand-over-mouth moments to please thrill-seekers in this B-movie follow-up but eyerolls soon prevail
Content: A still from Fall 2: Deadpoint.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenA still from Fall 2: Deadpoint.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentThrillersReviewFall 2: Deadpoint review – silly seat-edge sequel can’t reach heights of the originalThere are just about enough hand-over-mouth moments to please thrill-seekers in this B-movie follow-up but eyerolls soon prevailBenjamin LeeWed 2 Sep 2026 15.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 17.07 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was plenty of silliness but also plenty of suspense in 2022’s modestly successful don’t-look-down thrillerFall, a surprisingly well-made micro-budget marvel that ultimately found its audience on Netflix. While certain elements, such as the no-name leads and increasingly hokey script, might have made it seem like yet another churned out low-rent original for the streamer, it boasted more genuine thrills than we’ve come to expect there or really anywhere during this quantity over quality time for genre movies.Onslaught review – super soldier slasher doesn’t go hard enoughRead moreA sequel was financially inevitable (the original cost just $3m) but narratively questionable, given that the self-contained survival tale did not lend itself to the elasticity of a franchise. So here we are with Fall 2: Deadpoint, a palm-sweating formula regurgitated with only moderately jolting results. The first film saw two young women trying to get over the loss of a loved one by, naturally, climbing up an abandoned TV tower. So now the sequel has two young women trying to get over the loss of a loved one (who died in the first film) by, naturally, attempting a sky-high plank walk on the side of a mountain in Thailand. History then repeats itself when chaos strikes, this time courtesy of a rockslide, and our heroines have something more than grief to worry about.If, like me or any other sane person, you struggled to understand why someone would willingly put themselves into such a deeply stupid position in the first film then you’ll be unsurprised to hear that no one has figured out anything smarter for the sequel. The thrill-seeking dummy from Fall, whose death was used as a tiresome eyeroll twist, has since gone viral, as told to us in a cheaply unconvincing montage of social media posts (cheaper, but also funnier, still is the film using a bottle of “Jim Dandie’s” instead of Jack Daniel’s). She has left behind close friend Luce (Queen Charlotte’s Arsema Thomas) and sister Jax (British actor Harriet Slater, faking a solid American accent) who make the bizarre decision to honour her by also risking their lives doing something similarly reckless with help from a conveniently handsome American tour guide (another Briton, Tom Brittney). At one point, a character says to another: “I mean, remember why you’re here in the first place” and I honestly couldn’t tell you why.The series, as we now must call it, leans heavily on bland motivational thinking (“Fear is something you can control,” etc) but there is no amount of tea towel quotes that can explain why these characters are doing what they’re doing. It’s safest once again not to think too deeply about the hows and whys here and just focus on the horrors, of which there are plenty as disintegrating planks, rusty bars and unfortunate weather cause slipping, screaming and, you guessed it, falling.I can’t pretend that there aren’t effectively awful moments or that my hand didn’t cover my mouth on occasion, the formula working just the way it should in the film’s most superbly nauseating sequences. There are more ingredients involved here, as is often the case with a sequel, but the more the film explores anything that isn’t a scene aimed at stressing us out to the point of exhaustion, the more the soapy writing disappears into bubbles. The two women are solid leads, believably terrified throughout, but again they’re saddled with a harebrained twist that is conceptually fun but falls apart when thought about for longer than three seconds. The balance of suspense and stupidity ultimately teeters towards the latter in an overcooked finale which gives us another daft twist before, hilariously, setting up an already greenlit third film that promises to be an Avengers-style team-up. I think we might already be at Fall: Endgame.Fall 2: Deadpoint is out now in US cinemas, in Australia on 3 September and in the UK on 9 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsThrillersAction and adventure filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hungry review – hippo horror sees multi-ton mammal run amok among bayou boat-trippers | Film | The Guardian
description: A group of thinly drawn characters on a Louisiana tour fight for survival against a rampaging vegetarian
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: A group of thinly drawn characters on a Louisiana tour fight for survival against a rampaging vegetarian
Content: Meet-cute … Madison Davenport in Hungry.Photograph: © Sky UK/ Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenMeet-cute … Madison Davenport in Hungry.Photograph: © Sky UK/ Signature EntertainmentFilmReviewHungry review – hippo horror sees multi-ton mammal run amok among bayou boat-trippersA group of thinly drawn characters on a Louisiana tour fight for survival against a rampaging vegetarianLeslie FelperinWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 07.01 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis animal-attack horror plugs a gap with beasties – hippopotamuses – that may be deadly in real life but are hard to take seriously as a threat on screen. As someone says here, they have cute ears. Even the film’s title, evoking the kids’ game Hungry Hungry Hippos, diminishes the menace. That’s perhaps not the tone to set if you’re trying to persuade audiences that fatal consequences are in the offing. And as the script often reminds us, hippos are vegetarian, so hunger isn’t driving these multi-ton mammals to murder. Turns out they’re massively territorial, and especially dangerous when protecting their young. That, or they do just think killing people is fun.The film naturally spends less time worrying about the hippos’ motives and dwells more on the victims, who look pretty doomed given their thin characterisations. This lot certainly weren’t expecting to be attacked by a hippo when they woke up because they are on a bayou tour in Louisiana, where the biggest threats are normally alligators.Easily winning girl-least-likely-to-get-hippotomised because she’s nice is Sistine (Madison Davenport) – an all-American cute ingenue who has come along with her sassy best friend Hannah (Olivia Bernstone), who is mainly focused on hunky tour guide Rodrigo (Michel Curiel). Also on board the boat are an assortment of folk with varying degrees of likability, including a retired fireman (Jim Meskimen), his middle-aged daughter (Samantha Coughlan), her teenage son (River Codack), and finally a career lady (Tracey Bonner) clad in very bayou-unfriendly suit and stilettos.Writer-director James Nunn and his team are clearly less interested in developing character than in building suspense with ominous splashes at the edge of the frame. The film’s strongest suit, apart from the scary hippo itself, is the mechanics of rescue and beast evasion, with our girl Sistine’s gymnast training coming in handy, as does the fireman’s knowledge of pulleys and levers. But none of that cancels out the essential silliness of the premise.Hungry is on Sky Cinema from 4 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ready tae Drap review – clashing neighbours trapped in a lift get roars of approval | Stage | The Guardian
description: Comedy chemistry drives a play that asks if three contrasting characters – conspiracy theorist, pregnant mum, hen-do attendee – can find common ground
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Comedy chemistry drives a play that asks if three contrasting characters – conspiracy theorist, pregnant mum, hen-do attendee – can find common ground
Content: Rift in a lift … Tinashe Warikandwa, Éimi Quinn and Isabelle Joss in Ready tae DrapPhotograph: Eoin CareyView image in fullscreenRift in a lift … Tinashe Warikandwa, Éimi Quinn and Isabelle Joss in Ready tae DrapPhotograph: Eoin CareyStageReviewReady tae Drap review – clashing neighbours trapped in a lift get roars of approvalÒran Mór, GlasgowComedy chemistry drives a play that asks if three contrasting characters – conspiracy theorist, pregnant mum, hen-do attendee – can find common groundKatie HawthorneWed 2 Sep 2026 12.46 BSTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.30 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrapping three nightmare neighbours in the dodgy lift of their Glasgow high-rise, Ready tae Drap has lots of sparky, slapstick humour – but not so much nuance.Crotchety conspiracy theorist Pat (Isabelle Joss) is in her 70s and armed with barbed, uninvited observations. Saintly, exhausted Muslim mum of two Aaliyah (Tinashe Warikandwa) is on the verge of giving birth to her third child. Dry-humoured Lauren (performed by playwright Éimi Quinn) is the play’s millennial, fourth-wall-breaking narrator, clad in fishnets and bunny ears for a hen-do. It’s a classic setup: can these contrasting characters find common ground in a tight spot?Not really. Quinn’s vivid new play digs into chalk-and-cheese humour and an ever-present threat of body fluids, cracking jokes as blue as Lauren’s favourite flavour of WKD. Within the lift’s cramped confines (with concise design from Heather Grace Currie), Maureen Carr’s direction is dynamic and physical, bringing out the cast’s comedic chemistry: Pat’s gleeful descriptions of her post-menopausal sex life leave Aaliyah and Lauren wide-eyed and the Òran Mór’s full house roaring.But all this (literal, enjoyable) pissing about disguises the crux of the matter. For most of the hour, the older woman’s racism is watered down – although one sharply written line about Glasgow’s city centre fires has the audience nodding in agreement before it slides into blatant xenophobia. When Pat eventually tears off a vicious tirade against migrants, directed at Aaliyah whom she “doesn’t mean to offend”, both characters feel caricatured and underwritten. Even then, Pat’s lonely backstory is richer than Aaliyah’s, who is given a detail-free story about moving to Glasgow as a refugee – and all the while, Lauren, the audience’s direct contact, has fallen asleep in the corner.When she wakes, her own emotional reckoning is just as thin: Aaliyah and Pat team up to demand why “selfish” Lauren doesn’t want kids, and she skims over a vague answer in less time than the trio spent poking fun at hen-do inflatables.Ready tae Drap wisely doesn’t pretend that small talk will fix society’s deepening trenches. But despite its sleeves-rolled-up approach to life’s grubbier stuff, it shrinks away from emotional viscera.AtÒran Mór, Glasgow, until 5 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tupac’s murder: solved at last? – podcast | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: Thirty years after Tupac Shakur’s death, a man has been found guilty of killing the hip-hop legend. William Shaw on the star’s life, legacy and untimely death
Author: Helen Pidd
Headline: Thirty years after Tupac Shakur’s death, a man has been found guilty of killing the hip-hop legend. William Shaw on the star’s life, legacy and untimely death
Content: 00:00:0000:00:00Today in FocusTupac ShakurTupac’s murder: solved at last? – podcastThirty years after Tupac Shakur’s death, a man has been found guilty of killing the hip-hop legend.William Shawon the star’s life, legacy and untimely deathMore ways to listenApple podcastsSpotifyRSS FeedDownloadPresented byHelen PiddwithWilliam Shawand Jessica Hill, produced byGuy Szafman,Saskia Collette,Tom Glasser,Ruth Abrahams,Ivor ManleyandRoss Burns; executive producersHoma KhaleeliandSami KentWed 2 Sep 2026 03.00 BSTShareIn 1996,Tupac Shakurwas shot in a drive-by ambush in Las Vegas. He was only 25 years old and already one of the biggest artists in the US.He had just released a huge album, All Eyez on Me, which spawned two No 1 singles. He’d worked with some of hip-hop’s greatest stars. He’d starred in Hollywood films. It seemed he could do anything. And then, he died.For 30 years, no one was held to account for his murder. Meanwhile, his legend only grew, along with the conspiracies surrounding his death.Then, on Monday afternoon, in aLas Vegascourt, came a resolution – of sorts: the news that Duane Keith Davis had been found guilty of the murder of Shakur.The journalist Jessica Hill has been covering the case. She says there was little physical evidence of Davis’s wrongdoing. Instead, there were the accounts he had given himself – in books, podcasts and interviews – about his actions on the night. But although Davis was convicted of murder, he is not believed to be the person who pulled the trigger on the night Shakur was killed.William Shaw had met and interviewed Shakur, and remembers an erudite, multi-talented 25-year-old with a rich cultural life. His death, he says, should be seen in the context of the terrible situation in Los Angeles at the time. “It was about this terrible situation of massive drug sales going on, which was funding massive ongoing violence. And then this fact that this community was incredibly historically maltreated.”Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsTupac ShakurToday in FocusLas VegasHip-hop

title: Whisky galore – and now plenty more besides: exploring the Scottish island of Islay | Scotland holidays | The Guardian
description: Distilleries are the backbone of Islay’s economy and tourist trade. Thanks to their success, other businesses – from breweries and farms to restaurants and chocolatiers – are now thriving and adding to the island’s appeal
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: Distilleries are the backbone of Islay’s economy and tourist trade. Thanks to their success, other businesses – from breweries and farms to restaurants and chocolatiers – are now thriving and adding to the island’s appeal
Content: The village of Port Charlotte on Islay, located on the shore of Loch Indaal.Photograph: Mark Unsworth/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe village of Port Charlotte on Islay, located on the shore of Loch Indaal.Photograph: Mark Unsworth/AlamyScotland holidaysWhisky galore – and now plenty more besides: exploring the Scottish island of IslayDistilleries are the backbone of Islay’s economy and tourist trade. Thanks to their success, other businesses – from breweries and farms to restaurants and chocolatiers – are now thriving and adding to the island’s appealAilsa SheldonWed 2 Sep 2026 07.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 07.10 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Paps of Jura disappear into the mist as I pedal along the shores of Loch Indaal, and the rain cloud I’ve been racing finally catches up. I stash myhire bikeatPort Charlotte youth hostel, quickly change and make it toLochindaal Seafood Kitchenjust before the downpour.I’m soon warmed, by the welcome then by a bowl of creamy fish chowder. “We’ve plenty of fresh seafood just in,” is all the temptation I need to order the seafood plate. It’s a bowl for one, but a hungry one, and soon I’m picking and cracking my way through piles of fat langoustines and crab claws, with hot whisky-butter scallops and plenty of bread and butter.The island of Islay, off the west coast of Scotland, is far better known for its drinks than its food. With 10, soon to be 11, working whisky distilleries, Islay is synonymous with rich, heavily peated single malts. But, over several days cycling around the island, I find that whisky does much more than fill warehouses and attract tourists. It is helping to support an island where agriculture, fishing and hospitality have long struggled to provide year-round employment.View image in fullscreenLunch at Lochindaal Seafood Kitchen.Photograph: Ailsa SheldonAtBruichladdich, one of Islay’s smallest distilleries but the largest private employer, that begins with the barley. When the distillery was bought by a pair of wine merchants after being mothballed several times in the 1990s, they questioned why the barley arriving at the distillery was being sourced from so many different places. Surely, they thought, like vineyards, where the grain was grown would influence the whisky’sterroir.They began encouraging farmers to grow barley on Islay, which hadn’t been done since before the second world war. Farmers were understandably wary of taking on an unfamiliar crop, particularly as the tens of thousands of migratory geese from Greenland are partial to a field of young barley. When Islay’s last creamery closed in 2000, the dairy industry collapsed, so growing barley offered farmers another way to use their land, and Bruichladdich guaranteed to buy the crop regardless of the yield. Today, 21 Islay farms grow barley for the distillery, producing half of its requirements, and early experiments with rye have been promising.double quotation markGrowing up on Islay, whisky was a way of life. Every family has at least one person working in whiskyEva MacIntyre grew up on Islay, tried living on the mainland and came back. She now works for Bruichladdich as a brand ambassador and takes me up the hill to see the distillery’s water source.“Growing up on Islay, whisky was a way of life,” she tells me. “It’s not just a drink; it’s all about who you share it with.” Before her whisky presentations, she practises with her grandfather. Her story is not unusual. “Every family has at least one person working in whisky,” she tells me.View image in fullscreenRoom with a lighthouse view … at Port Charlotte youth hostel.Photograph: Ridgeline_PrintsI meet Kate Hannett, a full-time forager responsible for gathering the 22 botanicals used in the Botanist gin across peaty bogs and hillsides. Her brother, Adam, is Bruichladdich’s master blender, having started his career as a tour guide. Lisa Matthews, the assistant blender, is also anIleach(a person from Islay) and the distillery’s first female blender. Her brother is a brand ambassador in the US. There are jobs in whisky, and reasons to stay on the island, that most rural communities could only dream of offering their young people.The distilleries are woven into Islay life. I hear frequent stories of distilleries helping each other out and lending equipment when machinery breaks down. “It’s really not competitive,” Eva says. As well as the employment opportunities, whisky benefits the infrastructure. There’s a full-time fire service, unusual across rural Scotland. Even the swimming pool is heated by waste energy from Bowmore distillery.AtIslay Ales, another island-made drink begins with barley and soft west coast water. The brewery, founded in 2004, opened a new brewhouse last year. Its spent grain, or draff, goes to local farms for feed and wastewater is treated through a reed bed. On an island where the growing season is short and the weather can change before you’ve finished your pint, making food and drink locally is not necessarily easy. “After theAgricultural Show, which is the third Thursday in August, it’s winter,” I’m told.View image in fullscreenIslay Cocoa uses several local ingredients in its chocolates.Photograph: Islay CocoaEmma Goudie ofIslay Cocoabegan making chocolates as an easily transportable product that wouldn’t compete directly with other island food businesses. She uses local ingredients where they make sense, rather than simply because they are local.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s quality first, but I’m lucky that the produce we have here is excellent.” Her current range includes Orsay sea salt, Argyll coffee, and sourdough from neighbouring Jura. She also works with the whisky industry, creating chocolates designed to pair with Ardbeg and forCaol Ilatours. “It grew quite organically and in the best way,” she says.Iain and Alexander MacLellan are the fourth and fifth generations of a family whose hospitality business stretches back to the late 19th century. At Lochindaal Seafood Kitchen, Iain tells me he grew up with the fishers who supply the restaurant and remembers cooking mackerel and scallops on their boats. “I’ve been 52 years behind the bar,” he tells me. The restaurant grew out of the family pub atLochindall hotel, partly because, as Iain puts it, “we ran out of space to serve our seafood platters”.View image in fullscreenAilsa Sheldon enjoying a drink at Ardbeg House hotel.Photograph: Ailsa SheldonChef Ajish Johny came toPort Charlotte hotelafter working in India and Dubai, on cruise ships and in Wales, and has now been here for four years. His menus feature a curry of the day alongside Loch Gruinart oysters, locally caught fish and burgers made with beef from nearby Octomore Farm. “We never compromise on quality,” he says. “People on Islay are well travelled. They know what good food is.”And then there isArdbeg Housein Port Ellen, a once tired traditional hotel that has been transformed into a maximalist extension of the Ardbeg brand. There are 12 quirkily themed bedrooms, a fishing boat suspended over the bar and a theatrical restaurant with a beaten-metal ceiling, bold lighting and tables made from marble bathroom offcuts. It’s an exuberant place, but the food is excellent and well priced. I eat bread made with eight-year-old Ardbeg and thyme; langoustine bisque with pickled fennel and tarragon, then the catch of the day, sea bass, with cabbage, kale, roast potatoes and split beurre blanc. My taxi driver insisted that I try the sticky toffee pudding. My server does the same, so I take the hint and am rewarded with a treacly wedge of cake with whisky ice-cream. Outside, it’s raining again.Before the Clearances, about 15,000 people lived on Islay. Today, there are just over 3,000. Islay may have been built, in part, on whisky. But increasingly, the whisky is helping build something back: farms, breweries, restaurants, food businesses and reasons to stay.Ailsa Sheldon was a guest ofHostelling ScotlandandBruichladdich Distillery.Port Charlotteyouthhostelhas dorm beds from £28and private rooms from £78(open late March to early October). Travel to Islay from the Scottish mainland byCaledonian MacBrayne(CalMac) ferry fromKennacraigor by flying withLoganairfrom Glasgow. title: How to turn past-their-best bananas into a glorious ‘ice-cream’ – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Bananas often go off quickly, so use up over-ripe, brown specimens in a sugar-free dessert that will satisfy any sweet-tooth cravings
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Bananas often go off quickly, so use up over-ripe, brown specimens in a sugar-free dessert that will satisfy any sweet-tooth cravings
Content: ‘Really hits the spot’: Tom Hunt’s brown banana ‘ice-cream’.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian. Food styling: Tom Hunt.View image in fullscreen‘Really hits the spot’: Tom Hunt’s brown banana ‘ice-cream’.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian. Food styling: Tom Hunt.Waste notFoodHow to turn past-their-best bananas into a glorious ‘ice-cream’ – recipeBananas often go off quickly, so use up over-ripe, brown specimens in a sugar-free dessert that will satisfy any sweet-tooth cravingsTom HuntWed 2 Sep 2026 13.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.15 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith two young kids, we get through alotof bananas in our household. Perhaps surprisingly, though, most of them are frozen: our daughters eat them straight from the freezer most evenings, with frozen berries and yoghurt, for pudding. We normally order a stack of bananas every Saturday, and before the end of the week they inevitably start to turn brown. At this point, we peel, slice and freeze them for the children’s evening yoghurt, though sometimes, when we have a real excess, I turn them into today’s incredibly satisfying “ice-cream”. Its silky-smooth texture really hits the spot, and satisfies any ice-cream cravings without recourse to added sugar or excessive fat. The trick is to freeze the bananas in a single layer on a flat tray, so they don’t freeze into a homogeneous mass, then transfer to a container to enjoy as and when.Brown banana ‘ice-cream’This has to be in my top five everyday desserts, not least because brown bananas are very gooey and sweet, have a rich and creamy texture and a satiating flavour. Portion for portion, it feels luxurious and indulgent, even without the extra sugar, saturated fat, gums and stabilisers found in much commercial ice-cream and other ready-made desserts. Of course, blended fruit is itself a readily absorbable sugar, but the trade-off is worth it for the extra fibre, potassium, manganese and other vitamins. It’s also a fraction of the price of shop-bought ice-cream.This is best eaten fresh from the blender, but if you need to store a bumper batch, remember to take it out of the freezer at least 10 minutes before you want to scoop it.1 or more brown bananasHalf the bananas’ weight in liquid– water, yoghurt, milk or a plant-based alternativeToppings, all optional and to tasteChopped nutsCoconut flakesGrated chocolatePeel and chop the bananas into 2cm-thick slices (this makes them easier to blend later), then spread out on a tray and freeze for at least five hours. Once frozen, store in a sealed container in the freezer.To make the ice-cream, weigh the amount of banana you’ve taken out, then add half its weight in liquid – that is, water, yoghurt, milk or a plant-based alternative. Transfer to a jug blender and blitz smooth, but not for too long or the fruit will melt too much; stir, if need be, to get an even blend. Serve immediately as it is, or leave to soften like aMr Whippy-alike soft serve, or freeze for an hour or more for a firmer, scoopable texture, adding any optional toppings of your choice.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteFruitIce-cream and sorbetDessertfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Poppy O’Toole’s midweek timesavers: spicy chicken and baked rice, and Thai-style lemongrass fishcakes – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: You’ll thank yourself for making these batch-cooking beauties to store in the freezer until the next busy worknight
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: You’ll thank yourself for making these batch-cooking beauties to store in the freezer until the next busy worknight
Content: Poppy O’Toole’s midweek spicy chicken and baked rice.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenPoppy O’Toole’s midweek spicy chicken and baked rice.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.FoodPoppy O’Toole’s midweek timesavers: spicy chicken and baked rice, and Thai-style lemongrass fishcakes – recipeYou’ll thank yourself for making these batch-cooking beauties to store in the freezer until the next busy worknightPoppy O'TooleWed 2 Sep 2026 06.00 BSTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve called this spicy chicken and baked rice “midweek”, but you can enjoy this baby all week long. Juicy, spiced chicken, fluffy baked rice and enough flavour to make you bin that takeaway menu and raid your cupboards instead. Then some fragrant, delicate fishcakes with a lovely, bouncy texture, which are such a winner for the freezer. Taking only 10-ish minutes to cook from frozen, they save you from hungeranddistraction on a busy WFH day.Midweek spicy chicken and baked ricePrep10 minMarinate1 hrCook45 minServes8200gGreek yoghurtZest and juice of 1 lemon50g harissa paste1 tbsp garlic granules1 tbsp dried oregano2 tsp ground turmeric1 tbsp ras el hanout2 tsp ground coriander2 tsp ground cuminSalt and pepper16 skinless, boneless chicken thighsOlive oil3 red onions, peeled and roughly chopped into large pieces2 red peppers, deseeded and roughly chopped into large pieces4 garlic cloves, peeled and minced or grated2 tbsp tomato puree400g basmati rice1400g tincrushed tomatoes800ml chicken stockServing suggestions (optional)Sliced or pickled red onionCrumbled fetaFlat-leaf parsley leavesIn a bowl, combine the yoghurt, lemon zest and juice, harissa, garlic granules, dried oregano, ground turmeric, ras el hanout, coriander and cumin with a large pinch each of salt and pepper. Add the chicken thighs, give them a good mix to coat, then pop them in the fridge to marinate for at least an hour.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Meanwhile, put a glug of olive oil in an oven-safe saute pan on a high heat. Chuck in the onions and peppers, fry for two to three minutes, until colooured and slightly blackened, then add the garlic and fry for a minute more, until fragrant.Turn down the heat to medium, squeeze in the tomato puree and cook for one minute, until the mix darkens. Season generously, then tip in the rice and toast for a minute. Pour in the crushed tomatoes and chicken stock, and bring to a bubble.Put the chicken thighs on top of the rice – you want about half of each chicken thigh sitting above the level of the stock – then put the pot in the oven for 30 minutes, until the chicken is slightly charred and cooked through and the rice is tender. Serve immediately, piping hot, with the pickled red onion, feta and parsley, if you like.To eat later, freeze in an airtight container for up to three months. To reheat from frozen, heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 and reheat for 45–50 minutes, until piping hot throughout. Or defrost fully in the fridge overnight, then heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and reheat for 25–30 minutes, again until piping hot throughout.Lemongrass and ginger Thai-style fishcakesView image in fullscreenPoppy O’Toole’s lemongrass and ginger Thai-style fishcakes.Prep5 minChill1 hrCook15 minServes8500g skinless, boneless cod, or haddock200g shelled raw king prawns3 tbsp green Thai curry paste2 lemongrassstalks, bashed and roughly chopped50g fresh ginger, peeled and roughly chopped4 garlic cloves, peeled1–2 tbsp fish sauce, to taste2 tsp palm sugar1 tbsp light soy sauce2 eggsAbout 200g cornflourOlive oilTo serve (optional)Sweet chilli saucePickled vegCooked rice noodlesThai basil and mint leavesLime wedgesTip the fish, prawns, curry paste, lemongrass, ginger, garlic, fish sauce, palm sugar and soy sauce into a food processor. Crack in the eggs, then blitz to a paste. Tip the mixture into a bowl and stir through enough cornflour to make a wet dough (you may not need all of it, so add the cornflour in batches).Wet your hands so the fishcake mixture won’t stick to them, then weigh out 16 equal balls of about 70g each. Shape these into 2cm-thick patties, then arrange on a well-oiled baking tray – they will feel really wet, but that’s normal! - and refrigerate for at least an hour, to firm up.Put a little olive oil in a frying pan on a medium heat, then, working in batches, fry the fishcakes for three to four minutes on each side, until cooked through, piping hot and golden. Serve with sweet chilli sauce, rice noodles, herbs and lime, if you like.To eat later, freeze the raw fishcakes on a tray until solid, then transfer to an airtight container and freeze for up to three months.To cook from frozen,put a little olive oil in a frying pan on a medium-low heat, then fry the fish cakes in batches for about five to six minutes on each side, turning carefully, until cooked through, piping hot and golden.These reccipes are edited extracts from Poppy Cooks: The Actually Delicious Batch Cookbook, by Poppy O’Toole, published by Bloomsbury Publishing at £22.
